en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, [this work] titled *Sammohavinodanī* (The Dispeller of Delusion).
Commentary on the Vibhaṅga: 1.
Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Suttanta-Bhājaniya (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā)
The Lord, the Seer of the Four Truths,
the Fully Enlightened One, having revealed the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* in its fourfold manner, immediately thereafter, the Guide,
endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, [proceeded].
Since the turn has now arrived for the commentary on that Vibhaṅga which the Teacher taught by way of the eighteen sections of analysis beginning with the aggregates (khandha),
I shall therefore provide an explanation of its meaning.
"Having delved into the method of the ancient commentaries, and having shown reverence for the True Dhamma, I shall compose [this work]; listen to it with concentrated minds.
1. The Five Aggregates: the aggregate of form... pe ...the aggregate of consciousness. This [section] occurs at the beginning of the *Vibhaṅga* treatise.
In the Analysis of the Aggregates (*Khandhavibhaṅga*), there is that which is called the "Exposition of the Discourse" (*Suttantabhājanīya*). Therein, "five" is a delimitation by number;
by this, it shows that there are neither fewer nor more than that. "Aggregates" (*khandhā*) is an indication of phenomena as delimited.
In this regard, this word "aggregate" (*khandha*) is seen in several contexts: in the sense of a heap, a quality, a designation, and as a conventional usage.
“Bhikkhus, just as it is not easy to take the measure of the water in the great ocean—
saying there are this many gallons of water, or this many hundreds of gallons, or this many thousands of gallons,
or this many hundreds of thousands of gallons— but rather it is simply an incalculable, immeasurable mass of great water;”
In such passages as “it is reckoned as,” the term *khandha* (aggregate) refers to a mass. For a small amount of water is not called a “mass of water”;

only a large amount is so called. Likewise, a small amount of dust is not a “mass of dust,” a few cows are not a “mass of cattle,” a small force is not a “mass of strength,” and a small amount of merit is not a “mass of merit.”

It is so called. For indeed, a large amount of dust is called a "dust-heap" (*raja-kkhandha*); many cattle and so forth are called a "cattle-heap" (*go-kkhandha*); and [large amounts of] strength, merit, and so on are called "strength-heap," "merit-heap," and so forth.
However, in such expressions as "the aggregate of virtue" (*sīla-kkhandha*) and "the aggregate of concentration" (*samādhi-kkhandha*), it is called an "aggregate" (*kkhandha*) by way of its quality.
As in: "The Blessed One saw a great log being carried away by the current of the river Ganges."

Here, it is called a "aggregate" (khandha) by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*). In such passages as, "That which is mind, mentation, ideation... consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness," it is called an aggregate by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).
But here, it is intended in the sense of a heap (*rāsi*). For this meaning of "aggregate" is the meaning of a mass, the meaning of a multitude, the meaning of a collection, the meaning of a heap;
therefore, aggregates should be understood as having the characteristic of a heap. It also has the meaning of a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*).
It is appropriate to say so; for in the world, when people have taken a loan and are being pressed for payment, they say, "We will pay in two installments," or "We will pay in three installments.
Thus, it is also appropriate to say that "the aggregates (khandhā) are characterized by their constituent parts (koṭṭhāsa).
In this way, here "the aggregate of form" means a heap of form, a portion of form; "the aggregate of feeling" means a heap of feeling, a portion of feeling.
In this same manner, the meaning of the aggregate of perception and the others should be understood.
Up to this point, the Fully Enlightened One has analyzed that which consists of "the four great elements and the derived matter dependent on the four great elements" across eleven categories—
such as the past, future, present, and so forth— as "twenty-five divisions of matter."

And by showing that the entire mass of form— classified in such ways as "the ninety-eight components of form"— is, when all taken together, called the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*); and likewise,

that the entire mass of feeling belonging to the four planes— which is analyzed into those same eleven locations as "pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling"— when all taken together, [is called the aggregate of feeling].
He showed that the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is what is meant by "name.
Furthermore, he showed that the entire mass of perception belonging to the four planes, which is analyzed into those same eleven bases—beginning with "perception born of eye-contact... up to...

perception born of mind-contact"—is collectively called the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). And as for this [volition] beginning with "volition born of eye-contact... up to... volition born of mind-contact"...
"Cetanā" refers to the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), which he showed to be the entire mass of volition belonging to the four planes, analyzed into those same eleven bases;

having combined all of that together, it is called the aggregate of formations. Furthermore, as for this mass of consciousness belonging to the four planes, analyzed into those same eleven bases—namely, "eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)"—it is... [the aggregate of consciousness].
Having synthesized all of that together, he showed it as what is called the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*).
Furthermore, herein, all matter produced by the fourfold origination is the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*);

feeling co-arising with the eighty-nine states of consciousness, beginning with the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere, is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*); perception is the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*); contact and the others...

The mental objects are the aggregate of formations, and the eighty-nine types of consciousness are the aggregate of consciousness. In this way, the delimitation of phenomena within the five aggregates should be understood.
1. Description of the Aggregate of Form.
2. Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate those aggregates beginning with the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), he says:
"Therein, what is the aggregate of form? and so forth. In that context, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to within those five aggregates.

"What" (*katamo*) is a question expressing a desire to explain. "Aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandho*) is the indication of the phenomenon being inquired about. Now, analyzing that [aggregate], he says: "Whatever form there is," and so forth. Therein, "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*)...
"Kiñci" (whatever) is an expression that includes everything without remainder. "Rūpaṃ" (form) is a restriction to prevent over-extension.
Thus, by these two words, the complete inclusion of form is accomplished.
In this context, in what sense is it "rūpa"? It is "rūpa" in the sense of being "ruppana" (being affected). For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And what, bhikkhus, do you call ‘form’? It is deformed, bhikkhus, therefore it is called ‘form.

By what is it deformed? It is deformed by cold, it is deformed by heat, it is deformed by hunger, it is deformed by thirst, and it is deformed by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. It is deformed, bhikkhus, therefore it is called ‘form.’”
"Therefore it is called 'form' (rūpa).
In this context, "what" (kiṃ) is a question regarding the cause; the meaning is: for what reason do you say it is form? For what reason is it named "form"?
In the phrase "it is affected" (ruppati), the particle "iti" indicates the reason. The meaning is: because it is affected, therefore it is called "form."
"It is disturbed" (*ruppati*) means it is agitated, struck, oppressed, and broken; such is the meaning. Thus, by this much way, matter (*rūpa*) is described in the sense of being disturbed.
It is also appropriate to say that it is "matter" by virtue of the characteristic of being disturbed, for this is its characteristic of being disturbed.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "it is disturbed by cold," the disturbance by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell. Of the three...
Between three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there is an individual hell called the "inter-world hell" (*lokantarika-niraya*), measuring eight thousand *yojanas*.
There is no earth beneath it, nor is there the light of the moon, sun, stars, or jewels above; it is perpetually dark.
The physical form (*attabhāva*) of beings reborn there is three *gāvuta* in size. Like bats, they [cling] to the mountain bases with their long and broad...
Clinging with their claws, they hang head-downwards. When, crawling along, they come within arm’s reach of one another, they think, "We have found food!
and, intent upon it, they turn over and fall into the water that sustains the world. Even when struck by cold winds, they break off like ripe madhuka fruits and fall into the water.

As soon as they fall, they are dissolved by extremely cold water, while their skin, sinews, flesh, and bones break apart and crackle like a lump of dough dropped into hot oil. Thus, being disfigured by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell.
This is also evident in regions such as the Mahimsaka country where snow falls and the air is freezing. Therein—
For indeed, beings whose bodies are split and cut by cold even reach the end of their lives.

The ravaging by heat is evident in the Great Niraya of Avīci; for there, when beings are laid down upon a floor of glowing iron and subjected to the fivefold torture and other punishments, they experience great suffering.
The ravaging by hunger is evident both in the realm of the *peta*s and during times of famine. For in the realm of the *peta*s...
Beings do not take even two or three Buddha-intervals to put even a small amount of food into their mouths with their hands.
Their bellies are like hollow trees ablaze within. There is no measure to those who have reached death having failed to obtain even a mere ladle of sour gruel during a famine.
The affliction by thirst is evident in the case of the Kālakañjika hell-beings and others.
For there, for two or three intervals between Buddhas, those beings are unable to obtain even a single drop of water sufficient to moisten their hearts or their tongues.
Even when they go to a river thinking, "We shall drink water," the river turns into a bed of sand. Even when they plunge into the great ocean, [the same occurs].

The great ocean is like a slab of rock. As they wander about, parched and oppressed by intense suffering, it is said that one *kālakañjika* asura, unable to endure his thirst, descended into the Great Ganges, which is a league deep and wide.
Wherever he went, the water would dry up and smoke would rise from the scorching rock slab.
It was as if it were the time for walking meditation. As he wandered here and there upon hearing the sound of water, the night passed away.
Then, early in the morning, about thirty alms-collecting monks, while going out for alms, saw him and asked, "Who are you, good man?
"I am a peta, venerable sirs," he replied. "What are you searching for? they asked.
“Water, venerable sir,” he said. “This Ganges is full; do you not see it?
“It is of no use to me, venerable sir. “In that case, lie down on the bank of the Ganges; we shall pour water into your mouth.
He lay down flat on his back upon the sandy beach. The monks brought out about thirty bowls, and having fetched water again and again, they poured it for him.
They poured it into his mouth. While they were doing so, the time [for almsround] drew near.
Then they said, "It is time for us to go on our almsround, good sir; have you received some satisfaction?
The peta replied, "Venerable sirs, if even half a *pasata* of the water poured from thirty bowls by thirty noble ladies had entered my throat, [I would have been satisfied]."
He said, "May there be no liberation from one's own peta-existence. Thus, deformation through thirst is evident in the realm of petas.
Deformation by gadflies and the like is evident in places abounding with gadflies, flies, and so forth. And here, "gadflies" (daṃsa) refers to brown flies;
"mosquitoes" (makasa) refers to mosquitoes themselves, and they should be understood by way of abdominal winds, back winds, and so on.
For when a wind-disease arises within the body, it breaks the hands, feet, back, and so forth; it makes one blind, it makes one hunchbacked, and it makes one a cripple who crawls on a board.
"Heat" refers to the heat of the sun. By means of that, the deformation [of the body] is evident in places such as the desert wilderness (*marukantāra*).
It is said that a certain woman, having been left behind from a caravan at night in a desert wilderness, was [buried] in sand by day as the sun rose.
Unable to place her foot on the one that was burning, she lowered the basket from her head and stepped on it.
Gradually, unable to stand because the basket had become heated by the heat, she placed her upper garment over it and stepped on it.
When that too became hot, she laid the infant she was carrying in her arms face down and, while he was crying and crying, stepped on him along with—
Because of that, he died right there, scorched by the heat.
"Reptiles" refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling; their causing of physical disturbance should be understood through such things as being bitten by venomous snakes and so forth.
Now, that which is comprised by the phrase "whatever form" consists of twenty-five categories and ninety-four sub-categories.
In order to show all form by including it within the categories of the past and so forth, he said:
"past, future, and present. Following that, in order to show that same [form] by including it within the four dyads beginning with the internal dyad, he stated:
"either internal or external," and so on. After that, having encompassed all of this within eleven bases...
In order to show the manifested form as a single mass all together, it is said: "all that together," and so forth.
Therein, "all that together" means that [form] in one place; "having heaped up" means having brought together;
"having condensed" means having made a summary. This is what is meant: all this aforementioned kind of form, which is characterized by the nature of being afflicted (ruppana-lakkhaṇa),...
When all things of a single kind are gathered together by means of wisdom and made into a heap, it is called the "form aggregate" (*rūpakkhandha*).

By this, it is shown that all form whatsoever is the form aggregate because it attains the state of a heap within the characteristic of being subject to change (*ruppanalakkhaṇa*). For there is no such thing as a "form aggregate" other than form itself.

And just as it is with form, so too are feeling and the other aggregates [designated] by their attainment of the state of a heap within their respective characteristics, such as the characteristic of being felt (*vedayitalakkhaṇa*).
For there are no so-called aggregates of feeling and so forth other than the actual feelings themselves.
Now, having placed matter in each respective location, the author explains by dividing it individually, saying:
"In this context, what is past matter? and so forth. Therein, the phrase "in each" refers to the matrix (mātikā) established by placing [matter] within the eleven locations.

*Bhummaṃ*. This is what is meant: regarding the matrix (*mātikā*) established by way of the method beginning with "past, future, and present," as for that which is called "past matter" (*atītaṃ rūpaṃ*), what is it? In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all the questions.

The phrases such as "the past has ceased" (*atītaṃ niruddhaṃ*) and so forth have already been explained in the commentary on the analysis of the triad of the past (*atītattika-bhājanīya*) in the Section on Exposition (*nikkhepakaṇḍa*).
"The four great elements" is a demonstration of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of that which was stated as "past matter.

And just as it is here, so too should the meaning be understood everywhere. By this, he shows this: past matter consists both of the primary elements (*bhūta*) themselves and of matter produced dependent upon those elements;
likewise future matter... [and so on] ...even distant or near matter. For it is not the case that [matter] is other than the primary elements themselves.
There is no such thing as "matter" other than matter that exists by depending [on the primary elements].
Another method: "Included in the past" means it is included within the very category of the past; it has been counted right here. What is that?
The four great primaries and the derived matter of the four great primaries. Thus it is in all cases.
The meaning should be understood. The terms for the exposition of the future and the present have already had their meanings explained in the preceding sections.
This so-called past, future, and present is twofold: according to the method of the Suttantas and according to the exposition of the Abhidhamma.
In the method of the Suttantas, it is delimited by existence (*bhava*); for, starting from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), [it refers to] past existences.
Matter produced [in the present life], whether it be produced in the immediately following existence or at the end of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, is all termed "past.

Matter that produces birth in future existences, whether it be produced in the immediately following existence or at the end of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, is all termed "future. Immediately after death and rebirth-linking...
Materiality that is currently occurring is called "present. However, in the exposition of the Abhidhamma, it is defined by its moment.
For there are three moments of materiality: arising, presence, and dissolution.
Any materiality that has ceased after reaching these three moments—whether it has ceased immediately or a hundred thousand million eons ago—is entirely "past."

As for the term "name": matter that has not reached these three moments—whether it has not reached them by even a single moment of consciousness or by the limit of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons in the future—is all called "future.
However, matter that has reached these three moments is called "present. In this regard, although this is the Suttanta-bhājaniya, even so:
It should be understood that by means of the exposition of the Abhidhamma alone, matter of the past, future, and present has been demonstrated.
There is another method: for this matter is fourfold as "past" according to the divisions of extent (*addhā*), continuity (*santati*), moment (*samaya*), and instant (*khaṇa*).
Likewise for the future and the present. First, according to the division of extent: in the case of a single being in a single existence, prior to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)...
The past is that which follows death; the future is that which comes after; and the present is that which lies between the two.

By way of continuity, even though it proceeds by way of prior and subsequent moments, that which is produced by a homogeneous temperature or by a single nutriment is the present. Prior to that, what is produced by a heterogeneous temperature or nutriment is the past;
after that, it is the future. That which is mind-born, produced by a single cognitive series, a single impulsion, or a single attainment, is the present.
Prior to that is the past; subsequent to that is the future. For that which is produced by kamma, there is no distinction of past and so forth by way of a separate continuity.
However, its distinction as past and so forth should be understood by way of its support for those very [material phenomena] produced by temperature, nutriment, and consciousness.
By way of time, it exists through its continuity during periods such as one muhutta, forenoon, afternoon, night, day, and so on.
That which is occurring at any given moment is called "present. What precedes that is "past," and what follows it is "future.
By way of moment, that which is included within the three moments of arising and so forth is called "present"; what precedes that is "past," and what follows it is "future.
Furthermore, that which has completed its function as a cause is "past. That which has finished its function as a cause but whose function as a condition is not yet finished is "present."
That which has not yet reached both functions is future. Or, at the moment of its own function, it is present; prior to that, it is past; and subsequent to that, it is future.

And herein, only the discussion of the moment (*khaṇa*) and so forth is non-figurative (*nippariyāya*); the rest are figurative (*sapariyāya*). Among these, the non-figurative discussion is what is intended here.
The explanatory passages for the "Internal Dyad" (*ajjhattaduka*) also have the same meaning as those stated previously in the explanation of the "Internal Triad" (*ajjhattattika*).
The terms "gross" (*oḷārika*) and so forth have their meanings already explained in the commentary on the section on matter (*rūpakanda*). 6.
Regarding the exposition of the "pair of inferior" (*hīnaduka*): the phrase "of those various beings" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ*) is a genitive case used with reference to many beings.
For if one were to say "of another and of another," even if one were to speak for a whole day or for a hundred thousand eons, one would only be saying this much.
Thus the Teacher, encompassing all beings without exception by means of only two phrases, said: "of those various beings.
For by this much, the entire exposition of the others is established. *Uññātaṃ* means despised. *Avaññātaṃ* means known after having been reviled.
*Rūpaṃ* is not even recognized. *Hīḷitaṃ* means cast away or discarded in the sense of being unfit to be grasped.
They also say it is "disgusting. "Contemptible" means despised by speech, as in "what is the use of this?
"Disregarded" means not held in high esteem. "Lowly" means base. "Considered lowly" means regarded as lowly; known as base, having been made out to be contemptible.
"Agreed upon as lowly" means agreed upon as lowly by the world, or agreed upon by those who are themselves lowly, like excrement by dung-eaters. "Unpleasant."
"Unpleasant" (*appiya*) means not sought for the sake of acquisition; even if someone were to seek it out, that is still its name as an object.
"Unwanted" (*akanta*) means not desired, or lacking in splendor. "Disagreeable" (*amanāpa*) means not fixed in the mind.
For such an object is not fixed in the mind; or alternatively, it causes the mind to shrink away.
"It increases" means it is agreeable; that which is not agreeable is disagreeable. Another method:
it is undesirable because it is devoid of success. Among those things arising from kamma, it arises exclusively from unwholesome kamma.
It is "unloved" because it is not a cause of pleasure. It is "disagreeable" because it is a cause of suffering. "Forms, sounds..."—this refers to its [nature].
The Illumination of the Essential Nature. For in this passage, the five strands of sensual pleasure that are undesirable are analyzed by way of unwholesome kamma;
however, there is nothing called "undesirable" born of wholesome kamma—all such things are exclusively desirable.
The description of the "exquisite" should be understood by way of the method opposite to what was stated [above]. But in this present passage, by way of wholesome kamma...
The five strands of sensual pleasure are analyzed as desirable. For there is nothing born of wholesome kamma that is undesirable; everything is indeed desirable.
And just as it is with those things born of kamma, so too there is desirability and undesirability among things originated by temperature and so forth.
Thus, in this dyad, the desirable and undesirable objects are analyzed. This, first of all, is the teachers’ common explanation.
But the caviller says: "There is no such thing as the desirable and the undesirable separately distinguished; they are spoken of merely according to the individual preferences of this or that person.
As it has been said:"
“Great King, I say that among the five strands of sensual pleasure, the pleasant is the foremost.
For those very forms, Great King, are pleasant to some and unpleasant to others; those very sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects, Great King, are pleasant to some and unpleasant to others.”
Thus, because those very same forms and so forth are relished and delighted in by one person, who thereby gives rise to greed;

while they are resented and struck against by another, who thereby gives rise to hatred; and because they are desirable, lovely, and pleasing to one, yet undesirable, unlovely, and displeasing to another;
and because one person grasps them from the right side, thinking, "They are desirable, lovely, and pleasing," while another [grasps them] thinking, "They are undesirable..."
"Unpleasant" or "disagreeable" is on the left side. Therefore, there is no such thing as the desirable and the undesirable that is separately distinguished.
For even earthworms are desirable, lovely, and agreeable to those living in border regions, while they are extremely loathsome to those living in the Middle Country.
Furthermore, peacock flesh and the like are desirable to them, whereas they are extremely loathsome to others.
He should be asked: “But do you say that there is no such thing as a distinct, separately analyzed desirable or undesirable object?
If he says, “Yes, there is none,” then having established him in that position up to the third time, the question should be asked:
“Is Nibbāna desirable or undesirable? Knowing the answer, he will say, “It is desirable. Even if he does not...
...should one speak thus, let them not speak. But Nibbāna is exclusively desirable. "Was it not the case that when the praises of Nibbāna were being told, one person became angry and said:

'You are telling the praises of Nibbāna; is there food, drink, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, coverings, and the fivefold abundance of sensual pleasures there? When it was replied, 'There is none,' he said, 'Enough for me with your Nibbāna! regarding Nibbāna..."
"It is 'desirable' (iṭṭha) that when its praise is being spoken, one closes both ears in anger.
However, by virtue of this [reaction], Nibbāna would become 'undesirable' (aniṭṭha) in your doctrine. But it should not be understood in this way; for he speaks with a perverted perception (saññā).
And through a perversion of perception, that very same object becomes desirable to one person and undesirable to another."
However, there is a separate classification for desirable and undesirable objects. By way of what is it classified? It is classified by way of the "middle-class" being.
For this is not classified by way of those such as Mahā Sammata, Mahā Sudassana, or King Dhammāsoka, who were exceedingly powerful;
for even a celestial-like object would appear unpleasant to them. Nor is it classified by way of those who are extremely destitute.

It is classified according to those for whom food and drink are difficult to obtain; for even their meals of broken rice and boiled grain, or their putrid meat broth, become exceedingly sweet and like nectar.

It is further classified according to those of middle status—such as accountants, high officials, guild-leaders, householders, and merchants—who receive what is desirable at times and what is undesirable at others. For such people experience both the desirable and the undesirable...
“They are able to determine [the object].
However, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said: “What is called ‘the desirable and the undesirable’ is determined solely by way of kamma-result, not by way of impulsion.
But impulsion, through the perversion of perception, becomes attached only to what is desirable, and only to what is desirable.”
"One is attracted to what is undesirable, and one is repelled by what is undesirable. However, this is determined with absolute certainty by way of result (vipāka) alone.
For it is impossible to deceive a resultant consciousness.
If the object is desirable, a wholesome resultant arises; if it is undesirable, an unwholesome resultant arises. Indeed, even though...
When those with wrong view see sublime objects such as the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or great shrines, they close their eyes and fall into dejection;
when they hear the sound of the Dhamma, they plug their ears.
However, their eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness are exclusively wholesome resultant states.
Although dung-pigs and the like, having smelled the scent of dung, experience joy thinking, "We shall get to eat," yet when they see the dung, their eye-consciousness;
when they smell its scent, their nose-consciousness; and when they taste its flavor, their tongue-consciousness—all these are exclusively unwholesome-resultant (akusalavipāka).
This is illustrated by the case of the pig that was tied up and made to lie upon a luxurious bed.
And although he may cry out, it is through a perversion of perception that mental grief arises only during the impulsion stage;
the body-consciousness itself is exclusively a wholesome resultant. Why? Because of the desirability of the object.
Furthermore, desirability and undesirability should also be understood by way of the sense-door. For even excrement, which is pleasant to touch, [is undesirable] at the eye-door and the nose-door.

What is undesirable becomes desirable at the door of the body. For example, when one struck by the jewel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch or impaled upon a golden stake, those jewel-treasures and golden stakes are desirable at the door of the eye, yet undesirable at the door of the body. Why?
Because they give rise to great suffering. Thus, it should be understood that what is desirable and what is undesirable are definitively distinguished solely by way of kamma-result (vipāka).
Regarding the phrase "or this or that," the preceding method should not be looked back upon here. For the Blessed One does not break what is agreeable by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*);
rather, he breaks it by way of the individual person (*puggala*). Therefore, inferiority and excellence should be understood only by taking "this or that" as the basis.
For the form of those in hell is called "inferior" when it has reached the ultimate limit; taking that as the basis—
Among animals, the form of the *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas* is called "exquisite. Compared to theirs, the form of the *petas* is inferior;
compared to theirs, the form of the inhabitants of the countryside is called "exquisite. Compared to theirs, it is inferior;
compared to theirs, the form of the village headmen is called "exquisite. Compared to theirs, it is inferior; compared to theirs—
The form of the lords of the provinces is called superior. Compared to that, the form of regional kings is called inferior;
compared to that, the form of a wheel-turning monarch is called superior.
Compared to that, the form of the earth-dwelling devas is called inferior; compared to that, the form of the Cātumahārājika devas—

The form of the deities is called "exquisite. Compared even to that, the form of the Tāvatiṃsa deities is called "exquisite"… [and so on] …the form of the Akaniṭṭha deities, however, has reached the ultimate limit and is called "exquisite.
7. In the exposition of the pair on "distance," the female faculty and so forth have already been analyzed below. In this dyad, however, [they are included] in the sense of being difficult to grasp.
Subtle materiality is said to be "distant" because its characteristic is difficult to penetrate. Gross materiality is said to be "near" because its characteristic is easy to grasp.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the section on physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) and even at the point of summary, it is not stated that "this is called distant materiality. Why?
Because there are two kinds of "distance": by way of characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and by way of location (*okāsa*).
...and so on. Therein, it was not stated that [the distant] is distant by way of characteristic; rather, that should be stated by way of location. Therefore, it was not stated as "distant.
To show that gross matter is distant by way of location, he said, "or whatever else," and so forth, without having first defined it.
The same method applies to the description of the proximate. Therein, "not near" means not close; "not adjacent" means detached.
"Far" means at a distance; "not near" means not in close proximity. This is called "form far away. This fifteenfold subtle form is far in terms of its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*);
however, the tenfold gross form is said to be far in terms of location (*okāsa*) by way of inclusion (*yevāpanaka*).
The explanation of the term "near" is self-evident.
"This is called 'proximate matter'"—this refers to the tenfold gross matter which is proximate by way of its characteristic;
however, the fifteenfold subtle matter is called "proximate" by way of its location (*okāsa*) because it is included within the [gross] bases.
From what extent, then, is matter called "proximate" by way of location? And from what extent is it called "distant"? This is according to the discourse on the nature of matter.
For those who are speaking, the range of hearing is twelve cubits. Within that distance, a form is "near";
beyond it, it is "far. In this regard, a subtle form, when it is far, is far both by way of its characteristic and by way of location;
but when it is near, it is near only by way of location, not by way of its characteristic. A gross form, when it is near, is near both by way of its characteristic and...
It is near by way of location; that which is distant is distant only by way of location, not by way of characteristic.
As for the phrase "or this or that," the preceding method should not be referred to here, for the previous section proceeded by way of breaking [the continuity].
However, here one does not break it by way of characteristic, but breaks it only by way of location being distant. For distance and proximity are established relative to each other.
This is what is shown here. For one's own form is "near," while the form of another, even if located inside one's own belly, is "far.
The form inside the belly is near; the form standing outside is far. The form of one lying on the same bed is near; the form standing outside at the head of the bed is far.
Form inside the monastery compound is near; form outside the monastery compound is far. Form inside the monastic complex is near; form outside the monastic complex is far.
Far away. Within the boundary, visible form is near; outside the boundary, it is far away. Within the precincts of a village, visible form is near; outside the precincts of a village, it is far away.
Within the district, visible form is near; outside the district, it is far away. Within the boundary of a kingdom, visible form is near; outside the boundary of a kingdom, it is far away.
Within the ocean, visible form is near; outside the ocean, visible form is far away. Within the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), [visible form is near].
Form is near; that which is outside the world-system is far.
This is the exposition of the aggregate of form.
2. Exposition of the aggregate of feeling.
8. In the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) and so forth, we shall explain only what is new, setting aside that which has already been stated above.

"Whatever feeling" includes feeling belonging to the four planes of existence. The terms "pleasant feeling" and so forth are stated to show, by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), the feeling that was previously defined according to its temporal divisions such as the past and so on. Among these, pleasant feeling is both bodily and mental.
[There are] mental [factors]. Likewise, painful feeling [is mental]. However, regarding neutral feeling, with reference to the sensitive body of the eye and so forth, it is said figuratively:
"there is bodily, there is mental. Among these, all bodily [feeling] belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). Likewise, painful mental feeling [belongs to the sense-sphere].
Mental pleasant feeling, however, belongs to the three planes (tebhūmika). Neutral feeling belongs to the four planes.
Its state as past, present, and future should be understood both by way of its continuity (*santati*) and by way of moments (*khaṇa*), and so forth.

In this regard, by way of continuity, those [mental states] included within a single cognitive process (*vīthi*), a single impulsion (*javana*), or a single attainment (*samāpatti*), and which arise in conjunction with a single type of object, are present.
Those prior to that are past; those subsequent are future. By way of moments and so forth, those included within the three instants (*khaṇa-ttaya*) are present.
Feelings that have reached the past, future, or middle [periods] and are performing their own function are "present. Those prior to that are "past," and those subsequent are "future.
It should be understood that this description is made with reference to the state of being past and so forth by way of moment (*khaṇa*) and other such criteria.
11. In the description of the gross and the subtle, the phrases "unwholesome feeling" and so forth are stated to show the state of being gross or subtle by way of genus (*jāti*).

These have been stated. "Painful feeling is gross," and so forth, are stated by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption," and so forth, are stated by way of the person (*puggala*).
"With taints" (*sāsava*), and so forth, are stated to show the state of being gross or subtle by way of the mundane and supramundane.

In that regard, unwholesome [feelings] are first gross in the sense of being accompanied by distress and in the sense of having painful ripening (*vipāka*). Wholesome [feelings] are [subtle] in the sense of being free from distress and in the sense of having pleasant ripening.

And they are subtle. The indeterminate (abyākata) are subtle in the sense of being effortless and in the sense of being without karmic result (avipāka). The wholesome and unwholesome (kusalākusala) are gross in the sense of being with effort and in the sense of having karmic result.
The indeterminate are subtle in the manner already stated.
The painful (dukkha) are gross in the sense of being disagreeable and in the sense of suffering. The pleasant (sukha) are subtle in the sense of being agreeable and in the sense of happiness.

The neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] is subtle in the sense of peace and in the sense of refinement. Pleasant and painful feelings are gross in the sense of agitation and in the sense of pervasion.
For pleasant feeling agitates and pervades; likewise does painful feeling.
Indeed, when pleasure arises, it agitates the entire body, churns it, drenches it, massages it, and suffuses it, like a jar of cold water.
It arises as if being poured out. Suffering arises like a red-hot iron ball being thrust inside, or like a grass torch burning on the outside.
The neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, however, is subtle in the manner already described.

The feeling of one who has not attained meditative absorption is gross because it is distracted among various objects; the feeling of one who has attained absorption is [subtle] because it is directed toward a single-pointed object alone.

That which "moves" is subtle. That which is associated with taints (*sāsrava*) is coarse because it is the cause for the arising of taints. What is called the "movement of taints" is exclusively coarse.
By contrast, that which is without taints (*anāsrava*) is subtle.
In this regard, there is one who is neither skilled in the "Triplet of the Wholesome" nor in the "Triplet of Feeling. Thinking, "I shall protect the Triplet of the Wholesome," he...
One breaks the triad of feeling; thinking "I guard the triad of feeling," one breaks the triad of the wholesome.
One [thinks] "I guard the triad" and thus breaks the difference between planes; another does not break it. How so? For in the triad of feeling it is said:
"Pleasant and painful feelings are gross; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtle. One rejects this, saying: "No."
All [feelings] that are neither-painful-nor-pleasant are subtle. For they are indeed wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Among these, the wholesome and unwholesome are gross, while the indeterminate is subtle. Why? Because it is so stated in the Pāḷi of the *Kusalattika*.
Thus, the *Kusalattika* is preserved, but the *Vedanāttika* is split.
"Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate feeling is subtle"—as for this statement made in the *Kusalattika*, one person objects:
"Not all indeterminate feelings are subtle. For that [indeterminate feeling] is also pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Among these, the pleasant and painful are gross, while the neither-painful-nor-pleasant is subtle. Why? Because it is so stated in the *Vedanāttika* of the Canon."
In this way, the triad of feeling is protected, while the triad of the wholesome is split. However,

when explaining the relative grossness and subtlety of the wholesome factors and so forth by means of the characteristic of the wholesome triad at the places where the wholesome triad occurs— and without looking at the triad of feeling there—

or by means of the characteristic of the triad of feeling at the places where the triad of feeling occurs— and without looking at the wholesome triad there— one does not, indeed, split [the teaching].
Regarding that which was stated in the *Kusalattika*—namely, “Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross; indeterminate feelings are subtle”—therein one person says:

“Even though supramundane wholesome feelings are the same [as others], they are called gross; even though resultant [feelings] are the same, even when co-nascent with the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, they are called subtle.
Such a person [erroneously] characterizes the peaceful and sublime supramundane feeling as gross.

When designating [the consciousness] associated with the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness as "rootless," "inferior," "dull," and "subtle," one is said to "break the plane" (bhūmantara) in order to preserve the "triad.

However, when explaining wholesome states on their respective planes by associating them with the specific results (vipāka) of those same planes, one does not break the plane. In this regard, the method is as follows:

—For wholesome states of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are gross, while the resultant states of the sense sphere are subtle. Wholesome states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, as well as supramundane wholesome states, are gross;
the resultant states of the fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane spheres are subtle. Speaking in this manner, one does not "break" [the exposition].
However, the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka said: "The quality of grossness and subtlety should not be mentioned regarding unwholesome states. For..."
“It is exclusively coarse. Even in the supramundane, the distinction between the coarse and the subtle need not be extracted; for that is exclusively subtle.
Having brought forward this discussion, they told it to the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya, saying, “Thus was it spoken by the Elder.
The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya said: “When the Fully Enlightened One had mastered the Abhidhamma, even of a single word, or of two...”
There is no place where a method (naya) has not been given for the words that require it;
there is no place where a method has not been applied where it was appropriate to do so.

However, here someone who wanders about thinking "I am a teacher," while extracting the grossness and subtlety regarding unwholesome states, becomes anxious. But by the Perfectly Enlightened One, even in the supramundane, grossness and subtlety [have been established].
"...have been rescued. Having said this, he then cited this sutta:

"In that regard, Bhante, as for this practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge, this practice, Bhante, is declared inferior in both respects—on account of its painfulness and its sluggishness.
For here, the four practices are explained as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
Regarding the phrase "or this or that," the preceding method need not be consulted here;

it should be explained solely by way of "this or that. For unwholesome states are of two kinds: those accompanied by greed and those accompanied by hatred. Among these, those accompanied by hatred are gross, while those accompanied by greed are subtle.
Those accompanied by hatred are also of two kinds: fixed and unfixed. Among these, the fixed...

Coarse consciousness is undetermined, while subtle consciousness is determined. Furthermore, that which lasts for an eon (*kappaṭṭhitika*) is coarse, while that which does not last for an eon is subtle.
Even among those lasting for an eon, that which is unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is coarse, while that which is prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) is subtle. Greed-accompanied consciousness is also twofold:

associated with views (*diṭṭhisampayutta*) and dissociated from views (*diṭṭhivippayutta*). Among these, that which is associated with views is coarse, while that which is dissociated from views is subtle.

Subtle. Those associated with wrong view are gross when they are of fixed destiny, and subtle when they are of no fixed destiny. That too is gross when unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*), and subtle when prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*).
In brief, regarding unwholesome states, that which yields much result is gross, and that which yields little is subtle.

But having reached the wholesome, those with little result are gross, while those with much result are subtle. Among the fourfold wholesome, sense-sphere wholesome is gross, and fine-material-sphere wholesome is subtle.
That too is gross, while immaterial-sphere wholesome is subtle. That too is gross, while supramundane wholesome is subtle.
This, first of all, is the method according to the distinction of planes.

As for their classification, those pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are threefold by way of being produced by giving, virtue, and meditation. Among these, those consisting of giving are gross, while those consisting of virtue are subtle.

That [virtue] is also twofold: gross when it consists of giving, and subtle when it consists of meditation. That [meditation] is also twofold: that which is rooted in two roots (*duhetuka*) and that which is rooted in three roots (*tihetuka*).

Among these, that rooted in two roots is gross, while that rooted in three roots is subtle. That which is rooted in three roots is further divided into the prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) and the unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*).

It is twofold. Therein, that which is prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) is gross (*oḷārika*), while that which is unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is subtle (*sukhuma*). In the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), the wholesome feeling of the first jhāna is gross;
the wholesome feeling of the second jhāna is subtle... [and so on] ...the wholesome feeling of the fourth jhāna is subtle. That too is gross;
the wholesome feeling of the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) is subtle; the wholesome feeling of the base of infinite space is gross... [and so on].
The wholesome feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle. That too is gross; the [feeling] co-arising with insight (vipassanā) is subtle. That too is gross;
the [feeling] co-arising with the stream-entry path (sotāpatti-magga) is subtle. That too is gross... [and so on] ...the [feeling] co-arising with the arahant path (arahatta-magga) is subtle.

Among the fourfold resultants (vipāka), the resultant feeling of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) is gross, while the resultant feeling of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is subtle. That too is gross... [and so on] ...the supramundane (lokuttara) resultant feeling is subtle. Thus, first, according to the undifferentiated classification.

As for the classification by way of distinction: there are sense-sphere resultant states that are rootless, and there are those that are with roots. Among those with roots, there are those with two roots and those with three roots.
Therein, the rootless are gross; those with roots are subtle. Of those with roots, the two-rooted are gross; the three-rooted are subtle.
Even among those, the prompted are gross; the unprompted are subtle. [This applies to] the resultant states of the first jhāna.

The first jhāna resultants are gross; the second jhāna resultants are subtle... [and so on] ...the fourth jhāna resultants are subtle. That too is gross; the space-infinity-ayatana resultants are subtle. That too is gross...
[and so on] ...the neither-perception-nor-non-perception ayatana resultants are subtle.

That too is gross; the feeling of the fruit of stream-entry is subtle. That too is gross; the feeling of the fruit of once-returning... [and so on] ...the feeling of the fruit of arahantship is subtle.
Among the three types of functional consciousness, the feeling of sense-sphere functional consciousness is gross, while the feeling of fine-material-sphere functional consciousness is subtle.
That [fine-material-sphere feeling] is also gross, whereas the feeling of immaterial-sphere functional consciousness is subtle. Thus much by way of non-distinction.

By way of distinction, however, among the sense-sphere functional consciousnesses divided according to rootless and other factors, the feeling of rootless functional consciousness is gross, while that with roots is subtle. That [with roots] is also [divided], such as that with two roots...

The three-rooted [consciousness] is subtle. Even there, that which is prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*) is gross, while that which is unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is subtle. In the first jhāna, functional feeling (*kiriyavedanā*) is gross;
in the second jhāna, it is subtle. That too is gross; in the third... [and so on] ...in the fourth, it is subtle. That too is gross;
functional feeling in the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) is subtle. That too is gross; [functional feeling in] the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*)... [and so on] ...
The functional feeling of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle. That which is gross is inferior; that which is subtle is superior. 13.
In the exposition of the "Pair on Distance," unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings by way of being dissimilar and dissociated.
In this manner, distance is to be understood in all instances. For even if one is possessed of unwholesome feeling and so forth...
Furthermore, when three people possessing painful feelings and so forth sit together on one couch, even for them those feelings are indeed "distant" by way of being dissimilar and unassociated.
This same principle applies to those possessing feelings and so forth while in meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
Unwholesome states, however, are "near" by way of being similar and analogous to the unwholesome. By this...
By this method, proximity (*santikatā*) should be understood in all instances.

For even if among three persons—one possessing unwholesome feeling and so forth—each is in a different realm (one in the sense-sphere existence, one in the fine-material existence, and one in the immaterial existence), those feelings of theirs are still called "proximate" by virtue of their commonality and similarity.
This same principle applies to those possessing wholesome feeling and so forth as well.
Regarding the phrase "or this or that," one should explain it here by way of "this or that" alone, without looking back at the preceding method.
And when explaining, one should not extract [a distant term] from near; rather, one should extract a distant term from what is near.
For unwholesome states are twofold: those accompanied by greed and those accompanied by hatred. Among these, those accompanied by greed [should be extracted] from what is accompanied by greed.
"Near" means [near] to that which is accompanied by hatred; "far" means [far] from it.

That which is accompanied by hatred is "near" to what is accompanied by hatred, and "far" from what is accompanied by greed. Furthermore, that which is accompanied by hatred is "near" to the determinate [kamma], and so on. Thus it is for the indeterminate [kamma].

And among those accompanied by greed and so forth, there are distinctions such as those lasting for an eon (*kappaṭṭhitika*), the spontaneous (*asaṅkhārika*), and the prompted (*sasaṅkhārika*); and among those associated with views (*diṭṭhi-sampayutta*) and so forth, there are further distinctions.
Having followed all this in detail according to the exposition of the coarse dyads (*oḷārikaduka*),
it should be understood that each individual portion of feeling is near to that very portion of feeling, while it is distant from the other portions.
This is the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).

3. Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception (Saññākkhandhaniddesa) 14. In the exposition of the aggregate of perception, the phrase "whatever perception there is" encompasses perception belonging to the four planes.

The terms "perception born of eye-contact," and so forth, are stated in order to show the specific nature of perception as it has been defined according to its temporal dimensions—past, present, and future. Among these, from eye-contact...
Or, those born in eye-contact are called "born of eye-contact. The same method applies to the others as well.

And here, the first five have the sensitive matter of the eye and so forth as their physical basis (*vatthu*). Those born of mind-contact may have the heart-basis as their physical basis or may be without a physical basis.
All of them are perceptions belonging to the four planes of existence.

17. In the exposition of the dyad of the gross (*oḷārika-duka*): contact born of impingement (*paṭigha-samphassa*) is contact that has arisen by taking as its basis the sensitive matter of the eye and so forth, which possess impingement, and by having as its object visible forms and so forth, which possess impingement;

it is thus called "contact born of impingement. That which is born from that [contact], or in that [contact], is called "born of impingement" (*paṭigha-samphassaja*). Likewise for "perception born of eye-contact," and so on, up to "perception born of body-contact."

It is named after its basis (*vatthu*): "perception of visible form" … down to … "perception of tangible object. It is also named after its object (*ārammaṇa*): "perception of [an object such as] visible form," and so on.

This, however, is the name according to both basis and object. For because it arises depending on bases that possess resistance (*sappaṭigha*) and taking as its objects those things that possess resistance, it is called "perception born of impingement-contact" (*paṭighasamphassajā saññā*). It is also called "born of mind-contact" (*manosamphassajā*).
By way of a figurative expression, this indeed has that name. For visual consciousness is called "mind" (*mano*). Contact co-arising with it is called "mental contact" (*manosamphassa*).
That which is born from that mental contact, or from that mental contact, is therefore "born of mental contact" (*manosamphassajā*).
Likewise, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness are called "mind. Contact co-arising with them is called "mental contact."
"Born of mind-contact" (*manosamphassajā*) means that it is born from that mind-contact, or born out of that mind-contact.
"Perception born of designation-contact" (*adhivacanasamphassajā saññā*) is indeed another synonym for it.
For the three formless aggregates, being themselves the "backbone," are called "born of designation-contact" by way of the perception that arises simultaneously with them.

They even give it the name "perception" (saññā). However, in the non-figurative sense, perception born of impingement by resistance (*paṭigha-samphassajā saññā*) refers to the perceptions of the five doors, while perception born of designation (*adhivacana-samphassajā saññā*) refers to the perception of the mind door.
Among these, the perception of the five doors is coarse (*oḷārikā*), because one is able to know [objects] even after merely looking at them.
For when one looks with lustful intent, one is said to be "looking with lustful intent," and when one looks with anger...
When someone is looking intently, people know by merely observing that "he is looking with anger.
Here is an account of this: it is said that two women were sitting and spinning thread.
While two young men were wandering through the village, one walking in front looked at one of the women. The other woman asked him, "Why indeed..."
“Did he look at her with a mind of lust? “No, that bhikkhu did not look at me with a dissimilar mind; rather, he looked at me with the perception that I was his younger sister.
Later, when those [other] bhikkhus had wandered through the village and were sitting in the assembly hall, the other bhikkhu asked him:
“Was that woman looked at by you? “Yes, she was looked at. “For what purpose? “Because she resembled my own sister.”
"He looked at him," he said. Thus, it should be understood that perception belonging to the five sense doors is capable of knowing even after looking.
Moreover, this [perception] has only the physical bases as its object. Some, however, explain it as occurring through the impulsion (javana) process.

But as for perception belonging to the mind door, even when two people are sitting on the same bed or the same seat, if one is thinking or reflecting on something else, [the other perceives]: "What are you thinking?"
They are subtle because they must be understood by asking, "What are you thinking about? according to the person's own words. The rest is exactly like the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
This is the exposition of the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*). 4. Exposition of the Aggregate of Mental Formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*)
20. In the exposition of the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the phrase "whatever volitional formations" includes all formations belonging to the four planes.
The terms "volition born of eye-contact," and so forth, are stated in order to show, by way of their intrinsic nature, those formations already specified according to the past and other time periods.
The terms "born of eye-contact," and so forth, have meanings already explained. As for "volition" (*cetanā*), it is stated here by way of the primary formation within its own ultimate limit.
It has been stated thus. For at the very minimum, even with eye-consciousness, the four formations mentioned in the text arise.
Among these, volition (cetanā) is predominant because it is manifest in the sense of "exertion" (āyūhana). Therefore, this alone is taken [as the representative].

However, when that is taken, the formations associated with it are also taken by implication. Here too, the first five [bases] have the sensitive matter of the eye and so forth as their physical basis.
Those born of mind-contact have either a heart-basis or no basis. All volition belonging to the four planes [of existence] is included. The remainder is exactly like the aggregate of feeling.
This is the exposition of the aggregate of formations.
5. Exposition of the Aggregate of Consciousness.
26. In the exposition of the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*), the phrase "whatever consciousness" includes consciousness belonging to all four planes.
The terms "eye-consciousness" and so forth are stated to show the nature of consciousness as it has been defined according to its past and other temporal states.
Among these, the five beginning with eye-consciousness have their respective bases in the sensitive matter of the eye and so on; mental consciousness, however, has its base in the heart.
It is also baseless. All consciousness of the four planes [is included]. The remainder is exactly like the aggregate of feeling.
This is the exposition of the aggregate of consciousness.
Miscellaneous Discussion.
Now, with respect to all five aggregates, [one should contemplate them] by way of their emergence, by way of their sequence, by way of the delimitation of time,

by way of simultaneous arising and separate cessation, by way of separate arising and simultaneous cessation, by way of simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation, by way of separate arising and separate cessation, by way of the past, future, and present,
by way of internal and external, by way of gross and subtle, by way of inferior and superior, by way of distant and near, and by way of condition and origination.
The miscellaneous section should be understood through sixteen modes, beginning with "being fully accomplished" and "being conditioned.
Therein, the origin is twofold: origin from the womb and origin by spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).

Of these, the origin from the womb should be understood as follows: at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for beings born from a womb, the five aggregates arise neither sequentially nor simultaneously.
They appear simultaneously. At that moment, the material continuity designated as the *kalala* (the embryo in its first stage) that has appeared is minute.
Having stated that it is merely enough to be taken up by a single stroke of a small fly’s wing, it was further said: “This is too much;
it is merely the size of a drop remaining at the tip of a fine needle when it is withdrawn after being dipped in oil. Even that [comparison] was rejected.
It is said: "When a single hair is drawn out from oil and grasped, it is merely the size of a drop that remains at its tip after the oil has dripped off.
Having rejected even that, he said: "In this country, when a person’s hair is divided into eight parts, a single portion is the measure of a hair of those in Uttarakuru;
it is merely the size of a drop that remains at the tip of such a hair when drawn out from clear sesame oil."
This was said. But having rejected even that, it was further stated: "That is much; what is called 'birth-wool' (*jātiuṇṇā*) is indeed fine.
From a single strand of it, when placed into clear sesame oil and drawn out, it is merely the size of a drop that remains at the tip as it drips.
And this [drop] is transparent, clear, unclouded, and pure, with a color identical to a drop of clear sesame oil. For this has also been said:
"Just as a drop of ghee-cream, unmixed, upon sesame oil, so too is that which resembles it in color called *kalala*.
Thus, for this limited continuity of matter, there are three series-heads: the base-decad (*vatthudasaka*), the body-decad (*kāyadasaka*), and [the sex-decad].
The female-faculty-decad by way of the female faculty in a woman, and the male-faculty-decad by way of the male faculty in a man.

Therein, the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa), its four supporting great elements (mahābhūta), the color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence dependent upon them, and vitality—this is called the "basis-decad" (vatthudasaka).
The body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda), its four supporting great elements, the color, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence dependent upon them, [and vitality].

"Life" (jīvita) refers to what is called the "body decad" (kāyadasaka). The female state in a woman, the male state in a man, the four great elements that are its support, and the visible form, odor, flavor, and nutritive essence dependent upon them—this is called the "sex decad" (bhāvadasaka).
Thus, at the moment of rebirth-linking for those born from a womb, there are thirty material phenomena produced by kamma, according to the maximum limit.
There is what is called the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). However, the feeling (*vedanā*) co-nascent with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) is the aggregate of feeling;

perception (*saññā*) is the aggregate of perception; mental formations (*saṅkhārā*) are the aggregate of formations; and the rebirth-linking consciousness itself is the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*).
Thus, at the moment of rebirth-linking for those born from a womb, the five aggregates are complete. But if it is a neuter rebirth-linking...
The existence-decad (bhāvadasaka) ceases. By way of these two decads, the twenty material phenomena born of kamma constitute what is called the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha).
The aggregates of feeling and so forth are of the same nature as previously described. Thus, at the moment of rebirth-linking for those born from a womb, the five aggregates are complete.

At this point, the tradition concerning the three modes of origination (*tisamuṭṭhānika*) should have been explained; however, instead of explaining that, what is shown is called "the emergence of the spontaneously born" (*opapātika-samuggama*).

For in spontaneously born beings with complete sense bases, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), seven heads of the material continuity (*rūpa-santati*) become manifest: the three mentioned above, plus the decads of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue. Among these, the eye-decad and so forth...
They are exactly like the body-decad (*kāyadasaka*). However, for a neuter being, there is no sex-decad (*bhāvadasaka*).
Thus, for spontaneously born beings (*opapātika*) with complete sense bases, the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*) consists of seventy and sixty material phenomena born of kamma (*kammaja-rūpa*).

The aggregates of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth are of the types already described. In this way, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the five aggregates are complete for spontaneously born beings.
This is called "arising by spontaneous birth. Thus, first of all, the five aggregates should be understood from the perspective of their arising.

Regarding the perspective of "priority and posteriority," among the five aggregates that arise in a continuous succession for those born from a womb, does material form produce material form first, or does non-material form do so? Material form produces material form itself.
It is not immaterial (arūpa). Why? Because the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) does not produce matter.

For sixteen types of consciousness—the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the death-consciousness of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), the two fivefold sense-cognitions, and the four immaterial-sphere resultants—do not originate matter.
Among these, first, the rebirth-linking consciousness [does not produce matter] because of the weakness of the physical basis (vatthu) and its lack of stability.
Due to the deficiency of conditions and its adventitious nature, it does not produce matter.
For in that case, the co-nascent physical basis (vatthu) is weak at the moment of its own arising; thus, because of the weakness of the basis, it does not produce matter.
And just as a man falling down a precipice is unable to serve as a support for another, so too this [consciousness], being impelled by the force of kamma, [cannot do so].
It is like falling from a precipice, having no foothold. Thus, because it is impelled by the force of kamma and because it lacks a foothold, it does not produce material form.

Furthermore, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises simultaneously with the physical basis (vatthu), neither preceding nor following it; for that consciousness, the basis is "pre-arisen" (purejāta).
Having ceased, it is not able to become a condition. If it were able, it would produce matter.

Even in those cases where the physical basis, having arisen prior, is able to become a condition and the continuity is maintained, there too the mind produces matter only when it has not fallen away from its constituent factors.
For if the mind [were to do so] at the moment of its subsistence or at the moment of its dissolution...
Or it might produce matter; even the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) would produce matter. However, consciousness does not produce matter during those two moments.

But just as a cluster of *ahicchattaka* mushrooms arises from the earth only by taking up particles of dust as they emerge, so too, consciousness, depending on the pre-arisen physical basis, [produces matter] at the moment of its own arising.

It arises having already grasped eight types of material phenomena. Furthermore, at the moment of rebirth-linking, because the physical basis (vatthu) cannot function as a pre-arisen condition, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not generate material phenomena due to this deficiency of conditions.
And just as when a stranger goes to a place he has never visited before, others [say to him]: "Come, sir, enter the village..."
Just as one who is poor and lacks resources is unable to say, "I will give food, drink, perfumes, garlands, and so forth," because these things are beyond his reach,
even so, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta), being adventitious, does not produce materiality because it too is adventitious. Furthermore,
the rebirth-linking consciousness [cannot produce materiality] because the thirty types of kamma-born materiality already occupy the positions where consciousness-born materiality would arise.
It does not produce form.
However, the death-consciousness of one whose taints are destroyed does not produce [form] because the root of the round has been stilled.
For in all states of existence, the root of the round has been stilled for him; it is incapable of arising again, and thus there is no longer what is called a "succession" into a new becoming.
For the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), however, with the exception of seven more existences, the root of the round (*vaṭṭamūla*) has been stilled.
Therefore, his death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) produces material form within seven existences; for the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), it does so in two; for the non-returner (*anāgāmī*), in one.
Because the root of the round has been stilled in all existences for the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), it produces none at all.
In the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, however, there is no jhāna-factor, no path-factor, and no root;
thus, because the mental factor is weak, they do not produce matter due to that weakness of the mental factor.
The four immaterial-resultants do not produce matter because of the absence of matter in that existence. And it is not only these that [do not produce matter], but also those...
In that existence, forty-two other types of consciousness also arise— namely, the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, ten unwholesome consciousnesses, nine functional consciousnesses,
four formless-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, four formless-sphere functional consciousnesses, three path-consciousnesses, and four fruition-consciousnesses—
and because of the absence of matter there, these too do not generate matter.
Thus, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not produce matter.
However, temperature produces the first matter. What is this so-called "temperature"?

It is the fire element existing within the thirty-two types of kamma-born material phenomena that arise at the moment of rebirth-linking. Having reached its location, it produces eight types of matter.
This temperature is called "slow cessation," whereas consciousness has "quick cessation. While that [temperature] is still persisting, sixteen moments of consciousness arise and cease.
Among these, immediately after rebirth-linking, the first life-continuum consciousness produces eight material phenomena at the very moment of its arising.
However, when the time comes for sound to arise, then both temperature and consciousness [produce it].
They will produce the group of nine sounds. Even edible food, having reached its destination, produces eight types of material form.
But from where does this [embryo] derive its edible food? From the mother. And this has also been said:
"Whatever food, drink, and nourishment his mother eats,"
“By that [nutriment] he sustains himself there, the man dwelling within the mother’s womb.
Thus, while still in the womb, the child is sustained by the nutritive essence (*ojā*) of the food and drink swallowed by the mother.

That very essence, having reached its proper place, gives rise to the eight types of material form (*rūpa*). But is it not the case that this essence is coarse, while the physical basis (*vatthu*) is subtle? How then does it take its stand there?
At first it does not take root; it takes root after one or two weeks have passed.
Whether it takes root earlier or later, when the nutritive essence of the food and drink consumed by the mother settles in the body of the child, it then causes the eight material phenomena to arise.

In the case of one who is born spontaneously (*opapātika*), when he is reborn in a place where solid and soft foods have been naturally prepared, the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that has reached its proper state generates material form as he takes them and swallows them. There is also one who is reborn in a forest devoid of food and drink;
he becomes greatly famished and swallows his own saliva by turning it over with his tongue. Even there, for him...
Nutritive essence, having reached its proper state, produces material form.
Thus, among the twenty-five components, only two things produce material form: the fire element and physical food.
Even in the immaterial plane, only two factors produce material form: consciousness and kamma-intention. In this regard:
Form is weak at the moment of arising and at the moment of dissolution, but strong at the moment of presence;
thus it originates form during the moment of presence. Consciousness is weak at the moment of presence and at the moment of dissolution, but strong only at the moment of arising;
thus it originates form only at the moment of arising. Volitional action (kamma-cetanā) becomes a condition even though it has already ceased.
For even an action accumulated at the limit of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons in the past becomes a condition now;

and an action accumulated now will become a condition even at the end of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons in the future. Thus it should be understood "from the perspective of before and after.
Regarding "delimitation by duration": for how long a duration does matter (rūpa) persist? For how long does immateriality (arūpa)? Matter...
The material (rūpa) undergoes transformation slowly and ceases gradually; the immaterial (arūpa) undergoes transformation quickly and ceases rapidly.
While the material form is still persisting, sixteen moments of consciousness arise and cease; however, that [material form] ceases together with the seventeenth moment of consciousness.
For example, it is as if a man, thinking "I shall make the fruit fall," were to strike a branch of a tree with a mallet, and the fruits...
And let the leaves fall from their stalks at one and the same moment. In that case, because of their own weight, the fruits would fall to the earth first, and the leaves, being lighter, afterwards.

In exactly the same way, just as the time when the leaves and the fruits are released from the stalk by the blow of a club is simultaneous, so too at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the material and immaterial phenomena arise simultaneously.
Manifestation is like the earlier falling to the ground of fruits due to their heaviness:
it is the arising and ceasing of the sixteen consciousnesses while the material form is still persisting. Cessation is like the later falling to the ground of fruits due to their lightness:
it is the cessation of the material form together with the seventeenth consciousness.

In this regard, although matter has a slow cessation and a heavy transformation, while consciousness has a quick cessation and a light transformation, neither matter nor non-matter can proceed by abandoning the other; the proceeding of both is of equal measure.
Herein, this is the simile: there was one man with short legs and another with long legs. Of these two, traveling along a path together—
As they walked, for as long as it took Dīghapāda to take a single step, the other would walk sixteen steps, taking one footstep after another.
Dīghapāda, however, would stretch out his own foot and drag it along for those sixteen steps of the short-legged man, making only a single step himself. Thus, neither was able to overtake the other.
The gait of both is of exactly the same measure. This should be understood in the same way:
the formless (arūpa) is like the short-legged man, and the material (rūpa) is like the long-legged man;
just as when the long-legged man takes one step, the other takes sixteen steps, so too while the material phenomena persist, sixteen [moments] of the formless phenomena pass.

The arising and ceasing of consciousnesses; just as when two men walk together, one of whom is a lame man, the other draws up his own foot at every sixteen steps and makes them advance by a single step, so too does matter cease along with the seventeenth consciousness;
just as two men walk together without lagging behind one another, at exactly the same pace.
Just as movement is to the formless, so too does form and the formless proceed at the same measure without obstruction;
thus they should be understood "by way of delimitation of time.

As for the phrase "by way of simultaneous arising and separate cessation," this should be illustrated by excluding that which is born of the final karma. For first there is the rebirth-linking consciousness...
The second life-continuum, the third life-continuum... [and so on] ...the sixteenth life-continuum.

In each of these, there are three moments by way of arising, presence, and dissolution. Within those, during each of the three moments of every single consciousness, thirty-two material qualities born of kamma arise.
Among them, the kamma-born materiality that arose at the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness persists until the seventeenth [moment].

That which arises at the very moment of the arising of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) ceases at the moment of its dissolution; that which arises at the moment of its presence ceases at the moment of its presence;
and that which arises at the moment of its dissolution ceases at the moment of its dissolution.
In this way, beginning with the second life-continuum consciousness, the method should be applied by connecting each with its own seventeenth consciousness. Thus, sixteen [moments].
There are forty-eight triads. This is called the lineage of the forty-eight types of kamma-born materiality.
Furthermore, this [lineage] proceeds unceasingly, like the current of a river, whether one is eating or drinking by night or by day, or whether one is asleep or heedless.
Thus it should be understood as "arising together and ceasing separately."
