‘The state of non-arising and simultaneous cessation’ is to be illustrated by means of the final kamma-born [materiality].
In that context, when there is a series of sixteen consciousnesses at the conclusion of the life-formations, the lower set of sixteen and the upper set of sixteen must be joined together as one.
For in the lower set of sixteen, at the moment of arising of the first consciousness, thirty-two kamma-born materialities have arisen.

In the upper group of sixteen, that which arises at the very moment of the arising of the first consciousness ceases at its own moment of cessation; that which arises at its own moment of presence ceases at its own moment of presence;
and that which arises at its own moment of dissolution ceases at its own moment of dissolution.

However, in the lower group of sixteen, that which arises at the moment of the arising of the second consciousness... [and so on] ...up to that which arises at the moment of the arising of the sixteenth consciousness.

Materiality born of kamma ceases at the very moment of arising of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*); that which arose during its [the death-consciousness] moment of presence ceases at the very moment of presence of the death-consciousness;
and that which arose during its moment of dissolution ceases at the very moment of dissolution of the death-consciousness.
From that point on, the continuity of materiality born of kamma no longer proceeds. If it were to proceed, sentient beings...
They would be called indestructible, imperishable, ageless, and immortal.

However, in this context, according to the method beginning with "it ceases at the very moment of arising of the seventeenth bhavaṅga-consciousness," it is stated that "the material form arisen at the moment of arising of one consciousness ceases at the moment of arising of another."

It is stated [in the commentary] because it has come down in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, that contradicts this canonical text: “For whom bodily formation ceases, for him mental formation ceases?”—[the answer being] “Yes.
How so? For bodily formation is the wind of inhalation and exhalation, which is mind-originated (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*).
And mind-originated matter, having arisen at the moment of the mind’s arising, [persists] until other...
Sixteen consciousnesses arise while it remains. It ceases together with the very last of those sixteen.
Thus, starting from the consciousness with which it arises, it ceases together with the seventeenth;
it does not cease at the moment of arising or the moment of presence of any consciousness, nor does it cease during the moment of presence.

Or it arises at the moment of dissolution. This is the natural law (dhammatā) of mind-originated matter; because it necessarily ceases in the same moment as the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra), it is stated:
"Yes. And this rule regarding the moment of mind-originated matter applies equally to that which is originated by karma and so forth.
Therefore, the kamma-born materiality that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases along with the seventeenth [consciousness] from that point onward.
That which arose during the subsistence-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases during the arising-moment of the eighteenth.
That which arose during the dissolution-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases during the subsistence-moment of the eighteenth.
The application [of the method] here should be made according to this principle. Beyond that, however, only the sequence of those things originated by temperature (utu-samuṭṭhānika) persists;
it must be said, "Having removed it, burn it. Thus it should be understood "by way of different arising and single cessation.

Regarding "by way of single arising and single cessation": material form arises and ceases together with material form; immaterial form arises and ceases together with immaterial form. Thus it should be understood "by way of single arising and single cessation."
Furthermore, "the state of neither-arising-nor-ceasing" should be illustrated by means of the fourfold continuity of matter (*catusantatirūpa*).
For within this body—which extends from the soles of the feet upwards to the crown of the head and is bounded by the skin—the fourfold continuity of matter exists here and there as a dense mass.
Even though it exists in this way, its simultaneous arising and so forth should not be perceived. It is, however, like a row of ants.
Or when a line of ants is looked at, they appear as if joined together, yet they are not actually joined.
For near the head of one there are the head, belly, and feet of another; near the belly of one there are the head, belly, and feet of another;
and near the feet of one there are the head, belly, and feet of another. In the same way...
Even among the four types of continuity of matter, while one thing is in the moment of arising, there is also the arising, the presence, and the dissolution of another;

while one thing is in the moment of presence, there is also the arising, the presence, and the dissolution of another; and while one thing is in the moment of dissolution, there is also the arising, the presence, and the dissolution of another.
In this way, "the state of neither non-arising nor non-ceasing" is to be understood here.
Furthermore, the categories beginning with "past" and ending with "distant and difficult," as they appear in the Canon, have already been explained.
The "origination by way of conditions" has also been discussed below according to the method beginning with: "born of kamma, conditioned by kamma, and originated by temperature conditioned by kamma.
Moreover, all five aggregates are indeed fully accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*), not unaccomplished; they are indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Moreover, they are indeed produced. For among phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), only *nibbāna* is exclusively unproduced and non-produced.
But how is it with the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and mental designation (*nāmapaññatti*)?
The attainment of cessation should not be described as mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, or produced or unproduced. Yet, it is produced.
It exists because it must be attained by one who is attaining it. Likewise with the designation "name" (*nāmapaññatti*). For that too does not receive the classification of mundane and so forth;
rather, it is a produced phenomenon (*nipphannā*), not an unproduced one (*anipphannā*). Indeed, when one grasps the term "name," one grasps it precisely as such.
— Discussion on the Determination of Order and Other Factors —
Having thus understood the aggregates by way of miscellaneous analysis, one should further understand them— precisely these same aggregates—
by way of the classification of knowledge, by way of order, by way of distinction,
by way of neither deficiency nor excess, and likewise by way of similes.
Thus, from the perspective of what is to be seen, there are two ways; for one who sees thus, the goal is accomplished.
This method of determination should be correctly understood by the discerning person.
In this context, "by way of order" refers to many kinds of order: the order of arising, the order of abandoning, the order of practice, the order of planes, and the order of teaching.
In this context, “first there is the *kalala*, from the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*,” and so forth, is the sequence of arising (*uppattikkamo*).
“States to be abandoned by seeing, states to be abandoned by cultivation,” and so forth, is the sequence of abandoning (*pahānakkamo*).

“Purification of virtue, purification of mind,” and so forth, is the sequence of practice (*paṭipattikkamo*). “Belonging to the sense-sphere, belonging to the fine-material sphere,” and so forth, is the sequence of planes (*bhūmikkamo*).
The sequence of teaching is such as “the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors,” or “discourse on giving, discourse on virtue,” and so forth.

Among these, first of all, a sequence of arising is not applicable here, because the aggregates—unlike the embryo in its stages of *kalala* and so on—do not arise with a fixed priority of before and after;
nor is a sequence of abandoning applicable, because wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned.
It is not a sequence of practice, because unwholesome states are not to be practiced; nor is it a sequence of planes, because feelings and the other aggregates are included within all four planes.

Rather, it is a sequence of teaching that is appropriate. For, without making distinctions, the Blessed One—desiring the welfare of those people and wishing to liberate from the grasp of a self those disciples who have fallen into the view of a self regarding the five aggregates—intends to free them from that grasp by means of the analysis of the "lump" (the mass) into its constituent parts.
For the sake of easy comprehension, he first taught the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), which is coarse and serves as the objective domain for the eye and the other sense faculties.

Following that, he taught feeling (*vedanā*), which experiences desirable and undesirable forms; then perception (*saññā*), which grasps the mode of the object of feeling according to the principle "what one feels, that one perceives";
then volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), which construct by way of perception; and finally, the support for those [factors] beginning with feeling.
And consciousness is the dominant factor—thus, first of all, the method of analysis "by way of order" (*kamato*) should be understood.

As for "by way of distinction" (*visesato*), this refers to the distinction between the aggregates (*khandhā*) and the aggregates subject to clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*). What, then, is their distinction? The aggregates are stated without distinction, whereas the aggregates subject to clinging are distinguished by their state of being associated with the taints (*sāsava*) and being objects of clinging (*upādāniya*).
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five aggregates subject to clinging; listen to that. Which [are they]?"
And what, monks, are the five aggregates? Whatever form, monks, there is—whether past, future, or present...
far or near—this is called the aggregate of form. Whatever feeling... whatever perception...
whatever formations... whatever consciousness there is... far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
These, monks, are called the five aggregates. And what, monks, are the five aggregates subject to clinging?

Whatever form, monks—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—is accompanied by taints and conducive to clinging—this is called the aggregate of form subject to clinging.

Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever volitional formations... whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—is accompanied by taints and conducive to clinging—this is called the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
“Monks, this is the consciousness-aggregate of clinging. These, monks, are called the five aggregates of clinging.
And herein, while feeling and the others exist both with and without taints (*āsava*), form is not so.

However, because its status as an aggregate is appropriate in the sense of a “heap,” it is mentioned among the aggregates. And because it possesses the sense of a heap and the sense of being subject to taints—
And the status of being aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) is appropriate; therefore, it is said in reference to the aggregates of clinging.
However, feeling and the others are mentioned as "aggregates" (khandha) when they are free from taints (anāsava), and as "aggregates of clinging" (upādānakkhandha) when they are with taints (sāsava).

Furthermore, in the term "aggregates of clinging," the meaning should be understood as "aggregates that have clinging as their domain" (upādānagocara). But here, all of these are taken together as one.
“Aggregates” (khandhā) is what is intended here.
But why did the Blessed One speak of exactly five aggregates—neither fewer nor more? It is because they comprise all conditioned things that share a common nature;
because this is the ultimate extent of the basis for grasping at a self or what belongs to a self; and because other [categories] are included within them. Among the many various classifications...

For when conditioned phenomena are grouped together according to their common characteristics (*sabhāga*), matter becomes one aggregate by way of being grouped with the common characteristic of matter;
feeling becomes one aggregate by way of being grouped with the common characteristic of feeling. This same method applies to perception and the others as well.

Therefore, only five are mentioned because of the grouping of all conditioned things according to their common characteristics. And this is the ultimate basis for the grasping of "self" and "belonging to self."
That is to say, the five beginning with form. For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, when there is form, by clinging to form, by adhering to form, such a view arises:
'This is mine, this I am, this is my self. [The same applies] to feeling...
to perception... to volitional formations... When there is consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, such a view arises..."
"...arises: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self. Therefore, even in terms of the maximum number of bases for the grasping of a self and what belongs to a self, only five are mentioned.

Furthermore, as for the other five aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) mentioned, such as virtue and so forth, they too are included right here because they are comprised within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Therefore, even by way of their inclusion therein, there are no others.
"Only five are mentioned. In this way, the method of analysis should be understood "in terms of neither deficiency nor excess. Regarding "by way of simile":

here, the aggregate of clinging to form is like a sickroom, because it serves as the dwelling place for the aggregate of clinging to consciousness—which is like a patient—by way of its basis, doors, and objects;
and the aggregate of clinging to feeling is like the illness itself, because it is afflictive.

The aggregate of clinging to perception (saññupādānakkhandha) is like an illness, because it gives rise to feelings associated with lust and other defilements through perceptions of sensual desire and so forth.

The aggregate of clinging to volitional formations (saṅkhārupādānakkhandha) is like the indulgence in unwholesome things, because it is the cause for the illness of feeling. For it is said: “They form the conditioned [volitional formations] for the sake of feeling.
Likewise: “Because of having performed and accumulated unwholesome kamma...”
“Resultant body-consciousness has arisen accompanied by suffering. The aggregate of clinging to consciousness is like a patient because it is not free from the illness of feeling.
Furthermore, these are like a prison, the executioner, the criminal, and the offender;
and they are like a vessel, food, condiment, a server, and an eater. In this way, the method of determination “by way of simile” is to be understood.
‘To be seen in two ways’ means both in brief and in detail; thus, the method of exposition should be understood here as being twofold in its manner of seeing.
For in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are [to be seen] as an enemy with raised sword according to the method stated in the *Āsivisa-sutta* (The Snake Simile);
as a burden according to the *Bhāra-sutta* (The Burden Sutta); and as a consumer according to the discourse on the state of being devoured.
By means of the *Yamaka-sutta*, they are to be regarded as the murderers consisting of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and the conditioned.

In detail, however, form is to be regarded here like a lump of foam, feeling like a water-bubble, perception like a mirage, mental formations like the trunk of a plantain tree, and consciousness like an illusion. For this has been said:
"Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a water-bubble;"
“Perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusion—thus it was taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.
In this regard, the similarity of form and the other aggregates to a mass of foam and so forth should be understood as follows: for just as a mass of foam is devoid of essence...
In this way, form too is entirely without core, being devoid of permanence, solidity, and a self as its core.
And just as it is impossible to take hold of that [clod of earth], thinking, "I shall make a bowl or a dish," and even if taken, it does not serve that purpose but simply breaks apart;
so too, it is impossible to take hold of form, thinking, "It is permanent," or "It is stable," or "It is I," or "It is mine."
Even when grasped, it does not remain as such; it is simply impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Thus, it is "just like a lump of foam.

Or again, just as a lump of foam is perforated here and there, composed of many joints, and is a dwelling place for many creatures such as water-snakes, so too is form perforated here and there and composed of many joints. And herein, by way of its constituent parts (*kula*):
Eighty species of worms dwell there; that very place serves them as a maternity home, a latrine, a sickroom, and a cemetery.
They do not go elsewhere to give birth or perform such functions. Thus it is like a lump of foam.
And just as a lump of foam, though initially only the size of a ripe jujube fruit, gradually becomes even the size of a mountain peak, so too does this body grow.

In this way, even such a form as this, having initially been merely a *kalala*, gradually becomes the size of a fathom in the case of cows, buffaloes, elephants, and so forth, and even the size of a mountain peak in the case of fish, turtles, and others, reaching even hundreds of yojanas in measure.
Thus it is like a mass of foam. And just as a mass of foam breaks up immediately upon rising, or after traveling only a short distance, [so too does this body].
But having reached the ocean, it inevitably breaks apart; in the same way, form also breaks apart even in the state of the *kalala*, and in the states of the *abbuda* and so forth.
Even if it does not break in the interim, once it reaches its hundredth year for those with a lifespan of a hundred years, it inevitably breaks apart;
at the mouth of death, it becomes a mere mass of powder and dust. Thus, too, it is like a lump of foam.
Just as a bubble is insubstantial, so too is feeling.

And just as it is weak, not fit for grasping, and impossible to take hold of to make into a raft or a seat—indeed, even when grasped or not grasped, it simply breaks apart—so too is feeling weak and not fit for grasping;
it cannot be grasped as "permanent" or "stable," and even when grasped, it is not so.
It remains. Thus, even though it has reached a state of being ungraspable, feeling is "like a bubble.
Just as in each drop of water a bubble arises and ceases, not remaining for long, so too feeling arises and ceases, not remaining for long;
in a single moment of consciousness, its duration is reckoned at hundreds of thousands of millions.

Having arisen, it ceases. And just as a bubble arises dependent upon four causes—the surface of the water, a drop of water, the spray of water, and the gathering wind—so too does feeling arise dependent upon four causes:
the physical basis, the object, the net of defilements, and the impact of contact.
In this way, feeling (vedanā) is like a bubble.
Perception (saññā), too, is "like a mirage" in the sense that it is devoid of substance. Likewise, it is so in the sense of being ungraspable;
for it is not possible to take hold of it to drink from, bathe in, or fill a vessel with. Moreover, just as a mirage flickers, perception possesses a surging impulse.
It appears as such; likewise, perception—divided into the categories of blue-perception and so forth—quivers and throbs for the purpose of experiencing blue and other objects.

And just as a mirage deceives the multitude, making them say, "It looks like a full pond" or "It looks like a full river," so too does perception deceive, making them say, "This is blue, beautiful, pleasant, and permanent."
The same method applies to the yellow and other colors as well.
Thus, by way of deception, formations are like a mirage; and by way of being pithless, they are "like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Likewise, they are so because they cannot be grasped. For just as it is impossible to take anything from a plantain trunk and use it for purposes such as rafters, even if it were taken...
It is not so; likewise, the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) cannot be grasped as permanent and so forth, and even when grasped, they do not remain so.
Just as a plantain trunk is a combination of many layers, so too the aggregate of formations is a combination of many phenomena.
And just as a plantain trunk has various characteristics—for indeed, the color of the outer leaf-sheath is one thing, and another is...

Then there are those that are more internal than the internal; in the same way, the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) has one characteristic from contact (phassa), and another from volition (cetanā) and so forth.
But when combined, it is called simply the "aggregate of formations. Thus, too, the aggregate of formations is like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Consciousness too is "like an illusion" in the sense of being pithless; likewise, in the sense of not reaching a graspable state.
And just as an illusion is short-lived and quick to appear, so too is consciousness; for it is even more short-lived and quicker to appear than that.
Indeed, by that very mind, a person appears as if coming, as if going, as if standing, and as if sitting. It is one thing indeed...
The mind at the time of coming is one thing, while at the times of going and so forth it is another. In this way, consciousness is like an illusion (*māyā*).
An illusion deceives the great multitude, causing them to grasp at whatever it presents as "this is gold," "silver," or "pearl. Consciousness likewise deceives the great multitude;
by means of that very same mind, it makes them perceive as if coming, as if going, as if standing, or as if sitting.

Having made it appear as such, one causes it to be grasped. Furthermore, the mind directed toward coming is one thing, while that directed toward going and so forth is another. In this way, too, consciousness is like an illusion.
Moreover, specifically, even internal form—though its object be beautiful and gross—should be regarded as foul.

Feeling is suffering because it is not exempt from the three kinds of suffering; perception and mental formations are non-self because they are not subject to one's control; and consciousness [is likewise non-self].

It should be seen as impermanent because its nature is to arise and fall away. One who views the five aggregates of clinging as being like an enemy with a raised sword and so forth is not oppressed by the aggregates.
In detail, however, one who views form and the other aggregates as being like a lump of foam and so forth does not perceive a core in what is coreless.
Specifically, viewing internal form as foul, one fully understands physical nutriment; in that which is foul—

Seeing [the beautiful] as beautiful, one abandons the perversion [of perceiving the unattractive as attractive], crosses over the flood of sensual desire, becomes dissociated from the yoke of sensual desire, becomes free from the taint of sensual desire, shatters the bodily tie of covetousness, and does not cling to the clinging of sensual desire.
Seeing feeling as suffering, one fully understands the nutriment of contact; one abandons the perversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure, and crosses over the flood of existence.
One becomes dissociated from the bond of existence; one becomes free from the taint of existence; one breaks the bodily fetter of ill will;
one does not cling to the clinging to rules and observances. Seeing perception and mental formations as non-self, one fully understands the nutriment of mental volition;
one abandons the perversion of regarding what is non-self as self; one crosses over the flood of views and the bond of views.

One becomes dissociated; one becomes free from the taint of views and thus becomes taintless. This breaks the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence to "this is the truth," and one does not cling to the clinging to a self-theory.
Seeing consciousness as impermanent, one fully understands the nutriment of consciousness;
one abandons the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent; one crosses over the flood of ignorance and becomes dissociated from the yoke of ignorance.
Through the taint of ignorance, he becomes untainted; he breaks the bodily tie of clinging to rules and observances; he does not take up the clinging to views.
Since seeing [the aggregates] by way of the executioner and so forth brings such great benefit, therefore a wise person should view the aggregates by way of the executioner and so forth.
Commentary on the Suttanta-Bhajaniya.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-Bhajaniya. 32.
Now follows the Abhidhamma-Bhajaniya. Therein, the exposition of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is to be understood according to the same method as detailed previously in the Rūpa-Kaṇḍa.

34. In the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), "in one way" means by a single division. "Associated with contact" means associated with contact. All feelings belonging to the four planes [of existence] are included.
In the dyad of "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*), the feelings with root-cause belong to the four planes, while those without root-cause belong only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
By this method, the feelings described under the headings of "wholesome" (*kusala*) and so forth should be understood. Furthermore, this aggregate of feeling—
It is shown as onefold by way of association with contact; twofold by way of being with root-cause or without root-cause;
threefold by way of birth; fourfold by way of different planes; and fivefold by way of faculties.

Among these, the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of pain have the physical sensitivity as their basis and belong exclusively to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). The faculty of mental joy has either the sixth [mental] base as its basis or no specific basis at all.
Or it belongs to those [other] planes. The faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) has six bases and belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

The faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) has four bases—the sensitive organs of the eye and so forth—six bases, no base at all, and belongs to the four planes. Thus it is shown according to its bases in six ways.
Therein, the first five feelings have the five sensitive organs as their bases and belong only to the sense-sphere; the sixth is either without a base or with a base and belongs to the four planes.
Therein, it is shown by way of sevenfold division as that born of mind-contact; by way of eightfold division as that born of body-contact;
by way of ninefold division as that born of mind-consciousness-element-contact within the sevenfold division;
and by way of tenfold division as that born of mind-consciousness-element-contact within the eightfold division. For among these, in the sevenfold division, that born of mind-contact...
That born of mind-element contact and that born of mind-consciousness-element contact are divided into two.
In the eightfold division, together with that [mental feeling], bodily-contact-born [feeling] is also divided into two: pleasant and painful.

In the ninefold division, among the seven kinds mentioned, that born of mind-consciousness-element contact is divided into three according to the wholesome and so forth. In the tenfold division, among the eight kinds...
Those [mental phenomena] born of contact with the mind-consciousness element are stated to be divided into three types by way of the wholesome and so forth.
Herein, the "Triplet of the Wholesome" (Kusalattika) is mentioned solely for the purpose of completing the set.

However, in the sevenfold, eightfold, and ninefold classifications, the method is applied only where it is appropriate to provide that method. For when reaching the Abhidhamma, the Tathāgata provides the method [only as required].
There is no method that has not been applied in its proper place. This, first of all, is one section in the *Dukamūlaka* (the Root of Pairs).

For in this *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, while analyzing the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), the Teacher took the triplets (*tike*) and inserted them into the pairs (*duke*), took the pairs and inserted them into the triplets, and brought forth both the triplets and the pairs by means of the "mutual expansion" method (*ubhatovaḍḍhananīhāra*).
In seven ways, twenty-four ways, thirty ways, and many ways—in every respect he demonstrated the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) as being manifold.
Why? Both because of the inclinations of the individuals and because of the elegance of the teaching.
For among the assembly of devas seated to hear the Dhamma, those sons of the gods who were taking up triads and placing them within dyads while it was being explained—
He taught by arranging [the teaching] accordingly for those who were able to penetrate it through those [particular] ways;
and he taught by those other ways for those who were able to penetrate what was being spoken in those other modes. This, in this context, is "the inclination of the individual" (*puggalajjhāsayo*).
However, the Perfectly Enlightened One, due to his own vast range of scope, would include the triads within the dyads, or the dyads within the triads.
He is able to teach in whatever manner he wishes, whether by way of "increase in both" (*ubhatovaḍḍhana*) or by way of the sevenfold method (*sattavidha-ādi-naya*).
Therefore, because he taught by means of these modes, this is his "elegance of teaching" (*desanāvilāsa*).

Among these, the section where he takes the triads (*tika*) and inserts them into the dyads (*duka*) is called the "dyad-rooted" (*dukamūlaka*). [Conversely,] taking the dyads and inserting them into the triads...

The section taught by inserting [the factors] is called the "Rooted in Triads" (*tikamūlaka*). The section taught by increasing both the triads and the dyads is called the "Doubly Increased" (*ubhatovaḍḍhitaka*).
Finally, the section beginning with "in seven ways," etc., is called the "Manyfold" (*bahuvidha*); these, for now, are the four great sections.

Among them, in the "Rooted in Dyads" (*dukamūlaka*), each dyad found among the dyads is taken together with each triad not found among the triads—namely, the triad of feeling (*vedanāttika*), the triad of the pleasant (*pītittika*), and the triad of the visible (*sanidassanattika*).

Having removed [the first two], and having combined the remaining nineteen triplets that are available, there are nine hundred and fifty combinations beginning with the combination of the second dyad and the first triplet, and so forth.
All of these have been stated in the Pāḷi by way of abbreviation, showing only what is appropriate to be shown in each respective place;
however, they should be understood in detail by one who does not become confused.

In the *Tikamūlaka* as well, for each individual triad found among the triads, one removes those dyads not found in conjunction with that triad—such as the first dyad and so forth—and joins the remaining fifty dyads, such as the "rooted dyad" (*sahetuka-duka*) and others, to them.
Thus, there are nine hundred and fifty sections, beginning with the section on the combination of the first triad and the second dyad.
All of these have been condensed in the *Pāḷi* at their respective places.
Having shown what is appropriate to be shown, it has been stated. However, one who is not confused should understand this in detail.

In the two-fold division of the "increased on both sides" (*ubhatovaḍḍhitaka*), starting from the second dyad in the two-fold division and the first triad in the three-fold division, one should apply the nineteen triads that are obtainable through the nineteen dyads that are obtainable; thus, there are the application-sections beginning with the second dyad and the first triad.
Nineteen [triads] have been stated. This is the third great section, called the "Doubly Increasing" (*ubhatovaḍḍhitaka*), because it increases in both ways by way of the two triads.
Regarding the exposition of the sevenfold [section] of the manifold section, among the nineteen triads obtainable starting from the beginning:
By correlating four sections with each individual [term], nineteen sevenfold sets are stated.
In the twenty-fourfold exposition as well, nineteen sets are stated by way of those very triads. Likewise in the manyfold set.
Since the thirtyfold set is only one, there are fifty-eight sets in total. This, then, is the commentary on the text here according to the delimitation of the sets.
Now follows the commentary on the meaning. Therein, first, the sevenfold exposition is indeed clear in its meaning.

In the twenty-fourfold exposition, the statement "there is a wholesome aggregate of feeling conditioned by eye-contact" is to be understood by way of the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"There is an unwholesome [aggregate]" is to be understood by way of the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. "There is an indeterminate [aggregate]"...

It should be understood by way of twenty-four types of consciousness: the three mind-elements (*manodhātu*), the three rootless mind-consciousness elements (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*), the eight great resultants (*mahāvipāka*), and the ten sense-sphere functional states (*kāmāvacara-kiriya*).
Among these, the eight wholesome and twelve unwholesome states are obtained by way of impulsion (*javana*). [The remaining] is the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*).
It is obtained by way of adverting. The two resultant mind-elements are obtained by way of receiving; the three resultant mind-consciousness elements by way of investigating and registration;
the functional rootless mind-consciousness element by way of determining; the eight great resultant consciousnesses by way of registration;
and the nine functional consciousnesses are obtained by way of impulsion. This same method applies to the doors of the ear, nose, tongue, and body as well.

In the case of the mind-door (*manodvāra*), however, "there is wholesome" is stated by way of the four planes of wholesome consciousness; "there is unwholesome" is stated by way of the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness.

"There is indeterminate" is stated by way of thirty-four types of consciousness-arising: namely, the eleven sense-sphere resultant (*vipāka*) types, the ten functional (*kiriya*) types, the nine functional types of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). Among these, the wholesome of the four planes...

Unwholesome [consciousness] is obtained by way of impulsion (*javana*). From the functional (*kiriya*), the rootless mind-consciousness element is obtained by way of adverting (*āvajjana*); the eleven resultant consciousnesses are obtained by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*); and both the functionals of the three planes and the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) are obtained only by way of impulsion. These may be explained by taking any one among the sevenfold classification and so forth. Regarding the thirtyfold [classification]: [The text continues with the detailed breakdown of the thirty types of consciousness. ...the wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere arises as the first; the unwholesome consciousness arises as the second; the functional consciousness of the sense-sphere arises as the third; the resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere arises as the fourth; the wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere arises as the fifth; the wholesome consciousness of the immaterial sphere arises as the sixth; the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere arises as the seventh; the resultant consciousness of the immaterial sphere arises as the eighth; the functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere arises as the ninth; the functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere arises as the tenth. In the case of the wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere, there are eight types: the four accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), the two accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), and the two accompanied by grief (*domanassa*).

Among these, the four accompanied by joy arise through association with the four jhānas; the two accompanied by equanimity arise through association with the fifth jhāna; and the two accompanied by grief arise through association with the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) of the first jhāna. In the case of the unwholesome consciousness, there are three types: that accompanied by joy, that accompanied by equanimity, and that accompanied by grief. Among these, the one accompanied by joy arises through association with the first jhāna; the one accompanied by equanimity arises through association with the fourth jhāna; and the one accompanied by grief arises through association with the preliminary stage of the first jhāna. In the case of the functional consciousness of the sense-sphere, there are nine types: the four accompanied by joy, the two accompanied by equanimity, and the three accompanied by equanimity. Among these, the four accompanied by joy arise through association with the four jhānas; the two accompanied by equanimity arise through association with the fifth jhāna; and the three accompanied by equanimity arise through association with the preliminary stage of the first jhāna. In the case of the resultant consciousness of the sense-sphere, there are five types: the four accompanied by joy and the one accompanied by equanimity. Among these, the four accompanied by joy arise through association with the four jhānas; and the one accompanied by equanimity arises through association with the fifth jhāna. In the case of the wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere, there are five types: the four accompanied by joy and the one accompanied by equanimity. Among these, the four accompanied by joy arise through association with the four jhānas; and the one accompanied by equanimity arises through association with the fifth jhāna. In the case of the wholesome consciousness of the immaterial sphere, there are four types: the four accompanied by equanimity. Among these, they arise through association with the four immaterial attainments (*jhāna*). In the case of the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere, there are five types: the four accompanied by joy and the one accompanied by equanimity. Among these, the four accompanied by joy arise through association with the four jhānas; and the one accompanied by equanimity arises through association with the fifth jhāna. In the case of the resultant consciousness of the immaterial sphere, there are four types: the four accompanied by equanimity. Among these, they arise through association with the four immaterial attainments. In the case of the functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere, there are five types: the four accompanied by joy and the one accompanied by equanimity. Among these, the four accompanied by joy arise through association with the four jhānas; and the one accompanied by equanimity arises through association with the fifth jhāna. In the case of the functional consciousness of the immaterial sphere, there are four types:

the four accompanied by equanimity. Among these, they arise through association with the four immaterial attainments. Thus, the thirty types of consciousness have been explained. As for the remaining types, they should be understood according to their respective characteristics. This concludes the section on the thirtyfold classification. [The text concludes with a summary verse regarding the total number of consciousnesses across all classifications. ...there are fifty-four types of consciousness in total. This concludes the Compendium of Consciousness (*Cittasangaha*). [The text then transitions to the Compendium of Mental Factors (*Cetasikasangaha*). ...there are twenty-two mental factors. Among these, the universal factors (*sabba-citta-sādhāraṇā*) are seven: contact (*phassa*), volition (*cetanā*), initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and attention (*manasikāra*). The particular factors (*pakiṇṇaka*) are six: zeal (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokkha*), mindfulness (*sati*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*). The unwholesome factors (*akusala*) are fourteen: delusion (*moha*), lack of shame (*ahirika*), lack of dread (*anottappa*), restlessness (*uddhacca*), greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dosa*), conceit (*māna*), wrong view (*diṭṭhi*), envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), worry (*kukkucca*), sloth (*thina*), torpor (*middha*), and agitation (*vikkhepa*). The beautiful factors (*sobhana*) are twenty-five: faith (*saddhā*), conscientiousness (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), tranquility of body (*kāyapassaddhi*), tranquility of mind (*cittapassaddhi*), lightness of body (*kāyalahutā*), lightness of mind (*cittalahutā*), plasticity of body (*kāyamudutā*), plasticity of mind (*cittamudutā*), wieldiness of body (*kāyakammaññatā*), wieldiness of mind (*cittakammaññatā*), proficiency of body (*kāyapāguññatā*), proficiency of mind (*cittapāguññatā*), rectitude of body (*kāyujukatā*), rectitude of mind (*cittujukatā*), non-delusion (*amoha*), non-worry (*an-uddhacca*), non-agitation (*avikkhepa*), and equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*). Thus, the fifty-two mental factors have been explained. This concludes the Compendium of Mental Factors. [The text concludes with a summary verse regarding the total number of mental factors across all classifications. ...there are fifty-two mental factors in total. This concludes the Compendium of Abhidhamma (*Abhidhammasangaha*). [The text then transitions to the Compendium of Bases (*Vatthusangaha*). ...there are twenty-one bases. Among these, the material bases (*rūpa-vatthu*) are eighteen: the ten sense-bases (*āyatana*), the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), the sex organs (*bhāva*), and the physical life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*). The immaterial bases (*nāma-vatthu*) are three: the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element accompanied by root-cause (*sahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*). Thus, the twenty-one bases have been explained. This concludes the Compendium of Bases. However, since they are illuminated by standing upon [the thirty-seven factors], which serve as illuminators of happiness, they were illuminated by standing upon these very thirty kinds.

For all these consciousnesses are obtained in three ways: at the eye-door by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*), by way of transcendence (*samatikkama*), and by way of development (*bhāvanā*). Likewise at the ear-door and the mind-door. But at the nose, tongue, and body doors, [they are obtained] by way of transcendence and—
"By way of development": it should be understood that [these attainments] are obtained in two ways. How so?
Here, a bhikkhu, while walking on a monastery tour, sees a kasiṇa disk and asks, "What is this? When told, "It is a kasiṇa disk," he asks again, "What do they do with this?
Then they explain to him: "Having developed it in this way, the jhānas..."
“Having aroused [the jhānas], and having increased insight which has the attainment as its proximate cause, one attains arahantship.
A clansman endowed with aspiration, without perceiving it as a burden, thinks: “It is fitting for me too to produce this quality;
however, it cannot be produced by one who lies down and sleeps; from the very beginning, one must apply energy and virtue...”
Thinking, "It is necessary to purify it," he purifies his virtue (*sīla*). Then, being established in virtue, having severed the ten impediments (*palibodha*),

content with the minimum of the three robes (*ticīvara-parama*), having performed the duties and services toward his preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and teacher (*ācariya*), having mastered the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), having performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas,
and having produced the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), [he develops] insight (*vipassanā*) which has the attainments as its proximate cause.
Having increased [the practice], one attains Arahatship. In this context, all preparatory feelings belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara);
the feelings of the eight attainments belong to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpāvacara and arūpāvacara); and the feelings of the Path and its Fruit are supramundane (lokuttara).

Thus, eye-consciousness is a powerful condition for the production of feelings belonging to these four planes; therefore, feelings of the four planes are said to arise with eye-contact as their condition. Thus far.
They are obtained by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
However, when a visible form has come into the range of the eye-door, one thinks: "Lust has arisen toward this desirable object;

aversion toward the undesirable; delusion due to lack of equanimity; conceit has arisen in me who am bound; wrong view in me who have misapprehended; agitation in me who have fallen into distraction."
“Restlessness, doubt in one who has not reached a conclusion, and the underlying tendency (anusaya) that has become firmly rooted in one who has done so—these have arisen.
Thus, established in discernment, the noble son, having recognized the arising of his own defilements, thinks: “If these defilements of mine increase, they will lead to my ruin and disaster;
come now, I shall subdue them. He then reflects: “It is certainly not possible for one who is lying down and sleeping to [subdue them].”
Having practiced according to the method explained below—that "one must exert energy from the very beginning in order to purify one's virtue so as to suppress the defilements"—he attains Arahantship.

In this context, all preparatory-jhana feelings belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the feelings of the eight attainments belong to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpāvacara* and *arūpāvacara*);
and the feelings of the Path and Fruit are supramundane (*lokuttara*). Thus, [the practitioner] deals with the defilement that has arisen regarding a form-object.
"Having transcended and gone beyond" means that the feelings belonging to the four planes have arisen with eye-contact as their condition. Thus they are obtained "by way of transcendence.
However, when a visible form has entered the range of the eye-door, one person establishes an investigation thus: "What does this visible form depend upon?
Then, having understood it to be "dependent on the primary elements," he discerns: "The four great elements and derived matter are 'matter' (rūpa)."
He comprehends them; he comprehends the states that are their object as "formless.

Then, having comprehended name-and-form together with its conditions and having applied the three characteristics, he attains Arahatship by contemplating formations according to the sequence of insight.

In this context, all preparatory feelings belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the feelings associated with the eight attainments belong to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpāvacara* and *arūpāvacara*).

"The feelings of the paths and fruits are supramundane; thus, having been generated after comprehending visible form as their object, this feeling is said to have arisen with eye-contact as its condition.
In this way, they are obtained "by way of development.
Another bhikkhu hears: "It is said that, having performed the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and having produced the attainments, [the feeling] has the attainment as its proximate cause..."

"By increasing insight, they reach Arahantship. A clansman endowed with noble aspiration, without considering "this is difficult," thinks, "It is fitting for me too to produce this quality," and by practicing according to the previous method, he reaches Arahantship.
In that process, all the preliminary-jhana feelings belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while the feelings of the eight attainments...

Feeling pertaining to the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere, and feeling pertaining to the supramundane—namely, the feeling associated with the paths and fruits—is thus a powerful condition for the production of ear-consciousness.
Therefore, feeling pertaining to the four planes is said to arise by way of ear-contact as its condition.
Thus, first, they are obtained "by way of decisive support" (*upanissaya*).
Regarding the ear-door, however, when a sound has come into the range [of perception], everything should be understood in the same manner as explained for the eye-door.
Thus, having transcended the defilements that arise with respect to a sound-object, it is said: "The feelings belonging to the four planes have arisen conditioned by ear-contact.
In this way, they are obtained "by way of transcendence."
But when a sound has entered the range of the ear-door, one person establishes discernment thus: "What is this sound dependent upon?
All of this should be understood in the same manner as explained for the eye-door. Having thus comprehended the sound-object, [one realizes]:
"This feeling that has arisen is indeed born with ear-contact as its condition. In this way, they are obtained "by way of development" (bhāvanā).

Furthermore, regarding the doors of the nose, tongue, and body, when odor-objects and so forth have come into the range of perception, everything should be understood in the same manner as described for the eye-door—namely, by recognizing: "Lust has arisen in me toward this desirable object.

Thus, having transcended the defilements that arise with respect to odor-objects and so forth, they have gone beyond; therefore, the feelings belonging to the four planes are said to be conditioned by nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact.
Thus they are obtained by way of "surmounting" in respect of the three doors.
However, when odors and so forth have come into the range of the nose-door and the others, one person establishes discernment thus:
"This is an odor, this is a flavor, this is a tangible object; on what are they dependent? Everything is to be understood in the same manner as explained for the eye-door.

It should be understood thus. Having thus comprehended the objects of smell and so forth, this feeling that has arisen is said to be born with the contact of the nose, tongue, and body as its condition.
In this way, they are obtained "by way of development" (bhāvanā).
At the mind-door, however, they are obtained in all three ways. For a certain person sees birth as fearful, and aging and sickness...
He perceives death as fearful; having perceived it as fearful, he reflects: "It is necessary to be liberated from birth, aging, sickness, and death.
It is not possible to be liberated from birth and the rest while lying down and sleeping; therefore, one must apply energy from the very beginning and purify one's virtue.
Having reflected thus, he practices according to the method described for the eye-door and attains Arahantship.

It attains [that state]. In this context, all preparatory (parikamma) feelings belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); the feelings of the eight attainments belong to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpāvacara-ārūpāvacara);

and the feelings of the path and fruit are supramundane (lokuttara). Thus, birth, aging, sickness, and death constitute a powerful condition for the production of feelings belonging to the four planes;
therefore, feelings of the four planes are said to have mental contact as their condition. Thus, first of all...
They are obtained by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

Furthermore, regarding the mind-door (*manodvāra*), when mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*) have come into range, everything should be understood according to the method already explained for the eye-door.
Thus, having transcended the defilements arisen with respect to mental objects, the feelings belonging to the four planes [of existence] arise conditioned by mind-contact (*manosamphassa-paccayā*).
Thus they are obtained "by way of surmounting.

However, when an object consisting of mental phenomena (dhammārammaṇa) has come into the range of the mind-door, one person establishes an investigation in this way: "On what is this object of mental phenomena dependent?
"It is dependent on the physical basis (vatthu). "On what is the physical basis dependent? "It is dependent on the great primary elements (mahābhūta)."
Thus, he comprehends the four great elements and derived matter as "matter," and he comprehends the states that have those as their object as "non-material.

Then, having comprehended name-and-form together with its conditions, having applied the three characteristics, and having reflected upon formations according to the sequence of insight, he attains Arahantship.
In this process, all the preliminary preparatory feelings belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
The feelings of the eight attainments belong to the fine-material and immaterial spheres, while the feelings of the path and its fruition are supramundane;
having thus comprehended the object as a mental phenomenon (*dhammārammaṇa*), these feelings are produced. Thus, they are said to arise with mind-contact (*manosamphassa*) as their condition.
These are obtained "by way of development" (*bhāvanāvasena*). Furthermore, those [feelings] which arise from eye-contact at the conclusion of all the twenty-fourfold sets and so forth—

"Feeling... pe ... feeling born of mind-contact"—thus six kinds of feeling have been stated; these are stated by way of the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*). This is the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*).

The aggregates of perception (*saññā-khandha*) and the others should also be understood by this same method. For, in the exposition of the aggregate of perception, among the triads (*tike*), [the following applies]:
The triplets and dyads are also obtainable here, as are the dyads such as those accompanied by pleasure among the dyads.

In the exposition of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), because contact (*phassa*) is also included within the aggregate of mental formations, it is stated as "associated with consciousness" (*cittasampayutta*) rather than "associated with contact.

Among the dyads here, the dyads of causes (*hetuduka*) and so forth are also obtainable. The triplets are exactly like those in the exposition of the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*). In the exposition of the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*)...
Without specifying the state of being "born of eye-contact" and so forth, it is stated as "eye-consciousness" and so on. For it is not possible to designate consciousness as "born of mind-contact.
The rest here is exactly the same as what was stated regarding the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*).
However, from the very exposition of these three aggregates, the triads and dyads that exceed those in the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*) are obtained. Of these:
The classification by way of turns should be understood accordingly.
This concludes the commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*. 3.
Commentary on the *Pañhā-pucchaka* (Question-and-Answer Section).

150. Now follows the section on the interrogation of questions (*pañhāpucchaka*). In that section on the interrogation of questions, having asked everything—both what is applicable and what is not applicable—regarding the five aggregates by way of such questions as, "How many are wholesome? How many are unwholesome?
How many are indeterminate?", then, in the response, only that which is applicable is set forth by way of such statements as, "The aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) is indeterminate."

This should be understood. And wherever a definition is not made as "one aggregate" or "two aggregates," but the tradition (tanti) is established in such a manner as "it may have arisen, it may be unarisen," and so forth, there the inclusion of all five aggregates should be understood.
The remaining analysis of those respective aggregates—whether wholesome and so on—is [as explained] below.
This has indeed been stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, among the triplets of objects (*ārammaṇattika*), the four aggregates are "limited-objects" (*parittārammaṇā*) for one who is lustful,
hateful, deluded, restrained, comprehending, or reviewing with respect to the fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*).

There are twenty-seven [types of consciousness] that have sublime objects (mahaggatārammaṇa) when they take as their object the fine-material and immaterial-sphere phenomena while being lustful, hating, deluded, restraining, or establishing a mental grasp;
they have immeasurable objects (appamāṇārammaṇa) when reviewing the path, fruition, and Nibbāna;
and they have indeterminate objects (navattabbārammaṇa) at the time of reviewing a concept (paññatti).
These same [mental factors] are object-dominant (ārammaṇādhipati) for those in training (sekkha) and those beyond training (asekkha) at the time of reviewing the path;

they are path-rooted (maggahetuka) during the time of the path by way of the co-nascent root (sahajātahetu); they are path-dominant (maggādhipati) at the time of reviewing by esteeming the path through objective dominance (ārammaṇādhipati);
and for one developing the path where either energy or investigation is predominant, they are path-dominant by way of co-nascent dominance (sahajātādhipati).
However, for one who develops [the meditation] with desire as the primary factor or consciousness as the primary factor, the objects are said to be "indeterminate.
But for one who, with respect to past aggregates, elements, and bases, feels lust, feels aversion, is deluded, exercises restraint, or establishes a sense of ownership, they have past objects;
for one who does so with respect to future ones, they have future objects.
Taking present phenomena as their object, they have a present object; however, for one who contemplates a concept (*paññatti*) or Nibbāna, they have an indeterminate object.

Likewise, for one who is lustful, hateful, deluded, or exercising restraint toward one's own aggregates, elements, and bases (*khandha-dhātu-āyatana*), [the consciousnesses] have those as their objects.
For one who establishes [the mind] upon a personal acquisition, they have an internal object;

for one who proceeds by taking the aggregates, elements, and bases of others as the object, they have an external object; even at the time of reviewing designations and Nibbāna, they have an external object;
and for one who proceeds thus among phenomena sometimes internally and sometimes externally, they have both internal and external objects.
At the time of the base of nothingness, they should be understood as having an indeterminate object.
Thus the Blessed One, having extracted this Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga) by way of the three turnings beginning with the Suttanta-bhājaniya, displayed it by dividing it.
For in all three turnings, there is only one delimitation; for the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is present everywhere.
It belongs exclusively to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). The four aggregates belonging to the four planes, comprising a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane, have been explained.
Thus ends the commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) within the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga of the *Sammohavinodanī*.
2. Analysis of the Bases (Āyatanavibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 154.

Now, in the exposition of the analysis of the bases that follows immediately after this, the author first presents the exposition according to the discourses (*suttantabhājanīya*), saying: "The twelve bases: the eye-base, the form-base," and so forth. Regarding this, first, by way of a method independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka-naya*):
The exposition should be understood by way of its eight characteristics, its concise and detailed summaries, and likewise by way of how it is to be seen.
Therein, specifically: it "sees" (*cakkhati*), thus it is the "eye" (*cakkhu*); the meaning is that it relishes and discerns visible form (*rūpa*). It "forms" (*rūpayati*)...
"Rūpa" means that which undergoes transformation of color; the meaning is that it manifests a state present within the heart.
"Sota" means it hears. "Sadda" means it resounds; the meaning is that it is uttered. "Ghāna" means it smells.
"Gandha" means it causes fragrance; the meaning is that it indicates its own basis. "Jivhā" means it summons life. "Rasa" means that beings take delight in it; [the root] "ras" means they enjoy it.

Meaning: A "body" (*kāya*) is the accumulation (*āya*) of despicable, tainted phenomena (*sāsava-dhamma*). "Accumulation" (*āya*) refers to the locus of arising. That which is touched is the "tangible" (*phoṭṭhabba*).
It is called "mind" (*mano*) because it cognizes (*manati*). They are called "phenomena" (*dhammā*) because they bear their own characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).

Furthermore, in general, it should be understood as a "base" (*āyatana*) because it is a source of arrival (*āyana*), because it extends the arrivals (*āyāna-tanana*), and because it leads (*nayana*) that which has arrived (*āyata*).

For, in relation to the eye, visible forms, and so forth, it is said that the mental states (citta) and mental concomitants (cetasika), by means of their respective functions such as experiencing, "extend toward" (āyanti), "arise," or "exert themselves" (ghaṭṭenti vāyamanti).

And it is further said that these [bases] "stretch out" or "expand" (tanonti vitthārenti) those states which have become the source (āya). This [process] has been occurring throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
The suffering of saṃsāra is exceedingly long; as long as it does not cease, [the faculties] lead one on, which is to say they cause it to proceed.

Thus, all my phenomena (dhammas) are called "āyatana, āyatana" because of their being a source of arrival (āyatanato), because of their stretching out (āyānaṃ tananato), and because of their leading that which is long (āyatassa ca nayanato).
Furthermore, *āyatana* should be understood in the sense of a place of residence, a source, a meeting place, a place of birth, and a cause.
For instance, in common usage, in expressions such as "the abode of Īśvara" (*issarāyatana*) or "the abode of Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāyatana*), the term *āyatana* refers to a place of residence.
In expressions such as "a mine of gold" (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) or "a mine of silver" (*rajatāyatana*), it refers to a source. In the Teaching (*sāsana*), [it is used in these senses].
However, in such passages as “Birds frequent that delightful abode,” it means a place of gathering.

In such passages as “The southern region is the abode of cattle,” it means a place of origin. In such passages as “In each and every case, he attains the state of being a witness whenever there is a suitable occasion,” it means a cause.

Furthermore, because those various states of consciousness and mental factors dwell within the eye, visible forms, and so forth—since their existence is dependent upon them—the eye and the rest are their "dwelling place" (*nivāsanaṭṭhāna*).
And because they are crowded within the eye and the rest, owing to their dependence upon them and their taking them as objects, the eye and the rest are their "mine" (*ākaro*).
Moreover, the eye and the rest are their "convergence place" (*samosaraṇaṭṭhāna*), by way of being the basis, the door, and the object in their respective instances.
By way of convergence. The eye and so forth are their place of birth, because they arise right there by virtue of having those as their support and object.
The eye and so forth are also their cause, because in their absence [the consciousnesses] are absent.
Thus, by these reasons—namely, in the sense of a dwelling place, in the sense of a mine, in the sense of a place of convergence, in the sense of a place of birth, and in the sense of a cause—...
These phenomena are called "base, base. Therefore, in the sense already stated, because it is both the eye and a base, it is the "eye-base" (cakkhāyatana);
... pe ... because they are both mental objects and a base, it is the "mental-object-base" (dhammāyatana). Thus, first of all, the analysis here should be understood "by way of meaning" (atthato).

‘By characteristic’: here the exposition should be understood by way of the characteristics of the eye and so forth. And those characteristics of theirs are to be known according to the method already stated below in the Exposition of the Aggregate of Matter (Rūpakaṇḍa-niddesa).
‘By their number’: this means by way of their state as such. This is what is meant: the eye and the other factors are indeed just *dhammas*.

If that is so, why are twelve bases (*āyatanas*) mentioned instead of simply saying “the base of mental objects” (*dhammāyatana*)? Because of the defining of the doors, objects, and the arising of the six groups of consciousness.
Here, because they are defined by way of being the doors and the objects for the six groups of consciousness, this alone constitutes their distinction;

thus, twelve are mentioned. For the group of consciousness comprised within the cognitive process of eye-consciousness, the eye-base alone is the door of its arising, and the visible-object-base alone is its object.
Likewise, the others [are the doors and objects] for the remaining [groups of consciousness].

However, for the sixth [consciousness], only a portion of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) known as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is the door of arising, and the uncommon object-base (*dhammāyatana*) is the object.
Thus, because the doors of arising and the objects of the six groups of consciousness have been defined, twelve [bases] are stated.
In this way, the analysis should be understood here "by way of number."

Regarding the phrase “in order of preference” (*kamato*): here too, among the sequences previously mentioned—such as the sequence of arising and so forth—it is the sequence of teaching that is appropriate.
For among the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*), the eye-base is taught first because its object is visible and impinging, making it the most manifest.

Following that are the ear-base and the others, whose objects are invisible yet impinging. Alternatively, [they are ordered] by way of their being the causes for the unsurpassed vision and the unsurpassed hearing.
Because they are of great service, among the internal bases, the eye-base and the ear-base are taught first;
after them, the three beginning with the nose-base. Because it is the objective domain for all five, the mind-base is placed at the end.

Because they are the objective domains of the eye and so forth, the external bases beginning with the visible-form base are taught immediately after their respective [internal] counterparts. Furthermore, this is also due to the determination of the causes for the arising of consciousness.
This very sequence should be understood for them. For it has been said: “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises... pe...
dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. Thus, the exposition here should be understood “by way of sequence.

Regarding “in brief and in detail”: in brief, because the mind base (*manāyatana*) and a portion of the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) are comprised by the term “name,” while the remaining bases are comprised by the term “form,” all twelve bases are merely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
In detail, first among the internal bases, the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) consists merely of the sensitivity of the eye by way of its genus;
however, it has infinite subdivisions according to the distinctions of conditions, destiny, category, and individual. The same applies to the four bases beginning with the ear-base.

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) has eighty-one subdivisions according to the distinctions of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness belonging to the three planes, as well as according to the distinctions of physical basis, path of progress, and so forth.
However, they are of infinite variety. The bases of visible form, odor, and flavor are each fourfold according to their mode of origination; the base of sound is twofold.
Furthermore, all of them are of infinite variety according to the distinction between homogeneous and heterogeneous.

The base of tangible objects is threefold by way of the earth element, fire element, and air element; it is fourfold by way of its mode of origination, and [furthermore] twofold by way of the homogeneous and heterogeneous.
It has many divisions. The sense base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) has many divisions by way of having as its object the phenomena belonging to the three planes.
Thus the exposition should be understood both in brief and in detail.
Regarding the phrase "as to how they are to be seen": all these sense bases are to be seen as neither coming nor going.
For these do not come from anywhere prior to their arising, nor do they go anywhere after their passing away.
Rather, prior to their arising, they have not yet acquired their own nature; after their passing away, their nature has been dissolved.
In the interval between the past and the future, they proceed dependent on conditions, lacking any autonomy. Therefore, they should be viewed as neither coming nor going.
Likewise, it is because they are effortless and inactive. For it does not occur to the eye, visible forms, and so forth:
"O, may consciousness indeed arise through our combination! Nor do they strive for the purpose of producing consciousness by acting as a door, as a basis, or as an object;
nor do they engage in any exertion. Rather, this is simply the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
Since eye-consciousness and the rest arise from the coming together of the eye, visible forms, and so forth, they should therefore be regarded as inactive and devoid of effort.
Furthermore, the internal bases should be regarded as like an empty village because they are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and a self;
while the external bases should be regarded as like thieves who plunder that village because they strike down the internal bases. For this has been said: "The eye..."

“Monks, one is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms,” and so on in detail. Furthermore, the internal [bases] should be regarded as like six creatures, and the external [bases] as their respective domains.
In this way, the exposition should be understood here “by way of being regarded.
Now, in order to show the manner in which they are to be seen with insight (vipassanā), the passage beginning with “the eye is impermanent” is commenced. Therein, the eye...
Having existed thus, it should be understood as impermanent in the sense of non-existence. It is also impermanent for four other reasons:
because it possesses arising and passing away, because it is subject to change, because it is temporary, and because it is the opposite of the permanent.
That very same thing is suffering in the sense of oppression; or rather, because this [formation], having arisen, reaches a state of stability, and during that stability...
It is worn out by aging, and having reached old age, it inevitably breaks up;

therefore, because of these four reasons—because it is constantly oppressed, because it is painful, because it is the basis of suffering, and because it is the opposite of happiness—it is suffering (*dukkha*).
Furthermore, it is non-self (*anattā*) in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery. Or else, because this [body], once arisen, does not attain stability, and having attained stability...
In these three respects—“may it not grow old,” “may it not be subject to decay,” and “may it not break up”—there is no state of mastery for anyone;

it is empty of that mode of mastery. Therefore, it is non-self (anattā) by virtue of these four reasons: being empty, being ownerless, being incapable of acting according to one's will, and being the negation of a self.

It is subject to change because it goes toward a state of non-existence, because it proceeds to the transition from one existence to another in its prior and subsequent phases, and because it abandons its original nature;
this is indeed a synonym for impermanence. This same method applies to such passages as "forms are impermanent" and so forth.
Furthermore, in this context, with the exception of the eye, the phenomena of the three planes are impermanent, but not the eye itself; the eye, however, is both the eye and impermanent.
Likewise, the remaining phenomena are suffering, but they are not the eye. The eye, however, is both the eye and suffering.
The remaining phenomena are non-self, but they are not the eye. The eye, however, is both the eye and non-self. This same method applies to form and the other [objects] as well.
But what has been shown by the Tathāgata in this Suttanta-bhājaniya? It is the twelve bases (āyatana).

The characteristic of non-self. For when the Perfectly Enlightened One demonstrates the characteristic of non-self, he does so either by way of impermanence, or by way of suffering, or by way of both impermanence and suffering. In this regard: "If one were to say, 'The eye is self,' that is not tenable.
For the arising and the passing away of the eye are discerned. But for that which its arising and passing away are discerned, [it is] 'self'..."
‘It arises in me and passes away in me’—thus it occurs to him. Therefore, that [position] does not hold:
one who would say ‘the eye is self’ is incorrect; thus, the eye is non-self. In this sutta, he demonstrated the characteristic of non-self by means of impermanence:
“Form, bhikkhus, is non-self. For if form, bhikkhus, were self, then this form would not be subject to affliction...”
“It would lead to affliction; and one could obtain regarding form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.
But because, monks, form is non-self, therefore form leads to affliction; and one cannot obtain regarding form:
‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus. In this sutta, the characteristic of non-self is established by means of suffering.
He showed it thus: “Bhikkhus, form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self;
what is non-self is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self. In such passages as these, he showed the characteristic of non-self by means of impermanence and suffering.
Why? Because impermanence and suffering are manifest.
For when a bowl or a cup, or anything at all, falls from the hand and breaks, people say, "Oh, how impermanent!
In this way, impermanence is said to be manifest. But when boils, pustules, and the like arise upon the body, or when one is pierced by stumps, thorns, and the like, people say, "Oh, how painful!
In this way, suffering is said to be manifest. However, the characteristic of non-self is not manifest.
It is darkness, unmanifest, difficult to penetrate, difficult to illuminate, and difficult to establish.
The characteristics of impermanence and suffering are discerned whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise. However, the characteristic of non-self is not discerned without the arising of a Buddha;
it is discerned only when a Buddha arises. For those ascetics and wanderers possess great psychic power and great majesty.
Even teachers such as Sarabhaṅga were able to say, "It is impermanent, it is suffering," but they were not able to say, "It is non-self.
For if they had been able to declare "non-self" to an assembled assembly, there would have been a penetration of the Path and its Fruits by that assembled assembly.
Indeed, the proclamation of the characteristic of non-self is not within the domain of anyone else.
This is the domain of the omniscient Buddhas alone. Thus, this characteristic of non-self is not manifest.

Therefore, when the Teacher demonstrates the characteristic of non-self, he does so either by way of impermanence, or by way of suffering, or by way of both impermanence and suffering. Here, however, it should be understood that he demonstrates it by way of both impermanence and suffering.
But for what reason, through non-attention to what, through non-penetration of what, and because of being concealed by what, do these characteristics not appear?
First, the characteristic of impermanence does not appear due to non-attention to and non-penetration of arising and passing away, and because it is concealed by continuity.
The characteristic of suffering does not appear due to non-attention to and non-penetration of constant oppression, and because of the [concealment by] postures.
Because it is concealed, the characteristic of non-self does not appear;
because of a lack of attention to and a failure to penetrate the analysis of the various elements, and because it is concealed by its compactness, it does not appear.

However, having discerned arising and passing away, when the continuity is disrupted, the characteristic of impermanence appears according to its true nature. [The characteristic of] constant oppression...
Having brought this to mind, when the postures have been analyzed, the characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa) becomes manifest according to its actual nature.
Having resolved the various elements (nānādhātuyo), once the resolution of the compact has been made, the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) becomes manifest according to its actual nature.

And herein, the impermanent is the characteristic of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa), the painful is the characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa), and the non-self is the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa).
This distinction should be understood. Therein, "impermanent" refers to the pentad of aggregates. Why?

Because of their nature of arising, passing away, and change, or because of their non-existence after having existed; for arising, passing away, and change are the characteristic of impermanence, or it is the transformation of state characterized by non-existence after having existed.
Furthermore, according to the statement, "That which is impermanent is suffering," that same pentad of aggregates is suffering. Why?
Because it is constantly oppressed, the mode of being constantly oppressed is the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha*).
