Furthermore, because of the statement, "That which is suffering is non-self," that same pentad of aggregates is non-self. Why? Because it does not exercise mastery; the mode of not exercising mastery is the characteristic of non-self (*anatta*).
Thus, impermanence, suffering, and non-self are distinct things, and the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self are likewise distinct.
The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements—all this is indeed called impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
The aforementioned modes and transformations are the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

In brief, it should be understood that here the ten bases belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two belong to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*). It should also be known that the practice of comprehension (*sammasana*) has been explained for all of them.
Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya. 155.
In the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, just as previously for the benefit of those practicing insight (vipassaka), it was stated: "The eye-base is the form-base," and so forth.

The sense bases were previously mentioned in pairs; however, they are here stated by way of defining the internal and external bases—namely, as "the eye base, the ear base," and so on—in order to show their essential nature (sabhāva) in all its aspects.
In the section explaining them, the definitions beginning with "What is the eye base? and so forth, should be understood according to the method already explained above.

167. As for that which was stated in the exposition of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), namely: "In this context, what is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*)? It is the destruction of lust (*rāga*), the destruction of hatred (*dosa*), and the destruction of delusion (*moha*)," the meaning here is as follows:
"The unconditioned element" refers to Nibbāna, whose intrinsic nature is unconditioned.
Because lust and the other defilements are destroyed by coming to rely upon it, it is therefore called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
Thus it was said. This is the teachers’ concordant explanation on this point.
However, the caviller says: "There is no such thing as Nibbāna separate [from defilements]; the destruction of the defilements alone is Nibbāna.
When told, "Bring a sutta," he says: "'Nibbāna, Nibbāna,' friend Sāriputta, is what is said; which [is that Nibbāna]?"
“Is it then, friend, that Nibbāna exists? “Friend, that which is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this is called Nibbāna.
Having cited this Jambukhādaka Sutta, he says: “By this sutta it should be understood that there is no such thing as a separate Nibbāna;

rather, the destruction of the defilements (*kilesakkhaya*) itself is Nibbāna. He should be asked: “But how [is it that...]?”* *Note: The sentence fragment ending with "yathā" indicates the original text was cut off.*
“Is this the sutta and such its meaning? He will certainly say, “Yes, there is no meaning apart from the sutta.
Then he should be told: “This sutta has been brought by you; now bring the next sutta. The next sutta is as follows:
“‘Arahatship, Arahatship,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said. What, friend, is Arahatship?”
"Friends, that which is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this is called Arahantship.
This is the sutta cited immediately following that [passage].
But when this was cited, they said: "Nibbāna is a phenomenon included within the sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana); Arahantship..."

There are four aggregates. Even when the Dhamma-Senāpati, dwelling having realized Nibbāna, was asked about Nibbāna or asked about Arahantship, he spoke only of the destruction of the defilements (kilesakkhaya). [The questioner asks: "But are Nibbāna and Arahantship one, or are they different? [The reply is:
"Whether they be one or whether they be different—what is the point of your making such excessive mincemeat of this matter?"
“You do not know even a single thing,” he was told. “Is it not good to know? When questioned thus again and again, unable to evade him, he said:
“Because it arises at the end of the destruction of lust and so forth, Arahantship is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
Then they said to him: “A great deed you have done! Even one who speaks by giving a bribe would say this very same thing.”
He might cause it to be said: "Just as you have explained this by way of analysis, so too should you understand this:
for it is by coming to Nibbāna that lust and the other defilements are exhausted; thus Nibbāna is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
Indeed, all three of these are synonyms for Nibbāna itself."
If, when this is said, he complies, that is well. If not, he should be made to act through the principle of "many extinctions.
How so? He should first be asked thus: "Is what is called the destruction of lust the destruction of lust alone, or of hatred and delusion as well?
Is what is called the destruction of hatred the destruction of hatred alone, or of lust and delusion as well? Is what is called the destruction of delusion the destruction of delusion alone..."
Or rather, [is it] also the destruction of lust and hatred? He will certainly say: “The destruction of lust is indeed the destruction of lust alone;
the destruction of hatred is indeed the destruction of hatred alone; the destruction of delusion is indeed the destruction of delusion alone.
Then he should be told: “In your doctrine, the destruction of lust is one Nibbāna, the destruction of hatred is another, and the destruction of delusion is yet another.”
One; with the destruction of the three unwholesome roots, there are three *nibbānas*;
with the destruction of the four clingings, four; with the destruction of the five hindrances, five; with the destruction of the six classes of craving, six;
with the destruction of the seven underlying tendencies, seven; with the destruction of the eight wrongnesses, eight; [and with the destruction] of the nine states rooted in craving...

If one were to take it thus—that there are nine [Nibbānas] at the destruction of the nine fetters, ten at the destruction of the ten fetters, and a distinct Nibbāna for each of the destruction of the fifteen hundred defilements—then there would be many Nibbānas. However, there is no such measure of Nibbānas.
Rather, not grasping it in that way, but taking it as "having come to Nibbāna, lust and the rest are destroyed," there is only a single Nibbāna, which is the destruction of lust (*rāgakkhaya*).
“The destruction of hatred and the destruction of delusion are also spoken of; take it that these three are likewise designations for Nibbāna itself.
But if, even when this is said, he does not comprehend, he should be dealt with by means of the gross method. How so?
“For even blind fools, such as the bear, the deer, the monkey, and others, indulge in sexual intercourse while overwhelmed by the defilements. Now, as for them...”
Defilement is pacified at the limit of its experience. According to your doctrine, creatures such as the chaddīpi fish, deer, and monkeys would be said to have attained Nibbāna.
Indeed, your Nibbāna is coarse and gross; it could not even be worn as an ornament on the ears!

However, without grasping it in that way, one says that by resorting to Nibbāna, lust and the other defilements are exhausted; thus, Nibbāna is one alone: the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
‘It is called the destruction of delusion. You should understand that all three of these are synonyms for Nibbāna itself.
But if, even when this is said, he does not grasp it, he should be made to realize it by means of the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu). How? First, he should be asked thus:
‘Do you say that there is such a thing as change-of-lineage? ‘Yes, I say so. ‘At the moment of change-of-lineage...’
‘Have the defilements been destroyed, are they being destroyed, or will they be destroyed? ‘They have not been destroyed, nor are they being destroyed; however, they will be destroyed.
‘But what is the object of the lineage-change (gotrabhu)? ‘Nibbāna. ‘At the moment of your lineage-change, the defilements have not been destroyed, nor are they being destroyed;
rather, they will be destroyed. While the defilements are still undestroyed, you [claim] the destruction of defilements.’
He described Nibbāna as the abandoning of latent tendencies while those latent tendencies have not yet been abandoned. That does not accord with your view.
Rather, without grasping it in that way, one should understand that by resorting to Nibbāna, lust and the other defilements are exhausted;

thus, the single Nibbāna is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. Take it, then, that all three of these are merely designations for Nibbāna itself.
But if, even when this has been said, he does not perceive it, he should be made to act according to the path. How so? First, he should be asked thus:
“Do you say there is such a thing as a ‘path’? “Yes, I do. “At the moment of the path, are the defilements already exhausted, are they being exhausted, or will they be exhausted?
Knowing [the answer], he will say: “It is not permissible to say that they are exhausted, nor that they will be exhausted.”
"It is appropriate to say that they 'come to an end. "If that is so, what is the extinction of defilements (kilesakkhaya) as Nibbāna for the Path?
Which are the defilements to be extinguished by the Path? What is the Path? Having taken what extinction of defilements as its object (ārammaṇa), which defilements does the Path extinguish?
Therefore, do not hold such a view. Rather, it is by coming to Nibbāna that lust and the other defilements are extinguished."
“Nirvana is indeed one; it is called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. All three of these are merely designations for Nirvana itself.
When this was said, he replied: “Do you say ‘having come,’ having come? “Yes, I say so.
“From where did you obtain this term ‘having come’? “I obtained it from the Suttas. “Produce the Sutta. [He recited: “Thus ignorance and craving...”
"And having come to that, they are exhausted in it, shattered in it, and never again anything at all.
When this was said, the opponent fell silent.

Here too, it should be understood that ten of the sense-bases belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two belong to the four planes of existence and are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā). 3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā) 168.
Here too, in the Section of Questions, having asked about everything—both that which is applicable and that which is not—the [explanation] proceeds solely by way of what is applicable.
The answer has been stated; and not only here, but this same method applies to all the question-and-answer sections.
Here, however, it should be understood that the ten bases (āyatana) are indeterminate (abyākata) by virtue of their being material form (rūpa).

The status of the two bases as wholesome and so forth should be understood in the same way as the four aggregates (khandha) are explained in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*. For indeed, the four aggregates are exclusively conditioned (sappaccaya).
Furthermore, regarding the dhammāyatana, it is stated that "it may be without a cause (appaccaya) and may be unconditioned (asaṅkhata).

Among the triads concerning objects, the dhammāyatana—consisting of subtle matter which is without an object—belongs to the category of the "inexpressible" (na-vattabba). However, this is so because it lacks an object;
it is not inexpressible by way of being an object for states that are themselves inexpressible as limited (paritta) and so forth. This is the distinction here.

The rest is exactly the same. For here too, just as in the case of the four aggregates, the two bases have limited objects for one who is lustful, hateful, deluded, restrained, comprehending, or reviewing with respect to the fifty-five states of the sense-sphere;
thus everything is exactly as described in the section on the aggregates.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Bases (*Āyatanavibhaṅga*) in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, is completed. 3.
The Analysis of the Elements (*Dhātuvibhaṅga*).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta-Bhājaniya 172.

Now, immediately following that, in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*, he states "the six elements" and so forth, presenting the Suttanta-Bhājaniya by condensing all elements into three sets of six through six elements each. Therein, "six" is the delimitation by number.

“Elements” (*dhātu*) is a designation for delimited phenomena. In such terms as “earth element” (*pathavīdhātu*), the meaning of “element” (*dhātvaṭṭha*) is the meaning of “intrinsic nature” (*sabhāvaṭṭha*);
the meaning of “intrinsic nature” is the meaning of “emptiness” (*suññataṭṭha*); and the meaning of “emptiness” is the meaning of “insubstantiality” (*nissattaṭṭha*).

Thus, by way of being intrinsic nature, emptiness, and insubstantiality, earth itself is an element; hence it is the “earth element. The same method applies to the water element and the others. Such is the word-analysis here.
Having understood this, the meaning should be known as follows: the earth element is the element of support; the water element is the element of cohesion;
the fire element is the element of maturation; the air element is the element of distension; the space element is the element of non-obstruction;
and the consciousness element is the element of cognition.
173. "The two earth elements": this refers to the two earth elements. The meaning is that what is called the earth element is not just one;
rather, there are two elements due to the distinction between the internal and the external. For this very reason, it is said: "There is the internal, and there is the external.
In this context, "internal" means those included within the continuity of a living being (*sattasantāna*), pertaining to one's own internal self. "External" means...

Included within the continuity of formations (*saṅkhāra-santāna*), they are not bound by the sense faculties (*anindriya-baddha*). "Internally" and "individually" (*paccattaṃ*)—both of these are merely designations for one's own internal self (*niyaka-ajjhatta*).
Now, in order to show that [the earth element] according to its specific nature and mode, the words beginning with "hard" (*kakkhaḷa*) are stated.

Therein, "hard" (*kakkhaḷa*) means stiff. "Roughness" (*kharigata*) means harsh. "Hardness" (*kakkhaḷatta*) is the state of being hard. "The state of being hard" (*kakkhaḷabhāva*) is the essential nature of hardness.

“Internally acquired” (*ajjhattaṃ upādinnaṃ*) means that which is acquired within what is reckoned as one’s own internal [self]. That which is called “acquired” (*upādinnaṃ*) refers to the group of eight things belonging to the body.
For although the group of eight things belonging to the body may be either produced by kamma or not, with reference to it there exists both the acquired and the unacquired;
however, in order to show that all of this is indeed “acquired” in the sense of being taken up, grasped, and clung to, he said: “internally acquired.”
Now, in order to show that very same earth element by way of its physical bases, it is said: "That is to say: head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth.
In this context, *seyyathidaṃ* is a particle. Its meaning is: "What is that internal earth element?
Or rather, what is that which is called 'hardness' within oneself? "Head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth, [is the answer] to that internal [earth element].
This is the demonstration of the classification of the earth element by way of its physical basis (*vatthu*). This is what is meant:
"Head-hairs" refers to that which is internal, clung-to (*upādinnā*), residing in the body, characterized by hardness, and is a distinct portion within this body. "Body-hairs" refers to...
[and so on] ... "excrement" refers to... Furthermore, although not mentioned here, the brain (*matthaluṅga*) is included in the text of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.
Having brought it forth: that which is called "brain" (*matthaluṅga*) is an internal, clung-to (appropriated) constituent of the body, characterized by hardness;
it is a distinct part within this body. The same method applies hereafter for the description of the water element (*āpodhātu*) and so on, as well as for bile (*pitta*) and the rest.
What is demonstrated by this? It is the attention to elements (*dhātumanasikāra*). Having performed the work of attention to the elements in this way, however—
What must be done by one who, having established insight (*vipassanā*), desires to reach the supreme goal of Arahantship?
The fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) must be cleansed. For the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā*) succeeds for one who possesses virtue.

The method for its cleansing should be understood according to the system explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. However, having established oneself in virtue with purified virtue, [one should abandon] the ten prior impediments (*pubbapalibodha*).
These must be severed. The method for severing them should be understood according to the same system explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Once the hindrances have been severed, the meditation subject of attention to the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) should be learned.
The teacher, when instructing the student in the meditation subject of attention to the elements, should explain the seven kinds of skill in learning and the ten kinds of skill in attention.
The resident pupil, too, having recited the text many times in the presence of his teacher, should make the meditation subject free from tangles and well-mastered.
For this is said in the Commentary: "A beginner monk who desires to be liberated from aging and death should seek skill in learning in seven ways, and he should seek skill in attention in ten ways."

In this meditation subject of attention to elements, "skill in learning" should be sought in these seven ways: by way of verbal expression, by way of mind, by way of color, by way of shape, by way of direction, by way of location, and by way of delimitation.
Furthermore, it should be practiced by way of successive order, not too quickly, not too slowly, warding off distraction, transcending the conventional designation, and gradual relinquishing.
Skill in attention should be sought through these ten aspects: by way of characteristic and the three types of discourses.
Both of these will be made clear later in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga*.
However, one who has thus mastered the meditation subject should avoid the eighteen faults of lodgings as described in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Dwelling in a lodging endowed with the five factors, one who is himself endowed with the five factors conducive to striving should,
after returning from the alms round following the meal, go to a secluded place and attend to the meditation subject. And while attending to it,
one should [analyze] each individual part among the head-hairs and so forth by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.
Having brought this to mind, at the conclusion one should apply attention in this way: "These things called head-hairs are born on the skin that envelops the skull.

In this regard, just as when tufts of grass grow on the top of an anthill, the top of the anthill does not know, 'Tufts of grass are growing on me,' nor do the tufts of grass know, 'We are growing on the top of an anthill.'"
In the same way, the skin enveloping the skull does not know, "Hair has grown upon me," nor do the hairs know, "We have grown upon the skin enveloping the skull.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, what is called "hair" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, and soulless.
The earth element is rigid.

Hairs grow on the skin that envelops the body. In this regard, just as when *dabba* grass grows in the site of an empty village, the site of the empty village does not know, "The *dabba* grass has grown upon me," nor do the *dabba* grasses know, "We [have grown here]."

Just as hair grows in an empty village, so too the skin that envelops the body does not know, "Hair has grown on me," nor do the hairs know, "We have grown on the skin that envelops the body. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, what is called "hair" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
“Insentient and rigid is the earth element.
The nails are those grown on the tips of the fingers. In this regard, it is just as when children play by piercing madhuka-wood sticks with sticks;
there, the sticks do not know, “Madhuka-wood sticks have been placed upon us,” nor do the madhuka-wood sticks [know the same].

Just as they do not know, "We have been placed upon the fingers," even so the fingers do not know, "Nails have grown on our tips," nor do the nails know, "We have grown on the tips of the fingers. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intention or reflection.
Thus, what is called "nails" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
The earth element is insentient and rigid.

The teeth grow upon the jawbones. In this regard, just as when pillars are set up by carpenters on stone mortars after being bound together with some kind of cement, the mortars do not know, "Pillars are standing upon us," nor do [the pillars know, "We are standing on mortars"].

Just as pillars do not know, "We are standing on mortars," even so the jawbones do not know, "Teeth have grown upon us," nor do the teeth know, "We have grown upon jawbones. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, what are called "teeth" are a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
The earth element is insentient and rigid.

The skin stands enveloping the entire body. In this regard, just as a great lute covered with moist ox-hide does not know, "I am covered with moist ox-hide," nor does the moist ox-hide [know the same].

Just as one knows, "The great lute has been covered with skin," even so the body does not know, "I am covered with skin," nor does the skin know, "The body is covered by me. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "skin" is a distinct component within this body, insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
The earth element is insentient and rigid.

It remains coating the mass of flesh and bones. In this regard, just as when a wall is plastered with thick clay, the wall does not know, "I am plastered with thick clay," nor does the thick clay know, "By me, a great wall..."

"Besmeared": in the same way, the skeletal frame does not know, "I am besmeared by flesh divided into nine hundred pieces," nor does the flesh know, "The skeletal frame is besmeared by me. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, what is called "flesh" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
The earth element is insentient and rigid.
The sinews remain binding the bones within the body.
In this regard, just as when wooden posts of a wall are bound together by creepers, the wooden posts do not know, "We are bound by creepers," nor do the creepers know [the same].

"Just as we do not know, 'The rafters have been bound together by us,' so too the bones do not know, 'We are bound together by the sinews,' nor do the sinews know, 'The bones are bound together by us. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, that which is called 'sinew' is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty."
"Lifeless and rigid, it is the earth element.
Among the bones, the heel bone stands supporting the ankle bone; the ankle bone stands supporting the shin bone;
the shin bone stands supporting the thigh bone; and the thigh bone stands supporting the hip bone.
The hip bone stands supporting the backbone; the backbone stands supporting the neck bone;
the neck bone stands supporting the head bone. The head bone is established upon the neck bone; the neck bone is established upon the backbone;
the backbone is established upon the hip bone; and the hip bone is established upon the thigh bone.
The thigh bone is supported by the shin bones; the shin bone is supported by the ankle bones;
the ankle bone is supported by the heel bone.
In this regard, just as in a pile of bricks, wood, cow dung, and so forth, the lowermost layers do not know, "We are supporting those above us."
nor do those above know, "We are supported by those below us.
In the same way, the heel-bone does not know, "I am standing having lifted up the ankle-bone," nor does the ankle-bone know,
"I am standing having lifted up the shin-bone," nor does the shin-bone know [the same].
‘I stand having lifted up the thigh-bone,’ the thigh-bone does not know;
‘I stand having lifted up the hip-bone,’ the hip-bone does not know; ‘I stand having lifted up the backbone,’ the backbone does not know;
‘I stand having lifted up the neck-bone,’ the neck-bone does not know; ‘I stand having lifted up the head-bone,’ the head-bone does not know.
As for "standing": the skull bone does not know, "I am supported by the neck bone";
the neck bone does not know, "I am supported by the vertebrae"; the vertebrae do not know, "I am supported by the hip bone";
the hip bone does not know, "I am supported by the thigh bone"; the thigh bone does not know, "I am supported by the shin bone..."
As for "resting upon": the shin bone does not know, "I am resting upon the ankle bone," nor does the ankle bone know, "I am resting upon the heel bone.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality and reflection.
Thus, what is called "bone" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
"Insentient and rigid is the earth element.
Bone-marrow is that which resides within various bones.

In this regard, just as when bits of bamboo shoots and the like are inserted inside bamboo joints and so forth, the bamboo joints do not know, "Bits of bamboo shoots have been inserted into us," [so too with the body].
Nor do the tips of the bamboo shoots and so forth know, "We are situated upon the bamboo joints and such.
In the same way, the bones do not know, "Marrow is situated within us," nor does the marrow know, "I am situated within the bones.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus is that which is called marrow.
In this body, there is a distinct component that is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and called the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*).

The kidney is situated surrounding the heart-flesh, bound by a thick sinew that emerges from the throat, travels a short distance with a single root, and then divides into two. Therein, just as [a fruit] attached to its stalk...
Just as two mango fruits do not know, "The stalk has been attached to us," nor does the stalk know,
"I have been attached to these two mango fruits," even so, the thick sinew does not know, "The kidney has been bound to me," nor does the kidney know,
"I have been bound by the thick sinew. They are devoid of mutual intention or reflection.

These are the phenomena (*dhammā*). Thus, what is called the "kidney" (*vakkam*) is a distinct component within this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*).
The heart (*hadayam*) is situated inside the body, supported by the middle of the cage of the breast-bones. Therein, it is like the interior of an old chariot frame.

Just as a piece of meat placed within the frame of an old chariot does not know, "The piece of meat is placed supported by me," nor does the piece of meat know, "I am situated supported by the frame of an old chariot," even so,
the interior of the ribcage does not know, "The heart [is situated supported by me]..."
"Stationed": the heart does not know, "I am stationed supported by the interior of the cage of the breast-bones.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual awareness or reflection. Thus, that which is called the "heart" is a distinct component within this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
The liver is situated within the body on the right side between the two breasts. In that regard,
just as the sides of a mortar do not know, "A twin mass of flesh is attached to me," nor does the twin mass of flesh know, "I am attached to the sides of the mortar."

Just as one who is attached does not know that "the liver is situated within the breasts on my right side," nor does the liver know that "I am situated within the breasts on the right side," so too these phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus, what is called the liver in this body—
The separate portion that is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and called the earth element [is the skin].
Among the membranes, the concealed membrane lies surrounding the heart and the kidneys;
the unconcealed membrane lies beneath the outer skin, enveloping the flesh throughout the entire body. In this regard, it is as if wrapped in a cloth...
The flesh does not know, "I am wrapped in a membrane," nor does the membrane know,
"I have wrapped the flesh. In the same way, the kidneys, heart, and the flesh throughout the entire body do not know,
"I am covered by the *kilomaka* (spleen)," nor does the *kilomaka* know, "By me are the kidneys, heart, and the flesh throughout the entire body [covered]."
"And flesh that is concealed. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called *kilomaka* (the pleura) is a distinct constituent in this body: insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
*Pihaka* (the spleen) is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the upper side of the abdominal membrane. Therein—
Just as a lump of cow dung standing against the upper wall of a granary does not know,
"The lump of cow dung is standing supported by me," nor does the lump of cow dung know, "I am standing supported by the upper wall of the granary," even so,
the upper wall of the stomach does not know, "The spleen is supported by me..."
"Situated": the spleen does not know, "I am situated leaning against the upper side of the belly.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called the spleen is a distinct component in this body:
insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, solid, and the earth element.
The lungs are situated inside the body, hanging down between the two breasts, covering the heart and the liver above. In this regard, just as the interior of an old granary does not know,
"A bird's nest is hanging from me," nor does the bird's nest know, "I am hanging in an old granary."
Just as one does not know, "I am standing hanging inside an old granary," nor does the granary know,
"The lungs are hanging inside me," so too the body does not know, "The lungs are hanging within me," nor do the lungs know,
"I am hanging within such a body. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called "lungs" is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
The "intestines" (anta) reside within the interior of the body, from the gullet down to the opening of the rectum. Therein, just as in the case of a blood-bowl...
When a corpse has been laid down after being bent over, with its neck-vessels severed, the blood-filled bowl does not know,

"The corpse with its neck-vessels is situated within me," nor does the corpse with its neck-vessels know, "I am situated within the blood-filled bowl. In the same way, the interior of the body does not know,
"The intestines are situated within me," nor do the intestines know, "I am situated within the interior of the body."
"Situated": these phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "the bowel" (*anta*) is a distinct part within this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
The small intestine (*antaguṇa*) stands fast, binding together twenty-one coils of the large intestine. In that regard, it is like a circular rope used for wiping the feet.
When the cords have been sewn and remain so, the foot-wiping cloth does not know,
"The cords have sewn me and remain," nor do the cords know, "We have sewn the foot-wiping cloth and remain.
In the same way, the end does not know, "The cord of the end has bound me and remains," nor does the cord of the end know [the same].
‘I am standing having tied a knot. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called the “intestine” is a distinct component in this body: insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
The *udariya* (stomach contents) is that which remains in the stomach— the food, drink, chewed food, and tasted food. In this regard,
just as a dog’s trough does not know, “A dog’s vomit is situated in me,” nor does the dog’s vomit know,
“I am situated in a dog’s trough,” even so the stomach does not know, “Stomach contents are situated in me,” nor do the stomach contents [know].
One knows, "I am situated in the belly. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called "undigested food" (*udariya*) is a distinct component in this body: insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
Feces (*karīsa*) is situated at the end of the intestines, in what is known as the receptacle for digested food, resembling an eight-finger-breadth section of a bamboo joint. Therein—
Just as when fine yellow clay is pressed and placed inside a bamboo tube, the bamboo tube does not know,
"Yellow clay is situated within me," nor does the yellow clay know, "I am situated in a bamboo tube," even so, the receptacle of digested food does not know,
"Feces are situated within me," nor does the feces know, "I am situated in the receptacle of digested food."
"Stationed": these phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "feces" is a distinct component within this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
Brain matter is situated inside the skull. In that regard, it is like [the contents] placed inside an old gourd shell.
A gourd vessel does not know of the lump of dough, “The lump of dough is situated in me,” nor does the lump of dough know, “I am situated in the gourd vessel.
In the same way, the interior of the skull does not know, “The brain is situated in me,” nor does the brain know, “I am situated within the interior of the skull. Thus they are mutually [unaware].
These states are devoid of mental application and reflection. Thus, what is called "brain" is a distinct component in this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, rigid, and the earth element.
By the phrase "or whatever else," he shows that the earth element accompanying the three components beginning with water is included as a "concomitant earth" by way of its characteristic.

In the description of the external earth element: "iron" (*ayo*) refers to black iron. "Metal" (*loha*) is fourfold: metal of the same genus (*jātiloha*), metal of a different genus (*vijātiloha*), artificial metal (*kittimaloha*), and demon-metal (*pisācaloha*).

Among these, the seven types known as metal of the same genus are: iron (*ayo*), tin (*sajjhu*), gold (*suvaṇṇaṃ*), lead (*tipu*), zinc (*sīsaṃ*), copper (*tambalohaṃ*), and brass (*vekantaka*). Metal of a different genus is "elephant-nose metal. Bell-metal (*kaṃsalohaṃ*)...
Vatthaloha (round iron) and ārakūṭa are called the three artificial metals.
Morakkhaka, puthuka, malinaka, capalaka, selaka, āṭaka, bhallaka, and dūsiloha are called the eight pisāca-metals.
Among these, five are natural metals (jātiloha) that are mentioned separately in the Pāḷi. Tambaloha and vekantakaloha—by these [two], however...
Together with the two types of base metal (*jātiloha*), everything else here should be understood as "metal" (*loha*).
"Tin" (*tipu*) is white tin; "lead" (*sīsa*) is black tin; "silver" (*sajjhu*) is silver; "pearl" (*muttā*) is sea-pearl;

"gem" (*maṇi*) refers to all gems of the *jotirasa* variety and so forth, excluding those specifically mentioned in the text such as beryl (*veḷuriya*) and the rest. "Beryl" (*veḷuriya*) is a gem the color of bamboo.
*Saṅkha* means a sea-shell. *Sila* refers to all types of stone, such as black stone, yellow stone, white stone, and so forth.
*Pavāḷa* means coral itself. *Rajata* means a coin (*kahāpaṇa*). *Jātarūpa* means gold. *Lohitanka* means a red gem.
*Masāragalla* means a variegated gem. Regarding grass and the like, even coconuts and other such things that have no pith are considered "grass."
...is called "wood. Even a piece of wood, down to a mere fragment of timber, is called "wood.
"Gravel" refers to sand ranging from the size of a mung bean up to the measure of a fist; below the size of a mung bean, it is called "sand.
"Potsherd" refers to any kind of broken vessel. "Earth" refers to the ground. "Stone" refers to anything from the point where it no longer fits within the hollow of a closed fist.
A stone that has not yet reached the size of an elephant is called a "stone"; from the size of an elephant upwards, it is called a "mountain.
By the phrase "or whatever else," he includes the remaining types of earth, such as the stalks of palmyra palms and coconut fruits.
By the phrase "both the internal earth element and the external," he indicates that both earth elements possess the characteristic of hardness (*kakkhaḷattha*).
By way of characteristic, it shows that there is only one earth element. 174.

In the description of the water element and so forth, it should be understood according to the method explained below. In such terms as "water" (āpo) and "that which has become water" (āpogata), it is "water" by way of cohesion;

and because it has attained the state of being water, it is called "that which has become water. It is "moisture" (sneha) by way of viscidity; and that very same [element] is "moisture-natured" (snehasabhāva).
"Being gone-to" (gatattā) means having become affection (snehagata). "The state of being a bond for matter" (bandhanattaṃ rūpassa) refers to the binding nature of inseparable material phenomena.
Bile, phlegm, and so forth should also be brought to mind specifically as elements, after they have been discerned by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.
Here is the method: among the types of bile, unbound bile is connected with the life-faculty and pervades the entire body.
"Stationed" means the bound bile is stationed within the gallbladder. In this regard, just as when oil has pervaded a cake and is situated there,
the cake does not know, "Oil is situated pervading me," nor does the oil know,
"I am situated pervading the cake," even so, the body does not know, "Unbound bile is situated pervading me," nor does [the bile] know...
One knows unbound bile thus: "I am situated pervading the body.

And just as, when a kosātakī pod is filled with rainwater, neither does the kosātakī pod know, "Rainwater is situated in me," nor does the rainwater know, "I am situated in the kosātakī pod," even so the gall-bladder does not know, "Bound bile [is in me]."
As for "situated": even the bound bile does not know, "I am situated in the gall-bladder. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "bile" is a distinct component in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, insubstantial, liquid, adhesive in nature, and the water element.
Phlegm, measuring a full bowlful, rests upon the surface of the stomach. In this regard,
just as a cesspool covered by a layer of froth does not know, "A layer of froth rests upon me," nor does the layer of froth know,
"I rest upon a cesspool," even so the surface of the stomach does not know, "Phlegm rests upon me."
Nor does the phlegm know, “I am situated on the surface of the stomach. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, that which is called phlegm is a distinct component in this body:
insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid in nature, cohesive in form—the water element.

The *pubba* (pus) has no fixed location; wherever a part of the body is struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames of fire, and so forth, the blood coagulates and festers there, or boils, pustules, and the like arise, and it remains right in those very spots.

In this regard, just as when sap exudes from a tree due to a blow from an axe or similar cause, it is not the case that the axe-blow and other such factors belong to the tree [in the sense of being its inherent parts].
The sap does not know, "I am situated within us," nor does the sap know, "I am situated in such places as where the tree has been struck by an axe.
In the same way, the parts of the body that have been struck by stumps, thorns, and so forth do not know, "Pus is situated within us," nor does the pus know, "I am situated in those parts.
They are devoid of mutual mental engagement (*ābhoga*) or reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
These are the phenomena (*dhammā*). Thus, what is called "pus" is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, liquid, and of a binding nature;
it is the water element (*āpodhātū*).
Regarding blood, there is circulating blood, which, like uncongealed bile, remains pervading the entire body. Then there is stored blood.
It stands filling the lower part of the site of the liver, measuring about the capacity of a single bowl, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs.
Regarding the analysis of the blood that circulates there, it is similar to that of the "unbound bile" (*abaddhapitta*).
As for the other [blood], it is like water in a dilapidated pot where, while moistening clods of earth at the bottom, the clods do not know [the water].
Just as the clods of earth do not know, “We are being moistened by water,” nor does the water know, “I am moistening the clods of earth,” even so,
the region below the liver, or the kidneys and other organs, do not know, “Blood is situated within me,
or it is situated moistening us”; nor does the blood know, “I am filling the region below the liver.”
"Remaining moistening the kidneys and so forth. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "blood" is a distinct component in this body: insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, cohesive in nature, and the water element.
Sweat remains and trickles out, filling the pores of the head-hairs and body-hairs during times such as exposure to heat from a fire.

In this regard, just as when bundles of lotus roots, lily stalks, or lotus stems have been recently pulled up from the water, the openings within those bundles of lotus roots and so forth do not know,
"Water is trickling out from us," nor does the water trickling out from the openings of those bundles of lotus roots and so forth [know that it is doing so].

Just as one knows, "I am trickling out through the openings of the wounds from the *bhisā* grass," even so, the pores of the hair and body do not know, "Sweat is trickling out from us," nor does the sweat know, "I am trickling out through the pores of the hair and body.
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus, what is called "sweat" is a distinct [factor] in this body.
The water element is a constituent that is insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, liquid in nature, and characterized by cohesion.
Fat is a solid unctuousness that, in a stout person, pervades the entire body, while in a lean person, it resides supported by the flesh of the calves and other such parts.
In this regard, just as when a heap of meat is covered with a turmeric-dyed cloth, the heap of meat does not know, "Supported by me..."
Just as a turmeric cloth does not know, “I am standing supported by a heap of flesh,” nor does the heap of flesh know,
“A turmeric cloth is standing supported by me,” so too, within the entire body or in the calves and so forth, the flesh does not know,
“Fat is situated supported by me,” nor does the fat know, “I am situated supported by the flesh in the entire body or in the calves and so forth. They are mutually [unaware].
These states are devoid of mental application and reflection. Thus, what is called "fat" is a distinct component in this body;
it is insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, a viscous moisture, a thick liquid, and a form of cohesion—the water element.
As for tears: when they arise, they either remain filling the eye sockets or flow out. In that regard, just as...
Just as when young palm-tree hollows are filled with water, the young palm-tree hollows do not know,
"Water is staying within us," nor does the water know, "I am staying within the young palm-tree hollows"; even so, the eye-hollows do not know,
"Tears are staying within us," nor do the tears know, "I am staying within the eye-hollows."
"Stationed": these phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called "tears" is a distinct constituent within this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, insubstantial, liquid, and adhesive in nature; it is the water element.

Fat [is found] on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the tops of the shoulders, at times such as when heated by fire.

With its moisture dissolved and settled. In this regard, just as when oil is poured into gruel, the gruel does not know, "Oil is standing covering me," nor does the oil know, "I am standing covering the gruel";
even so, the area such as the palm of the hand does not know, "Fat is standing covering me," nor does the fat know, "I am [standing] on the area such as the palm of the hand."
“Having overspread [the body], they remain. These phenomena are devoid of mutual concern or reflection.
Thus, what is called “fat” is a distinct component in this body: insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, liquid, adhesive in nature, and belonging to the water element.
When there is such a cause for the arising of spittle, the spittle descends from both sides of the cheeks and rests upon the tongue.
In this regard, just as the bottom of a well on a riverbank where water flows without interruption does not know,
"Water is resting upon me," nor does the water know, "I am resting upon the bottom of the well," even so the surface of the tongue [does not know].

The tongue knows, "Saliva has descended from both sides of my cheeks and is situated [there]," yet the saliva does not know, "I have descended from both sides of the cheeks and am situated on the surface of the tongue. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, what is called "saliva" is a distinct constituent of this body, insentient, indeterminate, and empty.
The watery element (*āpodhātu*) is that which is insentient, liquid, and has the nature of cohesion.
When nasal mucus (*siṅghāṇikā*) arises, it either remains filling the nostrils or flows out.
In this regard, just as a bag filled with putrid curd does not know, "Putrid curd is contained within me," nor does the bag...

Just as putrid curd knows, “I am placed in a bowl,” even so the nostrils do not know, “Snot is situated within us,” nor does the snot know, “I am situated in the nostrils. These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection.
Thus, that which is called snot is a distinct constituent of this body, insentient and indeterminate.
The water element is that which is empty, devoid of a sentient being, liquid, and of a binding nature.
The synovial fluid, performing the function of lubricating the joints, resides within the one hundred and eighty joints.
In this regard, just as an axle oiled with oil does not know, "I have been lubricated with oil and am standing here," nor...

Just as oil knows, “I have lubricated the axle and remain [there],” even so the hundred and eighty joints do not know, “The synovial fluid has lubricated us and remains [there],” nor does the synovial fluid know, “I have lubricated the hundred and eighty joints and remain [there].
These phenomena are devoid of mutual intentionality or reflection. Thus, what is called “synovial fluid” in this [body]...
The urine is a distinct part of the body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a living being, liquid in nature, and cohesive in form; it is called the water element (*āpodhātu*).

It resides within the bladder. In this regard, just as when a porous jar is placed upside down in a cesspool, the porous jar does not know, "The cesspool liquid is contained within me," nor does the cesspool liquid [know the same].

Just as one standing in a bronze vessel does not know, "I am standing in a bronze vessel," so too the bladder does not know, "urine is contained within me," nor does the urine know, "I am contained in the bladder. These phenomena are devoid of mutual awareness or reflection.
Thus, what is called "urine" is a distinct component in this body—insentient, indeterminate, and empty.

The water element (*āpodhātu*) is that which is insentient, liquid, and has the nature of cohesion. The phrase "or whatever else" is said with reference to the water element among the remaining three portions.
In the description of the external water element, the flavor produced in dependence upon a root is called "root-flavor" (*mūlarasa*); this applies to trunk-flavor and so forth as well.
The same method applies here. Milk and so forth are already well known. However, unlike in the *Bhesajja-sikkhāpada* (the training rule on medicines), there is no restriction here;
any kind of milk is simply "milk. The same method applies to the remaining items as well. "Earthly" refers to water situated in pits and the like.

"From the sky" refers to rainwater that has not yet reached the earth. "Or whatever else" refers to snow-water, the water that destroys the world at the end of an eon, the water that sustains the earth, and so forth.
These have been included in the section on miscellaneous matters (*idha yevāpanaka*).
175. In the description of the fire element (*tejodhātu*): it is "fire" (*tejo*) by way of its fiery nature. It is "fire-constituted" (*tejogata*) because it has attained the state of being fire.

"Heat" (*usmā*) is the mode of warmth; it is "heat-constituted" (*usmāgata*) because it has attained the state of being heat. "Fervor" (*usuma*) is intense fervor; that very [fervor] is the state of fervor.
"Attained by going" means having become heated. "By which" means by which [element] that has become fire and is provoked. "It is warmed" means this body is warmed;
it becomes heated through the state of one-day-old aging and so forth.

"And by which it ages" means by which this body ages, reaching a deficiency of the faculties, the exhaustion of strength, and the state of wrinkles, grey hair, and so on. "And by which it is consumed" means...

When this body is burned by that which has become agitated, the person, crying out "I am burning! I am burning!", longs for an application of well-washed sappi, gosīsa, and sandalwood paste, as well as the breeze from a palm-leaf fan.

And it is by means of that [fire] that what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper digestion—namely, the food such as boiled rice that is eaten, the drinks such as beverages that are drunk, the snacks such as flour cakes that are chewed, and the tastes...
Or, it means that things such as mangoes, honey, and molasses undergo proper ripening and reach a state of differentiation in terms of their flavor and so forth.
Herein, the first three fire elements have four origins, while the last one has only a kamma-origin.
This, then, is the word-commentary for this section.

This, however, is the method of attention: here a bhikkhu attends thus: “That by which one is warmed—this is a distinct component in this body, insentient, indeterminate, empty, devoid of a being, having the mode of maturing—[it is] the fire element”;
and “that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested...”
One attends to it thus: ‘This is the fire element in this body, a distinct part, insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, of the nature of maturation.
Or else, whatever ordinary heat there is in this body, that is included within the category of “whatever there is” (yā-vā-panaka).
In the description of the external fire element (*bāhiratejodhātu*): a fire ignited dependent on wood, having wood as its fuel, is called a "wood-fire.
The same method applies to splinter-fires and so forth. "Refuse-fire" (*saṅkāraggi*) is a fire kindled by piling up rubbish.
"Indra-fire" (*indaggi*) is a lightning-fire. "Fire-heat" (*aggisantāpa*) is the heat of a flame or of glowing embers. "Sun-heat" (*sūriyasantāpa*)...
Heat (*ātapo*). "The heat of a pile of wood" means the heat at the place where a heap of wood is situated. The same method applies to the others as well.

Furthermore, the fire of hungry ghosts (*petaggi*), the fire at the destruction of an eon (*kappavināsaggi*), the fire of hell (*nirayaggi*), and so forth, are included here under the category of "and whatever else.

176. In the description of the air element (*vāyodhātu*): it is air by way of blowing (*vāyanavasena*). It is "air-ness" (*vāyogata*) because it has attained the state of being air. Rigidity (*thambhitattaṃ*).
"Of form" means the state of rigidity of inseparable (avinibbhoga) form. "Upward-moving winds" are the upward-ascending winds that produce belching, eructation, and so forth.
"Downward-moving winds" are the downward-descending winds that expel feces, urine, and so forth.
"Winds residing in the belly" are the winds outside the intestines. "Winds residing in the bowels" are the winds inside the intestines. "Winds following through the limbs and members" are...
The winds that follow along the network of vessels (*dhamanijālānusārena*) and pervade every limb throughout the entire body are those that produce the movements of flexing, extending, and so forth.
The "sword-winds" (*satthakavātā*) are winds that proceed as if cutting the joints and ligaments with a butcher’s knife.
The "razor-winds" (*khurakavātā*) are winds that cleave the heart as if with a razor. The "uppalaka-winds" (*uppalakavātā*) are winds that tear out the very flesh of the heart.
In-breathing (*assāsa*) is that which enters within through the nostrils; out-breathing (*passāsa*) is that which goes out from the nostrils.
Herein, all the preceding [factors] have a fourfold origination, whereas the in-breaths and out-breaths themselves originate solely from consciousness. This is the word-by-word commentary here.
As for this method of attention: here a bhikkhu [observes] the winds distinguished as "upward-moving" and so forth, by way of their being upward-moving and so on.
Having grasped this, he brings it to mind thus: "The winds called upward-moving are a distinct component in this body;
they are insentient, indeterminate, empty, soulless, and their mode is distension; they are the air element. The same method applies to the others as well.
As for the phrase "or whatever else," the winds included in the remaining wind-components have been entered here under the category of "and so forth" (idha yevāpanaka).
In the description of the external air element (*bāhiravāyodhātu*): "east winds" are winds coming from the eastern direction.
The same method applies to the west, north, and south. "Dusty winds" (*sarajā*) are those accompanied by dust; "dustless winds" (*arajā*) are those devoid of dust, pure, and thus called dustless.
"Cold" refers to those arising from the cold season, produced within cold clouds. "Hot" refers to those arising from the hot season.
"Arising within the warm clouds": these are "limited," meaning they are mild and thin winds; "excessive," meaning they are powerful winds. "Black":
these arise within black clouds, by which one who is struck becomes black in complexion;
some say this is also a designation for them. "Veramba winds": winds that blow at a height of one *yojana* or more. "Wing-winds."
"Even the winds arising from the flapping of a fly's wings. "Supaṇṇa-winds" means Garuḷa-winds.
Although these too are indeed wing-winds, they are mentioned separately by way of their specific intensity.
"Palmyra-fan winds" are winds produced by palm leaves or by anything else shaped like a circle. "Fanning-winds" refers to [winds produced by] a fan.
Winds have been stirred up. And these palm-leaf fans and whisks produce wind where none has arisen and redirect it where it has already arisen.
As for the phrase "or whatever else," here all winds other than those included in the canonical text (pāḷi) are entered under the category of "and so forth" (yevāpanaka).

177. In the description of the space element (ākāsadhātu): it is called "space" (ākāsa) because it does not strike against anything in the sense of being non-obstructive. Space itself is the state of space (ākāsabhāva).
Because it has gone there, it is "gone to space" (*ākāsagata*). Because it cannot be struck, it is "unstruck" (*agha*).

Because it has gone to the state of being unstruck, it is "gone to the unstruck" (*aghagata*). An opening is an interval. Because that very thing has gone to the state of being an opening, it is "gone to the opening" (*vivaragata*).
"Untouched by flesh and blood" means free from flesh and blood. The passage beginning with "ear-hole" (*kaṇṇacchidda*) is a demonstration of its specific divisions. Therein, "ear-hole" refers to—
"In the ear" means an opening or cavity, a space not touched by flesh or blood. The same method applies to the other [orifices] as well.
"By which" means by which opening one swallows—that is, causes to enter within—this edible food consisting of the varieties such as what is eaten and so forth.
"In which" means in that space known as the interior of the belly, where this very fourfold edible food remains.

"By which": that opening by which all this [waste], having reached the state of ripened dregs, exits—from the surface of the belly down to the path of the excrement—is a fissure measuring one span and four finger-breadths, untouched by flesh and blood;

it should be understood as the space element (*ākāsadhātu*) because it is free from them. Or else, "that which": here, the interior of the skin, the interior of the flesh, and the interior of the sinews.
The "space between bones" and the "space between body hairs"—all of this is included within the category of the *yevāpanaka* (miscellaneous).

In the description of the external space element, the phrase "not in contact with the four great elements" should be understood as that which is separated from the four great elements, such as wall-cavities, door-cavities, and so forth.
By this [definition], for one who performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) in that space...
It has been stated that the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise.
178. In the exposition of the consciousness element (*viññāṇadhātu*), the element known as eye-consciousness is the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*).
The same method applies to the remaining [consciousness elements] as well. Thus, when these six elements have been discerned, the eighteen elements are indeed discerned.
They exist. How so? First, by the inclusion of the earth, fire, and air elements, the tangible element (*phoṭṭhabba-dhātu*) is already included.

By the inclusion of the water and space elements, the mental-object element (*dhamma-dhātu*) is included. By the inclusion of the consciousness element (*viññāṇa-dhātu*), the mind element (*mano-dhātu*) is already included, because it acts as its precursor and its successor.
The eye-consciousness element and the others are already mentioned in the Sutta itself. The remaining nine are brought in [from elsewhere].
They should be shown. For by the inclusion of the eye-consciousness element, both the eye-element, which is its support, and the form-element, which is its object, are indeed included.
Likewise, by the inclusion of the ear-consciousness element and so forth, all eighteen elements—including the ear-element and the rest—are indeed included.
Among these, the discernment of the material (rūpa) is explained by way of ten elements; the discernment of the immaterial (arūpa) is explained by way of seven.
In the dhamma-element, there may be the inclusion of the material, and there may be the inclusion of the immaterial.

Thus, the inclusion of the material is stated by means of six and a half elements, and the inclusion of the immaterial by means of four and a half elements; this constitutes the exposition of the inclusion of the material and the immaterial.
The material and the immaterial are the five aggregates. That is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). The prior craving that originates them is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).
The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The knowledge of that is the path, which is the truth of the path.

It should be understood that this meditation subject on the Four Truths has been stated as the conclusion, having brought to its ultimate peak the monk who is intent upon it by way of the eighteen elements, up until the attainment of Arahantship.
179. Now, showing the second set of six, he said: "Furthermore, there are six elements," and so forth.
Therein, the "element of pleasure" and the "element of pain" refer to the pleasure and pain based on the physical sensitivity (kāyappasāda), presented as a pair by way of their mutual opposition.
For pleasure is the opposite of pain, and pain is the opposite of pleasure. Whatever place is pervaded by pleasure...
To whatever extent suffering pervades, to that same extent happiness pervades.
The "element of joy" and the "element of grief"—this too is made into a pair in the same way.
For joy is the opposite of grief, and grief is the opposite of joy. To whatever extent a place is pervaded by joy, to that same extent...
It pervades with displeasure (*domanassa*). To whatever extent it pervades with displeasure, to that same extent it pervades with joy (*somanassa*).
As for the pair consisting of the element of equanimity (*upekkhā-dhātu*) and the element of ignorance (*avijjā-dhātu*), these two are formed as a dyad by way of similarity.
For both of these are similar because they are unmanifested (*avibhūta*). In that context, by the inclusion of the elements of pleasure and pain, their associated [mental factors] are also included.

By the inclusion of the body-consciousness element (*kāyaviññāṇadhātu*), both the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) as its physical basis and the tangible-object element (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*) as its object are included.
By the inclusion of the elements of joy and grief (*somanassadomanassadhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) associated with them is included.

By the inclusion of the ignorance element (*avijjādhātu*), the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) is included. By the inclusion of the equanimity element (*upekkhādhātu*), the consciousness elements of eye, ear, nose, and tongue, as well as the mind-element (*manodhātu*), are included.
Since the eye-element, visible-object element, and so forth—which serve as the bases and objects for those [consciousnesses]—are also included, thus all eighteen elements are indeed included.
Now, regarding the discernment of matter by means of these ten elements and so forth, everything should be understood according to the method already explained below.
In this way, having brought it to its culmination for a single bhikkhu up to the stage of Arahantship—

It should be understood that the conclusion has been stated. In that regard, as for "What is the element of pleasure? That which is bodily gratification," and so forth, these follow the same method explained below.

181. In the third set of six, "sensual desire" (kāma) refers to two kinds of sensual desire: sensual desire as object (vatthukāma) and sensual desire as defilement (kilesakāma). Of these, regarding sensual desire as defilement:

The element associated with sensual desire is the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*); this is a name for sensual-desire thought (*kāmavitakka*). The element that is sensual desire itself, with reference to the object of sensual desire, is the sense-sphere element;
this is a name for the phenomena belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*). The element associated with ill will is the ill-will element (*byāpādadhātu*);
this is a name for ill-will thought (*byāpādavitakka*). The element that is ill will itself is the ill-will element; [this refers] to the ten bases of resentment (*āghātavatthu*).
This is the name for repulsion (*paṭigha*). An element associated with cruelty (*vihiṃsā*) is the “cruelty-element” (*vihiṃsā-dhātu*);
this is the name for thoughts of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*). Or, cruelty itself as an element is the “cruelty-element”; this is the name for the harming of other beings.

However, since this has not been mentioned below, it should be understood through the analysis of its meaning and so forth as follows: by means of this, beings are harmed, or it is the act of harming.

"Against these beings" refers to cruelty (*vihiṃsā*). It should be understood as having the characteristic of harming, or alternatively, the characteristic of being the opposite of compassion (*karuṇā*).

Its function is to produce agitation in the mental continuum of others, or alternatively, its function is to destroy compassion within one's own continuum. It is manifested as a basis for suffering, and its proximate cause is aversion (*paṭigha*).
Renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is called non-greed (*alobha*) because it has emerged from greed; [it is so called] because of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Because it has emerged [from unwholesome states], it is the first jhāna; because it has emerged from all unwholesome states, it is the wholesome.

An element associated with renunciation is the "renunciation-element" (*nekkhammadhātu*); this is a name for renunciation-thought (*nekkhammavitakka*). Renunciation itself is the element, thus it is the "renunciation-element"; this is a name for all that is wholesome.
An element associated with non-ill-will is the "non-ill-will-element" (*abyāpādadhātu*); this is a name for non-ill-will-thought (*abyāpādavitakka*).
"Name. The state of non-ill will is the "element of non-ill will" (*abyāpādadhātu*); this is a name for loving-kindness (*mettā*).
The state associated with non-cruelty is the "element of non-cruelty" (*avihiṃsādhātu*); this is a name for the thought of non-cruelty. Non-cruelty itself is the "element of non-cruelty";

this is a name for compassion (*karuṇā*). 182. Now, in order to demonstrate that very meaning, the word-commentary begins with: "In this context, what is the element of sensual desire? (*tattha katamā kāmadhātūti*).
In this context, "connected" (*paṭisaṃyutta*) means connected by way of association. "Reasoning" (*takka*), "applied thought" (*vitakka*), and so forth, have meanings already explained.
"Afflicts" (*viheṭheti*) means it oppresses or causes suffering. "Harming" (*heṭhanā*) is oppression or the production of suffering by means of blows with the hand and so forth.
"Violent harming" (*viheṭhanā*) is intense harming. "Injuring" (*hiṃsanā*) means they injure by means of this; "violent injuring" (*vihiṃsanā*) is intense injuring. "Provocation" (*rosanā*)...
*Ghaṭṭanā*: striking. *Virosanā*: forceful striking. Or, in all cases, the word has been augmented by the prefix *vi*.
That by which one harms is *upaghāta*; the harming of others is *parūpaghāta*.
That by which one is friendly is *metti*. The state of being friendly is *mettāyanā*. Of one who is friendly, that is, of one possessing loving-kindness (*mettāsamaṅgin*).
The state is the quality of being loving-kind. For a mind liberated from ill-will, that liberation is "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*).

Here, by the first three terms, loving-kindness is described as having reached both access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*); by the last term, it is described as having reached absorption alone.

One feels compassion through this, thus it is "compassion" (*karuṇā*). The mode of feeling compassion is "the act of feeling compassion" (*karuṇāyanā*). For one who feels compassion, that is, for one possessing compassion...
The state of being compassionate is *karuṇāyitattaṃ*. For one whose mind is liberated from cruelty, that liberation of the mind is "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*).

Here too, the distinction between access and absorption should be understood in the same manner as previously explained. In both cases, the final terms "loving-kindness" and "compassion" are stated for the purpose of specifying the particular types of liberation of mind.

Furthermore, in this context, sensual thought arises with respect to both sentient beings and formations; even when it arises in both instances, it constitutes a breach of the path of action (*kammappaṭha*).

However, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) that has arisen toward sentient beings alone constitutes a course of kamma (*kammappatha*), and not the other [type of ill-will]. The same principle applies to cruelty (*vihiṃsā*) as well.

In this regard, there are two ways of explaining: the inclusive and the non-inclusive. For, by the inclusion of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), the elements of ill-will and cruelty are also included.
Yet, having extracted them specifically from the sense-sphere element itself, both are [distinguished] separately.
"These have been shown. This, first of all, is the inclusive exposition (*sabbasaṅgāhika-kathā*) here.

However, with the exception of the elements of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), all the rest are simply the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*). This is called the unmixed exposition (*asambhinna-kathā*).

By the inclusion of the renunciation element (*nekkhammadhātu*), the elements of non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) and non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) are indeed already included. Yet, having extracted both of these from the renunciation element again and again—
"Shown"—this too is a comprehensive exposition here. "Excluding the elements of non-ill-will and non-cruelty, the remainder are the element of renunciation"—this is called the unmixed exposition.
For when these eighteen elements are encompassed by these six elements, they are indeed encompassed. All [of them]...
For indeed, having repeatedly extracted them from the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) alone, they must be made to obtain [the status of] the eighteen elements themselves;

thus, by way of three sets of six, they become eighteen. However, instead of taking it in that way, if one makes eighteen for each set of six according to the method stated, and then condenses all those groups of eighteen into one, they remain eighteen.

It should be understood that they exist. Thus, in this Suttanta-bhājaniya, it should be understood that the course of comprehension has been explained as follows: sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), and two belong to the three planes (tebhūmika).
This concludes the commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya.
2. Commentary on the Exposition by Way of Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya) 183.

In the Exposition by Way of Abhidhamma, showing all the elements (dhātus) in their own form, [the Blessed One] spoke of the eighteen elements beginning with "the eye element" and "the visible-form element. Regarding that, first, in the section on the enumeration (uddesa), it is said:
"In terms of meaning, characteristic, and so forth, In terms of order, and what is reckoned as 'just so much'..."
The conditions are now to be examined; the analysis is to be understood. Therein, as for "by way of meaning":
it sees, thus it is the eye (*cakkhu*); it is manifested, thus it is form (*rūpa*). Eye-consciousness is "consciousness of the eye" (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*);
in this manner, first of all, the analysis of the eye and the other [bases] is to be understood by way of their specific meanings. But without distinction:
It burns (vidahati), it is held (dhīyate), it is an arrangement (vidhāna), or it is prescribed (vidhīyate); or else, because it is held therein (ettha vā dhīyati), it is called a *dhātu*.

For the mundane elements (*dhātuyo*), being established as causal factors, burn forth the manifold suffering of saṃsāra—just as gold, silver, and other mineral ores produce gold, silver, and so on—and they are borne by sentient beings, just as a burden is borne by porters.
The meaning is "they are held. And these [elements] are merely the distribution of suffering because they do not come under one's control.

Furthermore, by means of these [elements] acting as instruments, the suffering of saṃsāra is distributed among sentient beings; and that [suffering], having been thus distributed, is held—that is, deposited—within these very [elements].

Thus, each individual phenomenon among the eye and the rest is called a "constituent" (dhātu) in the sense of "it distributes" (vidahati), "it is held" (dhīyati), and so forth, according to its occurrence.
Furthermore, just as the so-called "self" (attā) does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāva) for the non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiyā), these [aggregates] are not like that.

Rather, they are called "elements" (dhātuyo) because they bear their own intrinsic nature. And just as in the world various mineral constituents such as yellow orpiment and red arsenic are called "elements," so too are these "elements" (dhātuyo) because they are like elements; for they are diverse constituents of knowledge and the knowable. Or alternatively, just as...

The designation "element" (*dhātu*) is applied to the taste, blood, and so forth—which constitute the parts of the aggregate known as the body—because they are delimited by mutually distinct and dissimilar characteristics;
in the same way, the designation "element" should be understood for these [senses] as well, which are the parts of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) known as the five aggregates.
For these, beginning with the eye, are delimited by mutually distinct and dissimilar characteristics. Furthermore, regarding the term "element" (*dhātu*):

This is a designation for that which is merely devoid of a soul (*nijjīva*). For indeed, the Blessed One, in such passages as “This person, bhikkhu, consists of six elements,” gave a teaching on the elements (*dhātu*) for the purpose of uprooting the perception of a soul. Therefore, in the sense already stated:

it is the eye and it is an element, thus “eye-element” (*cakkhudhātu*); ... [and so on] ... it is mind-consciousness and it is an element, thus “mind-consciousness-element” (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). Thus:
Herein, the exposition should be understood according to meaning;

and by the phrase "according to characteristic, etc.," the exposition should also be understood here according to the characteristics of the eye and the other [faculties]. Furthermore, those characteristics and so forth should be understood in the same manner as stated below.
By the phrase "according to order," even here, among the orders previously mentioned—such as the order of arising—the order of teaching is what is appropriate. And this, moreover, is...
It is stated by way of the successive determination of cause and fruit. For this dyad—“eye element” and “visible-object element”—is the cause;
“eye-consciousness element” is the fruit. In this manner, the analysis should be understood in all instances according to their sequence.
“By way of that much” means by way of its extent. This is what is meant: for in those various passages from the Suttas and the Abhidhamma...
The element of light, the element of beauty, the element of the base of infinite space, the element of the base of infinite consciousness, the element of the base of nothingness,
the element of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the element of the cessation of perception and feeling, the element of sensual desire,
the element of ill will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, the element of non-cruelty, the element of pleasure, and the element of pain.
the element of joy, the element of grief, the element of equanimity, the element of ignorance, the element of exertion, the element of striving,
the element of perseverance, the inferior element, the middling element, the superior element, the earth element, the water element,
the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element, the conditioned element, the unconditioned element, and the world with its many and diverse elements.
Other elements such as these are also seen.
If this is so, why is the limit set at eighteen, rather than making no limit for all [elements]?
Because all elements that exist by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāva) are included within those [eighteen]. For it is only the material element (*rūpadhātu*)...
The light element (*ābhā-dhātu*). However, the beautiful element (*subha-dhātu*) is dependent upon form and so forth. Why? Because it has the sign of the beautiful as its object.

For the beautiful element is the sign of the beautiful; and that does not exist apart from form and so forth. Alternatively, since form and so forth—which are the objects of wholesome resultant consciousness—are themselves the beautiful element, this [element] consists merely of form and the rest.
In the case of the elements of the base of infinite space and so forth, the mind is the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇa-dhātu*).

The remaining phenomena are the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu). However, the element of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu) does not exist as a distinct intrinsic nature; for it is merely the cessation of those two elements.

The sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu) is either just the element of mental objects, as it is said: "In this context, what is the sense-sphere element? It is thought associated with sensual desire... wrong intention";
or it consists of all eighteen elements, as it is said: "Below, down to the Avīci hell..."

“Having set a limit above by including the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, whatever aggregates, elements, and bases are within this interval, occurring here and included herein—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu).
The renunciation-element (nekkhammadhātu) is indeed the Dhamma-element; all wholesome [states]...

Or, because of the statement, “Dhammas are the element of renunciation,” the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) also exists [as such].
