The elements of ill will, cruelty, non-ill will, non-cruelty, pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, ignorance, exertion, striving, and perseverance are simply the dhamma-element (dhammadhātu).
The inferior, intermediate, and superior elements are merely the eighteen elements themselves. For the inferior eye and so forth are the inferior element;
the intermediate and superior eye and so forth are both the intermediate and superior elements. But in the absolute sense, the unwholesome...

The dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element are the inferior element (*hīnadhātu*). Both the mundane wholesome and indeterminate states, as well as the eye-element and the rest, are the intermediate element (*majjhimadhātu*).

However, the supramundane dhamma-element and mind-consciousness-element are the superior element (*paṇītadhātu*). The earth, fire, and air elements are simply the tangible-object element (*phoṭṭhabbadhātu*).
The water element and the space element are simply the dhamma-element. The consciousness element is simply the compendium of the seven consciousness-elements, beginning with eye-consciousness.

The seventeen elements and a portion of the mental-object element (dhammadhātu) constitute the conditioned element (saṅkhatadhātu). The unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu), however, is only a portion of the mental-object element.

Furthermore, the world of "many elements" and "diverse elements" consists merely of the classification of the eighteen elements. Thus, because all elements existing by way of their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva) are included therein, exactly eighteen are stated.
Furthermore, eighteen [bases] are taught for the purpose of uprooting the notion of a "living being" (jīva) in regard to consciousness, whose intrinsic nature is cognizing.
For there are beings who perceive a living being in consciousness, whose intrinsic nature is cognizing.

Having demonstrated its manifoldness through the division into the elements of eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness, and its impermanence due to its existence being dependent on conditions such as the eye and visible forms, [the Buddha taught this] to those in whom that notion has long been latent...
The Blessed One revealed eighteen elements for one who wishes to eradicate the perception of a living being.

Furthermore, they were revealed as eighteen specifically because of the inclinations of those to be trained; that is, he taught exactly eighteen for the sake of those beings who are to be guided by this teaching, which is neither too concise nor too prolix.
For in whatever manner he reveals the Dhamma, whether by way of summary or in detail,
the power of the True Dhamma strikes down [the opposing views] so that they perish in an instant.
"Darkness prevails in the hearts of beings who are to be disciplined.
In this way, the analysis here should be understood "by way of number.
As for the term "conditioned," first of all, the eye-element is reckoned as a single dhamma by way of its genus, namely, the sensitivity of the eye.
Likewise, the elements of ear, nose, tongue, and body, and of visible form, sound, odor, and flavor, are reckoned as fourfold by way of the ear-sensitivity and so forth.
The tangible element, however, is reckoned as three phenomena by way of earth, fire, and air.
The eye-consciousness element is reckoned as two phenomena by way of wholesome and unwholesome resultants. Likewise are the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness elements. The mind element—
Furthermore, it is reckoned as three states by way of the five-door adverting consciousness, and the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant receiving consciousnesses.
The mental-object element (dhammadhātu) is reckoned as twenty states by way of the three immaterial aggregates, the sixteen subtle material phenomena, and the unconditioned element.
The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) consists of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousnesses.
"It is reckoned as 'sixty-seven dhammas'—thus here the exposition of the term 'conditioned' (saṅkhata) should be understood.

As for 'conditions' (paccaya), the exposition should be understood by way of the fact that the eye-element and so forth are conditions for the eye-consciousness-element and so forth. Furthermore, their state of being conditions will be made clear in the section on the detailed explanation (niddesa).
'Should be seen' (daṭṭhabba): the meaning is that the exposition should be understood here also by way of what is to be seen. For all [these] are indeed conditioned."
The elements (dhātuyo) should be seen as secluded from the past and the future, as empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood, and as occurring in dependence upon conditions.

Specifically, however, herein the eye-element (cakkhudhātu) should be seen like the surface of a drum, the visible-form element (rūpadhātu) like the drumstick, and the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu) like the sound. Likewise, the eye-element is like the surface of a mirror, and the face...
The visible-object element is like the object, and the eye-consciousness element is like the appearance of the face.

Alternatively, the eye element is like sugarcane or sesame seeds, the visible-object element is like the sugarcane press or the sesame millstone, and the eye-consciousness element is like the sugarcane juice or the sesame oil.

Likewise, the eye element is like the lower fire-drill, the visible-object element is like the upper fire-drill, and the eye-consciousness element is like the fire. This same method applies to the ear element and the others as well.
The mind-element (manodhātu), however, should be regarded as preceding and following the eye-consciousness element and the others according to their occurrence, like a forerunner and a follower.
Within the mental-object element (dhammadhātu), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) should be regarded as a dart and a stake;

the aggregates of perception (saññā) and formations (saṅkhāra) are like those afflicted by the application of the darts and stakes of feeling; or, for worldlings (puthujjana), perception is like an empty fist because it generates the suffering of hope.
Like a forest animal, because it perceives signs incorrectly; like a man throwing someone into a pit of glowing embers, because it casts the formations into rebirth-linking;
like thieves pursued by royal officers, because they are followed by the suffering of birth;

like seeds of a poisonous tree, because they are the cause for the continuity of the aggregates which brings all manner of harm; and like matter, because it is the sign of various kinds of calamities.
It should be viewed as being like a wheel of fire.
However, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) should be viewed as the deathless, the peaceful, and the secure. Why?

Because it is the direct opposite of all that is harmful. The mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇa-dhātu) is like a forest monkey, because it proceeds by grasping one object and then letting go of it to grasp another.
It should be regarded as being like a wild colt because it is difficult to tame; like a stick thrown into the air, falling wherever it may land;
and like an actor on a stage because of its association with various defilements such as greed and hatred.

In the section of the detailed exposition, regarding the phrase "dependent on the eye and forms," this pair [the eye and forms] and another, namely the functional mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*), are both dependent upon.

The meaning is: "and the three associated aggregates. For in the case of the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*), the eye is the support condition (*nissayapaccaya*), visible form is the object condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) is the disappearance condition (*vigatapaccaya*), and the three immaterial aggregates are the co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*).
Therefore, this eye-consciousness element is said to arise dependent upon these four. The same method applies to the phrases "dependent on the ear," and so forth.

“Immediately after the ceased” means immediately following that which has ceased. “The mind-element born thereof” refers to the two-fold mind-element—arising from that same object—consisting of wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant types, whose function is receiving.
Alternatively, “the first attention among all phenomena” means the first attention occurring when all these phenomena, beginning with eye-consciousness, arise.
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as "the first act of attention directed toward all phenomena comprised within the objects of the eye-consciousness element and so forth.
By this, it should be understood that the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) performing the function of five-door adverting is included.
In the phrase "immediately after [the mind-element] has arisen and ceased," the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). Therefore...
"Of the mind-element and also of the mind-consciousness-element"—this is the meaning to be understood here. By this, it refers to both:
(1) the resultant mind-consciousness-element that arises with the function of investigation immediately after the resultant mind-element has arisen and ceased;
and (2) the functional mind-consciousness-element that arises with the function of determining immediately after that [resultant mind-element] has arisen and ceased.

It should be understood that all those moments of mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) which arise as the functional consciousness (javanakicca) immediately after that [advertence] has arisen and ceased are included here.
"Dependent on the mind" refers to the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅgamana). "And mental objects" refers to the objects of the four planes of existence.
"Mind-consciousness arises" means that the impulsion (javana) together with the adverting consciousness is produced.

In this place, however, they took up what is called the "hand-held question. It is said that the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, taking the Elder Ābhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, by the hand, said: "In places where the word 'dependent' (paṭicca) occurs, advertence (āvajjana) should not be treated separately;
it should be understood as being based on the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) alone. Therefore, here the term "mind" (mano) includes advertence.
The life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). "Mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) refers to impulsion mind-consciousness (*javanamanoviññāṇa*).

However, in this Exposition of the Abhidhamma (*Abhidhammabhājanīya*), sixteen elements are stated to belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two are of four planes and are described as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā) 185.
In the Section of Questions, the state of being wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth regarding the eighteen elements should be understood according to the method already explained below.
Regarding the triads of objects (*ārammaṇattika*), however, as for the statement that six elements have limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*), this refers to the five [sensory] [elements].
This was stated with reference to the fact that eye-consciousness and the others, as well as the mind-element (*manodhātu*), invariably occur with respect to the five objects such as visible form.

However, the status of limited objects (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth for the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—which were mentioned as "two elements"—should be understood according to the same method explained for the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*). Thus, in this inquiry as well, there are sixteen elements.
Those pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and two belonging to four planes—comprising a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane—have been explained.
Thus, this *Dhātuvibhaṅga* (Analysis of Elements) has also been taught by dividing it after having extracted its threefold rotation.
From the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga) is finished. 4.
The Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition (Suttantabhājanīya).

189. Now, in the immediately following *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths), "four" is the numerical limit. "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*) is the indication of the specific phenomena being defined. Regarding the section on the summary beginning with "The Noble Truth of Suffering," it is said:
"In terms of classification, etymology, and the distinctions of characteristic and so forth;
likewise in terms of the extraction of meanings and their significance, as well as by way of neither deficiency nor excess."
By way of sequence, by way of function, by the analysis of what is included therein,
by way of simile, by way of the fourfold set, by way of emptiness,
the single-fold, and so forth, and by way of the similar and the dissimilar.
The exposition should be understood by the wise according to the sequence of the teaching.

In this context, "by way of analysis" means that four meanings each for suffering and the other [noble truths] have been analyzed as they truly are, not otherwise, and not differently—those which must be fully realized by those who are realizing suffering and the rest. As it has been said: "The meaning of suffering is oppression..."
The meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of changeability—these four are the meanings of suffering as suffering;

they are such, not otherwise, and not different. The meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, and the meaning of impediment... [as above] ...are the meanings of the origin.

The meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless... [as above] ...are the meanings of cessation. The meaning of outlet, the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, and the meaning of being unconditioned... [as above] ...are the meanings of the path.
“The meaning of cause, the meaning of seeing, the meaning of predominance—these four are the meaning of the path of the path, which are thus, not otherwise, and not different.
Likewise: “The meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of changeability, the meaning of convergence regarding suffering,” and so forth.
Thus, by way of these four sets of four meanings as they have been analyzed—
"Suffering and so forth are to be understood. This, first of all, is how the exposition should be understood here by way of analysis.
Regarding the phrase "by way of derivation, characteristic, and so forth," first, as for "derivation":
here the word *du* is seen in the sense of what is contemptible; for they call a contemptible son a *duputta* (a bad son). The word *khaṃ*, however, refers to what is empty.

For empty space is called *khanti*. And this first truth is "bad" (*kucchita*) because it is the basis for manifold calamities, and it is "empty" (*tuccha*) because it is devoid of the state of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood imagined by foolish people. Therefore, because it is bad and because it is empty, it is called "suffering" (*dukkha*).
Furthermore, this word *saṃ* indicates conjunction, as in such expressions as "coming together" (*samāgama*) and "united" (*sameta*).
The word *u* signifies arising, as in such expressions as "arisen" (*uppanna*) or "appeared" (*udita*). The word *aya*, however, indicates a cause.

Furthermore, this second truth is the cause for the arising of suffering when it is conjoined with the remaining conditions. Thus, because it is the cause for the arising [of suffering] through its conjunction with suffering, it is called the "origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*).

As for the third truth: since the word *ni-* signifies non-existence (*abhāva*) and the word *rodha* signifies confinement (*cāraka*), it is called "cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodha*) because there is an absence here of the confinement of suffering known as saṃsāra, owing to its being empty of all destinations;
or else, when that [cessation] is attained, there is the absence of the confinement of suffering known as saṃsāra, because it is the opposite of that [suffering]. Thus it is "cessation of suffering."
It is called "the cessation of suffering" because it is the condition for the non-arising and the cessation of suffering. As for the fourth truth,

it is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" because, by way of its object, it moves toward that cessation, and because it is the path for the attainment of the cessation of suffering.
However, because the Noble Ones—beginning with the Buddhas—penetrate these truths, they are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasacca*).
As it is said: "Monks, there are these four Noble Truths. Which are they... [as above] ...These, monks, are the four Noble Truths.
The Noble Ones penetrate these; therefore they are called 'Noble Truths'. Furthermore:
They are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*) because they belong to the Noble One (*ariya*). As it is said: "In this world with its devas...
[and so on] ...among gods and humans, the Tathāgata is the Noble One; therefore they are called 'Noble Truths.

Alternatively, they are called "Noble Truths" because the state of being noble (*ariyabhāva*) is established through their full awakening (*abhisambuddhattā*). As it is said: "Indeed, bhikkhus, regarding these four Noble Truths..."
“Because he has fully awakened to things as they truly are, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called ‘Noble.
Furthermore, they are called ‘Noble Truths’ because they are noble truths; ‘noble’ means that they are such, not otherwise, and non-deceptive.
As it was said: ‘Monks, these four noble truths are such, not otherwise, and not different.’”
"Therefore they are called 'Noble Truths'. Thus should the analysis of this term be understood by way of its etymology.
How [is it analyzed] "by way of the distinction of characteristics and so forth"? Herein, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of oppression;

its function is to torment; its manifestation is occurrence. The truth of origin has the characteristic of being a source; its function is to bring about non-interruption; its manifestation is an impediment.
The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace, the function of deathlessness, and the manifestation of signlessness.

The truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out, the function of effecting the abandoning of defilements, and the manifestation of emergence. Furthermore, they have respectively the characteristics of occurrence and its cause, and of non-occurrence and its cause.

Likewise, they have the characteristics of being conditioned and craving, and of being unconditioned and vision. Thus, here, [the truths are distinguished] "by way of the classification of their characteristics and so forth."
The exposition should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "and by way of extracting the meaning from the eightfold [truths]," if one asks what the meaning of truth (*saccaṭṭha*) is here:
it is that which, when investigated with the eye of wisdom, is deceptive like an illusion, misleading like a mirage, and of an unfindable nature like the self (*attā*) of the non-Buddhist sectarians.

And it does not exist [as a substantial entity]; rather, by way of its being real, non-erroneous, and factual—characterized by affliction, origin, and the path of escape—it remains the very objective domain of noble knowledge (*ariya-ñāṇa*).
This reality, which is real, non-erroneous, and factual, should be understood as the true meaning (*saccaṭṭha*), just like the characteristic of fire or the nature of the world.
As it has been said: "‘This is suffering,’ monks, this is real (*tatha*), this is not unreal (*avitatha*)."
“This is not otherwise,” and so on in detail. Furthermore:
Since suffering does not fail to afflict, and nothing other than suffering afflicts, it is considered a truth by virtue of its nature as an affliction.
Without that, suffering does not arise from anything else, nor does it exist apart from that;
by the fixed law of the cause of suffering, thus is clinging the truth.
There is no peace other than Nibbāna, nor is there peace that is not that; for that reason, it is the truth.
By way of its being peaceful, this is considered the Truth.
There is no other path leading to liberation, nor is it itself non-liberating;
because it possesses the state of true liberation, it is thus recognized as the Truth.

Thus, the wise have declared that the meaning of the truths, which consists in the state of things as they truly are and is free from perversion, applies without distinction to all four truths, beginning with suffering. In this way,
the analysis should be understood "by way of meaning."
How [is it] "by way of extracting the meaning"? Herein, this word *sacca* is seen in many meanings, as follows:

in such passages as "One should speak the truth, one should not be angry," it refers to verbal truth (*vācāsacca*). In such passages as "The recluses and brahmins are established in truth," it refers to the truth of abstinence (*viratisacca*).
In such passages as "Why do they proclaim various truths, these disputants who are skilled in eloquent speech? it refers to the truth of views (*diṭṭhisacca*).
In such passages as “For there is one truth, there is no second,” it refers to both Nibbāna and the Path as ultimate truths (paramatthasacca).

In such passages as “Of the four noble truths, how many are wholesome? it refers to the noble truths (ariyasacca). Since this [term] here also applies to the noble truths, the analysis should be understood in this way by way of the extraction of the meaning (atthuddhārato).
‘As to “neither deficient nor superfluous”: why, then, are exactly four noble truths stated—neither fewer nor more?
Because nothing else is possible, and because none of them can be removed.
For there exists nothing else that could be added to these, nor can even one of these be taken away. As it is said: “Here, monks, suppose someone were to come...”’
“Whether it be a recluse or a brahmin, it is impossible that he should say: ‘This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering;
there is another Noble Truth of Suffering than that which has been taught by the recluse Gotama.
Setting aside this Noble Truth of Suffering, I shall proclaim another Noble Truth of Suffering’—such a thing is not possible,” and so forth. And as it was said: “For whoever, monks...”
“Whether it be a recluse or a brahmin, it is impossible that he would say: ‘This is not the first noble truth of suffering as taught by the recluse Gotama;
rejecting this first noble truth of suffering, I shall proclaim another as the first noble truth of suffering. Such a thing cannot be. And so forth.

Furthermore, in explaining the process of existence (*pavatti*), the Blessed One explained it together with its cause; and in explaining cessation (*nivatti*), he explained it together with its means. Thus, at most, only four factors have been stated: the process of existence, its cause, cessation, and the means thereto.
Likewise, there are the things to be fully understood, the things to be abandoned, the things to be realized, and the things to be developed;

and the basis for craving, craving itself, the cessation of craving, and the means to the cessation of craving; and the attachment, the delight in attachment, the eradication of attachment, and the means to the eradication of attachment.
By way of basis as well, only four are mentioned. Thus, the analysis here should be understood “according to deficiency and excess.

Regarding “order,” this too refers to the sequence of the teaching. And herein, the truth of suffering is stated first because it is easy to understand due to its grossness and because it is common to all beings;
immediately after that, for the purpose of showing its cause, the truth of origin is stated.

The truth of cessation follows next for the purpose of making known that with the cessation of the cause comes the cessation of the fruit; and at the end, the truth of the path is taught for the purpose of showing the means to attain that cessation.
Alternatively, suffering was mentioned first in order to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in beings who are attached to the gratification of the pleasure of existence.
That [suffering] does not come unmade, nor does it arise from the creation of a Lord (*issara-nimmāna*) or similar causes; rather, it arises from this [cause].
Immediately after that, origination is taught for the purpose of making it known.

Then, for those whose minds are agitated because they are overwhelmed by suffering accompanied by its cause, and who are seeking an escape from suffering, cessation is taught for the purpose of generating consolation through the vision of that escape. After that, the path—which brings about cessation—is taught for the purpose of attaining cessation.
In this way, the determination of the "order" (kamata) here should be understood.
The meaning is that the exposition should also be understood by way of the function of the knowledge of the truths, according to the phrase "the knowledge regarding the Noble Truths.
For the knowledge of the truths is twofold: the knowledge of awakening (*anubodha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*). Therein, the knowledge of awakening is mundane;
it occurs with respect to cessation and the path by means of hearsay and so forth. The knowledge of penetration is supramundane, having cessation as its object.
Having performed its function, it penetrates all four truths as well. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—all this should be stated.
Furthermore, regarding that which is mundane (*lokiya*), therein the knowledge of suffering functions by way of overcoming the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
Knowledge of suffering turns back the prevailing view of a personal entity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); knowledge of origin turns back the view of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi);
knowledge of cessation turns back the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi); and knowledge of the path turns back the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi).

Alternatively, knowledge of suffering turns back the error regarding the fruit—namely, the perception of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood in the aggregates which are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood; and knowledge of origin...

The misconception regarding the cause is the false attribution of causality to that which is not a cause, such as the belief that the world proceeds from a creator, a primal substance, time, inherent nature, or other such factors.
The misconception regarding cessation is the grasping of non-liberation as liberation, such as the notion that the formless realm, the world-summit, or similar states constitute final emancipation.
The misconception regarding the path is the adherence to an impure path—such as the pursuit of sensual pleasures or the practice of self-mortification—as being the true way.
It turns back the misapplication regarding the means that occurs by way of grasping at the path to purification. Therefore, this is said:
“As long as a person is deluded regarding the world, the origin of the world, the auspicious cessation of the world, and the means thereto, so long does he not understand the Truths.”
In this way, the exposition should be understood here also from the perspective of the function of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca*).

Regarding the phrase "the divisions of those included within": within the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), with the exception of craving (*taṇhā*) itself and untainted phenomena (*anāsavadhamma*), all remaining phenomena are included;
within the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), there are the thirty-six modes of the movement of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*); the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*)... [is included].

It is unmixed: within the Truth of the Path, there are, by way of right view, the basis of psychic power consisting in investigation, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena.
By way of right intention, there are the three thoughts of renunciation and so forth; by way of right speech, the four types of verbal good conduct;
by way of right action, the three types of bodily good conduct; and by way of right livelihood, fewness of wishes and contentment.
Furthermore, because all these— right speech, right action, and right livelihood— are the virtue (sīla) beloved by the Noble Ones,
and because virtue must be received with the hand of faith (saddhā), there is the presence of the faculty of faith, the power of faith, the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal,
and, under the designation of right effort, the fourfold right exertion, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the factor of enlightenment that is energy.
Under the heading of right mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the mindfulness enlightenment factor are included;

under the heading of right concentration, the three types of concentration beginning with that accompanied by applied and sustained thought, as well as the concentration enlightenment factors of mental one-pointedness, rapture, tranquility, and equanimity, are included.
In this way, the analysis of what is "included herein" should be understood.

‘By way of simile’: for the truth of suffering should be seen as like a burden, the truth of origin as like the taking up of the burden, the truth of cessation as like the laying down of the burden, and the truth of the path as like the means for laying down the burden;
and likewise, the truth of suffering is like a disease, the truth of origin as like the cause of the disease, and the truth of cessation as like the subsiding of the disease.

The truth of the path is like medicine; or alternatively, the truth of suffering is like a famine, the truth of the origin is like a drought, the truth of cessation is like a good harvest, and the truth of the path is like a timely rain.
Furthermore, [they may be understood] by way of the enemy, the root of enmity, the eradication of enmity, and the means for that eradication;

or by way of the poisonous tree, the root of the tree, the cutting off of the root, and the means for that cutting off; or by way of fear, the root of fear, fearlessness, and the means for attaining it.
And having applied these [terms] by way of the effort that brings about the reaching from this shore to the further shore across the great flood, they are to be understood through their similes.
Thus, in this context, the exposition "by way of simile" is to be understood. Regarding "by way of the tetrads":
herein, there is suffering that is not a noble truth, and there is a noble truth that is not suffering.
There is that which is both suffering and a noble truth; there is that which is neither suffering nor a noble truth. This same method applies to the origin and the other [noble truths].

In this regard, the states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are suffering by way of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkhatā*), according to the statement "whatever is impermanent, that is suffering," yet they are not noble truths.
Cessation is a noble truth but not suffering. The remainder—

However, two noble truths may be suffering from the perspective of impermanence, yet not in the sense of that which is to be fully understood for the sake of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
In every respect, however, the five aggregates of clinging—excluding craving—are both suffering and a noble truth.
The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are for the purpose of full understanding of that [suffering] under the Blessed One.
The holy life is lived in its true sense as neither suffering nor a noble truth.

Having applied this principle accordingly to the origin and the other [truths] as well, the analysis here should be understood according to the tetrads. Regarding the phrase "by way of emptiness, the singlefold, etc.":

first, by way of emptiness, all truths should be understood as empty in the ultimate sense because of the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who attains Nibbāna, or one who goes [to it]. Thus it is said:
"There is only suffering, but no one who suffers; there is action, but no agent is found.
There is extinction, but no person who has extinguished; there is the path, but no traveler is found.
Alternatively:
The first two [truths] are empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self; the state of "mine" is empty of those two alone.
The Path is devoid of permanence, pleasure, and self—thus it is empty in those respects.

Alternatively, the three [truths of suffering, origin, and the path] are empty of cessation, and cessation is empty of the remaining three. Or else, here the cause is empty of its fruit, as is the case with the Origin.

Because suffering does not exist in the path and cessation does not exist in the fruit, the fruit is not "pregnant" [with its cause], unlike the *prakṛti* of those who propound a primal nature (*pakativādī*).
Furthermore, the fruit is empty of causes because there is no conjunction (*asamavāya*) between the origin of suffering and the cessation and the path;

the fruit of a cause is not conjoined with its cause, unlike the dyads (*dviaṇuka*) and so forth of those who propound the conjunction of cause and fruit (*hetuphalasamavāyavādī*). Therefore, this is said:
Likewise, here cessation is empty of that [conditioned state], and even by that [cessation] Nibbāna is empty;
the cause is empty of the fruit, and the fruit is empty of that cause.
In this way, first of all, the determination of “emptiness” (suññatā) should be understood.
‘Of one kind, etc.’: here, all suffering is of one kind in its state of occurrence; it is of two kinds by way of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

it is of three kinds by way of the distinction between rebirth-existence in the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere; it is of four kinds by way of the distinction between the four nutriments;

it is of five kinds by way of the distinction between the five aggregates of clinging. Origination (*samudaya*) is also of one kind in its state of causing occurrence; it is of two kinds by way of being associated with or dissociated from views.

Craving is threefold according to the division of craving for sense-pleasures, existence, and non-existence; fourfold according to what is abandoned by the four paths; fivefold according to the division of delighting in form and so forth;
and sixfold according to the division of the six groups of craving. Cessation is also singlefold in its nature as the unconditioned element;
but figuratively, it is twofold as *sopādisesa* (with residue remaining) and *anupādisesa* (without residue remaining); threefold as the pacification of the three types of existence; and fourfold...
It is fourfold because it is to be realized by means of the four paths; fivefold because of the subsiding of the five kinds of delight;

sixfold because of the destruction of the six groups of craving. The path itself is singlefold because it is to be developed; twofold because of the distinction between serenity and insight, or the distinction between vision and development;
threefold because of the distinction of the three aggregates. For this [Nibbāna], being without parts, is like a kingdom compared to a city which has parts.
It is comprised within three aggregates. As it was said:
"Friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path does not comprise the three aggregates;
rather, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is comprised within the three aggregates. And as for that, friend Visākha..."
“Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
Right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha).
Right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).”
For here, the three beginning with right speech are virtue itself; therefore, they are included in the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) by way of their own nature (*sajātito*).
Although in the text the designation "aggregate of virtue" is made in the locative case, the meaning should nevertheless be understood in the instrumental sense.
However, among the three beginning with right effort, concentration, by its own inherent nature, [remains] one-pointedness upon the object.
He is unable to apply himself; however, when energy performs its function of exertion and mindfulness performs its function of non-forgetfulness, he becomes assisted by them and is able to do so.

In this regard, there is this simile: just as when three friends have entered a park intending to play at a festival, [one friend is like the mind, another like energy, and the third like mindfulness].
Suppose a man, seeing a single *campaka* tree in full bloom, were unable to reach it even by raising his hand.
Then a second person might lean down and offer his back; yet even standing upon that person’s back, he would still be unable to reach it because of the shaking.
Then another might offer his shoulder to him; standing upon the back of one and the shoulder of the other—
Just as one might climb onto the shoulder of a tree, pluck flowers as desired, and wear them while sporting under the stars—this should be understood in the same way.
For the three qualities beginning with right effort, which arise together, are like the three friends who have entered the park together;
the object is like the well-flowered *campaka* tree; and it is like being unable to grasp [the flowers] even by raising one's hand.
Concentration, being unable by its own nature to settle upon the object with one-pointedness, is like a companion who has turned his back and bent over;
mindfulness is like a companion standing by, leaning against his shoulder.
Just as another person, standing on the back of the first and clutching the shoulder of the second, is able to pick a flower as he pleases, so too...

In the same way, when energy performs its function of exertion and mindfulness performs its function of non-forgetfulness, concentration, having received their assistance, is able to settle upon the object with one-pointedness.
Therefore, it is concentration alone that is here included in the aggregate of concentration by way of its intrinsic nature (*sajātito*).
Effort and mindfulness, however, are included by way of their functional activity (*kiriyato*).

Even in the case of right view and right intention, wisdom is unable by its own nature to determine the object as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self" without first striking at it with thought. How so?
Just as a money-changer, though he wishes to examine all sides of a coin while holding it in his hand, cannot do so merely by the surface of his eye;
Just as one is able to turn [a coin] over, and having turned it over again and again with the joints of the fingers, is able to look at it from this side and that,
even so wisdom is not able by its own nature to determine the object according to its characteristics such as impermanence;
rather, it does so through *vitakka* (initial application), which has the characteristic of directing [the mind] and the function of striking and rubbing, as if striking and turning [the object].

Just as one who has taken [something] repeatedly is able to determine that it has indeed been given, so too here, right view alone is included in the aggregate of wisdom by way of its intrinsic nature (*sajātito*), whereas right intention is included by way of its function (*kiriyato*).
Thus, the path is comprised by these three aggregates. Therefore it was said: "It is threefold, according to the division into the three aggregates."
It is fourfold by way of the path of stream-entry and so forth.

Furthermore, all the truths are of one kind because they are non-false or because they are to be directly known; they are of two kinds as mundane and supramundane, and as conditioned and unconditioned;
they are of three kinds in terms of being abandonable by vision, abandonable by cultivation, or neither abandonable nor not-unnecessary-to-abandon.

And, they are fourfold according to the division beginning with "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*). Thus, in this context, the analysis by way of "the singlefold and so forth" should be understood.

Regarding "by way of similar and dissimilar": all the truths are similar to one another because they are non-false (*avitatha*), empty of self (*attasuñña*), and difficult to penetrate. As it is said:
"What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult or more hard to accomplish..."

“Which would be more difficult and more hard to accomplish: one who, from afar, were to shoot an arrow through the narrow opening of a palm-leaf with such precision that it followed arrow after arrow without missing, or one who were to pierce the tip of a hair split sevenfold with the tip of another hair?”—“Venerable sir, this latter is indeed more difficult and more hard to accomplish:
one who [pierces] the tip of a hair split sevenfold with the tip of another hair.”

“...should penetrate it. [The Buddha said: “Ānanda, those who penetrate this as it really is—‘This is suffering’... [and so on] ...penetrate what is even more difficult to penetrate than that, namely, those who penetrate as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
[They are] dissimilar by way of the definition of their specific characteristics. And the first two are similar in the sense of being difficult to fathom because of their profundity.

The first two are similar because they are mundane (*lokiya*) and subject to taints (*sāsava*), and dissimilar because they differ as fruit and cause, and because one is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) while the other is to be abandoned (*pahātabba*).
The last two are also similar in that they are supramundane (*lokuttara*) and free from taints (*anāsava*), being difficult to fathom in their profound sense;

yet they are dissimilar because they differ as object and subject, and because one is to be realized (*sacchikātabba*) while the other is to be developed (*bhāvetabba*). Furthermore, the first and third are also similar.

They are similar by way of their fruit, but dissimilar by way of the conditioned and the unconditioned. Furthermore, the second and fourth are similar by way of their designation as causes, but dissimilar by way of being exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.
Moreover, the first and fourth are similar by way of being conditioned, but dissimilar by way of being mundane or supramundane.
And the second and third are similar by way of being neither-learner-nor-non-learner states, but dissimilar...
"By way of having an object and not having an object— thus, through such modes and methods,
the wise one should discern the similarity and dissimilarity of the Noble Truths."
The commentary on the summary of the Suttantabhājanīya is finished.
1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Suffering:
The Exposition of Birth.
190. Now, in order to explain in detail the suffering and other truths that were briefly mentioned, the section of the exposition beginning with "What therein is the noble truth of suffering?
Birth is suffering" is commenced. Therein, birth is to be understood, and the meaning of suffering in birth is to be understood;
likewise for aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

Association with the unpleasant is to be understood, as is dissociation from the pleasant; the meaning of suffering in association with the unpleasant and dissociation from the pleasant is to be understood;
desire is to be understood, and the meaning of suffering in desire is to be understood; the aggregates are to be understood, and the meaning of suffering in the aggregates is to be understood.
In this regard, for the purpose of explaining the Noble Truth of Suffering, there is this matrix:

for this so-called suffering is manifold and of various kinds, namely: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, the suffering of formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, figurative suffering, and non-figurative suffering.
Therein, bodily and mental painful feelings are called "the suffering of suffering" because they are suffering both by their intrinsic nature and by name.
Pleasant feeling is called "the suffering of change" because it is a cause for the arising of suffering through transformation.
Equanimous feeling and all remaining formations of the three planes are called "the suffering of formations" because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. Likewise...
However, there is also oppression in the case of the paths and fruits.
Therefore, these states should be understood as "suffering due to formations" (*saṅkhāradukkha*) by virtue of being included within the truth of suffering.

Physical and mental affliction—such as earaches, toothaches, the fever born of lust, and the fever born of hatred—and so forth, are called "concealed suffering" because they must be known through inquiry and because the cause [of the pain] is not manifest.

It is called "unmanifest suffering" (apākaṭadukkha). Illness arising from the thirty-two types of judicial torture and so forth is called "unconcealed suffering" (appaṭicchannadukkha) because it must be known even without being asked about and because its cause is manifest; it is also called "manifest suffering" (pākaṭadukkha).
With the exception of the suffering of suffering itself, all the rest—birth and so forth—as it appears in the *Vibhaṅga* of the Truth of Suffering, [is included].

Because it serves as the basis for various types of suffering, it is called "suffering by way of figurative expression" (*pariyāya-dukkha*). "Suffering-as-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*) is called "suffering not by way of figurative expression" (*nippariyāya-dukkha*).
Standing upon these two terms—suffering by way of figurative expression and suffering not by way of figurative expression—the Noble Truth of Suffering should be explained.
And this Noble Truth appears in the Canon both in brief and in detail. In brief:

In a place where [the subject] has been introduced in brief, it is appropriate to explain it either briefly or in detail. However, in a place where it has been introduced in detail, it is appropriate to explain it only in detail, not briefly. Since this [subject] is introduced in detail at this point, it should be explained in detail.
Therefore, that which was asked in the section on the exposition (*niddesa-vāra*)—"Therein, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering?"—[is to be explained as follows].
Having taken up such phrases as “Birth, too, is suffering,” it was said: “Birth is to be understood; the meaning of suffering in birth is to be understood,” and so forth.
Therein, birth and the other factors should first be understood by way of this word-commentary (padabhājanīya): “Therein, what is birth?
That which is the birth, the being born, of various beings into their respective classes of beings.”
191. Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning: “Of those various beings” is a concise, general designation for many beings.

For if one were to say, “The birth of Devadatta, the birth of Somadatta,” and so on, even if it were spoken for a whole day, beings would never be fully exhausted, nor would the entire explanation of the other terms be accomplished. But by these [terms]...
By these two words, no being whatsoever remains uncomprised, nor is any explanation of the ultimate purpose left unestablished.
Therefore it is said: “Of those various beings. In the phrase “in this or that,” this is a common designation for the many classes of beings according to their respective births and destinies.
“In a class of beings” (sattanikāye) means in a group of beings, in a multitude of beings, in a collection of beings; such is the meaning.
"Birth" (*jāti*): this word *jāti* has multiple meanings. For instance, in the passage "one birth, two births," it occurs in the sense of existence (*bhava*).
In the passage "There are, Visākhā, those called Nigaṇṭhas, a class of recluses," it occurs in the sense of a school (*nikāya*).
In the passage "A grass called *tiriyā*, a species of grass, having grown from the navel, stood reaching up to the sky," it occurs in the sense of a designation (*paññatti*). "Birth" (*jāti*)...
“Included within two aggregates”—this refers to the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*).
“Bhikkhus, that first mind which arose in the mother’s womb, that first consciousness which appeared; from that as its basis, there was his birth”—this refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
“The Bodhisatta, Ānanda, had just been born”—this refers to the act of giving birth (*pasūti*). “Unreproached... [the rest of the passage follows].

Regarding the phrase "by way of birth" (*jātivādena*), here it refers to family. In the passage, "Sister, since I was born with noble birth" (*ariyāya jātiyā*), it refers to noble virtue (*ariyasīla*).
However, here [in the present context], this term applies to the first aggregates produced along with their concomitants.

Therefore, "birth" (*jāti*) in the sense of the process of being born is its specific intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapaccatta*); "rebirth" (*sañjāti*) is the same word augmented by a prefix in the sense of the process of being born again.
"Descent" (*okkanti*) is by way of descending (*okkamana*). Or, "birth" (*jāti*) is in the sense of being born; it is associated with the case of incomplete sense bases (*aparipuṇṇāyatana*).
"Rebirth" (*sañjāti*) is in the sense of being fully born; it is associated with the case of complete sense bases. "Descent" (*okkanti*) is in the sense of descending;

it is associated with the egg-born and the womb-born, for they descend into both the shell of the egg and the membrane of the womb, and while descending, they are as if entering into rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
They seize [the rebirth-linking]. In the sense of being produced, it is "production" (*abhinibbatti*).

That is applicable in the case of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, for they are produced having already become manifest. This, first of all, is the conventional explanation. Now follows the ultimate explanation.
For in the ultimate sense, it is only the aggregates (*khandhā*) that appear, not a "being" (*satta*). In this regard:

"And aggregates" (khandhānaṃ) should be understood as referring to the grasping of one aggregate in a one-aggregate existence, of four aggregates in a four-aggregate existence, and of five aggregates in a five-aggregate existence.
"Manifestation" (pātubhāvo) means arising. Regarding "bases" (āyatanānaṃ), here the inclusion should be understood according to the bases that arise in their respective locations.
"Acquisition" (paṭilābho) is simply the manifestation within the continuity (santati).
For it is precisely when they become manifest that they are said to be "obtained. This is called "birth" (jāti); this is what is designated by the term "birth.
Furthermore, its characteristic is the first manifestation in various states of existence; its function is to bring forth;
its manifestation is the emergence here from a past existence, or, by way of its fruit, the manifestation of the diversity of suffering.
Now, it must be understood that "birth has the characteristic of suffering. For this birth itself is not suffering;
rather, it is called suffering because it serves as the basis for the arising of suffering. But what kind of suffering does it serve as the basis for?

It is the suffering pertaining to the states of deprivation (āpāyika-dukkha), which was illustrated by the Blessed One through similes in such discourses as the *Bālapaṇḍita-sutta*, as well as the various types of suffering in the human world within the happy destinies (sugati), beginning with the descent into the womb (*gabbhokkantimūlaka*).
Suffering arises; this is the basis for all of it. Herein, this suffering—classified as beginning with that rooted in descent into the womb—is as follows:
for when this being is being reborn in a mother’s womb, he is not reborn among blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and so forth.
Rather, he is between the stomach below and the intestines above, amidst the abdominal membranes and the spinal vertebrae.
In a place of extreme confinement, thick darkness, permeated by the stench of various corpses, buffeted by winds carrying the most foul odors of impurity,
and utterly loathsome— a region of the belly— he is reborn like a worm among putrid fish, rotten gruel, cesspools, and the like. Having been reborn there,
for ten months he is cooked like a sealed pot by the heat arising from the mother’s womb.
Like a lump of dough being steamed, deprived of the ability to contract or extend its limbs, it experiences excessive suffering.
This, first of all, is the suffering rooted in the descent into the womb (*gabbhokkantimūlaka*).
Furthermore, when that [embryo] is in the hands of a drunken gambler, as it were, during the mother’s sudden stumbling, walking, sitting, standing, turning over, and so forth—
Like a goat in the hands of a snake-charmer, or like a young serpent, he experiences extreme suffering through such procedures as being dragged forward and backward, shaken, and tossed about;
and when his mother drinks cold water, he is as if fallen into a cold hell;
when she swallows hot gruel, rice, and so forth, he is as if surrounded by a rain of glowing coals; and when she swallows salt, sour liquids, and the like—
The intense suffering experienced like one undergoing judicial punishment such as being smeared with caustic lye is the "suffering rooted in the maintenance of the pregnancy.

Furthermore, the suffering that arises through cutting, tearing, and so forth, in a place unfit even for friends, ministers, or relatives to behold—a mother whose fetus has become stuck—is the "suffering rooted in the failure of the pregnancy. That which [arises] for her while she is giving birth...
As he is turned by the mother’s kamma-born winds and pushed along the birth canal— which is as terrifying as a precipice into hell—
and as he is being expelled through the extremely narrow opening of the womb like a great elephant through the hole of a palm tree,
suffering arises for him as he is crushed by the mountain-like contractions, like a being in hell.

— this is the suffering rooted in the process of birth. Furthermore, when the newborn’s delicate body—resembling a fresh wound—is subjected to being grasped by the hands, washed, bathed, rubbed with cloth, and so forth, the suffering that arises, comparable to being pierced by the point of a needle or the edge of a razor, is the suffering rooted in emerging from the mother’s womb. That which follows from there...

Furthermore, the suffering that arises for one who kills oneself during the course of existence; for one devoted to the practice of self-mortification and austerity through such means as the naked ascetic’s observances;
for one who refuses to eat out of anger; and for one who hangs oneself—this is suffering rooted in one's own initiative (*attūpakkamamūlaka*).
However, the suffering that arises for one who experiences killing, imprisonment, and so forth at the hands of others—this is suffering rooted in the initiative of another (*parūpakkamamūlaka*).
"It is suffering. Thus, this birth is the very basis for all this suffering. Therefore, it is said:
"If a being were not born in the hells, There would be no unbearable things such as the burning of fire there."
"Where could suffering find a footing?"—
thus the Sage said here that birth is suffering.
Suffering among animals [arises from] whips and goads...
How could that manifold suffering arising from blows with sticks and the like exist there without birth?
Even apart from that, birth itself is suffering.
Furthermore, among the petas, suffering is manifold,
arising from hunger, thirst, wind, heat, and so forth;
since that does not exist for one who is unborn there.
Therefore, the Sage has declared that birth is suffering.
So too is the suffering among the Asuras in the world-intervening realms, which are of intense darkness and unbearable cold.
There would be no existence there for him, nor would there be birth;
yet even that from which this birth arises is suffering.
And even the womb of a mother is like a hell of excrement.
A being who has long been subject to this [existence] attains even this most terrible suffering upon departing from here;
yet even this does not exist without birth— thus, indeed, this birth is suffering.
What is the use of much speaking?
Indeed, wherever it may be, there is never any suffering whatsoever here for one who is free from birth;
therefore, O Great Sage, [there is no suffering].
"‘Suffering’—this ‘birth’ he spoke of first of all. 192.

In the description of aging (*jarā*), "aging" (*jarā*) is the specific intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapaccatta*). "The state of decaying" (*jīraṇatā*) is a description of its mode. "Brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*) and so forth...
Three [terms] are descriptions of functions in relation to the passing of time; the latter two are descriptions of the natural state.

For by this term "aging" (*jarā*), it is illuminated according to its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); therefore, this is its description of intrinsic nature. By the term "decay" (*jīraṇatā*), it is [described] according to its mode; therefore, this is its description of mode.
By the term "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*), it is [described] according to the function of causing the teeth and nails to become broken upon the passing of time.
"Graying" (*pālicca*) is stated by way of the function of causing the hair of the head and body to become gray.
"Wrinkling of the skin" (*valittacatā*) is explained by way of the function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to become wrinkled.

Thus, these three—beginning with "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*)—are descriptions of its functions at the time of the passing of age. Because they have become manifest through the perception of these transformations, it is called "manifest aging" (*pākaṭajarā*).

It has been shown. For just as a path traversed by water, wind, fire, or by grass, trees, and so forth, becomes evident through their contact and destruction or through their burning, yet that traversed path is not those very waters and so on themselves;
even so, the path traversed by aging through the breaking and decay of the teeth and other parts is evident, and it is perceived even when one opens one's eyes.
Decay is not merely brokenness and so forth; for decay is not something cognizable by the eye.

However, by these two terms—"the dwindling of the life-span" and "the ripening of the faculties"—the natural process consisting of the exhaustion of the life-span and the ripening of the eye and other faculties is made manifest specifically at the time of passing away. Therefore, these latter two [terms]...

These should be understood as a description of their intrinsic nature (*pakatiniddesa*). In this context, because the life-span (*āyu*) of one who has reached old age diminishes, old age is described as "the destroyer of life" (*āyuno saṃhānī*) by way of a metaphorical designation of the result for the cause.
Because the sense-faculties, such as the eye, which were very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects during youth, become fully ripened and disordered when one reaches old age.
They are unable to grasp even their own gross objects; therefore, they are called "the ripening of the faculties" by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
Furthermore, all this aging thus described is twofold: manifest and concealed. Among these, in the case of the teeth and so forth...
Because the state of being broken and so forth is visible among material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), aging among them is called "manifest aging" (*pākaṭajarā*).
However, because such a transformation is not visible among immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), aging among them is called "concealed aging" (*paṭicchannajarā*).

In this context, that which is seen as the state of being broken and so forth is simply the color (*vaṇṇa*) of such things as teeth, because they are easily discernible; having seen that with the eye, one [perceives it] through the mind-door (*manodvāra*).

Having reflected, "These teeth have been struck down by old age," one knows old age; it is like observing the horns of cattle and other such things tied up on the bank of a river and knowing that there is water beneath them.

Furthermore, this old age is twofold: it is both "without interval" (avīci) and "with interval" (savīci). In this regard, [it is seen] in gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so forth, as well as in those with weak sense-faculties and the like.

Because the specific variations in color and so forth are difficult to discern among both living beings—such as in their flowers, fruits, and sprouts—and non-living things, aging is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīci-jarā*);

the meaning is that it is continuous aging. However, because those aforementioned specific variations in color and so forth are easy to discern among other things, aging is called "interrupted aging" (*savīci-jarā*).
In this context, aging with intervals should be illustrated by way of both the acquired and the unacquired:
for infants, first of all, what are called milk-teeth appear; these are not firm. When they have fallen out, teeth appear again.
These are white at first, but when struck by the wind of aging, they turn black. [The same applies to] the hair.
However, at the very beginning, they are copper-colored, black, and white. But the skin is reddish.
As they grow and grow, the whiteness of the white parts and the blackness of the black parts become apparent; yet, when struck by the wind of old age, it takes on wrinkles.
Just as all grain is white when first sown, but later turns blue, so too [does the skin change] through the wind of old age.
But at the time it is struck, it becomes pale. It is indeed appropriate to illustrate this with the sprout of a mango as well.
This is called "aging" (*jarā*); this is what is designated by the term "aging. Furthermore, its characteristic is the maturation of the aggregates; its function is to bring about death;
and its manifestation is the destruction of youth.
Regarding the statement, “The meaning of suffering should be understood through aging”: here, this [aging] itself is not suffering;
rather, it is called suffering because it is the basis for suffering. For what kind of suffering? For both bodily suffering and mental suffering (domanassa-dukkha).
For the physical frame of one who has aged becomes as weak as an old cart; whether standing, walking, or sitting—
Or, while he is speaking, a powerful bodily pain arises; or, no longer perceiving his wife and children as before, mental distress arises.
Thus, it should be understood as "suffering" because it serves as the basis for both these types of suffering. Furthermore:
Because of the slackening of the limbs and the transformation of the sense faculties;
Through the destruction of youth, the impairment of strength,
the separation from one's own wife and children and from mindfulness and the like,
through being offensive, and through further falling into folly.
Whatever suffering a mortal experiences, whether physical or mental—all this has aging as its cause; therefore, aging is suffering.
The Exposition of Death.

193. In the exposition of death (*maraṇaniddesa*): *cuti* (falling away) is by way of the process of passing away. This is a general term for the falling away of the aggregates, whether one, four, or five.

"The state of falling away" (*cavanatā*) is an indication of the characteristic by means of an abstract noun. "Dissolution" (*bhedo*) is a demonstration of the arising of the breakup of the aggregates at the moment of death.
"Disappearance" (*antaradhāna*) refers to the aggregates at the moment of death, which have broken up like a broken jar, by whatever method of description.
This is an exposition of the impossibility [of escape]. "Death" (maccu) refers to death known as "Māra. "Kāla" means the Ender;
his activity is "kālakiriyā" (the act of passing away). Up to this point, conventional death has been illustrated.

Now, in order to illustrate it according to the ultimate sense (paramattha), he said: "The breaking up of the aggregates," and so forth. For, in the ultimate sense, it is only the aggregates that [constitute death].

The aggregates break up, but no so-called "being" dies at all. However, when the aggregates are breaking up, there is the conventional expression that "a being dies," and when they have broken up, that "the being is dead.
And here, the breaking up of the aggregates occurs by way of the four- or five-aggregate planes, while the laying down of the corpse occurs by way of the one-aggregate plane;
or else, the breaking up of the aggregates occurs by way of the four-aggregate plane, while the laying down of the corpse occurs by way of the remaining two.
The laying down [of the body] is to be understood. Why? Because in both states of existence there occurs the laying down of the physical frame, which is reckoned as the material body (*rūpakāya*).

Alternatively, because in the realms of the Four Great Kings and so forth, the aggregates (*khandha*) simply break up and nothing at all is laid down, the breaking up of the aggregates is described with reference to those realms.
In the human realm and so forth, there is the laying down of the physical frame. And here, it is because of the act of laying down the physical frame that [the term is used].
Death is described as "the casting off of the physical body.
By the phrase "the cutting off of the life-faculty," it is shown that what is called death applies only to that which is bound by faculties;
there is no such thing as death for that which is not bound by faculties. Expressions such as "the crop is dead" or "the tree is dead" are merely conventional designations.
In terms of meaning, however, such statements merely illustrate the state of exhaustion and passing away of crops and the like.
"This is called death"—all of this is designated as "death.

Furthermore, one should understand that there is also this classification: momentary death (*khaṇika-maraṇa*), conventional death (*sammuti-maraṇa*), and death by total cutting off (*samuccheda-maraṇa*).
In this context, "momentary death" (*khaṇikamaraṇa*) refers to the dissolution of material and immaterial phenomena during the course of existence (*pavatta*).

"Tisso has died, Phusso has died"—this is called "conventional death" (*sammutimaraṇa*). The passing away of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), without further rebirth-linking, is called "death by eradication" (*samucchedamaraṇa*).

However, in this present sense, conventional death is intended. [The other types are] death at the exhaustion of birth (*jātikkhayamaraṇa*) and death by means of an external instrument (*upakkamamaraṇa*).
It is also called death by exhaustion of life, death by exhaustion of merit, and death by exhaustion of both. Its characteristic is falling away;
its function is separation; it is manifested as being parted from what one possesses.
As for the statement, "The meaning of suffering should be understood in relation to death," this [death] itself is not suffering; rather, it is the cause of suffering.
However, it is called "suffering" by way of being the basis for suffering.

For even bodily feelings at the point of death, like a burning grass torch held against a headwind, consume the body. And at the time when the signs of hell and so forth appear, powerful mental distress arises.
Thus, it should be understood that both of these are "suffering" by way of being the basis for suffering. Moreover—
For one who contemplates the signs of evil, such as wicked deeds,
and for the fortunate one who cannot endure separation from beloved objects—
the mental suffering experienced by one who is dying is, without distinction, the same.
And for all [beings], whatever bodily suffering there is— such as the severing of joints and ligaments—
that arises for those whose vital spots (*marmans*) are being pierced, which is unbearable and incurable: this is the source of that suffering.
"Death is the basis for this; therefore it is spoken of simply as 'suffering.
Furthermore, these things called birth, aging, and death roam about seeking an opening in these beings, like murderous enemies.
For just as when a man has three enemies roaming about seeking an opening, one might say:
“I will praise a certain forest by name, take this [man], and go there; for me, there is nothing difficult about this.
The second would say, “When you have taken him and gone, I will beat him and make him weak;
for me, there is nothing difficult about this. The third would say, “When you have beaten him in this [forest]...”
"Let the decapitation of me with a sharp sword while I am rendered weak be my burden. Having spoken thus, they would do exactly so.

In this context, just as the first enemy, after praising the forest, took him and went there, so too is the duty of birth (jāti) to cast one out from the circle of dear friends and relatives and cause one to be reborn anywhere at all.

The function of aging should be understood as being like the weakening of a second person by beating him; it consists in causing the aggregates that have arisen to fall into a state of dependence on others and a destiny toward the bed of death.
The function of death should be understood as being like the decapitation of a third person with a sharp sword; it consists in bringing about the destruction of life.
Furthermore, in this context, the suffering of birth should be regarded as like entering a great wilderness fraught with danger;
the suffering of aging should be regarded as like the weakness of one deprived of food and drink;
and the suffering of death should be regarded as like bringing ruin and calamity through wild beasts and the like upon a weak person whose progress in maintaining the postures has been thwarted.
194. In the exposition of sorrow (*soka-niddesa*), "calamity" (*byasana*) means that which casts away or destroys welfare and happiness.
"Calamity of relatives" (*ñātibyasana*) means the ruin or destruction of relatives due to thieves, disease, fear, and so forth. By that calamity of relatives...
"Of one who is touched" (*phuṭṭhassa*) means of one who is overwhelmed, overpowered, or possessed; this is the meaning. The same principle applies to the others as well.
However, this is the distinction: the misfortune of wealth is "wealth-misfortune" (*bhogabyasana*);

the meaning is the loss or destruction of wealth through kings, thieves, and so forth. Disease itself is the misfortune, "disease-misfortune" (*rogabyasana*); for disease "misfortunes" (*byasati*), that is, destroys health.
*Byasana* (ruin). *Sīlabyasana* is the ruin of virtue; it is a name for immorality (*dussīlya*).
A view that arises destroying right view is itself the ruin, namely *diṭṭhibyasana*.

Here, the first two are unconditioned (*anipphanna*), while the latter three are conditioned (*nipphanna*) and struck by the three characteristics. Furthermore, the first three are neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
The two calamities of virtue and view are unwholesome.
"By one or another" means by whichever among those already mentioned or by whichever among those not yet mentioned, such as the calamities of friends and relatives.
"Of one who is possessed" means of one who is pursued [by them] and not released from them. "By one or another painful state" means...
By whatever cause sorrow and suffering arise. "Sorrow" (*soka*) means sorrow by way of the act of grieving; this is the specific intrinsic nature of the sorrow produced by those causes.
"Grieving" (*socanā*) is the manner of grieving. "State of having grieved" (*socitatta*) is the condition of having grieved.
"Internal sorrow" (*antosoka*) is sorrow within; the second term is augmented by the prefix *anta-*. For that [sorrow] is indeed within.
Because it arises as if drying up and completely parching [the mind], it is called "inner grief, inner parching.
"The burning of the mind" refers to the manner in which the consciousness is consumed. For when grief arises, like a fire, it burns and scorches the mind;
it causes one to say, "My mind is burning, nothing occurs to me. Thus, one is pained.
The mind is *dummana*; its state is *domanassa*. In the sense of having entered [into the heart], sorrow itself is a dart, thus it is "the dart of sorrow" (*sokasalla*).
This is called "sorrow"; this is what is designated by the name "sorrow.

Although this, in its actual meaning, is indeed the feeling of mental distress (*domanassavedanā*), nevertheless, it is characterized by inward brooding, has the function of consuming the mind, and is manifested as constant grieving.

Regarding the statement, “The meaning of sorrow (*soka*) is to be understood as suffering (*dukkha*”), it is called “suffering” here both because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is suffering and because it serves as the basis for suffering.
Which suffering? It is bodily suffering and, at the moment of the impulsion (*javana*), the suffering of mental grief (*domanassa*).
For through the force of sorrow, a great boil arises in the heart; having ripened, it bursts.
Either black blood issues from his mouth, or a powerful bodily pain arises.
Furthermore, as he thinks, "So many of my kinsmen have come to destruction; so much of my wealth has perished," a powerful mental grief arises.
Thus, this should be understood as suffering by virtue of being the basis for these two kinds of suffering. Moreover—
Sorrow pierces the hearts of beings like a dart;
it burns intensely, like an iron arrow heated in fire.
Furthermore, it brings about the breaking apart of disease, old age, and death.
“Because there is manifold suffering, therefore it is called ‘suffering.
(195) In the exposition of lamentation:
“My daughter! My son!”—thus, naming them one by one, they wail and weep.
"By this they cry out," thus it is *ādeva*. "Crying out again and again after having repeatedly praised various qualities," thus it is *parideva*.
The two pairs of words following that are stated by way of describing the manner and the cultivation of the preceding pair. *Vācā* means speech.
*Palāpa* is empty, meaningless speech. It is "disfigured" (*virūpa*) by way of being half-spoken, spoken otherwise, and so forth.
"Palāpa" means empty talk; "vippalāpa" means the same. "Lālappati" is speaking again and again. The manner of such speaking is "lālappanā.
The state of one who has spoken thus is "lālappitattaṃ. This is called "parideva"; this is what is designated by the term "lamentation.
It has the characteristic of repeated wailing; its function is the proclaiming of virtues and faults; it is manifested as agitation.
Regarding the statement, “Lamentation should be understood as having the sense of suffering (*dukkha*”), this too is not itself suffering;
rather, it is called suffering because it serves as the basis for bodily pain and the suffering of mental distress (*domanassa*).
For one who laments strikes his own limbs with his fists, beats and crushes his chest with both hands, and even clashes his head against a wall. Therefore, for him—
A powerful bodily pain arises. He reflects on such things as, "So many of my kinsmen have gone to destruction, decline, and passed away.
Consequently, a powerful mental grief arises. Thus, it should be understood as suffering by way of being the basis for both these types of suffering. Moreover—
One who is struck by the dart of sorrow and wails aloud encounters even greater and more excessive suffering, born from the parching of the throat, lips,
and palate, which is difficult to endure.
"‘Suffering’—by this the Blessed One meant lamentation.
This is the exposition of suffering and mental grief (196–197).

Since the exposition of suffering and mental grief has already been described in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*, it is well known. Furthermore, their characteristics and other features have already been stated therein.

Regarding the statement, “The meaning of suffering should be understood in the case of physical pain; the meaning of suffering should be understood in the case of mental grief,” both of these are called “suffering” because they are themselves suffering and because they serve as the basis for bodily and mental suffering.
For instance, in the case of one who is pained by the cutting off of hands and feet or ears and nose in an almshouse for the destitute...
For one who lies down with a skull of leavings placed before him, intense physical pain arises as maggots emerge from the openings of his wounds;
and seeing the great multitude sporting under the stars, adorned with garments dyed in various colors and wearing permitted ornaments, intense mental distress arises.
In this way, first of all, the state of being the basis for both types of suffering within suffering should be understood. Furthermore—
Because it oppresses this bodily suffering and, moreover, mental suffering even more,
it is specifically called "suffering. Furthermore,
those afflicted by mental suffering tear out their hair, beat their breasts, twist and wriggle about.
They throw themselves down precipices; they take up weapons; they eat poison; they hang themselves with ropes; they enter fire.
Thus, being remorseful for various mistaken actions and with their minds burning, they reflect.
In this way, it should be understood that mental grief (domanassa) is the basis for both kinds of suffering. Furthermore—
Because it oppresses the mind and brings about oppression of the body, it is called "suffering" (dukkha) and also "mental distress" (domanassa);
thus, from that [suffering], mental distress arises. This is the exposition of despair (upāyāsa).
198. In the exposition of despair (*upāyāsa*): it is "exertion" (*āyāsa*) in the sense of being a source of weariness;

this is the name for the exhaustion of the mind that occurs in the mode of sinking and despondency. Intense exertion is "despair" (*upāyāsa*). The state of having been exerted is "the state of being exerted" (*āyāsitatta*); the state of having been despaired is "the state of being despaired" (*upāyāsitatta*).
This is called "despair"—this is what is designated as despair. Furthermore, its characteristic is distraction, and its function is sighing.
It is manifested as despondency.
Regarding the statement, “The meaning of despair should be understood as suffering,” this too is not itself suffering;
