rather, it is called suffering because it serves as the basis for both types of suffering. For instance, when a king, being enraged, strips one of power and deprives them of their children and brothers—

For those who, having entered the forest out of fear of being commanded to be executed, remain hidden there and have fallen into great despair, intense bodily suffering arises from lying down in pain and sitting in pain.
Furthermore, as they think, "So many of our kinsmen have been lost, so much wealth has been destroyed," intense mental grief arises.
Thus, for both of these [types of people], there are two kinds of suffering.
It should be understood as suffering by way of being its basis. Furthermore:
Because it excessively burns the mind and withers the body, the suffering that despair produces is therefore called suffering.
And here, sorrow (*soka*) should be regarded as like the cooking of oil and other substances within a vessel by a mild fire;
lamentation (*parideva*) as like the overflowing of what is being cooked by a fierce fire out of the vessel;
and despair (*upāyāsa*) as like the continued cooking of what has overflowed and can no longer even remain outside, until it is completely consumed within the vessel itself.
199. In the exposition on association with the unloved (*appiyasampayoga-niddesa*): "Of whom" (*yassa*) means "of those who belong to him. "Unwanted" (*aniṭṭhā*) means not sought after.
Whether they have been sought or not sought, this is merely a name for objects that are disagreeable. They do not move toward the mind, nor do they enter it.

Unpleasant (*akanta*). They are not dear to the mind, nor do they increase the mind’s favor, thus they are disagreeable (*amanāpa*). The terms "forms" (*rūpa*) and so forth are a demonstration of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Those who desire or wish for what is harmful are "those who desire harm" (*anatthakāma*). Those who desire or wish for what is detrimental are "those who desire detriment" (*ahitakāma*).

Those who desire or wish for discomfort and an unhappy state of being are "those who desire discomfort" (*aphāsukakāma*). [They oppose] the security, fearlessness, and turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) from the four yokes (*yoga*).
They do not desire it; rather, they desire only the fearful round of existence (*saṃsāra*). Thus, they are "those who desire the yoke and security" (*āyogakkhemakāmā*).

Furthermore, because they do not desire the benefit (*attha*) consisting of the growth of faith and the other [faculties], and because they desire the disadvantage (*anattha*) consisting of the decline of those very same things, they are "those who desire what is harmful" (*anatthakāmā*). This is also because they do not desire the welfare (*hita*) that serves as the means for faith and the others.

Because they desire what is harmful—which serves as a means for the loss of faith and so forth—they are "those who desire harm. Because they do not desire dwelling in comfort but rather desire dwelling in discomfort, they are "those who desire discomfort.
Because they do not desire anyone who is fearless but rather desire fear, they are "those who desire lack of security from the yoke";
such is the meaning to be understood here.
*Saṅgati* means meeting together after having gone [to one place]. *Samāgama* means meeting with those who have arrived. *Samodhāna* means being together in standing, sitting, and so forth.
*Missībhāva* means performing all activities together. This is the application according to sentient beings (*sattavasena*).

However, whatever is applicable according to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāravasena*) should be understood. "This is called" means this is what is termed "association with the unpleasant" (*appiyasampayoga*).
Thus, it has the characteristic of being a combination of undesirable things; its function is to cause mental distress;
and it is manifested as a state of misfortune. In terms of its actual nature, there is no single dhamma called "suffering.

It is merely called "suffering" because it serves as the basis for both kinds of suffering (bodily and mental) in those associated with what is disagreeable. For when undesirable objects come together, they lead to piercing, cutting, cleaving, and so forth.
They produce bodily suffering as well, and mental suffering because they generate agitation. Therefore this is said:
"Upon seeing what is unpleasant, suffering first arises in the mind;
thereafter, it arises in the body through the application [of that mental state] in this world."
Therefore, it should be understood that by way of its basis,
even among the two types of suffering, that which was called "suffering" by the Great Seer is the meeting with what is unpleasant.
This is the exposition on separation from the beloved.
200. The exposition on separation from the beloved (*piyavippayoganiddesa*) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "mother" (*mātā*) is spoken here in order to show those who desire one's welfare in their own form. In that context: she cherishes (*mamāyati*) him, thus she is a mother (*mātā*); he loves (*piyāyati*) him, thus he is a father (*pitā*);

he shares (*bhajati*) with him, thus he is a brother (*bhātā*); likewise for a sister (*bhaginī*). They feel loving-kindness (*mettāyanti*), thus they are friends (*mittā*); or, they measure (*minanti*) [him], thus they are friends; they include him within all their secrets.
This is the meaning. They are called *amaccā* because they are together (*amā*) in the sense of sharing in duties and obligations.

They are called *ñātī* because they know (*jānanti*) or are known as "this one is our own. They are called *sālohitā* because they are connected by blood. Thus these terms should be understood according to their meanings.
"This is called" means this is what is designated as separation from the beloved. Its characteristic is the separation from a desired object.
Its essence is the production of sorrow, and its manifestation is calamity.
In terms of its actual nature, there is no single dhamma called "suffering" (dukkha).

It is merely called "suffering" because it serves as the basis for both kinds of suffering for those separated from what is dear. For when desirable objects are lost, they cause the body to wither, waste away, and so forth.
They produce bodily suffering as well, and mental suffering because they cause one to lament, thinking, "What we once had is no longer ours. Therefore it is said:
"Because of separation from relatives, wealth, and so forth, fools, pierced by the arrow of sorrow, are tormented here and there;
therefore, separation from what is dear is considered suffering."
201. In the exposition of desire (*icchā-niddesa*): "Of things subject to birth" means of those whose nature is birth, whose inherent character is birth.
"Desire arises" means craving (*taṇhā*) arises. "O, may it be! is an aspiration (*patthanā*). "But this is not to be attained by mere desire" refers to that which...

“O, may we not be subject to birth, and may birth not come upon us!”—thus, the state of being non-subject-to-birth existing in virtuous ones who have abandoned the origin [of suffering], and the non-arrival of birth existing in those who have attained final Nibbāna, is what is desired.
Yet, even for one who desires this, it cannot be reached without the cultivation of the Path; and for one who does not desire it, [it is reached] through that very cultivation.
That which is to be attained cannot be called "attained" merely by wishing for it.

The phrase "this too" (*idampi*)—the particle *pi* is used here to include the remaining items mentioned below—means that whatever object one desires but cannot obtain through any means, that very desire for an unobtainable object should be understood as suffering.
This same principle applies to the passages beginning with "those subject to aging" (*jarādhammānaṃ*), and so forth.
Thus, in this context, the very desire for things that cannot be obtained is what is called "not to get what one desires is suffering.
It has the characteristic of desiring unobtainable objects; its function is the pursuit of them; it is manifested as the failure to attain them.
Furthermore, it is called "suffering" because it serves as the basis for the two kinds of suffering. For instance, someone might think, "May I become a king..."
He is highly esteemed. Surrounded by a band of men who have been cut off or scattered, he enters a mountain ravine or a dense forest thicket.
Then the king, having learned of this occurrence, dispatches an army.
His followers being struck down by the king’s men, and himself having received wounds, he flees and enters among the trees or among the rocks. In that—
At such a time, a great cloud arises and a thick, dark, black storm sets in.
Then, creatures such as black ants surround it from all sides and seize it. Consequently, a powerful physical pain arises for it.
Thinking, "Because of me alone, so many kinsmen and possessions have been destroyed," a powerful mental grief arises.
It arises. Thus, this desire should be understood as suffering because it serves as the basis for both of these types of suffering. Furthermore:
"The distress consisting of frustration that arises here in the world for beings who, while longing for this or that, do not obtain it—[that is the suffering of not getting what one wants]."
The cause for his aspiration toward things that should not be obtained is precisely this;
therefore, the Conqueror declared suffering to be "the non-attainment of what one desires.
This concludes the exposition of the aggregates of clinging.
202. In the exposition of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the phrase "in brief" is said with reference to the teaching.
For suffering cannot be summarized as "there are this many hundreds of sufferings," or "this many thousands of sufferings," or "this many hundreds of thousands of sufferings";
however, the teaching can be summarized. Therefore, it is said: "There is nothing else whatsoever called suffering."
Summarizing the teaching as “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering,” he spoke thus.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is “What are they? The meaning of the terms “the aggregate of clinging to form,” and so forth, has already been explained in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*.
Regarding the statement, “The meaning of suffering should be understood for the aggregates”:
The suffering beginning with birth, which has been described here by the Tathāgata,
and that which has not been mentioned— all of this does not exist without these [aggregates].
Therefore, in brief, these are the aggregates of clinging.
"Suffering" is what was said by the Great Seer,
the teacher who points out the end of suffering. For in various ways, birth and the other [afflictions] relate to the five aggregates of clinging just as fire relates to fuel,
as blows relate to a target, as gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like relate to cattle, as birds relate to a field, and as village-robbers relate to a village.
Oppressing them, they arise within the very aggregates of clinging—just as grass, creepers, and the like arise upon the earth, or as flowers, fruits, and shoots arise upon trees.
Of these aggregates of clinging, birth is suffering at the beginning, aging is suffering in the middle, and death is suffering at the end.
Sorrow is the suffering of being scorched by the impact of the pain at the moment of death; lamentation is the suffering of wailing because one cannot endure that [pain].
Lamentation (*parideva*). Then, from contact with undesirable tactile objects characterized by the disturbance of the elements, there is bodily pain as suffering (*dukkha*).
For worldlings (*puthujjana*) who are afflicted by that, mental affliction as suffering arises due to the occurrence of aversion;

this is grief (*domanassa*). For those whose despondency is produced by the increase of sorrow and so forth, there is the suffering of brooding, which is despair (*upāyāsa*). For those who have met with the frustration of their desires...
The suffering of the frustration of desires and the non-attainment of what is desired— when the aggregates of clinging are examined in such various ways as these,
it cannot be fully described even in many eons if one were to point out each one individually;
yet all that suffering is contained within any five [aggregates], just as the taste of the waters of the entire ocean is contained within a single drop of water.
In order to show [the truth of suffering] by summarizing it within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the Blessed One said: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
The commentary on the exposition of the truth of suffering is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Origination (*samudayasacca*).
203. In the exposition of the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), "that which is this craving" (*yāyaṃ taṇhā*) refers to this very craving.

"Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobbhavikā*): renewed existence is the making of renewed existence (*punabbhava*); that which has the nature of renewed existence is "leading to renewed existence. Furthermore, it gives renewed existence, it conduces to renewed existence, and it produces existence again and again; thus it is "leading to renewed existence. Moreover, it is the giver of renewed existence.
There is that which does not give, yet there is that which leads to renewed existence and that which does not;

there is that which, once rebirth-linking has been given, consists merely in the ripening of the substrate. Whether it gives renewed existence or does not give it, whether it leads to renewed existence or does not lead to it, and whether it consists merely in the ripening of the substrate once rebirth-linking has been given—it is nevertheless called "leading to renewed existence."
She obtains [it]. "Accompanied by delight-and-lust" (*nandirāgasahagatā*) means accompanied by the delight-and-lust known as rejoicing (*abhinandana*);
it is said that she has reached a state of essential identity with delight-and-lust.

"Rejoicing here and there" (*tatratatrābhinandinī*) means rejoicing wherever there is a personal existence (*attabhāva*), or rejoicing here and there among objects such as visible forms (*rūpa*); she is one who delights in visible forms.
The meaning is: "delighting in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. *Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is "what is that? or "of what kind is it?
*Kāmataṇhā* means craving for sense pleasures (*kāme taṇhā*); this is a designation for attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
*Bhavataṇhā* means craving for existence (*bhave taṇhā*); it refers to that which arises by way of longing for existence and is accompanied by the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

This is a designation for passion for existence in the realms of form and formlessness, as well as for attachment to meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) is craving for non-existence;
it is a designation for passion accompanied by the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).
Now, in order to show the basis of that craving in detail, he said: "But that [craving]... and so forth. Therein, "arises" means:

It is born. It settles means it establishes itself through repeated occurrence. "Whatever in the world is of a pleasant nature and of a gratifying nature" refers to that which in the world has both a quality of being dear and a quality of being sweet.
In the passages beginning with "the eye in the world," beings who are attached to the eye and so forth in the world through the notion of "mine" become established in prosperity;
they [perceive] their own eye in mirrors and such, following the grasping of signs.
They consider the fivefold translucent clarity of the eyes to be like a jeweled lion-lattice opened within a golden palace;
they consider the ear to be like a silver tube or an anklet-string;
they consider the nose, which has acquired the designation "high-bridged," to be like a stalk of green palmyra placed upright; and they consider the tongue to be like a piece of red woolen cloth.
They consider their own body to have a soft, smooth, and sweet flavor; they consider it like a sal-tree trunk or a golden archway.
They consider their own mind to be unsurpassed and sublime compared to the minds of others. They consider their own form to be like the color of golden *kaṇikāra* flowers and the like;
their own sound to be like the gentle cooing of a rutting *karavīka* cuckoo or the resonance of a jeweled flute; [all these] things obtained by themselves.
They think, "Who else has such objects of smell and so forth arising from the four origins?
As they think thus, those forms of the eye and so forth become both dear and pleasant to them.
Then, craving that had not yet arisen arises in them toward those things, and that which had already arisen becomes firmly established through repeated occurrence.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises,” and so forth.
In this context, “when arising” means that whenever it arises, it arises therein. This same method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of the Origin is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation (Nirodhasaccaniddesa) 204.

Regarding the phrase "of that very craving" (*tassāyeva taṇhāya*) in the exposition of the truth of cessation: here, although it should have been said "of that very suffering" (*tasseva dukkhassa*), it is stated thus because suffering ceases only through the cessation of its origin (*samudaya*) and not otherwise.
As it has been said: "Just as when the root is firm and undamaged... (*Yathāpi mūle anupaddave daḷhe*)... [and so forth].
"Even a tree that has been cut down grows again; even so,
as long as the underlying tendency of craving is not uprooted,
this suffering arises again and again."
Therefore, in order to show that cessation of suffering by means of the cessation of its origin, he spoke thus. For the Tathāgatas conduct themselves like lions;
when they bring suffering to cessation and demonstrate the cessation of suffering, they apply themselves to the cause, not to the fruit.
But the followers of other sects conduct themselves like dogs; when they bring suffering to cessation and [demonstrate] the cessation of suffering...
Those who desire [liberation] practice both through self-mortification and through the fruit of that very teaching, rather than through its cause.
Because he lives like a lion, the Teacher, practicing through the cause, said: "That which is of that very...
and so forth. In this context, "of that very" refers to that very arising which was explained above by way of its establishment. "The fading away and cessation without remainder," and so on.
All these are indeed synonyms for Nibbāna. For it is by coming to Nibbāna that craving fades away and ceases without remainder;
therefore, it is called "the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving.
And because it is by coming to Nibbāna that craving is relinquished, renounced, released, and no longer clung to, therefore Nibbāna is "relinquishment" and "renunciation."

"Liberation, non-attachment"—thus it is said. For there is indeed only one *nibbāna*. However, its synonyms are numerous, being various designations for *nibbāna* according to their opposition to all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*), such as:

the cessation through the fading away without remainder, relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, and non-occurrence.
The signless, the wishless, the non-accumulation, the non-relinking, the non-arising, the non-going, the unborn, the ageless, the diseaseless,
the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentationless, the non-affliction,
the undefiled, and so forth. Now, regarding those objects in which craving— though cut off by the Path and having reached non-arising by resorting to Nibbāna— [remains].
The arising of that [defilement] has been shown; now, in order to show its non-existence in that very place, he said, "But as for this...
and so forth. In this regard, it is just as if a man, seeing a bitter gourd vine growing in a field, were to seek out its root starting from the tip and cut it;
then, having gradually withered away, it would reach a state of non-occurrence. Consequently, the bitter gourd would have ceased in that field.
It might be said that [craving] has been abandoned. In the same way, craving for the eye and so forth is like a bitter gourd in a field.
When its root is cut by the Noble Path, it reaches Nibbāna and goes to non-occurrence. Having thus gone, it is no longer perceived within those bases, just as the bitter gourd in the field.
And just as when bandits have been brought from the forest to the southern gate of the city...
They might be killed, and then it would be said that the robbers in the forest were either dead or slain;

even so, craving for the eye and the other [senses], which is like the robbers in the forest, has been extinguished upon reaching Nibbāna—like the robbers at the southern gate—and thus it is extinguished in Nibbāna.
But being thus extinguished, it is no longer perceived in those bases, just as the robbers in the forest are no longer seen.
Showing its cessation right there, he said: "The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world;
it is here that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; it is here that, when ceasing, it ceases," and so forth. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the exposition of the Truth of Cessation is finished.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Truth of the Path 205.
In the exposition of the truth of the path, the phrase "this very [path]" is a restriction intended to exclude any other path.

It is called "noble" (ariya) because it is remote from the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path, because it brings about the state of a noble one, and because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruits. There are eight factors.
"Assa" means "eightfold. This [path], like an army with four divisions or a musical ensemble with five components, consists merely of its parts;

there is nothing apart from the parts. It is called the "magga" (path) because it is sought by those desiring *nibbāna*, or because it seeks *nibbāna*, or because it proceeds while slaying the defilements (*kilesas*).
"Seyyathidaṃ" means "what is that? or "how is it constituted?"
Now, showing that there is no path apart from its constituent factors—that it is merely the factors themselves that constitute the path—he says:
"Right view... pe... right concentration. Therein, right view has the characteristic of seeing rightly; right intention has the characteristic of directing [the mind] rightly;
right speech has the characteristic of encompassing rightly; right action has the characteristic of originating rightly.
Right livelihood has the characteristic of complete purification. Right effort has the characteristic of exertion.
Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing. Right concentration has the characteristic of unification.
And each of these has three functions, as follows: first, right view also [performs its function] by others...

Together with their own opposing defilements, they abandon wrong view, take cessation as their object, and see the associated states through non-delusion by way of dispelling the delusion that conceals them.
Right intention and the others likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take cessation as their object. However, specifically in this case:
Right intention directs the co-nascent states; right speech correctly grasps them; right action correctly originates them;
right livelihood correctly purifies them; right effort correctly exerts them; right mindfulness correctly establishes them; and right concentration correctly steadies them.

To begin with, what is called right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) has various moments and various objects in its preliminary stage, but at the time of the Path (magga), it has a single moment and a single object.
However, by way of function, it receives four names, such as "knowledge regarding suffering" (dukkhe-ñāṇa) and so forth.

Right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) and the others likewise have various moments and various objects in their preliminary stages, but at the time of the Path, they have a single moment and a single object. Among these, right intention—
By way of its function, it receives three names beginning with "the intention of renunciation.

Right speech and the other two [right action and right livelihood] are, in the preliminary stage, both abstinences and volitions that occur at different moments and have different objects; however, at the moment of the Path, they are abstinences only.
As for right effort and right mindfulness—this pair also, by way of their functions as the four right strivings and the four foundations of mindfulness, [are so called].
It receives those names. Right concentration, however, is simply right concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path.

Thus, among these eight factors, because they are of great assistance to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna, the Blessed One taught right view first. For this has been described as "the lamp of wisdom" and "the sword of wisdom. Therefore—
By means of this right view—known as insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa)—during the preliminary stage, the practitioner destroys the darkness of ignorance and slays the thieves of the defilements;
thus, through safety, the yogāvacara reaches Nibbāna. Therefore it was said:
"Right view is taught first because it is of great assistance to the yogi who is practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna."
Right intention, however, is of great assistance to that [concentration], and therefore it is mentioned immediately after it. For just as a money-changer,
turning a coin over and over in his hand and examining it with his eye,

knows "this is counterfeit" or "this is genuine," so too the practitioner of yoga, having reflected with initial application (*vitakka*) during the preliminary stage, examines with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
He knows: “These phenomena belong to the sense sphere; these phenomena belong to the fine-material sphere, and so forth.

Or, just as a carpenter, having taken a great tree by its end and turned it over and over again, fashions it with an adze and brings it to his work, even so the practitioner of yoga, having applied thought to the phenomena presented by thought after thought, [examines them] with wisdom.

Having delimited them by way of such categories as, "These phenomena belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), these phenomena belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)," he applies them to action.
Therefore it was said: "Right intention, moreover, is of great assistance to that [right view]; therefore it is stated immediately after it.

And this [right intention] is helpful not only to right view, but also to right speech. As it is said: "Householder, having first thought and deliberated, one subsequently utters speech. Therefore, right speech is stated immediately after it.

However, because people in the world first agree by means of speech, saying, “We shall do this and that,” and then engage in their various tasks, speech is thus an aid to bodily action; therefore, right action is mentioned immediately after right speech.

Furthermore, since it is only for one who abandons the fourfold misconduct of speech and the threefold misconduct of body and fulfills both types of good conduct that the morality consisting of the eight factors of right livelihood is fulfilled—and not for anyone else—right livelihood is mentioned immediately after those two.
Thus, one who lives by a pure livelihood should not be satisfied merely with the thought,
"My livelihood is pure," and it is not fitting to dwell heedlessly; rather, to show that this energy must be exerted in all postures,
right effort is taught immediately thereafter.

Next, right mindfulness (sammāsati) is taught immediately after that in order to show that even by one who has initiated energy, mindfulness must be made well-established upon the four bases, beginning with the body. Furthermore,
it should be understood that right concentration (sammāsamādhi) is taught immediately after right mindfulness because mindfulness, when thus well-established,
is capable of concentrating the mind on a single object after having investigated the courses of those phenomena that are either helpful or unhelpful to concentration.
In the exposition of right view, the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths is shown by the passage beginning with “knowledge of suffering.
Therein, the first two truths are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and the latter two are the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*).

Among these, a bhikkhu’s application of the meditation subject is directed toward the round, whereas there is no such application toward the cessation of the round. For the first two truths consist of the five aggregates as suffering, and...
Having learned from the teacher both in brief—“Craving is the origin”—and in detail by way of the method beginning with “Which are the five aggregates?
The aggregate of form,” and so forth, the practitioner performs his work while repeatedly turning over [the teaching] with his speech.
As for the other two truths, [he understands]: “The truth of cessation is desirable and lovely.”
"The Noble Truth of the Path is agreeable, desirable, lovely, and pleasing"—thus he performs the work by the mere hearing [of this].
Performing the work in this way, he penetrates the four truths with a single penetration and realizes them with a single clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*):

he penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding (*pariññā*), origination through the penetration of abandoning (*pahāna*), and cessation through the penetration of realization (*sacchikiriyā*).

One penetrates the path through penetration by development; one fully understands suffering through the clear realization of full understanding... [and so on] ...one clearly realizes the path through the clear realization of development.
Thus, in the prior stage, there is for him penetration regarding two truths by way of learning, interrogation, hearing, retention, and comprehension;
regarding the other two, there is only penetration by way of hearing. In the subsequent stage, there is penetration regarding three truths by way of function, and regarding cessation—
Penetration of the object. In this context, all knowledge of penetration is supramundane;

however, the knowledge of hearing, retention, and comprehension is mundane and belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Reflective knowledge, moreover, belongs to one who has already attained the truths.

But this [monk] is a beginner; therefore, that [reflective knowledge] is not mentioned here. And prior to his full discernment, this monk thinks: "I fully understand suffering, I [fully understand] the origin..."
There is no mental application, attention, or reviewing consisting of the effortful thought, ‘I abandon [craving], I realize cessation, I develop the path’;
rather, this occurs starting from the moment of full comprehension. At a later stage, however, suffering has indeed been fully understood...
[and so on] ...the path has indeed been developed.
In this context, two truths are profound because they are difficult to see, and two are difficult to see because they are profound.
For the truth of suffering is evident in its arising; even when one encounters the striking of stumps or thorns and the like, it is subject to being called "Oh, what suffering!
The origin [of suffering] is also evident in its arising through such things as the desire to eat and the desire to consume. [This is so] from the penetration of their characteristics...
However, both [of these] are profound. Thus, they are profound because they are difficult to see.

As for the application toward the other two, it is like stretching out one's hand to grasp the peak of existence, like stretching out one's foot to touch the Avīci hell, and like joining the tip to the tip of a hair split a hundredfold. Thus, because they are profound...

They are difficult to see. Thus, with reference to the arising of preliminary-stage knowledge by way of apprehension and so forth regarding the four truths—which are profound because they are difficult to see and difficult to master—this statement beginning with “knowledge of suffering” was spoken. However, at the moment of penetration (*paṭivedha*), there is only a single knowledge.

In the exposition of right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*): “Escaped from sensual desire” is the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*). “Escaped from ill will” is the intention of non-ill will (*abyāpāda-saṅkappa*).
"Delivered from cruelty" refers to the intention of non-cruelty. In that regard, the thought of renunciation arises as it strikes down and cuts off the thought of sensual desire;
the thought of non-ill will [strikes down] the thought of ill will; and the thought of non-cruelty [strikes down] the thought of cruelty.
Furthermore, the thought of renunciation arises as the direct opposite of the thought of sensual desire.
Non-ill-will and non-cruelty thoughts [are the opposites] of ill-will and cruelty thoughts.
Therein, for the purpose of destroying the footprint of sensual-desire thought, the practitioner either contemplates sensual-desire thought itself or some other formation.
Then, at the moment of insight, the intention associated with insight, by way of its specific factor, [destroys that thought].
It arises making a strike and a severance against sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*), and having accelerated insight (*vipassanā*), it brings about the Path.
Then, at the moment of the Path, the intention (*saṅkappa*) associated with the Path arises, making a strike and a severance against sensual thought by way of its total eradication.
Likewise, for the purpose of striking and severing ill-will thought (*byāpādavitakka*), [it arises] against ill-will thought...
Or he comprehends another formation; or, for the purpose of striking down the thought of cruelty, he comprehends the thought of cruelty or another formation.
Then, at the moment of insight, everything should be applied in the same manner as before.
However, among the thirty-eight objects analyzed in the text for the three types of thoughts beginning with sensual desire, even a single meditation subject—
There is nothing that is not an opponent [to these thoughts]. However, exclusively for sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*), the first jhāna among the foul objects (*asubha*) is the opponent;
for ill-will thought (*byāpādavitakka*), the three or four jhānas of loving-kindness (*mettā*); and for cruelty thought (*vihiṃsāvitakka*), the three or four jhānas of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Therefore, for one who has performed the preliminary work on the foul objects and entered jhāna, at the moment of attainment:
Volition associated with jhāna arises as an antidote to sensual thought by way of suppression.

For one who establishes insight having made jhāna the basis, at the moment of insight, volition associated with insight arises as an antidote to sensual thought by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*). Having brought insight to its culmination...
When one is attaining the path, at the moment of the path, a thought associated with the path arises as the opposite of sensual thought by way of its complete eradication.
It should be understood that such an arisen state is called "the thought of renunciation" (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that after having performed the preliminary work for loving-kindness (*mettā*) and having performed the preliminary work for compassion (*karuṇā*), one enters into jhāna; thus, all [of this] is the same.

It should be applied in the same manner as before. Thus, it should be understood that what has arisen in this way is called "thought of non-ill-will" (abyāpāda-saṅkappa) and also called "thought of non-cruelty" (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa). In this way, these thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) and so forth are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of their arising by way of insight-meditation (vipassanā-jhāna);
however, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), regarding the unwholesome thought that has arisen in these three instances—
By means of establishing the word-breaks through the method of proving non-occurrence, while fulfilling the factor of the path, a single wholesome intention arises.
This is called right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*).

Furthermore, in the exposition of right speech (*sammāvācā*), because one abstains from false speech with one state of mind, and from malicious speech and so forth with another distinct state of mind, [they are distinct].
Therefore, while the fourfold abstentions are diverse in the preliminary stage, at the moment of the Path, there arises only a single wholesome abstention termed Right Speech (*sammāvācā*).

This fulfills the factor of the Path by way of preventing, through the severing of its basis, the fourfold unwholesome and immoral volition known as wrong speech (*micchāvācā*). This is what is called Right Speech.
In the exposition of right action (*sammākammanta*) as well, because one abstains from killing living beings with one state of consciousness,
from taking what is not given with another, and from sexual misconduct with yet another, these three abstinences are distinct in the preliminary stage. However, at the moment of the path,

by way of severing the continuity [of defilements] and accomplishing non-arising, they function through the cutting off of the threefold unwholesome and immoral volition known as wrong action (*micchākammanta*).

While fulfilling the factors of the path, there arises only one [factor] called right action, which consists in the abstinence from unwholesome deeds. This is what is known as right action (*sammākammanta*).
In the description of right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*): "here" means in this teaching; "noble disciple" means a disciple of the Noble One, the Buddha;
"having abandoned wrong livelihood" means having abandoned an evil way of life; "by right livelihood" means by a wholesome way of life praised by the Buddha.

"He makes his living" means he maintains the continuity of life. Here too, because one abstains from transgressions of the body-door by one consciousness and from transgressions of the speech-door by another, it arises at various moments during the preliminary stage.
However, at the moment of the Path, regarding the unwholesome volition of wrong livelihood that had arisen through the seven courses of action at the two doors:
By way of fulfilling the path factor through the establishment of non-arising according to the analysis of words, there arises precisely one wholesome abstention termed right livelihood.
This is what is called right livelihood.
The exposition of right effort will be made clear by way of a word-by-word commentary in the Vibhaṅga on the Right Strivings. This...

However, in the preliminary stage, it is obtained within various states of consciousness. For with one state of consciousness one exerts effort for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
with another, for the abandoning of arisen ones; and with yet another, for the arising of unarisen wholesome states;
and with another, for the stability of those that have arisen. But at the moment of the Path, it occurs within a single state of consciousness alone.
It is so obtained. For indeed, the single energy associated with the path receives four names in the sense of accomplishing the four functions.
The description of right mindfulness will also become clear through the word-by-word commentary in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga*.
And this [mindfulness] is also obtained in various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage; for one comprehends the body with one consciousness, and with another and yet another...
[The same applies to] feeling and the other [mental factors]. However, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), they are obtained within a single consciousness alone.
For mindfulness associated with the Path receives four names in the sense of accomplishing the four functions.
In the description of Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi), the four jhānas are distinct both in the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) and at the moment of the Path. In the preliminary stage...
They are diverse by way of attainment; at the moment of the path, they are diverse by way of the various paths.
For one person, the first path belongs to the first jhāna, and the second path and so forth may also belong to the first jhāna, or they may belong to any one of the second jhānas and so on.

For another person, the first path belongs to any one of the second jhānas and so on, while the second path and so forth may belong to any one of the second jhānas and so on, or they may belong to the first jhāna.
Or so it is. Thus, all four paths—whether similar, dissimilar, or partially similar—are [determined] by way of the jhāna.
However, this distinction occurs according to the rule of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*). First, according to the rule of the foundational jhāna:

for one who has attained the first jhāna, the path that arises when they emerge from the first jhāna and practice insight (*vipassanā*) is a first-jhāna path; its path-factors (*maggaṅga*) and enlightenment-factors (*bojjhaṅga*) [are likewise of the first jhāna].
In this case, however, they are indeed complete. For one who, having emerged from the second jhāna, develops insight, the path that arises belongs to the second jhāna;

here there are seven path-factors. For one who, having emerged from the third jhāna, develops insight, the path that arises belongs to the third jhāna; here there are seven path-factors and six enlightenment factors.
This same method applies from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is stated that in the formless realm, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise; however, these are supramundane (*lokuttara*), not mundane (*lokiya*).
How is this so? Even here, in the case of the first jhāna and the others, it is when one has emerged from them and attained the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*)...
For one who has developed an immaterial attainment and is reborn in the immaterial realms, the three paths arise there based on that very jhāna.
Thus, it is the foundational jhāna itself that determines [the path]. Some elders, however, say that "the aggregates which serve as the object for insight determine it.
Others say that "the inclination of the individual determines it. Still others say that "insight leading to emergence [determines it]."

They say, “It brings [the mind] to its proper course. The determination of their doctrine is to be understood according to the method already stated below, in the commentary on the Exposition of the Supramundane Terms in the Section on the Arising of Consciousness.

This is called right concentration: that one-pointedness (ekaggatā) within these four jhānas is called mundane right concentration in the prior stage, and supramundane right concentration in the subsequent stage. Thus, by way of the mundane and the supramundane—
The Blessed One taught the Truth of the Path.
In that regard, on the mundane path, all the factors of the path have as their object one or another of the six objects, according to their respective suitability.
On the supramundane path, however, for the noble [path] that proceeds toward the penetration of the Four Truths, [the factor of concentration] has Nibbāna as its object.
The eye of wisdom, right view, is that which eradicates the underlying tendency of ignorance.
For one endowed with such a view, right intention is the directing of the mind toward the state of Nibbāna associated with that [view], which eradicates the threefold wrong intention.
For one who thus sees and reflects, there is also [right speech] associated with that [view], which eradicates the fourfold verbal misconduct.

Abstention from wrong speech is right speech (*sammāvācā*). For one who abstains in that way, the abstention from the three kinds of bodily misconduct—which is associated with that [right speech] and cuts off wrong action (*micchākammanta*)—is right action (*sammākammanta*).

Right livelihood (*sammāājīva*) is the abstention from wrong livelihood associated with those same right speech and right action, which serves as their purification and cuts off hypocrisy and the like. Of this [path factor] designated as right speech, right action, and right livelihood...

For one established upon the plane of virtue, right effort—right exertion—is the application of energy that corresponds to and is associated with that virtue; it cuts off sloth and accomplishes the non-arising and abandoning of unwholesome states and the arising and maintenance of wholesome states as they arise.

For one who exerts himself in this way, there is likewise mindfulness associated with that effort which shakes off wrong mindfulness and accomplishes the contemplation of the body and so forth regarding the body and other objects.

And non-forgetfulness of the mind is right mindfulness. Thus, for one whose protection of the mind is well-established through unsurpassed mindfulness, the unification of mind associated with that [mindfulness] which eradicates wrong concentration is right concentration.
This is the supramundane noble eightfold path, which, together with the mundane path, is designated as "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."

Furthermore, this path is both *vijjā* (clear vision) and *caraṇa* (conduct), because right view and right intention are comprised within *vijjā*, while the remaining factors are comprised within *caraṇa*.

Likewise, it is both *samatha* (tranquility) and *vipassanā* (insight), because those two [factors] are comprised within the vehicle of insight (*vipassanā-yāna*), while the others are comprised within the vehicle of serenity (*samatha-yāna*).
Alternatively, it is both *samatha* and *vipassanā* because those two are comprised within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññā-khandha*), while the subsequent ones...

Because it is comprised of the three aggregates of virtue for the first three [trainings], and for the remainder by the aggregate of concentration and the trainings in higher wisdom, higher virtue, and higher mind, there are both the three aggregates and the three trainings. Endowed with these,
the noble disciple is like a traveler possessed of eyes capable of seeing and feet capable of walking— one who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*).
Having abandoned the two extremes— the pursuit of sensual pleasure by means of the vehicle of insight and the pursuit of self-mortification by means of the vehicle of serenity—
and having entered upon the Middle Way, he crushes the aggregate of delusion with the aggregate of wisdom,
the aggregate of hatred with the aggregate of virtue, and the aggregate of greed with the aggregate of concentration, through the training in higher wisdom.
Having attained the three excellences— perfection in wisdom, perfection in virtue through the training in higher morality, and perfection in concentration through the training in higher mind—
he realizes the deathless Nibbāna and enters the noble plane known as the "certainty of rightness," which is auspicious in its beginning,
middle, and end, and variegated with the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment as its jewels.
Commentary on the Suttanta-Bhājaniya.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya (206–214).
Now follows the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya. Therein, instead of saying "the Noble Truths," it is stated without omission:
In order to show the origin (samudaya) which is defined as the condition, it is said: "the four truths.

For if one were to say simply "the Noble Truths," the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots associated with the outflows (sāsavā), and the remaining wholesome states associated with the outflows would not be included. Moreover, it is not craving alone that brings about the origin of suffering.
These and all other remaining conditions, such as the defilements (kilesa), likewise bring about suffering.

Thus, because these conditions also bring about suffering, in order to show the origin (samudaya) comprehensively as being synonymous with "conditions," it is stated as "the four truths" rather than "the Noble Truths.
Furthermore, in the section of the detailed exposition (Niddesa), suffering is not explained first; rather, this is for the purpose of providing a thorough explanation of that very suffering.

The origin of suffering has been demonstrated. For when that has been demonstrated, the truth of suffering becomes easy to explain by way of the method beginning with the words, "and the remaining defilements.

Here, the truth of cessation is also demonstrated in five ways as the abandoning of craving, namely, "the abandoning of craving and of the remaining defilements," by way of the abandoning of the aforementioned origin.

Here, however, the truth of the path is presented merely as an illustration of the method of teaching analyzed in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* by way of the stream-entry path associated with the first jhāna. The distinctions of that method should be understood;
we shall explain them further below.
However, since it is not only the eightfold path that is the practice (*paṭipadā*),

for according to the statement, "But previously his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were already quite purified," even a fivefold path is taught as the practice by way of the individual's inclination;
therefore, in order to show that method, the fivefold set has also been explained.

And since it is not only the eightfold and fivefold paths that are the way, but rather the more than fifty associated states are also the way, the third all-inclusive section is set forth in order to demonstrate this principle.
In that context, the phrase "the remaining states are associated with the way leading to the cessation of suffering" is omitted. The rest...
It is exactly the same in all respects. Therein,
regarding the section on the Eightfold Path, among the five divisions beginning with "the abandoning of craving and the remaining defilements," first,
in the first division, at the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), there is the pure practice (suddhika-paṭipadā) and pure emptiness (suddhika-suññatā) in the application of jhāna.

In these five sections—the way of emptiness (*suññatapaṭipadā*), the pure wishless (*suddhika-appaṇihita*), and the way of the wishless (*appaṇihitapaṭipadā*)—there are ten methods by way of two sets of fourfold and fivefold methods respectively. The same applies to the remaining [sections]; thus, for the twenty types of misinterpretation (*abhinivesa*), there are two hundred methods.
These, multiplied fourfold by the four predominances (*adhipati*), become eight. Thus, there are two pure [methods] and [eight] with predominance.
"Eight" means that there are one thousand methods in total. And just as it is for the path of stream-entry, so it is for the remaining paths;
thus, there are four thousand methods. And just as there are four in the first section, so it is for the others;
thus, in the five sections of the Eightfold Chapter, there are twenty thousand methods. Likewise, in the Fivefold Chapter and in the All-Inclusive Chapter...
Thus, all sixty thousand methods were analyzed by the Teacher; however, the Pāḷi has come down in brief.
In this way, it should be understood that the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, consisting of three great sections and fifteen divisions, adorned with sixty thousand methods, has been expounded.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchaka). 215.
In the Section of Questions, the status of the four truths as wholesome and so forth is determined according to the same method explained in the Analysis of the Aggregates (Khandhavibhaṅga).

It should be understood. Regarding the triads of objects (*ārammaṇattika*), however, the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) has a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) when one relishes phenomena of the sense-sphere;
it has a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*) when one relishes sublime phenomena; and it has an indeterminate object (*navattabbārammaṇa*) when one relishes a concept (*paññatti*).

The truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) has a limited object when it arises directed toward phenomena of the sense-sphere; [it has a sublime object] when directed toward phenomena of the fine-material or immaterial spheres...
At the time of its arising directed toward a noble object, it has a sublime object; at the time of reviewing the nine supramundane states, it has an immeasurable object;
at the time of reviewing a conceptual designation (paṇṇatti), it has an indeterminate object.
As for the path-truth, by way of being a conascent cause, energy or investigation is always made predominant during the cultivation of the path, and thus the path is dominant through that cause.

When any one of the [four] mental states beginning with desire (*chanda*) is predominant, it is called "indeterminate" (*navattabba*). The truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) has the Path as its object (*maggārammaṇa*) at the time when Noble Ones review the Path;
it has the Path as its predominance (*magga-adhipati*) at the time when they review that very Path, holding it in esteem; and it is indeterminate at the time when they review other phenomena.
"Two truths" refers to the truths of suffering and its origin (*samudaya*). For these arise by taking as their object phenomena classified as past and so forth.
The objects are past and so forth. For one who relishes phenomena classified as internal and so on, the truth of origination has an internal object and so forth;
it should be understood that the truth of suffering may also have an indeterminate object at the time of the base of nothingness.
Thus, in this set of questions, two truths are mundane and two are supramundane. And as it is in this case, so too...
In the first two [divisions] as well. For by the Fully Enlightened One, in all three—the *Suttantabhājaniya* and the others—only mundane and supramundane truths were taught.
Thus, this *Saccavibhaṅga* too has been shown by dividing it after having extracted those three turnings.
From the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Sammohavinodanī*.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga) is finished.
5. Analysis of the Faculties (Indriyavibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition (Abhidhammabhājanīya).
219. Now, in the subsequent Analysis of the Faculties (*Indriyavibhaṅga*), "twenty-two" is the delimitation by number. "Faculties" (*indriyāni*) is the indication of the phenomena so delimited.
Now, showing them according to their specific forms, he says: "the eye-faculty," and so forth. Therein, it is the "eye-faculty" because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) at the eye-door.
It is the "body-faculty" because it exercises lordship at the doors of the ear, nose, tongue, and body. [It is the mind-faculty] because its characteristic is cognizing.
It exercises lordship (indaṭṭha) over the mind, thus it is the mind-faculty (manindriya). It exercises lordship over the state of femininity, thus it is the femininity-faculty (itthindriya).

It exercises lordship over the state of masculinity, thus it is the masculinity-faculty (purisindriya). It exercises lordship over the characteristic of preservation, thus it is the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).
It exercises lordship over the characteristic of pleasure, thus it is the pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya). [It exercises lordship] over the characteristics of pain, joy, grief, and equanimity...

It exercises lordship in the characteristic of equanimity, thus it is the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*). It exercises lordship in the characteristic of resolution, thus it is the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).

It exercises lordship in the characteristic of exertion, thus it is the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*). It exercises lordship in the characteristic of establishment, thus it is the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*).
It exercises lordship in the characteristic of non-distraction, thus it is the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*). [It exercises lordship] in the characteristic of seeing...

It exercises lordship over wisdom, thus it is the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*). It exercises lordship over the characteristic of knowing during the course of existence with the thought, "I shall know the unknown," thus it is the faculty of "I-shall-know-the-unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).
It exercises lordship over the further understanding of those very phenomena already known, thus it is the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*).
It exercises lordship over the state of one who has already known, thus it is the faculty of one who has known (*aññātāvindriya*).
Here, what is called the "Suttanta-bhājaniya" (the analysis according to the Discourses) is not included.
Why? Because these twenty-two faculties do not appear in this specific sequence within the Suttantas.

For in the Suttantas, two faculties are mentioned in some places, three in others, and five in still others; thus, there is no place where all twenty-two appear consecutively. This, then, is the point here.
This is the method according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). However, there is this other method:

"One should understand the exposition of these [factors] by way of their meaning, characteristics, and so forth, as well as their order, their divisions and non-divisions, their functions, and their planes."
In this context, the meaning of the eye and the other [faculties] has first been explained by way of such methods as: "It sees, therefore it is the eye.

Regarding the last three, however, the first is called the *anaññātaññassāmītindriya* (the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown") because it arises in one who has practiced with the thought, "In the prior stage, I shall know the deathless state or the Dhamma of the Four Truths which was previously unknown," and because it possesses the sense of a faculty (*indriya*).
It has been stated. The second is the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) because of its nature as a full comprehension and because it arises in the sense of a faculty.

The third is the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) because it arises only in one whose taints are destroyed and who has completed the task of knowledge regarding the four truths, and because it arises in the sense of a faculty.

But what is this so-called "sense of a faculty" (*indriyaṭṭha*)? The sense of a faculty is the sense of being a mark of a lord (*indaliṅgaṭṭha*); the sense of a faculty is the sense of being taught by a lord (*indadesitaṭṭha*).

The meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is the meaning of what is seen by the Lord (*inda*); the meaning of "faculty" is the meaning of what is permitted by the Lord; the meaning of "faculty" is the meaning of what is favored by the Lord. All of these meanings apply here as appropriate.
For the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the "Lord" (*inda*) because of his state of supreme sovereignty.
And wholesome and unwholesome karma [is the Lord] among karmas, because no one else possesses sovereignty over karmas. Therefore, in this context, those things produced by karma...

The faculties indicate wholesome and unwholesome karma; thus, they are "faculties" (*indriya*) in the sense of being signs of the lord (*indaliṅga*) and in the sense of being authorized by the lord (*indasiṭṭha*).

Furthermore, because all of these have been both revealed and fully awakened to by the Blessed One exactly as they are, they are "faculties" in the sense of being taught by the lord (*indadesita*) and in the sense of being seen by the lord (*indadiṭṭha*). By that very same Blessed One, the Lord of Sages (*muninda*), some...

Because some are cultivated for the sake of frequenting their objective fields (*gocara*) and others for the sake of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they are called "faculties" (*indriya*) in the sense of being "mastered" (*indajuṭṭha*).
Furthermore, these are faculties in the sense of sovereignty (*issariyattha*) known as predominance (*ādhipacca*).

For the predominance of the eye and so forth is established in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and the rest; for when that [faculty] is keen, [the consciousness] is keen, and when it is dull, it is dull. This...
This is the analysis of these [faculties] "by way of meaning.

Regarding the phrase "by way of characteristics, etc.," the meaning is that one should understand the analysis of the eye and the other faculties by means of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*).
Their characteristics and so forth are exactly as described in the method set forth below. For the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) and the others—
In terms of meaning, all four are simply non-delusion (*amoha*). The remaining factors are included therein by their very nature.

Regarding the "order," this too refers to the sequence of the teaching. In that regard, because the attainment of the plane of the Noble Ones occurs through the full understanding (*pariññā*) of internal phenomena, the faculties such as the eye-faculty, which are comprised within one's own personal existence (*attabhāva*), are taught first. Furthermore, that personal existence...
That phenomenon depending upon which one comes to be designated as "woman" or "man"—this is [the female faculty and the male faculty] for the purpose of illustration.
Since both of these two function in dependence upon the life-faculty, the life-faculty is mentioned next for the purpose of making this known.
As long as that [life-faculty] continues to proceed, there is no cessation of these feelings. Whatever...
The faculties of pleasure and so forth are mentioned next for the purpose of making known that all that is felt is either pleasure or pain.
Then, for the purpose of showing the practice—that these states must be developed for the sake of the cessation of that [feeling]—the faculties of faith and so forth are mentioned.
Finally, for the purpose of showing the fruitfulness of the practice—that through this practice this state first becomes manifest within oneself—the [following] is mentioned.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*). Because it is the fruit of that very [faculty] and because it must be developed immediately after it, the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) follows it.

Beyond this, for the purpose of making known that its attainment occurs through cultivation and that once it is attained there is nothing further to be done, the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*), which constitutes the ultimate consolation, is taught at the end. This is the sequence here.

Regarding "distinction and non-distinction": here, the distinction pertains only to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). For that material life-faculty is twofold: the material life-faculty and the immaterial life-faculty. For the remaining faculties, there is no distinction. Thus, one should understand the determination of these faculties here by way of their distinction and non-distinction.

Regarding "function" (*kicca*): if it is asked what the function of the faculties is, first, as for the eye-faculty, from the statement, "The eye-base is a condition, by way of faculty-condition, for eye-consciousness and for those states associated with it," that which exists by way of being a faculty-condition—

That which is to be accomplished is the causing of the mental states such as eye-consciousness to conform to one’s own mode of being—characterized as sharp, dull, and so forth—which is designated as "function" (*kicca*).
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties. For the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), however, it is the bringing of its co-nascent states under its own control;
for the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), it is the preservation of its co-nascent states.

The female and male faculties conform to the signs, gestures, dress, and physical forms of females and males; the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and grief, having overwhelmed their co-nascent states, bring about their respective coarse modes of manifestation;
the faculty of equanimity brings about a mode that is peaceful, sublime, and neutral;
and the faculties of faith and so forth overcome their opposites and bring about a state of clarity and other such qualities in the associated mental factors.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya) effects both the abandoning of the three fetters and the making of its associated states inclined toward that abandonment;
the faculty of knowledge (aññindriya) effects both the thinning out and abandoning of sensual lust, ill will, and so forth, as well as the bringing of its co-nascent states under its own control;
and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya) effects both the abandoning of all exertion regarding duties and the state of being a condition for being directed toward the Deathless.
One should understand the analysis here according to function (*kicca*) as "of the associated [states]. Regarding "by way of plane" (*bhūmito*):
herein, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, masculinity, pleasure, pain, and grief belong exclusively to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
The faculties of mind, life, equanimity, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom [belong to all planes].

And [the remaining faculties] are included within the four planes. The faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) is included within three planes by way of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the supramundane.
At the end, the three [faculties] are exclusively supramundane. Thus one should understand the analysis according to the planes. For one who understands in this way:
The bhikkhu, full of a sense of spiritual urgency, remains established in the restraint of the faculties.
"Having fully understood the faculties, one reaches the end of suffering.

In the section on the exposition (niddesa), everything beginning with "The eye, which [arises] from the four great elements," etc., is to be understood according to the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
Furthermore, regarding the exposition of the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), and so forth, [the term] right effort (*sammāvāyāma*)...
Wrong effort, right concentration, wrong concentration, and so forth, are not mentioned here.
Why? Because they are all-inclusive. For it is the faculties that are described here as being all-inclusive. Even so, among these ten faculties, ten are mundane and belong only to the sense-sphere;
three are supramundane; and nine are a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 2. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchaka) 221.
In the Section of Questions, the classification of all the faculties (indriya) as wholesome and so forth is to be understood according to the method of the canonical text itself.
223. Regarding the triads of objects (*ārammaṇattika*), however, the statement that "seven faculties are without objects" refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, female, and male faculties.
The life faculty (*jīvitindriya*), on the other hand, is not included here because it is mixed with the formless.
"Two faculties" means two faculties; this is said with reference to the pair of pleasure and pain, for those have exclusively limited objects. The faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*)...

"It may have a limited object (parittārammaṇa), or it may have a sublime object (mahaggatārammaṇa)": when it occurs by taking sense-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhamma) as its object, it has a limited object;
when it occurs by taking fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) phenomena as its object, it has a sublime object;
and when it occurs by taking a concept (paṇṇatti) as its object, its object is not to be defined. Nine faculties may have a limited object.
This was said with reference to the faculty of mind, the life-faculty, the faculties of mental joy and equanimity,
and the pentad beginning with faith. For the life-faculty, because it is mixed with material form, although it is included among the immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) that lack an object,
it may also be included in the category of the immaterial (arūpakoṭṭhāsa) on the side of what is not matter.
"The four faculties" refers to the faculties of pleasure, pain, mental grief, and "I-have-known-the-unknown.
For these do not belong to the triad of having the Path as their object. "Having the Path as its cause" is said with reference to the co-nascent cause (*sahajāta-hetu*).
At times when energy or investigation is predominant, it may have the Path as its dominant influence (*adhipati*); at times when desire or consciousness is predominant, it cannot be so designated.
"Ten faculties may be arisen and may be arising" is said with reference to the seven material faculties and the three resultant faculties.
The ten faculties together with mental grief have already been discussed above. Among them, the faculty of mental grief has an indeterminate object at the time it occurs by way of a designation;
the remaining ones [have an indeterminate object] even at the time of reviewing Nibbāna.
"Three faculties have external objects" refers to the three supramundane (lokuttara) faculties. "Four" refers to pleasure, pain, joy, and grief;

for these occur by taking both internal and external phenomena as their objects. "Eight faculties" refers to the mind faculty, the life faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the pentad beginning with faith.
Among these, at the time of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), it should be understood that they have an indeterminate object.

Thus, in this section on the interrogation of questions as well, ten faculties are stated as belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), three as supramundane (*lokuttara*), and nine as both mundane and supramundane (*lokika-lokuttara-missaka*).
This too constitutes a single chapter together with the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya*.
However, this analysis of the faculties (*indriya-vibhaṅga*) is presented by extracting and dividing it into two cycles of exposition.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Faculties (*Indriyavibhaṅga*) within the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, is completed. 6.
The Analysis of Dependent Origination (*Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*).
1. Explanation of the Section on Enumeration in the Suttanta-Bhājaniya. 225.

Now, immediately following this, in the Vibhaṅga of Dependent Origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), there is a textual tradition (*tanti*) set forth in the manner beginning with, "This is 'volitional formations conditioned by ignorance'.
By providing a commentary on its meaning, one enters the circle of those who teach through analysis (*vibhajjavāda*).
Because one must not misrepresent the Teacher, must not deviate from one's own system, must not distort the systems of others,
must not contradict the Suttas, must conform to the Vinaya, must look to the Great Authorities, must illuminate the Dhamma, must summarize the meaning,
and must demonstrate that very meaning again by repeating it through other methods.
An exposition of the meaning must be made; yet an exposition of the meaning of dependent origination is difficult even by its very nature, as the ancients have said:
“The truth, a being, rebirth-linking, and the mode of conditions— These four things are hard to see, and even harder to teach.”
Therefore, having reflected that "it is not easy to explain the meaning of dependent origination except for those who have attained the scriptures and realization," [the author says]:
"Desiring today to speak the exposition of the mode of conditions,
I find no foothold, like one who has plunged into the ocean."
This Dispensation, adorned with various methods of teaching,
and the path of the ancient masters continue to proceed without interruption.
Therefore, relying upon both of these, I shall provide this commentary on the meaning.
I shall undertake this; listen to it with concentrated minds.
For this was said by the ancient teachers:
"Whoever should listen to this, making it their very bone..."
One may attain distinction between what precedes and what follows;
having attained distinction between what precedes and what follows,
one shall go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Regarding the passage beginning "With ignorance as condition,
volitional formations [arise]," the detailed exposition should be understood first of all through: the different modes of teaching, the meaning, the characteristics,
the various classifications, and the definition of the factors.
In this context, "by way of the different modes of teaching" means that the Blessed One’s teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is fourfold:

like the grasping of a creeper by four men carrying it, it may proceed from the beginning or from the middle to the end, or likewise from the end or from the middle to the beginning. For just as among those carrying the creeper...
Among four men, one first sees the very root of a creeper; having cut it at the root and pulled out everything, he takes it and brings it for use.

In this way, the Blessed One teaches dependent origination from beginning to end, starting from: "Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise... [and so on] ...with birth as condition, aging and death arise."
Just as one among those men who first sees the middle of the creeper cuts it at the middle, pulls out the upper portion, takes it, and brings it for use, so too the Blessed One [said]:
"For one who delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, delight arises; whatever delight there is in feelings, that is clinging; with that clinging as condition..."
“Becoming; with becoming as condition, birth”—thus he teaches starting from the middle all the way to the end.

And just as one of those men first sees the tip of the creeper, and having grasped the tip, takes up the whole thing following the tip down to the root and brings it to his work, even so the Blessed One [teaches]: “With birth as condition, aging-and-death.”
"But this has been said: 'Monks, is aging-and-death conditioned by birth, or not?
And how does it come to be so? " 'Venerable sir, aging-and-death is conditioned by birth; that is how it comes to be for us: aging-and-death is conditioned by birth.

" 'Birth is conditioned by existence... [and so on] ... volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance. Thus indeed it has been said: [aging-and-death is conditioned by birth]... " 'Ignorance is conditioned by what? "
“Bhikkhus, what now are volitional formations, or how is it in this regard? “Ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, venerable sir;
such is our understanding in this regard: ‘ignorance is the condition for volitional formations. Thus he teaches dependent origination from the conclusion back to the beginning.

Just as one among those men first sees the middle of the creeper, cuts it in the middle, and descending, takes it down to its root and brings it for use; even so the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, what is the source of these four nutriments?
What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their provenance? These four nutriments have craving as their source..."
“With craving as their origin, with craving as their source, with craving as their provenance. And what, bhikkhus, is the cause of this craving?
Feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness. What is the cause of volitional formations?...

Volitional formations have ignorance as their cause, with ignorance as their origin, with ignorance as their source, with ignorance as their provenance. Thus he taught starting from the middle back to the beginning.

But why does he teach in this way? Because dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is all-encompassing and excellent, and because the Blessed One himself has attained mastery in the art of teaching.
Dependent origination is indeed all-encompassing and excellent, for it leads to the penetration of the truth from every perspective.

Furthermore, the Blessed One has attained mastery in teaching through his possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) and the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), as well as by having reached a fourfold profundity. He...

Because he has attained mastery in the elegance of teaching, he teaches the Dhamma by means of various methods. In particular, it should be understood that his "teaching in forward order" (*anulomadesanā*), which begins from the very start,
was delivered for the purpose of demonstrating how the process of existence (*pavatti*) arises through its own respective causes, and for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of its origination,
as he perceived that those to be trained were confused regarding the analysis of the causes of that process.

The teaching that proceeds in reverse order from the conclusion is for the purpose of demonstrating to him—by following the sequence of prior-stage penetration—the respective causes of suffering such as aging and death, which he has himself realized, as he surveys the world fallen into hardship according to the method beginning: "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; it is born, it ages, and it dies. As for that which...
That which proceeds from the middle back to the beginning is for the purpose of carrying it back as far as the past by following the determination of the source of nutriment;

and that which proceeds from the middle to the end is for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of cause and fruit starting from the past, [and] from the origination of the causes of the future period within the present period.
This is for the purpose of showing the future half [of the cycle] beginning from that point. Among those [teachings],

it should be understood that the teaching given here is that which was previously stated as a progressive (anuloma) exposition starting from the beginning, for the purpose of showing the process of occurrence through their respective causes to those to be trained who are confused about the cause of occurrence, and for the purpose of showing the order of arising.
But why is ignorance mentioned first here? Is it because, like the "primordial nature" (*pakati*) of the proponents of primordial nature, ignorance is also a causeless root-cause of the world?
It is not causeless; for the cause of ignorance has been stated: "With the arising of the taints (*āsava*), there is the arising of ignorance.
