However, there is a way in which it may be considered a root-cause. What, then, is that way? It is in the context of the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).
The state of being the head. For when the Blessed One speaks on the discourse of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakatha*), he speaks having made two things the head:

either ignorance (*avijjā*) or craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). As it is said: "Bhikkhus, no prior limit is discerned of ignorance, such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist;
then afterwards it came into being. Even though this is said, bhikkhus, yet..."
And yet, ignorance is discerned as having this specific condition; or craving for existence, as it is said:
"Bhikkhus, no prior limit of craving for existence is discerned, such that one could say, 'Before this, craving for existence did not exist, and only afterwards did it come into being.
Even though this is said, bhikkhus, nevertheless craving for existence is discerned as having this specific condition."
But why did the Blessed One, when speaking on the discourse of the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), speak making these two very factors the head?
Because they are the specific causes for karma that leads to happy and miserable destinies. For ignorance is the specific cause of karma leading to a miserable destiny.
Why? Because an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) overcome by ignorance is like a cow to be slaughtered, overcome by the distress of heat from fire and the blow of a club.

Just as one who is weary from exhaustion might undertake drinking hot water—though it provides no refreshment and even brings harm to oneself—so too, due to the fever of the defilements (*kilesa*), one undertakes various kinds of karma leading to miserable rebirths, such as killing living beings, which provide no satisfaction and bring harm to oneself through falling into the lower realms.
However, craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is the specific cause for karma that leads to happy rebirths. Why is this?
Because the worldling, overcome by craving for existence, undertakes various kinds of action leading to a happy destination—
such as abstaining from taking life— which, like the cow described above, provides satisfaction and dispels one's own exhaustion through drinking cool water,
and which, being free from the torment of the defilements, provides satisfaction and dispels the exhaustion of suffering in an unhappy destination by bringing about rebirth in a happy state.
Now, among these phenomena which constitute the head of the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), in some places the Blessed One gives a teaching rooted in a single phenomenon, such as:
"Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness," and so forth.
Likewise: "Monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are subject to clinging..."
“Craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises,” and so forth. In some instances, it is rooted in both [ignorance and craving], as follows:
“Bhikkhus, for the fool who is hindered by ignorance and associated with craving, this body has thus come to be.
Thus, this body and external name-and-form—this is the dyad. Dependent upon this dyad is contact; there are six sense bases.”

“Touched by which [feelings], the fool experiences pleasure and pain,” and so forth. Among those various teachings, the statement “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise” should be understood here as a teaching based on a single factor (ekadhammamūlikā) by way of ignorance.
Thus, first, the exposition should be understood here according to the distinction of the teachings.

‘In terms of meaning’ means in terms of the meaning of the terms beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*). That is to say: bodily misconduct and so forth are called “unfindable” (*avindiya*) in the sense that they are unfit to be fulfilled;
the meaning is that they are not to be obtained. Ignorance is that which finds what is unfindable.
Conversely, bodily good conduct and so forth are called “findable” (*vindiya*). Ignorance is that which does not find what is findable. The meaning of “aggregate” (*khandha*) is a heap.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is so called because it makes unknown the meaning of the sense-bases as "bases," the meaning of the elements as "emptiness," the meaning of the truths as "suchness," and the meaning of the faculties as "predominance.
Furthermore, ignorance is so called because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning—namely, the fourfold meanings of suffering and so forth, described by way of oppression and so on.
[It functions] within the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), amidst all the modes of birth, destinies, states of being, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

It is called ignorance (*avijjā*) because it causes beings to run about. It is ignorance because it runs toward things such as "woman" or "man" which do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), yet it does not run toward things that do exist, such as the aggregates (*khandha*).

Furthermore, it is ignorance because it conceals the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and so forth, as well as the phenomena of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently originated (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) states.
That depending upon which a fruit comes into being is the condition (*paccaya*). "Depending upon" (*paṭicca*) means not without that; the meaning is "not having abandoned it.
"Comes into being" (*eti*) means both arises and proceeds. Furthermore, the sense of "condition" (*paccaya*) is the sense of "being helpful.
Ignorance (*avijjā*) and that which is a condition (*paccayo*) together constitute "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccayo*). Therefore: "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*).
They are called *saṅkhārā* because they construct the conditioned (*saṅkhata*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of *saṅkhārā*:

those that arise with ignorance as their condition (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), and those included under the term *saṅkhāra* itself. Among these, there are three types of formative activities—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—and three types of formations of body, speech, and mind;
thus, these six are the *saṅkhārā* conditioned by ignorance. All of them are merely mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*).

Furthermore, there are these four types of formations (saṅkhāra) conveyed by the term *saṅkhāra*: conditioned formation (*saṅkhatasaṅkhāra*), formed formation (*abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhāra*), formative formation (*abhisaṅkharaṇasaṅkhāra*), and functional formation (*payogābhisaṅkhāra*).

Among these, all conditioned phenomena (*sappaccaya-dhammā*) spoken of in such passages as “Impermanent indeed are formations” are called “conditioned formations. Those belonging to the three planes produced by kamma...

In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), material and immaterial phenomena are called "conditioned formations" (*abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra*). These too are included within the phrase, "Impermanent indeed are formations.
However, no separate place for them is found [in the suttas].

But wholesome and unwholesome volition belonging to the three planes is called the "formative formation" (*abhisaṅkharaṇaka-saṅkhāra*). Regarding it, [it is said]: "Bhikkhus, this person, immersed in ignorance..."

The sense in which it occurs in such passages as “If one forms a meritorious volitional formation” (puññañce abhisaṅkharoti) is evident. However, bodily and mental energy is called “volitional formation as exertion” (payogābhisaṅkhāra).

This is found in such passages as: “Having gone as far as the range of volitional formation, he stood still as if struck by a bolt” (yāvatikā abhisaṅkhārassa gati, tāvatikaṃ gantvā akkhāhataṃ maññe aṭṭhāsi).

And it is not only these; there are also many other formations (saṅkhāra) mentioned by way of the term "formation" in such passages as: "Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu enters the cessation of perception and feeling, first his verbal formation ceases, then his bodily formation, then his mental formation.
Among those, there is no formation that exists apart from conditioned formations.

It would not be included [in the causal sequence]. From this point onward, in such passages as "with formations as condition, consciousness," and so forth, what has been stated should be understood according to the method already explained.
However, regarding what has not been explicitly stated: it cognizes, thus it is *viññāṇa* (consciousness); it bends toward, thus it is *nāma* (mentality); it is affected, thus it is *rūpa* (form);

it extends into the future and leads that which is extended, thus it is *āyatana* (base); it touches, thus it is *phassa* (contact); it feels, thus it is *vedanā* (feeling); it is agitated, thus it is *taṇhā* (craving); it grasps, thus it is...
Grasping (*upādāna*). It exists and it causes [existence] to come into being, thus it is existence (*bhava*). Birth (*jāti*) is the act of being born. Aging (*jarā*) is the state of decaying.
Death (*maraṇa*) is that by which beings die. Sorrow (*soka*) is grieving. Lamentation (*parideva*) is wailing. It causes suffering, thus it is suffering (*dukkha*);

or, it cuts [the heart] in two ways—by way of arising and by way of persistence—thus it is suffering. The state of one who is dejected is dejection (*domanassa*). Intense distress is despair (*upāyāsa*).
“Arise” means they are produced. And this connection of the word “arise” should be made with all the terms, not only with sorrow and the rest.
For otherwise, if it were merely stated that “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise],” it would not be understood what they are doing.
But when the connection “they arise” is applied, then: “ignorance which is also a condition is ‘ignorance-condition’ (avijjāpaccayo); [and so on for the subsequent links].
"Therefore, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be"—thus the determination of the conditions and the conditioned has been made.
This same method applies everywhere.

"In this way" indicates the method already demonstrated. By this it is shown that [volitional formations arise] through causes such as ignorance alone, and not through the creation of a Lord (issaranimmāna) or other such causes.
It shows this. "Of this" means of what has been stated above. "Entirely" means unmixed or in its totality.
"Of the mass of suffering" means of the aggregate of suffering, not of a sentient being, nor of pleasure, beauty, and so forth. "Origin" means arising. "Occurs" means it comes into existence.
Thus, in this context, the exposition should be understood according to its meaning.
‘From the characteristic, etc. means from the characteristic and so forth of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest; that is to say:

ignorance has the characteristic of non-knowing, the function of deluding, the manifestation of concealing, and the proximate cause of the taints (*āsava*). Formations (*saṅkhāra*) have the characteristic of volitional construction, the function of accumulating, the manifestation of volition (*cetanā*), and the proximate cause of ignorance. Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) has the characteristic of cognizing, the function of being the forerunner, and...
Rebirth-linking has the manifestation of re-arising, and its proximate cause is volitional formations, or else it has the physical basis and the object as its proximate cause.
Name has the characteristic of bending toward [the object], the function of association, the manifestation of inseparability, and consciousness as its proximate cause.

Matter has the characteristic of being affected (ruppana), the function of dispersal, the manifestation of the indeterminate, and consciousness as its proximate cause. The sense base has the characteristic of being a door for the arrival [of consciousness].
The six sense bases have the function of seeing and so forth; they are manifested as the state of being the physical bases and doors [of consciousness];
and their proximate cause is name-and-form. Contact has the characteristic of touching; its function is impingement; it is manifested as conjunction;

and its proximate cause is the six sense bases. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing; its function is the enjoyment of the flavor of the object; it is manifested as pleasure and pain; and its proximate cause is contact.
Craving has the characteristic of being a cause; its function is delighting; it is manifested as insatiability; and its proximate cause is feeling.
Clinging has the characteristic of grasping; its function is not letting go; it is manifested as intensified craving and views; and its proximate cause is craving.

Becoming has the characteristic of action and the fruit of action; its function is the process of becoming and the state of having become; and it is manifested as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states.

Its proximate cause is clinging. The characteristics and other attributes of birth and the rest should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths).
Thus, the exposition here should be understood by way of its characteristics and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "as being of one kind, etc.": herein, ignorance is of one kind because it consists of non-knowing, non-seeing, delusion, and so on; it is also twofold as non-practice and wrong practice.
Likewise, formations are twofold by way of being formations and non-formations; threefold by way of association with the three kinds of feeling;
fourfold by way of non-penetration of the Four Truths; fivefold by way of concealing the danger in the five destinies;
and, moreover, it should be understood that among all immaterial phenomena, there is a sixfold nature by way of doors and objects.
Volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are of one kind insofar as they possess the nature of being subject to taints (*sāsavā*) and having a result of maturation (*vipākadhammadhamma*);

they are of two kinds as wholesome (*kusala*) and unwholesome (*akusala*), and likewise as limited (*paritta*) and sublime (*mahaggata*), inferior (*hīna*) and intermediate (*majjhima*), and fixed in wrongness (*micchattaniyata*) and unfixed (*aniyata*); they are of three kinds insofar as they are volitional formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth;
they are of four kinds insofar as they lead to the four modes of birth (*yoni*); and they are of five kinds insofar as they lead to the five destinations (*gati*).
Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is of one kind by way of being mundane resultant and so forth; it is of two kinds by way of being with root-cause (*sahetuka*) or without root-cause (*ahetuka*);

it is of three kinds by way of being included within the three realms of existence, by way of association with the three types of feeling, and by way of being without root-cause, with two root-causes, or with three root-causes; and it is of four and five kinds by way of the modes of birth and destinations.

Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is of one kind by way of being dependent on consciousness and by way of being a condition for kamma; it is of two kinds by way of having an object (*sārammaṇa*) or not having an object (*anārammaṇa*); it is of three kinds by way of being past and so forth; and it is of four and five kinds by way of the modes of birth and destinations.

The sixfold sense base (*saḷāyatana*) is of one kind from the standpoint of being the place where birth and convergence occur; it is of two kinds by way of the primary elements, the sensitive organs, and consciousness;

it is of three kinds by way of its domain being favorable, unfavorable, or neither; and it is of four and five kinds by way of inclusion within the various modes of birth (*yoni*) and destinations (*gati*).
In this manner, the singlefold nature and so forth of contact (*phassa*) and the other factors should also be understood. Thus, herein, even from the perspective of being of one kind and so on—
The analysis should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "and the definition of the factors," sorrow and the rest are mentioned here for the purpose of showing the uninterrupted continuity of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).
For these arise in the fool who is struck down by aging and death. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, the uninstructed person..."
“When a worldling is touched by a painful bodily feeling, he sorrows, languishes, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
As long as these [feelings] continue to occur, there is ignorance;

thus, the cycle of existence remains connected through the formula “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. Therefore, for them as well, it is by means of aging and death that [the cycle is completed].

By making them into a single group, it should be understood that there are exactly twelve factors of dependent origination. Thus, the exposition here should be understood also by way of the defining of the factors.
This, then, is the brief explanation according to the section on the enumeration.
The commentary to the section on the enumeration is finished.
The Exposition of the Foundation of Ignorance (Avijjāpada-niddesa) 226.
Now follows the detailed explanation by way of the section on exposition. For it was said: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise].
In that context, when the volitional formations conditioned by ignorance are to be shown, since the father must first be mentioned when speaking of the son—
It is so explained. For if this were the case, one would be properly called "the son of a friend" or "the son of Datta.
Therefore, the Teacher, skilled in teaching, first showed ignorance—which is like a father in the sense of being the producer of the formations—by saying:
"What is ignorance? It is non-knowing regarding suffering," and so forth.
In this context, because this ignorance does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the characteristic of the actual nature of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*),
but rather remains by concealing, enveloping, and binding it, it is therefore called "ignorance regarding suffering" (*dukkhe aññāṇa*). Likewise,

because [it does not allow one to do so] regarding the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering— each with its characteristic of the actual nature— ...
It does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate; it remains concealing, enveloping, and binding.

Therefore, it is called "ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. In these four instances, ignorance (*avijjā*) is explained according to the method of the Suttantas as "lack of knowledge" (*aññāṇa*).
In the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa*, however, according to the Abhidhamma method, ignorance regarding the "prior limit" (*pubbantāññāṇa*) is included, as well as ignorance regarding four other points.
Therein, "the prior limit" (*pubbanta*) refers to the past time, that is, the past aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).

"The subsequent limit" (*aparanta*) refers to the future time, that is, the future aggregates, elements, and bases. "The prior and subsequent limits" (*pubbantāparanta*) refers to both of these together. "Specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*)...

The factors such as ignorance (*avijjā*) are the causes of formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the other links. "Dependently arisen phenomena" refers to the phenomena such as formations that have been produced by ignorance and the rest.

In this context, ignorance is so called because it does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate the true nature and characteristics of the past aggregates and so forth; rather, it remains having concealed, enveloped, and bound them.
Therefore, it is called "ignorance regarding the past. Likewise, because it does not allow one to know, see,
or penetrate the true nature and specific characteristics of future aggregates and so forth, of past and future aggregates and so forth,
and of dependently arisen phenomena— remaining instead by concealing, enveloping, and binding them— it is so termed.
Therefore, it is said that there is "ignorance regarding things that are dependently originated through specific conditionality.
In these eight instances, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, ignorance is described as "avijjā" (nescience).
What, then, has been stated in this way? Ignorance has been described both by way of its function and by way of its nature. How so?
For this ignorance is described in terms of its function because it does not allow one to know, see, or penetrate these eight points;
and it is also described in terms of its arising because when it arises, it arises in relation to these eight points.
Having explained it thus, twenty-five phrases beginning with "that which is such ignorance, non-seeing" are taken up to show the characteristic of ignorance.
In this regard, although this ignorance has been explained by these eight terms, it is not yet well-explained unless its characteristic is further stated by twenty-five terms;
however, when the characteristic is stated, it is indeed well-explained.
Just as a man searching for a lost ox might ask people: "Venerable sirs, is there perhaps a white [ox]?"
“Look at the ox! Look at the red ox! They would say, “In this kingdom there is no ox that is white and red;
what is the characteristic of that ox? Then, if he were to say “saṅghāṭi” or “plough,” the ox would indeed be well-described; even so, because this ignorance [is defined] by eight terms...
Even though it has been explained, if the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) are not stated by means of the twenty-five terms, it cannot be said to be well-explained;

only when the characteristics have been stated is it truly well-explained. Therefore, it should be understood by way of those twenty-five terms which were spoken for the purpose of showing its characteristics.
To explain: "Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is wisdom (*paññā*). It makes known and clarifies the meaning of things, the reasons for those reasons, and the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
However, this ignorance (*avijjā*), having arisen, does not allow that which is known to be made clear;

thus, it is "non-knowledge" (*aññāṇa*) because it is the opposite of knowledge. "Vision" (*dassana*) is also wisdom. That too sees that aspect [of reality]. But ignorance, having arisen, [prevents] that...
"Non-seeing" (*adassana*) means not allowing one to see. "Clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) is also wisdom; it clearly realizes that mode [of truth].
Ignorance (*avijjā*), however, having arisen, does not allow that clear realization to occur; thus, it is "non-realization" (*anabhisamaya*).

"Subsequent awakening," "complete awakening," and "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) are also wisdom; it subsequently awakens to, completely awakens to, and penetrates that mode [of truth]. However, ignorance, having arisen...

Because it does not allow one to awaken to, fully comprehend, or penetrate that [object], there is non-awakening (*ananubodha*), non-full-comprehension (*asambodha*), and non-penetration (*appaṭivedha*).

Wisdom is also called "grasping" (*saṅgāhanā*); having taken up and rubbed against that aspect, it grasps it. Ignorance (*avijjā*), however, having arisen, does not allow one to take up, rub against, and grasp that;
thus, it is "non-grasping" (*asaṅgāhanā*). Wisdom is also called "thorough penetration" (*pariyogāhanā*); it [penetrates] that...
Having plunged into and entered that mode [of appearance], it grasps it. Ignorance, however, having arisen, does not allow one to plunge into, enter, and grasp it;
thus there is "non-plunging" (apariyogāhanā). Wisdom is also "equal viewing" (samapekkhanā); it views that mode equally and correctly.
Ignorance, however, having arisen, does not allow one to view it equally and correctly; thus there is "non-viewing" (asamapekkhanā).

Insight is also called *paccavekkhaṇā* (reflective observation). It reflects upon that mode [of activity]. However, because ignorance, having arisen, does not allow for such reflective observation, it is called *apaccavekkhaṇā*.
Since it has no direct perception (*paccakkha*) regarding any action, and since it performs actions itself without reflecting, it is called *apaccakkhakamma* (action without direct perception).
Due to its state of being dull-witted, it is *dummejjha*; due to its state of being foolish, it is *bālya*.
Clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) is also wisdom (*paññā*). It correctly understands the meaning of things, their causes, and the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

Ignorance (*avijjā*), however, having arisen, does not allow that mode [of understanding] to be known; thus it is "lack of clear comprehension" (*asampajañña*). Through its deluding nature it is delusion (*moha*);

through its stupefying nature it is extreme delusion (*pamoha*); through its utterly confusing nature it is total delusion (*sammoha*). It is so called because, by way of such expressions as "finding what should not be found," and so forth.

Ignorance (*avijjā*). It hurls one down and causes one to sink within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), thus it is the "flood of ignorance" (*avijjogha*). It yokes one to the cycle of existence, thus it is the "yoke of ignorance" (*avijjāyoga*).

Because it arises again and again by way of not being abandoned, it is the "latent tendency of ignorance" (*avijjānusaya*). Just as thieves who have overpowered a traveler on the road seize and plunder him, so too does ignorance "overpower," seize, and plunder the wholesome consciousness;
thus it is the "obsession of ignorance" (*avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna*). Just as at the city gate, by means of that which is called a crossbar...

Just as when a gatekeeper falls, the movement of people from within the city to outside and the entry of people from outside into the city is cut off, even so, for one upon whom this has fallen in the city of *sakkāya*, the movement of knowledge that leads to the attainment of *nibbāna* is cut off;
thus it is called the "gatekeeper of ignorance" (*avijjā-laṅgī*). And it is unwholesome.
And it is the root, or the root of the unwholesome, thus it is an "unwholesome root" (*akusalamūla*). But that is nothing other than what is intended here as delusion (*moha*);
thus, delusion is the unwholesome root. This is called ignorance (*avijjā*): this [state] with such characteristics is called by the name "ignorance.
In this way, the characteristic of ignorance should be understood by way of twenty-five terms.
This ignorance, characterized in this way, although described as "non-knowing" regarding suffering and the other truths, is a portion of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*);
it is co-nascent with it, takes it as its object, and conceals it. It is not a portion of the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*);
it is co-nascent with it, takes it as its object, and conceals it. It is neither a portion of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*), nor is it co-nascent with it.
It does not take that as its object; it merely conceals it. It is not even a portion of the truth of the path, nor is it co-nascent with it, nor does it take it as its object;

it merely conceals it. Ignorance arises with suffering as its object, and it conceals that. Ignorance arises with the origin as its object, and it conceals that. Ignorance [arises] with cessation as its object...
Ignorance does not arise with respect to that, yet it conceals it. Ignorance does not arise with respect to the fact that the Path is its object, yet it conceals it.

Two truths are profound because they are difficult to see; two truths are difficult to see because they are profound. Furthermore, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is both profound and difficult to see.
In this regard, "suffering" is indeed manifest, but as for its characteristic—
Because it is difficult to see, it is called "profound. The same method applies to the origin as well.
Just as it is a great task to churn the great ocean and extract its essence, or to remove sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, or to press a mountain and extract its sap;
even so, these two truths are difficult to see precisely because of their profundity.
The truth of cessation, moreover, is exceedingly profound and exceedingly difficult to see.
Because it is thus difficult to see and because it is profound, the darkness of delusion that obscures these four noble truths is called ignorance (*avijjā*).
This concludes the exposition of the term "ignorance."

The Exposition of the Terms for Volitional Formations (*saṅkhāra-pada-niddesa*). Without referring to those formations mentioned previously under the term "formations" (*saṅkhāra*), and instead showing specifically those formations that arise with ignorance as their condition, [the text] asks:
"In this context, what are the formations conditioned by ignorance? and states: "Volitional formation of merit," and so forth.
In this context, it is called *puñña* because it purifies (*punāti*) its own doer, fulfills his intention (*ajjhāsaya*), and produces a state of existence worthy of honor (*pujja*).
It is called *abhisaṅkhāra* because it constructs (*abhisaṅkharoti*) both ripening (*vipāka*) and the form of what has been done (*kaṭattārūpa*).

Thus, merit itself as a construction is "meritorious volitional formation" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). That which is the opposite of merit is "demerit" (*apuñña*). Demerit itself as a construction is "demeritorious volitional formation" (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*).

It does not waver, thus it is "imperturbable" (*āneñja*). Volitional formation itself is imperturbable; because one forms existence that is imperturbable, it is called "imperturbable volitional formation" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).

That which proceeds by way of the body, or proceeds from the body, or is the formation of the body, is "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāra*). The same method applies to vocal formation and mental formation as well.
Therein, the first triad is taken according to the *Parivīmaṃsana-sutta*; for therein it says: "If one forms a meritorious formation..."

"If one performs a meritorious volitional formation, consciousness becomes one that goes toward merit. If one performs a demeritorious volitional formation, consciousness becomes one that goes toward demerit.
If one performs an imperturbable volitional formation, consciousness becomes one that goes toward the imperturbable. Thus it was said.
The second triad is taken according to the *Vibhaṅga-sutta* immediately following [the first], by way of the discourse on right view.
It is indeed appropriate to say that they have been "taken" as well. For in that context it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these three formations. Which three?
The bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation. But why are they taken on the basis of these suttas?
This so-called Abhidhamma was not composed recently, nor was it by non-Buddhist seers or disciples.
Or was it spoken by deities? But this was spoken by the Omniscient Victor. Indeed, the textual tradition (tanti) is shown to be exactly the same in both the Abhidhamma and the Suttas;
it is for the purpose of illustrating this point that he now says, "In that regard, what is the meritorious formation? and so forth. Therein:
"Wholesome volition" (*kusalā cetanā*) is stated without restriction, thus including volition of all four planes.

However, because it is specified as "belonging to the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere," thirteen types of volition—namely, the eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere and the five wholesome volitions of the fine-material sphere—are called the "volitional formation of merit" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
By the terms "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) and so forth, the occurrence of those very same volitions is shown according to the bases for performing meritorious deeds (*puññakiriyavatthu*).
In this regard, eight types of merit consist of giving and virtue pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*). However, thirteen types also consist of meditation (*bhāvanā*).
For just as one who is reciting a familiar text may not know even one or two connected passages at first, but knows them later when reflecting upon them;
even so, for one performing the preliminary work of the *kasiṇa* and reviewing the familiar jhāna and the familiar meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), [the same occurs].
For one who is attending [to these], there is also development dissociated from knowledge. Therefore it was said: "But thirteen are made of development.

In that context, regarding those consisting of giving and so forth: "The volition, intention, and state of having intended that arises with giving as its object, having giving as its basis—this is called the formation of merit consisting of giving.
With virtue as its object... pe ...with development as its object, having development as its basis..."
“The volition that arises, the act of intending, the state of having intended—this is called the formation of merit consisting in development.
This is the brief teaching.
However, [it applies] to the four requisites such as robes, or to the six objects such as visible forms, or to the ten [types of food] beginning with alms-food.

Regarding the bases of giving (*dānavatthu*), the volition (*cetanā*) that occurs during three periods— beginning from the production of those things to be given, through the time of relinquishment in the preliminary stage,
and finally at the time of recollection with a joyful mind— is called "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*).

Furthermore, regarding virtue (*sīla*), for one who goes to a monastery thinking, "I shall go forth," in order to fulfill [the precepts], and for one who is actually going forth, [the volition] directed toward that aspiration...
The volition that arises when one has reached the culmination [of the training], reflecting, "I have indeed gone forth;

this is excellent, very good," while exercising restraint according to the Pātimokkha, reviewing the requisites such as robes, restraining the eye-door and other sense doors regarding forms and other objects that come into range, and purifying one's livelihood—this is called virtue consisting in moral discipline (*sīlamaya*).
This is according to the path of insight (*vipassanāmaggā*) described in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
For one who develops the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self;

forms … [and so on] … mental objects; eye-consciousness … [and so on] … mind-consciousness; eye-contact … [and so on] … mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact … [and so on] … feeling born of mind-contact;
perception of forms … [and so on] … perception of mental objects; and aging-and-death as impermanent and suffering—
This is the detailed explanation: for one developing [the perception] as non-self, the volition that occurs is called "consisting of development.

In the description of the formation of demerit, "unwholesome volition" refers to the volition associated with the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. Regarding the term "belonging to the sense sphere":
although—with the exception of the two types of volition accompanied by displeasure—the remaining ones arise even in the fine-material and immaterial realms.
In that context, however, they do not draw forth rebirth-linking; rather, they cause resultant [kamma] to flow only within the sense sphere by way of rebirth-linking.
Thus, they are described as belonging specifically to the sense sphere.

In the exposition of the imperturbable volitional formations (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), "wholesome volition pertaining to the immaterial sphere" refers to the four types of wholesome volition of the immaterial sphere.
These four are called "imperturbable volitional formations" (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) both in the sense of being imperturbable (aniñjana) and in the sense of forming (abhisaṅkharaṇa).

For fifteen states—namely, three types of wholesome, resultant, and functional volition belonging to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, and twelve types of volition belonging to the immaterial sphere—are called "imperturbable" (āneñja) in the sense of being motionless and in the sense of being unshakable. Among these, those of the fine-material sphere are wholesome...
Volition (*cetanā*), although itself unmoving (*aniñjā*), produces both the similar and dissimilar, as well as the moving and the unmoving, whether material or immaterial;
therefore, it is not called "the formative action of the imperturbable" (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).

However, resultant and functional volitions do not form a result because they are themselves without result; likewise for the resultant and functional volitions of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*). Thus, these eleven [types of volition]—

Volition that is immovable is not a formative action (*abhisaṅkhāra*). However, the fourfold wholesome volition of the formless realm is called "immovable formative action" because, just as the shadows of elephants, horses, and so forth are similar [to their sources], it produces a formless state that is itself immovable and similar to itself.
Thus, there are thirteen by way of meritorious formative actions, twelve by way of non-meritorious formative actions, and [four] by way of immovable formative actions.
Thus, when all these eighty-four are combined together, they constitute twenty-nine volitions (*cetanā*). In this way, the Blessed One—
having delimited with his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) the wholesome and unwholesome volitions arising in immeasurable beings within immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*),
as if holding them on a great scale or weighing them by putting them into a measure— showed that there are exactly twenty-nine.
Now, showing the three doors of action through which immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) perform wholesome and unwholesome karma as they accumulate it, he says:
"In this context, what is bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*)? It is bodily volition (*kāyasañcetanā*)," and so forth.
Therein, "bodily volition" refers to the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome volition that proceed from the door of the body after having originated a bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).

The twelve unwholesome volitions (akusalacetanā) together with [the eight wholesome ones] constitute twenty volitions; it is also appropriate to say that twenty wholesome and unwholesome volitions arise at the door of the body (kāyadvāra), performing the acts of taking up, grasping, and moving.
The "volitions of speech" (vacīsañcetanā) are those same twenty volitions which, having originated vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), proceed from the door of speech.

It is also appropriate to say that the twenty volitions (cetanā) that have arisen, which bring about the movement of the jaw and the differentiation of speech at the door of speech, are likewise conditions for consciousness.
However, the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cetanā) is not included here because it does not serve as a condition for subsequent consciousness.
And just as with the volition of direct knowledge, so too the volition of restlessness (uddhacca-cetanā) is not a condition; therefore, it is also excluded from being a condition for consciousness.
[These] are to be removed. However, all of these [kinds of volition] have ignorance as their condition.
"Mental volition" refers to all twenty-nine types of volition that arise at the mind-door without producing either of the two forms of intimation (*viññatti*).
Thus, the Blessed One [taught] that in the immeasurable world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), immeasurable beings are exerting themselves in wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
"Accumulating through these three doors"—thus he showed the door of kamma as accumulation (*āyūhana*).
Furthermore, the mutual association between these two triads should be understood. How so?

For the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) may be a bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) for one who abstains from bodily misconduct, and it may be [a verbal formation] for one who abstains from verbal misconduct.

Vocal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*). Thus, the eight wholesome volitions (*cetanā*) of the sense sphere constitute both the meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) as well as bodily and vocal formations.
Furthermore, the thirteen volitions arising at the mind-door constitute both the meritorious formation and mental formation (*citta-saṅkhāra*).
Likewise, non-meritorious formation may, by way of bodily misconduct during its occurrence, become a bodily formation.

Through the occurrence of verbal misconduct, there may be verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*); through occurrence at the mind-door, excluding the two [other] doors, there may be mental formation (*citta-saṅkhāra*).
Thus, unwholesome formation (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) is both bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation.
However, bodily formation may be wholesome formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), it may be unwholesome formation, but it is never imperturbable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).
Likewise for the verbal formation. As for the mental formation, it may be a meritorious formation, it may be a non-meritorious formation, or it may be an imperturbable formation.
These are what are called "formations conditioned by ignorance.
But how is this to be known—that these formations have ignorance as their condition? Because they exist when ignorance exists.
For one in whom ignorance— known as non-knowing— regarding suffering and the other truths has not been abandoned, he first, through non-knowing regarding suffering and the past and so forth,
grasps the suffering of saṃsāra with the perception of pleasure and initiates the three kinds of formations that serve as its cause;
and through non-knowing regarding the origin, he [grasps] the formations conditioned by craving— which are actually causes of suffering— as being causes of pleasure.

One undertakes [volitional formations] through conceiving; however, due to ignorance regarding cessation and the path, one perceives as the cessation of suffering those specific destinies that are not actually the cessation of suffering, and perceives as the path to cessation those things such as sacrifice, self-mortification, and asceticism which are not the path to cessation.
Thus, aspiring for the cessation of suffering, one undertakes the three kinds of volitional formations by way of sacrifice, self-mortification, and asceticism.
Furthermore, because of that ignorance which has not been abandoned regarding the Four Truths,
he does not understand as suffering the suffering known as the fruit of merit— which is specifically permeated by numerous disadvantages such as birth, aging, sickness, and death—

and thus undertakes the formation of merit consisting of the various volitional activities of body, speech, and mind for its attainment, like one desiring celestial nymphs who leaps from a mountain peak. And even regarding that which is considered happiness...
Even though he does not perceive that at the end of the fruit of that merit there is the suffering of change which produces great fever and little satisfaction,
he nevertheless initiates a volitional formation of merit of the kind already described, like a moth flying into the flame of a lamp,
or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking the edge of a blade smeared with honey.

Furthermore, failing to see the danger in the pursuit of sensual pleasures and other such actions that entail karmic results, and due both to his perception of them as pleasant and to being overwhelmed by the defilements,
he initiates unwholesome volitional formations even through the three doors— like a child playing with excrement, or like one wishing to die consuming poison. And likewise,
failing to comprehend the suffering inherent in the change and transformation of conditioned phenomena, even regarding the results of the formless realms...

Through the perversion of eternalism and so forth, one initiates the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), which is a mental volitional formation, like a person who is disoriented setting out on a path toward a city of demons.
Thus, since the state of being a formation arises only from the presence of ignorance and not from its absence, this must be understood: these...

“Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition. And this has also been said: “Bhikkhus, one who is ignorant, possessed by ignorance, performs a meritorious volitional formation, performs a demeritorious volitional formation, and performs an imperturbable volitional formation.
But when, bhikkhus, ignorance has been abandoned by a bhikkhu and true knowledge has arisen, through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge...”
“...nor does he form a formation of merit. Here it may be asked:
“Let us grant for now that ‘ignorance is a condition for formations. But this must be explained: ‘For which formations is it a condition, and in what way? To this it is said:
It is a condition for meritorious [formations] in two ways and in many ways;”
For others, that [ignorance] is considered a condition in one way for subsequent [states].

In this context, regarding the statement "for merits it is twofold," it is a condition in two ways: by way of object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and by way of decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
For when one comprehends ignorance as destruction and as vanishing, it serves as the object-condition for the meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) of the sense-sphere; and...
It is a condition by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) at the time of knowing a deluded mind with a mind of direct knowledge (abhiññā-citta).
Furthermore, for one who fulfills the bases of meritorious action pertaining to the sense sphere— such as giving— in order to transcend ignorance,
and who arouses jhānas of the fine-material sphere, it is a condition for both of those by way of decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

Likewise, for one who, being deluded by ignorance, aspires to success in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) and performs those very same meritorious deeds, it becomes a condition in many ways for the formative forces of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*). How so?

For when passion and the other [defilements] arise with this ignorance as their object, it serves as an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*); and when one esteems it and relishes it, [it serves as a condition].

By way of object-predominance and object-strong-dependence; by way of strong-dependence condition for one who, deluded by ignorance and not seeing the danger, commits killing and so forth; by way of proximity, contiguity, immediate-strong-dependence, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions for the second impulsion and those following;
and by way of root, co-nascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions for one who performs any unwholesome action whatsoever.
It is a condition in many ways.

Regarding the statement, “For the latter, it is considered a condition in one way,” this means that for the formations of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), it is considered a condition in only one way, namely, by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*). Furthermore, its status as a decisive support should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the formations of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
Here it may be asked: “Is this ignorance alone the condition for the formations, or are there other conditions as well?”

Now, what is the point here? If, first of all, it follows that there is only a single cause, then does it not follow that the description of a single cause—namely, "there are also other formations conditioned by ignorance"—is untenable? It is not untenable. Why? Because:
Here, the one is not from the one, nor is the many from the many; nor is the one from the many.
There is fruit, but there is no purpose in illustrating it as having a single cause and a single fruit.
For here, from a single cause, there is neither a single fruit nor a manifold fruit; nor does a single fruit arise from multiple causes.
Rather, from multiple causes, there is indeed a manifold fruit. Thus, from multiple factors consisting of season, earth, seed, and water—
It is observed that a single fruit, consisting of form, odor, taste, and so forth, as well as the sprout, arises from multiple causes.

However, as for this demonstration of individual cause and effect—“with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises”—there is a meaning therein, and a purpose exists.

For the Blessed One, in some instances, illuminates either a single cause or a single fruit—due to its preeminence, its obviousness, its uniqueness, or in accordance with the elegance of his teaching and the disposition of those to be trained.
Thus, in the statement "with contact as condition, feeling arises," he mentions only a single cause and a single fruit.
For contact is the preeminent cause of feeling, since feeling is established according to the nature of the contact.
Feeling is the primary fruit of contact, because contact is defined according to the feeling it produces.
One cause is stated—namely, phlegm—as it is the most evident [cause] in the case of "diseases arising from phlegm"; for here, phlegm is evident, whereas karma and the other causes are not.
Furthermore, [a specific cause is mentioned] because of its non-commonality, as in: "Bhikkhus, whatever unwholesome states there are, they all have unwise attention as their root."
He states one reason: for improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) is the uncommon cause of unwholesome states, whereas the bases, objects, and so forth are common causes.

Therefore, although other bases, objects, co-nascent factors, and so on exist as causes of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), this ignorance (*avijjā*) alone is [specified] here because of the statements:
"Craving increases in one who contemplates gratification" and "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints (*āsava*)."

It should be understood that ignorance is explained as the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) because it is the primary cause among other causes such as craving, because it is evident [in the Sutta], and because it is unique [to this context]. And by this very statement—

which serves as a rebuttal to the objection regarding the illustration of single causes and single fruits— it should be understood that the illustration of single causes and single fruits applies everywhere.
"The purpose should be understood.

Here it is asked: "Even this being so, how is it appropriate for ignorance—which has exclusively undesirable fruit and is blameworthy—to be a condition for the formative forces of merit and the imperturbable?
For sugar-cane does not arise from a nimba seed. How could it not be appropriate? For in the world—
The condition of phenomena is established as both contradictory and non-contradictory, as well as similar and dissimilar; yet these are not themselves results of kamma.

For in the world, a condition that is either contradictory or non-contradictory in terms of location, intrinsic nature, function, and so forth, is established for phenomena. Indeed, the preceding consciousness...
The state of another’s mind is a condition opposed in location; and prior training in crafts and so forth is a condition for later occurrences of craft-activities and the like.
Kamma is a condition opposed in intrinsic nature to matter; and milk and such things are conditions for curds and the like.
Light is a condition opposed in function to eye-consciousness; and molasses and such things are conditions for fermented liquors and the like. But the eye, visible forms, and so forth—

The conditions for eye-consciousness and the rest are non-opposed in terms of their basis (*ṭhāna*). Likewise, preceding impulsions (*javana*) and so forth are non-opposed in terms of both nature (*sabhāva*) and function (*kicca*) to succeeding impulsions and the like.

Just as conditions are established as being either opposed or non-opposed, so too are they similar or dissimilar. For indeed, matter consisting of temperature (*utu*) and nutriment (*āhāra*) is a condition for matter that is similar to it;
and rice seeds and the like are conditions for rice fruits and the like. Dissimilar matter, however, is also a condition for immaterial phenomena (*arūpa*).
And the formless is a condition for form; and cow-hair, sheep’s wool, horns, curd, sesame flour, and so forth, are conditions for mats, grass-roofs, thatch, and so forth.

And those phenomena which are conditions—whether opposed or non-opposed, similar or dissimilar—for other phenomena, those phenomena are not exclusively the resultants (*vipāka*) of those [other] phenomena.
Thus, this ignorance (*avijjā*), by way of being a resultant and by virtue of its nature as an exclusively undesirable fruit, is also blameworthy (*sāvajja*).

It should be understood that ignorance is a common condition for all these formations of merit and so forth, acting as a condition according to its specific role, function, and nature—whether in opposition or non-opposition—and by way of being a similar or dissimilar condition. Furthermore, its status as a condition is such that:
"For one in whom the ignorance known as lack of knowledge regarding suffering and the rest has not been abandoned..."

Thus it has been stated in such a manner: "First, through ignorance regarding suffering and concerning the past and so forth, having grasped the suffering of saṃsāra with the perception of pleasure, one undertakes the three kinds of formations that are its causes," and so on.
Furthermore, there is this other method:
He who is deluded regarding birth and death, the cycle of existence, the characteristics of formations,
and those phenomena that have arisen dependently— he, therefore,
constructs these three kinds of formations.
“Ignorance is the condition for those three kinds [of formations] because it exists in them.
But how is it that one who is deluded regarding these performs those three kinds of formations?
First, being deluded regarding death, and failing to grasp death anywhere as “the breaking up of the aggregates is death,” [one thinks]: “A being dies; of a being...”

He conceptualizes such things as "transmigration to another world. Being confused about rebirth (*upapāta*), he does not grasp that "the manifestation of the aggregates is birth" in any respect, but instead conceptualizes such things as "a being is reborn" or "the manifestation of a new body for a being.
Being confused about *saṃsāra*, he [conceptualizes] this which is—
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases, occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra.
Thus is saṃsāra described. Not grasping at it in this way [as a self], one does not think: “This being goes from this world to the next world.”
One conceptualizes such things as, "He comes from the other world to this world," and so forth.

Being deluded regarding the characteristics of formations (*saṅkhāra*), and failing to grasp both their specific characteristic (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*) and their general characteristic (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*), one conceptualizes formations as self, as belonging to a self, as permanent, as beautiful, and as pleasant.
Being deluded regarding dependently arisen phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma*), [one conceives] through ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest...
Not grasping at the occurrence of formations and so forth, [one might think]: "The self either knows or does not know; it is that very one who acts and causes others to act;
it is that which is reborn at the moment of conception. Atoms, Īśvara, and so forth, having fashioned the body from the stage of the *kalala* onwards, provide the sense faculties for it.
Endowed with these faculties, it touches, feels, craves, clings, and undergoes conflict."
Or he conceptualizes: "He will exist again in another state of being," or "All beings are determined by their destiny, their meeting, their nature, and their transformation.

Being thus blinded by ignorance and conceptualizing in this way, just as a blind man walking upon the earth might tread upon both the path and the non-path, upon dry land and the lowlands, upon the level and the uneven, even so does he [tread upon] merit...
One forms a volitional formation that is either unwholesome or imperturbable. Therefore, this is said:
"Just as a man blind from birth, Without a guide, Goes sometimes by the right path, And sometimes by the wrong path."
Wandering in saṃsāra, the fool, being thus without a guide,
at one time performs merit and at another time even demerit.
But when, having understood the Dhamma, he realizes the Truths;
"Then, with the subsiding of ignorance, he will live in peace.
This is the detailed explanation of the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise].
This concludes the exposition on the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations."

227. In the exposition of the section on consciousness with the condition of formations (*saṅkhāra-paccayā viññāṇa*), regarding "eye-consciousness" and so forth: eye-consciousness is twofold, being either wholesome resultant (*kusalavipāka*) or unwholesome resultant (*akusalavipāka*).
The same applies to ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. However, mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*)...

There are twenty-two types [of resultant consciousness]: two mind-elements (manodhātu) that are wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant; three rootless mind-consciousness-elements (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu);
eight root-endowed sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses; five fine-material-sphere consciousnesses; and four immaterial-sphere consciousnesses.
Thus, by means of these six types of consciousness, all thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses are included.
[These states] exist. However, supramundane states are not included because they do not fit within the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).
Herein, one might ask: how is it to be known that "this consciousness of the aforementioned kind has formations as its condition"?
Because there is no result (*vipāka*) in the absence of accumulated karma. For this is a result, and a result does not occur in the absence of accumulated karma.
It arises. If it were to arise [indiscriminately], then all results would arise for everyone; but since they do not so arise, this should be understood:
"This consciousness exists with volitional formations as its condition.
If one asks, "With what kind of volitional formations as condition does what kind of consciousness arise?"—first, with the volitional formation of sense-sphere merit...

There are sixteen [types of consciousness] that are wholesome-resultants: the five beginning with eye-consciousness; in the case of mind-consciousness, one mind-element and two mind-consciousness-elements;
and the eight great sense-sphere resultants. As it is said:
"Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness has arisen..."
Likewise, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness arise; resultant mind-element arises;
mind-consciousness-element arises accompanied by joy; mind-consciousness-element arises accompanied by equanimity;
mind-consciousness-element arises accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge; [mind-consciousness-element arises] accompanied by joy...
“Associated with knowledge and with volitional effort; accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge; accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge and with volitional effort;
accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge; accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge and with volitional effort;
accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge; and accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge and with volitional effort.”
With the volitional formation of merit pertaining to the fine-material sphere as condition, however, there are five resultant states of consciousness of the fine-material sphere. As it is said:

"Because of having performed and accumulated that very wholesome kamma of the fine-material sphere, with the abandoning of sensual pleasures... [and so on]... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna... [and so on]... up to the fifth jhāna.
Thus, by way of the volitional formation of merit, consciousness is twenty-one-fold.

But with unwholesome volitional formations as condition, there arise seven kinds of consciousness consisting of the five unwholesome-resultant types beginning with eye-consciousness, one mind-element, and one mind-consciousness-element. As it is said:

"Due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome kamma, resultant eye-consciousness arises; likewise, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, resultant mind-element, and resultant mind-consciousness-element arise."
But with the immovable formative volition as condition, there are four immaterial resultant states; thus consciousness is fourfold. As it has been said:

"Due to the performance and accumulation of that very wholesome karma of the immaterial sphere, as a result, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, [there arises] consciousness accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space...
[and so on] ...accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness... and so forth.
“Accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness…pe… accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
with the abandoning of pleasure…pe… he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Having thus understood that consciousness has formations as its condition, one should now understand its mode of occurrence as follows:
Indeed, all this occurs in two ways: by way of the process-of-becoming (*pavatti*) and the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Among these, the two fivefold sense-consciousnesses, the two mind-elements (*manodhātu*), and the rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—these thirteen occur only during the process-of-becoming within the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*).
The remaining nineteen occur, as appropriate, both during the process-of-becoming and at rebirth-linking across the three planes of existence.
They also occur at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

How so? First, the five types of wholesome-resultant consciousness, beginning with eye-consciousness, [arise] when an object—whether desirable or undesirable—has come within the range of the eyes and other sense bases of one who has been reborn through either a wholesome or an unwholesome resultant [kamma], and whose faculties have reached their respective maturity in due order.

Or else, taking as their object a desirable, neutral, or undesirable form and so forth, they proceed by depending on the sensitivity of the eye and other faculties, accomplishing the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching.
Likewise, there are five unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses]. For them, however, the object—consisting of forms and so forth—is exclusively undesirable or undesirable-neutral;
this alone is the distinction. All ten of these are fixed as to their door, object, physical basis, and place of arising.
And they have fixed functions. Therefore,
immediately after the wholesome resultant eye-consciousness and so forth, the wholesome resultant mind-element (manodhātu) arises, taking the same object as those [preceding consciousnesses],
depending on the heart-base (hadayavatthu), and accomplishing the function of reception (sampaṭicchana).
Likewise, immediately after unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses], there arise unwholesome-resultant [consciousnesses].
Furthermore, this pair has indeterminate doors and objects, fixed bases and locations, and fixed functions.
However, the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy arises immediately after the wholesome-resultant mind-element.
Taking that very object as its support and depending upon the heart-base (hadayavatthu), it performs the function of investigation (*santīraṇa*).

Furthermore, when a powerful object appears at any of the six sense-doors, for beings in the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it generally interrupts the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) following the impulsion (*javana*) associated with greed;
it then occurs once by way of registration (*tadārammaṇa*) regarding the object grasped by that impulsion.
Or it occurs twice. In the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness, however, only two mental moments are mentioned for the registration (tadārammaṇa) at all doors.
This consciousness receives two names: "registration" and "subsequent life-continuum" (piṭṭhibhavanga).
It has an indeterminate door and object, a determinate basis, and an indeterminate place and function.
Thus, first of all, it should be understood that thirteen [types of consciousness] occur only during the course of existence (*pavatti*) within the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra-bhava*).
Among the remaining nineteen types of consciousness, there is none that does not occur in a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) corresponding to itself.

However, during the course of existence, as for the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant [consciousness], the two rootless mind-consciousness elements (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu*) occur at the five sense doors.

Immediately following the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant mind-elements (manodhātu), it performs the function of investigation; through the six doors, in the manner previously described, it performs the function of registration (tadārammaṇa);
after the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) provided by itself, in the absence of any thought-moment that interrupts the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), it performs the function of the life-continuum;
and at the end, it performs the function of death. Thus, accomplishing these four functions, it proceeds with its basis fixed, while its doors, objects, locations, and functions remain undetermined.

The eight sense-sphere wholesome-with-root consciousnesses perform three functions: during the course of existence, they perform the function of registration at the six doors in the manner already described;
after the rebirth-linking provided by themselves, they perform the function of life-continuum (bhavaṅga) whenever there is no interrupting thought-moment;

and finally, they perform the function of death. Thus, while performing these three functions, they proceed with their objects and bases fixed, but with their doors, objects, and locations being variable.
The five fine-material-sphere consciousnesses and the four immaterial-sphere consciousnesses, following the rebirth-linking moment provided by themselves, proceed by accomplishing two functions:
the function of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)—provided there is no intervening consciousness that cuts off the life-continuum—and finally, the function of death (*cuti*).

Among these, the fine-material-sphere consciousnesses have fixed bases and objects but indefinite locations and functions; the others [the immaterial-sphere consciousnesses] have indefinite bases and objects, and their location and function are also indefinite.
They proceed as being without a physical basis, having fixed objects, and performing functions in indeterminate locations.
Thus, first of all, even the thirty-two-fold consciousness proceeds during the course of existence conditioned by formations (*saṅkhāra*).
In that regard, those various formations serve as conditions for it both as kamma-conditions and as decisive-support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

In this context, among these eleven types of resultant consciousness mentioned as having that [object] as their object (*tadārammaṇa*), not even one occurs as a resultant object in the fine-material or immaterial realms.

Why? Because of the absence of the seed. For there, the seed of rebirth known as sense-sphere resultant consciousness does not exist, which could produce it during its occurrence with respect to objects such as visible forms. This is also the case for eye-consciousness and the others.
If it is argued that non-existence [of the object] follows in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*), we say no;

because of the power of the functioning of the faculties and because of the restriction of consciousness according to the distinction between the doors and the cognitive process (*vīthi*). Just as this registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) does not function at all in the fine-material or immaterial realms, so too it does not follow after any states belonging to the non-sensual sphere (*akāmāvacara*). Why? Because it is not a producer, and because it is dissimilar to the producer. For, just as...
Just as a young child, wishing to go outside after leaving his house, takes hold of his own father— the one who gave him birth—
or another relative similar to his father who desires his welfare, and follows after them, and not some other person such as a royal official;
so too, this [consciousness], wishing to emerge from the object of the *bhavaṅga*, [takes hold of] its own progenitor due to their commonality.
Or it follows only a sense-sphere javana similar to its predecessor, and not any other sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (anuttara) state.

And just as this [sublime javana] does not follow sublime or supramundane states, so too, when these sense-sphere states occur with a sublime object, it does not follow them either. Why? Because they are unfamiliar domains.

And because its object is exclusively limited (*paritta*). For just as a young child following his father or a relative like his father follows him only within familiar places such as the house, the door, the street, or the crossroads, and not when he goes to the forest or a battlefield;
so too, even while following objects of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it does not follow those that are sublime (*mahaggata*) and so forth.
It follows only those states that arise in a limited (paritta) sphere, and not those arising with reference to sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara) states.

For its object is exclusively extremely limited, as it is said: "All resultant mind-element of the sense-sphere, functional mind-element, and functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy—these states have limited objects. Thus, its object is indeed entirely limited.
It has been stated; therefore, it should be understood that this [registration] does not even follow after sense-sphere phenomena when the object is sublime (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara).
Or rather, what is the use of this discussion on reasoning? For in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated categorically:

"The eleven registration-consciousnesses do not take registration when they have impelled in the javana stage by taking a name or clan as their object. When impelled by taking a concept (paññatti) as their object..."
When a javana has occurred, the registration (tadārammaṇa) is not obtained. In insight (vipassanā) that takes the three characteristics as its object, the registration is not obtained.

In powerful insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī), the registration is not obtained. When a javana occurs taking material and immaterial phenomena as its object, the registration is not obtained.
Among those phenomena fixed in the wrongness (micchattaniyata), the registration is not obtained.

In the case of phenomena fixed in rightness (*sammattaniyata-dhamma*), registration (*tadārammaṇa*) is not obtained. When impulsion (*javana*) occurs with supramundane phenomena as its object, registration is not obtained.
When impulsion occurs with direct knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) as its object, registration is not obtained.

When impulsion occurs with the knowledge of the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*) as its object, registration is not obtained. In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), when the object is weak...
That registration [consciousness] is not obtained; it is obtained only when a strong object has entered the range of the six doors.
And when it is obtained, it is obtained only in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*). In the fine-material and immaterial realms (*rūpa- and arūpa-bhava*), there is no such thing as registration.
As for what was said regarding the remaining nineteen types of consciousness: "In none of them is there any rebirth-linking corresponding to itself..."
“...it does not proceed,” this is difficult to understand because it is so concise. Therefore, in order to show the method of detailed exposition for this, it is said:
“How many kinds of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) are there? How many kinds of rebirth-linking consciousnesses are there? By what means and where does rebirth-linking occur?
What is the object of rebirth-linking?”
There are twenty types of rebirth-linking, including that of the non-percipient beings. There are nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness of the kinds already described.
Among these, rebirth-linking in the woeful states occurs through the rootless mind-consciousness element, which is the result of unwholesome kamma;

rebirth-linking in the human world occurs through the wholesome-resultant [mind-consciousness element] for those born blind, deaf from birth, insane, mute, eunuchs, and so forth. Rebirth-linking occurs through the eight great resultant consciousnesses accompanied by roots.
Rebirth-linking occurs among the sense-sphere deities and humans for those possessing merit;

it occurs in the fine-material Brahma-world through the five types of fine-material-sphere resultant [consciousness], and in the immaterial world through the four types of immaterial-sphere resultant [consciousness].
And wherever rebirth-linking occurs by means of a particular [consciousness], that very [consciousness] is called its corresponding rebirth-linking.
In brief, there are three kinds of objects for rebirth-linking: kamma, the sign of kamma, and the sign of destiny.
Therein, "kamma" refers to wholesome or unwholesome volition that has been accumulated. "The sign of kamma" is the object-base which was taken as an object when the kamma was being accumulated.
In this regard, even if the kamma was performed in the past, reaching back to the limit of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons—
At that moment, either the kamma or the sign of the kamma (kamma-nimitta) appears. Here is an instance of the appearance of a sign of kamma:
It is said that a man named Gopakasīvalī had a cetiya built at the Tālapiṭṭhika Monastery.
As he lay upon his deathbed, the cetiya appeared to him; he took that very image as his sign.
Having taken [the requisites] and passed away, he was reborn in the world of the devas. There is such a thing as a "death in confusion.
For while one is departing from the presence [of others], they cut off one's head with a sharp sword from behind;
or even while one is lying down and asleep, they cut off one's head with a sharp sword; or they kill one by drowning in water. At such times as these, one of the following occurs:
Either a kamma or a sign of kamma appears. There is indeed another kind of easy death:
for instance, when they crush a fly settled on the tip of a toothpick by striking it with a mallet, even at such a time as this, either a kamma or a sign of kamma appears.
However, while that fly is being crushed, first there is a mind-door adverting consciousness, then the life-continuum...
It does not advert; rather, it is the mind-door adverting consciousness alone that adverts. Then, having impelled the javanas, it sinks back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
On the second occasion, the body-door adverting consciousness adverts the life-continuum. Thereafter, the process-consciousnesses proceed:
body-consciousness, receiving, investigating, and determining. Having impelled the javanas, it sinks back into the life-continuum.
On the third occasion, the mind-door adverting consciousness turns back the life-continuum. Then, after the impulsion has impelled, it sinks back into the life-continuum.
At this point, one passes away. For what purpose is this brought forward? It is for the purpose of showing that the domain of immaterial phenomena is so exceedingly swift.
The sign of destiny (gatinimitta) is a certain appearance that manifests in the place where one is to be reborn.
When it manifests for one destined for hell, it appears like a cauldron of molten iron. When it manifests for one destined for the human world, it appears like a mother’s womb or a palanquin.
When it manifests for one destined for the deva world, the wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha), celestial mansions (vimāna), couches, and so forth appear.
Thus, in brief, there are three objects for rebirth-linking: kamma, the sign of kamma, and the sign of destiny.
Another method: There are three objects for rebirth-linking—the past, the present, and the indeterminate—and the non-percipient rebirth-linking is objectless.
In that regard, [the objects] of the rebirth-linkings of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are...
The object is exclusively past. For the ten sense-sphere consciousnesses, it is either past or present; for the remaining types, it is not to be stated.

Furthermore, since rebirth-linking occurring with respect to these three types of objects arises immediately after a death-consciousness that has either a past object or an unspecified object—there being no such thing as a death-consciousness with a present object—it is thus.

Therefore, the manner in which death with one of two types of objects is followed by rebirth-linking with one of three types of objects—occurring according to a happy or miserable destination—should be understood. To illustrate:
first, in the case of a person of evil deeds who is situated in a happy destination of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), [it occurs as follows]: "Then, for him, in that..."
From such statements as "at the time of hanging down," etc., it follows that for one lying on the bed of death,
the evil kamma accumulated or the sign of the kamma (*kamma-nimitta*) comes into the range of the mind-door. Taking that as its object,

after a pure cognitive series (*javana-vīthi*) ending in registration (*tadārammaṇa*), the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*) arises by making the object of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) its support.

When that [death-consciousness] has ceased, the rebirth-linking consciousness— pertaining to an unhappy destiny and impelled by the power of unabated defilements— arises, taking as its object that very same kamma or sign of kamma which has come into range. This is rebirth-linking with a past object immediately following death with a past object.

In the case of another person, at the time of death, a sign of an unhappy rebirth—such as the color of a mass of flames in hell and so forth—arises within the range of the mind-door by way of the aforementioned type of kamma.
After the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen and ceased twice, there occurs one adverting consciousness (āvajjana) directed toward that object;
then, because its momentum has been weakened by the proximity of death, five impulsion moments (javana) arise.
With "two [moments] having that as their object," three process-consciousnesses arise.
