Then, taking the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as its object, one death-consciousness (cuticitta) arises. At this point, eleven mind-moments have passed.

Then, in that very same object which has a remaining lifespan of five mind-moments, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta) arises. This occurs immediately after a death-consciousness whose object is past.
Rebirth has a present object.
At the moment of death for another person, a low object—serving as a cause for lust and so forth—comes into the range of one of the five sense-doors.
Following that, at the conclusion of the *voṭṭhabbana* consciousness that has arisen in due order, because of the proximity of death...
Due to the slowing of its momentum, five impulsion moments (*javana*) and two registration moments (*tadārammaṇa*) arise.

Following that, one death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) arises, taking as its object the same object as the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). At this point, there are fifteen moments: two life-continuums, adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, five impulsions, two registrations, and one death-consciousness.

The moments of consciousness have passed. Then, while that same object still endures for the duration of one remaining moment of consciousness, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises with respect to that very object.
This too is a rebirth-linking with a present object immediately following a death with a past object.
Such, then, is the manner in which a rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination—with an object both past and present—occurs immediately after a death in a happy destination with a past object.

But for one situated in an unhappy destination (duggati) who has accumulated blameless kamma, that blameless kamma or the sign of the kamma (kamma-nimitta) enters the range of the mind-door in the same manner already described.
Thus, setting aside the bright side (sukkappakka) from the dark side (kaṇhappakka), everything should be understood according to the previous method.
This [refers to the process] immediately following a death in an unhappy destination whose object is past, [resulting in rebirth] with an object that is either past or present.
The mode of occurrence for rebirth-linking in a happy destination (*sugati*). Furthermore,
for one established in a happy destination who has accumulated blameless kamma, as stated in the passage beginning, "At that time,
those [signs] hang down before him," the blameless kamma accumulated according to its nature, or the sign of the kamma (*kamma-nimitta*), appears at the mind-door to one lying on the bed of death.
It comes into range. And that occurs only for one who has accumulated blameless kamma pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
However, for one who has accumulated sublime kamma (*mahaggata-kamma*), only the sign of the kamma (*kammanimitta*) comes into range.

Taking that as its object, immediately after a pure cognitive series (*javanavīthi*)—which culminates in registration (*tadārammaṇa*)—the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) arises, making the object of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) its own object.

When that [death-consciousness] has ceased, there arises a rebirth-linking consciousness included within a happy destination, directed toward that very same object— whether it be a kamma or a kamma-sign—

that has come into the range of perception and is impelled by the power of unabated defilements. This is the rebirth-linking with a past object immediately following a death with a past object, or with an unspecified object.

In another person, at the time of death, due to blameless kamma pertaining to the sense-sphere, a sign of a happy destination— appearing as the color of a mother’s womb in the human world, or as the color of pleasure groves,
wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth in the deva world— comes into range at the mind-door.
Following the same sequence shown for the appearance of signs of an unhappy destination, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises immediately after the death-consciousness.
This is the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with a present object immediately following a death-consciousness (cuti) that had a past object.
In another case, at the time of death, relatives say, "Dear one, this offering to the Buddha is being made for your sake;

gladden your heart," and [present] a visible object by means of flower garlands, banners, flags, and so forth, or [a mental object] by means of listening to the Dhamma, musical offerings, and so forth.
Or a sound-object; or a smell-object by way of incense, perfumes, and so forth;
or a taste-object by saying, "Dear son, taste this; it is a gift to be given for your sake," such as honey, molasses, and so forth;
or [a tangible-object] by saying, "Dear son, touch this; it is a gift to be given for your sake," such as Chinese silk, Somāra cloth, and so forth.

Or they bring tactile objects to the five doors. When that object—be it a visible form or another—has come into range, following the sequence ending with the arising of determining consciousness (*votthapana*), five impulsion moments (*javana*) and two registration moments (*tadārammaṇa*) arise; this is because their momentum has weakened due to the proximity of death.
Thereafter, taking the life-continuum’s own object as its object, one [moment arises].
At the conclusion of the death-consciousness, rebirth-linking consciousness arises with respect to that very same object which persists for only a single moment of consciousness.
This too is a case where, immediately following a death-consciousness with a past object, there is a rebirth-linking consciousness with a present object.
However, in the case of another person who has attained a sublime state by means of the earth-kasiṇa jhāna or other such meditations and remains in a happy destination (sugati):

At the time of death, either one of the following—wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere, the sign of that kamma, or the sign of the destination—or else a sign such as the earth-kasiṇa or a sublime consciousness, comes into the range of the mind-door;
or else a sublime object that serves as a cause for the arising of wholesome states comes into the range of either the eye-door or the ear-door.
Following this, at the conclusion of the javanas that have arisen in due order, [the process proceeds].
Because its momentum has been weakened by its proximity to death, five impulsion moments arise. However, for those whose destiny is the sublime (mahaggata), there is no registration (tadārammaṇa).
Therefore, immediately after the impulsions, a single death-consciousness (cuticitta) arises, taking as its object the same object as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
At the conclusion of that, [there arises a rebirth-linking consciousness] included within one of the happy destinies—either of the sense-sphere or the sublime—among the various happy realms.
Among the objects as they have appeared, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises taking one particular object.

This is the mode of occurrence of rebirth-linking, which takes one among the past, present, or indeterminable objects immediately following a death in a happy destination that has an indeterminable object.

Following this same principle, rebirth-linking immediately following a death in the formless realms should also be understood. This is the manner in which rebirth-linking—with an object that is either past or indeterminable—occurs immediately after a death in a happy destination with an object that is past or indeterminable.

But for one who has committed evil deeds and is situated in an unhappy destination (duggati), that kamma—either as a kamma-sign (kammanimitta) or a destiny-sign (gatinimitta)—appears at the mind-door in the manner already described;
or else, at the five doors, an object that serves as the cause for the arising of unwholesome states enters the range of perception.
Then, in due order, at the conclusion of the death-consciousness (cuticitta), one of those objects belonging to the unhappy destination becomes the object [of the rebirth-linking consciousness].

The rebirth-linking consciousness arises. This is the mode of occurrence of rebirth-linking, which has objects belonging to the past and present, immediately following a death in an unhappy destination that had an object in the past.
Up to this point, the occurrence of all nineteen kinds of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking has been illustrated.
All of this occurs as follows:
while it is occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking, it proceeds in two ways by way of kamma;
and through the divisions such as the mixed and so forth, the division is of two kinds and more.
Indeed, this nineteenfold resultant consciousness, while occurring at rebirth-linking, functions in two ways by way of kamma.
For its own respective productive kamma acts as a condition for it both as a asynchronous kamma-condition and as a decisive-support condition.
For this has been said: "Wholesome and unwholesome kamma [acts] as a decisive-support condition for the result..."
“...the condition. For one who proceeds in this manner, however, the classification into two types and so forth should also be understood through the divisions such as the mixed and the unmixed;
that is to say—although this [continuity] proceeds in a single way by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it is twofold according to the division of the mixed and unmixed with matter;

it is threefold according to the division of existence in the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial realms; and [it is fourfold] by way of the egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously born modes of birth.
It is fourfold, fivefold by way of destiny, sevenfold by way of stations of consciousness, and eightfold by way of abodes of beings.
Therein: The mixed [consciousness] is twofold according to the distinction of states, and the intrinsic nature therein is likewise twofold.
Two or three decads, including the first [decad], in brief.
Regarding the statement, “Mixed is twofold due to the difference in existence”:

that rebirth-linking consciousness which arises here mixed with matter—excluding the immaterial existence—arises in the fine-material existence without the state known as the female faculty and male faculty.
In the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), apart from the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of those born as hermaphrodites (*jātipaṇḍaka*), [existence] is twofold:

with intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and without intrinsic nature (*abhāva*). Regarding the phrase “And therein, that which has intrinsic nature is twofold,” even there, that which possesses intrinsic nature is indeed twofold because it arises together with either the female or male state.
Regarding the phrase “Two or three decads arise together with the first,” this refers to the two categories here: the mixed and the unmixed.
The materiality at the beginning of existence is mixed with rebirth-linking consciousness;

together with that, two or three decads arise—either by way of the decad of the physical basis and the body, or by way of the decad of the physical basis and the sex-organ. There is no further reduction of materiality beyond this.
Now, when arising in such a minimal measure, this occurs in two types of birth: those called egg-born and moisture-born.
In one moment of birth, it arises having received the designation "kalala" (embryonic jelly), measuring the size of a drop of oil or clarified butter skimmed from the surface with a single hair.
Therein, the classification of origins should be understood according to the modes of rebirth.
For among these—there are no origins in the hells, nor in the devas, excluding those on earth.
There are three previous births (*purimikā*) in all three destinies (*gatittaya*).

In that context, regarding the phrase "and among the gods" (*devesu ca*), by the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that just as there are no three previous births among the hell-beings and among the gods excluding those on earth, so too there are none among the *nijjhāmataṇhika* ghosts;
for they are exclusively of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). As for the remainder, however...

In the three realms consisting of animals, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and humans, as well as among the earth-dwelling devas excluded from the previous [categories], there are four modes of birth (*yoni*). Regarding this:
"In the fine-material realms, there are thirty-nine; at the maximum, there are seventy forms."
Among those born from moisture and those of spontaneous birth—or at least in the case of the latter—there are thirty [material phenomena].

First, among the material Brahmās who are of spontaneous birth, thirty-nine material phenomena arise together with the rebirth-consciousness, by way of four groups: the eye-decad, the ear-decad, the base-decad, and the life-nonad.

However, excluding the fine-material Brahmās, among the other moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, there are at most seventy [material qualities], by way of the decads of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the base-decad.

And these are always present among the devas. Therein, the group of ten material qualities consisting of color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, the four elements, the sensitive eye, and the life faculty is called the "eye decad."

...so it is named. In this way, the rest are to be understood. At the very minimum, however, thirty material phenomena arise in one who is blind from birth, deaf, noseless, and asexual, by way of the tongue-decad, the body-decad, and the physical-basis-decad.
Between the maximum and the minimum, the appropriate variations are to be understood accordingly.
Having understood this, again—

The distinction between difference and non-difference regarding death and rebirth-linking is to be fully understood by means of the aggregates, the object, the destiny, the root-cause, feeling, zest, applied thought, and sustained thought.

The meaning is that this distinction between difference and non-difference, by way of these factors— aggregates and so forth— should be known for both types of rebirth-linking (mixed and unmixed) and for the death-moment that immediately precedes it.

How so? Sometimes, immediately after a four-aggregate formless death-consciousness, there arises a rebirth-linking consciousness that is likewise four-aggregate and has an object not different [from the previous one].
Sometimes, following a four-aggregate formless death-consciousness with an object that is non-magnificent and external, there arises one with a magnificent and internal object.

This, first of all, is the method regarding the formless planes themselves. However, sometimes, immediately after a four-aggregate formless death-consciousness, there arises a five-aggregate [rebirth-linking consciousness].

Rebirth-linking belongs to the sense-sphere. Sometimes, immediately after a death-moment of the sense-sphere consisting of five aggregates, or after a death-moment of the fine-material sphere, there is a four-aggregate rebirth-linking in the immaterial sphere.
Thus, from a death-moment with a past object, there may be a rebirth-linking with a past, an inexpressible, or a present object;

from a death-moment in certain happy destinies, there may be a rebirth-linking in certain miserable destinies; and from a death-moment that is rootless, there may be a rebirth-linking that possesses roots.
With a death accompanied by two roots, there is a rebirth-linking accompanied by three roots; with a death accompanied by equanimity, there is a rebirth-linking accompanied by joy;

with a death without rapture, there is a rebirth-linking with rapture; with a death without applied thought, there is a rebirth-linking with applied thought; with a death without sustained thought, there is a rebirth-linking with sustained thought;
and with a death without applied or sustained thought, there is a rebirth-linking with both applied and sustained thought—such is the case for each respective instance.
And the opposite should be applied accordingly.
This mere phenomenon, having acquired its conditions, passes on to another state of existence;
there is no transmigration from that [state], nor does it exist without a cause.
Thus, this mere collection of material and immaterial phenomena, arising when the necessary conditions are met, is said to "enter another existence";
it is not a "being" (satta), nor a "life-principle" (jīva). For it, there is no transmigration from a past existence to this one, nor is there its manifestation here without a cause.
We shall illustrate this by means of the manifest process of human death and rebirth-linking:
For in a past existence, when death was imminent— whether by natural causes or through violence—
and while unable to endure the convergence of death-bed sensations that sever all the joints and bonds of the limbs and members, his body gradually withered like a green palm leaf placed in the sun;
and when the eye and other sense-faculties had ceased, they remained established only in the heart-base (*hadaya-vatthu*).
At the moment when the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, and the life-faculty remain, consciousness— supported by the heart-base—
proceeds by taking as its object either a specific kamma characterized as a residual formation whose conditions have been obtained through being weighty, habitual, proximate, or previously performed,
or the objective field presented by that kamma, known as the sign of kamma or the sign of destiny.
Thus, as this [consciousness] proceeds, because craving and ignorance have not been abandoned, craving inclines it toward that object whose dangers are concealed by ignorance;

the co-nascent formations propel it. Being thus inclined by craving and propelled by formations in the course of the continuum, it is like one who, while crossing a stream, clings to a rope tied to a tree on the near bank, and [clings] to the previous [moment of consciousness].
It abandons its support; furthermore, whether it relishes or does not relish the support produced by kamma, it proceeds solely through conditions such as the object.
In this context, the former is called "death" (cuti) because of passing away, and the latter is called "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) because of connecting with the beginning of another existence.
It is said: "This [consciousness] has neither come here from a previous existence, nor has it arisen there without a cause such as kamma, formations, or objects.
There may be illustrations for this, such as echoes and the like.
In terms of the continuity of the stream, there is neither identity nor difference.

Herein, regarding this consciousness's non-arrival here from its previous existence and its arising through causes comprised within that past existence, phenomena such as an echo, a lamp, a seal, and a reflection would serve as illustrations. For just as:
Just as an echo, a lamp, a reflection, or a shadow arises from causes such as sound and so forth without going elsewhere, even so is this mind.
And here, "due to the continuity of the stream, there is neither identity nor difference.

For if, while there is a continuity of the stream, there were absolute identity, curd would not arise from milk. On the other hand, if there were absolute difference, [curd] would not be dependent upon the milk.
It might be curd. This same principle applies to all things produced by causes and conditions. And if this were so, there would be the abolition of all worldly conventions, which is undesirable.
Therefore, in this matter, one should not adhere exclusively to either identity or difference.
Here it may be asked: "But if there is thus manifestation without transmigration, then as for those aggregates (khandhas) that exist in this human existence—"

Since the condition for the fruit—the karma—has ceased, and since that karma does not go there [to the new existence], would that fruit arise from something else, or from something other than its cause?
And if there is no experiencer, to whom would that fruit belong? Therefore, this formulation is not sound. Regarding this, it is said:
“That fruit which occurs within a continuum belongs neither to another nor from another.”
The conditioning of seeds is the proof for this point.
For when a fruit arises within a single continuum, since identity and difference are absolutely excluded therein, it does not arise "from another" or "as something other.
And the conditioning of seeds is the proof for this very point.
For when preparations have been made for seeds such as mangoes, a specific fruit arises at a later time within the continuity of that seed once it has obtained the necessary conditions;

yet this fruit does not arise from other seeds nor from other preparatory conditions, and those seeds or preparations do not themselves reach the place where the fruit appears. This should be understood as being exactly like that.

This meaning should also be understood by way of such things as knowledge, spells, and medicinal herbs, which, though applied to the body of a child, yield their fruit at a later time in the body of an adult and so forth.
As for what was said: “And if there is no enjoyer, to whom would that fruit belong?”—to that we reply: [as follows].
The designation "eater" is established precisely by the arising of the fruit;
just as the designation "the tree bears fruit" is established by the production of the fruit of the tree.
For indeed, it is by the arising of the fruit of the tree—which is but one part of those phenomena designated as "the tree"—that [the designation is established].
Just as a tree is called "fruit-bearing" or "fruited" because of the production of fruit,
so too a god or a human— being merely a portion of the aggregates (khandhas) designated as "god" or "human"—
is called "one who enjoys," "happy," or "suffering" solely through the arising of the fruit of pleasure and pain known as experience. Therefore, there is no separate enjoyer here other than this.
"There is no such thing as an object. Even if one were to say: "Even so, these formations must either exist as conditions for a fruit or not exist.
If they exist, their result must occur at the very moment of their occurrence. But if they do not exist..."
"If it were said that these [conditions] always bring forth their fruit both before and after they have been set in motion," he should be told this:
"These conditions are effective because they have been performed, and they do not always bring forth their fruit;
in this regard, examples such as surety-bonds and the like should be understood."
For volitional formations (saṅkhāra) become conditions for their own fruit solely by virtue of having been performed (katattā), not because of being present or being absent.
As it is said: "Because wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere has been performed and accumulated, its result, eye-consciousness, arises," and so forth.
Having become conditions for their respective fruits as appropriate, they do not again bring about those fruits.
They exist because their result has already matured. To clarify this meaning, this illustration beginning with "surety" should be understood.

For in the world, when someone acts as a surety for the delivery of something, or buys goods, or incurs a debt, the mere performance of that action becomes the condition for the delivery of that object and so forth.
There is neither existence nor non-existence of the action. Nor does one remain merely a "holder" after the handing over of that object and so forth.

Why? Because the handing over and other such acts have been performed. Just as it is because they have been performed that volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) become conditions for their own fruit, yet they do not continue to bring about the fruit after the giving of the fruit according to its fitness. Up to this point, [the discussion has been] by way of the mixed and unmixed.
Thus, the occurrence of the rebirth-linking consciousness as it proceeds in both ways has been illustrated by way of the condition of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya*).
Now, in order to dispel confusion regarding all these thirty-two types of consciousness, [the author says]:
"By way of rebirth-linking and occurrence, these [consciousnesses] in the states of existence and so forth..."
The formations (saṅkhāras) should be understood, as well as their conditions.

In this context, "existence" (bhava) and so forth refers to these: the three existences (bhavas), the four modes of birth (yoni), the five destinations (gati), the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).
Among these existences and so on, during both rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and the course of existence (pavatta), these [formations] belong to those resultant consciousnesses (vipākaviññāṇa).
The meaning is that the conditions must be understood exactly as they are.

In this regard: first, as for the volitional formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), the volitional formation of merit—consisting specifically of the eight types of sense-sphere volition—acts, without distinction, as a "kamma-condition" (at a different time) for the rebirth-linking of the nine resultant consciousnesses within a fortunate rebirth in the sense-sphere existence.

And the condition is twofold: by way of decisive support (upanissaya-paccaya) and [the other]. The volition of the fivefold wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is the formation of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra);
it is a condition for the five [mental aggregates] at rebirth-linking in the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava).

However, the aforementioned classification of sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) volition is a condition, by the same method already stated, for the seven limited resultant consciousnesses (paritta-vipāka-viññāṇa) in a happy destination within the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava), excluding the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity.

In the course of existence (*pavatta*), it is a condition in two ways, but not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). In the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*), that same [condition] is likewise a condition for the five resultant consciousnesses during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking.

However, in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*)—specifically in the miserable destinies—it is likewise a condition for all eight limited-resultant consciousnesses during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking.

In that regard, in the hells, during the Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s wanderings through the various hells and similar occasions, that [object] serves as the condition for the encounter with desirable objects.
Furthermore, among the animals—specifically those such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and petas who possess great psychic power—desirable objects are indeed obtained.

In the same way, within the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava) in the happy destinies, during the course of existence, that very [object] serves as the condition for all sixteen types of wholesome resultant consciousness.

And [it is] at rebirth-linking. Without distinction, the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) is a condition for ten resultant consciousnesses in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), both during the course of existence (*pavatta*) and at rebirth-linking.

The formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), consisting of the twelve types of unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*), is a condition for one consciousness in the miserable destinies (*duggati*) within the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*).

Likewise, in the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is a condition for those [seven] but not during the course of existence (*pavatta*); for six [consciousnesses], it is a condition during the course of existence but not at rebirth-linking;

and for all seven unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses, it is a condition both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking. Furthermore, in the sensual realm (*kāmabhava*) within a happy destination (*sugati*), it is a condition for those same seven during the course of existence but not at rebirth-linking;
in the fine-material realm (*rūpabhava*), it is a condition for four resultant consciousnesses.

In the same way, the condition [of the imperturbable formation] exists during the course of existence (*pavatta*), but not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). And that occurs in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) by way of seeing undesirable forms and hearing undesirable sounds.
However, in the Brahma-world there are no such things as undesirable forms and so forth; likewise, it is the same in the sense-sphere divine world.

The imperturbable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) is a condition for the four resultant consciousnesses in the formless existence (*arūpabhava*) both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.

Furthermore, by way of the all-inclusive method (*sabbasaṅgāhikanaya*), the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), which consists of twenty types of volition (*cetanā*)—both wholesome and unwholesome of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*)—acts as a condition in two ways for the ten resultant consciousnesses (*vipākaviññāṇa*) at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*):

namely, as a asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*) and as a decisive support-condition (*upanissayapaccaya*). That same [bodily formation] acts in the same two ways for thirteen [resultant consciousnesses] in the sense-sphere existence and for nine [resultant consciousnesses] in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*).

In the course of existence (*pavatta*), that same [volitional formation] is a condition for the twenty-three resultant consciousnesses in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) in exactly the same way, but not at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

This same principle applies to verbal formations (*vacīsaṅkhāra*) as well. Furthermore, the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*), which is divided into twenty-eight or twenty-nine types of volition (*cetanā*), is a condition for nineteen resultant consciousnesses in the three existences in the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.
In the same way, it is a condition for the resultant consciousnesses at rebirth-linking, but not during the course of existence.

That same [kamma] is a condition in the same way for twenty-two resultant consciousnesses—namely, the thirteen mentioned below and the nine—in both types of existence during the course of existence, but not at rebirth-linking.
However, in all three types of existence, it is a condition in the same way for all thirty-two resultant consciousnesses during the course of existence.

And also at rebirth-linking. Thus, first of all, with respect to the various states of existence, those formations for which these [volitions] are conditions, and how they serve as conditions, should be understood. This same method should be understood regarding the modes of birth (*yoni*) and so forth.
Herein, this is a mere introductory explanation starting from the beginning: among these formations, since the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*)...
Having given rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in two types of existence (*bhava*), it produces its entire result;
likewise in the four modes of birth (*yoni*), such as egg-born and so forth; in the two destinations (*gati*), namely gods and humans;

and in the four stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), which consist of those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, those with diverse bodies and unified perceptions, those with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, and those with unified bodies and unified perceptions—this being by way of humans and the planes of the first, second, and third jhānas.

However, in the abode of non-percipient beings, this [kamma] produces only material form; thus, having given rebirth-linking in only four of the seven abodes of beings, it generates its entire result.

Therefore, within these two types of existence, four modes of birth, two destinations, four stations of consciousness, and four abodes of beings, this [kamma] [produces] twenty-one types of resultant consciousness.
In the manner already stated, it serves as a condition for rebirth-linking and for the course of existence (pavatta) according to what is possible.

As for the unwholesome formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), however, because it occurs only within a single sensual existence (kāmabhava)— in four modes of birth (yoni), in the remaining three destinations (gati),
in one station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) known as "diversity of body and unity of perception," and in such a single [station]— it is [restricted].
It ripens by way of rebirth-linking in the abodes of beings; therefore, in a single existence, within the four modes of birth,
the three destinations, one station of consciousness, and one abode of beings, it serves as a condition for the seven resultant consciousnesses according to the method already stated,
both at the moment of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.

As for the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*), however, because it ripens by way of rebirth-linking in a single existence— that is, in one formless existence, in one mode of birth (the apparitional), in one destiny (the divine),
in three stations of consciousness (the base of infinite space and so forth), and in four abodes of beings (the base of infinite space and so forth)—
therefore, it occurs in only one existence, in one mode of birth, and in one divine destiny.
In the three stations of consciousness and the four abodes of beings, bodily formation acts as a condition for the four types of consciousness—
both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence—

in the manner already described. This is because bodily formation occurs within a single sensual-sphere existence, across the four modes of birth, the five destinations, and two stations of consciousness.
Having given rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in two of the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*), it produces its entire result;

therefore, in one existence, across the four modes of birth (*yoni*), the five destinations (*gati*), the two stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and the two abodes of beings, it is likewise a condition for twenty-three resultant consciousnesses during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence (*pavatta*). The same method applies to verbal formations (*vacī-saṅkhāra*) as well.
However, because the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) does not ripen anywhere except within one of the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*),

it serves as a condition for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for the thirty-two types of resultant consciousness (*vipākaviññāṇa*) accordingly, within the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the eight abodes of beings.

And [it occurs] during the course of existence (*pavatta*). However, in the non-conscious abodes of beings (*aviññāṇaka sattāvāsa*), there is no consciousness conditioned by formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya-viññāṇa*).

Furthermore, the meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) is a condition for the kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) in the non-percipient beings by way of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*).
Thus—by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence—these [formations] [are conditions] in the realms of existence and so forth.
Formations are to be understood, as well as their conditions.
This is the exposition of the section on consciousness with formations as its condition.
This is the exposition of the section on name-and-form.
228. In the exposition of name-and-form conditioned by consciousness:
the detailed analysis is to be understood through the diversity of the teaching, its occurrence in all states of existence and so forth, its inclusion, and the method of conditions.

‘By way of the difference in teaching’ means: first, in the Suttanta and here [in this work], the teaching is made identical and uniform because there is no difference in the term *rūpa*, as in: “What is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements”;
however, it is different in the case of the term *nāma*.
For in the Suttanta it is said: "In this context, what is name (nāma)? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention.
Here, however, it is stated as: "The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations.

For in that [Suttanta], even that name which arises conditioned by eye-consciousness, and which—once arisen—is the persistence of consciousness and the life-span of immaterial phenomena, is described thus by way of its dependence on other factors.

Because it is evident as something to be grasped, he showed that by dividing the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) into three parts—by way of volition, contact, and attention—and taught it together with the other two aggregates. Here, however, including all names mentioned there as well as those not mentioned, he said:
"Three aggregates: the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)."
But why are these three aggregates alone called "name," while consciousness is not? It is not that it is not;
however, if that consciousness were included, it would result in the coexistence of two types of consciousness: the consciousness as name and the consciousness as condition.
Therefore, setting aside consciousness in its capacity as a condition, [the other three] are called "name" as that which is produced by conditions.
It is said that only three aggregates are mentioned in order to demonstrate this. Thus, first, the analysis should be understood "by way of the distinction of the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "occurring in all states of existence, etc.": here, name occurs in all remaining states of existence—namely, all existences (*bhava*), modes of birth (*yoni*), destinations (*gati*), and stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*)—with the exception of one single abode of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
Matter occurs in two existences, four modes of birth, five destinations, and the first four stations of consciousness.

And it proceeds within the five abodes of beings. While the mind is thus proceeding, since for those born from non-existence, those born from a womb, and those born from an egg, at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), two stream-heads of materiality arise by way of the physical basis and the body, along with three immaterial aggregates;
therefore, for them, in detail, twenty states arise as materiality and three as immateriality.
Regarding "aggregates" (khandhā): these twenty-three states, conditioned by consciousness, should be understood as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
By the method of taking what has not been taken, if one removes nine material phenomena from one stream-head, there are fourteen;

then, adding the existence-decad of intrinsic natures, there are thirty-three. Again, by the method of taking what has not been taken among those, if one removes eighteen material phenomena from two stream-heads, there are fifteen.
And because, among spontaneously born beings (*opapātika-satta*), at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-kkhaṇa*)—

such as those belonging to the Brahma-world (*brahmakāyika*) and others— four continuities of material form (*rūpa-rūpa*) and three immaterial aggregates (*arūpin-khandha*) manifest by way of the eye-decad,
ear-decad, base-decad, and the nonad of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya-navaka*), therefore, in detail, for them there are forty-nine states by way of material form and three [immaterial aggregates].
And the immaterial aggregates—these forty-two states should be understood as "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.
However, by taking what has not yet been included, and excluding twenty-seven states from the three heads of the continuity, there remain fifteen.
In the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), however, because the remaining types of spontaneous birth (opapātika) or moisture-born beings possess complete sense bases by their very nature...
At the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), seven heads of the material continuity (*rūpasantatisīsa*) and three immaterial aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*) become manifest.

Therefore, in detail, these seventy-three phenomena—consisting of seventy from the material continuity and the three immaterial aggregates—should be understood as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by consciousness (*viññāṇapaccaya*).
However, by taking what has not yet been taken [from the previous analysis], from the six heads of the continuity...
Having excluded fifty-four factors, nineteen remain. This is the maximum number.

At the minimum, however, for those lacking the head of this or that continuity of material form, one should understand—both briefly and in detail—that name-and-form, reckoned as the condition for rebirth-linking consciousness, is to be understood by omitting each respective factor.
For non-material beings, there are only the three non-material aggregates. For non-percipient beings, [there is only] material form.
"Only the vital-nonad. This, first of all, is the method regarding rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

However, during the course of existence (*pavatta*), in every place where matter arises, at the moment of the presence of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the temperature-born pure octad (*suddhaṭṭhaka*)—arising from the heat that functions together with the rebirth-linking consciousness—becomes manifest. As for the rebirth-linking consciousness itself...

It does not originate matter. For, just as a person who has fallen over a precipice is unable to serve as a condition for another, so too, due to its weakness resulting from the weakness of the physical basis (*vatthu*), it is unable to originate matter.

However, after the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), beginning from the first life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), there is the pure octad originated by consciousness. At the time of the manifestation of sound—
From the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, there is the sound-nonad consisting of both the temperature and the consciousness that occur.
However, for those womb-born beings who subsist on physical nutriment, it is said:
"Whatever food, drink, and nourishment his mother eats..."
"By that he sustains himself there, the person while still in the mother's womb"— from this statement,
when the body has been sustained by the food swallowed by the mother, at the time of swallowing the saliva that has first entered one's own mouth,
there arises the "pure octad produced by nutriment. This is [the example] of that which is produced by nutriment.
Pure octad, together with the temperature-born and consciousness-born [octads], consists of twenty-six types at most by way of two sets of nine;
and the previously mentioned action-born [octads], which arise three times in each single moment of consciousness, consist of seventy types.
Thus, there are ninety-six types of material phenomena (rūpa) and the three immaterial aggregates (arūpino khandhā), making ninety-nine states (dhammā) in total. Since—
The word "or" (*vā*) is indefinite because it appears only at certain times; therefore, setting aside both of those,
these ninety-seven states should be understood as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by consciousness for all beings,
as far as possible, whether they are sleeping, heedless, walking about, eating, or drinking, by day or by night.
These proceed with consciousness as their condition; we shall explain later how that [consciousness] serves as their condition.

Now, as for this material form born of kamma herein: although it establishes itself first of all within the states of existence, the modes of birth, the destinations, the stations of consciousness, and the abodes of beings, it is unable to remain stable if it is not supported by material form originated by the three [other causes];
nor can the [form] originated by the three [causes] [remain stable without it].

They were not supported by that [earth]. Rather, like bundles of reeds established in the four directions when struck by the wind, or like a wrecked ship that has found some foothold in the great ocean when battered by the force of the waves, these beings remained standing together without falling, mutually supporting one another, for one year, two years...
[and so on]... even for a hundred years, until those beings [perished].

"Or until the exhaustion of the life-span, or the exhaustion of merit, they continue to proceed. In this way, the analysis should be understood here as "proceeding through all states of existence and so forth.

And regarding the term "compendia," herein [it refers to] that which occurs in the immaterial realm during the process of occurrence and rebirth-linking, and in the five-aggregate existence during the process of occurrence.
With consciousness as condition, there is name alone; and that which occurs among non-percipient beings and throughout the five-aggregate existence as form alone with consciousness as condition;

and that which occurs everywhere in the five-aggregate existence as both name and form with consciousness as condition—all that, having been subsumed by the method of "single-remainder" (*ekadesasarūpeka-sesa*) as "name-and-form," [arises] with consciousness as condition.
It should be understood as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). If it is argued that this is inappropriate because consciousness is absent among the non-percipient beings (*asaññī*), that is not incorrect.
For this is said: "That which is the cause of name-and-form, consciousness, is considered to be twofold:
resultant (*vipāka*) and non-resultant (*avipāka*); therefore, this [definition] is indeed appropriate."
For that consciousness which is the cause of name-and-form is considered to be twofold, by way of the distinction between resultant and non-resultant. And this is indeed logical:

because it is produced by kamma among the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), and likewise, in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*), it is produced by kamma during the moments of wholesome and other types of consciousness occurring in the course of existence. Thus...
The exposition here should also be understood by way of grouping.
For in this context, regarding "the method of conditions": for name, the resultant consciousness is a condition in nine ways.
The materiality of the physical basis is ninefold; that of the remaining materiality is eightfold.
Volitional consciousness relates to materiality in one way;
other types of consciousness relate to it in their respective appropriate ways.

That which is called name— consisting of resultant [consciousness] at rebirth-linking or during the course of existence— is a condition in nine ways for its associated materiality, whether mixed with materiality or unmixed with materiality,
and for other resultant consciousnesses, whether at rebirth-linking or otherwise, by way of the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, association,

resultant, nutriment, faculty, presence, and non-disappearance. For the physical basis (vatthurūpa) at rebirth-linking, it is a condition by way of the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, resultant, nutriment, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

There are nine kinds of conditions. However, with the exception of the physical basis (vatthurūpa), all other material phenomena serve as conditions for one another through eight of these nine conditions, excluding the mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya).

Furthermore, kamma-forming consciousness serves as a condition for the matter of non-percipient beings or for kamma-born matter in the five-aggregate plane in only one way, namely, by way of decisive support (upanissaya) according to the Suttanta method.
It exists. It should be understood that all remaining consciousness from the first bhavaṅga onwards serves as a condition for its respective name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as appropriate.
However, if the method of its conditions were to be shown in detail, the entire exposition of the *Paṭṭhāna* would have to be set forth; therefore, we do not undertake it here.
In this regard, it may be asked: "How is it to be known that the name-and-form of rebirth-linking has consciousness as its condition?

It is to be known from both scripture (sutta) and reasoning (yutti). For in the Suttas, the fact that feeling and the other mental factors have consciousness as their condition is established in many ways through such methods as the passage beginning, "Phenomena that follow upon the mind. As for reasoning:
"For it is established here by means of material form born of mind that is seen;
for even regarding material form that is not seen, consciousness is its condition.
For when the mind is either confident or dispirited, material forms corresponding to that state arise and are seen. By means of what is seen...

And by the statement "there is inference of what is unseen," it should be understood here that consciousness is a condition for the rebirth-linking materiality even though it is unseen, by means of the mind-born materiality which is seen.
For in the *Paṭṭhāna*, it is stated that even that [materiality] originated by kamma has consciousness as its condition, just like that originated by mind.
Thus, the exposition should be understood here according to the method of conditions.
And here, when the Blessed One says, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form," since to the wise who investigate,
only name-and-form itself is seen occurring in the ultimate sense— neither a being nor a person—
therefore this is irrefutable by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else.
"Or, in the world, the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion.
This is the exposition of the terms regarding name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.
The exposition of the terms regarding the six sense bases.
229. In the exposition of the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form:
"Name" is considered to be the three aggregates, and "form" is considered to be the primary elements, the physical bases, and so forth.
That [name] is a condition for that [form], and vice versa, in the manner already described.
Regarding that name-and-form which serves as the condition for the six sense bases: therein, "name" refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling;

"form," however, should be understood as consisting of the four primary elements, the six bases, and the life-faculty—thus comprising the elements, bases, and so forth—as included within one's own continuity.
Furthermore, it is called "name-and-form" because it is both name and form, or "name-and-form" [as a compound].

When the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) compound is thus formed as "the sixth base and the six bases are the 'six bases'," it should be understood that this very six bases—formed by the *ekasesa*—is the condition. Why?
Because in the immaterial realm (*ārūpa*), only name (*nāma*) is the condition; and that [name] belongs only to the sixth base, not to any other.
For he will state in the section on the indeterminate (*abyākata*): "The sixth base has name as its condition. This is indeed included here.
For it should be understood that it is analyzed therein.
Herein, one might ask: "How is it to be known that 'name-and-form is the condition for the sixfold base'?
Because of its presence when name-and-form are present. For each respective sense-base exists when its corresponding name and form exist, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, the fact that this [condition] exists when that [state] exists will become clear precisely within the method of conditions (*paccayanaya*). Therefore:

"Whether in rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or in the course of existence (*pavatta*), whatever is a condition for whatever, and in whatever manner it is a condition—that should be understood by one who discerns."
Herein, this is the exposition of the meaning:
In the immaterial plane, name alone is the condition for rebirth-linking and the course of existence in seven ways; the sixth [condition] exists there at its minimum.

How so? First, at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), name is a condition for the sixth base in seven ways—at minimum—by way of the co-nascent, mutuality, support, association, resultant, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
However, some of these also act as conditions in other ways, such as by way of the root condition (*hetupaccaya*) or the nutriment condition (*āhārapaccaya*);
thus, the full range of conditions should be understood according to their respective maximum and minimum applications.
In the case of the active state (*pavatta*), the resultant (*vipāka*) acts as a condition in the manner already described.

However, in the other case [the passive state], at its minimum, it acts as a condition by way of six conditions—excluding the resultant condition—from among the types of conditions mentioned above. Yet, some of these act as a condition through the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), and some through the nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*);
thus it acts as a condition in other ways as well. The maximum and minimum [of its conditioning role] should be understood by way of this.
In another existence as well, the name [at rebirth-linking] is likewise;
for the sixth [consciousness], that is a condition for the others in six ways.
For even in the five-aggregate existence other than the formless realm, that resultant name, acting as an associate to the heart-base, [serves as a condition].
For the sixth, the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it is a condition in seven ways at minimum, exactly as stated for the immaterial plane (*ārūpa*).

However, for these other five—the eye-base and so forth—it is a condition in six modes by way of conascence, support, result, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance, acting as an associate to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Furthermore, in this context...

By way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), or by way of the nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*)—thus there are other ways as well in which a condition exists. By means of that, the superior and inferior grades should be understood.
It is likewise in the course of existence (*pavatta*):
"The resultant is a condition for the resultant; the non-resultant is a condition for the non-resultant; [and] it is a condition for the sixth in six ways."

For even in the course of existence within the five-aggregate plane, just as in the case of rebirth-linking, resultant name is a condition for resultant sixth base in seven ways by way of its capacity.

Non-resultant [name], however, is a condition for non-resultant sixth base only by way of its capacity, and thus, excluding the resultant condition, it is a condition in six ways. In this context, according to the method already stated—
The maximum and minimum [number of conditions] should be understood.

In that very same way, for the remaining five [types of consciousness], the resultant [consciousness] is a condition in four ways; likewise, the non-resultant [consciousness] is explained in the same manner.

For in that very same process, the five bases—such as the eye-faculty and so forth—of the remaining [mental states] are a condition in four ways for both types of resultant-named phenomena (vipāka-nāma) by way of postnascent dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.
And just as with the resultant, the non-resultant is likewise explained. Therefore, their wholesome and other classifications are also fourfold.

It should be understood that it serves as a condition. Thus, first of all, it should be understood in what way each [mental] base (āyatana) serves as a condition for whichever [base] during rebirth-linking or in the course of existence, and how it does so.
However, in this context, material form (rūpa) serves as a condition in the immaterial realm (ārūpya-bhava).
Not even for a single base (āyatana), but rather within the existence of the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha).
Regarding the connection [of rebirth], the physical basis (vatthu) is a condition for the sixth [consciousness] in six ways;
the primary elements (bhūtāni) are a condition for the five [senses] in four ways, without distinction.

For, in terms of material form (*rūpa*), at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the basis-form (*vatthurūpa*) is a condition for the sixth base, the mind-base (*manāyatana*), in six ways: by way of the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance.

Furthermore, the four primary elements (*bhūta*), both generally at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence (*pavatta*), act as conditions for whichever base arises—whether it be the five bases beginning with the eye-base—by way of the conditions of conascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance.
The conditions are fourfold.
For these [five aggregates], life-faculty is threefold and nutriment is [threefold] during the course of existence;
for the sixth [consciousness-element], those same two are sixfold; and for that very [element], the physical basis is fivefold.

Furthermore, for these five—beginning with the eye—the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvita*) serves as a condition in three ways: by way of presence (*atthi*) and non-disappearance (*avigata*), both at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and during the course of existence (*pavatta*).
"And nutriment" means that nutriment also serves as a condition in three ways: by way of presence and non-disappearance.

However, this applies only to those beings who subsist on nutriment, and only during the course of existence when the body is sustained by nutriment, not at the moment of rebirth-linking. As for those [faculties]...

The five bases, beginning with the eye-base, act as conditions for the sixth base—the mind-base, which consists of the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness—in six ways during the course of existence (pavatta), namely:

as support-condition (nissaya), pre-existence-condition (purejāta), faculty-condition (indriya), dissociation-condition (vippayutta), presence-condition (atthi), and non-disappearance-condition (avigata);

however, this does not apply at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Excluding the five types of consciousness, the physical heart-base (vatthurūpa) acts as a condition for that same mind-base in the remaining ways.
In the course of existence (pavatta), but not at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), conditionality occurs in five ways:

by way of dependence, prenascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, it should be understood exactly how and for which sense base (āyatana) materiality serves as a condition, both at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence.
But as for name-and-form, it is both together that constitute the condition for whatever [consciousness];
and how this applies in all cases must be understood by one who is discerning. To illustrate:
first, in the case of rebirth-linking in the five-constituent existence, [name-and-form] consists of the three aggregates and the materiality of the physical basis.
Name-and-form is a condition for the sixth base by way of such conditions as co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, association, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance;
this is merely an outline here. However, since it is possible to apply all these [conditions] according to the method already stated, no detailed exposition is given here.
The Exposition of the Conditioned Arising of the Six Sense Bases by way of Name-and-Form.
The Exposition of Contact by way of the Six Sense Bases (230). In the exposition of contact conditioned by the six sense bases:
In brief, there are six types of contact, beginning with eye-contact;
in detail, they become thirty-two, just like consciousness.
For in the Pāli, "in brief," only six contacts are mentioned, beginning with "eye-contact. In detail...
Furthermore, there are ten [types of consciousness] consisting of the five wholesome-resultants and the five unwholesome-resultants beginning with eye-contact;

and the remaining twenty-two associated with mundane resultant consciousness. Thus, all together, there are thirty-two types of consciousness conditioned by formations, just as were stated for the [resultant] consciousnesses.
Now, the condition for these thirty-two kinds of contact is the sixfold sense base (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Regarding that:
Together with the sixth [consciousness-element], the wise maintain that the sixfold sense base (*saḷāyatana*) consists of the internal eye and so forth, along with the external [objects].

In this regard, as for those who hold that "this is a discourse on the occurrence of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*)," they consider the condition to be comprised within a single continuum (*ekasantati*).

They also teach that [the sixfold base] is conditionally arisen. Following the scriptural passage, "Contact has the sixfold base as its condition," they maintain that in the formless realm it is the sixth base, while elsewhere—by way of a comprehensive inclusion—it is the sixfold base;

thus, making a partial *sarūpa-ekasesa* (an elliptical compound based on similarity), they accept that the internal eye-base and so forth, together with the sixth, constitute the "sixfold base. For that indeed is the sixth base...
The six sense bases (saḷāyatana) go only to the category of the six sense bases. However, those who maintain that only what has arisen from conditions is included within a single continuum,
while the conditions themselves may belong to different continua— when they explain each and every sense base that serves as a condition for contact—
they include even external factors and, together with the sixth [base], [classify them] internally and externally.
They maintain that the "sixfold base" (saḷāyatana) consists of the six bases together with the sense-base of visible form and the others.
For even that [term]—by applying the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*) to the phrase "the sixth base and the sixfold base"—comes to be designated simply as "sixfold base.
Here it is said: contact does not arise from all the bases together, nor do all contacts arise from a single base.
And this [contact] is stated as being "only one" in the formula "with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises. Why is that? Here is the answer:
This is true. It is not possible for all [conditions] to produce one, nor for one to produce all; however, it is possible for many to produce one.
For example, visual contact arises from the eye base, the form base, the mind base—which is comprised of eye-consciousness—and the remaining [bases].
And "the associated mental-object base"—in this way, it should be applied everywhere as appropriate. Therefore, indeed:
"But this contact, which arises from many bases, is shown here by the One Who Is Such (the Tathāgata) by means of the singular grammatical designation."

‘By means of the singular designation’: for by this singular designation, “with the six sense bases as condition, contact [arises],” it is shown that from many sense bases there is a single contact; such is the meaning. Regarding the sense bases, however:
Five are sixfold, and one is threefold; the external ones are ninefold.
One should discern how these function as conditions for this [contact] according to their occurrence.

Herein, this is the analysis: first, the five bases beginning with the eye-base are conditions in six ways—by way of support, prenascence, faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance—for the fivefold contact divided into eye-contact and so forth.

Following that, one resultant mind-base is [a condition] for the various types of resultant mind-contact by way of conascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, faculty, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

There are nine kinds of conditions. Among external phenomena, however, the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) is a condition for eye-contact in four ways: as object-prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance.
Likewise, the sound-base and the others are conditions for ear-contact and so forth.
For mind-contact, those [bases] and the mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*) are likewise conditions, but only by way of the object-condition alone. Thus, the six external bases...
"Explain its status as a condition as far as possible.
This is the exposition of the section on contact with the six sense bases as its condition.
This is the exposition of the section on feeling.
231. In the exposition on feeling conditioned by contact:
Feeling is stated according to the doors, beginning with that born of eye-contact;
these are sixfold by way of division, and are considered to be eighty-nine in total.

By the method beginning with "feeling born of eye-contact" and so forth, these six types of feeling—beginning with that born of eye-contact—are stated in the Pāḷi according to their doors. However, when analyzed, they are considered to be eighty-nine because they are associated with eighty-nine types of consciousness.
Among these feelings, it is said that here thirty-two feelings are intended, as they are associated only with resultant consciousness.
In that regard, there are eight ways in which the five [faculties] act as conditions at the five doors;
for the remaining [mental factors], it is one way, namely contact (phassa), and it is the same at the mind-door.
For there, at the five doors, visual contact and the rest are the conditions for the five feelings based on the physical bases of the eye-sensitivity and so forth.
Contact is a condition in eight ways: by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance.

However, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings that arise at each of the remaining doors by way of reception, investigation, and registration, contact such as eye-contact and so forth is a condition in only one way: by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).

‘In the mind-door too it is likewise’: for in the mind-door as well, that contact—consisting of the co-nascent mental impression (*manosamphassa*)—is a condition in eight ways for the sense-sphere resultant feelings that occur by way of the object (*tadārammaṇa*), and also for the fine-material and immaterial plane resultant feelings that occur by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
As for those [feelings] which occur in the mind-door by way of the object...
Sensations of the sense-sphere: for these, the mental contact associated with the adverting consciousness at the mind-door is a condition in one way, by way of decisive support.
This concludes the exposition of the section on sensation conditioned by contact.
232. Exposition of Craving as Conditioned by Feeling:
Here, craving is explained as being of six kinds, distinguished as craving for forms and so forth.
In this context, each [craving] is considered threefold according to its mode of occurrence.
For in this description of craving conditioned by feeling, just as a son is designated by his father’s name as “the merchant’s son” or “the brahmin’s son,” these six types of craving—
namely, craving for forms … up to … craving for mental phenomena— are explained by way of their names according to their objects.
The meaning is "revealed" or "declared. In this context, the meaning of the terms should be understood according to the method: craving for form is *rūpataṇhā*, and so forth.

Furthermore, among those cravings, each individual craving is considered to be threefold according to its mode of manifestation: craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
For indeed, when craving for form itself [arises] toward a visible object that has come within the range of the eye by way of the gratification of sensual pleasure...
When it proceeds by relishing [the object], then it is called craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).

When that same object proceeds together with the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), which regards it as permanent and everlasting, then it is called craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*); for lust accompanied by the view of eternalism is termed craving for existence.
However, when that same object proceeds [with the thought] "it is cut off, it perishes," [then it is called craving for non-existence].

When it occurs together with the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), it is then called craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*). For lust accompanied by the annihilationist view is termed craving for non-existence.
This same method applies to craving for sound and the others; thus, these constitute eighteen types of craving.
These eighteen occur with respect to internal forms and so forth, and eighteen with respect to external ones, making thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six past [types of craving].
There are thirty-six types of craving regarding the future and thirty-six regarding the present, making one hundred and eight cravings in total.
When these are condensed, they should be understood as six, by way of their objects such as visible forms and so forth, or as three, by way of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*) and the rest.

For these beings, having relished a son, through the sense of "mine" regarding that son—just as a nurse [feels toward her charge]—there arises [craving] by way of objects such as visible forms and so forth.

Having relished feeling and through attachment to feeling, people pay great honor to painters, musicians, perfumers, cooks, weavers, formulators of elixirs, physicians, and others who provide the objects of perception such as forms and so forth;
therefore, it should be understood that all these [types of craving] have feeling as their condition.
Furthermore, it is the feeling of resultant pleasure that is intended here.
This [craving] is single and of one kind; therefore, it is a condition for craving.
“Of one kind” means it is a condition by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Or rather: The suffering person longs for happiness; the happy person desires even more.
But because equanimity is peaceful, it is described as "pleasure.
Therefore, through craving as a condition, all three kinds of feeling arise;
and with feeling as a condition, craving arises—thus it was said by the Great Seer.
"And because feeling does not exist without a latent tendency,
therefore that [feeling] does not exist for a brahmin who is possessed of virtue.
This is the exposition of the section on craving with feeling as its condition.
233. Exposition of the Footing of Clinging (Upādāna-pada-niddesa).
In the exposition of clinging as conditioned by craving:
There are four kinds of clinging; they are [to be understood] according to their analysis of meaning.
One should explain the categories of phenomena both briefly and in detail, according to their sequence.
For in the Canon, these four kinds of clinging are mentioned: clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), and so forth, up to clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
This is the analysis of their meaning: one clings to sensual pleasure, which is reckoned as the objective basis, thus it is "clinging to sensual pleasures. And sensual pleasure...

Thus, "clinging" (*upādāna*) refers to clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). "Clinging" means firm grasping; here the prefix *upa-* has the sense of "firmness," as in words such as *upāyāsa* (agitation) and *upakaṭṭha* (near).
Likewise, it is "view-clinging" (*diṭṭhupādāna*) because it is both a view and a form of clinging.
Or, it is "view-clinging" because one clings to a view. For in such expressions as "the self and the world are eternal," a subsequent view [clings to] a preceding view.

It clings. Likewise, because one clings to virtue and observances (*sīlabbata*), it is "clinging to virtue and observances" (*sīlabbatupādāna*). Alternatively, it is "clinging to virtue and observances" because it is both virtue and observances and it is clinging.
For practices such as the cow-virtue and the ox-virtue are themselves clingings due to the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) that they alone constitute purity.
Likewise, it is called "doctrine" (*vāda*) because one speaks by means of it; it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because one clings by means of it. What do they speak of, or what do they cling to?

“Self” (attā). Or, the clinging to one’s own doctrine of self is “clinging to the doctrine of self” (attavādupādāna). Alternatively, it is called “clinging to the doctrine of self” because by means of it they cling to the mere doctrine of self as being the self.
This, for now, is the analysis of their meaning.

In the “Summary and Detailed Exposition of the Phenomena” (Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāra), however, first regarding sensual clinging (kāmupādāna): “In this context, what is sensual clinging? That which, in regard to sense-pleasures...”

Because it is stated: "Sensual desire, sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, and sensual clinging—this is called clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna)," it is therefore said, in brief, to be the intensification of craving.
This intensification of craving is simply subsequent craving that has become strong by means of preceding craving acting as its decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). However, some say:
Craving (*taṇhā*) is the longing for objects not yet attained, like a thief reaching out his hand in the dark.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is the seizing of objects already attained, like that same thief seizing the goods.

These two states are the opposites of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and contentment (*santuṭṭhitā*), and likewise they are the root of the suffering of seeking and guarding. As for the remaining three types of clinging, they are in brief merely views (*diṭṭhi*).

In detail, however, *kāmupādāna* (clinging to sense-pleasures) is the state of firmness of craving (*taṇhā*), which—as previously stated regarding form and so forth—is divided into eight hundred types.
*Diṭṭhupādāna* (clinging to views) is wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) having ten bases. As it is said: "In this context, what is clinging to views?
It is that kind of view, such as: 'There is no giving, there is no offering... [etc. ...they declare to have realized for themselves'—such a view... [etc. ...a perverted grasp."
“This is called clinging to views. Furthermore, the grasping at purification through rules and observances is clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).

As it is said: “In this regard, what is clinging to rules and observances? It is the view, and so forth, up to the mistaken grasp, that outside of this [teaching], there is purification through the ascetics’ and brahmins’ moral conduct (*sīla*), purification through their observances (*vata*), and purification through both moral conduct and observances.”
“This is called clinging to rules and observances. Clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*) consists of the twenty-based view of a personal entity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
As it is said: “In this regard, what is clinging to a doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling...
not trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones... regards form as self... [and so on] ...this perverted grasping—this is called clinging to a doctrine of self.”
This is the summary and detailed exposition of the Dhamma herein. Regarding “by way of order,” there is a threefold order: the order of arising, the order of abandoning, and the order of teaching.
Among these, since it is impossible to point to a first arising of these defilements within the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no literal order of arising for them.

It is not said [that they arise simultaneously]. However, in a figurative sense, for the most part in a single existence, the adherence to eternalism or annihilationism is preceded by the grasping at a self.
From that, for one who grasps "this self is eternal," there arises the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) for the sake of purifying the self;

and for one who grasps "it is annihilated" and is indifferent to the next world, there arises the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Thus, first there is the clinging to the doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*), followed by the clingings to views, rules and observances, and sensual pleasures.
This is the order of their arising within a single existence.

Furthermore, among these, the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and the others are abandoned first, because they are to be eliminated by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). Clinging to sensual desire (*kāmupādāna*) is abandoned last, because it is to be eliminated by the path of Arahantship. This is the order of their abandonment.
However, among these, clinging to sensual desire is taught first because its scope is vast and it is more manifest. Indeed, its scope is vast...
That [craving] is associated with eight types of consciousness; the others have limited objects and are associated with four types of consciousness.
Furthermore, because people generally delight in the *ālaya* (the substrate), sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*) is prominent, whereas the others are not.

One who possesses sense-desire clinging is intent on the acquisition of material objects and is full of curiosity, auspicious rites, and so forth, rather than holding the view of eternalism; therefore, view-clinging (*diṭṭhupādāna*) follows immediately after that. That...
When analyzed, it becomes twofold by way of clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbata*) and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavāda*).
Between these two, because it can be understood even upon seeing the practice of cows or the practice of dogs, clinging to rules and observances is coarse; thus it was taught first.
Because of its subtlety, clinging to a doctrine of self is taught last. This is their order of teaching.
And here, craving is a condition for the first [type of clinging] in one way;
for the remaining three, it is a condition in seven or eight ways.

And here, when the fourfold set of clingings has been taught in this manner, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*) serves as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the first, which is clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).

It is a condition in one way by way of arising in relation to objects that are relished through craving. However, for the remaining three [mental aggregates], it is a condition in seven ways—by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root—or in eight ways when including the decisive-support condition.
And when it is a condition by way of decisive support, it is necessarily not conascent.
The exposition of the section on clinging with craving as condition.
The exposition of the section on existence: 234.
In the exposition of existence with clinging as condition—
The exposition should be understood according to its meaning, its nature, its purpose, its analysis, its synthesis, and what is the condition for what.
In this context, "becoming" (*bhava*) means that which comes to be. "In two ways" means it occurs by way of two modes. Alternatively, "in two ways" means...
