The term "karaṇa" (instrument) is used in the sense of that which is cooked; thus it is said to be twofold. "Atthi" means "exists. "Kamma-bhava" is existence as action;
"upapatti-bhava" is existence as rebirth. And here, existence is called "bhava" because rebirth comes into being (*upapatti bhavati*).
Just as action is described as "the arising of Buddhas is blissful" because it is a cause of happiness, so too [action] is [called existence] because it is a cause of existence.

It should be understood that "existence" (*bhava*) is spoken of here in the sense of its result. In this context, what is "kamma-existence"? The meaning is: among those two types of existence, which one is called "kamma-existence"?
The terms "meritorious formations" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth have already been explained. "All" means without exception.
It is "leading to existence" (*bhavagāmi*) because it goes toward or causes one to go toward existence; by this, he excludes the supramundane (*lokuttara*).
For this is a discourse on the round (vaṭṭa), and it is based on the turning away from it (vivaṭṭa). It is called *kamma* because it is "done" (*karīyati*).

Among the realms of existence such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), existence characterized by sense-desire is "sense-sphere existence. This same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial realms of existence.

Existence belonging to those possessing perception is "perception-existence" (*saññābhava*), or alternatively, it is "perception-existence" because perception exists therein. By contrast, there is "non-perception-existence" (*asaññābhava*). [And] coarse perception...

Because it is neither a subtle state of being nor a non-state of being, and because there is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" in this existence, it is called "the existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*nevasaññānāsaññābhava*).
An existence mixed with a single aggregate of form is "existence with one base" (*ekavokārabhava*); or, because that existence has only one base, it is "existence with one base.
The same method applies to the existences with four bases and five bases. This is called "existence as rebirth" (*upapattibhava*).
This ninefold [existence] is called "rebirth-existence" (*upapattibhava*). Thus, first, the exposition should be understood here "by way of meaning" (*atthato*).

However, "by way of phenomena" (*dhammato*), here the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) consists of thirteen volitions (*cetanā*), the formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) of twelve, and the formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) of four. By the phrase "all kamma leading to existence," all these are included.
States associated with volition are comprised of those states designated as kamma that lead to accumulation.

Sensual existence consists of the five aggregates of clinging; likewise, fine-material existence consists of the five; immaterial existence consists of four; perception-existence consists of four or five;
non-perception existence consists of one aggregate of clinging; neither-perception-nor-non-perception existence consists of four. [These include] the one-aggregate existence and so forth.

The single, fourfold, and fivefold aggregates are [to be understood] by way of the aggregates subject to clinging; thus, in this context, the exposition should be understood "by way of the phenomena" (*dhammato*).

As for "by way of the purpose" (*sātthato*): although it is true that in the description of existence (*bhava*)—and likewise in the description of formations (*saṅkhāra*)—only the formative acts of merit and so forth were mentioned, nevertheless, these former ones are mentioned here because they serve as the condition for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) by way of past karma. These...
The repetition is indeed purposeful, as it indicates that present karma serves as a condition for future rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Alternatively, previously it was stated that volition alone constitutes the formations (*saṅkhārā*) by way of such methods as: "In this context, what is the formation of merit? It is wholesome volition belonging to the sense-sphere.
However, here, because of the statement "all karma leading to existence," they include those associated with volition as well.

Previously, it was stated that volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are simply karma conditioned by consciousness; now, however, it includes even those that produce the non-percipient realm (*asaññābhava*).

What need is there for much more? In the formula “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,” only wholesome and unwholesome phenomena—namely, the meritorious volitional formations and so forth—are mentioned.

But here, in the formula “with clinging as condition, existence arises,” because the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is also included, [the volitional formations] may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
The phenomena have been stated. Therefore, this repetition is purposeful in every respect. Thus, the analysis here should be understood "also by way of its purpose.

Regarding "classification and inclusion": this refers to both the classification and the inclusion of existence (bhava) based on the condition of clinging (upādāna). For that which [arises] with sensual clinging (kāmupādāna) as its condition...
Kamma that produces existence in the sense-sphere is *kammabhava*. The aggregates produced by that [kamma] are *upapattibhava*.

This same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpabhava* and *arūpabhava*). Thus, with craving-fuel as condition, there are two types of sense-sphere existence, which include the perception-existence (*saññābhava*) and the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*);

two types of fine-material existence, which include the perception-existence, the non-perception-existence (*asaññābhava*), the one-aggregate existence (*ekavokārabhava*), and the five-aggregate existence.

There are two immaterial existences (*arūpabhava*); together with those included within them—the existence of perception (*saññābhava*), the existence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaññānāsaññābhava*), and fourfold-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*)—there are six existences along with their inclusions.
And just as there are six existences along with their inclusions conditioned by sense-desire clinging (*kāmupādāna*), so too are there [six] conditioned by the remaining types of clinging;
thus, by way of the divisions of clinging as a condition, there are twenty-four existences along with their inclusions.

Furthermore, by way of grouping, taking kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) together, there is one sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) conditioned by clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), along with those included therein;
likewise for form and formless existences—thus there are three existences. Similarly, this applies to the conditions of the remaining types of clinging as well.
Thus, by way of grouping according to the condition of clinging, there are twelve existences, including those included therein. Moreover, without distinction:
With clinging as condition, there is kamma that leads to sense-sphere existence; this is *kamma-bhava*. The aggregates produced by that are *upapatti-bhava* (rebirth-existence).

This same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial existences. Thus, with clinging as condition, including what is included therein, there are two types of sense-sphere existence, two of fine-material existence, and two of immaterial existence;
by way of this further classification, there are six existences (*bhava*). [This is] the division into *kamma-bhava* and *upapatti-bhava*.
Or, without entering into those [subdivisions], there are three existences (*bhava*) by way of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth, together with what is included within them.
Furthermore, without entering into the divisions of sensual existence and so forth, there are two existences by way of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

And without entering into the divisions of kamma and rebirth existences, there is one existence by way of existence as "existence conditioned by clinging" (*upādānapaccayā bhavo*). Thus, herein, regarding the condition of clinging...
The exposition should also be understood by way of the classification of the breakup of existence (*bhava*).

Regarding the phrase “whatever is the condition for whatever”: the meaning is that the exposition should also be understood from the perspective of which clinging (*upādāna*) serves as the condition for what. But here, what is the condition for what? Whatever [clinging] is a condition for anyone.
It is indeed so. For the worldling is like one who is insane;

without investigating whether "this is appropriate" or "this is inappropriate," he merely performs whatever action he might, having aspired to some kind of existence by means of any kind of clinging whatsoever.
Therefore, when some say that "the form and formless realms of existence do not arise through clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*)," that should not be accepted.
However, it should be understood that "by all [means] one becomes [all]" is as follows:

here, someone—either by way of hearsay or by following their own views—thinks, "These sensual pleasures are abundant both in the human world among such families as the great khattiya clans, and in the six celestial worlds of the sense-sphere devas";
and, being deceived by listening to false doctrines and other such means for the sake of attaining them, [he thinks], "By this action..."

Thinking, "May my sensual desires be fulfilled," one commits bodily misconduct and so forth due to the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Through the fulfillment of such misconduct, one is reborn in the woeful states.
Alternatively, aspiring for sensual pleasures visible in this life, or seeking to preserve those already obtained, one commits bodily misconduct and so forth due to the clinging to sensual pleasures.
Through the fulfillment of such misconduct, one is reborn in the woeful states. Therein, that which has become the cause for his rebirth...

Kamma is kamma-existence (*kammabhava*); the aggregates produced by that kamma are rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), while the existence of perception (*saññābhava*) and the five-constituent existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) are included within that very [rebirth-existence].
Furthermore, one whose knowledge has been nurtured by hearing the true Dharma and so forth understands: "By this kamma, sensual pleasures are accomplished."
One who conceives performs good bodily conduct and so forth by way of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). Through the fulfillment of that good conduct, one is reborn among gods or humans.
Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for that rebirth is *kammabhava* (kamma-existence), while the aggregates produced by that karma are *upapattibhava* (rebirth-existence).
The existence of perception (*saññābhava*) and the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) are indeed included within these. Thus is clinging to sensual pleasures.
It is a condition for sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), which includes its various divisions and is comprised within [the three realms].

Another person, having either heard or imagined that "sensual pleasures are more abundant in the fine-material and immaterial existences," produces the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the fine-material and immaterial realms by means of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
By the power of those attainments, he is reborn in the fine-material or immaterial Brahma-worlds. Therein, for him—
Kamma that serves as the cause for rebirth is *kammabhava*; the aggregates produced by that kamma are *upapattibhava*.

Furthermore, the states of non-perception (*asaññā*), neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññā-nāsaññā*), the one-aggregate (*ekavokāra*), four-aggregate (*catuvokāra*), and five-aggregate (*pañcavokāra*) existences are included within these very categories.

Thus, clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is a condition for both the fine-material (*rūpa*) and immaterial (*arūpa*) existences, along with their various subdivisions and what is included therein.

Another, adopting the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi) with the thought, “This so-called self is utterly annihilated, completely destroyed, whether in the fortunate existence of the sense-sphere realm or in either of the form or formless realms,” performs karma leading to that [annihilation].
For him, that karma is the kamma-bhava; the aggregates produced by that karma are the upapatti-bhava. As for the saññā-bhava and the others...

They are indeed included within that. Thus, the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is a condition for all three types of existence—sensual, fine-material, and immaterial—along with their subdivisions and their respective inclusions.

Furthermore, by means of the clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*), one thinks, "This so-called self is happy and free from feverish distress in either a fortunate rebirth in the sensual sphere or in one of the fine-material or immaterial existences," and thus performs karma leading to those states. For such a person...
That karma is *kammabhava*; the aggregates produced by it are *upapattibhava*. The *saññābhava* and the others are indeed included within that.
Thus, the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*) is a condition for the three types of becoming (*bhava*), together with their subdivisions and as they are so included.

Another [teacher] says: "This so-called virtue-and-observance (*sīlabbata*) [is a condition] either for the fortunate existence of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-sampattibhava*) or for one of the two, the fine-material or immaterial existences."
"Of one who fulfills it, happiness reaches fulfillment"—thus, by way of the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), one performs karma leading to that [state].
That karma of his is *kammabhava*; the aggregates (*khandhā*) produced from that are *upapattibhava*.

However, the existence of perception (*saññābhava*) and the others are indeed included within that. Thus, clinging to rules and observances also includes the three types of existence along with their subdivisions.
"It is a condition for the states of existence"—thus, the analysis should be understood here according to what serves as a condition for what. But if it is asked:
"In this context, how does what serve as a condition for which state of existence?
[The answer is: For the material and immaterial states of existence, clinging is the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
It should be understood that this [clinging] is also [a condition] for existence in the sense-sphere (*kāmabhava*) by way of co-nascence and so forth.

For these four kinds of clinging are a condition in one way—by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*)—for existence in the sense-sphere, for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms, and for rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) resulting from wholesome karma within the sense-sphere itself. Within the sense-sphere, by oneself...

It is a condition for unwholesome kamma-existence that is associated [with consciousness] by way of the classifications of conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root-conditions;
and for that which is dissociated, it is a condition solely by way of decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
This concludes the exposition of the section on existence with clinging as its condition.
235. The Exposition of Terms such as Birth, Aging, and Death:

In the expositions of birth and so forth under the condition "with existence as condition," the analysis of birth and the other terms should be understood according to the method stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths).
Here, however, by "existence" (*bhava*), only *kamma-bhava* (karmic existence) is intended; for that is the condition for birth, not *upapatti-bhava* (rebirth-existence).
Furthermore, it acts as a condition in two ways: by way of the kamma-condition and the decisive-support-condition.
Herein, one might ask: "How is it to be known that existence is a condition for birth?

It is because even when external conditions are equal, distinctions such as inferiority and superiority are observed. For among the external conditions—namely, the father, the mother, semen, blood, food, and so forth—[there is no such distinction].
Even among beings who are twins, a distinction such as inferiority or superiority is observed.
And this is not without cause, because it does not exist at all times for all beings;

nor is it caused by anything other than kamma, because there is no other cause within the internal continuum of those beings produced thereby. Thus, it has kamma as its cause. For kamma is [the cause] of beings...

It is the cause for the distinction between the inferior, the superior, and so forth. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Kamma divides beings, that is to say, according to their inferiority and superiority.
Consequently, this must be understood: "Becoming is a condition for birth.
And because, in the absence of birth, there is no such thing as aging and death, nor do sorrow and the other states exist, [it follows] from birth...

However, when there is mindfulness, there arise both aging-and-death and the states such as sorrow that occur either through the connection with aging-and-death for a fool touched by the phenomena of suffering designated as "aging-and-death," or through the lack of such connection for one touched by those various phenomena of suffering;

therefore, it should be understood that this [mindfulness] is the condition for both aging-and-death and for sorrow and the rest. Furthermore, it is [the condition] by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"It is a condition in a single way" means:
the exposition of the terms beginning with "birth" (jāti) conditioned by "existence" (bhava). 242.

The meaning of "evam etassa" and so forth should be understood in the same manner as stated in the section on the enumeration (uddesa-vāra). "Conjunction" (saṅgati) and the others are synonyms for origination (samudaya).

But because sorrow and the rest are mentioned here at the end, therefore that ignorance which was stated at the beginning of this wheel of existence as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]"—that ignorance is established by means of sorrow and the rest:
"This wheel of existence has its beginning unknown;
it is devoid of a doer or an experiencer, and it is empty of the twelvefold emptiness."
It should be understood that [this wheel] proceeds constantly and continuously. But how is ignorance established here by means of sorrow and the rest?
How is this wheel of existence "beginningless"? How is it devoid of an agent or an experiencer? And how is it empty of the twelvefold emptiness?
For herein, sorrow, pain, grief, and despair are inseparable from ignorance, and lamentation belongs to one who is deluded.
When those [defilements] are established, ignorance is established as well. Furthermore, it is said: "With the arising of the taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance.

And these states, beginning with sorrow, arise from the arising of the taints. How so? First, in the case of separation from the objects of sensual desire, sorrow arises from the arising of the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava).
As it is said: "If that person, desiring and full of longing for sense-pleasures..."
“Those sensual pleasures perish, and one is tormented as if pierced by an arrow.
And as it is said: “From sensual desire sorrow is born. All these, moreover, arise from the influx of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), as it is said:
“For one who dwells obsessed with the thought ‘form is mine,’ that form undergoes change and alteration.”
...there is. From the change and alteration of that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
And just as there is the arising of the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), so too is there the arising of the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), as it is said:
“Even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abounding in happiness, and long-dwelling in lofty palaces—even they, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma...”
"Having heard this, they mostly fall into fear, agitation, and terror"—this is like the case of the gods who, having seen the five portents, are terrified by the fear of death.
And just as there is the arising from the outflow of existence (*bhavāsava*), so too is there the arising from the outflow of ignorance (*avijjāsava*);
as it is said: "That fool, bhikkhus, experiences three kinds of suffering and mental distress even in this very life."
Thus, because these [states] arise from the origination of the taints (*āsava*), therefore, when they are established, they establish the taints that serve as the cause for ignorance (*avijjā*).
And when the taints are established, ignorance is also necessarily established, since it exists by virtue of being their condition.
In this way, it should be understood that "ignorance is established here through sorrow and the rest."
Since, however, ignorance is thus established by its very existence as a condition,
there is no end to the succession of cause and effect— such as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness"— therefore,
this twelvefold wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*), which proceeds by way of the connection between cause and fruit, is established as "beginningless" (*aviditādi*).
If it is argued that, this being so, the statement "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" contradicts the teaching of the mere beginning, we reply:
this is not a teaching of the mere beginning; rather, it is a teaching of the predominant factor. For among the three rounds (vaṭṭa), ignorance is the predominant one.
By the mention of ignorance, the remaining round of defilements, the round of kamma, and so forth, are all encompassed by the fool, just as by the seizing of a snake's head.

The rest [of the body] is like the snake’s body, while the arm is like the snake’s coils. But when ignorance is completely severed, liberation occurs through those [factors], just as the arm encircled by the snake is liberated when the snake’s head is cut off.
As it is said: “With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance itself, there is the cessation of volitional formations,” and so forth.
Thus, this is the explanation of that primary factor which, when grasped, constitutes bondage, and when released, constitutes liberation.
"It is not a statement concerning a beginning" means that this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) should be understood as having an unknown beginning.

Since the occurrence of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and the rest proceeds by way of causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, it cannot be said to have been created by some other agent—such as Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, the Best, or the Creator—as is imagined by others; for [the Buddha has said]: "Indeed, this [wheel] of mine..."
It is devoid of a self that speaks or feels, as imagined in such ways;
thus, it should be understood as "devoid of an agent or an experiencer.
Furthermore, because ignorance here possesses the nature of arising and passing away, it is not permanent; and because it is defiled, it is subject to corruption.

And it is empty of the nature of beauty because of its impurity, empty of the nature of pleasure because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, and empty of a self-entity that possesses mastery because its existence is dependent on conditions;

likewise for the factors such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Or, since ignorance is not the self, does not belong to a self, is not in a self, and does not possess a self, so too are the factors such as volitional formations; therefore, "this is empty of twelvefold emptiness."
It should be understood as the "wheel of existence.
And having understood it thus, furthermore:
"Its roots are ignorance and craving; its times are the three periods beginning with the past."
Among these, the constituent factors are two, eight, and two respectively according to their specific forms.
Furthermore, within this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*), it should be understood that the two phenomena—ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*)—are the roots.
Thus, with ignorance as its root and ending with feeling (*vedanā*), it is drawn from the past; with craving as its root, it extends through the continuity of the future.

The phrase "ending in aging and death" is twofold. Therein, the former is stated with reference to those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*), and the latter with reference to those of craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*).
For ignorance is the leader of the round of existence for those of speculative temperament, while craving is the leader for those of craving temperament.

Alternatively, the first [version] is for the purpose of uprooting the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), because it demonstrates that there is no interruption of the causes for the arising of results.
The second [truth] is for the eradication of the eternalist view, because it reveals aging and death as they have arisen;

alternatively, the first is by way of those born from a womb, because it illustrates sequential occurrence, while the latter is by way of those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), because it illustrates simultaneous arising.
Furthermore, there are three times: past, present, and future. Among these, ignorance (*avijjā*) is presented in its own form according to what has come down in the Canon.
It should be understood that two factors—formations (*saṅkhārā*) and ignorance—are of the past time; eight factors from consciousness (*viññāṇa*) up to existence (*bhava*) are of the present time;
and two factors—birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are of the future time. Furthermore:
"And this [Dependent Origination] comprises four divisions: cause, fruit, preceded by cause, and the three links."
It should be understood that it revolves with twenty spokes, three rounds, and without a fixed point.
In this regard, between the formations (*saṅkhārā*) and rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*), there is one connection called "cause-and-effect" (*hetu-phala-sandhi*).
Between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*taṇhā*), there is one connection called "effect-and-cause" (*phala-hetu-sandhi*). Between existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*)...
And in between, there is one link consisting of cause and fruit. Thus, this should be understood as a sequence of links beginning with cause and fruit, preceded by cause and fruit.
Furthermore, its four groupings are established according to their beginning and end, as follows: ignorance and formations constitute one grouping;

consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute the second; craving, clinging, and becoming constitute the third; [and birth and aging-and-death constitute the fourth].
"Birth, aging, and death are the fourth. Thus, this should be understood as comprising four divisions:
"In the past, there were five causes; now, there is a pentad of results.
Now, there are five causes; in the future, there will be a pentad of results."
Furthermore, by means of these twenty aspects, it should be understood that there are "twenty aspects" (vīsati-ākāra).

In this context, regarding the statement “In the past, there were five causes,” first, ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhārā)—these two have already been mentioned. However, because one who is ignorant becomes agitated, and being agitated, grasps;
and because for him, with grasping as condition, there is becoming (bhava), therefore craving (taṇhā), grasping (upādāna), and becoming are also included.

Thus it is said: "In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance (avijjā), the exertion is volitional formations (saṅkhāra), the attachment is craving (taṇhā), the approaching is clinging (upādāna), and the intention is becoming (bhava).
These five factors in the previous kamma-existence are the conditions for rebirth-linking here [in this life].
In that context, "in the previous kamma-existence" means in the prior kamma-existence, while the kamma-existence was being performed in a past birth.
The meaning is as follows: "Delusion is ignorance" means that the delusion regarding suffering and so forth at that time—by which one who is deluded performs kamma—is ignorance (*avijjā*).
"Accumulation is volitional formations" refers to the prior volitions of one performing that kamma;
for example, the prior volitions that arise in one who, having generated the thought "I shall give a gift," prepares the requisites for giving for a month or even a year.
However, when one places the offering into the hands of the recipients, that volition is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Alternatively, among the six impulsive moments (*javana*) consisting of a single thought-moment, the volition is called the "formations of exertion" (*āyūhana-saṅkhāra*); the seventh volition is "existence.

Or, whatever volition constitutes existence, the factors associated with it are called the "formations of exertion. Craving (*taṇhā*) is attachment (*nikanti*), which [arises] for one performing karma...
The longing and aspiration for the fruit in the state of rebirth is what is called craving (*taṇhā*). Appropriation (*upādāna*) is the approaching:

that karma which serves as the condition for existence (*bhava*), proceeding in such a manner as, “Having done this, I will enjoy sensual pleasures in such-and-such a place, or I will cut off [the world],” etc.;
this approaching, grasping, and clutching is what is called appropriation. Volition (*cetanā*) is existence (*bhava*).
The meaning should be understood thus: "existence" (*bhava*) is the volition stated at the conclusion of the process of accumulation (*āyūhana*).
Now, regarding the "fivefold fruit," that beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling has already appeared in the text.
As it is said: "Here, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent [into the womb] is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense-base; the touched is contact; what is felt is feeling."
"These five factors—feeling and so forth—arise here in the state of rebirth (upapattibhava) as conditions for karma performed in the past.
In this context, "rebirth-linking consciousness" (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) refers to that consciousness which is called "linking" because it arises by way of connecting to another existence.
"Descent" (*okkanti*) refers to the descent of the material and immaterial phenomena into the womb, their arrival and entry [therein].
"Like this"—this refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "The sense-base is clarity"—this is stated by way of the five sense-bases, beginning with the eye.
"Contact is what is touched"—that which has arisen having touched or contacting an object is contact (*phassa*).
"Feeling is what is felt"—that which is the resultant feeling arisen together with either the rebirth-linking consciousness or with contact conditioned by the six sense-bases.
"Feeling" (vedanā)—the meaning should be understood in this way.
"Now, the causes are five": craving and the others mentioned in the text are indeed craving, clinging, and existence.

When existence is included, its antecedents or the formations associated with it are necessarily included; and by the inclusion of craving and clinging, [the remaining factors are likewise encompassed].
The ignorance associated with that [craving], or rather, that by which one who is deluded performs kamma, is already included; thus there are five. Therefore he said:
"Here, due to the ripening of the sense bases, there is delusion as ignorance; the exertion is volitional formations (saṅkhāra);

the attachment is craving (taṇhā); the approaching is clinging (upādāna); and the intention is becoming (bhava). These five factors here, in this kamma-becoming, lead to rebirth-linking in the future."
"Because of the conditions. In this context, by the phrase "because the sense-bases have matured," the delusion at the time of performing the kamma that results in a matured sense-base is shown.
The rest is self-evident.
"'The five fruits in the future' refers to the five beginning with consciousness; these are stated by way of taking birth. Aging-and-death..."

But for those very same [beings], there is aging and death. Therefore he said: "In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent [into the womb] is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense base;
what is touched is contact; what is felt is feeling. These five states, as conditions for the karma performed here, arise in the future existence of rebirth. Thus, this [wheel] has twenty spokes.

In this regard, there are five accumulations of kamma in the previous existence, five accumulations of result in the present, five accumulations of kamma in the present, and five phenomena subject to result in the future—thus, ten things are kamma and ten are result.
In two instances it is called "kamma," and in two instances it is called "result"; all of this is thus.

The wheel of existence (*bhavacakkam*) is the cycle of dependent origination (*paccayākāravaṭṭam*), consisting of both karma and the result of karma (*kammavipāko*). Likewise, in two instances it is karma, which is the summary of karma (*kammasaṅkhepo*);
and in two instances it is the result, which is the summary of the result (*vipākasaṅkhepo*). Thus, all of this is both the summary of karma and the summary of the result.
In two instances it is karma, which is the cycle of karma (*kammavaṭṭam*); and in two instances it is the result, which is the cycle of the result (*vipākavaṭṭam*).

All of this is both the round of kamma and the round of result. Likewise, in two instances kamma is kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), and in two instances result is result-existence (*vipākabhava*); thus all of this is both kamma-existence and result-existence.

In two instances kamma is the turning of kamma (*kammapavatta*), and in two instances result is the turning of result (*vipākapavatta*); thus all of this is both the turning of kamma and [the turning of result].
And [there is] the occurrence of ripening. Likewise, in two instances there is karma and the continuity of karma;
in two instances there is ripening and the continuity of ripening—thus all this is both the continuity of karma and the continuity of ripening. In two instances there is karma called "functional";
in two instances there is ripening called "the fruit of the functional"—thus all this is both the functional and the fruit of the functional.
Thus this suffering has arisen with a cause;
it is impermanent, shifting, fleeting, and unstable.
From phenomena, phenomena arise according to their causes.
Herein, neither a self nor another is found.
Phenomena produce phenomena through the conditions of causes and constituent parts.
And for the cessation of those causes, the Dhamma was taught by the Buddha.
When the causes have been obstructed, the cycle, being severed, does not turn.
Thus, for the making of an end to suffering, the holy life exists here;
and since beings are not apprehended, there is neither annihilation nor eternalism.
Regarding the phrase "it revolves as a threefold cycle, unstable": here, the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) constitute the cycle of kamma;

ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), and clinging (*upādāna*) constitute the cycle of defilements (*kilesa*); and consciousness (*viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) constitute the cycle of result (*vipāka*).
This wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) is "threefold" by virtue of these three cycles; and as long as the cycle of defilements is not cut off, it continues because its conditions remain unsevered.
It should be understood that because it revolves again and again,
it indeed wanders without stability. And as it wanders in this way—
by way of the origin of truth, by function, by prevention, and by similes—
And the distinctions of the profound method should be understood as appropriate.
In this context, since wholesome and unwholesome kamma are stated without distinction to be the truth of origin in the *Saccavibhaṅga*,

therefore, regarding "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations [arise]," the volitional formations produced by ignorance are the second truth (the truth of origin) which gives rise to the second truth (suffering).
From volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), consciousness arises; from consciousness and so forth, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the rest, ending with resultant feeling, arise;

from feeling, craving (*taṇhā*) arises; from craving, clinging (*upādāna*) arises; and from clinging, becoming (*bhava*) arises—all these being the first truth arising from the second truth. From the first truth [arise] the first truth [itself]. From feeling, craving arises—the second truth arising from the first truth.
From craving, clinging arises—the second truth arising from the second truth. From clinging, becoming [arises].
The first and second truths originate from the second truth; birth originates from becoming, which is the second truth;
and aging-and-death originates from birth, which is the first truth—the first truth itself.
Thus, this should be understood "by way of origination from the truths" according to what is appropriate.
But because here ignorance deludes beings regarding the bases and is a condition for the manifestation of volitional formations;
likewise, volitional formations construct the conditioned and are conditions for consciousness;
and consciousness too recognizes the basis and is a condition for name-and-form; and name-and-form also mutually supports one another.
It is a condition for the six sense bases; the six sense bases also function within their respective domains and are a condition for contact.
Contact touches the object and is a condition for feeling. Feeling experiences the flavor of the object and is a condition for craving.
Craving also becomes attached to phenomena that are provocative of attachment and is a condition.
Existence (*bhava*) is a condition for clinging (*upādāna*); clinging also clings to the phenomena that are objects of clinging and is a condition for becoming (*bhava*).
Becoming, too, disperses into various destinies and is a condition for birth (*jāti*).
Birth also produces the aggregates (*khandha*) by way of their manifestation and, as the process of their arising, is a condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Aging and death, too...
It also determines the state of the ripening and breaking up of the aggregates and serves as a condition for the manifestation of another existence, because it is the basis for sorrow and so forth;
therefore, in all instances, this should be understood according to its appropriate twofold activity.
And herein, the statement "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations" is a preclusion of the view that there is an agent; [the statement] "with volitional formations as condition..."

“Consciousness” is the prevention of the view that there is a transmigration of a self; “with consciousness as condition, name-and-form” is the prevention of the perception of a solid mass, because it shows the differentiation of the bases imagined to be a self;
and in such passages as “with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,” etc., it is the prevention of views such as “the self sees...
[and] cognizes, touches, feels, craves, clings, exists, is born, ages, and dies.”
Therefore, this wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) should be understood as "a warding off" (*nivāraṇa*) by way of warding off wrong view (*micchā-dassana*), as appropriate.

Furthermore, because herein there is a non-seeing of phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), ignorance (*avijjā*) is like a blind man;
the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*) conditioned by ignorance are like the stumbling of a blind man; and the formations conditioned by ignorance are like the falling of one who has stumbled.
Consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form is like the appearance of a boil on one who has fallen [into it];

conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases are like the bursting of the boil and the formation of pustules; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact is like the rubbing of the boil and the pustules;
conditioned by contact, feeling is like the pain from that rubbing; and conditioned by feeling, the longing for a remedy for that pain...

Craving (*taṇhā*) is like grasping for what is unwholesome through a desire for its remedy; conditioned by craving is clinging (*upādāna*), which is like smearing on what is unwholesome that has been grasped.

Conditioned by clinging is existence (*bhava*), which is like the manifestation of an abscess due to the smearing of what is unwholesome. Conditioned by existence is birth (*jāti*), which is like the bursting of an abscess from the condition of the abscess itself.
Conditioned by birth are aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which are like the breaking open of the abscess resulting from the condition of the abscess.
Or rather, because here ignorance overcomes beings by way of non-practice and wrong practice, just as a film covers the eyes;
and being thus overcome, the fool envelops himself with formations leading to renewed existence, like a silkworm with its cocoon-filaments.
Consciousness, when grasped by formations, gains a footing in the various realms of existence, just as one who is protected by a guide [finds safety].
Just as a prince [ascends] to kingship, consciousness— by way of conceiving the sign of rebirth— produces manifold name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking,
just as a magician produces an illusion; and the six sense-bases established upon that name-and-form reach growth,
increase, and fullness, like a forest thicket established on fertile ground, due to the friction of the sense-bases.
Contact arises like fire from the friction of two fire-sticks; for one touched by contact, feeling becomes manifest like the burning of one touched by fire;
for one experiencing feeling, craving increases like thirst in one drinking salt water;
the one thus tormented forms a longing for states of existence like a thirsty man for water; that is his clinging, and through clinging—
One clings to existence through greed for material things, like a fish seizing a hook; when there is existence, birth occurs, like a sprout when there is a seed;
for one who is born, aging and death are inevitable, like the falling of a tree that has grown.
Therefore, this wheel of existence should be understood through such similes, as appropriate.
And because the Blessed One, with reference to its profundity in meaning, in nature, in teaching, and in penetration,

said: "Ānanda, this dependent origination is profound and appears profound," therefore this wheel of existence should be understood according to the circumstances through its classification by way of profundity.

In this context, because aging-and-death does not exist apart from birth, nor does it arise from anything other than birth, but rather originates precisely from birth—since the meaning of its origination through the condition of birth is thus difficult to comprehend—the meaning of aging-and-death as having originated and arisen through the condition of birth is profound.
Likewise, [the same applies] to birth through the condition of existence... down to volitional formations.
The sense of being produced and brought about with ignorance as its condition is profound; therefore, this wheel of existence is "profound in meaning.

This, then, is the "profundity of meaning" here: for "meaning" (attha) is said to be cause and fruit, as it is said, "Knowledge regarding cause and fruit is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)."

However, because the manner and the specific condition in which ignorance acts as the cause for its respective formations is difficult to comprehend, the causal function of ignorance toward formations is profound; likewise, the causal function of formations...
[and so on] ...up to birth and aging-and-death is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence is "profound in its phenomena" (dhamma-gambhīra).

This is what is meant here by "profundity of the Dhamma. For "Dhamma" is a name for a cause, as it is said: "Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
And because it must be practiced in various ways according to various reasons, the teaching itself is profound;
no knowledge other than omniscience finds a footing therein. For instance, in a certain Sutta:
It is taught in forward order in some places, in reverse order in others; in some places in both forward and reverse order;

in some places starting from the middle in either forward or reverse order; in some places with three links and four groups, in some places with two links and three groups, and in some places with one link and two groups.
Therefore, this wheel of existence (bhavacakra) is profound in its teaching.
This is the profundity of the teaching. Furthermore,

because the intrinsic nature of ignorance and the other factors herein— which, when penetrated, causes the phenomena of ignorance and so forth to be penetrated according to their specific characteristics—
is profound due to its difficulty of fathoming, this wheel of existence is therefore profound in terms of penetration.

Thus, herein, the meaning of ignorance as non-knowing, non-seeing, and non-penetration of the truths is profound; the meaning of volitional formations as volitional construction, accumulation, and the presence or absence of lust;

the meaning of consciousness as emptiness, lack of agency, and the manifestation of rebirth-linking through non-transmigration; the meaning of name-and-form as simultaneous arising, analysis and non-analysis, and the bending and deformation;
the meaning of the six sense bases as predominance, world, doors, fields, objects, and subjects; and the meaning of contact as touching, collision, conjunction, and meeting.
The meaning of feeling (*vedanā*) is the state of experiencing the taste of the object, whether as pleasure, pain, or neutrality, and the state of being felt.

The meaning of craving (*taṇhā*) is the state of delighting in, clinging to, and being like a stream, a creeper, a river, or an ocean of craving that is difficult to fill. The meaning of clinging (*upādāna*) is the state of taking up, grasping, adhering to, misapprehending, and the difficulty of transcending.

The meaning of becoming (*bhava*) is the state of accumulating, forming, and hurling one into the various wombs, destinies, stations, and abodes. The meaning of birth (*jāti*) is the state of being born, being conceived, descending [into the womb], being produced, and manifesting.
The meaning of aging-and-death as destruction, passing away, breaking up, and transformation is profound; this is its profundity in terms of penetration.

Furthermore, because there are four methods of meaning herein—the method of unity, the method of diversity, the method of non-agency, and the method of suchness—therefore, this wheel of existence should be understood according to its appropriate division of methods. Therein:
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises.
Thus, just as a seed attains the state of a tree through the sequence of sprout and so forth, the non-interruption of the continuum is called the “method of identity” (*ekattanaya*).

Seeing this correctly, one abandons the view of annihilationism by understanding the non-interruption of the continuum proceeding through the connection of cause and fruit; whereas seeing it incorrectly—
One clings to the view of eternalism by grasping at a unity due to the uninterrupted continuity of the stream as it proceeds through the connection of cause and fruit.
However, the precise determination of the specific characteristics of ignorance and the other factors is called the "method of diversity" (*nānattanaya*);
seeing this correctly, one abandons the view of eternalism by perceiving the arising of ever-new [phenomena], whereas seeing it incorrectly, one [clings] to that which falls within a single stream...
Because it perceives multiplicity only within a single, distinct continuum, one clings to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

The "method of non-agency" (*abyāpāranaya*) refers to the absence of such functional activity as ignorance thinking, "Formations (*saṅkhārā*) must be produced by me," or formations thinking, "Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) belongs to us.
Seeing this correctly, one abandons the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*) through the realization of the non-existence of an agent.

One who views incorrectly, failing to grasp the causal nature of ignorance and the other factors—which is established by the fixed law of their own intrinsic natures even in the absence of a conscious agent—clings to the view of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*).
For it is only through causes such as ignorance that formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth arise, just as curd and the like arise from milk and the like; it is not otherwise.

This is called the "method of the nature of things" (*evaṃdhammatānaya*); seeing it correctly, one abandons the view of causelessness (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*) and the view of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*) by understanding the fruit according to its conditions.

Seeing it wrongly, however, one fails to grasp the occurrence of the fruit according to its conditions, and by apprehending that anything whatsoever could arise from anything whatsoever, one falls into both the view of causelessness and the doctrine of fatalism (*niyatavāda*).
"It appropriates"— thus is this wheel of existence (bhavacakra) to be understood,
as appropriate, by way of its arising from the truths, its functions, its prevention, its similes, and its profound distinctions of method.

For this [Abhidhamma], being unfathomable in its profundity and difficult to master due to its manifold methods, cleaves the wheel of existence— constantly grinding it down like the wheel of a thunderbolt—
when wielded by the well-sharpened sword of knowledge upon the excellent stone of concentration.
There is no one, even in a dream, who has transcended the fear of saṃsāra.
And this was said by the Blessed One: "This dependent origination, Ānanda, is profound and appears profound."
“It is, Ānanda, because of the non-awakening to and non-penetration of this Dhamma that this generation has become like a tangled skein,
like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, and does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realms, and the cycle of saṃsāra. Therefore,
one who is practicing for the welfare and happiness of oneself or others should abandon all other duties—
"In this world, the wise person, regarding the profound distinctions of the mode of conditions,
should always apply themselves with mindfulness so that they may find a firm footing.
This concludes the commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 243.

Thus, with knowledge unimpeded regarding all phenomena—as if stretching out the great earth and as if expanding the sky—the Teacher, having presented the conditionality that is free from knots and tangles according to various types of consciousness in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, [proceeds further].
Having thus shown this, he now established the matrix (mātikā) by way of the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya in the sequence beginning with "with ignorance as condition,
volitional formations," in order to demonstrate in various ways the mode of conditions occurring within a single moment of consciousness—
since this mode of conditions exists not only in various types of consciousness but also in a single consciousness. Now, with the matrix thus established:
By means of the roots beginning with ignorance, there are nine root-terms and nine methods (*naya*);
therein, one should illuminate the tetrads and the divisions of the sections.

Herein, this is the illumination: for here [the dependent origination] is analyzed by way of the distinctions of ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the sixfold base, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and so forth.

By means of the nine root-terms beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), there are nine methods (*naya*) consisting of these: the method beginning with ignorance, that beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), that beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*), that beginning with mentality (*nāma*), that beginning with the sixth sense-base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*), that beginning with contact (*phassa*), that beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), that beginning with craving (*taṇhā*), and that beginning with clinging (*upādāna*).
Among these, first as for this method beginning with ignorance, therein are the tetrad of conditions, the tetrad of causes, and the tetrad of associated factors.

The "mutuality tetrad" consists of four tetrads. Just as it is here, so it is with the remaining [methods]; thus, according to each method, there are thirty-six tetrads by way of four tetrads for each.
Therein, because each individual tetrad comprises four sets of four sections, by way of these four tetrads, in each method—
It should be understood that sixteen times sixteen makes one hundred and forty-four rounds. 1.
The Tetrad of Conditions:
In this regard, concerning that tetrad of conditions which is first of all in the method rooted in ignorance, the first [condition] is in the place of name-and-form.

The first is called the twelvefold cycle because, while *nāma* is mentioned in the place of *nāmarūpa* and the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) is mentioned in the place of the six bases, it is thus connected with two incomplete factors.

The second is called the elevenfold cycle because, since *nāma* alone is mentioned in the place of *nāmarūpa* and nothing at all is mentioned in the place of the six bases, it is connected with one incomplete factor.
The third is connected with one complete factor because the sixth base is mentioned in the place of the six bases.
This is called the "twelvefold section. The fourth, however, is indeed complete with all twelve factors. Herein, one might ask:
"Is this too incomplete, being joined with only a single factor, since it is stated that 'contact has the six sense bases as its condition'? No, because that [sixth base] is not a factor here.
For in this context, contact alone is the factor, not the sixth base. Therefore, because that is not a factor, [the series remains complete].
"This one is not lacking any factor. However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "The first is taken in the sense of being all-inclusive;
the second, in the sense of specific conditions; the third, by way of beings born from a womb; and the fourth, by way of spontaneously born beings (*opapātika*).
Likewise, the first is in the sense of being all-inclusive; the second, in the sense of specific conditions; the third..."
"The first is taken by way of incomplete sense bases, and the fourth by way of complete sense bases. Likewise, the first is taken in the sense of being all-inclusive;
the second, by way of the Mahānidāna Sutta; the third, by way of the form existence (rūpa-bhava); and the fourth, by way of the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava).

In this context, the first is called "all-inclusive" because it is not excluded from any of these three subsequent sections. The distinction between the others will be clarified further on. To explain that:
Whatever has been stated differently in various places, whatever has not been stated anywhere, and whatever is the condition for what—all that one should examine. Herein is the method:
first, without making distinctions, instead of saying "formations" (saṅkhārā) in all four of these as is done in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, [one should proceed as follows].

It was stated as "volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*); why is that? Because [the present context] pertains to a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*). For therein, the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) was analyzed as spanning various moments of consciousness;

here, however, what pertains to a single moment of consciousness is undertaken. And since there are not many volitions (*cetanā*) within a single moment of consciousness, it was stated as "a volitional formation" (*saṅkhāro*) rather than "volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*).

In the first instance here, however, having set aside material form—because it comprises phenomena included within a single moment of consciousness and because it is common to all locations—it is stated simply as "with consciousness as condition, name. For that [name] is comprised within a single moment of consciousness and is common to all locations;
there is no place where the occurrence of consciousness does not take place. And because:

Included within a single moment of consciousness, there is indeed only a single contact; therefore, when taking up the sense-base that serves as its corresponding condition, [the Buddha] spoke of only the single mind-base (*manāyatana*) in the place of the six sense-bases, stating: "With name as condition, the sixth base.
For that [mind-base] is the corresponding condition for that single unwholesome contact. And although this [sixth base] arises with volitional formations as its condition...
"Consciousness" was mentioned there as well; however, it is taken up again here for the purpose of showing the distinction between cause and fruit, and for the sake of completing the factors.
For in that context, specifically, *saṅkhāra* is the cause and generally, *nāma* is the fruit.
Here, however, generally, *nāma* is the cause and specifically, *phassa* is the fruit. As for sorrow and the rest, since they are all...
They do not occur in a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*), nor do they arise in every instance of the occurrence of consciousness or within every state of mind;

therefore, they are not included. Birth, aging, and death, however, although they may last for more than a mere moment of consciousness, are included for the sake of completing the factors of dependent origination because they are contained within the moment of consciousness.
Thus, first, regarding that which was stated otherwise: "And what..."
That which has not been stated here should be understood.

As for what is stated here and in the subsequent sections, its meaning should be understood in the same manner already explained. However, whatever specific distinction appears in each respective section, we shall clarify that very point in that very place.

Regarding the phrase "that which is the condition for which," here [it is said] that for the *saṅkhāra*, ignorance (*avijjā*) [acts as a condition] by way of those factors common to associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
It is a condition in seven ways: by way of the six conditions—conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance—and by way of the root-condition.

In this context, since the three sets of four conditions beginning with the "root" have already been explained elsewhere by way of the non-disappearance, association, and mutuality conditions, those should be excluded here;
thus, ignorance should be understood as a condition for volitional formations in four ways by way of the remaining conditions.
Volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*) is a condition for consciousness (*viññāṇa*) in eight ways: by way of the six common conditions and by way of the two conditions of kamma and nutriment.

Here, however, excluding those same three [conditions], it is fivefold. Consciousness is a condition for mentality (*nāma*) in nine ways: by way of the six common conditions and by way of the three conditions of faculty, nutriment, and predominance.
Here, however, excluding those same three, it is sixfold. Mentality is a condition for the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) by way of the common...
Sixfold: some [factors] here act as the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), some as the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*), and so on, in many ways.
Here, however, excluding those same three, it is threefold, fourfold, or fivefold.

Just as the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) is to contact (*phassa*) as consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is to name-and-form (*nāma*), so too is contact to feeling (*vedanā*). Together with the six common conditions, including the nutriment condition, it is sevenfold.
Here, however, by excluding those same three, it is fourfold. By way of feeling together with the six common conditions of jhāna-factors and faculties, it is eightfold.
Here, however, by excluding those same three, it is fivefold. Just as ignorance is related to volitional formations, so craving is related to clinging.
Thus, by way of clinging together with the six common conditions of the path-factors, it is sevenfold.
But here, having excluded those same three, it is fourfold: existence is a condition for birth.

Since "birth" is intended here as a conditioned characteristic (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), it is therefore a condition by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) in a figurative sense. Likewise, birth is a condition for aging-and-death.

However, those who say: "In this tetrad, for all [factors] beginning with formations, ignorance and the rest are conditions by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*)"—[their view is incorrect].
“...are conditions. Indeed, it is by way of the co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) alone that the first section was commenced.
Having thus shown the absence of such [co-nascence] for existence (*bhava*) and the rest, and the presence of other conditions, those [objections] should be rejected.

For existence is not the co-nascence condition for birth, nor is birth for aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*). And as for the remaining conditions for these, such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth, which have been stated—those too...

They simply come to be. Therefore, it is not possible to discard them. Thus, first of all, in the first section, whatever has been stated differently, whatever has not been stated, and whatever is the condition for what—in whatever place and in whatever manner—that should be understood. The same method applies to the second section and those that follow.
However, this is the distinction: in the second section, after stating "with name as condition, contact," nothing is said in place of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*).
It has been stated; for what purpose? It is for the purpose of showing a specific condition and for the purpose of including it within the teaching of the *Mahānidāna Sutta*.
For contact (*phassa*) does not have the sixth sense-base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) alone as its condition; rather, the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) are also conditions.
And in the *Mahānidāna Sutta*, when asked, "Is there a specific condition for contact? [it was replied:]...
“Ānanda, regarding what exists, one should say: ‘It exists. If it were asked, ‘With what as condition is contact?
one should say: ‘Contact has name-and-form as its condition. Thus, setting aside the six sense bases, dependent origination was taught with eleven factors.
Therefore, for the purpose of showing this specific distinction of conditions and for the sake of this teaching in the Mahānidāna Sutta:
In the second round, for the purpose of inclusion, it says "with name as condition, contact," yet nothing is stated in place of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*).
This, then, is the distinction in the second round.
In the third round, however, the fourth factor—"with consciousness as condition, mind-and-body" (*nāmarūpa*)—is indeed that which has come down in the Suttanta-bhājaniya.
If it is argued that what was stated is inappropriate here because the mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, that is not incorrect. Why?

Because it functions as a condition at its own time. For even if the material form (*rūpa*) there persists beyond the moment of consciousness, that consciousness still serves as its condition at its own time.
How so? First, in the case of the mind-originated (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*) [matter] that has arisen prior [to the consciousness]:...

Or it is a condition for another by way of posteriority-condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*). For this has been said: "Mentally originated states, namely mind and mental factors, are conditions for this pre-arisen body by way of posteriority-condition.

However, it is a condition for the co-arisen mind-originated [matter] by way of support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). As it was said: "Mind and mental factors are conditions for mind-originated matter..."
“...is a condition by way of dependence-condition.
If this is so, why was it not stated in the same way in the preceding sections? Because it was taught with reference to the location where matter arises.

For this mode of conditionality [pertains] to the location where matter arises, specifically in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) for those born from a womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*) and for those of apparitional birth (*opapātika*) whose sense bases are incomplete.

And it is taught by way of the gods of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). For that very reason, instead of saying here "the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana*), it is stated as "the sixth sense base.
Therein, "name" (*nāma*) is exactly according to the method explained below. "Form" (*rūpa*), however, should be understood as heart-form (*hadayarūpa*).
And that serves as the support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*) and the prenascence-condition (*purejātapaccaya*) for this sixth sense base.
Thus, it is a condition in two ways; this is the distinction in the third section.

The fourth section, however, is stated by way of the mode of birth (*yoni*) as those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*), by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*) as those with complete sense bases, and by way of existence (*bhava*) as beings of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
For that very reason, it is said here: "With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base."
In this context, name [is related] to the sixth base by way of co-nascence and so forth, and to the eye-base and the others by way of postnascence condition.
As for materiality, heart-basis matter is related to the sixth base by way of support condition and pre-nascence condition;

the four great elements are related to the eye-base and the others by way of co-nascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Furthermore, since this mode of conditionality pertains to a single moment of consciousness, it is called "momentary."
Therefore, instead of saying "with the sixfold base as condition" (*saḷāyatanapaccayā*) here, it is stated as "with the sixth base as condition" (*chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phasso*);
this is the distinction in the fourth section.
Having thus understood their differences, one should further note that among all of them, specifically in the first two sections, [these factors] exist in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*).

It should be understood that these were stated for the purpose of showing the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). For in the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), the factors of dependent origination proceed unmixed with form (*rūpa*).
The third was stated for the purpose of showing the mode of conditions in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*);

for although there is a mixing with form in the fine-material existence, the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) do not proceed [there]. The fourth was stated for the purpose of showing the mode of conditions in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*).

It has been stated [thus]. For in the sensuous existence (*kāmabhava*), the entire sixfold sense base (*saḷāyatana*) occurs. Or, the third [alternative] was stated with reference to the moment of unwholesome occurrence for those whose sense bases are incomplete in both the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) and the sensuous existence.
Or, the fourth was stated with reference to those whose sense bases are complete in the sensuous existence.
Or, the first was stated with reference to the state of going everywhere (*sabbatthagāmita*); for that indeed does not [fail to occur] anywhere.
It does not occur in a place where consciousness is active. The second [type] is stated with reference to a specific condition;

here, the specific condition consists in the contact having eleven factors and its being conditioned by the mental aggregates (*nāma*). The third is stated with reference to the first two modes of birth (*yoni*);
for it occurs in those first two modes of birth, since there the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) are never absent. The fourth...
This was said with reference to the last two modes of birth (*yoni*). For he arises in those last two modes of birth;
therein, the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) arise at all times.
And up to this point, that which was stated regarding all four sections—
"Whatever has been stated otherwise in a particular place, whatever has not been stated anywhere,
and the condition by which anything [arises]— one should observe all of that.
Thus is the elucidation of the meaning of the verse completed.
Following this same method, one should understand all this principle from hereon;
and whatever distinction there may be, one should know it in the subsequent tetrads as well. 2.
The Tetrad on Causes (Hetucatukka).
244. In this regard, the method already stated here is evident everywhere. However, the distinction should be understood as follows:

first, in the tetrad of causes, "having ignorance as its cause" means that ignorance is the cause for it. What is meant is that ignorance is the driver of its occurrence from the moment of co-arising until its dissolution.
And by the phrase "with ignorance as condition," it is indicated by way of such conditions as conascence and the rest.

Having shown in general that ignorance (*avijjā*) is the condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), it is further shown specifically as a non-disappearance condition by the phrase "rooted in ignorance" (*avijjāhetuka*).
This same method applies to such cases as "consciousness conditioned by volitional formations is rooted in volitional formations.

But why is the term "rooted in" (*hetuka*) not used for existence (*bhava*) and the others? Because there is no fixed rule regarding non-disappearance conditions, and because [such a condition] is absent.
And [this applies] to the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*). Regarding this, it is asked: "What is existence conditioned by clinging (*upādāna-paccayā bhavo*)?

Because of the statement: "Excluding clinging itself, the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*), the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇa-khandha*)—this is called 'existence conditioned by clinging,'" here the name "existence" refers to these four aggregates conditioned by clinging. Within the aggregate of mental formations...
And because of such statements as, "Birth is comprised within two aggregates," birth, aging, and death are included therein.
In that context, since birth, aging, and death are not found until the stage of clinging (*upādāna*), clinging is not invariably a condition for becoming (*bhava*).
This is because of such statements as, "That which is the birth of this or that phenomenon," regarding the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*).

Because existence (*bhava*), which is comprised of birth, aging, and death, does not exist even at the very moment of birth, it cannot function as a non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*) for birth.

Likewise, because birth does not exist at the moment of aging and death, [it cannot function as such]. Furthermore, since existence is a condition for birth only by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), and birth is a condition for aging and death [only through other conditions], there is no rule whatsoever regarding a non-disappearance condition.

It should be understood that the mention of "root-cause" (*hetu*) among the [five] types of existence (*bhava*) was not made because the condition of non-disappearance (*avigata-paccaya*) is absent there.
However, some say: "Because of the statement 'existence is twofold,' existence includes both rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) and kamma-existence;

and since grasping (*upādāna*) is not a non-disappearance condition for rebirth-existence, one does not say 'existence conditioned by grasping has grasping as its root-cause,' but rather 'conditioned by grasping..."
It is called "existence" (*bhava*). Since it has been cut off here [in the present life], it is not mentioned from the future [life] either.
That is incorrect here because existence mixed with rebirth is not intended; for here, the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandhā*) are what have come under the heading of "existence.
And in the formula "with existence as condition, birth," it is the remainder of existence—excluding birth, aging, and death—that serves as the condition for birth.

It should be understood. Why? Because birth and the other factors have no further conditions for their own arising. If that is so, should it not be stated that "existence (bhava), excluding birth, aging, and death, is the condition for birth"? Yes, it should be stated;

however, it was not mentioned because there is no specific passage [in the text] where it ought to be stated. For in the exposition of the tenth factor, it is stated that "existence arises with clinging as its condition. In the exposition of the eleventh factor, it is [birth].

It should be stated. However, as for that existence which is the condition for birth, there is no phrase to be stated regarding it; thus, because of the absence of such a phrase, it was not mentioned.

Nevertheless, even though unstated, it must be understood through logical reasoning. Furthermore, in such passages as "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form," the expression "having consciousness as its cause" and so forth is employed because the state of being a non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*) is possible for consciousness and the rest. This is the distinction in this tetrad of causes.
3. The Tetrad on Association (Sampayutta-catuṣka) 245.

In the tetrad on association as well, by the phrase "conditioned by ignorance" (avijjā-paccayā), the fact that volitional formations (saṅkhāra) have ignorance as their condition is shown by way of such conditions as co-nascence (sahajāta).
Then, by the phrase "associated with ignorance" (avijjā-sampayutto), the state of being a condition through association (sampayutta-paccayatā) is further demonstrated.

The same method applies to the remaining sections as well. However, because there is no association (*sampayoga*) between immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) and material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), in the third and fourth sections—such as "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form" (*viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ*)—only that which is applicable according to the method beginning with "name associated with consciousness" (*viññāṇasampayuttaṃ nāmaṃ*) is included. This is the distinction in the tetrad of association.
4. The Tetrad on Mutuality (Aññamaññacatukka) 246.

In the tetrad on mutuality as well, having shown that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations by way of such conditions as co-nascence and so forth through the phrase "conditioned by ignorance," the state of mutual conditionality is then shown by the statement, "ignorance is also conditioned by volitional formations. The same applies to the remaining sections.

This is the method. However, because *bhava* (existence) is universal (*nippadesa*) while *upādāna* (clinging) is partial (*sappadesa*), and a partial phenomenon can serve as a condition for a universal phenomenon but not vice versa, it is therefore not stated here that "with *bhava* as condition, there is also *upādāna*.
Alternatively, it was not stated in this way because the teaching [of the previous section] has already been concluded. And because [the phrase] "with *nāmarūpa* as condition" [is present].

The six sense bases exist, yet within a single moment of consciousness, there is no name-and-form conditioned by the six sense bases for which the six sense bases could serve as a mutuality condition;
therefore, in the fourth section, only that which is applicable—namely, "name-and-form [conditioned] even by the sixth base"—is taken. This is the distinction in the tetrad on mutuality.
The Matrix of the Method Based on Ignorance as the Root. 247. The Matrix of the Method Based on Formations, etc., as the Root:
Now begins the method based on formations, namely, "with formations as condition, ignorance. Therein, just as in the case of the matrix based on ignorance...

In this way, four tetrads and sixteen turns should be understood. However, in the first tetrad, the teaching is abbreviated by showing only the first turn. And as it is here, so it is with those [tetrads] rooted in consciousness and so forth.
Therein, in all eight methods beginning with those rooted in formations, according to the method starting with "with formations as condition, ignorance," by way of conascence and other conditions—

Having shown that ignorance is the condition for the formations and so forth, the manner in which the wheel of conditions operates even within a single moment of consciousness is further demonstrated by the method beginning with, "With ignorance as condition, there are formations.
Why, however, were methods rooted in existence (*bhava*) or rooted in birth, aging, and death not stated? Is ignorance conditioned by existence?
Is it not the case that [ignorance] does not exist? It is not that it does not exist.

However, when such statements as "with volitional formations as condition, ignorance" are spoken, there is no phenomenon included within existence (bhava) that is not said to be a condition for ignorance.

Therefore, since there is no other previously unstated condition for ignorance to be mentioned, the method based on existence was not stated. And by the inclusion of "existence," ignorance is also subsumed.
It proceeds. Therefore, if it were said that "ignorance has existence as its condition," it might also be said that "ignorance has ignorance as its condition.
Yet, within a single moment of consciousness, ignorance does not truly function as a condition for itself.

Consequently, because [the causal sequence] is thus severed, the methods based on birth, aging, and death have not been included here. Furthermore, birth, aging, and death are already inherently contained within existence (*bhava*).
