Since these do not serve as conditions for ignorance within a single moment of consciousness, the methods based on existence (*bhava*) or based on birth, aging, and death have not been stated.
This concludes the commentary on the matrix (*mātikā*). This is the commentary on the exposition of the unwholesome (*akusala*).

248–249. Now, just as in the preceding *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* (Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness), the wholesome was first analyzed according to the sequence of the matrix (*mātikā*) beginning with the triad of the wholesome, so here, because no such matrix has been set forth, the wholesome is not mentioned first;
rather, it begins with "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations [arise]," since the matrix is set forth here by way of unwholesome phenomena.

In order to classify and demonstrate the factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), beginning with ignorance (avijjā) and so forth, according to the sequence of their presentation, he said: "Which states are unwholesome?
and so on. The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as explained previously in the section on the arising of consciousness (cittuppādakaṇḍa).
However, since craving (taṇhā) and sense-desire clinging (kāmupādāna) cannot coexist within a single moment of consciousness, that which [is mentioned] here...
Grasping (upādāna) is obtained with craving (taṇhā) as its condition; in order to demonstrate that very point, it is said: "views, the course of views," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the description of existence (bhava), since grasping is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), it is therefore stated:
"Excluding grasping, there is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness."
If it were stated in this way, then clinging would result in being the condition for itself; yet a thing cannot be its own condition.

Furthermore, in the descriptions of birth and so forth, because these are the birth and other characteristics of immaterial phenomena, "brokenness, graying, wrinkling, death, and the state of passing away" are not mentioned.

250. Having thus concluded the first section, in the second section, at the very same time when the mode of conditionality was shown by the first section, the teaching is given by way of the formula beginning with "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations," and so on, rather than presenting a separate section defining the time-periods in order to show the mode of conditionality by another method. Therein, setting aside...
"Contact" (phassa): since contact is also included within the category of the mental (nāma), this is stated for the purpose of extracting it by name from that category.

252. In the third section, when consciousness—which is the condition for the mind-originated matter—is occurring, the accumulation of the eye-base and so forth, which are sustained by that [consciousness], becomes manifest; therefore, regarding the eye-base...

"Accumulation," and so forth, has been stated. Furthermore, because consciousness is also a condition by way of the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) for the bodily form born of kamma that exists at that same time, it was stated thus.

In this context, although only two continuums—namely, the kamma-born and the mind-originated—are mentioned, the other two continuums must also be included; for consciousness is indeed a condition for them as well.

254. However, in the fourth section, because even in a single moment of consciousness all bases—beginning with the eye-base—arise through the condition of the great primary elements (mahābhūta-rūpa), the sixth base arises through the condition of heart-basis matter (hadaya-rūpa), and all of them arise as appropriate through the conditions of mind (nāma) by way of post-nascence, conascence, and so forth, it was therefore said therein:
"Which is the sixfold base conditioned by mind and matter? The eye-base," and so on.
256. In the second tetrad, everything is self-evident. 264.

In the third tetrad, in order to show separately those for which there is no state of being a concomitant condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*) and those for which there is, it is said: "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with consciousness as condition, the name associated with consciousness," and so forth. 272.
In the fourth tetrad, regarding the description of name conditioned by contact (*phassa*), although it says: "Excluding contact, the aggregate of feeling... [and so on]," etc.

Although it is not explicitly stated that "the aggregate of consciousness—this is called 'name' conditioned by contact," nevertheless, because it is stated in the description of the immediately preceding term as "excluding contact, the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness," even though it was not mentioned, it is indeed as good as mentioned.
For whatever is called name is a condition for contact, and contact is likewise a condition for that very same name.

Just as this first method, which has ignorance (*avijjā*) as its root and is divided into sixteen turns consisting of four tetrads, has been explained in relation to this first unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), so too should the eight methods beginning with that which has formations (*saṅkhāra*) as its root be understood. However, the text (*pāḷi*) has been abbreviated.
In this very same way, within that same first unwholesome consciousness, there are nine methods and thirty-six tetrads, and [the total number of factors is] forty-four... [and more].
It should be understood that there are one hundred and twenty-eight [occasions].
Now, in order to show the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) in the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses by this same method, the passage beginning "Which phenomena are unwholesome?
is commenced. Therein, because in those states dissociated from views (*diṭṭhivippayutta*), there is no clinging (*upādāna*) conditioned by craving (*taṇhāpaccayā*).
Therefore, in the place of clinging (*upādāna*), the footing is filled by resolution (*adhimokkha*) which falls firmly like clinging itself.

And in those states accompanied by grief (*domanassa*), since there is no craving (*taṇhā*) conditioned by feeling, the footing is filled in the place of craving by resistance (*paṭigha*), a powerful defilement, just as craving would be;
and in the place of clinging, by resolution alone. However, in those associated with doubt (*vicikicchā-sampayutta*)...
Since there is no resolve due to the absence of determination, there is consequently no faith;
therefore, in the place of craving, the position is filled by doubt, which is a powerful defilement. The place of clinging is thus entirely omitted.
However, in the case of the consciousness associated with restlessness, since there is resolve, the position in the place of craving is filled by restlessness, which is a powerful defilement.
In the section on clinging (*upādāna*), it is by means of resolve (*adhimokkha*) alone. And throughout, the text has been abbreviated after showing merely the specific distinction.
Of this distinction that has been shown, only the exposition of resolve is new; the rest has already appeared below.
In the exposition of resolve, however, it is "resolve" by way of resolving; or else, one resolves upon the object by means of it.
Resolve (*adhimokkha*) is that by which the mind reaches a state of certainty through the absence of doubt. The mode of resolving is "resolving" (*adhimuccanā*).
It is "being resolved upon that" (*tadadhimuttatā*), meaning the state of being resolved upon that mind or upon that object.

In all types of consciousness, the classification according to the fourfold method should be understood in the same manner as explained for the first type of consciousness; however, this is not the case in the consciousness associated with doubt (*vicikicchā-sampayutta*).
Because there is no method rooted in clinging (*upādāna*), there are eight methods, thirty-two tetrads, and one hundred and twenty-eight [items].
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome (*akusala-niddesa*). Now begins the commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome (*kusala-niddesa*).
292. Now, in order to show the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) regarding wholesome consciousness and so forth by this same method, the passage beginning "Which states are wholesome? is commenced.
However, it is not done here in the same way as in the unwholesome section, where the matrix (*mātikā*) was first laid down and the exposition (*niddesa*) followed later.

Why? Because of the possibility of diversity in the section on absorption (*appanā*). For in the case of mundane wholesome states and so forth, these states— [The text continues with an explanation of the various wholesome factors.]
Because it is included within the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), there is a fixed application (*appanā*) of the phrase "thus for this entire mass of suffering";
whereas for supramundane wholesome states (*lokuttarakusala*) and so forth, there is the phrase "thus for these phenomena" (*dhammā*).

Therefore, since it is not possible to establish a common matrix (*mātikā*) here, the exposition has been made by setting out the matrices for each of those respective wholesome states and so forth separately.
In this context, because ignorance does not exist together with a wholesome formation within a single moment of consciousness, that [ignorance] is not mentioned.
Just as there are unwholesome roots for unwholesome states, so for wholesome states there is the "wholesome root" from the perspective of its being a root.

Furthermore, due to the absence of craving and clinging, there is a clarity that plunges deeply into the object in place of craving—just like craving—and what is called "firmly established" in place of clinging—just like clinging.
Resolution has been explained. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated below.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome. Now begins the commentary on the Exposition of the Indeterminate.
306. The indeterminate [states] have been analyzed according to the sequence already presented in the preceding section on the arising of consciousness (cittuppādakaṇḍa).
In all these sections, the methods based on ignorance (*avijjāmūlaka*) are omitted. Why? Because there is no factor to be placed in the position of ignorance.

For while in wholesome states of consciousness there is a wholesome root (*kusalamūla*) to be placed in the position of ignorance, this is not the case in the visual consciousness and so forth. This applies to those states accompanied by roots (*sahetuka*).
However, although such things exist, even so they are not included here because they have been cut off;
it should be understood that the teaching was given as having entered the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness.
Specifically, in this context, the place of craving and the place of clinging are absent in eye-consciousness and the others. Why?

Because of the absence of strong phenomena that serve as the basis for craving (*taṇhā*), and because they lack resolute confidence (*adhimokkha*). In the remaining rootless (*ahetuka*) states, the very basis for craving is absent.
In those with roots (*sahetuka*), because of the presence of clarity (*pasāda*), the place of craving is filled by clarity.

Thus, herein, in the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant eye-consciousnesses and so forth, there are the factors rooted in formations, consciousness, name, the sixth sense-base, contact, and feeling.

Cha cha. In the cases of those without roots, seven methods each should be understood together with that rooted in resolution; in the cases of those with roots, eight methods each should be understood together with that rooted in confidence.
Therein, regarding eye-consciousness and the rest, only the first section of each of the four tetrads has been stated. The second section is by way of the distinction of conditions.
Even though it is obtainable, it was not mentioned. The third and fourth sections are impossible for that very reason;

for those [objects] are mixed with material form (*rūpa*), and eye-consciousness and the rest do not originate material form. And just as two sections are obtainable in the first tetrad, so too are they in the remaining tetrads.
Therefore, there is the second section in the first tetrad, and two sections each in the remaining tetrads.

It should be understood that even those not explicitly mentioned are as if they have been mentioned. In all fourfold sets (*catukka*) concerning the remaining rootless indeterminate states (*ahetuka-abyākata*), all permutations (*vāra*) are obtainable;
however, because they have already been concluded here, they are not included further on. The teaching was given precisely because they are already included within the scope of the discourse.

This same principle applies to the remaining root-possessing resultant states (*sahetuka-vipāka*), with the exception of the immaterial-sphere resultants (*arūpāvacara-vipāka*). For, in the case of the immaterial-sphere resultants—
It is obtained only twice. This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Indeterminate (Abyākataniddesa).
Now begins the commentary on the Exposition of Wholesome States Rooted in Ignorance (Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddesa).

334. Now, in order to show the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) within a single moment of consciousness by another method, the section beginning with "Which states are wholesome? is commenced again.
Therein, the phrase "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*) is stated with reference to the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

For that very reason, in the section of the exposition, instead of analyzing it by asking "What therein is ignorance?", it says: "What therein is [the condition] through ignorance as condition? (*tattha katamo avijjāpaccayā*).
"Volitional formation" is thus analyzed. For at that time, it is volitional formation—consisting of wholesome volition—that is co-nascent with the mind, not ignorance.
In that regard, for mundane wholesome states, ignorance serves as a condition in the manner already stated below in the Suttanta-bhājaniya.

However, because one who has not yet abandoned ignorance develops the supramundane for the sake of abandoning that ignorance, it therefore serves as a condition for that [wholesome consciousness] by way of its transcendence.
For only one possessed of ignorance accumulates wholesome karma, not the other.

In this regard, accumulation occurs in the wholesome states of the three planes both by way of delusion and by way of development through transcendence; whereas in the supramundane, it occurs by way of development through eradication.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
However, this is the distinction: whereas below, in each single wholesome [consciousness], nine sets of sixteen were obtained by way of four tetrads, they are not obtained here.
Why? Because of the absence of the conditions of non-disappearance, association, and mutuality for ignorance.
However, here only the first tetrad is obtained by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). That too was shown only in the first instance and then abbreviated;
it should be demonstrated by extracting [the details].
This concludes the commentary on the description of wholesome states rooted in ignorance.
Commentary on the Exposition of Resultants Rooted in the Wholesome (Kusalamūlakavipākaniddesavaṇṇanā) 343.

Now, in order to show the structure of conditions (paccayākāra) regarding the indeterminate (abyākata) states as well by means of another method, the passage beginning "Which states are indeterminate?
is commenced. Therein, the phrase "conditioned by wholesome roots" (kusalamūlapaccayā) is also stated with reference to the decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya).

For a wholesome root is the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for wholesome-resultant [consciousness], and an unwholesome root is the decisive support condition for unwholesome-resultant [consciousness];
however, there is nothing at all to be said regarding asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*).

Therefore, this [root] serves as a condition both by way of the decisive support condition and by way of the asynchronous kamma-condition. For this very reason, in the section on the exposition, it says: "In that regard, what is..."
Without analyzing it as "wholesome root," it is analyzed there as: "In this context, what is the volitional formation conditioned by the wholesome root?
This same method applies to unwholesome resultant [formations] as well.
And just as in the description of the wholesome rooted in ignorance, in this description of the resultant as well, first of all, only the tetrad of conditions is presented.
It is possible. That too was shown in the first section and then abbreviated.

Therefore, in each resultant consciousness, the classification of sections according to the method based on the roots of the wholesome and the roots of the unwholesome should be understood by way of each respective tetrad.
As for functional states (*kiriyādhamma*), however, because neither ignorance nor the wholesome and unwholesome roots act as decisive-support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) [for them],...
Therefore, it is said that the mode of conditionality was not explained by way of functional (kiriyā) states.
Thus, having described these phenomena— unwholesome, wholesome, and indeterminate— in their many varieties;
Furthermore, for the wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as for their results, [the decisive support condition] acts by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
Again, the entire system of conditions was stated in a single way by the eminent teacher Vādippavara,
for the purpose of generating the differentiation of knowledge regarding the various types of dhamma-conditions.
And because the differentiation of knowledge never occurs in one who is devoid of the sequence of study, hearing, reflection, and practice; therefore,
the wise person should always [engage] through study, hearing, reflection, and practice.
"In that regard, one should do no harm; there is nothing more to be done than this.
Furthermore, this mode of conditionality (paccayākāra) has been presented by extracting and dividing it into exactly two cycles according to the Suttanta-bhājaniya and the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.
This concludes the commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.
The explanation of the Analysis of Dependent Origination in the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga entitled *Sammohavinodanī* is finished. 7.
The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga*).
1. Commentary on the Section of Enumeration in the Suttanta-Bhājaniya. 355.
Now, in the immediately following *Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga*, "four" is the delimitation by number.
By this, it indicates the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness as being neither less than nor more than that. "Foundations of mindfulness" refers to the three foundations of mindfulness.

—The domain of mindfulness (*satigocara*) is also [a reason for its being called *satipaṭṭhāna*]. Furthermore, it is because the Teacher has transcended both aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways.
For in such passages as: “Monks, I shall teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Listen to that... And what, monks, is the arising of the body? With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body,” the domain of mindfulness is indeed [the foundation of mindfulness].
It is called *satipaṭṭhāna*. Likewise [it is used] in such passages as: “The body is the *upaṭṭhāna*, not the mindfulness;
mindfulness is both the *upaṭṭhāna* and the mindfulness. Its meaning is as follows: it is a *paṭṭhāna* because mindfulness is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) in it.
What is established? Mindfulness. The *paṭṭhāna* of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*; or, *paṭṭhāna* means a primary station (*padhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ*). The *paṭṭhāna* of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*.
It is like the elephant’s station, the horse’s station, and so forth.

Regarding the passage: “The three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is worthy to instruct a following as a Teacher”—here, the foundation of mindfulness is defined as the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways.
It has been stated. Its meaning is as follows: it is a *paṭṭhāna* because it is to be established (*paṭṭhapetabba*);

the meaning is "that which should be set forth. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness (*sati*); thus, the establishment by means of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*. However, in such passages as, "The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," it is mindfulness itself that is called the foundation of mindfulness. Its meaning is as follows:
It is called *paṭṭhāna* because it establishes (*patiṭṭhāti*); the meaning is that it stands near, having leaped up and plunged in.
Mindfulness itself is *satipaṭṭhāna* in the sense of establishing. Alternatively, mindfulness is so called in the sense of remembering, and establishment in the sense of standing near.
Thus, it is *satipaṭṭhāna* as both mindfulness and that which is its establishment. This is what is intended here. If this is so, why [is it called "the foundations of mindfulness"]?
Why is the plural form "satipaṭṭhānā" used? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness; for there are many such mindfullnesses due to the diversity of their objects.
But why has the Blessed One taught exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more?

Because it is for the benefit of those to be trained. For among those of craving-temperament and view-temperament, and those who rely on serenity and those who rely on insight, there are two types each according to whether they are dull or sharp.

For one of dull faculties whose temperament is dominated by craving, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body is the path to purification when it is practiced in a gross manner;
for one of sharp faculties, it is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings when it is practiced in a subtle manner.

For one of dull faculties whose temperament is dominated by views, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind is the path to purification when it is not overly differentiated; for one of sharp faculties, it is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of mental objects when it is highly differentiated.
For one of dull faculties who follows the vehicle of serenity (*samatha*), the first foundation of mindfulness is the path of purification, as its sign is easily attained;
for one of sharp faculties, it is the second, because their mind does not settle upon a coarse object.

For one of dull faculties who follows the vehicle of insight (*vipassanā*), the third is appropriate, as its object has not reached too great a degree of differentiation; for one of sharp faculties, the fourth is appropriate, as its object has reached a very high degree of differentiation.
Thus, exactly four are stated, neither fewer nor more.

Or rather, they are for the purpose of abandoning the perversions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and selfhood. For the body is indeed impure; therein, beings are perverted by the perversion of beauty.
Therefore, the first [foundation of mindfulness] is for the purpose of abandoning that perversion by means of showing the state of impurity therein.

The foundation of mindfulness has been explained. Furthermore, although feeling and the other aggregates are apprehended as pleasant, permanent, and self, feeling is actually suffering, the mind is impermanent, and mental phenomena are non-self. Beings are distorted by the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self regarding these things.
Therefore, the remaining three foundations were taught in order to abandon those perversions by showing that feeling and the others are, in fact, suffering and so forth.

Thus, it should be understood that exactly four [foundations of mindfulness] were taught—neither fewer nor more—for the purpose of abandoning the perversions (*vipallāsa*) of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.

Furthermore, it should be understood that they were taught as four not only for the purpose of abandoning the perversions, but also for the purpose of abandoning the four floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), taints (*āsava*), fetters (*gantha*), and clingings (*upādāna*), as well as for the purpose of fully understanding the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*). This, first of all, is the method according to the treatise (*pakaraṇanaya*).
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "By way of refuge and by way of convergence into unity, there is only one foundation of mindfulness;

yet by way of object, it is fourfold. For example, in a city with four gates, those coming from the east take merchandise produced in the eastern direction and enter the city itself through the eastern gate; likewise from the south... [and so on].
Those coming from the west or the north take their goods from the northern marketplace and enter the city itself by the northern gate;
in this way, this matter is to be understood. For the great city of Nibbāna is like the city;
the supramundane Eightfold Path is like the gate; and the body and so forth are like the eastern direction and so on.
Just as those coming from the east, having taken merchandise produced in the eastern region, enter the city itself by way of the eastern gate,
so too those coming by way of the contemplation of the body, having developed the fourteenfold contemplation of the body,
descend into the single Nibbāna alone by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of that development of the contemplation of the body. Just as...
Those coming from the south take goods produced in the southern region and enter the city through the southern gate;

likewise, those coming by way of the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā), having developed the ninefold contemplation of feelings, descend into the single Nibbāna alone by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of that development of the contemplation of feelings. Just as...
Those coming from the west take their wares produced in the western region and enter the city through the western gate;

likewise, those coming by way of the contemplation of mind develop the sixteenfold contemplation of mind and, by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of that development of the contemplation of mind, they converge upon the single Nibbāna. Just as...
Those coming from the north, taking goods produced in the northern region, enter the city itself through the northern gate; likewise,
those coming by way of the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā), having developed the fivefold contemplation of phenomena,
descend into the single Nibbāna alone by means of the Noble Path produced through the power of the development of the contemplation of phenomena.

Thus, it should be understood that although there is only one single foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) by way of its refuge and by way of its convergence into unity, it is said to be fourfold by way of its objects.
Regarding the phrase "here, monks" (*idha bhikkhū*):
although this analysis of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga*) was delivered by the Blessed One while seated in the world of the gods (*devaloka*), [it is addressed here].
It has been stated that not even a single bhikkhu was sitting there in the presence of the Blessed One.
Even so, because these bhikkhus are developing the four foundations of mindfulness—and since they are indeed the "range" (gocara) of bhikkhus—the Blessed One addresses them here as "bhikkhus.
But do only bhikkhus develop these foundations of mindfulness, and not bhikkhunīs and the others?
Bhikkhunīs and others also cultivate this; however, the bhikkhus are the foremost assembly (aggaparisā). Thus, because they are the foremost assembly, he addresses them here as "bhikkhus.
Alternatively, he speaks thus because the state of being a bhikkhu is seen to consist in the practice itself. For whoever practices this way of practice is called a "bhikkhu.
Indeed, whether one is a deva or a human, if one is practicing, one is reckoned simply as a "bhikkhu. As it has been said:
“Even if one were adorned and should walk with composure,
being peaceful, tamed, self-controlled, and living the holy life,
having laid aside the rod toward all beings— ”
“Such a one is a brahmin, such a one is a recluse, such a one is a bhikkhu.
Commentary on the Summary of the Contemplation of the Body:
“Inwardly” (ajjhattaṃ) refers to what is internal to oneself (niyakajjhattaṃ). Therefore, “inwardly in the body” (ajjhattaṃ kāye) means “in one’s own body” (attano kāye).

In this context, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical body (*rūpakāya*). For here, the physical body is intended as a "body" in the sense of being a collection of parts and limbs, such as hair and so forth—just as one speaks of a "body of elephants," a "body of horses," or a "body of chariots.
And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too is it in the sense of being the source (*āya*) of what is loathsome.
For it is the source (*āya*) of things that are loathsome, even supremely disgusting; thus it is called a "body. *Āya* means the place of origin.
Herein, this is the etymological explanation: it comes (*āyati*) from that, thus it is "coming" (*āya*). What comes? The loathsome things, such as hair and so forth.
Thus, the coming of the loathsome things, hair and so forth, is the "body" (*kāya*).

"Contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) means one whose nature is to contemplate the body, or one who is contemplating the body. Even though it has already been stated "the body," [the word] is repeated again...

Regarding the phrase "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*), it should be understood that the second mention of "body" is made for the purpose of demonstrating its definition, its separation from density, its analysis, and so forth, without confusion.
By this, it is shown that one is not contemplating feelings in the body, nor contemplating mind or mental objects;
rather, one is specifically contemplating the body in the body—that is, by showing the mode of contemplation of the body within the basis known as the "body," it is demonstrated without confusion.
Thus, the establishment [of the meditation object] has been shown.

Likewise, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon in the body apart from its limbs and members, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man apart from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth. Furthermore, even regarding that body which is a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya)—consisting of hair of the head, body hair, and the rest—one does not contemplate a single phenomenon apart from those primary elements and derived matter;
rather, one is like one who contemplates the constituent parts of a chariot.

By viewing the body— designated as a "mass"— as a collection in various ways, such as viewing it as a collection of limbs and members like one observing the parts of a city, or viewing it as a collection of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth like one observing the components of a city,

or viewing it as a collection of primary elements and derived matter like one separating the leaf-sheaths of a plantain trunk or like one untying an empty fist, the analysis of the compact mass is demonstrated.
It exists. For herein, neither a body, nor a woman, nor a man, nor any other phenomenon whatsoever is perceived apart from the aforementioned collection [of elements].
Yet, beings form various false attachments to that mere collection of phenomena as described.
Therefore, the ancients said:
“What one sees, that is not seen; what is seen, that one does not see. Not seeing, the deluded one is bound;
being bound, he is not released. This is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the analysis of the compact mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*) and so forth.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), this further meaning is also to be understood here: [the demonstration of the analysis of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases].
For this person is indeed a contemplator of the body in this very body, and not a contemplator of other phenomena. What is meant by this?

Just as people might contemplate water even in a mirage where no water exists, so too, one does not contemplate this body—which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul—as being permanent, pleasant, self, or beautiful;
rather, one is a contemplator of the body precisely as a contemplator of the collection of modes that are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul.
This has been said. Alternatively, that body which was described in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* by way of the passage beginning, “Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest...
he breathes in mindfully,” and ending with the dust, the atoms, and the bones;
and that [body] which is described as, “Here, someone contemplates the earth-body as impermanent, likewise the water-body, the fire-body, ... [and so forth].

In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, "body" (*kāya*) is explained as: "the body of air, the body of head-hair, the body of body-hair, the body of skin, the body of hide, the body of flesh, the body of blood, the body of sinews, the body of bone, and the body of bone-marrow.
Since one contemplates all of these within this very body, the meaning should also be understood as "one who contemplates the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*).
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows:

because one does not contemplate anything in the body that could be grasped as "I" or "mine," but rather contemplates each respective collection of various phenomena such as head-hairs and body-hairs, one is called "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) in the sense of contemplating the collection of phenomena consisting of head-hairs and so forth within the body.
Furthermore, it is said: "In this body, one contemplates [it] as impermanent, not as permanent," and so on.

Furthermore, the meaning should also be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" by way of contemplating the entire collection of aspects— beginning with the characteristic of impermanence— that have been set forth in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* in their proper sequence.
For it is in this way that the bhikkhu who has entered upon the practice of contemplation of the body in the body contemplates this body through the contemplations of impermanence and so forth.
By means of the seven contemplations, he contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent; he contemplates as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates as non-self, not as self; he becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not passionate;
he causes cessation, not origination; he relinquishes, not grasps. Contemplating that [body] as impermanent, he [abandons] the perception of permanence...
It should be understood that one who contemplates as suffering abandons the perception of pleasure; one who contemplates as non-self abandons the perception of self;
one who becomes disenchanted abandons delight; one who becomes dispassionate abandons lust; one who brings about cessation abandons origination;
and one who relinquishes abandons grasping.
"Abides" (*viharati*) is an expression indicating association with any one of the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).
The meaning is that he carries and maintains his personal existence (*attabhāva*) by interrupting the obstruction of one posture with another, so that it does not fall [into collapse].
"In the external body" means in the body of another. "In the internal and external body" means sometimes in one's own body and sometimes...
Regarding another's body: for by the first method, the comprehension of the body is stated with respect to one's own body; by the second method, with respect to another's body;
and by the third method, sometimes with respect to one's own body and sometimes with respect to another's body. However, there is no such thing as an object that combines both internal and external.
What is described here is the time when one who is proficient in the meditation subject moves from one to the other. "Ardent" (ātāpī) means...
This is an illustration of the conjunction of energy that encompasses the body.

For at that time, he is possessed of that energy which, because it scorches the defilements within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), is called "scorching" (*ātāpa*); therefore, he is called "ardent" (*ātāpī*).

"Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means being endowed with the knowledge termed clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) that encompasses the body. "Mindful" (*satimā*) means [endowed] with mindfulness that encompasses the body...

He is endowed with mindfulness. Now, because he discerns the object by means of mindfulness and contemplates it by means of wisdom—for there is no such thing as contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness—it was said: "Bhikkhus, I declare mindfulness to be all-beneficial.
Therefore, up to this point—"he dwells contemplating the body in the body"—the meditation subject of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in body-contemplation is established.
This has been said. Alternatively, because one who lacks ardor finds inner contraction to be an obstacle;
one who lacks clear comprehension is confused regarding the adoption of skillful means and the avoidance of unskillful means;
and one who lacks mindfulness is simply incapable of relinquishing unskillful means and adopting skillful means, his meditation subject does not succeed. Therefore, by the power of which qualities...
It should be understood that this was said—namely, "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful"—for the purpose of showing how that [foundation of mindfulness] is accomplished for them.

Thus, having shown the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body and its associated factor, he now says "having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world" in order to show the factor of abandoning.
Therein, "having removed" means either by removal through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by removal by suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).
Or, having removed [them]. Here, "the world" (*loka*) refers to this very body, which has been defined as being divided into internal and other categories;
the meaning is that one has removed covetousness and dejection regarding that world.

Since, in this context, the mention of "covetousness" includes sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and the mention of "dejection" includes ill-will (*byāpāda*), therefore, by showing these two powerful factors included among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), [the five hindrances are shown].
It should be understood that the abandoning of the hindrances has been stated.
Moreover, it should be understood specifically that by the removal of covetousness, there is the removal of attachment rooted in bodily success;

by the removal of ill-will, there is the removal of aversion rooted in bodily failure; and by the removal of covetousness, there is the removal of delight in the body, while by the removal of ill-will...

The abandoning of non-delight in the cultivation of the body, the removal of unreal qualities such as beauty and pleasure from the body through the removal of covetousness, and the removal of real qualities such as foulness and suffering from the body through the removal of displeasure is thus stated.
By this, the power of yoga and the capability for yoga of the practitioner are illustrated. This is the power of yoga.
For this is what it means: he is free from attraction and repulsion, enduring both the unpleasant and the pleasant, and is devoid of adding what is unreal or removing what is real.
Being thus free from attraction and repulsion, enduring the unpleasant and the pleasant, and neither adding the unreal nor removing the real, he is capable of yoga.

Another method: In the phrase "contemplating the body in the body," the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is stated by way of contemplation (*anupassanā*). In the phrase "he dwells" (*viharati*), the protection of the body for one who possesses the meditation subject is stated by way of the dwelling already mentioned.
In the words "ardent" (*ātāpī*) and so forth, "ardency" refers to right effort (*sammappadhāna*);

"mindfulness and clear comprehension" (*satisampajañña*) refers to the meditation subject that is beneficial in all circumstances, or else it refers to the means for protecting the meditation subject; or alternatively, it refers to mindfulness itself.

It should be understood that serenity is attained by way of contemplation of the body, insight through clear comprehension, and the fruit of development through the removal of covetousness and dejection.

This, then, is the commentary on the meaning of the summary of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body. Now follows the commentary on the summaries of the contemplation of feelings and so forth.

In the sections on the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, the terms "internal" and so on should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. For in these cases too, a threefold comprehension is taught:
namely, one's own feelings and so forth, another's feelings and so forth, and at times one's own and at times another's feelings and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the repetition of the terms "feelings" and so on in such phrases as "contemplating feelings in feelings," [the purpose is as follows:]...
The purpose should be understood in the same manner as that stated for the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).

Regarding the phrases "contemplating feelings in feelings," "contemplating the mind in the mind," and "contemplating phenomena in phenomena": here, "feelings" refers to the three kinds of feeling, and these are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*);
likewise, the "mind" and the "phenomena" are mundane. Their detailed classification will become clear in the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*).
However, here one who contemplates feeling in the manner that it should be contemplated is to be understood as "one who contemplates feelings in feelings.
This same method applies to the mind and mental objects. And how should feeling be contemplated?
First, pleasant feeling [should be contemplated] as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it has been said:
“He who has seen pleasure as suffering, and has seen suffering as a dart,
and has seen that which is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as peaceful yet impermanent—
that bhikkhu indeed possesses right vision and will wander in peace.”
All these should also be contemplated as suffering. And this has been said: "Whatever is felt, that I call suffering.

Furthermore, they should be contemplated according to their pleasantness and painfulness, as it was said: "Pleasant feeling, friend Visākha, is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change"—all of this should be expanded in detail. Moreover, they should also be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence.
They should be contemplated. The rest will become clear in the section on the exposition (Niddesavāra) itself.

Regarding mental states (cittadhamma), first, consciousness (citta) should be contemplated by way of its various classifications—such as object-conditioned, dominant, conascent, belonging to the planes, kamma-resultant, functional, and so forth—as well as by way of the contemplations of impermanence and so on, and by way of the classifications such as "with lust" and so on that appear in the section on the exposition. As for mental factors (dhammā):

It should be contemplated by way of the specific and general characteristics, the nature of emptiness, the contemplations of impermanence and so forth, and the various classifications such as "peaceful" and "unpeaceful" found in the section on the exposition (*niddesa*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Furthermore, it is certainly the case that for one who has abandoned covetousness and dejection regarding the world known as the body, those same states have also been abandoned regarding the worlds of feeling and so forth.
However, it is stated in all instances both with reference to various individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness occurring at various moments of consciousness.

Or else, what has been abandoned in one instance is abandoned in the others as well; therefore, it should be understood that this was stated in that manner for the purpose of showing its abandonment therein.
The commentary on the Section of Enumeration is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Contemplation of the Body (Kāyānupassanāniddesa). 356.
Now, just as a skilled basket-maker [produces] coarse mats, fine mats, boxes, baskets, bags, and so forth...
Suppose one desiring to make various utensils were to obtain a single large bamboo, cut it into four parts, and then taking each individual section of bamboo,
split it and fashion those respective utensils; or alternatively, suppose a skilled goldsmith,
desiring to make various kinds of jewelry, were to obtain a piece of perfectly pure gold and break it into four parts.

Just as one might take each individual portion and fashion it into various ornaments, even so the Blessed One, desiring to bring about manifold specific attainments for beings through the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, presented the single right mindfulness according to its objects by way of the formula: "There are four foundations of mindfulness;
here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally," and so forth.

Having divided [the *satipaṭṭhānas*] into four ways and then taking each one individually, he begins the section on the detailed exposition by analyzing them according to the method starting with, "And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu [regard] internally as body... and so forth.
Therein, the phrase beginning with "And how" is a question of desire to speak in order to explain in detail. This, however, is the summarized meaning here:
“And in what manner and by what method does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body as a body internally?
This same method applies to the remaining sections of the questions. “Here, a bhikkhu” means a bhikkhu in this dispensation (*sāsana*).
Here, the word “here” (*idha*) indicates the dispensation which serves as the support for the person who produces all modes of contemplation of the body, beginning with the internal.
And it is a negation of the existence of such [ascetics] in other teachings. For this has been said: “Right here, monks, is there an ascetic...
empty are the doctrines of others of ascetics who are different. Therefore it is said: “Monks in this teaching. “Internally, the body” means one’s own body.
“From the soles of the feet upwards” means from the soles of the feet upward. “Down to the crown of the head” means...
"Down to the tips of the hairs": [it extends] from below the hair-tips. "Ending at the skin": it is bounded on all sides by the skin.

"He contemplates it as full of various kinds of impurity" means he sees that this body is filled with various kinds of impurities such as hair and so forth. How? "In this body there are head-hairs... down to... urine.
Therein, "there are" (*atthi*) means they exist (*saṃvijjanti*). "In this" refers to this very [body].
It is said that from the soles of the feet upwards, from the crown of the hair downwards, and across to the skin’s surface, it is filled with various kinds of impurities.

"In the body" means in the physical frame. For this physical frame is called "body" (*kāya*) because it is a collection of impurities, and because it is the source (*āya*) of the loathsome things such as the hair and so forth, as well as the hundreds of diseases such as eye-diseases.
"Head-hairs, body-hairs": these are the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs.
In this context, the connection should be understood as follows: "In this body there are head-hairs; in this body there are body-hairs.

For within this entire frame, measuring one fathom—from the soles of the feet upwards, from the crown of the head downwards, and from the skin across the sides—in every respect, [these are to be found].
Searching through it, no one sees even the slightest trace of purity—neither a pearl, nor a beryl, nor aloeswood, nor saffron, nor camphor, nor scented powders and the like;
rather, one sees only various kinds of impurity, such as head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and unsightly. Therefore it was said:
“There are in this body head-hairs, body-hairs... [etc. ... urine. This is the commentary on the connection of the words here.

Now, a clansman who desires to reach Arahantship by developing this meditation subject must first purify his fourfold virtue and become established in perfectly pure virtue. Among the ten impediments, that which is an impediment...
There is [a case] for one who, having cut that off, has generated the first jhāna through the cultivation of the meditation subject of attention to repulsiveness,
and having made that jhāna a basis, has established insight and attained either Arahantship or one of the fruits beginning with Non-returning—
even for a master of the lineage (tanti-ācariya) who has thoroughly mastered the Pāḷi together with its commentaries to the very last extent.
It should be learned in the presence of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitta).
If one does not find such a pure virtuous friend in the same monastery, one should go to the place where he dwells and learn it there.

Therein, everything—including the purification of the fourfold moral discipline (sīla), the obstacles (palibodha), the removal of obstacles, and the procedure for approaching the teacher—is [to be explained].
This has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.
However, when a teacher explains a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he should do so in three ways. There may be a bhikkhu who has already mastered the meditation subject by nature;
for him, the teacher should explain it after having him recite it once or twice during the sitting session.
One person, having lived nearby, wishes to learn; for him, the teaching should be given at every opportunity as he arrives.

Another, having learned it, wishes to go elsewhere; for him, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) should be explained without being overly prolix nor overly abbreviated, making it free from tangles and free from knots.
When explaining, what should be pointed out? The sevenfold skill in learning.
And the skill in attention should be explained in ten ways. Therein, skill in learning should be explained in seven ways as follows:
by way of word, by way of mind, by way of color, by way of shape, by way of direction, by way of location, and by way of delimitation.
For in this meditation subject of attention to repulsiveness, even one who is a master of the Tipiṭaka—
Therefore, at the time of attention, one should first perform the recitation with the voice.
For some, the meditation subject becomes clear even while they are reciting, as was the case for two elders who had received their meditation subjects from the Venerable Mahādeva Thera of Malaya.
It is said that when those two requested the meditation subject from the Thera, he told them: "For four months, in this way..."
"Recite the text," he said, and gave them the Pāḷi of the Thirty-two Aspects.

Although they were already proficient in two or three Nikāyas, because of their aptitude for grasping what is well-turned, they became stream-enterers while still reciting the Thirty-two Aspects for four months.
Therefore, a teacher explaining a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should say to his pupil: "First, by means of speech..."
“Recite the meditation subject. And while reciting it, you should analyze the five groups beginning with the skin and perform the recitation in both forward and reverse order.
For after saying, “Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin,” one must then say in reverse order, “Skin, teeth, nails, body-hairs, head-hairs.
Immediately after that, regarding the five groups beginning with flesh: “Flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow...”
Having said "kidney," one should again state them in reverse order: "kidney, bone marrow, bone, sinew, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body hair, head hair.
Then, regarding the fivefold lungs, having said "heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs," one should again state them in reverse order: "lungs, spleen, midriff, liver, heart, kidney."
"One should say: 'marrow, bone, sinew, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body hair, and head hair.
Then, although it has not ascended this sequence, the brain—which appears in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*—is added to the sequence following excrement;
thus, in this "pentad of brains," [it is said]: "intestines, mesentery, stomach, excrement, and brain."
Having spoken thus, one should further recite it in reverse order: "brain, feces, stomach-contents, intestines, large intestine,
lungs, spleen, kidneys, liver, heart, kidneys [repeated], bone-marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, teeth, nails, body hair, head hair."
Then, regarding the group of six consisting of fat, it says: “bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, and fat. Having stated this, it then proceeds again in reverse order:

“fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, brain matter, feces, stomach contents, small intestines, large intestines, lungs, spleen, midriff, liver, heart, kidneys, marrow, bones, sinews, flesh, skin, and teeth.”
"nails, body hair, and head hair" should be stated.
Then, regarding the group of six excretions (*muttachakka*), having stated "tears, fat, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine," one should again state them in reverse order:
"urine, synovial fluid, snot, spittle, fat, tears, grease, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile, and brain matter."
“Feces, urine, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints,

synovial-fluid, head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, gorge, feces, brain— in this way,

the recitation should be performed verbally even for a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred-thousand times. For by verbal recitation, the continuity of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is maintained.”
It becomes proficient; the mind does not wander here and there;
the constituent parts become manifest, appearing like a row of fingers or like a fence and its posts.

Just as the recitation is done with the voice, so too should the recitation be performed with the mind. For recitation with the voice is a condition for recitation with the mind. Recitation with the mind...
It is a condition for the penetration of characteristics. The penetration of characteristics is a condition for the penetration of the path and its fruit.
Regarding "by way of color," the color of the hair and so forth must be defined. Regarding "by way of shape," the shape of those very things must be defined.
Regarding "by way of direction," in this body, the region above the navel is the upper direction, and the region below is the lower direction. Therefore...
“The direction should be defined thus: ‘This part belongs to this particular direction.
‘By way of location’ means that the location of each part should be defined thus: ‘This part is situated in this particular place.
‘By way of delimitation’ refers to two kinds of delimitation: delimitation by the similar and delimitation by the dissimilar. Therein, ‘this part [is delimited] below’...”
“...and above, and across, it is delimited by this name”—thus should the delimitation by way of similarity be understood.
“Head-hairs are not body-hairs, and body-hairs are not head-hairs”—thus should the delimitation by way of dissimilarity be understood without confusion.
While explaining the sevenfold skill in learning in this way, [he says]: “This meditation subject is found in such-and-such a Sutta...”
Having understood that it was taught by way of repulsiveness, or "in such-and-such a place by way of elements," one should explain it accordingly.
For this [method] was taught by way of repulsiveness alone in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, while it was taught by way of elements in the Mahāhatthipadopama, Mahārāhulovāda, and Dhātuvibhaṅga Suttas.
However, in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, with reference to one for whom it appears by way of its color, the four jhānas are attained.

They have been analyzed. Therein, that which is explained by way of the elements is a subject of meditation for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna), while that which is explained by way of repulsiveness is a subject of meditation for serenity (samatha-kammaṭṭhāna).
They say that this [present subject] is indeed explained here as a subject of meditation for serenity, specifically as something common to all without distinction.
Having thus explained the sevenfold skill in learning, one should explain the tenfold skill in attention as follows:
"By way of succession, not too fast, not too slow, warding off distraction, surmounting the description, gradual relinquishing, absorption, and the three discourses.
In this context, "by way of succession" refers to starting from the time of recitation.
It should be brought to mind in regular succession, not by skipping over intervals. For if one brings it to mind by skipping intervals,
just as an unskilled man climbing a thirty-two-rung ladder by skipping rungs falls with a weary body and does not complete the ascent, even so,
because he fails to attain the gratification that is to be reached through the perfection of meditation, [he fails in his purpose].
With a weary mind, one falls [into negligence] and does not bring meditation to completion.
Even when attending to it in successive order, one should attend to it "not too quickly.
For if one attends to it too quickly, it is as if one were to set out on a three-league road and, without observing the turns and descents, proceed at a rapid pace.
Just as a man who travels back and forth seven times in rapid succession may indeed exhaust the distance, yet he must still proceed by asking for directions;
even so, when one reaches the very end of the meditation subject, it remains unclear and does not bring about distinction. Therefore, it should not be given attention too quickly.

And just as it is not too fast, so too it is not too slow. For if one attends to it too slowly, it is just as when a man wishing to travel a three-league road on that very day fails to reach the end of his journey because he lingers among trees, mountains, thickets, and the like along the way;
thus the road is not exhausted, and it must be completed over two or three days. In the same way, [the path is not traversed].
If the meditation subject does not reach its conclusion, it does not become a condition for the attainment of distinction.
Regarding the phrase "by warding off distraction": having set aside the meditation subject, the distraction of the mind toward various external objects must be warded off;
for if it is not warded off, it is as if one has entered upon a narrow, precipitous path.
If a person, failing to observe the footprints of a man and looking here and there, misses the sequence of his steps, he will then fall into a precipice a hundred fathoms deep;
even so, when there is outward distraction, the meditation subject declines and is lost. Therefore, one should attend to it by warding off distraction.
‘By transcending the designation’: having transcended this designation beginning with “head-hairs, body-hairs,” one should establish the mind on the repulsive.
For just as, in a time when water is scarce, people seeing a well in the forest tie some kind of signpost there such as a palm leaf, and then come back by means of that signpost and bathe.
They both bathe and drink whenever they wish. But when their path has become familiar through constant movement, there is no need for a sign; they go at any desired moment and bathe and drink.
In exactly the same way, for one who attends to the mind by way of the designation "head hairs, body hairs" during the preliminary stage, the state of repulsiveness becomes manifest.
Then, having transcended the designation "head-hairs, body-hairs," one should fix the mind on the state of repulsiveness itself.
Regarding "by successive relinquishing": whichever part does not appear should be relinquished; thus it should be brought to mind by relinquishing them one by one.
For when a beginner brings the mind to "head-hairs," the attention proceeds until it reaches "urine."

It remains fixed right at this final portion. And when one brings "urine" to mind, the attention proceeds until it remains fixed right at this initial portion, "head-hairs. Then, as he brings them to mind, some portions appear clearly while others do not.
Therefore, for as long as those portions that do appear are present, he should perform the work upon them.
It should be practiced until, when two [images] appear, one of them appears more clearly.
When it has appeared in this way, absorption (appanā) should be induced by repeatedly bringing that very same image to mind.
In this regard, there is this simile: just as a hunter wishing to catch a monkey living in a palm grove of thirty-two palm trees...
Having pierced the leaf of the palm tree standing at the beginning with an arrow, he should raise a shout;

then that monkey, falling from one palm tree to the next in succession, would go only as far as the last palm tree; having gone there, when the hunter has done exactly the same thing again, it would return by that same path to the first palm tree;
thus it would go back and forth in succession again and again.

Having risen right at the place where the shout was raised, and then gradually descending until he falls upon a single palm fruit, if he were to grasp firmly the bud or the leaf-spike in the middle of that fruit while being pierced, he would not rise; in this same way should this be understood.
Herein, this is the application of the simile: just as there are thirty-two palms in the palm grove, so too in this body there are thirty-two [bones].
The body parts; the mind is like the monkey; the practitioner is like the hunter;

the monkey’s roaming through the grove of thirty-two palm trees for the sake of an object is like the practitioner’s mind roaming through the body consisting of thirty-two parts for the sake of an object;
when the hunter pierces the leaf of the palm tree standing at the beginning with an arrow and lets out a shout, the monkey—

Just as a monkey, having fallen from one palm tree, goes to the last palm tree, so too when a meditator begins the mental attention on "head-hairs," his mind comes to rest only at the final stage after proceeding through the sequence;
the same method applies to returning again; and for the monkey going through the sequence again and again, there is a rising at each place where it had previously let out a cry.

When, while attending to [the object] again and again, some images appear while others do not, one should let go of those that do not appear and perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on those that do.

Gradually, it becomes like this: as if one were to fall upon a single palm leaf, firmly grasp its central bud-like palm-leaf needle, and continue piercing it without rising even when being pierced; likewise, when two images appear at the conclusion, whichever one appears more clearly—
It is established by repeatedly attending to that very object until absorption (*appanā*) is produced.

There is another simile: just as a bhikkhu who lives on almsfood, residing near a village of thirty-two families, might receive two alms at the first house and send one beyond; then, on the following day, he receives three.
On the following day he should give two [meals]; on the third day, having received a bowlful at the very beginning, he should go to the refectory and eat.
This should be understood as being analogous to that. For the thirty-two modes of meditation (dvattiṃsākāra) are like the village of thirty-two families;

the practitioner (yogāvacara) is like the alms-collector (piṇḍapātika); and the meditator’s dwelling in dependence upon that village is like the practitioner’s dwelling in the thirty-two modes of meditation.

This is the preparation: as one attends to the object again and again, one should discard those [images] that do not appear and retain those that do appear—just as when, having received two alms at the first house, one discards the subsequent one;
or as when, having received three on the second day, one discards the subsequent two—until the two sections [of the body] are established.

The preparation consists in this: just as on the third day one receives a bowlful at the very beginning and, sitting in the refectory, consumes it, so too does one repeatedly bring to mind whichever of the two [parts] presents itself more clearly, thereby producing absorption (*appanā*).

"From absorption" means from the stage of absorption. The intention here should be understood as follows: absorption occurs within each individual constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*), such as the head-hairs and so forth.

‘And three discourses’: the discourse on higher consciousness (*adhicitta*), the discourse on coolness (*sītibhāva*), and the discourse on skill in the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgakosalla*). These three discourses should be understood as being for the purpose of yoking energy with concentration; this is the intended meaning here. In that regard:
“Monks, by a monk devoted to higher consciousness, three signs should be attended to from time to time...
From time to time the sign of concentration should be attended to; from time to time the sign of exertion should be attended to...”
From time to time, the sign of equanimity should be brought to mind.
Monks, if a monk devoted to higher consciousness were to attend exclusively to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would lead to indolence.
Monks, if a monk devoted to higher consciousness were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion, [it is possible that his mind would lead to agitation].

That state of mind would lead to restlessness. If, monks, a monk devoted to higher consciousness were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not become rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
But when, monks, a monk devoted to higher consciousness attends from time to time—
He attends to the sign of concentration, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity.
That mind becomes pliant, wieldy, radiant, and not brittle; it is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
“Just as, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice prepares his furnace, and the furnace—”
Having bound it, he heats it in the mouth of a furnace; having heated it in the mouth of the furnace, he takes the gold with tongs and places it in the mouth of the furnace;

having placed it in the mouth of the furnace, he fans it from time to time, sprinkles it with water from time to time, and observes it from time to time. If, monks, the goldsmith or the goldsmith’s apprentice...
If a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to blow upon that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would burn.

But if, monks, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to sprinkle that gold thoroughly with water, it is possible that the gold would go out. If, monks, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice...
Or if the goldsmith, or his apprentice, were to look on at that gold with total indifference, it is possible that the gold would not reach proper maturity. But when, monks,
the goldsmith or his apprentice repeatedly blows upon that gold from time to time,
repeatedly sprinkles it with water from time to time, and repeatedly looks on at it from time to time, [it reaches proper maturity].
That gold is soft, workable, radiant, and not brittle; it is well-suited for craftsmanship,
and whatever kind of ornament one desires— whether a flat band, an earring, a neck-ornament,
or a golden garland— it serves that purpose.
“Even so, bhikkhus, for one devoted to the higher mind... rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints;

and whatever state realizable by direct knowledge his mind inclines toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge, he attains the capacity to be a witness therein, in each and every case where there is a suitable basis”—this sutta should be understood as the higher mind (*adhicitta*).
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness.
With which six? Here, bhikkhus, at the time when the mind should be restrained, the bhikkhu restrains the mind;
at the time when the mind should be exerted, he exerts the mind...”
He exerts himself; at the time when the mind should be gladdened, he gladdens the mind;
at the time when the mind should be looked upon with equanimity, he looks upon it with equanimity;
and he is one who is intent on the sublime and delights in Nibbāna. Possessed of these six qualities, monks, a bhikkhu...
This Sutta—"one is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness"—is to be understood as "the state of coolness.
Furthermore, skill regarding the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga-kosalla) has indeed been handed down in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, in the Mahāvagga, within the Bojjhaṅga-saṃyutta, as follows:
"In the same way, monks, at whatever time the mind is sluggish, that is not the time for the development of the tranquility factor of enlightenment (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga)."
Thus, having properly mastered these seven kinds of skill in learning and having well-defined this tenfold skill in attention,
the yogi should thoroughly master the meditation subject by means of both these skills.
However, if it is more comfortable for him to stay in the same monastery as his teacher, he need not have it explained in such detail.
One who is devoted to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should, having attained distinction, have it explained further and further.
One who wishes to dwell elsewhere should have it explained in detail according to the method already stated;

then, having repeatedly rehearsed it and severed every knot-like difficulty, he should abandon a lodging unsuitable for the cultivation of the meditation subject and [seek one] free from the eighteen faults, such as being too large.

While dwelling in a suitable abode and having severed the minor impediments, one who is of a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*) must, since lust is to be abandoned, perform the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the contemplation of repulsiveness (*paṭikkūla-manasikāra*).
While performing it, he should first take up the sign (*nimitta*) in the hair. How? Having plucked out one or two hairs—
Having placed it on the palm of the hand, the color should first be defined. It is permissible to look at the hair even at the place where it has been cut;
it is likewise permissible to look at it in a bowl of water or a bowl of rice-gruel soup. When it is black, one should attend to it as "black"; when it is white, as "white.
But when it is mixed, they should be attended to according to whichever is predominant. And just as with the hair, so too...
In this way, the sign must be grasped even after seeing the entire set of thirty-two parts.

Having thus grasped the sign, one should define all the components by way of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation; then, they should be defined as repulsive in five ways: by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location.
Herein, this is the progressive exposition for all the components: first, as to natural color, the head-hairs are black, the color of green *ariṭṭhaka* fruit;
as to shape, they are long and cylindrical, the shape of a balance-beam; as to direction, they grow in the upper direction;
as to location, they are bounded on both sides by the ears and the temples, in front by the edge of the forehead, and behind by the nape of the neck. They encircle the skull.

The space for the head-hairs is the moist skin. By way of delimitation, the head-hairs are delimited below by their own root-bases, which are established having entered the skin covering the head to the extent of a grain of rice; above, by space; and across, by one another.
Since two head-hairs do not exist together, this is the delimitation by homogeneity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).

‘Hair is not body-hair, body-hair is not hair’—in this way, hair is a distinct constituent unmixed with the remaining thirty-one constituents; this is the delimitation by way of dissimilarity. This is the definition of hair by way of its color and so forth.

Now, however, is the fivefold definition of it as repulsive by way of its color and so forth: these hairs are repulsive by way of color, by way of shape, by way of smell, by way of habitat, and by way of location. Even though they may be pleasant...
For when they see anything hair-colored in a bowl of conjey or in a bowl of rice, they feel disgust, saying, "This is mixed with hair; take it away!

Thus, hair is repulsive by way of its color. Even those who eat at night feel the same disgust upon touching the shape of hair, even if it is merely a grain husk or a flax seed. Thus, hair is repulsive by way of its shape.
The smell of hair that is devoid of preparations such as oil-anointing, flowers, and incense is extremely loathsome;
it is even more loathsome when it has been cast into a fire. For although hair might not be repulsive in terms of its color or shape, it is certainly repulsive by its smell.
Just as the excrement of a young child is yellow like turmeric in color, yet [repulsive nonetheless].

In terms of shape as well, it has the shape of a lump of turmeric. Furthermore, the carcass of a black dog that has been discarded in a place of refuse is, in color, the color of a ripe palm fruit; in shape, it has the shape of a discarded round mudiṅga gourd;
and its fangs are like jasmine buds. Thus, both might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, but they are indeed repulsive by their odor.
In this way, even though hair might be non-repulsive in terms of its color and shape, it is indeed repulsive by way of its odor.
Just as vegetables grown in a place of filth through the runoff from a village are loathsome and unfit for consumption to city-dwellers,
so too are hairs repulsive because they are produced from the runoff of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so forth.
"Exceedingly disgusting"—this refers to their repulsiveness "by way of their location. These things called hairs grow upon a heap of thirty-one parts, like a sprout arising from a mound of excrement.

Because they grow in an impure place—like vegetables grown in a cemetery or a rubbish heap, or like lotuses and water lilies growing in a ditch—they are supremely disgusting; this is their [repulsiveness].
‘By way of location’ refers to repulsiveness.

And just as with head-hairs, so too for all the parts, the fivefold repulsiveness should be defined by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location. Furthermore, all [the parts] are distinct by way of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.
They should be defined individually.
Therein, first, as to natural color, the body hairs are not entirely black like the head hairs, but are blackish-brown;
as to shape, they have the shape of the base of a palmyra tree with its top bent downward; as to direction, they are produced in two directions; as to location, setting aside the head hairs...
The soles of the feet and palms of the hands are mostly covered by the skin that envelops the rest of the body;

as for their boundaries, they are delimited below by their own root-base which has entered a hair’s breadth into the enveloping skin of the body, above by space, and across by each other. There are no two hairs together.
This is their delimitation by way of similarity. Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Nails" is the name for the twenty nail-pads. All of them are white in color; in shape, they are the shape of fish scales;
in terms of direction, the toe-nails are born in the lower direction and the finger-nails are born in the upper direction, thus they are born in two directions.
By way of location, they are established on the upper surfaces of the tips of the fingers.

By way of delimitation, they are bounded on two sides by the flesh at the ends of the fingers, internally by the flesh of the back of the fingers, externally and at the tip by space, and crosswise by one another.
There are no two nails together. This is their delimitation by similarity. Their delimitation by dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
Regarding "the teeth": for one with complete teeth, there are thirty-two tooth-bones. As to their color, they are white; as to their shape, they are of various shapes.
For first, in the middle of the lower row of teeth, four teeth have the shape of gourd seeds placed in a sequence upon a lump of clay.
On both sides of these, there is one [tooth] each, which has a single root and a single point.
It has the shape of a jasmine bud. From there, each [bone] has two roots and two ends, shaped like a cart-supporting prop.
Then, two by two, they have three roots and three ends. Then, two by two, they have four roots and four ends. The same method applies to the upper row as well.
As for direction, they are born in the upper direction. As for location, they are established upon the two jaw-bones. As for delimitation:
They are delimited below by their own root-bases resting upon the jawbone, above by space, and across by one another.

There are no two teeth together. This is their delimitation by way of common characteristics (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of uncommon characteristics (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is exactly the same as that of the head-hairs.
The skin is that which stands enveloping and covering the entire body. Above that is the "cuticle," which is black, brown, yellow, and other colors;
even when squeezed from the whole body, it is only the size of a jujube seed. As for the skin itself, it is white in color.
And this whiteness of its remains even when the cuticle has been destroyed by the impact of a flame, a blow from a weapon, or similar causes.
It is evident. As for its shape, it has the very shape of the body.
This is the summary here. In detail, however: the skin of the toes is the shape of a weaver’s shuttle; the skin of the back of the foot is the shape of a bag-bound sandal;
the skin of the calf is the shape of a palm leaf used as a food packet; the skin of the thigh is the shape of a long pouch filled with rice.
