The skin of the buttocks has the shape of a water-strainer made of cloth filled with water. The skin of the back has the shape of leather stretched over a wooden board.
The skin of the belly has the shape of leather stretched over the sound-box of a lute. The skin of the chest is for the most part square in shape.
The skin of both arms has the shape of leather stretched over a quiver. The skin of the back of the hands has the shape of a sheath for a razor.
Or it is shaped like a bundle of fans. The skin of the fingers of the hand is shaped like a key-case. The skin of the neck is shaped like a collar.
The skin of the mouth is perforated and shaped like the nest of an insect. The skin of the head is shaped like a bundle of leaves.
And by the meditator who is discerning the skin, he should direct his knowledge upward toward the face, starting from the upper lip.
First of all, one should define the skin covering the face. Then the skin of the frontal bone.
Then, as if inserting a hand between a bag and the bowl placed inside it, one should direct knowledge between the skull and the scalp, [observing] how the skin is joined as one with the bone.
While separating [the skin], one should define the skin of the head. Then the skin of the shoulders.
Then the skin of the right hand, both in the forward and reverse directions. Then, by that same method, the skin of the left hand. Then the skin of the back.
Having defined each of those, [one defines] the skin of the right foot, both in the forward and reverse directions. Then, by that same...
By this method, one should define the skin of the left foot. Then, in successive order, the skin of the bladder, the belly, the heart, and the neck should be defined.
Next, after defining the skin of the neck, one should define the skin of the lower jaw and bring it to a conclusion by reaching the edge of the lower lip.
Thus, for one who grasps the grosser parts, even the subtle becomes manifest.
By direction, it arises in two directions. By location, it stands enveloping the entire body.

By delimitation, it is delimited below by its supporting surface and above by space; this is its delimitation by way of similarity. Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is exactly the same as that of the head-hairs.
There are nine hundred pieces of flesh. All of these, by way of color, are red, like the *kiṃsuka* flower. By way of shape:
the flesh of the calves is shaped like rice placed in a palm-leaf basket; the flesh of the thighs is shaped like a young *nisada* fish;
the flesh of the buttocks is shaped like the edge of a hearth; the flesh of the back is shaped like a layer of palm-sugar; and the flesh of the two sides...
The flesh in the belly of the potthali-like [stomach] has the shape of a coating of fine clay; the flesh of the breasts has the shape of lumps of clay thrown down after being rolled into balls;
the flesh of the two arms has the shape of two large, skinless rats placed side by side.
Thus, as one discerns the grosser flesh, the subtler flesh also becomes manifest. As for direction, it is produced in two directions. As for location, [it is located...]

It stands smeared with more than three hundred bones. By way of delimitation, it is bounded below by the surface resting upon the skeletal mass, above by the skin, and across by each other [bone]; this is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
‘Sinews’ refers to nine hundred sinews. By way of color, all the sinews are white; by way of shape, they are of various shapes.
For among them, starting from the upper part of the neck, five great sinews bind the body and descend along the front side of the heart;
five along the back side, five along the right side, and five along the left side.
While binding the right hand, there are five [fingers] on the front side of the hand and five on the back side;

likewise while binding the left hand. While binding the right foot, there are five [toes] on the front side of the foot and five on the back side; likewise while binding the left foot. Thus, these are the body-supporting [muscles].
There are sixty major sinews that penetrate and bind the body; these are also called *kaṇḍaras*.
All of them are shaped like the buds of a *kandala* lily.
Others, however, which cover various parts of the body, are finer than those and are shaped like cords or ropes.
Others than those are even more subtle, shaped like rotting creepers. Others than those are even more subtle, shaped like the strings of a great lute (*vīṇā*).
Others are shaped like thick threads. The sinews on the backs of the hands and feet are shaped like the feet of birds.
The sinews of the head are shaped like the hair-net of children. The sinews of the back are shaped like a wet net spread out in the sun. The remaining ones...
The sinews, following each respective limb and member, are shaped like a net-sack fastened upon the body. As to direction, they are found in two directions.
As to location, they remain binding the bones throughout the entire body. As to delimitation: below, by their surfaces resting upon the three hundred bones;
above, by the portions where they touch the flesh and skin; and across, [by the spaces between them].

They are delimited by one another; this is their delimitation by way of homogeneity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of heterogeneity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.

Regarding "bones": setting aside the thirty-two teeth-bones, there are the remaining sixty-four hand-bones, sixty-four foot-bones, sixty-four soft bones supported by flesh, and two heel-bones—[these being] in each foot.
Two ankle bones, two shin bones, two knee bones, two thigh bones, two hip bones,
eighteen vertebrae, twenty-four ribs, fourteen breast bones, one heart bone, two collarbones,
two shoulder blades, two upper-arm bones, and two each for the forearm bones.
There are seven neck vertebrae, two jawbones, one nose bone, two eye bones, two ear bones, one forehead bone, one skull bone, and nine cranial plates; thus there are exactly three hundred bones.
All of these are white in color and various in shape. Among them, the bones of the toes of the feet...
The bones of the middle joints are shaped like *kataka* seeds. The bones of the middle sections immediately following those are shaped like jackfruit stones.
The bones of the lower sections are shaped like small drums (*paṇava*). The bones of the back of the foot are shaped like crushed kanda-lotus roots.
The heel bone is shaped like the single stone of a palmyra fruit. The ankle bones are shaped like the balls used in the game of *bandhakī-ḷā*. As for the shin bones...
The place where it is fixed upon the ankle bones is shaped like a sindika reed with its bark unremoved. The small shin bone is shaped like the handle of a bow;
the large one is shaped like the back of a withered snake. The knee bone is shaped like a piece of foam that has decayed on one side.
Therein, the place where the shin bone is fixed is shaped like the tip of a cow’s horn that has become excessively worn down. The thigh bone is shaped like the handle of a poorly whetted axe or adze.
The place where the hip-bone is fixed is shaped like a play-ball. Therefore, the place where the two hip-bones are fixed is shaped like a large *puṇṇāga* fruit with its tip cut off.
Both hip-bones, being joined together as one, are shaped like a potter’s kiln;
individually, they are shaped like a blacksmith’s bellows-fastening. The sacrum bone situated at the corner is positioned facing downwards.
It has the shape of a grasped cobra’s hood, with openings and perforations in seven places.
The vertebrae of the backbone are shaped like copper-plate headbands placed one upon another on the inside, and like round beads on the outside.
Between them, there are two or three thorns resembling the teeth of a saw. Regarding the twenty-four ribs:
The incomplete [bones] have an incomplete white shape; the complete [bones] have a complete white shape.
All of them also have the shape of a white cock with its wings spread out.
The fourteen breast-bones have the shape of the frame of an old chariot. The heart-bone has the shape of the pommel of a spear.
The collarbones are shaped like small iron handles for axes. The shoulder-blade bones are shaped like a worn-out Sinhalese hoe on one side.
The upper-arm bones are shaped like the handles of mirrors. The lower-arm bones are shaped like twin palm-bulbs.
The wrist bones are shaped like leaden headbands placed together and set down. The back-of-the-hand bones are shaped like a heap of crushed kandaḷa roots.
In the hands and fingers, the bones of the root joints are shaped like small drums (*paṇava*); the bones of the middle joints are shaped like incomplete jackfruit seeds;
the bones of the tip joints are shaped like *kataka* seeds. The seven neck bones, when pierced with a rod and placed in succession, are shaped like the rings of a bamboo pole.
The lower jawbone is shaped like the iron hammer-strap of smiths.
The upper [bone] has the shape of a scraping knife.

The bones of the eye-sockets and nose-sockets have the shape of young palm stalks from which the pith has been removed. The frontal bone has the shape of the bowl of a conch-shell vessel turned upside down.
The bones of the ear-lobes have the shape of a barber’s razor-case. Above the frontal bone and the ear-lobes, in the place where a headband would be tied...
The bone [of the jaw] has the shape of a broken fragment of a bowl filled with constricted vessels. The skull-bone has the shape of a curved coconut with its top cut off.
The bones of the head have the shape of a worn-out gourd-pot placed together by stitching.
As to direction, they are located in two directions. As to location, they generally reside throughout the entire body; specifically, however, here—
The bones of the head rest upon the bones of the neck; the bones of the neck upon the vertebrae of the spine; the vertebrae of the spine upon the bones of the hips;
the bones of the hips upon the bones of the thighs; the bones of the thighs upon the bones of the knees;
the bones of the knees upon the bones of the shanks; the bones of the shanks upon the bones of the ankles; and the bones of the ankles rest upon the bones of the heels. As for their delimitation:
They are delimited internally by the bone marrow, above by the flesh, and at the tip and the base by one another.
This is their delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Their delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Bone marrow" refers to the marrow located inside those various bones. By way of color, it is white. By way of shape, it is...
As for the large bones, it has the shape of the moistened tip of a large bamboo shoot inserted inside a bamboo tube;
as for the small and minute bones, it has the shape of the moistened tips of thin bamboo shoots inserted among the joints of bamboo stalks inside [the bones].
As for its direction, it is found in two directions. As for its location, it is situated within the bones. As for its delimitation:
It is demarcated by the inner surfaces of the bones. This is its delimitation by way of similarity. Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
The kidneys are two lumps of flesh bound together by a single ligament. As to color, they are pale red, the color of *pālibhaddaka* wood.
As to shape, they are shaped like children’s twin play-balls, or like a pair of mango fruits attached to a single stalk.
Or: by direction, it is born in the upper direction. By location, having emerged from the throat-passage, it proceeds a short distance as a single root and then divides into two;
being bound together by thick sinews, it stands surrounding the heart-flesh.
By delimitation, the kidney is delimited by its own kidney-parts. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind.
The section on dissimilar parts, however, is the same as that for the head-hairs.
"Heart" refers to the heart-flesh. As to color, it is red, the color of the back of a lotus leaf.
As to shape, it has the shape of a lotus bud placed upside down with its outer petals removed. It is smooth on the outside; on the inside, it is like the interior of a *kosātakī* fruit.
It is like the interior [of a lotus]. For those with wisdom it is slightly opened, while for those of dull wisdom it remains merely as a bud.
Inside it there is a hollow about the size of a *punnāga* seed, wherein a half-*pasata* measure of blood collects;
depending upon this, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) function. Furthermore, that [blood] is red in one of a lustful temperament.
For one of a hateful temperament, it is black; for one of a deluded temperament, it resembles water in which meat has been washed;
for one of a discursive temperament, it has the color of pea-soup; for one of a faithful temperament, it has the color of a *kaṇikāra* flower;
and for one of a wise temperament, it appears clear, serene, undisturbed, bright, and utterly pure, radiant like a polished gem of fine quality. As for its direction, it is upward.
Regarding its direction, it is born in the upper region. Regarding its location, it is situated within the body between the two breasts.

Regarding its delimitation, the heart is delimited by its own heart-portion; this is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Liver" (*yakana*) refers to a twin-layered mass of flesh. By way of color, it consists of a reddish-yellow element, like a slightly red water-lily.
It has the color of the back of a leaf. In terms of shape, it is like a *koviḷāra* leaf: single at the base and double at the tip.
For those who are dull-witted, there is only one large one; for those possessed of wisdom, there are two or three small ones.
In terms of direction, it is born in the upper direction. In terms of location, it stands within the space between the two breasts, resting against the right side.

As for its delimitation: the liver is delimited by the portion that is the liver. This is its delimitation by way of its own kind (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of what is not of its own kind (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
The "membrane" (*kilomaka*) is the flesh that envelops [the internal organs], which is twofold according to the distinction between the covered and the uncovered.
Both kinds are white in color, the color of *dukūla* cloth or a rag. As for its shape, it has the shape of its own location. As for its direction, the covered membrane...
That which is born in the upper direction [is one type]. The other is born in the two directions.

By way of location, the concealed *kilomaka* (pericardium) stands covering the heart and the kidneys. The unconcealed *kilomaka* stands enveloping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body.
By way of delimitation, it is bounded below by the flesh, above by the skin, and across...

It is delimited by a portion of a kilo. This is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"The liver" (*pihaka*) refers to the flesh of the stomach and the tongue. By way of color, it is blue, the color of the *nigguṇḍika* flower.
By way of shape, it measures seven finger-breadths, is unattached, and has the shape of the tongue of a black calf. By way of direction, it is in the upper direction.
As for its birth: spatially, it is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the upper part of the abdominal membrane;

it is by a blow to this spot that beings meet their end when struck. As for its delimitation: it is delimited by its own surface area. This is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of what is other than itself (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Lungs" refers to the lung-flesh, which is divided into thirty-two pieces of flesh. By way of color, it is red, like the color of a slightly ripe udumbara fruit.
By way of shape, it has the shape of thick, unevenly cut pieces of cake.
Because it is struck by the heat of the kamma-born fire when there is an absence of food and drink within, it is tasteless and sapless, like a lump of chewed straw.
By direction, it is born in the upper direction. By location, it is situated within the body between the two breasts, hanging down so as to cover the heart and the liver.
By delimitation, it is delimited by its own proximate parts. This is its delimitation by way of similar parts;
however, its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In a man, the intestinal coil (*antavaṭṭi*) is thirty-two hands long; in a woman, it is twenty-eight hands long. It is coiled in twenty-one places.
As for its color, it is white, the color of lime-plastered pebbles. As for its shape, it has the shape of a snake with its head cut off and placed coiled inside a red bowl.
As for its direction, it is found in two directions. As for its location, it is above...
Because it is bound below at the throat-pit and at the path of the dung, it resides within the body bounded by the throat-pit and the path of the dung.

In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own internal parts. This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Entrails" (*antaguṇa*) refers to the binding in the places where the coils of the intestines reside. As for its color, it is white, the color of the root of the *dakasītalika* plant.
By way of shape, it has the shape of the root of a water-cooling plant (*dakasītalika*). By way of direction, it is produced in two directions.
By way of location, for those performing work with a hoe, an axe, and so forth, when pulling a machine, it is like the cord of a machine;

it is like a cord that remains sewn between the foot-wiping rope-circle and the machine-boards, binding them together so that they do not slip apart at their inner edges—thus [it is located] among the twenty-one [parts].
Regarding its location, it is situated within the internal cavities. Regarding its delimitation, it is delimited by its portion as part of the entrails; this is its delimitation by way of similarity.
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Udariya" (stomach contents) refers to what has arisen in the stomach from what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. As for its color, it has the color of the food that has been swallowed.
By way of shape, it has the shape of loose grains of rice in a strainer. By way of direction, it is located in the upper direction.
By way of location, it resides in the stomach. The stomach is a fold of the intestinal membrane resembling a bulge formed in the middle of a wet cloth when squeezed at both ends;
it is smooth on the outside, and on the inside it resembles a dirty curtain-purse enveloping a raw muscle.
It is even appropriate to say that it resembles the interior of a boiled *panasa* fruit;

for therein dwell, in a state of utter confusion and crowded together in dense throngs, thirty-two species of worms such as the *takkoṭaka*, *gaṇḍuppādaka*, *tālahīraka*, *sūcimukhaka*, and *paṭatantasuttaka*.
When food, drink, and other necessities are unavailable, they leap up...
Roaring, they strike at the flesh of the heart;
and at the time of swallowing food, drink, and so forth, turning their faces upward, they greedily snatch away two or three morsels of what was first swallowed.
This place serves as a birth-chamber, a latrine, a sickroom, and a charnel ground for those worms.
Just as, for example, at the gate of a village of outcasts, during the heat of the summer season, when the rain falls in thick drops,
various kinds of filth— urine, feces, skin, bones, pieces of flesh, phlegm, snot, blood, and so forth— are carried along by the water and fall into a cesspool;
there they lie, churned by muddy water, and after two or three days have passed, swarms of worms have arisen within them, and they are heated and steamed by the force of the sun’s heat.
Just as a mass of froth and bubbles, emitting an intense blue color and being supremely foul-smelling and loathsome,
stands having reached a state where it is not even fit to be approached or looked at, let alone smelled or tasted; even so,
food and drink of various kinds, once crushed by the pestle-like teeth and smeared with saliva and drool turned over by the hand of the tongue—
At that very moment, its excellence of color, fragrance, taste, and so forth vanishes; it falls [into the womb] like the vomit from a weaver’s donkey,
becomes enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind, is heated by the force of the digestive fire in the stomach,
swarms with hosts of worms, and emitting layers of froth and bubbles, it remains in a state of extreme impurity, foul stench, and loathsomeness.
Having heard this, even the repulsiveness of food, drink, and so forth becomes established; how much more so when one has observed them with the eye of wisdom!
And wherever that food, drink, and so forth falls, it undergoes a fivefold division:

one portion is consumed by the microbes, one portion is burned by the digestive fire, one portion becomes urine, one portion becomes feces, and one portion becomes the state of nutritional essence (*rasa*).
Having entered [the stomach], it nourishes the blood, flesh, and so forth. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the membrane of the abdomen and by the portion of the abdominal contents;
this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of head-hairs.
"Feces" (*karīsa*) means excrement. By way of color, it is for the most part the very color of the food that has been swallowed. By way of shape...
Its shape is that of a space. By way of direction, it is produced in the lower direction. By way of location, it resides in the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*).
The receptacle for digested food is situated below, between the navel and the base of the spinal column at the end of the intestines;
it is eight finger-breadths in height and resembles a bamboo tube, just as rainwater falling on successive levels of ground collects therein.
Having flowed down and filled the lower part of the ground, it remains there; even so, whatever food, drink,
and so forth has fallen into the stomach is cooked by the digestive fire until it becomes like froth, and as each portion is cooked, it passes through the interior of the intestines,
flowing down repeatedly and being churned until it attains a smooth consistency, becoming accumulated like yellow clay being poured into a bamboo tube.
It remains after being offered as an oblation. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the membrane of the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*) and by its own portion of excrement;
this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Brain" (*matthaluṅga*) refers to the mass of marrow situated within the skull. By way of color, it is white, having the color of a cluster of *ahicchattaka* mushrooms.
It is also appropriate to say that it has the appearance of spoiled milk that has not yet reached the state of curd. In terms of shape, it is the shape of its location.
In terms of direction, it is born in the upper direction.

In terms of location, it remains heaped together, like four lumps of dough placed in dependence upon the four suture-lines within the skull. In terms of delimitation, [it is delimited] by the skull...
It is delimited by the inner lining and by the portion of the brain. This is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Bile" (*pitta*) refers to two types of bile: bound bile (*baddha-pitta*) and unbound bile (*abaddha-pitta*). Among these, bound bile, in terms of color, is...

The *baddhapitta* (bound bile) is thick and the color of *madhuka* oil; the *abaddhapitta* (unbound bile) is the color of withered and shriveled flowers. Regarding their shape, both are shaped according to the space they occupy.
Regarding direction, the *baddhapitta* is produced in the upper direction, while the other is produced in two directions.
Regarding location, setting aside the *abaddhapitta*, [the *baddhapitta* is found] in the places where hair, body hair, teeth, and nails are detached from the flesh.
The "stiff" bile (thaddha-pitta) remains pervading the rest of the body like a drop of oil on dry, stiff skin;

when it is disturbed, the eyes become yellow and roll, and the limbs tremble and itch. The "bound" bile (baddha-pitta) resides within a gall-bladder (pittakosa) resembling the pod of a large kosātaki gourd, situated between the heart and the lungs and supported by the liver. When this [bile]...

When it is provoked, beings become insane; with their minds deranged, they cast aside shame and fear of wrongdoing, and do what should not be done, say what should not be said, and think what should not be thought.
As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of bile. This is its delimitation by way of similarity.
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of head-hair.
Phlegm (*semha*) is the phlegm within the interior of the body, measuring the size of a single bowlful. By way of color, it is white, like the color of the juice of the *nāgavalli* leaf.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By way of location, it resides on the surface of the stomach;
at the time of swallowing food, drink, and so forth, it is just as if duckweed or moss were upon water, or as if [it were stuck] to a piece of wood.
Just as when [food] falls into a skull, it breaks into two pieces and remains spread out over it, even so when food, drink, and so forth fall into the belly,
they break into two pieces and remain spread out over it; and when that [digestive fire] has become dull,
the belly becomes supremely loathsome, smelling of a corpse, like a festering boil or a rotten hen’s egg.
Then, because of that intense odor, even his breath and mouth become foul-smelling, like a putrid corpse;
and that man comes to be called upon as "Go away, you stinking woman!
Furthermore, having increased and reached a state of thickness, it is like a lid-plate for a privy, completely containing the stench of a corpse within the lining of the belly itself.

It remains. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of phlegm; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Pubbā" (pus) refers to that which occurs by way of putrid blood. As to color, it is the color of a withered leaf; however, on a dead body, it has the color of thick, putrid gruel.
As to shape, it has the shape of its location. As to direction, it is born in two directions.
As to its location, there is no fixed place where pus might remain accumulated;

rather, wherever a part of the body is struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames, and the like, and the blood coagulates and suppurates, or wherever boils, pustules, and so forth arise, it remains right there. As to its delimitation, it is bounded by what precedes it.

It is delimited. This is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Blood": there are two kinds of blood—the stored blood and the circulating blood. Therein, the stored blood, in terms of color, is the color of thick, boiled lac-juice;
the circulating blood is the color of clear lac-juice. In terms of shape:
Both have the shape of their respective locations. By way of direction, the accumulated blood is found in the upper direction, while the other is found in both directions.

By way of location, the circulating blood—excluding the places where hair, body hair, teeth, and nails are detached from the flesh, as well as the stiff, dry skin—remains pervading the entire acquired body following the network of veins.
The stored blood fills the lower portion of the site of the liver;
measuring about one bowlful, it remains trickling drop by drop over the heart, kidneys, and lungs, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs.
For when that [blood] does not reach the kidneys, heart, and so forth, beings become thirsty. As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of blood.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity. Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
Sweat (*seda*) is the water element oozing from the pores of the body hairs and so forth. By way of color, it is the color of clear sesame oil.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it arises in two directions. By way of location, there is no fixed location specifically called "the location of sweat."
Where it would always remain like blood;

however, when the body is heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, changes of season, and so forth, then it trickles out from all the pores of the head-hairs and body-hairs like a cluster of lotus stalks that have been pulled up from water and cut unevenly.
Therefore, its shape is that of the very pores of the head-hairs and body-hairs.

It should be understood by way of its characteristic and so forth. Furthermore, the meditator who is discerning perspiration should attend to it as existing filling the openings of the pores of the head hairs and body hairs.
In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion that is perspiration; this is its delimitation by the similar.
Its delimitation by the dissimilar, however, is the same as that of the head hairs.
Meda means fat. As to its color, it is the color of split turmeric.
As to its shape, in one with a stout body, it has the shape of a turmeric-colored linen rag placed between the skin and the flesh;
in one with a lean body, it is doubled over, depending upon the flesh of the calves, the flesh of the thighs, the flesh along the spine, and the flesh of the belly-wall.
Having been multiplied threefold, it has the appearance of a piece of fine cloth or rags dyed with turmeric.

As for its location, it is found in two locations. As for its spatial extent, in the case of a stout person, it covers the entire body; in the case of a thin person, it rests upon the flesh of the calves and other such areas.
Although it is reckoned as "moisture" (*sineha*), because of its extreme loathsomeness, it is used neither for oil on the head nor for nasal oil and the like.
They take it for the sake of [the body]. By way of delimitation, it is delimited below by the flesh, above by the skin, and across by the portion of fat;
this is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of head-hair.
"Tears" refers to the water-element (*āpo-dhātu*) that trickles from the eyes. By way of color, it has the color of clear sesame oil. By way of shape—
Its location is the shape of a space. As for its direction, it is born in the upper direction. As for its location, it resides in the eye-sockets.
However, this does not remain constantly accumulated in the eye-sockets like bile in the gall-bladder;
rather, when beings are filled with joy and laugh with loud laughter, or when they are filled with grief and weep and lament, such a [humor] arises from unsuitable food.

They bring [tears], and when their eyes are struck by smoke, dust, sand, and so forth, then—having arisen from these dissimilar nutriments of joy, grief, and temperature—they remain filling the eye-sockets or flow out.
However, the yogi who is grasping tears should grasp them precisely by way of their remaining to fill the eye-sockets. As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion that is the tear.

It is delimited. This is its delimitation by way of similar things (*sabhāga-pariccheda*). Its delimitation by way of dissimilar things (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of head-hair.
"Fat" (*vasā*) refers to liquefied grease. As to color, it is the color of coconut oil; it may also be said to be the color of oil poured over rice-scum (*ācāma*).
As to shape, at the time of bathing, it has the shape of a spreading drop of grease revolving on the surface of clear water.

By direction, they are born in two directions. By location, they mostly reside on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the tops of the shoulders.
And it is not the case that these always remain dissolved in those locations;

rather, when those parts become heated by the heat of a fire, the heat of the sun, an imbalance of the seasons, or an imbalance of the bodily elements, then—just as a drop of oil spreads upon clear water at the time of bathing—they [spread] there.
It circulates here and there like [a liquid]. In terms of its delimitation, it is delimited by a portion of fat; this is its delimitation by way of similar parts (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Spittle" (*kheḷa*) is the water element mixed with froth inside the mouth. In terms of color, it is white, the color of froth. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location.
It is also appropriate to say that it has the shape of foam. As for its direction, it is produced in the upper direction.
As for its location, it descends from both sides of the cheeks and rests upon the tongue. It does not remain there constantly accumulated;
however, when beings see or remember such food as is hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour, [it arises].

Or whenever they place something in the mouth, or when their heart becomes weary, or when a sense of disgust arises toward anything, then saliva arises and flows down both cheeks to settle upon the tongue.
This is thin at the tip of the tongue and thick at the root of the tongue; and as for unhusked grain or rice placed in the mouth—
Or any other kind of solid food, like water in a pit dug in the sand of a riverbed, it is capable of moistening without itself being exhausted.
As for its delimitation, it is delimited by the portion that is saliva; this is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
"Snot" (*siṅghāṇikā*) is the impurity that trickles from the brain. By way of color, it is the color of the pith of a young palmyra palm.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it arises in the upper direction.
By way of location, it remains filling the nostrils. And this does not remain here always accumulated; rather, it is just as when a man [uses] a lotus leaf...
If one were to tie up curd and pierce it from below with a thorn, and then the whey of the curd were to drip out and fall away through that hole;
even so, when beings weep or when their bodily elements become disturbed due to incompatible food or temperature,
then the brain matter— which has reached a state of putrid phlegm— oozes from within the head through the opening of the palate and the mouth.
Having descended, it fills the nostrils and remains there or flows out. However, by a yogi who is discerning snot, it should be discerned only by way of its filling the nostrils.
In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion that is snot; this is its delimitation by way of its own nature (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
Its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar (*visabhāga-pariccheda*), however, is the same as that of head-hair.
Lasikā is the slimy secretion within the joints of the body. By way of color, it is the color of *kaṇikāra* resin.
By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it is found in two directions.
By way of location, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints, it resides within the one hundred and eighty joints. And for one in whom this is deficient, when they rise up...
As he sits, walks forward, walks backward, bends, or stretches, his bones creak;
he moves about as if making the sound of snapping fingers. When he has traveled even a distance of one or two leagues, the air element becomes disturbed and his limbs ache.
However, for one who possesses it in abundance, [this occurs] during standing, sitting, and so forth.
The bones do not creak; even after traveling a long distance, the air element does not become disturbed, nor do the limbs ache.

In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its portion of synovial fluid. This is its delimitation by way of similarity. Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of head hair.
As for urine: in terms of color, it has the color of bean-brine water. In terms of shape, it has the shape of water contained within a water-jar placed with its opening facing downwards.
By direction, it is born in the lower direction. By location, it is situated within the bladder.

"Bladder" (vatthi) refers to the bladder-sack, just as when a mouthless earthenware pot is placed in a cesspool, the liquid from the cesspool enters it, yet no path of entry is apparent; even so, urine [enters] from the body.
It enters, yet its path of entry is not apparent, while its path of exit is clearly visible;

furthermore, when it is released and the bladder is full, beings experience the urge, thinking, "Let us void urine. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the interior of the bladder and by the portion of urine itself.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity. Its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, however, is the same as that of the head-hairs.
Thus, having defined the parts beginning with head-hair according to their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation,
one who attends to them as "repulsive, repulsive" in five ways— by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location— following the method of "not too fast,
not too slow," and so forth, transcends conceptual designation, just as one with sight [transcends darkness].
Just as when a man gazes at a garland made of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung on a single thread, all the flowers become clearly manifest as if they were neither before nor after one another;

even so, for one who gazes upon this body thinking, "In this body there are head-hairs," all those phenomena (dhammas) become clearly manifest as if they were neither before nor after one another. Therefore, it was said in the Discourse on Skillfulness in Attention:
“For the beginner, indeed, as he brings his attention to bear on ‘hair,’ that attention proceeds until it comes to rest,
having reached this very final section, ‘urine. But if he also applies his attention externally, then when all these sections have become clear to him,
humans, animals, and so forth, as they wander about, abandon their appearance as sentient beings and appear merely as a collection of bodily sections.”
And as one swallows those drinks, foods, and so forth, they appear like being cast into a heap of bodily parts.
Then, for one who repeatedly brings them to mind as "repulsive, repulsive" through the process of gradual release and so on, absorption (*appanā*) eventually arises.
In that context, the appearance of the head-hairs and other parts by way of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation is the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*).
The counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) is the appearance [of the object] by way of its repulsiveness in all its aspects.
For one who repeatedly adverts to it, attends to it, and strikes it with thought and applied thought, the four aggregates have repulsive objects;

absorption (*appanā*) occurs by way of the first jhāna. In the preliminary stage, the preparatory and access consciousnesses are accompanied by both applied and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicārā*).

They are accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*) and associated with joy (*somanassasahagata*), having a repulsive sign as their object; the absorption (*appanā*) itself is also with initial and sustained application (*savitakka-savicāra*), accompanied by rapture, and associated with joy.
However, in terms of the plane of existence, they belong to the sublime realm (*mahaggata*) of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
Furthermore, even regarding this repulsive object, joy arises through the perception of its advantages, solely by the power of the object’s unification (*ekattārammaṇa*).
Or rather, that [hindrance] arises. However, the second jhāna and the others do not arise here. Why? Because of its coarseness.
For this object is coarse; here, one-pointedness of mind is produced by the power of applied thought (*vitakka*) itself, not by the transcendence of applied thought.
This, first of all, is the discourse on the meditation subject by way of serenity (*samatha*).
In general, however, it should be understood by way of what is common to all: one who wishes to develop this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should first learn the meditation subject,
and at the time of recitation, strike out each individual part with the voice again and again— namely, the sign of color, the sign of shape, the sign of direction,
the sign of location, and the sign of delimitation— and perform a threefold recitation for each part, thinking, "This is similar to that."

It should be practiced. How so? First, regarding the "fivefold skin" (tacapañcaka), one should practice recitation for half a month—five days in direct order, five days in reverse order, and five days in both direct and reverse order, according to the method already explained below.
Then, having gone into the presence of the teacher and mastered the "fivefold membrane" (vakkapañcaka), one should likewise practice recitation for half a month. After that...
Having combined those ten sections together, [he meditates] for half a month. Again, having mastered each one among the five sections beginning with the lungs, [he meditates] for half a month.
Then, those fifteen sections [together] for half a month. The five sections beginning with the brain for half a month.
Then, twenty-three sections for half a month. The six sections beginning with the fat for half a month. Then, those twenty-six sections [together].
Having grouped them together, one half-month for the urine-group; then, having grouped all thirty-two parts together, another half-month—thus the recitation should be performed over six months.
In this regard, for a wise bhikkhu endowed with the necessary support (upanissaya), even as he is learning the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna):
Some parts appear clearly to some people, while they do not appear to others. Therefore, one should not abandon one's effort on the grounds that "they do not appear.
One should instead perform the recitation by taking up as many parts as do appear.
Furthermore, when explaining this meditation subject, one should explain it neither according to the case of the person of sharp wisdom nor according to the case of the person of dull wisdom.
This should be explained by way of one of medium intelligence. For it was by way of one of medium intelligence that the teachers established the tradition (tanti), having delimited it at six months.
However, for one whose sections are still not clear even after this much time, recitation must certainly be continued beyond that;
yet it should not be done without delimitation, but rather by delimiting it in periods of six months each.
When performing recitation (*sajjhāya*), one should not review the colors, nor should one attend to the characteristics;
the recitation should be performed solely by way of the constituent parts (*koṭṭhāsa*). Even the teacher should not instruct, "Perform the recitation by way of the colors.
What is the fault in giving such an instruction? It is the arising of the perception of failure even when there is success. For if the teacher—
When it is said, “Recite by way of color,” if the meditation subject does not appear to this bhikkhu while he is doing so by way of color,
but appears instead by way of repulsiveness or by way of elements,
then he perceives, “This meditation subject is not of a different characteristic,” and he accepts it, taking it exactly as it was told by the teacher. [By way of repulsiveness...]

Even when told, "Recite the meditation subject," if, while he is doing so, it does not appear as repulsive to him, but appears instead by way of its color or by way of its elements, then he perceives, "This meditation subject is not of the right character," and he accepts it only after rationalizing what was said by the teacher. [The teacher should say: "Recite that meditation subject by way of the elements."

Even when this has been said, if for him who practices accordingly the meditation subject does not appear according to its elements, but appears either by way of color or by way of repulsiveness, then he perceives:
"This meditation subject is not of a different characteristic," and he accepts it, taking it as exactly what was told by the teacher.
This is the fault in what was told by the teacher after having fixed [the object].
But how should he be instructed? He should be told: "Recite by way of the constituent parts.

How so? He should be told: "Recite thus: 'The head-hair constituent, the body-hair constituent. However, if while he is reciting in this way by way of the constituent parts, [the object] appears to him according to its color, then he must inform his preceptor-instructor: "I..."
“I am reciting the thirty-two aspects by way of the bodily parts, but they appear to me according to their color.
The teacher must not deceive him by saying, “This is like a non-subject for meditation; it is of a different character.
[He should rather say: “Well done, good man! You must have previously performed the preliminary work on the color-kasiṇa. This very...”
"The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for you is this: recite it by way of its colors alone.
He should be told this, and he too should perform the recitation by way of the colors alone.
While doing so, he [contemplates] the four color-kasinas internally: blue, yellow, red, and white.
He attains it. How? For when he brings to mind the color in the hair, body-hair, bile, and the black parts of the eyes as "blue, blue," the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise;
having made jhāna the basis and established insight, he reaches Arahantship. But in the case of fat and the yellow parts of the eyes...
For one who attends to the color in the flesh and blood, and in the red parts of the eyes, as "yellow, yellow," the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise;
having made jhāna the basis and established insight, one attains Arahantship.
However, for one who attends to the color in the flesh and blood, and in the red parts of the eyes, as "red, red," the fourfold and fivefold jhānas [arise].
The fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise; having made jhāna the basis and established insight, one attains Arahantship.
Furthermore, for one who attends to the color in the nails, teeth, skin, bones, and the white parts of the eyes as "white, white," the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise;
having made jhāna the basis and established insight, one attains Arahantship. This...
For a bhikkhu who is intent upon [the body] by way of its color, there is a conclusion leading up to Arahantship.
For another who recites it by way of its constituent parts, it appears as repulsive. Then he should inform his preceptor for instruction.
The preceptor should not say, "This is like a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that is not a meditation subject; it is of a different character."
He should be told: “It is well, good man! You must have previously applied yourself to the contemplation of the repulsive.
This very meditation subject is suitable for you. Recite it by way of the repulsive.
He too should recite it by way of the repulsive: “Hair is called ‘unlovely, foul-smelling, disgusting…’”
When one recites the text with the thought, "It is repulsive," the first jhāna arises in regard to that repulsive object.
Taking that jhāna as a basis and establishing insight, he attains Arahantship.
This is the conclusion for a bhikkhu intent upon the repulsive, leading all the way to Arahantship.
For another who recites by way of the body parts, it appears by way of the elements (*dhātu*). How does it appear when appearing by way of the elements?
First, the head-hairs appear like the tufts of grass growing on the top of an anthill.
The body-hairs appear like the *dabba* grass growing in the ruins of an old village. The nails appear like the husks of *madhuka* fruits placed upon sticks.
The teeth are like gourd seeds that have been inserted and fixed within a lump of clay. The skin is like the moist ox-hide stretched over the body of a lute.
The flesh is like the clay smeared upon a wall. The sinews are like creepers bound together with bundles of reeds.
The bones are like the bundles of reeds set up to support a wall. The bone-marrow is like the end of a bamboo shoot placed inside a large bamboo stalk and kept moist.
The kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, and lungs—these six parts appear like the interior of a butcher’s shop.
The thirty-two-cubit-length intestine lies coiled within the bowl of blood like a house-snake.
The mesentery is like a cord sewn to a foot-wiping cloth. The undigested food in the stomach is like [food] in a strainer.
It appears like loose-grained rice; like the grey clay placed inside a bamboo tube;

like four lumps of rice-flour paste set down after pressing down the brain; and it appears as if filled with water in twelve water-cups placed in succession, representing the twelve kinds of water element.
Then he should inform the instructor of advice. The instructor must not deceive him by saying, "This is not a meditation subject;
it is unlike one," or "This is of a different character. Instead, he should say: "Excellent, good man!
You must have previously applied yourself to the contemplation of the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*). This very meditation subject is suitable for you. Recite it according to the elements..."
He should be told, "Do it. He should also perform the recitation by way of the elements (*dhātu*).
Herein, this is the method of recitation by way of attention (*manasikāra*): here, a monk [reflects] that "the head-hairs grow on the skin covering the head;
they do not know, 'We grow on the skin covering the head'; the head..."
Even the skin covering [the body] does not know, "Hair has grown upon me"; one attends to it thus:
"These are insentient, indeterminate, empty, rigid, and solid—this is the earth element. "Body hairs have grown on the skin that covers the body.
They do not know, 'We have grown on the skin that covers the body. And the skin that covers the body..."
They do not know, "Hair has grown upon me," for these too are insentient. The nails have grown on the tips of the fingers;
they do not know, "We have grown on the tips of the fingers. Nor do the finger-tips know, "Nails have grown upon us";
these too are insentient. The teeth have grown on the jawbone; they do not know, "We have grown on the jawbone."
Even the jawbone does not know, “Teeth have grown upon me. These too are insentient. The skin does not know, “The body is enveloped by me.
The body also does not know, “I am enveloped by skin. This too is insentient.
The flesh does not know, “The body is smeared with me. The body also does not know, “I [am smeared] with flesh.”
"Anointed": this too is insentient. The sinew does not know, "I stand having bound together the heap of bones.
The heap of bones also does not know, "I am bound by a network of sinews. This too is insentient.
The skull-bone does not know, "I am established upon the neck-bones. The neck-bone also does not know, "Upon me..."
The skull-bone does not know, “I am supported by the neck-bone. The neck-bone does not know, “I am situated upon the vertebrae.
The vertebrae do not know, “I am supported by the hip-bone, the thigh-bone, the shin-bone, and the ankle-bone.
The heel-bone does not know, “I am standing having lifted up the ankle-bone,” and so on.
The neck bone does not know, "I am standing having lifted up the head bone.
The bones stand in succession reaching to the end;
measured by many joints, they are not joined by anything.
Bound by sinews and impelled by decay, it is insentient, like a wooden puppet.
"This too is insentient: the marrow of the bones... the kidneys... [and so on] ...the brain is insentient, indeterminate, and empty."
He attends to it thus: ‘The earth element is stiff and solid. He attends to it thus: ‘Bile, phlegm...
down to urine—insentient, indeterminate, empty, liquid, and mobile—is the water element.
For one who comprehends these two great elements, the fire element, which predominates in the abdomen, becomes evident; [and] that which predominates in the nose...
The air element becomes manifest. For one who discerns these four great elements, derived form (upādārūpa) becomes manifest.
Great element is delimited by derived form, and derived form is delimited by the great element.
Just as sunlight is delimited by shade, and shade by sunlight, even so the great element is delimited by derived form.

Derived form [is classified] by way of the great primary elements. Then, as he thus comprehends the aggregate of form—thinking, "The four great primary elements and the twenty-three derived forms are the aggregate of form"—the immaterial aggregates become clear to him by way of the bases and doors.
Thus, the comprehension of the material and immaterial consists of the five aggregates; the five aggregates are the twelve bases; the twelve bases...

Thinking, "There are eighteen elements," he defines name-and-form by dividing it into two portions—just as one splitting a twin-trunked palmyra tree—by way of the aggregates, bases, and elements. He [reflects]:
"This name-and-form has not arisen without cause or without condition; it has arisen with cause and with condition."

Investigating, "What is its cause? What is its condition? he determines its conditions as follows: "It is conditioned by ignorance, conditioned by craving, conditioned by kamma, and conditioned by nutriment.
Having established these conditions, he reflects: "In the past there were only conditions and phenomena arisen from conditions;
in the future there will be only conditions and phenomena arisen from conditions; and at present there are only conditions and phenomena arisen from conditions. Beyond that, there is no being."
"Or there is no person; it is merely a heap of pure formations"—thus one dispels doubt regarding the three periods of time.
This is what is called the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), which consists in the observation of formations through insight.
For a bhikkhu who stands having thus observed formations, the root has entered deep into the teaching of the One of Ten Powers.
He is said to have gained a footing; he is called a "minor stream-enterer" (cūḷasotāpanna) whose destination is fixed.

Then, having obtained such favorable conditions regarding the season, favorable conditions regarding the person, favorable conditions regarding food, and favorable conditions regarding the hearing of the Dhamma, seated upon a single seat in the excellent cross-legged posture, he applies the three characteristics and, through the sequence of insight, [contemplates] formations...
“Contemplating thus, he attains Arahantship”: this is the conclusion for a bhikkhu intent upon the elements, leading up to Arahantship.
However, if the subject does not appear to him either as beautiful, or as repulsive, or as empty, he should not abandon the meditation subject thinking, “It does not appear to me.
Rather, he should apply himself to the very attention directed toward the constituent parts.
It is said that the ancient elders stated: “Attention to the parts alone is sufficient.
Thus, for one who repeatedly performs the recitation by way of the parts, those parts become familiar. But when are they said to be familiar?
When, upon merely adverting to “hair,” the attention proceeds until it comes to rest on the final part, “brain matter”—then [the parts are familiar]. “Brain matter”...
As soon as he has brought it to mind, his attention comes and becomes established upon the first section, beginning with "hair.
Then, for him, it is just as when a man with good eyesight looks at a garland made of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung on a single thread,
or when he looks back at thirty-two hundred footprints that have been dug out in a row.
Just as thirty-two-colored flowers or a patterned cloth become clearly visible when arranged in sequence,
even so, thirty-two sections appear; beings, whether they be animals or humans, do not appear as they move about,
but rather as sections, like food and edibles being placed into the intervals between those sections.
From the time one becomes proficient with the constituent parts, one will be liberated through one of three doors.
The meditation subject appears either as beautiful, or as repulsive, or as empty.
It is just as when a woman wishing to bake cakes takes whatever she desires from the kneaded dough that has been set aside; or as when something placed on a level patch of ground...

Just as water flows out from whichever part one strikes a jar filled with water, even so, from the time the constituent parts become familiar, the meditation subject will indeed appear through one of the three doors: to one who wishes it, as beautiful;
to one who wishes it, as repulsive; and to one who wishes it, as empty.
This much is called the "learning junction" (uggahasandhi). Standing at this learning junction, the number of bhikkhus who have attained arahantship is beyond calculation.
However, for one to whom the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not become manifest at the learning junction, that person should master the meditation subject and—
If the monastery where the teacher resides is suitable, that is good; if not, one should dwell in a place that is suitable.
While dwelling there, one should live in a lodging endowed with five factors, having avoided the eighteen faults of a dwelling, and one should also be oneself endowed with those five factors.
Then, after the meal, having returned from the alms round—
Having entered either a night-quarters or a day-quarters, one should attend to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). How?
First of all, it should be attended to in successive order, exactly according to the method explained below, and not by skipping over sections.
For one who attends to it in successive order is like someone climbing a thirty-two-rung ladder step by step to reach the palace.

Just as a person who, having ascended [a palace], experiences its advantages does not fall from the palace while attending to the advantages, so too one who attends to the meditation subject in its proper sequence— starting with "hair of the head, hair of the body"—
does not fall away from the meditation subject and experiences the nine supramundane states that resemble the advantages of the palace.
Furthermore, when attending to it in successive order, one should attend neither too quickly nor too slowly.
For one who attends to it too quickly, although the meditation subject becomes familiar, it remains unmanifest;
the simile for this has already been stated above.
For one who attends to it too slowly, the meditation subject does not reach its conclusion, but must be dropped midway.
It is so. For example, suppose a man sets out on a three-league journey at evening, having girded his loins;

starting from the place of departure, he rests upon seeing cool shade, stretches out his back upon seeing a delightful sandy beach, drinks and bathes upon seeing a forest lotus pond, and climbs a mountain upon seeing it, [experiencing] the mountain's beauty.
As he looks, a lion, a tiger, a leopard, or a thief seizes and kills him right there in the midst of it; or else the thieves plunder and kill him.
In the same way, for one who attends to the meditation subject too slowly, it does not reach its conclusion, but must be abandoned midway.
Therefore, one should attend to it thirty times in a single day—neither too quickly nor too slowly.
One should perform the recitation ten times in the morning, ten times at midday, and ten times in the evening; it is not permissible not to do so.
For just as it is not permissible, having risen early in the morning, not to wash one's face, or not to eat solid or soft food, [so it is with this].
It is not permissible to eat [that], but this [other thing] would be permissible; however, this alone is absolutely not permissible to do.
One who does it stands having grasped a great benefit. For example, suppose a man has three fields:
one field yields eight jars, one sixteen, and one thirty-two; by means of those three fields...
If one is unable to look after all [three], having abandoned two, one should look after only the one that provides the thirty-two pots;
plowing, sowing, and giving gifts should be performed right there. That very one will provide the share for the other two upon their rising.
In the same way, even if one abandons other tasks such as washing the face, work should be performed right here.
It is not improper to do it. By the statement, "One who does so stands having grasped a great benefit," the Middle Way is thus described.
Even by one practicing in this way, distraction must be warded off; for if one abandons the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), the mind [wanders] externally.
If one falls into distraction, one falls away from the meditation subject and is unable to transcend the fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
For example, it is like a man who, having secured a loan of a thousand [coins] and received interest, sets out on a journey;
along the way, he encounters a single footpath laid over a deep mountain ravine where crocodiles, sea-monsters, sharks, and *rākṣasa* demons have arisen.
Just as one walking along the Daṇḍaka causeway might let go of his foothold and, looking here and there, fall down to become food for crocodiles and other creatures,
even so this person, having let go of the meditation subject, falls away from the meditation subject when his mind wanders outwardly,
and is unable to transcend the fear of the round of existence.

Herein, this is the correlation of the simile: the time when the man had completed the recovery of his thousand coins and obtained interest is like the time when this bhikkhu has mastered the meditation subject in the presence of his teacher.

The deep mountain cleft in between is like *saṃsāra*. His being bitten by crocodiles and other creatures is like the great sufferings rooted in the round of existence. The single-path bridge made of sticks is...
It is like the path of recitation for this bhikkhu; it is like the time when that man,
having ascended a narrow footbridge made of sticks and released his foothold, looked here and there and fell, becoming food for crocodiles and other creatures—
so it is for this bhikkhu who, having abandoned the meditation subject, has a mind distracted externally.
One should understand that having fallen away from the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), one is incapable of transcending the fear of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).

Therefore, the head hairs (kesā) should be brought to mind. Having brought the head hairs to mind and having warded off the outward distraction of the arising of consciousness, one should bring to mind with a purified mind:
“Head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin. While bringing it to mind in this way, [one remains] from the meditation subject...
He does not fall away; he transcends the fear of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). In this regard, the simile should be understood by reversing the previous one:

just as a clever man, having settled his debt of a thousand and obtained interest, ascends a causeway of planks, prepares his lower and upper garments, steadies his body with the elements, and reaches the further shore in safety—so it is for the clever bhikkhu.
Having brought the hair to mind and warded off outward distraction of the arising consciousness, for one who attends with a pure mind to “hair,
nails, teeth, skin,” it should be understood that there is a surmounting of the fear of the round [of existence] without falling away from the meditation subject.
Thus, even by warding off outward distraction, through the surmounting of the description in the manner already stated below—
One should attend to it thus: having set aside the designation "head-hairs, body-hairs," mindfulness should be established as "the repulsive, the repulsive.
However, at first it does not appear as repulsive. As long as it does not so appear, the designation must not be set aside.
When it does appear, then one should set aside the designation and attend to it simply as "the repulsive."
Furthermore, it should be brought to mind as repulsive in five ways according to the method explained below.
For within the "fivefold skin" (the skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and bone marrow), all five kinds of repulsiveness are found: by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location.
In the remaining parts as well, the attention should be applied according to whichever [type of repulsiveness] is applicable.
In this context, the five parts beginning with head-hairs are reckoned as the sign of beauty, a basis for lust, and a desirable object.
Whatever beings there may be who are subject to lust, they all lust after these five parts.
Yet this bhikkhu brings about absorption (appanā) regarding what is "repulsive" in that which is the very place where the multitude lusts. In this regard, because of the attainment of absorption—
From that point onward, without becoming weary, he reaches absorption (*appanā*).

Here is an illustration: just as a skilled archer, having pleased a king and received a choice village yielding a hundred thousand coins, sets out for it fully equipped with his five weapons, and on the way encounters thirty-two bandits—
Having seen them, he would execute the leader of those five thieves; from the time they were executed, those two would no longer be said to be traveling along the same path.

This should be understood as being exactly like that. For it is just as when the archer, having pleased the king, received an excellent village, so too is it for this bhikkhu who has learned the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of his teacher.
The time of their execution is the time of stability. The thirty-two parts are like thirty-two thieves. The five, beginning with head-hair, are like five chief thieves.
The time of executing the chief thieves is the time when this bhikkhu brings about absorption on the "repulsiveness" of the five skins—the objects of lust for all beings.
The time of the remaining thieves fleeing by the mere stroke of a hand is [the attainment of insight].
In the same way, it should be understood that absorption is attained without even becoming fatigued in the remaining sections.
Thus, by one who is transcending the designation (*paṇṇatti*), attention should be exercised through successive relinquishing:
while attending to the head-hairs, as soon as one has attended to them, mindfulness should be directed toward the body-hairs while still maintaining concern for the head-hairs.
As long as the body hairs do not appear clearly, one should direct attention to them, thinking, “head hairs, head hairs.
But when the body hairs appear, then one should set aside the head hairs and establish mindfulness on the body hairs. In this same way, attention should be applied to the nails and so forth.
Here is an illustration: just as a leech moving along does not stop until it has gained a foothold in front of it...
It does not let go of the place where it was grasped by the tail from behind;
but when it gains a foothold in front, it then raises the tail and places it at the place grasped by the mouth.

In exactly the same way, while attending to the head-hairs again and again, one should direct mindfulness toward the body-hairs with a mind still concerned with the head-hairs. This continues until the body-hairs appear.

At first, one should direct attention to them as "head hairs, head hairs. When body hairs appear [in the mind's eye], then one should set aside the head hairs and establish mindfulness on the body hairs.
In this way, attention should be applied to the nails and so forth as well.
For one who proceeds in this manner, absorption (*appanā*) arises; thus, one should perfect the skill in attention as it has been described. How so? For this—
For one who is attending to a meditation subject for absorption, absorption is attained; however, it does not appear at first.

For the mind, which has been developed toward various objects throughout the beginningless round of saṃsāra, when the mere thought "head-hairs" is adverted to, it follows along the stream of its habitual recitation and settles upon the brain. When the mere thought "brain" is adverted to...
Having arrived by way of the stream of recitation (*sajjhāya*), it becomes established upon the head-hairs.
However, as one attends to it again and again, each respective component (*koṭṭhāsa*) becomes manifest. Mindfulness also proceeds while remaining supported by concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, whichever component manifests most clearly, one should apply double the effort toward that very part and bring it to absorption (*appanā*).
Thus, from the time he has brought about absorption, he brings about absorption without becoming weary in the remaining sections.
In this regard, the simile is that of a monkey in a palm grove.
Furthermore, the application of the simile should be understood in this way as well: a monkey dwells in a palm grove consisting of thirty-two palm trees.
Desiring to capture him, the hunter stood at the foot of a palmyra tree situated at one end and raised a shout.
Being of a proud nature, the monkey leaped from that tree to another and stood upon a peripheral palmyra tree. The hunter went there as well and raised a shout.
The monkey then returned and settled back on the original tree. Thus pursued from one place to another, he became exhausted.
Standing at the foot of each respective palm tree, whenever there was a shout, he would rise up and, as he went along, becoming very exhausted,
he would firmly grasp the pointed leaf-spike of a palm tree, pierce it with the tip of his bow,
and even while being pulled, it did not slip away.
In this context, there are thirty-two sections like thirty-two palm trees; the mind is like the monkey; the practitioner is like the hunter.

Just as when the hunter stands at the base of the palm tree and shouts, the monkey—which is of a proud nature—flees and settles on the edge of the perimeter, so too does the mind, which has grown accustomed to various objects throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), [think] "head-hairs."

Just as when one has called out "Ukkuttha! at the far limit and, following the stream of the recitation, reaches the near limit upon merely reflecting on it, so too, upon merely reflecting on "brain," one reaches the hair of the head by following the stream of the recitation;
and for one who follows it back and forth until weary, [it stops] at the place where the "Ukkuttha" was first called out.
It is like the act of walking, establishing mindfulness again and again as each respective part appears to one who is repeatedly attending to them as if it were the time for rising;
and it is like the time of not fleeing when one has pierced with the tip of a bow and seized [the target],
which is the bringing about of absorption by applying double the attention to whichever part appears most clearly.
From the moment he has brought [the mind] to absorption (appanā), he will bring it to absorption without becoming weary in the remaining sections.
Therefore, "repulsive, repulsive"—this should be adverted to and attended to again and again; it should be struck by reasoning and struck by applied thought (vitakka).
For one who acts in this way, the four aggregates become objects that are repulsive, and absorption is reached.
[He] attains [it]. The preliminary-stage consciousnesses, known as the preparation (*parikamma*) and access (*upacāra*), possess both applied and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*);
all of this is exactly as stated below. However, for one who brings a single portion to mind, only a single first jhāna is produced.
For one who brings each separately to mind, thirty-two first jhānas are produced. In the hand...
The subject matter of the question remains as it was originally.
"He [cultivates] that sign" means that the bhikkhu cultivates that sign of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-nimitta*). "Practices" means he serves and frequents it.
"Develops" means he increases it. "Cultivates repeatedly" means he does it again and again. "He defines it well-defined" means he defines it as being well-defined.
He does so. "He directs his mind toward the external body" means that having done so, he directs, places, and sends his own mind toward the external body of another.
"There is [feeling] in his body" means there is feeling in his body. "He directs his mind toward the internal and external body" means at times...

At times he directs his mind toward the body of another. Regarding the phrase "there is the body," this is stated because it is intended neither exclusively as one's own body nor exclusively as another's body.

In this context, for one who performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) by contemplating one's own living body as "repulsive" (*paṭikūla*), both absorption (*appanā*) and access concentration (*upacāra*) arise. [The same applies] regarding the living body of another.

For one who attends to it as "repulsive," neither absorption (*appanā*) nor access (*upacāra*) concentration arises. But does not both of these arise in the case of the ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*)?
Yes, they do arise; for those are situated on the side of what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*). Therefore, in their case, both absorption and access concentration arise.
But this [the corpse] is situated on the side of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*). For that very reason, neither of these two arises here.
It is not born. However, it should be understood that this is the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) consisting in the contemplation of foulness (asubhānupassanā).
What is explained in this section? Tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are explained.
Now, in this context, all these miscellaneous points common to mental attention (manasikāra) should be understood as follows. For of these—
The analysis of the head-hairs and so forth should be understood by way of their signs (*nimitta*), characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), elements (*dhātu*), emptiness (*suñña*),
and the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. Therein, "by way of signs" means that within the thirty-two aspects there are one hundred and sixty signs, by means of which the practitioner...
One discerns the thirty-two aspects by way of their components as follows:

for the head-hair, there are five characteristics—the characteristic of color, the characteristic of shape, the characteristic of direction, the characteristic of location, and the characteristic of delimitation. The same method applies to body-hair and the rest.
Regarding "by way of characteristics": within the thirty-two aspects, there are one hundred and twenty-eight characteristics, by means of which the practitioner...
He attends to the thirty-two aspects by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), as follows:

in the case of head-hairs, there are four characteristics—the characteristic of stiffness, the characteristic of binding, the characteristic of heat, and the characteristic of distension. The same method applies to body-hairs and the rest.
Regarding "by way of elements" (*dhātu*): among the elements spoken of in the thirty-two aspects as "This person, monk, consists of four elements," [he considers] one hundred and twenty-eight...
There are elements, by means of which the practitioner grasps the thirty-two aspects according to their elements as follows:
in the head-hairs, there are four elements—solidity is the earth element, cohesion is the water element, heat is the fire element, and distension is the air element.
The same method applies to the body-hairs and the rest.
‘Emptiness’: there are ninety-six kinds of emptiness in the thirty-two aspects, by means of which the practitioner of yoga contemplates the thirty-two aspects as empty, namely:

“Head-hairs are empty of a self or of what belongs to a self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternalness, or of a nature that does not change. Thus, first, head-hairs are empty of self and empty of what belongs to a self.

There are three kinds of emptiness: emptiness of permanent being (*niccabhāva-suññatā*). The same method applies to the body hairs and so forth. Regarding the phrase “from the perspective of the aggregates, etc.”:
when the thirty-two aspects, beginning with head hair, are being analyzed by way of the aggregates and so on, one considers such questions as: how many aggregates are there in head hair?
How many bases (*āyatana*), how many elements (*dhātu*), how many truths (*sacca*), and how many foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are there? And so forth.
The detailed analysis here should be understood according to this method.
Having thus shown body-contemplation in detail through its threefold division into internal and so forth,
the passage beginning with "anupassī" is now commenced in order to explain the phrases "he dwells contemplating the body, ardent, clearly comprehending," and so on.
In this context, in order to show that contemplation by means of which one is called "contemplating the body," it is said: "What is contemplation?
It is wisdom, understanding," and so forth. The same method applies to the terms "ardent" and the rest.

Therein, "wisdom, understanding," and so on, should be understood according to the method already explained below in the commentary on the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* (The Section on the Arising of Consciousness).

All terms beginning with "endowed" (*upeta*) are synonyms for one another. Furthermore, one is "endowed" (*upeta*) by way of repetition (*āsevana*), and "thoroughly endowed" (*samupeta*) by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
