This same method applies to these two pairs as well: "approached" (*upāgata*) and "thoroughly approached" (*samupāgata*), and "attained" (*upapanna*) and "fully attained" (*sampanna*).
However, "possessed" (*samannāgata*) should be understood here in the sense of frequent practice (*bahulīkāra*). By this...
The same method applies to such phrases as "endowed with ardor" (*ātāpena upeto*).

Regarding the word "dwells" (*viharatī*), without posing the question "What therein is dwelling?", he speaks of "conducts himself" (*iriyati*) and so forth, teaching by way of a discourse focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya*).
Its meaning is: because of being possessed of one or another of the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).
It moves. By means of those four modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), it proceeds through the turning of the chariot of the body.
It protects [the body] by maintaining its long-term endurance, warding off the suffering of one mode of conduct with another mode of conduct.
It sustains itself by not remaining fixed in any single mode of conduct, but by turning through all the modes of conduct. In each respective mode of conduct, in that manner...
Likewise, it "maintains" because it sustains the body; it "conducts" because it carries on for a long duration;
it "dwells" because, having interrupted one posture with another, it preserves life. 362.
That very body is the "world" (loka) in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating, in that very body wherein one dwells contemplating the body.
The world (*loka*). Furthermore, because covetousness and dejection (*abhijjhā-domanassa*) are abandoned in the body, they are likewise abandoned in feeling and the other aggregates;
therefore, it is said that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are the world.

Regarding the terms "peaceful" (*santa*) and so forth: it is "peaceful" (*santa*) because of its state of peace by way of cessation (*nirodha*); it is "calmed" (*samita*) because it has been stilled through cultivation (*bhāvanā*); [and] through the full understanding of the objective basis (*vatthupariññā*)...
They are "stilled" (*vūpasantā*) by way of the subsiding of their occurrence. They are "gone to rest" (*atthaṅgatā*), meaning they have gone to the goal known as cessation (*nirodha*).
Because they have been warded off from repeated arising, they have "gone utterly to rest" (*abbhatthaṅgatā*).
"Appitā" means destroyed; it also means established in non-occurrence. "Byappitā" means well-destroyed; it also means established in utter non-occurrence.

The meaning is as follows: because they have been dried up so that they do not flow again, they are "dried up" (*sositā*). Because they are thoroughly dried up, they are "completely dried up" (*visositā*); the meaning is that they have been made parched.

Because their end has been brought about, they are "brought to an end" (*byantīkatā*). And herein, for one who dwells in the meditation subject, the preservation of the body is achieved through the dwelling in the meditation subject via contemplation;
right effort is achieved through ardor; and the means for preserving the meditation subject is through mindfulness and clear comprehension.
It should be understood that serenity is obtained through mindfulness by way of contemplation of the body, insight through clear comprehension,
and the fruit of development through the removal of covetousness and displeasure.
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of the body is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Contemplation of Feeling (Vedanānupassanāniddesa) 363.
In the exposition of the contemplation of feeling as well, it should be understood in the same manner and according to the method already stated above.
Regarding the phrases "experiencing a pleasant feeling" and so forth, "pleasant feeling" refers to either bodily or mental pleasant feeling.
The meaning is that one who is experiencing [a feeling] understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.

In this regard, it may be granted that even infants lying on their backs understand, at the time of drinking milk and so forth, while experiencing a pleasant feeling, that "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling";
however, this was not said with reference to such a kind of knowing. For such a kind of knowing does not abandon the perception of a self (sattūpaladdhi).

If one does not eliminate the perception of a being (*sattasaññā*), there is neither the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) nor the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā*).

However, for this bhikkhu, knowing [this] abandons the apprehension of a being, eliminates the perception of a being, and thus both the meditation subject and the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness come to be.
For [one asks]: "Who feels this? To whom does the feeling belong? By what cause does the feeling arise?"
This was said with reference to such clear comprehension and experiencing.
In this regard, who experiences? No being whatsoever, nor any person, experiences. Whose feeling is it?
It is not the feeling of any being or any person. For what reason is it called "feeling"? Because this feeling has a physical basis and an object.
Therefore, he understands thus: “It is feeling alone that feels, having made this or that basis for pleasure and so forth its object;
but based on that occurrence of feeling, there is the mere conventional expression, ‘I feel.
Thus, perceiving that it is feeling alone that feels by making the basis its object, [he knows]: “I am feeling a pleasant feeling.”
"He understands" is how it should be understood, as was the case with a certain elder at Cittalapabbata.
It is said that when the elder was unwell, he groaned from intense pain and rolled back and forth.
A young monk asked him, "Venerable sir, which part of your body is aching? "Friend, there is no specific place that is aching," [he replied].
“There is no ‘I’; it is feeling alone that feels, having made the physical basis its object.
“From the moment one knows this, is it permissible, venerable sir, to endure [the pain]? “I endure it, friend. “Endurance, venerable sir, is better. The elder endured.
The wind cut him open as far as the heart. His intestines were heaped up upon the bed. The elder—
He showed it to the junior monk, saying, “Is such endurance appropriate, friend? The junior monk remained silent.

The elder, having applied energy and concentration, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and as one who had reached the summit, he passed away into Parinibbāna.
And just as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling... pe... while experiencing a non-worldly feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, [he thought]: “Non-worldly...”

“I experience a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant,” he understands. Thus, having taught the meditation subject of form (*rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*), the Blessed One taught the meditation subject of the formless (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of feeling (*vedanā*).
For there are two kinds of meditation subjects: the meditation subject of form and the meditation subject of the formless;
these are also called the discernment of form and the discernment of the formless. Therein, the Blessed One—

When teaching the meditation subject of the material (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), he taught the analysis of the four elements (catudhātu-vavatthāna) either by way of concise attention or by way of detailed attention;
both of these have indeed been shown in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*.

But when teaching the meditation subject of the immaterial (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), he generally taught it by way of feeling (vedanā). For in the meditation subject of the immaterial, there are three kinds: [feeling, mind, and mental objects].
Adherence—by way of contact, by way of feeling, and by way of consciousness. How so?

For some, when the meditation subject of form has been grasped either briefly or in detail, the first impact of the mind and mental factors upon that object is evident as contact arising while touching that object. For another, it is [evident] as experiencing that object...
When feeling arises, it becomes manifest. For some, when consciousness arises cognizing that object after having grasped it, it becomes manifest.
In this regard, for one to whom contact is manifest, he understands: "It is not contact alone that arises; together with it..."
“Feeling also arises experiencing that very same object; perception also arises perceiving it; volition also arises intending it;
and consciousness also arises cognizing it. Thus, one discerns precisely the pentad beginning with contact.
Furthermore, for one to whom feeling is clear, [it becomes evident]: “It is not merely feeling that arises; together with it, while contacting that very same object...”
‘Contact also arises; perception, which is the act of perceiving, also arises; volition, which is the act of intending, also arises; and consciousness, which is the act of cognizing, also arises.
Thus he discerns precisely this pentad beginning with contact. Even for one to whom consciousness is clear, it becomes evident that ‘it is not consciousness alone that arises;
along with it, there also arises contact, which touches that very same object.’
“Feeling that is being experienced arises, perception that is perceiving arises, and volition that is intending arises”—thus he discerns precisely these five factors beginning with contact.
Then, investigating, “On what are these five factors beginning with contact dependent? he understands: “They are dependent on a physical basis.”
"Basis" (vatthu) means the body born of kamma. With reference to this, it was said: "And this consciousness of mine is supported here, bound up here.
In terms of its actual meaning, it consists of both the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived forms (upādārūpa).

Thus, one sees here that "matter" (rūpa) is the physical basis, while "name" (nāma) consists of the four mental aggregates with contact as the fifth; this is precisely what is meant by "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa). Herein, "matter" refers to the aggregate of form, and "name" refers to the [other] four [mental aggregates].
"Immaterial aggregates" refers to the mere five aggregates. For there are no five aggregates apart from name-and-form (nāmarūpa), nor is there name-and-form apart from the five aggregates.
Examining them with the thought, "What is the cause of these five aggregates?", he sees that they have ignorance and so forth as their cause; thereafter—
This is both condition and conditionally arisen; there is no other being or person, but only a mere heap of pure formations.

Thus, having applied the three characteristics by way of name-and-form together with their conditions, he wanders about contemplating them as “impermanent, suffering, and non-self” according to the sequence of insight.
Desiring penetration day after day, he [remains] in such a state.
Having obtained what is favorable to the season, favorable to the individual, favorable as food, or favorable for hearing the Dhamma during the day,
he sits in a single cross-legged posture and, having brought insight to its culmination, establishes himself in Arahantship. Thus,
the meditation subject has been explained for these three types of persons up to the attainment of Arahantship.
Now, here the Blessed One, while teaching the formless meditation subject (*arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna*), taught it by way of feeling (*vedanā*).
For when it is taught by way of contact (*phassa*) or by way of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), it is not clear; it appears as if in darkness.
But when taught by way of feeling, it becomes clear. Why? Because the arising of feelings is clearly manifest. Indeed, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings—

It is manifest. When happiness arises, it shakes and massages the entire body, pervading and overflowing it, as if making one eat clarified butter refined a hundred times, or as if anointing one with oil refined a hundred times, or as if extinguishing a fever with a thousand pots of water, while one utters the words, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! indeed.

It arises. When suffering arises, it agitates, crushes, pervades, and drenches the entire body, as if inserting a red-hot iron bar, as if pouring molten copper, or as if throwing a mass of wood-torches into a forest of dry grass and trees—“Alas, what suffering! Alas! [it cries].
‘It is suffering! Thus it arises even while one is still lamenting. In this way, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is evident.
However, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is difficult to illustrate; it is dark and obscure.

That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling becomes evident to one who grasps it by way of its method—that is, as a state of neutrality consisting in the negation of what is pleasant and unpleasant when pleasant and painful feelings have passed away—just as [the following example shows].

What is it? Just as a deer-trapper, following the tracks of a deer that has fled after climbing onto a back-rock, sees its footprints both on the near side and on the far side of the rock, yet seeing none in between, nevertheless knows by inference: "It climbed up from here;
it descended from there; it must have gone through this particular spot across the middle of the back-rock."
For just as a footprint at the place where one has ascended is evident, so too is the arising of pleasant feeling evident;
and just as a footprint at the place where one has descended is evident, so too is the arising of painful feeling evident.

Just as grasping the path by way of inference—thinking, "He ascended from here, he descended from there, and he went thus in the middle"—so too, when pleasure and pain have ceased, [the neutral state] is understood by way of the negation of the agreeable and the disagreeable.
For one who grasps it by way of its method, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that consists in the mode of neutrality becomes evident.

Thus, after first teaching the formal meditation subject (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), the Blessed One, while subsequently teaching the formless meditation subject (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), demonstrated it by turning [the mind] away by means of feeling.
And he does not demonstrate it in this way only here; in the Dīgha Nikāya as well—
In the Mahānidāna Sutta, the Sakkapañha Sutta, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, and in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya,
as well as in the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta,
the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, in the Cūḷanidāna Sutta, the Rukkhopama Sutta, and the Parivīmaṃsana Sutta.
In many suttas, such as "All [feelings] are associated with feeling," after first explaining the meditation subject of the material (rūpa),
he subsequently demonstrated the meditation subject of the immaterial (arūpa) by way of feeling. And just as in those various instances, so too in this Vibhaṅga on the Foundations of Mindfulness,
after first explaining the meditation subject of the material, he subsequently [explains] the meditation subject of the immaterial.
Having turned it back by way of feeling, he showed it.
In this regard, concerning the phrases "pleasant feeling" and so forth, there is this further method of understanding: "He understands, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.
This is because at the moment of a pleasant feeling, there is an absence of painful feeling; thus, while feeling a pleasant feeling...

He understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling. Because of the absence now of that painful feeling which previously existed, and because this pleasant feeling did not exist before, he is fully aware therein that what is called "feeling" is impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time, one experiences only a pleasant feeling.
Aggivessana, at whatever time one experiences a painful feeling... [or] a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time...”
At that time, one experiences a pleasant feeling; one does not experience a painful feeling, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling at that time.

Yet, Aggivessana, even a pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Even a painful feeling... [and] even a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is likewise.
“Feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned... [and so on] ...of a nature to cease.
Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, disenchanted with painful feeling, and disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated...”
“‘It is liberated’—such knowledge arises; he understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

Regarding the phrases “sensual pleasure” and so forth: sensual pleasures (*sāmisā sukhā*) are the six types of worldly joy-feelings (*gehassita-somanassa-vedanā*) based on the bait of the five strands of sense pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

The so-called "unworldly pleasant feeling" refers to the six types of joy and happiness based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*); the so-called "worldly painful feeling" refers to the six types of grief and sorrow based on household life (*geha*);
the so-called "unworldly painful feeling" refers to the six types of grief and sorrow based on renunciation;

the so-called "worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" refers to the six types of equanimity based on household life; the so-called "unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" refers to the six types of equanimity based on renunciation.
The classification of these is found in the text itself in the following section. "That sign" means that sign of feeling.
"In external feelings" means in the feelings of another person. "Experiencing a pleasant feeling" means experiencing a pleasant feeling in another person.
"Internally and externally" means at times in one's own feelings and at times in another's feelings.

He applies the mind. In this section, because neither self nor another is restricted, only the mere discernment of feeling is shown by saying, "Here, a bhikkhu [regards] a pleasant feeling as 'a pleasant feeling,'" and so forth. The rest here is self-evident.
However, in this section, only pure insight (suddhavipassanā) is discussed.
The commentary on the description of the contemplation of feelings is finished.
Commentary on the Description of the Contemplation of Mind (365):
In the description of the contemplation of mind as well, it should be understood in the same manner and according to the same method as stated below. [The mind] with lust...

In the passages beginning with "or mind," however, "with lust" refers to the eightfold [consciousness] accompanied by greed; "free from lust" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate [consciousness].
Since this, however, is an analysis of mental states (sammasana) rather than a combination of phenomena (dhammasamodhāna), no supramundane consciousness is found here even in a single term.
Because they occur together with and are abandoned along with lust and the other [defilements] by way of their being objects to be abandoned, [the terms apply] to the two [types of consciousness].
The [remaining] unwholesome states are not included because they cannot be found in these categories in a non-figurative sense.
The other four unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the first category nor to the second. "With hatred" is twofold, being accompanied by displeasure (*domanassa*).
"Free from hatred" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate states. The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the first category nor to the second.
They associate with it. Delusion (moha) is twofold: that accompanied by doubt and that accompanied by restlessness.
Since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining [mental factors] are also certainly included here.
For within this very dyad, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are fully encompassed. "Free from delusion" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate [states]. "Contracted" (saṃkhitta) means...
“Overcome by sloth and torpor” means this is what is called a contracted mind. “Distracted” means accompanied by restlessness;
for this is what is called a scattered mind.
“Exalted” refers to the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere. “Not exalted” refers to the sense-sphere. “Surpassable” refers to the sense-sphere.

“Anuttara” (supreme) refers to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*). Even therein, the fine-material sphere is with-superior (*sauttara*), whereas the immaterial sphere alone is supreme (*anuttara*).
“Samāhita” (concentrated) means that for which there exists either absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) or access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*).

“Asamāhita” (unconcentrated) means devoid of both types of concentration. “Vimutta” (liberated) means liberated by means of liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhanavimutti*). “Avimutta” (unliberated) means...
It is devoid of liberation through both [tranquility and insight]. However, there is no occasion here for liberation by eradication, subsidence, or escape.
"A mind with lust" means a mind that has lust for it. The rest is of plain meaning because it follows the method already explained below.
In this section as well, only pure insight (suddhavipassanā) is discussed.
The commentary on the exposition of the contemplation of mind is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Contemplation of Phenomena:
Explanation of the Chapter on the Hindrances.
367. To this extent, since the discernment of the aggregate of form has been explained through body-contemplation,

the discernment of the aggregate of feeling through feeling-contemplation, and the discernment of the aggregate of consciousness through mind-contemplation, now, by way of the associated mental states,
the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is explained in order to include the discernment of the aggregates of perception and mental formations as well.
He said, "And how does a bhikkhu show [this]? and so forth. Therein, "existent" (*santa*) means existing by way of frequent occurrence;
"non-existent" (*asanta*) means not existing by way of non-occurrence or because it has been abandoned.
"And how" (*yathā ca*) means the reason by which the arising of sensual desire occurs. "And he understands that" (*tañca pajānāti*) means he understands that reason. By this method...
The meaning should be understood in all instances.
Therein, sensual desire arises through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward a beautiful object (*subha-nimitta*).
A "beautiful object" refers both to that which is beautiful and to that which has beauty as its objective support. "Improper attention" refers to...

Improper attention is attention that follows a wrong path; it is attention that regards what is impermanent as permanent, what is suffering as happiness, what is non-self as self, or what is foul as beautiful. For one who frequently engages in such attention, sensual desire arises.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the beautiful (*subhanimitta*). Therein, the frequent practice of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), or for the increase and expansion of sensual desire that has already arisen.
However, its abandonment occurs through proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) directed toward the sign of the foul (*asubhanimitta*).
Now, the sign of the foul refers both to the foul itself as the sign and to the foul object as the sign. Proper attention means skillful attention (*upāya-manasikāra*).
Attention is the act of attending to impermanence as "impermanent," or to suffering as "suffering," or to non-self as "non-self," or to the unattractive as "unattractive.
For one who frequently engages in that attention therein, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the unattractive. Frequent, systematic attention directed toward it is the means by which unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned, increases no further, and reaches its full development."
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire:
apprehending the sign of the foul, devotion to the development of the foul, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends, and appropriate talk.
For sensual desire is abandoned by one who apprehends the tenfold sign of the foul, by one who develops it, and by one who guards the doors of the sense faculties.
Even for one who is moderate in eating, having the habit of sustaining himself by drinking water when there is space for four or five morsels, it is said:
“Having eaten four or five morsels, One may drink water;
This is sufficient for a well-disposed dwelling For a bhikkhu of resolute mind.”
Even for one who serves spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta) such as the Elder Tissa the Impurity-worker—who delights in the meditation on foulness (asubha)—sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is abandoned;
it is also abandoned through appropriate talk concerning the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it is said:
"Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire. Now, for one by whom [sensual desire] has been abandoned through these six things...
One understands: "Through the path of Arahantship, there is the non-arising of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) in the future.
However, through unwise attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) toward the sign of repulsion (paṭigha-nimitta), ill will (byāpāda) arises.
In this context, both the repulsion itself is called the "sign of repulsion," and the object of repulsion is also the "sign of repulsion. Unwise attention [is the cause] in all cases.
It has but a single characteristic. When one frequently applies the mind to that sign, ill will arises. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there is the sign of repulsion.
Frequent unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will.
However, through wise attention to the liberation of mind by loving-kindness, its abandonment occurs. In this context, when “loving-kindness” is mentioned—

Both absorption (appanā) and access (upacāra) are suitable; "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) refers specifically to absorption. "Careful attention" (yonisomanasikāra) has the characteristic already described.
For one who frequently practices that [attention] therein, ill will (byāpāda) is abandoned.

Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettācetovimutti). Frequent practice of careful attention toward it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill will: the grasping of the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on one’s own kamma as one’s own property, frequent practice of reflective discernment, having virtuous friends, and talk that is conducive [to such states].

For ill will is abandoned even by one who grasps loving-kindness by means of any one of these methods: directed toward specific individuals, directed toward unspecified individuals, or by suffusing the directions.
It is also for one developing loving-kindness by means of directional pervasion—either limitedly or unlimitedly—who reflects: "What will you do by being angry with this person?
Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so forth? Are you not one who has come by your own karma and will go away by your own karma alone?
To be angry with another is like taking glowing coals, red-hot iron rods, or excrement and [throwing them] at another..."
"It is like a desire to strike. What will this angry person do to you?
Will he be able to destroy your virtue and the other qualities? Having come here by his own karma, he will depart by his own karma alone;
like an unaccepted gift or a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger of his will fall back upon his own head. Thus...
Ill will is abandoned by one who reflects upon the fact that both oneself and others are the owners of their own karma;

by one who, having reflected on the ownership of karma for both, stands firm in discernment; and by one who serves spiritual friends like the Elder Assagutta, who delight in the cultivation of loving-kindness.
It is also abandoned through appropriate talk centered on loving-kindness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it was said:

“Six things lead to the abandoning of ill will. Furthermore, he understands that for ill will abandoned by these six things, there is no further arising in the future through the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*).
Regarding “discontent” (*arati*) and so forth, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise through unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). Discontent means a state of dissatisfaction.
*Tandī* is bodily languor. *Vijambhikā* is stretching the body. *Bhattasammada* is drowsiness after eating or a feverish state caused by food.

*Cetaso līnattaṃ* is a state of mental sluggishness. When one frequently applies improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) to these states such as aversion and the rest, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Monks, there are discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after a meal, and mental sluggishness. Therein,
the frequent application of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor,
or for the increase and expansion of sloth and torpor that have already arisen.”

However, its abandonment occurs through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) toward the element of initiative (*ārambhadhātu*) and the others. The "element of initiative" is the energy of the initial undertaking.
The "element of exertion" (*nikkamadhātu*) is stronger than that because it has emerged from indolence.
The "element of perseverance" (*parakkamadhātu*) is stronger still because it advances to ever-higher stages. Regarding this threefold energy, wise attention [is required].
For one who frequently practices [this], sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of perseverance.
Cultivating wise attention toward these frequently is the non-nutriments for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, and for the abandonment of arisen sloth and torpor."
“...for their increase and for their abundance.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor:

taking note of the sign of overeating, changing one’s posture, attending to the perception of light, dwelling in the open air, having virtuous friends, and engaging in appropriate conversation. (From the *Āharahatthaka Sutta*)
For one who has eaten food such as *bhuttavamitaka*, *tatravaṭṭaka*, *alaṃsāṭaka*,
or *kākamāsaka* and is sitting in a night station or a day station practicing the duty of a recluse, sloth and torpor come sweeping over him like a great elephant. However,
for a bhikkhu whose habit is to subsist by leaving space for four or five mouthfuls and then drinking water, that [sloth and torpor] does not [overcome him].
"Occurs": by taking this as a sign, even for one who observes moderation in eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned.

By changing from whichever posture sloth and torpor have descended upon, by attending to the light of the moon, the light of a lamp, or the light of a torch at night, or to the light of the sun during the day, by dwelling in the open air, and by [associating with] those like the Elder Mahākassapa—[sloth and torpor are abandoned].

For one who has abandoned sloth and torpor, sloth and torpor are abandoned even by associating with virtuous friends; they are also abandoned by talk concerning the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that are conducive to them while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor.
Furthermore, for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, [it is abandoned] by the path of Arahantship.
He understands: "In the future, there is non-arising.

Through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) regarding the lack of tranquility of the mind, restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*) arise. "Lack of tranquility" refers to the state of being untranquil; in terms of its meaning, it is simply restlessness and remorse.
In that regard, [he understands] the frequent occurrence of improper attention...
While one is engaged in [unwholesome] conduct, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, there is non-tranquillity of mind. Therein, the frequent application of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the increase and expansion of restlessness and remorse that have already arisen."
But the abandoning of this occurs through wise attention directed toward the tranquility of the mind known as concentration. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"There is, bhikkhus, a tranquility of the mind. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the non-nutriments for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and for the waning away, the increase, and the fullness of arisen restlessness and remorse."
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse:
being well-versed in the teachings, asking many questions, knowing the formulated rules of the Vinaya, associating with the elders, having virtuous friends, and engaging in appropriate conversation.
For even by means of great learning—when one acquires one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas according to both the text and the meaning—[restlessness and remorse are abandoned].
Restlessness and remorse are abandoned. They are abandoned by one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is unallowable;
by one who has mastered the Vinaya regulations through practice and thus knows them well; by one who approaches elder and senior Theras;
and by one who serves spiritual friends such as the Elder Upāli who are experts in the Vinaya—whether while standing, sitting, or otherwise engaged.
It is also abandoned by talk that is connected with what is allowable and what is unallowable, and is beneficial. Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.

Furthermore, he understands: “When restlessness and remorse have been abandoned by means of these six things, there is their non-arising in the future—restlessness through the path of Arahantship, and remorse through the path of Non-returning.”
Through improper attention toward things that are a basis for doubt, doubt arises.
Things that are a basis for doubt are themselves called "doubt" because they are the cause of repeated doubting.
In this regard, doubt arises in one who frequently engages in improper attention. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, there are things that are grounds for doubt. Therein, the frequent application of improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the increase and expansion of arisen doubt.
However, its abandonment occurs through the application of proper attention to wholesome and other such states. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states,
and dark and bright states with their counterparts. In this regard, the frequent practice of wise attention is the non-nutriments for the arising of unarisen doubt,
or for the increase and expansion of doubt once it has arisen.”
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt:
great learning, inquisitiveness, knowledge of the Vinaya, abundance of resolute confidence, friendship with the virtuous, and appropriate talk.
For even in one who possesses great learning—whether they have mastered one or, as the case may be, up to five Nikāyas by way of both the text and the meaning—doubt [arises].
It is abandoned. Doubt is abandoned by one who frequently inquires about the Three Jewels; by one who has attained mastery over the Vinaya;
by one who possesses abundant resolve known as unwavering faith in the Three Jewels; and by one who serves a spiritual friend such as the Elder Vakkali, who is resolved through faith.
Regarding the relinquishing of one's position and so forth, [it concerns] the Three Jewels...
It is also abandoned through talk that is dependent on the qualities [of the Buddha] and is conducive to progress. Therefore it was said:
“Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt. Furthermore, one understands that for doubt abandoned by these six things, there is non-arising in the future by means of the path of stream-entry.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Hindrances. Commentary on the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment.

In the chapter on the factors of enlightenment, "present" means existing by way of having been acquired; "absent" means not existing by way of not having been acquired. Furthermore, regarding the phrases "as to how it has not arisen," and so forth, first, as regards the mindfulness factor of enlightenment:
“Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the mindfulness enlightenment factor.

Frequent, thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen mindfulness enlightenment factor. Thus there is its arising. In this regard:
Mindfulness itself is the state conducive to the mindfulness enlightenment factor. Proper attention has the characteristic already described.
When one frequently practices that therein, the mindfulness enlightenment factor arises.
Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor: mindfulness, clear comprehension,
Avoiding persons who are unmindful, associating with persons who are established in mindfulness, and being intent upon that [mindfulness]. For,
by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances beginning with "the excellent" (*abhikkanta*),

by avoiding persons who are unmindful— who are like crows cast out from a meal— and by associating with persons who are established in mindfulness— such as the Elder Tissa-datta and the Elder Abhaya— one [achieves this].

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises for the purpose of arousing mindfulness during standing, sitting, and so forth, and through the state of the mind being inclined, leaning, and bent towards it.
Furthermore, he understands that for this factor, once arisen through these four causes, there is the fulfillment of its development by means of the path of Arahantship.
As for the enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena—
“There are, bhikkhus, wholesome and unwholesome states... [and so on] ...states that are dark, bright, and their counterparts.

Frequent, thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of investigation of states, and for the increase, expansion, development, and cultivation of the arisen enlightenment factor of investigation of states.”
“...it leads to fulfillment”—thus there is arising.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment: being a thorough questioner; ... [and so forth].

These are: making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, avoiding persons of poor wisdom, associating with persons of wisdom, reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge, and being intent upon that.

Therein, "being inquisitive" means being abundant in inquiry based on the meaning of the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path-factors, jhānas, serenity, and insight.
"Making the basis pure" refers to the internal and external bases.
Making things clear and clean. For when one's hair, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is full of humors and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclear and impure.
But when the robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or when the lodging is dirty, then the external basis...

It becomes unclean and impure. Therefore, by means of cutting the hair and so forth, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives, and by anointing and bathing, the internal basis must be made clean.
By means of sewing, washing, dyeing, and trimming, the external basis must be made clean. For in this regard—
When the internal and external bases are unclear, the knowledge regarding the arisen states of mind and mental factors is also unclear and impure,
like the radiance of a lamp flame arising from impure wicks, a lamp-stand, and a circle of ghee-oil.
But when the internal and external bases are clear, the knowledge regarding the arisen states of mind and mental factors is also clear.
It is like the radiance produced by the flame of a lamp depending on a clean lamp-stand, a bowl, and refined oil.
Therefore it is said: "The act of making the basis pure leads to the arising of the investigation-of-dhammas factor of enlightenment.
"Balancing the faculties" means bringing the faculties, such as faith and the rest, into a state of equilibrium. For if...

The faculty of faith becomes strong while the others are weak; consequently, the faculty of energy is unable to perform its function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing.
Therefore, by means of reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena, or by attending to them in whatever way makes [faith] strong...
Likewise, that which has arisen should be abandoned through non-attention; the story of the Elder Vakkali is the illustration here.

However, if the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is too strong, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution (*adhimokkha*), nor can the others perform their respective functions.
Therefore, it should be diminished by the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the other factors; in this regard as well, the story of the Elder Soṇa is the illustration.
This must be demonstrated. In the same way, when one of the remaining factors is predominant, the inability of the others to perform their respective functions should be understood.
In particular, however, they praise the balance between faith and wisdom, and between concentration and energy.
For one who has strong faith but weak wisdom is blindly devoted; he places his confidence in what is not a proper basis. One who has strong wisdom but weak faith...

If one sides with the miserly faction, it becomes incurable—like a disease arising from medicine—and by overreaching, thinking "merit arises merely through the mere thought," one fails to perform meritorious deeds such as giving and is reborn in hell.
However, through the balance of both, one has faith in the object itself. But strong concentration with weak energy, and [weak concentration with] strong energy... of concentration...
Because it belongs to the side of indolence, indolence overcomes [concentration]. Strong energy overcomes weak concentration;
because energy belongs to the side of agitation, agitation overcomes it. However, when concentration is joined with energy, it cannot fall into indolence;
when energy is joined with concentration, it cannot fall into agitation. Therefore, both of these should be balanced.
It should be done. For absorption (*appanā*) occurs through the balancing of both [faith and wisdom]. Furthermore, for one whose task is concentration (*samādhi*), even strong faith is appropriate.
By thus having faith and resolving, he will reach absorption.
Regarding concentration and wisdom, for one whose task is concentration, a strong one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) is appropriate. For in this way, he reaches absorption.
He attains it. For one who practices insight (vipassanā), wisdom must be strong; for in this way he attains penetration of the characteristics.
However, through the balance of both, absorption (appanā) certainly occurs. But mindfulness must be strong in all cases.
For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation under the influence of faith, energy, and wisdom—which belong to the side of agitation—and from the side of indolence.
And by means of concentration, it protects [the mind] from falling into indolence.
Therefore, like salt seasoning all condiments, or like a minister for all royal affairs, mindfulness is desirable in every situation. Thus he said:
"Mindfulness, moreover, has been described by the Blessed One as 'all-beneficial. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge; it is manifested as protection."
"And when mindfulness is present, there is no exertion or restraint of the mind without mindfulness.
Avoidance of persons of poor wisdom means keeping far away from dull-witted individuals who have not plunged into the analysis of the aggregates and so forth.
Service to persons of wisdom means [relying on] those who possess the discernment of the fifty characteristics of the factors of enlightenment.

Associating with persons endowed with the wisdom of rise and fall; reflection on the conduct of those with profound knowledge means reflecting on the distinctions made by the profound wisdom that occurs regarding the profound aggregates and so forth;
being intent upon that means having a mind that is inclined, directed, and leaning toward the arousal of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor while standing, sitting, and so forth.
He understands: "When it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of arahantship.
Regarding the energy enlightenment factor:
"Bhikkhus, there is the element of instigation, the element of exertion, and the element of perseverance. Therein, there is frequent application of wise attention..."
“This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy”—
thus there is its arising.
Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the energy factor of enlightenment:
reflecting on the fear of the states of misery; seeing the benefits; reflecting on the path to be traversed; honoring the alms-food received; reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance;

reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher; reflecting on the greatness of one's birth; reflecting on the greatness of one's fellow practitioners of the holy life; [and reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma].
Avoiding indolent persons, associating with those who have initiated energy, and being intent upon that [energy]. In this regard,
even at the time of experiencing great suffering in the hells— starting from the fivefold execution by binding—
and even when caught in the animal realm by means of nets, fish-traps, and so forth, or when pierced by the blows of threshing spikes and the like...

Furthermore, even at times such as when pulling carts, or during the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) for many thousands of years or even throughout an entire interval between Buddhas while suffering from hunger and thirst,
or among the Kālakañjika asuras while experiencing the sufferings of wind, heat,

and so forth with a physical body (attabhāva) measuring sixty or eighty cubits consisting of nothing but skin and bone— it is impossible [to lose] the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga).

To arouse [it]. “This, monk, is precisely the time for you to exert energy”—thus, even for one reflecting on the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*) arises.
“It is not possible for one who is indolent to attain the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*); it is only possible for one who has initiated energy—this is the benefit of energy.
Thus, it also arises for one who perceives the benefits. “By all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples alone...”
"It is the path already traveled that must be gone upon, and it cannot be traversed by one who is lazy"—thus it arises even for one reflecting on the route of travel.

"Those people who attend upon me with alms-food and so forth are neither my relatives, nor my slaves or laborers, nor do they give me choice alms-food and such out of the thought, 'We shall live depending on him'; rather, it is because of their own merit..."
They give while hoping for great fruit. It was not with the thought, “Having used these requisites, he will dwell in comfort, full of physical vigor,” that the Teacher permitted you these requisites;
rather, it was with the thought, “While using these, he will practice the duty of a recluse and be liberated from the suffering of the round,” that those requisites were permitted.
"Therefore, if you dwell indolent, you will not honor that almsfood; for it is only for one who has aroused energy that there is what is called 'honoring almsfood.
Thus it arises even for one reflecting on the honoring of almsfood, as it did for the Elder Mahā Mitta.
It is said that the Elder resided at a place called Kassakaleṇa. In the village where he went for alms, there was a great female lay devotee who looked after the Elder as if he were her own son.
One day, while she was going to the forest, she said to her daughter: "My dear, in such-and-such a place there are old rice grains;
in such-and-such a place there is milk; in such-and-such a place there is ghee; in such-and-such a place there is molasses. Your..."
“Cook some rice and give it to my noble brother Ayyamitta when he arrives, along with milk, ghee, and sugar;
you too should eat. “But what will you eat yourself, mother?
“As for me, yesterday I ate leftover rice that had been cooked the day before with sour gruel. “What will you eat during the day, mother? “Just potherbs.”
“Mother, having added broken rice, cook some sour gruel and set it aside.
When the Elder heard that sound while putting on his robe and taking out his bowl, he admonished himself:
“It seems the Great Laywoman is eating discarded food with sour gruel; even during the day she will be eating broken leaves and sour gruel.”
But she mentions old rice and so forth for your sake. Relying on that, she indeed does not expect a field, nor a dwelling, nor food, nor clothing;
rather, desiring the three kinds of excellence, she gives.
Will you be able to grant her those excellences, or will you not? This, moreover—
Thinking, "Alms-food cannot be eaten by one who is still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion," he placed the bowl into its bag,
released the cord, and turned back. He went straight to Kassakalena,
set the bowl below his bed and the robes on the robe-rack, and resolved upon energy, vowing, "I shall not leave until I have attained arahantship."
He sat down. Having lived for a long time as one diligent and having increased his insight, that bhikkhu attained Arahantship even before breakfast;
like a blooming lotus, he sat smiling, a great one whose taints were destroyed.
The deity residing in the tree at the entrance of the cave—
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
You whose taints are exhausted—you are worthy of offerings, O venerable sir.
Having uttered this inspired utterance, she said: “Venerable sir, by giving almsfood to Arahants like you who have entered for alms, these elderly women will be freed from suffering.”
The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking for the time, realized it was already morning; he took his bowl and robe and entered the village.
The girl, having prepared the meal, sat waiting with the door open, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now my brother will come. When the Elder arrived at the door of the house, she—
Taking a bowl and filling it with a gift of milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, she placed it in his hands.
The Elder, having offered a blessing of "May there be happiness," departed. She remained standing, gazing after him;
for at that time, the Elder’s complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were serene, and his face—
Freed from her bonds, she shone exceedingly like a ripe palm fruit.
When the great female lay devotee returned from the forest, she asked, "What is it, my daughter? Has your brother come? She related the entire account of what had occurred.
The lay devotee, realizing, "Today my son’s duty of going forth has reached its culmination," said, "Is your brother, my daughter, finding delight in the Buddha’s teaching?"
“He does not grow weary,” he said.
“Now, this inheritance of the Teacher is indeed great—namely, the so-called seven treasures of the noble ones (ariyadhana).
It is not possible for one who is indolent to grasp it. For just as parents [might say] of a son who has gone astray, ‘This one is no son of ours’...”

They cast him out; upon their passing, he does not receive their inheritance. In the same way, the lazy person does not obtain this inheritance of the noble wealth, whereas only one who has aroused energy obtains it—this arises even for one reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance.
"Furthermore, your Teacher is great. For at the time your Teacher took rebirth in his mother’s womb, and also at the time of his Great Departure..."
"Even at the time of his full enlightenment, during the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the twin miracle, the descent from the heavens,
the relinquishing of the life-force, and at the time of his final Nibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system shook. Is it fitting for you,
having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Teacher, to be lazy?"— thus it arises even when one reflects upon the greatness of the Teacher.
“Even by birth, you are not of low birth now; you are born into the lineage of King Okkāka, which has descended from the unadulterated tradition of the Great Elect (Mahāsammata);
you are the grandson of the great King Sīrisaddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā; you are the younger brother of the auspicious Rāhula.
It is not fitting for one such as you, a son of the Conqueror, to dwell in indolence. Thus is the greatness of birth.
It also arises when one reflects: "Sāriputta and Moggallāna, as well as the eighty great disciples, penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone.
You are following the path of these fellow practitioners of the holy life; are you not following it?
Thus, it arises even from reflecting upon the greatness of one's fellow practitioners of the holy life.

It arises even for one who avoids lazy persons—resembling python snakes that remain with their physical and mental energy spent—and who instead associates with persons who have initiated energy and are resolute;
and it arises for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the arousal of energy during standing, sitting, and so forth.
Furthermore, he understands that when it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.
Regarding the factor of enlightenment that is rapture:

"Monks, there are states conducive to the factor of enlightenment that is rapture. Therein, frequent and thorough attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment that is rapture, or for the increase and fulfillment of the arisen factor of enlightenment that is rapture."
“...it leads to increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment”—thus there is arising.
In this context, rapture itself is what is called the states conducive to the rapture enlightenment factor. The attention that produces it is called wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the rapture enlightenment factor: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the deities; [and so forth].
The recollection of peace, avoiding persons of harsh character, associating with kindly persons, reflecting on discourses that inspire confidence, and being intent upon those qualities.
For when one recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the factor of enlightenment consisting of rapture arises, pervading the entire body up to the stage of access concentration;
and likewise for one recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, [which have been] protected for a long time without breach.
For one reflecting on the fourfold purified virtue; for a layperson reflecting on the ten precepts or the five precepts;
for one who, during times of famine or fear and so forth, has given excellent food to fellow practitioners of the holy life and reflects on that generosity, thinking, “Thus indeed have we given”;
and for a layperson as well, reflecting on the gift given to those possessed of virtue at such a time.
When one reflects upon the presence within oneself of such qualities as those endowed with which the deities attained the state of a deity;
when one reflects that even for sixty or seventy years the defilements do not manifest, having been suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti);
and when one reflects on the lack of reverence shown during visits to shrines, visits to the Bodhi tree, and visits to the elders—[these are the causes of rebirth among the deities].
Even for one who avoids coarse persons—like the dust on a donkey’s back—who are indicated by their harsh nature and lack of serene confidence and affection toward the Buddha and the others;
even for one who serves gentle-minded, affectionate persons who abound in serene confidence toward the Buddha and the others;
and even for one who reflects upon the inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem while standing, sitting, or otherwise engaged.
It arises even for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and leaning toward the production of rapture.
He understands that when it has thus arisen, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.
As for the tranquility enlightenment factor—
“Bhikkhus, there is tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. In this regard,
frequent and thorough attention is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility if it has not yet arisen,
or to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has arisen.”
Thus there is arising. Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the tranquility factor of enlightenment:

the use of refined food, the use of a comfortable climate, the use of a comfortable posture, the practice of equanimity, avoidance of persons with agitated bodies, association with persons whose bodies are tranquil, and devotion thereto.

Tranquility arises even for one who eats refined, unctuous, and suitable food, and even for one who resorts to a suitable climate and posture during cold and hot seasons or while in various postures such as standing.
However, this was not said with reference to one who is of the nature of a Great Man (mahāpurisa), for such a person is capable of enduring all climates and postures. As for him...
There is similarity and dissimilarity. It arises even in one who avoids dissimilar postures and resorts only to similar ones.
"Neutral application" refers to reflecting on the fact that both oneself and others are the owners of their own karma;
it arises through this neutral application. This refers to one who wanders about actually harassing others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth.
It arises for one who avoids a person whose body is agitated, even while attending upon a person whose hands and feet are restrained and whose body is tranquil;
and it arises for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of tranquility during standing, sitting, and so forth.
Furthermore, he understands that when it has thus arisen, its cultivation reaches completion through the path of Arahantship.
Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration:
"Monks, there is the sign of serenity, the sign of non-distraction.

Frequent, thorough attention directed toward that is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration."
"It leads to increase, to expansion, to development, and to fulfillment"—thus there is arising.
In this context, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, and in the sense of non-distraction, it is the sign of non-confusion.
Furthermore, eleven factors lead to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor: making the basis pure; ... [and so forth] ... [the rest of the eleven factors]. Thus there is arising.
The balancing of the faculties, skill in signs, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time,
gladdening the mind at the proper time, maintaining equanimity at the proper time, avoiding persons who are unconcentrated,
associating with persons who are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and being intent upon them. Therein, "making the basis pure" means:
And the balancing of the faculties should be understood in the manner already described.
Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the sign of the kasiṇa.

"Exerting the mind at the proper time" means that at whatever time the mind becomes sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, at that time [one should exert it] by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture.

Its uplifting; "restraining the mind at the proper time" means that at whatever time the mind has become over-aroused due to excessive energy and so forth, at that time its restraint is achieved by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
"Encouraging it at the proper time" means at whatever time the mind [is sluggish] due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom...
Or, if it becomes unpalatable due to the failure to attain the bliss of tranquility, at that time one should arouse a sense of spiritual urgency by reflecting upon the eight grounds for urgency.
The eight grounds for urgency are: the four consisting of birth, aging, sickness, and death; the suffering of the states of deprivation as the fifth;
the suffering rooted in the round of existence in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
"It is suffering. And by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, he generates confidence. This is called "encouragement at the proper time.

As for "equanimity at the proper time": when, by means of right practice, the mind becomes free from sluggishness, free from over-exertion, free from dissatisfaction, proceeding evenly toward the object, and has entered the path of serenity (*samatha*), then—at that time—one should maintain equanimity regarding exertion, restraint, and encouragement.
He does not exert effort, like a charioteer with horses moving at an even pace. This is called equanimity toward the occasion (*samaye ajjhupekkhanatā*).

Avoidance of persons who are not concentrated means staying far away from persons whose minds are distracted and who have not attained either access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*). Cultivation of persons who are concentrated means [cultivating those] through access concentration or absorption...

It is the service, cultivation, and attendance upon those whose minds are concentrated. What is called "being intent upon that" is the state of having a mind that is inclined, directed, and leaning toward the production of concentration itself during standing, sitting, and so forth.
For when one practices in this way, this [concentration] arises.
Furthermore, he understands that once it has arisen in this manner, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.
Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity:

"Bhikkhus, there are states conducive to the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Frequent, thorough attention directed toward them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or for the growth and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity."
“It leads to increase, to expansion, to development, and to fulfillment”—thus there is arising.
In this context, equanimity itself is what is called the states conducive to the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

Furthermore, five things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: neutrality toward beings, neutrality toward formations, [neutrality toward pleasant and unpleasant feelings, neutrality toward mental objects, and neutrality toward the body]. Thus there is arising.
Avoiding persons who dally with the formations of beings, associating with persons who are neutral toward the formations of beings, and being intent upon that [neutrality].
Therein, one arouses neutrality toward beings in two ways:
"You have come by your own kamma and will go by your own kamma; this person too has come by his own kamma and will go by his own kamma."
"Whom do you cherish?"—thus by reflecting on the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*); and "In the ultimate sense, there is no self at all.
Who are you that cherishes anyone?"—thus by reflecting on the absence of a sentient being (*nissatta*). By these two modes he arouses equanimity toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-majjhattatā*):
"This robe, having gradually undergone changes in its color and reached a state of decay..."
"Having become a foot-wiping cloth, it will be discarded at the end of a staff.
Furthermore, by reflecting on its ownerless state thus: "If it had an owner, he would not allow it to be destroyed like this";
and by reflecting on its temporary nature thus: "This is not lasting; it is merely for the time being. And just as...
The same application should be made regarding the bowl and other requisites as well.
Regarding the phrase "avoiding persons who cherish the seven conditioned things":

here, a person—whether a householder who cherishes their own sons, daughters, and so forth, or one gone forth who cherishes their own pupils, co-residents, preceptors, and so forth—performs for them with their own hands such tasks as cutting hair, sewing with a needle, washing robes, dyeing them, boiling bowls, and so on.
Not seeing him for even a moment, he asks, "Where is that novice? Where is that young man?

Like a wandering deer, he looks here and there; and even when asked by another for the sake of shaving hair and so forth, "Please send such-and-such for a moment," he replies, "We ourselves do not perform that work; you will only weary yourselves by taking him."
He does not give it away—this is what is called the "Seven-fold Clinger" (*sattakelāyana*).
But he who treats robes, bowls, water-strainers, walking sticks, and so forth as his own property, and does not even allow another’s hand to touch them, even when asked for them temporarily, says:
"We ourselves do not use these because we treat them as our own; what business is it of yours?"

When one says, "I shall give," this is called a person who dotes on formations (*saṅkhārakelāyana*). However, one who is neutral and indifferent toward both of those two grounds is called a person who is neutral toward beings and formations (*sattasaṅkhāramajjhatta*).

Thus, this factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*) belongs to one who avoids from afar such persons who dote on beings and formations, as well as to a person who is neutral toward beings and formations.
It arises even for one who is serving [the path], and even for one whose mind is inclined, prone, and leaning toward its production while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Furthermore, he understands that for what has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of development through the path of Arahantship. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the section on the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).

In these two sections as well, pure insight (suddhavipassanā) alone is discussed. Thus, these four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are found in various states of mind during the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga);
for one comprehends the body with one state of mind, feeling with another, the mind with another, and mental phenomena (dhamma) with yet another.
However, at the moment of the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga), they are found within a single state of mind alone.
For one who has arrived after first investigating the body, the mindfulness associated with insight is called "contemplation of the body" (kāyānupassanā).

A person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one who contemplates the body. For one who has reached the noble path by bringing insight to its culmination, the mindfulness associated with the path at the moment of the path is called "contemplation of the body. One endowed with that mindfulness—
A person is called "one who contemplates the body" (*kāyānupassī*). Having grasped feeling (*vedanā*)... having grasped the mind (*citta*)...

for one who has come [to practice] having grasped phenomena (*dhamma*), the mindfulness associated with insight is called "contemplation of phenomena" (*dhammānupassanā*). A person endowed with that mindfulness is called "one who contemplates phenomena.
For one who, having intensified insight, has attained the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), at the moment of the Path, [the mindfulness] associated with the Path...
This is called mindfulness of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*). A person endowed with that mindfulness is called one who contemplates phenomena.

Thus, for the time being, the teaching rests upon the person. However, regarding the body, mindfulness that grasps the body is accomplished by means of the Path through the abandoning of the perversion that [views] it as "beautiful";
thus it is called contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*). Through the abandoning of the perversion that [views] feeling as "pleasure,"...
Mindfulness that grasps feelings succeeds through the Path; this is called the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*).
Mindfulness that grasps the mind succeeds through the Path by abandoning the perversion [of perceiving] the mind as permanent; this is called the contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*).
Mindfulness that grasps phenomena succeeds through the Path by abandoning the perversion [of perceiving] phenomena as a self; this is called the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*).
Thus, mindfulness associated with the path receives four names in the sense of accomplishing the four functions.
Therefore it was said: “But at the moment of the supramundane path, they are obtained in one and the same consciousness.
This concludes the commentary on the Suttantabhājanīya.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 374.

Since the teaching in the Abhidhammabhājanīya is undertaken by way of the supramundane foundations of mindfulness (lokuttara-satipaṭṭhāna), one should not establish the sequence in the same way as it was established for the mundane foundations of mindfulness (lokiya-satipaṭṭhāna) with respect to the objects such as the body; rather, all the foundations of mindfulness, beginning with the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), [should be treated] in their entirety.
These have been pointed out by one who shows merely the opening of the method of teaching as analyzed in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

In this regard, the classification of the methods should be understood. How so? First, in the case of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*), there is the pure practice (*suddhika-paṭipadā*) with a focus on jhāna, the pure emptiness (*suddhika-suññatā*), the practice of emptiness (*suññata-paṭipadā*), the pure wishlessness (*suddhika-appaṇihita*), and the practice of wishlessness (*appaṇihita-paṭipadā*).
In these five instances, there are ten methods (naya) by way of two sets of fourfold and fivefold methods respectively.
Likewise for the others; thus, in the twenty modes of misapprehension (abhinivesa), there are two hundred methods. These, multiplied by four through the four predominances (adhipati), become eight.
Thus, including the two pure [methods] and the eight with predominance, there are one thousand methods in total. The same applies to the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) and the rest.

And in the case of the bare foundations of mindfulness (*suddhika-satipaṭṭhāna*), there are five thousand methods regarding the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). And just as it is for the path of stream-entry, so it is for the remaining paths;
thus, in the wholesome (*kusala*), there are twenty thousand methods.

Furthermore, when divided according to emptiness (*suññatā*), the wishless (*appaṇihita*), the signless (*animitta*), and so forth, there are sixty thousand methods in the resultant (*vipāka*), which is three times that number. In this very way, [this applies] both to those who accomplish their own functions and to those whose functions are already perfected.
The exposition of the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya is twofold by way of the exposition of the wholesome and the wholesome-resultant foundations of mindfulness;

it is tenfold by way of the ten sections of exposition—five for the wholesome and five for the resultants—according to the modes of contemplation of the body and so forth, both in their pure form and in their detailed forms;
thus adorned with eighty thousand methods, it is the exposition of the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā) 386.
In the Section of Questions, the status of the foundations of mindfulness as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the text itself.
Regarding the triads of objects, however, all of these have exclusively immeasurable objects (*appamāṇārammaṇa*), because they proceed by taking as their object the immeasurable Nibbāna.
They do not have the Path as their object; rather, they have the Path as their cause by way of being co-nascent causes (*sahajātahetu*).

At the time of the cultivation of the Path, when either energy (*vīriya*) or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is made predominant, they have the Path as their predominance (*adhipati*). In the case of the cultivation of the Path where desire (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) is predominant, it cannot be said that they have the Path as their predominance;
thus, even at the time of the fruit (*phala*), they cannot be so described. This remains the case even regarding past objects and so forth, by virtue of having a single common object.
They are not to be spoken of [as internal or external]; however, because Nibbāna is an external phenomenon (*bahiddhādhamma*), they are called "having an external object" (*bahiddhārammaṇa*).

Thus, in this *Pañhāpucchaka*, only the supramundane (*lokuttara*) foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) have been explained. For it was in the *Suttantabhājanīya* alone that the Fully Enlightened One taught the foundations of mindfulness as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane; whereas in the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* and the *Pañhāpucchaka*, [only the supramundane ones are treated].

But [the latter] are exclusively supramundane. Thus, this Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga) has also been presented by extracting and distributing it according to its three turnings.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Foundations of Mindfulness in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga, is finished.
8. Analysis of the Right Strivings (Sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Suttanta Portion (Suttantabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā) 390.
Now, in the subsequent Analysis of the Right Strivings, "four" is the delimitation by number. By that [number], it is not...
From this point downward, it elucidates the section on the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).
"Right exertions" means exertion as the cause, exertion as the means, and exertion through proper method. "Here, a bhikkhu" refers to a bhikkhu practicing in this dispensation.
"Of those that have not arisen" means of those not yet produced. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states born of lack of skill.
"Anuppādāya" means not for the purpose of arising. "He generates desire" means he generates and produces wholesome desire (kusala-chanda), which is characterized by the wish to act.
"He exerts effort" means he applies himself and strives. "He arouses energy" means he exercises physical and mental energy.
"He uplifts the mind" means he raises the mind by means of that very co-nascent energy. "He strives" means...
He exerts the energy of striving. Furthermore, these four terms should be connected respectively with the practices of cultivation, development, frequent exercise, and persistence.
"Of evil states that have arisen" refers to those evil phenomena that have reached the state of having already arisen (and thus cannot be said to be "unarisen").
"For the abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing. "Of wholesome states that have not yet arisen" refers to those things produced by skill that have not yet come into being.

Of phenomena (*dhammānaṃ*). "For the arising" (*uppādāya*) means for the purpose of producing. "Of those that have arisen" (*uppannānaṃ*) means of those that have been generated. "For the stability" (*ṭhitiyā*) means for the purpose of persistence.

"For non-confusion" (*asammosāya*) means for the purpose of not being lost. "For increase" (*bhiyyobhāvāya*) means for repeated becoming. "For abundance" (*vepullāya*) means for the state of vastness. "For development" (*bhāvanāya*) means for growth.
"For fulfillment" (*pāripūriyā*) means for the purpose of complete perfection. This, first of all, is [the explanation] of the four right endeavors (*sammappadhāna*).
The extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*) consists of a single word by way of the section on the headings (*uddesavāra*).

Now, in order to explain those words by dividing them in their proper sequence, the section on the exposition (*niddesavāra*) is commenced with the method beginning: "And how, monks, [does a bhikkhu] regarding unarisen [states]...
Therein, that which is similar to what has already appeared in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* below is [to be understood] as such.
This should be understood according to the method already stated in the commentary. As for what has not yet been discussed therein, regarding the description of desire (*chanda*) first:
