"that which is desire" (*yo chando*) refers to desire by way of its quality of being desirable. "Zeal" (*chandikatā*) is the state of being zealous, or the mode of producing zeal.
"Desire to act" (*kattukamyatā*) is the wish to do. "Skilled" (*kusalo*) means clever. "Desire for the Dhamma" (*dhammacchando*) is desire for the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For this—

"Zeal" (*chanda*) is of many kinds and various types, such as the zeal of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*), the zeal of views (*diṭṭhi-chanda*), the zeal of energy (*vīriya-chanda*), and the zeal for the Dhamma (*dhamma-chanda*).
Among these, by "zeal for the Dhamma" in this context, the zeal for wholesome states consisting of the desire to act is intended.

To "generate this zeal" means that one generates zeal precisely while making zeal itself; thus it is called "generating. By means of the prefix (*upasagga*), it is said: "he brings about thoroughly" (*sañjaneti*).
The word is expanded [to *samuṭṭhapeti*]. "He raises it up" (*uṭṭhapeti*) means that while generating desire, he is said to raise it up.
"He fully raises it up" (*samuṭṭhapeti*) is the word expanded by means of a prefix. "He produces it" (*nibbatteti*) means that while generating desire, he is said to produce it.
"He fully produces it" (*abhinibbatteti*) is the word expanded by means of a prefix. Furthermore, while generating desire, he gives rise to desire.
It is called "producing" (*sañjaneti*) when one constantly performs that very same [action]. It is called "raising up" (*uṭṭhapeti*) when one picks up again what has fallen due to some obstacle.
It is called "re-erecting" (*samuṭṭhapeti*) when one brings about a continuous stability. It is called "generating" (*nibbatteti*) when one makes that manifest.
It is called "generating" by way of facing toward it, through non-neglect, through living without dejection, and through living without shrinking back.
It is called "producing.
394. In the description of energy (*vīriya*), one who is actually performing energy is said to "arouse energy" (*vīriyam ārabhati*); the second term is augmented by a prefix.
One who is actually performing energy is also said to "cultivate" (*āsevati*) and "develop" (*bhāveti*). Performing it again and again, one "makes much of it" (*bahulīkaroti*).
One who performs [the action] from the very beginning "undertakes" it. One who performs it again and again "commences" it.

One who devotes oneself to it by way of cultivation "cultivates" it. One who increases it "develops" it. It should be understood that one who makes that very same thing habitual in all duties "makes much of" it. 395.
In the exposition of the exertion of the mind, one "exerts the mind" by applying it through the exertion of energy; the meaning is that one raises it up.
Exerting again and again, he fully exerts. Having thus fully exerted it, he supports it with the support of energy so that it does not fall;
thus he supports it. Even when supported, supporting it again and again for the sake of its stability, he is said to "re-support" it.

406. In the exposition of the three terms for "stability" (*ṭhiti*), it is stated that "whatever is stability, that is non-confusion," and so forth, in order to show that all [qualities] such as non-confusion are synonyms for stability.
For here, it is appropriate to say that each preceding term is the meaning of each subsequent term, and each subsequent term is the meaning of each preceding term.
The rest is clear in meaning everywhere; this concludes, for now, the commentary on the text.
However, here is the analytical exposition (*vinicchaya-kathā*). This discourse on the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) is indeed twofold: mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Among these, the mundane occurs at all prior stages. It [is explained] by way of the method in the *Kassapa-saṃyutta* as occurring at the moment of the mundane path.
They should be understood. For it is said therein:
"Friends, there are four right endeavors. Which four?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu thinks: 'If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, that would lead to my harm.'"
“He applies energy, thinking: ‘If these evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in me are not abandoned, they will lead to my harm’;
he applies energy, thinking: ‘If these wholesome states that have not yet arisen in me do not arise, they will lead to my harm’;
he applies energy, thinking: ‘If these wholesome states that have arisen in me cease, they will lead to my harm.’”
And here, “unarisen wholesome states” refers both to serenity and insight as well as the path. “Arisen wholesome states” refers only to serenity and insight.
As for the path, once it has arisen, there is no such thing as its ceasing while leading to harm;
for it ceases only after having provided the condition for the fruit. Or else, in the former case, it refers only to serenity and insight.
It was said that [the passage] should be accepted, but that is not correct.
To clarify the meaning therein—that "serenity and insight, when arisen, lead to harm when they cease"—this is the story:
it is said that a certain elder whose taints were exhausted thought, "I shall pay homage to the Great Shrine and the Great Bodhi Tree."
Having come from the countryside to the Great Monastery together with a novice who was a keeper of the goods and who had attained meditative absorption, he entered the courtyard of the monastery.
At the time of evening, while the great community of monks was worshipping the shrine, he did not go out to worship the shrine himself. Why?
Because those whose taints were destroyed possessed great reverence for the Three Jewels. Therefore, toward the community of monks...
Having paid homage and returned, at the time when people were eating their evening meal, he went out alone, thinking, "I shall pay homage to the cetiya," without even informing the novice.
The novice thought, "Why is the elder going out alone at an improper time?
I shall find out," and set out following right behind his preceptor's footsteps. The elder, however, did not perceive his arrival through mental advertence.
Unaware [of the elder’s intention], he ascended the courtyard of the Great Cetiya by way of the southern gate. The novice monk ascended immediately after him.
The great elder, having gazed upon the Great Cetiya and experienced joy directed toward the Buddha, focused his entire mind and, with a radiant countenance, paid homage to the Great Cetiya.
Seeing the manner of the elder’s homage, the novice thought: “My preceptor...”
"He pays homage with a mind exceedingly serene; what if I were to obtain flowers and perform an offering? he thought.
As the elder stood there, having paid homage, risen, and placed his hands in añjali upon his head while gazing up at the Mahācetiya, the novice cleared his throat to let him know that he had arrived.
The elder turned around and looked, asking, "When did you arrive?"
He asked: “Venerable sir, when you were paying homage to the cetiya, you paid homage with great faith.
Having obtained flowers, would you not have offered them? “Yes, novice, there is no other relic deposit (*dhātunidhāna*) equal to that in this cetiya.
Having obtained flowers for such an incomparable Great Thūpa...”
“Who would not worship it? “In that case, venerable sir, please consent;

I shall bring it. Having immediately entered into meditative absorption and gone to the Himālaya by means of psychic power, he took flowers endowed with excellent color and fragrance, filled a water-strainer with them, and returned before the Great Elder had even reached the western gate from the southern gate, [carrying] the flower-strainer.
Placing [the flowers] in his hand, he said, "Venerable sir, offer them in worship. The Elder said, "The flowers are too small for us, novice.
"Go, venerable sir, and offer them in worship while reflecting upon the virtues of the Blessed One.
The Elder ascended by the staircase situated at the western entrance and proceeded to perform the flower offering on the floor of the inner railing.
He began. The terrace was completely filled; the flowers fell and covered the second level with a depth reaching up to the knees.
Then, descending, he honored the footstool rail; that too was filled.
Knowing it was full, he proceeded scattering them on the lower floor; the entire courtyard of the shrine was filled. When that was full—
“The flowers do not diminish, novice,” he said. “Venerable sir, turn the water-strainer upside down,” [the novice] replied.

Having turned it upside down, he shook it; then the flowers were exhausted. The Elder gave the water-strainer back to the novice, and together with him, circumambulated the Cetiya three times by way of the elephant-rampart, and paid homage at four places.
As he was going to his own cell, he thought: "How great indeed is this novice's psychic power!
Will he be able to preserve this mastery of supernormal power? Then, seeing that he would not be able to do so, he said to the novice:
"Novice, you are now possessed of great psychic power; yet, having destroyed such a power, at the end of your life you will be like a blind weaver, with your hand—
“Will you drink sour gruel that has been stirred? Such is the fault of childhood:
though he was moved by his preceptor’s words, he did not ask, “Venerable sir, please explain a meditation subject to me”;
instead, he went along as if he had not heard what his preceptor said.
The Elder, having paid homage to the Mahācetiya and the Mahābodhi tree, had the novice take his bowl and robes and proceeded by stages until he reached the Kuṭeḷitissa Mahāvihāra.
The novice followed step by step behind his preceptor and did not go out for alms.
Having asked, "To which village are you entering, venerable sir? [the Elder replied], "Now my preceptor..."

Knowing that he would arrive at the village gate, [the novice] took his own bowl and robes and those of his preceptor, came through the air, gave the bowl and robes to the Elder, and entered the village for alms. The Elder constantly exhorted him:
"Novice, do not act in this way; the psychic power of an ordinary person is indeed unstable and unsteady; it is unsuitable when directed toward objects such as forms."
"Having attained [a state], it breaks apart with even the slightest [distraction]; having fallen away from a peaceful attainment, one is unable to steady oneself while living the holy life.
The novice did not wish to hear what his preceptor was saying, so he acted accordingly.
The elder, gradually performing the worship of the cetiya, arrived at Kammupendavihāra.
He went by that name. While he was staying there, the novice monk acted in exactly the same way.

Then one day, a weaver’s daughter—beautiful and in the prime of her youth—departed from Kammupendagāma, descended into the lotus pond, and was gathering flowers while singing. At that moment, the novice monk [was at] the edge of the lotus pond.
But as he was going along, like a blind fly attracted by the scent of *sakkarala* resin, he became captivated by the sound of her singing;
at that very moment, his supernormal power (*iddhi*) vanished, and he became like a crow with severed wings.

However, by the power of his attainment of the peaceful meditative absorptions (*santasamāpatti*), he did not fall into the water there, but descending like a *simbali* cotton-wool, he gradually reached the bank of the lotus pond.
He stood there. He went quickly, gave his preceptor’s bowl and robes, and turned back. The Great Elder thought, “I saw this already;
even if he is restrained, he will not turn back,” and without saying anything, he entered for alms.
The novice went and stood on the bank of the lotus pond, waiting for her to come across. She too [saw] the novice...
Seeing him traveling through the air and then returning to stand there, she realized, "Surely he has become weary because of me," and said, "Step back, novice!
He stepped back. She climbed out [of the water], put on her garment, approached him, and asked, "What is it, venerable sir?
He explained the matter to her. She [convinced him] by means of many reasons...
Although she exhorted him by showing the dangers of the household life and the benefits of living the holy life, she was unable to dispel his weariness.
Thinking, “Because of me, he has fallen away from such supernatural power;
it is no longer right for me to abandon him,” she said, “Stay right here! and having gone home, she reported the matter to her parents.
Approaching the bank and advising him in various ways, they said to him as he refused to accept their words:
"Do not regard us as being from a noble family; we are weavers. Will you be able to perform the work of a weaver? The novice replied:
"Lay follower, when one has become a householder, one might indeed engage in the work of a weaver or the work of a basket-maker; what is the use of this?"
"Do not set your greed on a mere garment. The weaver, having given her the garment tied around his waist, took her home and gave her to him as a daughter-in-law.
Having learned the craft of weaving, he worked in the workshop together with the other weavers.
While the wives of the others brought their food prepared early in the morning, his wife had not yet arrived. He [watched] the work of the others...
While they were eating after having set aside [the food], he sat spinning his spindle. She arrived later.
Then he rebuked her, saying, "You have come too late. Now, women—even when it is known that a Universal Monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) has his heart bound to them—regard him as if he were a slave.
Therefore, she spoke thus: "In the houses of others, there is wood, leaves, salt, and so forth..."
“[The food] is already prepared; there are donors and weavers who have brought it from outside.
But I am all alone, and you do not even know whether this or that exists in my house. If you wish to eat, eat; if you do not wish to eat, do not eat.
He became angry, thinking, “Not only have you served the meal late, but you have also provoked me with your words.”
Seeing no other weapon, she tore a piece from that very shuttle-stick at the weaving beam and hurled it.
Seeing it coming toward her, she turned slightly away. Now, the tip of a shuttle-stick is sharp;
as she turned, the stick entered the corner of her eye and remained there. She grasped the eye with both hands with great force, and blood flowed from the punctured spot.
Then, at that moment, he recalled his preceptor’s words:
"It was with reference to this that my preceptor said to me, 'In the future, you will drink sour gruel kneaded by the hand of a blind weaver. This must have been seen by the Elder.
Oh, what a man of far-reaching vision this noble one is! Thinking thus, he began to weep with a loud cry. Others said to him, "Enough!..."
"Friend, do not weep; for once an eye is broken, it cannot be restored to its original state by weeping," they said.
He replied, "It is not for this reason that I weep; rather, it is with reference to this that I weep," and he related the entire sequence of events.
Thus, serenity and insight, when they have arisen, lead to harm when they cease.

Another story: About thirty bhikkhus, having paid homage to the Mahācetiya at Kalyāṇī, were descending from the forest path toward the main road when they saw a man coming along the way who had returned from working in a cremation ground.
His body was smeared with ashes, and he wore a single saffron robe that was likewise smeared with ashes.
It was wrapped around him so tightly that when looked at, he appeared like a charred log.
Having finished his work during the day, he lifted a bundle of half-burnt wood, came along a by-path with his hair disheveled over his back, and stood before the monks.
Seeing him, the novices looked at one another and said, "Friend,..."
“Your father, your grandfather, your maternal uncle! they said, laughing, and having approached, asked his name: “What is your name, lay follower?
Being thus questioned about his name, he became remorseful;
he threw away the bundle of wood, adjusted his cloth, put it on, paid homage to the great elders, and said, “Wait a moment, venerable sirs. The great elders waited.
The young novices came and even mocked the great elders in their presence. The lay devotee said: “Venerable sirs, you mock me upon seeing me;
do not think that you have reached the pinnacle by this alone.
In the past, I too was a recluse just like you. Yet, you possess not even a modicum of one-pointedness of mind. I—”
"In this teaching, I was one of great psychic power and great majesty; taking up the sky, I made it earth, and making earth, I made it sky;
taking what was far, I brought it near, and bringing what was near, I made it far; in an instant, I pierced through a thousand world-systems.
Look at my hands; yet now they are like the hands of a monkey. With these very same hands—"
"Seated right here, I touched the sun and the moon. Using these very footprints as a footstool for the sun and the moon, I sat upon them.
Such supernormal power of mine was lost through negligence. You must not be negligent;
for through negligence, people encounter such calamity. By dwelling heedfully, they make an end to birth, aging, and death."
"Therefore, venerable sirs, being heedful, take me alone as your object," he said, and after thus admonishing them with a word of exhortation,
they were so moved by spiritual urgency that while still listening to his speech, thirty of them attained Arahantship right there through insight.
Thus, even serenity and insight, when they arise and then cease, lead to what is disadvantageous.
This much, then, is the exposition of the discourse on mundane right effort (*lokīyasammappadhāna*).
At the moment of the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*), however, this single energy (*vīriya*) receives four names by way of accomplishing four functions.
Among these, "of those that have not arisen" refers to those that have not arisen either because they do not manifest or because their object has not been experienced.
For otherwise, there are no evil unwholesome states that have not arisen in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Yet, when they arise, it is only these that arise; and when they are abandoned, it is only these that are abandoned.

In this regard, for some, the defilements (*kilesa*) do not manifest due to the practice of the observances (*vatta*); for others, [they do not manifest] due to the bonds (*gantha*), the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), concentration (*samādhi*), and insight (*vipassanā*).
By way of being one of those engaged in new construction work. How so? For a certain person is endowed with the proper conduct (*vatta*).

While he performs the eighty-two minor conducts, the fourteen major conducts, and the conducts regarding the shrine courtyard, the Bodhi-tree courtyard, the water shed, the Uposatha hall, and the duties for visitors and those departing, the defilements find no opportunity.
However, later on, having abandoned that conduct...
They arise for one who has broken the training rules and wanders about, owing to improper attention and the loss of mindfulness.
Thus, by way of non-occurrence, those not yet arisen are said to "arise.
A certain person is devoted to the texts: he learns one Nikāya, or two, or three, or four, or even five.
For one who grasps, recites, reflects upon, teaches, and explains that very word of the Buddha contained in the Three Pitakas—
according to its meaning, its text, its sequence, and its internal consistency—
the defilements find no opportunity. However, later on, for one who has abandoned the work of study and wanders about indolent, there arise improper attention and the loss of mindfulness.
They arise by coming together. In this way, too, they are said to "arise" when previously unarisen, by virtue of their non-occurrence.
Furthermore, there is a certain person who is a bearer of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); having undertaken the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices, he conducts himself accordingly.
While he maintains those ascetic qualities, the defilements find no opportunity; however, at a later time, having abandoned those ascetic practices...

They arise by way of the negligence of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the abandonment of mindfulness (*sati-ossagga*) as one wanders about for the sake of abundance and the [five] hindrances (*āvaṭṭa*).
Thus, even by way of non-occurrence, they are said to "arise" when not yet arisen.
Furthermore, someone may have mastery over the eight attainments (*samāpatti*); for him, regarding the first jhāna and so forth, there is mastery in adverting (*āvajjana-vasī*) and so on.
While one dwells by means of this [practice], the defilements find no opportunity.

However, at a later time, for one whose jhāna has degenerated or been abandoned, and who dwells intent on idle talk and the like, the defilements arise due to unwise attention and the lapse of mindfulness.
In this way, even by way of non-occurrence, previously unarisen defilements are said to "arise."
But another is a practitioner of insight (vipassaka); he dwells performing work upon either the seven insights or the eighteen great insights.
As he dwells in this way, the defilements find no opportunity.
Later on, however, having abandoned the work of insight and dwelling with an abundance of physical rigidity, through improper attention and the neglect of mindfulness—
They arise by coming together. In this way too, unarisen defilements are said to arise by way of non-occurrence.
Furthermore, a certain person is a supervisor of building works and constructs a Uposatha hall, a dining hall, and so forth.
While he is thinking about those requisites, the defilements find no opportunity; however, later on, when his building work is finished or abandoned...

Or they arise by way of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the abandonment of mindfulness (*sati-ossagga*). In this way, too, unarisen defilements (*kilesa*) are said to "arise" by virtue of their non-occurrence.
Furthermore, someone who has come from the Brahma-world is a pure being (*suddhasatta*); because of his lack of habituation (*anāsevanā*), the defilements find no opportunity [to arise].
They obtain [them]; however, at a later stage, when he has become habituated to them, they arise due to improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the abandonment of mindfulness (*sati-ossagga*).

In this way too, defilements that have not yet arisen are said to "arise" by virtue of their non-occurrence. Thus, first of all, their state of being unarisen should be understood by way of non-occurrence.
How do they arise by way of an object never before experienced? Here, someone obtains an object previously unexperienced, such as one that is pleasing and so forth.
Through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the lapse of mindfulness regarding that object, the defilements such as lust arise.
Thus, by way of an object never before experienced, those not yet arisen are said to "arise. However, at the moment of the supramundane path, there is only a single effort.

And as for those [unwholesome states] that have not yet arisen which might arise in this way, he accomplishes their non-arising so that they do not arise at all, and he accomplishes the task of abandoning those that have already arisen.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "of evil states that have arisen," there are four kinds of "arisen":

arisen as currently occurring (*vattamānuppanna*), arisen having been experienced and then passed away (*bhutvā vigatuppanna*), arisen by providing an opportunity (*okāsakatuppanna*), and arisen by reaching the plane of manifestation (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*).
In this context, those defilements that exist and are possessed of arising and so forth—this is called "presently arisen" (*vattamānuppanna*).
Furthermore, when an action has impelled and the resultant state has ceased after having experienced the flavor of the object, it is called "past" (*vigata*).
When an action has arisen and ceased, it is called "past. Both of these, having been and having passed away, are designated as "arisen by way of having been and passed away" (*bhūtvā vigatuppanna*).
It proceeds. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma, having obstructed the fruition of other kamma, makes room for its own fruition.
When the fruition arises once this room has been made, it is said to have "arisen from the making of room. This is what is called "arising by way of making room" (*okāsakatuppanna*).
The five aggregates, moreover, are called the "ground" for insight (vipassanā).
They are divided into the past and so forth. Regarding these, it cannot be said that the latent defilements (anusaya) dwelling within them are past, future, or present.
For even those latent defilements dwelling in past aggregates remain unabandoned; likewise, those dwelling in future and present aggregates also remain unabandoned.
These are what is called "arisen by way of having attained a plane. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"Defilements that have not been eradicated in their respective planes are designated as 'arisen by way of having attained a plane.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold classification of what is arisen: arisen as manifestation, arisen by way of apprehending an object, and arisen as unobstructed.
"Arising that has not been eradicated. In this context, only that which is currently occurring is called "arising through manifestation.
Once the eyes have been opened and the sign of the object has been grasped, it cannot be said that defilements will not arise at every moment of recollection.
Why? Because the object has been apprehended. How so? Just as with a milky tree [being cut] by an axe...
It cannot be said that milk will not come out from a place where it has been struck; it is the same here.
This is what is called "arisen by apprehending an object. However, it cannot be said that defilements which have not been suppressed by attainment will not arise in this particular place.
Why? Because they have not been suppressed. How so? Just as if one were to strike a milky tree with an axe—
In the same way, one cannot say, "Milk will not flow from this particular spot. This is called "arisen but not suppressed" (*avikkhambhituppanna*).

However, as for the defilements that have not been eradicated by the Path, it should be explained in detail according to the previous method that they will not arise even for one reborn in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
This is called "arisen but not eradicated" (*asamugghātituppanna*).

Among these, when they have arisen, there are four kinds of "arisen" that are not to be abandoned by the Path: arisen as occurring, arisen as having been experienced and passed away, arisen as making room, and arisen as manifest activity.

There are four kinds of "arisen" that are to be abandoned by the Path: arisen as obtained through the plane, arisen as grasped by the object, arisen as un-suppressed, and arisen as un-eradicated. For when the Path is arising...
He abandons these defilements. Those defilements which he abandons cannot be said to be past, future, or present.
And this has been said:
"If he abandons past defilements, then he is exhausting what is already exhausted, ceasing what is already ceased, and removing what is already gone."
He makes it vanish; he causes that which has reached its end to go to its end; he abandons that which is past and non-existent.
If he abandons future defilements, then indeed he abandons the unborn, the unproduced, the unarisen, and the unmanifested;
he abandons that which is future and non-existent. If he abandons present defilements, then indeed one who is lustful...
One who is lustful abandons lust; one who is hating abandons hatred; one who is deluded abandons delusion; one who is bound up abandons conceit;

one who is misapprehending abandons wrong view; one who has fallen into distraction abandons restlessness; one who has gone to what is undesirable abandons doubt; one who has become entrenched abandons underlying tendency.
Dark and bright states proceed yoked together and equally; thus there is a path-cultivation that leads to defilement... [as before] ...Therefore, indeed, there is no cultivation of the path.
“There is no realization of the fruit, there is no abandoning of the defilements, there is no breakthrough to the Dhamma. “There is cultivation of the path...
[and so on] ...there is breakthrough to the Dhamma. “In what way? “Just as a young tree...
[and so on] ...those things that had not yet appeared do not appear.”
Thus, although a tree with unripened fruit is mentioned in the Pāḷi, it should be illustrated by means of a tree with ripened fruit.
For example, there is a young mango tree bearing fruit. People might eat some of its fruits and fill their baskets with the remainder that has fallen.
Then, another person might cut it down with an axe. By doing so, he does not destroy the fruits that have already passed away.
Neither those that are future nor those that are present have been destroyed. For those that are past have already been consumed by people;
those that are future have not yet arisen and thus cannot be destroyed. Furthermore, at the very moment the tree is cut down, there are no fruits at all;
therefore, even those that are present have not been destroyed. However, if the tree were not cut down, then its earth-essence and...
Just as those fruits that would have arisen depending on water are destroyed— since they do not arise even when unarisen,
do not come into being even when unproduced, and do not manifest even when unmanifested— in the same way,
the Path neither abandons nor does it not abandon the defilements categorized as past and so forth. For those defilements [which have been abandoned] by the Path...
When the aggregates have not been fully understood, their arising may occur;

but once the aggregates have been fully understood through the Path, those defilements—having not yet arisen—do not arise, having not yet been produced—do not come into being, and having not yet become manifest—do not become manifest.
This is like a woman with young children who does not give birth again, or like those afflicted by disease whose ailments are pacified by medicines they have drunk.

Furthermore, this meaning must be clarified: it cannot be said that the defilements which the Path abandons are past, future, or present; nor is it the case that the Path does not abandon defilements.
However, with reference to those defilements which the Path does abandon, it was said: "Of evil states that have arisen," and so forth.
Not only does the path abandon the defilements alone, but because of the non-abandonment of the defilements, it also abandons those aggregates of clinging that would otherwise arise.

And this has been said: "By means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, through the cessation of volitional consciousness, name-and-form which would have arisen in the beginningless cycle of existence—setting aside the seven [remaining] existences—are abandoned."

“Here these cease,” and so on in detail. Thus, the path emerges from both the acquired (*upādinna*) and the unacquired (*anupādinna*). Furthermore, by way of existence (*bhava*): the stream-entry path emerges from the existence of the states of misery (*apāyabhava*);
the once-return path emerges from one portion of the existence of happy destinations (*sugatibhava*); the non-return path emerges from the existence of sensual desire in happy destinations;
the path of Arahantship emerges from the existence of the fine-material and immaterial realms, that is, from all forms of existence.
Some even say that it emerges [from the attainment].
Now, at the moment of the Path, how is there development for the arising of those [states] not yet arisen?
Or how is there stability for those already arisen? It is simply through the occurrence of the Path itself; for while the Path is occurring, it is "unarisen" because it has never arisen before.
This is what is called "name. For having gone to a place never before reached, or having experienced an object never before experienced, people say:
"We have come to a place not yet reached; we are experiencing an object not yet experienced.
And its process is precisely what is called "station" (ṭhiti); thus it is appropriate to say that one develops [the mind] for the sake of station. In this way, for him—

At the moment of the supramundane path, this energy of a bhikkhu receives four names, beginning with "for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. This is the discourse on the right exertions at the moment of the supramundane path.
Thus, herein the right exertions, both mundane and supramundane, have been demonstrated.
Commentary on the Suttanta-Bhājaniya.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya. 408.
In the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya, all the right efforts (sammappadhāna) follow the method of teaching as analyzed in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
These have been pointed out by the Teacher merely as a mere indication of the beginning. In this regard, the distinction of the methods (*nayabheda*) should be understood. How so?

First, regarding the first right exertion (*sammappadhāna*), within the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), there are five points: the pure practice (*suddhikapaṭipadā*), pure emptiness (*suddhikasuññatā*), the practice of emptiness (*suññatapaṭipadā*), the pure wishless (*suddhikaappaṇihitā*), and the practice of the wishless (*appaṇihitapaṭipadā*).
In these five places, there are two sets of fourfold and fivefold methods (*catukkapañcakanaya*).
By way of these [factors], there are ten methods (*nayā*). Thus, with the remaining [factors] as well, there are two hundred methods for each of the twenty types of misapprehension (*abhinivesa*).
These, multiplied fourfold by the four predominances (*adhipati*), become eight. Thus, including the two pure [methods] and the eight with predominance, there is a total of one thousand methods.
Likewise, in the case of the second right effort (*sammappadhāna*) and so forth, including the pure right efforts themselves, this applies to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
There are five thousand methods. And just as it is for the path of stream-entry, so it is for the remaining paths; thus, by way of the wholesome alone, there are twenty thousand methods.
However, since there is no function to be performed by the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) in the case of fruition (*vipāka*), the section on fruition has not been included.
It should be understood that the right efforts mentioned here refer exclusively to those supramundane states that have already been produced.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchaka). 427.
In the Section of Questions, the status of the right efforts as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the text itself. Regarding the triads of objects (ārammaṇattika):
However, all of these have only the immeasurable Nibbāna as their object because they proceed by taking that as their focus, and not the Path as their object;
yet, by way of the co-nascent cause, they have the Path as their cause. At the time of developing the Path by making investigation predominant, they have the Path as their predominance;
but they cannot be said to have the Path as their predominance when the development of the Path is performed with desire or consciousness as the predominant factors.

Furthermore, because there is no other energy superior to this energy, it cannot be said that these [factors] have the Path as their predominance (*maggādhipati*), nor can it be said that they do not.
Nor can they be said to have the past and so forth as their object by virtue of having a single object.

However, because Nibbāna is an external phenomenon (*bahiddhādhamma*), they are called "having an external object" (*bahiddhārammaṇa*). Thus, in this set of questions, only those supramundane states that have been produced are [discussed].
The right efforts (sammappadhānāni) have been explained. For by the Fully Enlightened One, in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, the right efforts mixed with both mundane and supramundane states were explained;
however, in the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya and the Pañhāpucchaka, they are explained as exclusively supramundane.
Thus, this analysis of the right efforts (sammappadhāna-vibhaṅga) has also been presented by dividing it after having extracted its threefold turnings.
The explanation of the Analysis of the Right Strivings in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, is completed. 9.
The Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power (*Iddhipādavibhaṅga*).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta-Bhājaniya 431.
Now, in the immediately following *Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga*, "four" is the delimitation by number. Regarding the term *iddhipādā*:
here, it is called *iddhi* because it succeeds (*ijjhati*); the meaning is that it is accomplished and brought to fruition. Or else, beings succeed by means of it; they become successful (*iddhā*).
It is also called *iddhi* because it is grown and has reached its peak. In the first sense, *iddhipāda* means "the foot of success" (*iddhi* itself is the foot);
the meaning is "a factor of success. In the second sense, *iddhipāda* means "the foot for success"; "foot" here means a foundation or a means of attainment.
For it is by means of this that one goes to and reaches success, which is designated as successive distinction; therefore, it is called a "foot."
Thus, first, the meaning of the phrase "the four bases of psychic power" (cattāro iddhipādā) should be understood.
Now, in order to explain them by way of analysis, the passage beginning with "Here, monks... is commenced.

In that context, "here, monks" means a monk in this dispensation. Regarding the term "endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving" (chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata): here, it refers to that which has desire as its cause and desire as its predominant factor.
Or "concentration" refers to *chandasamādhi*. This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) predominant.
"Exertive formations" (*padhāna-saṅkhārā*) are formations that constitute exertion; this is a designation for the energy of right effort (*sammappadhāna-vīriya*) which accomplishes the four tasks.
"Endowed with" means possessed of both *chandasamādhi* and the exertive formations. "Basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*).
Alternatively, by way of the sequence of accomplishment, or by the sense of succeeding— whereby beings succeed through this [power], becoming successful, prosperous, and reaching the pinnacle—

it is the entire collection of remaining consciousness and mental factors that serves as the foundation for the "bases" (pāda), namely the volitional formations of desire-concentration and exertion, which are associated with wholesome states such as access concentration and so forth, and which have attained the designation of "success" (iddhi) in this manner.

This is the meaning. For that which is stated later—“The basis of psychic power is the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness of one who has become thus”—is consistent with this meaning.
In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining [bases] as well.
Just as concentration obtained by making desire the dominant factor is called “concentration due to desire,” so too [is it for] energy... [and so on].
Regarding the mind: concentration attained by making investigation the dominant factor is called "investigative concentration" (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi*).
Now, in order to explain and demonstrate the terms beginning with "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*) and so forth, the passage beginning with "And how, monks...

is commenced. Therein, "if a monk makes desire the dominant factor" means: if a monk makes desire the dominant factor—that is, desire— *Note: The provided source text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on the *Visuddhimagga*. The sentence is left incomplete at the end.*
Making desire the eldest, the leader, and the precursor, one attains and produces concentration;
the meaning is that this concentration, thus produced, is called "concentration through desire" (*chandasamādhi*).

The same method applies to the phrases beginning with "energy" (*vīriya*) and so forth. Up to this point—namely, "these are called the formations of striving"—it concerns one who is developing the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chandiddhipāda*).
The energy described as accomplishing the four functions comprised within the volitional formations of striving for a bhikkhu is what is meant.
"Having gathered that together" means having made all of that into a single heap; "it comes to be reckoned" should be understood to mean that it receives this designation.

433. Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate the factors such as desire (*chanda*) within this group of terms, "the volitional formation of concentration through desire" (*chandasa-mādhipadhānasaṅkhāra*), the passage beginning with "What is desire? is commenced. Its meaning is self-evident.
"He is possessed of" means he is possessed of the mass of Dhamma known as the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). "Of those states" refers to those associated states, such as desire and the rest.
"Success" (*iddhi*), "accomplishment" (*samiddhi*), and so forth—all these are synonyms for the result of attainment. Even though this is so...

*Iddhi* (success) is so called in the sense of succeeding (*ijjhanaka*). *Samiddhi* (complete success) is *iddhi* that is fulfilled; alternatively, the word has been expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*).

*Ijjhanā* (succeeding) is the mode of succeeding. *Samijjhanā* (attaining) is the word expanded by means of a prefix. *Lābha* (gain) is the obtaining [of something] by way of its manifestation within one's own continuity (*santāna*).
*Paṭilābha* (re-gain) is the obtaining again, even of those things previously lost, by way of the exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*); [this too is expanded] by means of a prefix.
Or "pada" is increased. "Attainment" (patti) means reaching [the goal]. "Accomplishment" (sampatti) means reaching correctly by way of non-decline.

"Touching" (phusana) is the touching of acquisition. "Realization" (sacchikiriyā) is indeed the realization of acquisition. "Full attainment" (upasampadā) should be understood as the full attainment of acquisition.
"Of one who has become such" (tayābhūtassa) means of one who has become in that manner; the meaning is: of one who stands having acquired those states beginning with desire (chandādi).

By the phrases beginning with "the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandha*), all four aggregates are spoken of, having included desire (*chanda*) and the others within them. "Those phenomena" (*te dhamme*) refers to those four immaterial aggregates;
alternatively, it is also stated that it refers to the three phenomena beginning with desire. "He cultivates" (*āsevati*) and so forth have meanings already explained.
In the remaining explanations of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the meaning should be understood by this same method.
What has been stated thus far? A meditation subject that has reached its ultimate perfection for four types of bhikkhus has been explained.

For one bhikkhu relies upon desire: through the wholesome desire for the Dhamma and the wish to act, when there is the accomplishment of the goal, he thinks, "I shall produce the supramundane Dhamma; I have no burden in its production."
Making zeal the chief, zeal the burden, and zeal the precursor, one generates supramundane states.
One relies on energy; another relies on consciousness; another relies on wisdom. When the goal is accomplished through wisdom, [one thinks]:
"I shall generate supramundane states; there is no burden for me in their generation."
Making wisdom the chief, wisdom the yoke, and wisdom the forerunner, one brings about supramundane states.

How so? Just as when four sons of ministers wander about seeking positions of authority—one relies on attendance, one on bravery, one on noble birth, and one on counsel—how so? Among them, the first [relied] on attendance...
The first [minister] relied on the readiness [of the troops], thinking: "If there is diligence and the accomplishment of the objective, we shall obtain this position.
The second [minister] thought: "Even one who is diligent in his readiness may not be able to hold his ground when battle is actually joined;
moreover, the king's frontier will surely revolt, and when it revolts, the task will fall upon the chariot-commander."
The first thoughted, "By making myself a king and pleasing him, we shall have this position brought to us," and thus he relied upon his valor.

The second thoughted, "Even when one possesses valor, there are some of low birth; if they grant a position after purifying their lineage, they will grant it to me," and thus he relied upon his birth.
The third thoughted, "Even one of noble birth may be unconsultable; in matters that must be done by means of counsel..."
Thinking, "When [an opportunity] arises, we shall cause him to obtain this position," they took refuge in counsel.
All of them, by the power of their respective refuge, attained positions of authority.

Just as one who, being diligent in attendance there, attains a position of authority, so too by taking refuge in zeal—that is, through the wholesome desire for action (*kattukamyatā*) and the desire for wholesome states (*kusaladhammacchanda*).

When the production of the supramundane state (*lokuttara-dhamma*) is to occur, one should be seen as a producer of the supramundane state by making zeal (*chanda*) the chief, the burden, and the precursor—thinking, "I shall produce the supramundane state;
there is no burden for me in its production"—just like the Elder Raṭṭhapāla. For that venerable one, having made zeal his burden, [realized] the supramundane state.

He brought it forth. Just as one who, having pleased a king by his courageous nature, attains a high position, so too should he be regarded as one who brings forth supramundane states by making energy the eldest, the leader, the burden-bearer, and the precursor—just like the Elder Soṇa.
For that venerable one, making energy his burden-bearer, brought forth supramundane states.

Just as one who has attained a high position through the excellence of his birth, one should be seen as a producer of supramundane states by making the mind the eldest, the leader, the chief, and the precursor—just like the Elder Sambhūta. For that venerable one produced supramundane states by making the mind his chief.
Just as one who has attained a high position by relying on a mantra, [one should rely on] investigation...

One should be regarded as a producer of supramundane states by making investigation the foremost, the burden, and the precursor—just like the Elder Mogharāja. For that venerable one produced supramundane states by making investigation his primary focus.

And herein, the three factors consisting of desire-concentration, energy-concentration, and volitional-formation-concentration are both supernormal powers (*iddhi*) and bases for supernormal power (*iddhipāda*).
The remaining four associated aggregates, however, are simply bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

The three factors consisting of the volitional formations of exertion—namely, energy, consciousness, and investigation-concentration—are both psychic powers (*iddhi*) and bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). The remaining four associated aggregates, however, are simply bases of psychic power.
This, then, is the explanation according to the undifferentiated perspective.

As for the classification: "zeal" (*chanda*) is called the psychic power (*iddhi*). The four aggregates (*khandha*) developed through the predominance of zeal are called the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal (*chandiddhipāda*).

The two factors—concentration (*samādhi*) and the volitional formations of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*)—enter into the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal by way of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);
it is indeed appropriate to say that they have entered into that basis. In that very context, "concentration" is called the psychic power. Through the predominance of concentration...
The four aggregates when cultivated are called the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration (*samādhiddhipāda*).

The two phenomena—the desire (*chanda*) and the volitional formation of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*)—enter into the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration by way of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); it is indeed appropriate to say that they have entered into that basis.
In that very context, "volitional formation of striving" is what is called psychic power (*iddhi*). The four aggregates cultivated through the volitional formation of striving [are the basis].

This is called the basis of psychic power consisting of the volitional formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra-iddhipāda*). The two factors—zeal (*chanda*) and concentration (*samādhi*)—enter into the basis of psychic power consisting of the volitional formations of striving by way of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);
it is indeed appropriate to say that they have entered into that basis.

In that very same [basis], "energy" (*vīriya*) is called psychic power, "mind" (*citta*) is called psychic power, and "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) is called psychic power... [and so on] ...it is also appropriate to say that they have entered into that basis.
It is indeed appropriate to speak thus.

This is what is called the discourse on analysis (*bhedato kathā*). However, there is nothing new here; that which was already grasped has simply been made clear by its constituent elements (*dhātuka*). How so?

These three factors—zeal (*chanda*), concentration (*samādhi*), and the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*)—are both supernormal powers (*iddhi*) and bases of supernormal power (*iddhipāda*). The remaining four associated [mental states] are...
The aggregates are themselves the bases of success (*iddhipāda*). For these three factors, when they succeed, succeed only together with the four associated aggregates, not apart from them.

However, the four associated aggregates are called "success" (*iddhi*) in the sense of succeeding, and "base" (*pāda*) in the sense of being a foundation. Thus, neither "success" nor "base of success" refers to anything other than these.
It is a designation for something; it is a designation for the four associated aggregates themselves.

The three factors—energy, mind, and the volitional formation of investigation-concentration (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra*)—... [as before] ... are a designation for the four aggregates themselves.
Furthermore, it should be understood that each preceding stage is called a "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*), while each attainment is called "psychic power" (*iddhi*).
This meaning should be illustrated either by way of access concentration (*upacāra*) or by way of insight (*vipassanā*).

For the preliminary work for the first jhāna is called the "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*), while the first jhāna itself is called "psychic power" (*iddhi*). The preliminary work for the second, third, and fourth jhānas, as well as for the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is called the "basis of psychic power," while the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called "psychic power. Insight into the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) is the basis of psychic power.

The stream-entry path is called "success" (iddhi). The insight of the once-returner, non-returner, and arahant paths is called the "basis of success" (iddhipāda), while the arahant path itself is called "success. It is indeed appropriate to explain it by way of acquisition as well:
for the first jhāna is called the basis of success, and the second jhāna is called success; the second jhāna is called the basis of success, and the third jhāna...
What is called "success" (iddhi) ... [and so on] ... the path of non-returning is called a "basis for success" (iddhipāda), while the path of arahantship is called "success.
In what sense is it "success"? In what sense is it a "basis"? It is "success" in the sense of succeeding; it is a "basis" in the sense of being a foundation.
Thus, here too, the terms "success" or "basis" are not designations for anything else, but rather for the associated mental states.
"It is merely a designation for the four aggregates. When this was said, they replied:
"It would indeed be a designation for the four aggregates alone, if the Teacher had not brought forward later on what is called the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*. But in the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, it says:
'Zeal itself is the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal; energy itself, mind itself, and inquiry itself is the basis of psychic power consisting of inquiry.'"
It has been explained. However, some said, "Supernormal power (iddhi) is unconditioned, whereas the basis of supernormal power (iddhipāda) is conditioned.
Rejecting their statement, it was concluded that both supernormal power and the basis of supernormal power are "conditioned and struck by the three characteristics.
Thus, in this Suttanta-bhājaniya, the bases of supernormal power are explained as being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya. 2.
Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya. 444.
The Abhidhamma-bhājaniya is of self-evident meaning. However, the methods (nayā) herein should be enumerated: “Endowed with the concentration of desire and the volitional formations of striving...”
For in the passage where it is said, “he develops the basis for spiritual power,” four thousand methods (naya) are analyzed regarding the supramundane states.

The same method applies to energy-concentration and the others as well. Likewise, in the *Uttara-cūḷa-bhājanīya*, four thousand methods are analyzed for the basis for spiritual power consisting of desire;
and four thousand each for the bases of spiritual power consisting of energy, mind, and investigation—all of them together.
By way of eight tetrads, thirty-two thousand methods are analyzed.

Thus, it should be understood that this *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* has been explained as adorned with thirty-two thousand methods, pertaining exclusively to the supramundane bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) that have been generated.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions and Answers (*Pañhāpucchaka-vaṇṇanā*)
462. In the *Pañhāpucchaka*, the status of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the text itself.
Regarding the triads of objects, all of these have only the immeasurable Nibbāna as their object because they proceed by taking it as their object; they do not have the Path as their object.
However, by way of the co-nascent cause, they have the Path as their cause, but they do not have the Path as their predominance. For the four kinds of predominance are mutually exclusive.
They do not show respect [to one another]. Why? Because each is senior by its own nature.

For just as four princes of equal birth, equal age, equal strength, and equal skill do not pay honor to one another due to their respective seniority, so too these four predominants do not show mutual respect because each possesses its own distinct quality of seniority.

"They do not make it heavy" means that they are by no means dominated by the Path (magga-adhipati). Even though they share a single object among the past and so forth, they cannot be so described [as path-dominated].
However, because Nibbāna is an external phenomenon (bahiddhā-dhamma), they are called "having an external object" (bahiddhā-ārammaṇa).

Thus, in this section of questions and answers, only the supramundane (lokuttara) bases for psychic power (iddhipāda) that have been produced are discussed. For it was by the Fully Enlightened One himself, in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, that—
The bases for psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are said to be a mixture of mundane and supramundane;

however, in the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya*, the *Pañhāpucchaka*, and the *Pañhāpucchaka* [of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī], they are exclusively supramundane. Thus, this *Iddhipādavibhaṅga* has also been presented by extracting it through three cycles of exposition.
—From the *Sammohavinodanī*, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power (Iddhipādavibhaṅga) is finished.
10. The Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga). 1. Commentary on the Sutta-Method Exposition (Suttantabhājanīya).

466. Now, in the immediately following *Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga*, "seven" is the numerical limit. "Factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) means factors of enlightenment (*bodhi-aṅga*) or limbs of enlightenment;

thus they are called *bojjhaṅgas*. This is what is meant: that collection of states which, when arising at the moment of the supramundane path, [counteracts] sluggishness, agitation, stagnation, exertion, devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, adherence to annihilationism, adherence to eternalism, and so forth.

Because the noble disciple awakens by means of the harmony of qualities—consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—which serves as the antidote to manifold calamities, it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*);
he awakens, rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, penetrates the four noble truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself. Of that...

They are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they are factors (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), which is defined as the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), just like the factors of jhāna, the factors of the path, and so forth.

Furthermore, since the noble disciple is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) by virtue of awakening through this aforementioned harmony of states, these are also called *bojjhaṅgas* because they are factors of that enlightenment (*bodhi*), just like the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot. Thus say the teachers of the commentaries:
“Or, they are called ‘factors of enlightenment’ because they are factors for a person who is awakening.
Furthermore: “In what sense are they ‘factors of enlightenment’ (bojjhaṅga)? They are factors of enlightenment because they conduce to enlightenment;

they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken further; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken thoroughly; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken fully.”
The meaning of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) should also be understood by way of this analysis of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Regarding the terms "mindfulness-enlightenment-factor" (*satisambojjhaṅga*) and so forth: an enlightenment factor that is praised and beautiful is a "perfect enlightenment factor" (*sambojjhaṅga*);

mindfulness itself as a perfect enlightenment factor is the "mindfulness-enlightenment-factor. Among these, the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor has the characteristic of establishing (*upaṭṭhāna*), while the investigation-of-phenomena-enlightenment-factor has the characteristic of investigating (*pavicaya*).
The energy enlightenment factor has the characteristic of exertion; the rapture enlightenment factor has the characteristic of pervasion;

the tranquility enlightenment factor has the characteristic of peace; the concentration enlightenment factor has the characteristic of non-distraction; the equanimity enlightenment factor has the characteristic of reflective discernment.
Among these, because of the statement: "And mindfulness, monks, I declare to be beneficial in all circumstances."
Because it is beneficial to all the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (satisambojjhaṅga) is mentioned first.

Following that, the purpose for their sequential arrangement is already stated in the Pāḷi itself by way of the passage beginning: "Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that state with wisdom," and so forth.
But why are these stated as exactly seven, neither fewer nor more?
Because they are the opposites of lethargy and agitation, and because they are beneficial in all circumstances. For here, three factors of enlightenment are the opposites of lethargy, as it is said:
"Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is lethargic, that is the time for the development of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena..."
"It is the time for the development of the energy enlightenment factor; it is the time for the development of the rapture enlightenment factor.

There are three antidotes to restlessness, as it is said: "But on whatever occasion, bhikkhus, the mind is restless, on that occasion it is the time for the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor;
it is the time for the development of the concentration enlightenment factor."
"...the time for the development of the equanimity enlightenment factor.

Now, among these, mindfulness is "beneficial in all respects" because it is desirable in all the enlightenment factors—just as salt is in all sauces, or as the minister of all affairs is in all royal duties—as it is said: "And mindfulness, monks, I call beneficial in all respects."
There is also a textual reading, “sabbatthaka. The meaning is that both [of these qualities] are desired everywhere.

Thus, it should be understood that exactly seven [factors] have been stated because they are the opposites of lethargy and agitation, and because they are beneficial in all circumstances (sabbatthika).
Now, in order to show the distinction between them according to their respective functions even upon a single object:
Therein, the section beginning with "What is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness? is commenced. Regarding that, "a bhikkhu here" means a bhikkhu in this teaching.
"He is mindful" means he possesses mindfulness through mindfulness, just as one is "possessed of wisdom" through wisdom, "possessed of fame" through fame, or "possessed of wealth" through wealth;
the meaning is that he is endowed with mindfulness. "Supreme" means highest; for that [mindfulness] is the supreme truth of the ultimate goal (*paramattha-sacca*).
Because it is in conformity with both Nibbāna and the Path, it is called "supreme"—that is, most excellent and best. "With mindfulness and circumspection":
"circumspection" (nepakka) is a term for wisdom (paññā); thus the meaning is "with both mindfulness and circumspection.
But why is wisdom included in this distribution of mindfulness? It is for the purpose of illustrating the powerful nature of mindfulness.
For mindfulness arises both together with wisdom and apart from it. When arising together with wisdom, it is powerful;
when arising apart from it, it is weak. Therefore, wisdom is included [in this context] for the purpose of illustrating its state of power.
For example, suppose two royal ministers were standing in two directions; of these two, one might stand holding the prince.
Just as one who stands alone by his own nature, having taken a prince with him among those [others],
becomes possessed of splendor through both his own splendor and the prince’s splendor; yet, standing by his own nature, he does not become equal in splendor to him— just so,
mindfulness that has arisen together with wisdom is like a great minister who stands having taken the prince with him, standing by its own nature.

It arises without wisdom. In this regard, just as one who stands having taken hold of a prince becomes majestic both by his own majesty and by the majesty of the prince, so too mindfulness that arises together with wisdom is powerful;
just as one who stands by his own nature does not possess such majesty, so too mindfulness that arises without wisdom is weak.
"Is" is included [in the definition] for the purpose of illustrating the state of possessing strength.
"Even what was done long ago" refers to a duty performed by oneself or another with the body long ago, or a *kasiṇa* circle, or the preparatory work (*parikamma*) for a *kasiṇa*.
"Even what was spoken long ago" refers to much that was spoken by oneself or another with speech long ago, even at the head of a formal duty (*vattasīsa*).

Having stood [to deliver] either a discourse on the Dhamma or a determination of the meditation subject, or having stood at the head of the "bases of liberation" (*vimuttāyatana*), he delivers a discourse on the Dhamma.

"He remembers" means that he remembers the category of immaterial phenomena—which arose by originating that bodily intimation and verbal intimation—thinking, "Having arisen thus, it has ceased thus. "He recollects" means that he remembers again and again. This...

"It is called the mindfulness enlightenment factor": this mindfulness associated with insight, which has arisen in this way and gives rise to the remaining enlightenment factors, is what is termed the "mindfulness enlightenment factor.
"Dwelling thus mindful" means that the bhikkhu dwells having become mindful by means of the mindfulness that has arisen in that manner.
"That phenomenon" (*taṃ dhammaṃ*) refers to that phenomenon previously described as having been done long ago or spoken long ago.
"He investigates with wisdom" (*paññāya pavicinati*) means he investigates it with wisdom as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

"He scrutinizes" (*pavicarati*) means he scrutinizes it by causing his wisdom to move within that [investigation] as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self. "He enters upon a thorough examination" (*parivīmaṃsaṃ āpajjati*) means he enters upon looking and searching.

"This is called" means that this aforementioned kind of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) which arouses the factors of enlightenment is called the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor (*dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga*).
"For him, that dhamma" refers to that aforementioned kind of dhamma for that bhikkhu. "Has been undertaken" means it has been fulfilled, exerted, and grasped.
"Unflagging" means unflagging precisely because it has been undertaken. "This is called" [refers to the following].
This energy, which gives rise to the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) and is associated with insight (*vipassanā*), is called the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*).

"Unworldly" (*nirāmisā*) means pure due to the absence of the bait of sensual desire (*kāmāmisā*), the bait of worldly existence (*lokāmisā*), and the bait of the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭāmisā*). "This is called" means that this joy (*pīti*), which gives rise to the factors of enlightenment and is associated with insight, is called the joy factor of enlightenment (*pīti-sambojjhaṅga*).

"Of a joyful mind" (*pītimanassa*) refers to a consciousness associated with joy. "The body also becomes tranquil" (*kāyopi passambhati*) refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*), which consists of the three aggregates (*khandha*).
It becomes tranquil through the subsiding of the distress of the defilements. The mind and the aggregate of consciousness likewise become tranquil in that same way.
"This is called" means this tranquility associated with insight, which gives rise to the enlightenment factor, is called the enlightenment factor of tranquility (*passaddhisambojjhaṅga*).
"For one whose body is tranquil and who is happy" means for one who is made happy by the happiness arising from the state of bodily tranquility. "He becomes concentrated" means...
It is rightly directed; having become motionless, it is fixed upon the object, as if it has reached absorption (*appanā*).

This is called: this one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) associated with insight (*vipassanā*) that gives rise to the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) is called the concentration factor of enlightenment (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*).
"Thus concentrated" means concentrated by that concentration which is as if it had reached absorption. "Thoroughly looked upon with equanimity."
"He is one who looks on with equanimity" means he looks on with perfect equanimity; being unoccupied with the abandoning or increasing of those states, he looks on with equanimity.

"This is called" means this neutral mode of being, which accomplishes the non-declining and non-transcending state of the six factors of enlightenment, is called the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*).

What has been stated thus far? It has been stated that, simultaneously and without sequence, within a single moment of consciousness, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are the insight into the various flavors and characteristics of the preliminary stage.
This is the first method.
468–469. Now, in order to explain the manner in which the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen:
Showing the second method, he again said, "The seven factors of enlightenment," and so forth. Herein, this is the word-by-word commentary in sequence:
"Mindfulness with regard to internal states" is the mindfulness that arises in one who is comprehending internal formations.
"Mindfulness with regard to external states" is the mindfulness that arises in one who is comprehending external formations. "Whatever" means whichever. "That too" means...
That too: "for direct knowledge" means for the purpose of directly knowing the phenomena that are to be directly known. "For full enlightenment" (*sambodhāya*): full enlightenment is called the Path;
the meaning is "for the sake of the Path. "For Nibbāna": *vāna* is called craving; because that [craving] is not there, it is Nibbāna.

The meaning is that it leads to the realization of that unconditioned Deathless Element. This same method applies to the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) as well.

Bodily energy (*kāyika-vīriya*) is the energy that arises when one is intent upon walking meditation (*caṅkama*). Mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*) is the energy that arises without bodily exertion, such as the resolve:
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) is the subsiding of the distress of the three aggregates.
“Tranquility of mind” (*cittapassaddhi*) is the subsiding of the distress of the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*).

The exposition for the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*) is the same as that for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*). According to this method, the seven factors of enlightenment are explained as being a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
However, the ancient elders, thinking that “this much alone does not make it clear,” have presented them by way of analysis. For among these internal phenomena:

Mindfulness, investigation, and equanimity—these three, because they have the aggregates of one's own continuum as their object, are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*). Likewise, bodily energy that has not yet reached the Path is mundane.

However, joy and concentration that are without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*) are supramundane (*lokuttara*). The remaining factors are a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
In that regard, first, mindfulness and investigation-of-states equanimity directed toward internal phenomena have the internal as their object;

however, since those that are supramundane have the external as their object, it would not be logical for them to be considered supramundane. One who asserts that even the energy produced through the practice of walking meditation is mundane does not contradict [the scriptures].
But when are joy and concentration without applied thought and sustained thought supramundane?

Do they exist? First, in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), the joy factor of enlightenment (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) is found, but joy that is without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicārā pīti*) is not found.

In the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), joy without applied thought and sustained thought is found, but the joy factor of enlightenment is not found. In the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*), it is not found at all.
Here, however, by taking what is not found as the basis, even those things that are found are excluded.
Thus, this factor of enlightenment of rapture (pītisambojjhaṅga), which is without applied thought and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra),
is said to be exclusively supramundane (lokuttara) once it has emerged from the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere. Likewise,
while the factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhisambojjhaṅga) is found in the sense-sphere, concentration that is without applied thought and sustained thought is not found there.

In the fine-material and immaterial spheres, concentration without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*) is found, but the enlightenment factor of concentration (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*) is not found.
Here, however, even that which is found is excluded by virtue of what is not found.
Thus, this concentration without applied thought and sustained thought has emerged from the sense sphere, as well as from the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
It is stated that [the path] is indeed supramundane once it has been generated.
Furthermore, having taken up the mundane, the supramundane should be practiced; having taken up the supramundane, the mundane should be practiced.

For among internal phenomena, there is also a time for the development of mindfulness, investigation, and equanimity that is supramundane. In this regard, there is this sutta: “Internal liberation...”
"Friends, I speak of the destruction of all clinging; thus these taints do not flow on," by this sutta they are supramundane.

But when, while bodily energy produced through the practice of walking meditation is still unpacified, insight is joined with the path, then that is supramundane. As for those elders [who say], "In kasiṇa-jhāna, in ānāpāna-jhāna..."

They say that when one extracts a factor of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) from the meditations of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), it should not be prohibited; according to their doctrine, the factors of enlightenment of rapture and concentration (pītisamādhi-sambojjhaṅga) that are without applied thought and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra) would be mundane (lokiya).
This is the second method.

470–471. Now, in order to show the third method as it occurs by way of the development of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), he again says, "The seven factors of enlightenment," and so forth.
Herein, this is the word-by-word commentary on the sequence: "He develops" means he increases;
he generates and produces them repeatedly within his own continuum. "Dependent on seclusion" means dependent upon seclusion. "Seclusion" refers to...

Seclusion (*vivittatā*). This seclusion is fivefold: seclusion by way of its own nature (*tadaṅga-viveka*), seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhana-viveka*), seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), seclusion by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*), and seclusion by escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*).
Among these, seclusion by way of its own nature is insight (*vipassanā*). Seclusion by suppression refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
Seclusion by eradication refers to the path (*magga*). Seclusion by subsiding refers to the fruit (*phala*). Seclusion by escape refers to—
Nirvana is the escape from all signs. Thus, in this fivefold seclusion, that which is dependent on seclusion is "dependent on seclusion";

one should understand the meaning as follows: one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor dependent on seclusion by way of seclusion as a factor of penetration (*tadaṅgaviveka*), seclusion as abandonment (*samucchedaviveka*), and seclusion as escape (*nissaraṇaviveka*).

For in this way, the yogi devoted to the practice of developing the mindfulness enlightenment factor (satisambojjhaṅga) develops it at the moment of insight (vipassanā) as being based on seclusion by way of its function,
and based on seclusion as escape by way of his inclination; but at the time of the Path (magga),
he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor as being based on seclusion by eradication by way of its function, and based on seclusion as escape by way of its object.
Some say that joy based on the five kinds of seclusion [is present] as well.

For they extract the enlightenment factor not only at the moments of powerful insight, the path, and the fruit, but also extract it during the kasiṇa-jhānas, the ānāpāna-jhānas, the asubha-jhānas, and the brahmavihāra-jhānas which serve as the basis for insight;
nor has this been prohibited by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā. Therefore, according to their opinion, in these jhānas...
At the moment of its occurrence, it is based on seclusion by suppression precisely through its function.

And just as it is said at the moment of insight that it is "based on seclusion by escape" from the standpoint of aspiration, so too it is appropriate to say that "one develops it as based on seclusion by subsidence.
This same method applies to [the phrases] "based on dispassion" and so forth; for dispassion and the rest have the very same meaning as seclusion.
And herein, relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāgavossagga*) and relinquishment as leaping forward (*pakkhandanavossagga*).

Therein, “relinquishment as giving up” is the abandoning of defilements through their partial overcoming (*tadaṅgavasena*) at the moment of insight, and through their total eradication (*samucchedavasena*) at the moment of the Path.
“Relinquishment as leaping forward” is, at the moment of insight, by way of being inclined toward that [object], and at the moment of the Path...

Furthermore, there is the leaping forward into Nibbāna by taking it as an object. Both of these are appropriate within this method of explaining the meaning that is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
For in this way, this mindfulness factor of enlightenment abandons the defilements in the manner already described and leaps forward into Nibbāna.
By this entire phrase, "leading to relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*), it is meant that [the mind] is transforming toward relinquishment, has transformed, is maturing,

and has matured. For this bhikkhu devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment acts so that the mindfulness factor of enlightenment serves the purpose of relinquishing the defilements and the purpose of inclining toward Nibbāna through relinquishment.
"He brings it to maturity; he develops it in such a way that it becomes matured. This same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) as well.
According to this method, the factors of enlightenment are explained as being a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
This concludes the commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
2. Explanation of the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya 472.

In the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya, there are two methods: one by asking about all seven factors of enlightenment together and answering them collectively, and another by asking and answering each individually.
