The explanation of their meaning should be understood according to the method already stated below.

In the exposition of the equanimity enlightenment factor (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*), however: it is "equanimity" (*upekkhā*) by way of being equanimous. It is "equanimizing" (*upekkhanā*) as the mode of being equanimous.

It is "equanimity" because it looks upon (*ikkhati*) those states that are appropriate for equanimity and proceed in balance, and does not urge them on. It is "equanimizing" because it causes a person to become equanimous.
"Higher equanimizing" (*ajjhupekkhanā*) is an equanimizing that is superior to mundane equanimizing, having reached the state of an enlightenment factor.
Equanimity (*majjhattatā*) is the state of neutrality (*majjhattabhāva*) arising from the absence of involvement.
To show that this belongs to the mind and not to a "being," it is stated as "equanimity of the mind. This is the word-by-word commentary on this section.
As for the method of analysis (*naya*), it should be counted here: for when all seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are questioned together and answered collectively—
In each path, there are a thousand modes (*naya*); thus, four thousand modes are analyzed.
When asked and answered individually according to each enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅga*), there are four for each, making seven tetrads, which total twenty-eight.
Together with the previous four, these make thirty-two; thus, all of them together in the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* are thirty-two.
The thousands of methods have been analyzed as exclusively wholesome. However, since the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are found even at the moment of the fruit,
and since the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) have wholesome roots, the method of resultant (vipāka) is undertaken following the same sequence as the description of the wholesome—
namely, by way of a single question and answer for both, rather than treating them separately.
It is twofold by way of questioning and answering. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated below.
However, in the case of the resultant [consciousness], the methods should be made threefold compared to the wholesome.
This concludes the commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā) 482.
In the Section of Questions, the status of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the canonical text (pāḷi) itself.

Regarding the triads of objects (ārammaṇattika), however, all of these have only the immeasurable Nibbāna as their object because they arise directed toward it; they do not have the Path (magga) as their object.

However, here, by way of the co-nascent cause (*sahajāta-hetu*), wholesome states have the Path as their cause; at the time of cultivating the Path, having made either energy (*vīriya*) or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) predominant, they have the Path as their predominance (*maggādhipati*).

When the cultivation of the Path has zeal (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) as its predominant factor, it should not be said that they have the Path as their predominance, neither at the time of cultivation nor at the time of the fruit.
They cannot be said to have past objects, etc., even by way of having a single object; however, because Nibbāna is an external phenomenon (*bahiddhādhamma*), they are called "having external objects.
Thus, even in this section of questions and answers, only the supramundane (*lokuttara*) factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) that have been produced are discussed.

For it is in the first method of the Suttanta-bhājaniya that the mundane ones were taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One, while in the second and third [methods], [only the supramundane are treated].
The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) have been explained as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

However, in all four methods of the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya and in this section on the interrogation of questions, they are exclusively supramundane. Thus, this analysis of the factors of enlightenment has also been presented by applying it to the three turnings.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Factors of Enlightenment in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga, is finished. 11.
The Analysis of the Factors of the Path (*Maggaṅgavibhaṅga*).
1. Commentary on the Analysis by Way of the Suttas (Suttantabhājanīya) 486.

Now, in the immediately following *Maggavibhaṅga*, everything beginning with "the Noble Eightfold Path" should be understood according to the same method already explained in the *Saccavibhaṅga* under the description of the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering. [This section] is treated separately by way of its cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In the second method as well, everything beginning with "he develops right view dependent on seclusion" is to be understood according to the very method stated in the *Bojjhaṅgavibhaṅga*.
Thus, by means of these two methods, the Suttanta-bhājaniya has been explained as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya:
490. In the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*, instead of saying "the Noble One," it says "the Eightfold Path.
Even though this is not explicitly stated there, this [Path] is indeed noble (*ariya*).
For just as the son born of a consecrated king and a consecrated queen is a prince even if he is not called a "prince," so too is this [Path] noble even if it is not called "noble."
Thus it should be understood. The rest here also should be understood according to the method stated in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths).
Regarding the section on the fivefold path, even though "eightfold" is not explicitly mentioned, it should be understood as eightfold;
for there is no such thing as a supramundane path that is fivefold. This is the teachers' common explanation of this point. However, the caviller says:

“There is no such thing as an eightfold supramundane path; it is only fivefold. When told, “Bring a sutta [to prove this],” he, seeing no other way, will surely bring this passage from the Mahā-Ṣaḷāyatana Sutta:
“The view of one who has become thus—that is his right view. The intention, effort, mindfulness, and [concentration] of one who has become thus...”
“His concentration becomes right concentration. Furthermore, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood have already been thoroughly purified beforehand.
Then he should be told: “Bring the next passage from the sutta. If he brings it, that is well; if not, [the teacher should explain].
If he does not bring it himself, then after bringing it oneself, one should say: "In this way, this Noble Eightfold Path reaches the fulfillment of its development.
One should then say: "By this teaching of the Teacher, your position is refuted; there is no so-called 'five-factored supramundane path'—there is only the eight-factored one."
These three factors, however, function as purified even previously, but at the moment of the supramundane path, they become even more purified.
Now, for what purpose is this "five-factored path" included? It is for the purpose of showing its additional functions.
For at the very time one abandons wrong speech and fulfills right speech, at that same time, right action and right livelihood [are fulfilled].
There are none. These five factors that cause one to act abandon wrong speech, while right speech fulfills itself through the mode of abstinence.
At the time when one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action, at that time there is no right speech or right livelihood.
These five factors that cause one to act abandon wrong action.

Right action, however, fulfills itself by way of abstinence. At the time when one abandons wrong livelihood and fulfills right livelihood, at that time there is no right speech or right action. These five factors that cause [the path] to be performed abandon wrong livelihood;
right livelihood, however, fulfills itself by way of abstinence. Of these five...

The term "five-factored path" (pañcaṅgiko maggo) was used to show that the factors which cause [the path] have an abundance of functions. However, the supramundane path (lokuttaramaggo) consists of only eight factors; there is no such thing as a five-factored [supramundane] path.
"If you say it is eight-factored together with right speech and so forth, then there would be four types of volition regarding right speech and three..."
“Since there is such a multiplicity of volitions—namely, the volition of right action and the seven volitions of right livelihood—how will you be released?

Therefore, the supramundane path consists of only five factors. “We shall be released despite the multiplicity of volitions, and we shall say that the supramundane path consists of eight factors. “You are indeed a reciter of the *Mahācattārīsaka*; are you not?”
He should be questioned. If he says, "I am not," he should be told, "Because you are not a reciter, you do not know.
If he says, "I am a reciter," he should be told, "Bring forth a sutta. If he brings forth a sutta, that is well;
if he does not bring it forth, he himself should bring it from the latter fifty [discourses].
“And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Right speech, I say, bhikkhus, is twofold:

there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is subject to taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
“And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is subject to taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions?
Refraining from false speech, refraining from malicious speech, refraining from harsh speech, and refraining from idle chatter— this, bhikkhus,
is right speech that is subject to taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.”
“And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path?

It is, bhikkhus, the refraining, abstaining, desisting, and abstinence from the four kinds of verbal misconduct in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path— this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path….”
“And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Right action, bhikkhus, I declare to be twofold... [as above] ...resulting in the acquisitions.
“And what, bhikkhus, is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane...
[as above] ... “And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Right livelihood, bhikkhus, I declare to be twofold... [as above] ...resulting in the acquisitions.”
“And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? It is, bhikkhus,

the refraining, abstaining, desisting from, and avoidance of wrong livelihood in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path, and who is developing the noble path— this, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.”

Thus, in this context, each single abstinence from the four verbal misconducts, the three bodily misconducts, and wrong livelihood is called a noble, untainted, supramundane path-factor. "Where, then, is there a multiplicity of volitions here?
Where is there a five-factored path? This sutta demonstrates that, even against your will, the supramundane path is eight-factored."
If he perceives it by this much, that is well; if he does not perceive it, he should be persuaded by bringing forward other reasons.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, therein a true ascetic..."
"In that [other systems], it is not found...pe... But in this Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found;
here alone, Subhadda, is there a true ascetic...pe... Empty are the doctrines of others of true ascetics.
In many hundreds of other suttas as well, only the Eightfold Path is mentioned. It is also stated in the *Kathāvatthu* treatise:
“The Eightfold Path is the best of paths; the Four Truths are the best of truths;
Dispassion is the best of states; and the One with Vision is the best of bipeds”—is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes. “In that case, there is an Eightfold Path. But if even by this much...
If he does not comply with the request, he should be dismissed with the words: "Go, enter the monastery and drink the gruel.
It is impossible that he would state any further reason; this is not possible. The rest here is of plain meaning.
However, the methods (naya) should be enumerated here. For when four questions are asked together regarding the Eightfold Path and answered together, [there are...]
Regarding the paths, four thousand methods (naya) are analyzed. When the five-factored path (pañcaṅgika-magga) is asked about collectively and answered collectively, there are four [methods];
when asked about individually and answered individually, there are four for each of the five factors, making twenty.
Thus, the previous eight and these twenty make twenty-eight in total within the analysis of the path (maggavibhaṅga).

The methods are analyzed into thousands; these, moreover, are exclusively wholesome states pertaining to the supramundane that have been produced. Regarding the resultant [states], however, the methods should be made threefold compared to the wholesome.
This concludes the commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā) 504.
Regarding the Section of Questions, the status of the path-factors as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the text itself.

As for the triads concerning the object (*ārammaṇattika*), all of these have only the immeasurable Nibbāna as their object because they arise in reference to it; they do not have the path as their object.
Indeed, neither the path nor the fruit takes the path as its object. However, by way of the co-nascent cause (*sahajātahetu*), wholesome states herein have the path as their cause (*maggahetuka*).
At the time of developing the path, having made either energy (*vīriya*) or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) predominant, they have the path as their predominance (*maggādhipati*).

When the development of the path has zeal (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) as its predominant factor, it should not be said that they have the path as their predominance; this remains the case even at the time of the fruition (*phala*).

They cannot be described as having the past, etc., as their object even by way of being a single object; however, because Nibbāna is an external phenomenon (*bahiddhādhamma*), they are called "having an external object" (*bahiddhārammaṇa*).
Thus, in this section of questions and answers as well, only the supramundane path-factors (*lokuttaramaggaṅga*) that have been produced are discussed.
For it was in the Suttanta-bhājaniya alone that the Blessed One taught both mundane and supramundane path-factors.
In the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya* and in the *Pañhāpucchaka*, however, [the factors] are exclusively supramundane;
thus, this *Maggavibhaṅga* is also presented by dividing it after having extracted it through three rounds.
— From the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Factors of the Path is finished.
12. Analysis of Jhāna. 1. The Exposition according to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya).
Commentary on the Schedule (Mātikāvaṇṇanā) 508.
Now, regarding the Analysis of Jhāna (Jhānavibhaṅga) that follows immediately after this, there was first established a schedule for the entire Suttanta-bhājaniya;
therein, the word "here" (*idha*) refers to one who is perfected in the preliminary duties.
This is an exposition of the Teaching as the support for the person who produces all kinds of jhāna, and a refutation of the fact that other teachings possess such a quality.
For it has been said: “Only here, monks, is there a recluse... empty are the doctrines of others of recluses other than these.
The word “monks” (bhikkhū) is an exposition of the persons who produce those jhānas. “Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha” (pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto): [this refers to their conduct].
This is an exposition of his state of being established in the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "He dwells" is an exposition of his possession of a dwelling that is appropriate thereto.
"Perfect in conduct and resort" is an exposition of those qualities that are conducive to the restraint of the Pātimokkha mentioned below and to the application to jhāna mentioned above.
"Seeing fear in even the slightest faults" is [an exposition] of his [restraint] from the Pātimokkha...
This is an exposition of the state of being subject to non-decay. "Having undertaken" is an exposition of the undertaking of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) in its entirety.
"Trains" is an exposition of his state of being endowed with the training. "In the training rules" is an exposition of the things to be trained in.
"In the faculties" is an exposition of the ground for guarding the doors; it is also an exposition of the sphere that is to be protected.
They say thus: "One with guarded doors" is a description of his state of having established protection at the six sense-doors.

"Moderate in eating" is a description of his qualities such as contentment and so forth. "Devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night" is a description of the causal basis for this.
"Constancy and discernment" refers to that which is embraced by wisdom (*paññā*).
"By means of energy, he is characterized by constant practice": this illustrates his application to the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhika-dhamma*).
"He is devoted to the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment": this illustrates that his practice pertains to the portion leading to penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*).

"He acts with clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) regarding going forward... [and so on]... and regarding silence": this illustrates that he is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in all circumstances.
"Thus he resorts to a secluded lodging": this illustrates his taking possession of a suitable lodging. "The forest... [etc. ...fit for seclusion":
this illustrates the classification of that lodging, its lack of disadvantages, and its advantages.
"Having gone to the forest": this illustrates his being endowed with the aforementioned type of lodging. "He sits down": [this indicates the posture].
This is the description of his deportment (iriyāpatha) in accordance with his practice (yoga). "Having established mindfulness before him" is the description of his commencement of the practice.
"Having abandoned covetousness for the world," and so forth, is the description of the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) through his application to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
For him, whose hindrances have been abandoned, "quite secluded from sensual pleasures," and so forth, follows in sequence.
This is an exposition on the arising of jhāna.
Furthermore, "here a bhikkhu" means a bhikkhu who produces jhāna in this Dispensation.
Now, since a bhikkhu who produces jhāna must purify the four kinds of virtue, he is therefore described by the phrase "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha."
By the phrase "endowed with proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara-sampanno*), he teaches the purity of virtue consisting in livelihood-purification (*ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla*).
By the phrase "having undertaken, he trains in the rules of training" (*samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu*), he teaches the undertaking of those two types of virtue in their entirety.

By the phrase "guarded in the doors of the sense faculties" (*indriyesu guttadvāro*), he teaches the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-sīla*). By the phrase "knowing the proper measure in food" (*bhojane mattaññū*), he teaches the virtue dependent on the requisites (*paccaya-sannissita-sīla*).

By the passage beginning with "In the first watch of the night and the last watch of the night," [the Blessed One taught] the qualities conducive to the development of jhāna for one established in virtue.

By the passage beginning with "That which is excellent," [He taught] the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension for the non-decline of those qualities and the non-forgetting of the meditation subject.

By the passage beginning with "Secluded," [He taught] the selection of a dwelling suitable for development. By the passage beginning with "Having gone to the forest," [He taught] that very dwelling...
For one who has approached, there is both a posture conforming to jhāna and the commencement of the cultivation of jhāna.
By the commencement of the cultivation of jhāna—beginning with the phrase "he abandons covetousness, etc."—there is the abandoning of those states that are adverse to jhāna.
With the passage beginning "having abandoned these five hindrances," he thus indicates the sequence of the arising of all jhānas for one whose states adverse to jhāna have been abandoned.
Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā). Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavaṇṇanā) 509.
Now, in order to explain the matrix as it was set forth by dividing it according to its sequence, [the text begins with] "Herein" (*idha*), "of this view" (*imissā diṭṭhiyā*), and so forth.

It has been undertaken. In this context, by the ten phrases beginning with "of this view" (*imissā diṭṭhiyā*), the entire teaching of the Omniscient Buddha—comprising the three trainings—is described.
For that [teaching] is called "view" (*diṭṭhi*) because it was seen by the Blessed Buddha; it is called "acceptance" (*khanti*) by way of its being acceptable;

"inclination" (*ruci*) by way of its being pleasing; "taking up" (*ādāya*) by way of its being grasped; "Dhamma" (*dhamma*) in the sense of its intrinsic nature; and "training" (*sikkhā*) in the sense of its being something to be practiced.
It is the Vinaya; by both together it is the Dhamma-Vinaya. By way of being proclaimed, it is the Pāvacana (the Word); in the sense of the best practice, it is the Brahma-cariya;
and in the sense of giving instruction, it is called the Satthu-sāsana (the Teacher’s Dispensation).
Therefore, in such passages as "of this view," etc., [it means] of this Buddha-view, of this Buddha-approval, of this Buddha-preference, and in this Buddha-tradition.
In this Dhamma of the Buddha, in this Vinaya of the Buddha:
"And as for those things you might know, Gotamī, such that: 'These things lead to passion, not to dispassion;
they lead to bondage, not to liberation; they lead to accumulation, not to diminution; they lead to grasping...'"
‘They lead to non-renunciation, not to renunciation; they lead to great desires, not to fewness of wishes;
they lead to lack of contentment, not to contentment; they lead to socializing, not to seclusion; they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy;
they lead to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support. You should certainly hold this, Gotamī: ‘This is not the Dhamma…’” [and so on].
“This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction. But those teachings you should know, Gotamī, as follows:
“These teachings lead to dispassion, not to passion... [and so on] ...they lead to ease of maintenance, not to difficulty of maintenance.
Then, Gotamī, you should definitely hold: “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.”

When this has been said, it should be understood that the meaning is as follows: in this Buddha’s Dhamma-Vinaya, in this Buddha’s dispensation (pāvacana), in this Buddha’s holy life (brahmacariya), and in this Buddha’s teaching as Teacher (satthusāsana).

Furthermore, this entire dispensation, which consists of the three trainings, is called "view" (diṭṭhi) because it was seen by the Blessed One, because it is a condition for right view, and because it is preceded by right view; it is called "patience" (khanti) by way of the Blessed One’s acceptance, and by way of his approval.
It is taken up by way of inclination and grasping. It is called *dhamma* because it supports (*dhāreti*) its own agent from falling into the states of misery (*apāya*).
That same thing is called *vinaya* because it subdues (*vineti*) the side of defilement. Thus, it is *dhammavinaya* as both *dhamma* and *vinaya*.

Alternatively, it is *dhammavinaya* because this is the subduing (*vinaya*) of unwholesome states by means of wholesome states. For this very reason it was said: "And those things which you, Gotamī..."
"You should know the teachings thus: 'These teachings lead to dispassion, not to passion... [as before] ...you should hold them with absolute certainty, Gotamī, thinking:
"This is the Teaching, this is the Discipline, this is the Master’s instruction.
Because it is through the Teaching, and not by means of punishment and so forth, it is called the 'Teaching-Discipline' (dhamma-vinaya). And this has also been said:"
“Some are tamed by means of the rod, and others by hooks and whips;
but the elephant was tamed by the Great Seer without rod and without sword.
Likewise—
“For those who are led by the Dhamma, what envy can there be for one who understands?

Thus, the Vinaya is the discipline for the sake of the Dhamma; it is the Dhamma-discipline (*dhammavinaya*). For this discipline is for the purpose of the blameless Dhamma, not for the purpose of the bait of existence and worldly enjoyment.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “This holy life, monks, is not lived for the sake of deceiving people,” and so forth in detail.
The Elder Puṇṇa also said: "Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
Or, it leads to what is distinguished, thus it is *vinaya*. It is the discipline (*vinaya*) regarding the Dhamma, thus it is *dhammavinaya*.
For this leads to Nibbāna, which is distinguished from the phenomena of saṃsāra or from the phenomena of sorrow and so forth. Or, it is the discipline of the Dhamma, not that of other teachers.
The Dhamma-Vinaya: for the Blessed One is the embodiment of the Dhamma, and his is the Vinaya.

Or, because it is only phenomena (dhammas) that are to be directly known, fully understood, abandoned, developed, and realized, therefore this is the Vinaya regarding phenomena, not regarding sentient beings or living souls;
thus it is called the Dhamma-Vinaya. It is the preeminent teaching because, through its possession of meaning, phrasing, and other qualities, it surpasses the words of others.
It is the teaching (*pavacana*); it is the very teaching that is the *pāvacana*. It is the *brahmacariya* because it is a conduct distinguished from all other forms of conduct.
It is the *satthusāsana* because it is the instruction of the Blessed One who has become the Teacher of gods and humans;

or alternatively, it is the *satthusāsana* because the instruction itself has become the Teacher. For it was said: "After my passing, the Dhamma and Vinaya shall be your Teacher. Thus, the Dhamma and Vinaya alone are the Teacher.
Thus the meaning of these words should be understood as they have been stated.
Furthermore, because it is only in this very teaching that a bhikkhu who produces jhāna in all its modes is seen, and not elsewhere,
one should understand that the restriction "of this" and "in this" was established in various places for that reason.
This is the meaning of the explanation of the heading-word (*mātikāpada*) “here” (*idha*). 510.

In the description of a bhikkhu, “by designation” (*samaññāya*) means by way of a concept (*paññatti*), that is to say, by conventional usage (*vohāra*). For it is precisely by designation that a certain person is known as a “bhikkhu.
Thus, when bhikkhus are being counted during an invitation (*nimantana*) and so forth, even a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is included among them.
“They say, ‘a hundred bhikkhus,’ ‘a thousand bhikkhus. By way of admission (*paṭiññāya*) means by one’s own acknowledgment. For even by way of admission, someone is recognized as a bhikkhu.
Its occurrence should be seen in such instances as: ‘Who is here, friend? ‘I am a bhikkhu, friend,’ and so forth.
This, however, is a legitimate admission because it was spoken by the Elder Ānanda.”
Furthermore, at night, even those who are immoral, when traveling along the road and being asked, "Who is there?", respond with an unrighteous claim and a false statement, saying, "We are bhikkhus.
One "bhikkhati" means one begs; for whoever begs, seeks, or searches for alms (bhikkhā), let him receive it.
Whether he does or not, he is nonetheless called a *bhikkhu* because he "begs" (*bhikkhati*). By adding the syllable *-ka*, the word is expanded;
the meaning is that he is a *bhikkhu* by virtue of having the nature of begging (*bhikkhana-dhammatā*).

"One who has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering" means that he is called one who has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering because he has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering as undertaken by the Buddha and others. For whoever [possesses] a mass of wealth, whether small or great—

He is called a *bhikkhu* because he has gone forth from the home into homelessness, having abandoned making a living through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth, and has undertaken the practice of wandering for alms by merely accepting the outward signs of his status.

Alternatively, because his livelihood is dependent on others, even while eating solid food in the midst of the monastery, he is called a *bhikkhu* because he has undertaken the practice of wandering for alms. It is by depending on the meal of scraps obtained as alms that one goes forth.
He is called a *bhikkhu* because he has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering due to having developed energy (*ussāha*).
He is called a wearer of tattered robes (*bhinna-paṭadhara*) because he wears a robe that has been torn by means of its value, touch, and color.
In this context, the destruction of value should be understood through cutting with a knife; for even a robe worth a thousand pieces, when cut into fragments by a knife, [loses its original value].
It becomes of broken value; it is not worth even half its former price. Through the sewing together with thread, a difference in touch should be understood.
For even a cloth that was pleasant to the touch, once sewn together with threads, becomes a different touch and attains a state of roughness.
Through the needlework and so forth, a difference in color should be understood. For even a perfectly pure cloth, starting from the needlework...
By means of very fine combs, hand-sieves, water-strainers, and so forth, as well as by means of dyeing materials at the end, it becomes a different color and abandons its natural hue.
Thus, because he wears a cloth that has been altered in these three ways, a bhikkhu is called a "wearer of a dyed cloth" (bhinnapaṭadhara).
Alternatively, he is a "wearer of a dyed cloth" simply by wearing the saffron robes which are dissimilar to the garments of householders.
He "breaks" (bhindati) evil, unwholesome states; thus he is a bhikkhu. He breaks five defilements by means of the stream-entry path; thus he is a bhikkhu.
He breaks four [defilements] by means of the once-return path, four by means of the non-return path, and eight defilements by means of the arahant path;
thus he is a bhikkhu. Up to this point, those established in the four paths have been shown. By the word "because of having broken" (bhinnattā),...
Furthermore, there are four who have attained the fruits. For the stream-enterer stands having shattered five defilements by means of the stream-entry path;
the once-returner [stands] having shattered four by means of the once-returning path; the non-returner [stands] having shattered four by means of the non-returning path;

and the arahant stands having shattered eight defilements by means of the arahant path. Thus, this fourfold one who has attained the fruit is so called because of the shattering of evil unwholesome states.

"A monk" refers to one who has the abandoning of defilements by way of limits (*odhiso*) among phenomena. Here, there are two kinds of limits: the limit of the path (*maggodhi*) and the limit of defilements (*kilesodhi*). A "limit" (*odhi*) means a boundary or a demarcation.
In this context, a stream-enterer is a monk because of the abandoning of defilements by way of the limit of the path; for him, [in regard to] the four...

Defilements are abandoned by a single category (*odhi*) within the paths, not by the entire fourfold path. This same principle applies to the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*) and the non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
Furthermore, the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) is a bhikkhu because he has abandoned defilements categorically (*odhiso*), even though he has abandoned them by a single category;

for among the defilements to be abandoned, his defilements have been abandoned only by a single category, and not in their entirety. However, the arahant [has abandoned them] without such categorization (*anodhiso*).
A bhikkhu by the abandoning of defilements without exception. For his defilements have been abandoned by the fourfold path without exception, not merely by a single boundary of the path.
And among the defilements to be abandoned, the defilements have been abandoned without exception; for there is not even a single boundary of defilements that remains.
Thus he is a bhikkhu by the abandoning of defilements in both ways without exception.
"Trainee" (*sekkha*) refers to the seven noble ones together with the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*). They are called "trainees" because they train in the three trainings (*sikkhā*).
Among them, any one who is a trainee should be understood as a "monk in training" (*sekha-bhikkhu*). One who does not train is a "non-trainee" (*asekkha*).

Having transcended the states of a trainee and being established in the highest fruit, the non-trainee is called such because there is nothing further to be trained in; he is one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). The remainder...
An ordinary monk (*puthujjana-bhikkhu*) who neither trains in the three trainings nor remains having trained in them should be understood as "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (*nevasekkhanāsekkha*).

One is called an "excellent monk" (*agga-bhikkhu*) because he stands having reached the excellence consisting of the summit of virtue, the summit of concentration, the summit of wisdom, and the summit of liberation.
"Bhadra" means one who is not evil; for from the virtuous ordinary person up to the Arahant, they possess excellent virtue (*bhadra-sīla*).
Because they are endowed with concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are reckoned as "noble monks" (*bhadra-bhikkhu*).
A "monk who is the cream" (*maṇḍa-bhikkhu*) is a monk who is confident; the meaning is that he is untroubled and serene, like the cream of ghee.

He is called "the essence" (*sāra*) because he is endowed with those very same essences, such as the essence of virtue, just as a cloth is called blue because it is endowed with the quality of blueness.

He should be understood as a "sāra-bhikkhu" (a bhikkhu who is the core). Alternatively, because he has removed the state of being like the sapwood of defilements (*kilesa*), only one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) should be understood as the "sāra.
And therein, among these three instances—"he breaks (*bhindati*) evil unwholesome states, thus he is a bhikkhu; a bhikkhu through the specific abandonment of defilements;
a bhikkhu who is a trainee (*sekkha*)"—the seven trainees (*sekkhā*) are mentioned. [And] "because of having broken evil unwholesome states..."

Regarding the phrase "of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*): in these five instances—"a bhikkhu through the abandoning of defilements without remainder," "an *asekkha* bhikkhu," "the foremost bhikkhu," and "the essence bhikkhu"—only one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is spoken of.

In the expression "neither *sekkha* nor *asekkha*," it is the worldling (*puthujjana*) who is spoken of. In the remaining instances, the "virtuous worldling," the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*), and the one whose taints are destroyed are [all] spoken of.
All these have been explained.

Having thus shown the monk by means of his conventional designation and so forth, [the text] now says "by a unanimous Saṅgha" and so on, in order to show him by way of his full ordination (*upasampadā*).
In that context, "by a unanimous Saṅgha" refers to as many [monks] as are required for a formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by a quorum of five at the very least.

The monks have reached the stage for the formal act (*kamma*); because they have arrived, because the consent (*chanda*) has been brought from those entitled to give it, and because there is no protest from those present, one has attained a state of unanimity regarding a single formal act.
"By a motion followed by three proclamations" means that which is to be performed with one motion (*ñatti*) and three proclamations (*anussāvana*).

"By a formal act" means by a legitimate (*dhammika*) disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*). "Irreversible" means because it is endowed with the perfection of the subject matter, the motion, the proclamations, the boundary (*sīmā*), and the assembly (*parisa*).
By one who has approached [the state] that is not to be provoked and not to be reviled. "Worthy of the standing" means worthy of the reason, worthy of the Teacher’s instruction.
"One who is ordained" (*upasampanna*) means one who has attained a superior state; the meaning is "one who has reached it. For the state of being a bhikkhu is indeed a superior state.

And because he has attained that through the aforementioned procedure, he is called "ordained. By this, [it refers to] these various forms of ordination, such as the *ehibhikkhu* (come, bhikkhu) ordination...

Eight forms of ordination (*upasampadā*) have been taught: ordination by going for refuge, ordination by receiving instruction, ordination by answering questions, ordination by accepting the heavy rules (*garudhamma*), ordination by messenger, ordination by eight proclamations (*aṭṭhavācika*), and ordination by the formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements (*ñatticatutthakamma*).
Among these, [the following are mentioned]: ordination by the formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements, ordination by messenger, and ordination by eight proclamations.

These three were permanent. The others occurred only while the Buddha was still living. Among those forms of full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is this very ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) that is intended here. 511.

In the exposition of the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*, "the *Pātimokkha*" refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). For that which protects—meaning, guards—one who observes it, [is called the *Pātimokkha*].
It liberates—that is, it releases one—from the sufferings of the states of deprivation and so forth; therefore, it is called *pātimokkha*.

"Virtue" (*sīla*), "foundation," and so on, are synonyms for that very same term. In this context, while "virtue" is indeed a synonym for the *pātimokkha* which comes into being simultaneously with the conclusion of the formal ritual (*kammavācā*), nevertheless, from the perspective of its essential nature (*dhammata*), this is called virtue because it is the abstention from killing living beings and so forth.
One should understand that for one who is abstaining or fulfilling the practice of the duties, there are mental states such as volition (cetanā) and so forth.
For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "What is virtue (sīla)? Volition is virtue; mental concomitants are virtue; restraint is virtue; non-transgression is virtue.
Therein, what is called "volition as virtue" belongs to one who is abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, or to one who is fulfilling the practice of the duties.
Volition (*cetanā*). What is called mental virtue (*cetasika-sīla*) is the abstinence of one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth.
Furthermore, what is called volitional virtue is the sevenfold volition of the paths of action belonging to one who abandons killing living beings and so forth.

Mental virtue refers to the states of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, as described in the *Mahāvagga* of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* by way of the passage: "Having abandoned covetousness, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness," and so on.

"Restraint is virtue": here, restraint should be understood as fivefold—restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. The distinction between these is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Non-transgression is virtue": this refers to the bodily and verbal non-transgression of one who has undertaken the precepts. And herein, there is the virtue of restraint.
The virtue of non-transgression is virtue in the primary sense; it should be understood that volition as virtue and mental factors as virtue are virtue in a secondary sense.
However, because a bhikkhu is said to be "established" in the Dispensation by means of the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, that [restraint] is called "the foundation";
for either the bhikkhu is established therein, or wholesome states themselves are established therein.
It is a foundation. This is the meaning:
“A wise man, established in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom, ardent and discerning, that bhikkhu shall unravel this tangle. And: [the rest of the verse].

“It is virtue, O Great King, that is the foundation for all wholesome states,” and “For one established in virtue, O Great King, no wholesome states decline”—it is through such suttas as these that this should be understood.
This [virtue] is the “beginning” in the sense of being what arises first. And it has been said:
“Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the beginning among wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? Virtue that is well-purified and a view that is straight.”
Just as a city-builder, desiring to construct a city, first clears the site for the city and subsequently builds it by demarcating it with streets, crossroads, junctions, and so forth; even so,
the practitioner of yoga first purifies his virtue, and thereafter realizes serenity, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
Or just as a dyer first washes a cloth with three alkaline substances and then applies whatever dye he desires to that perfectly clean cloth;
or just as a skilled painter, wishing to paint a figure,
first performs the preparatory work on the wall and only afterwards brings forth the figure— exactly so does the practitioner of yoga first purify his virtue (*sīla*).
In the subsequent stage, one realizes such states as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Therefore, virtue (*sīla*) is called the "beginning" (*ādi*).
This is termed "footing" (*caraṇa*) because of its similarity to a foot. For "feet" (*caraṇa*) are indeed called "feet" (*pāda*).
Just as the volitional formation of moving toward the various directions does not arise in a person whose feet have been cut off, but arises only in one whose feet are complete; even so, for whom...
When virtue is broken, torn, and incomplete, the progress of knowledge toward Nibbāna does not succeed for that person.
But for one whose virtue is unbroken, untorn, and complete, the progress of knowledge toward Nibbāna succeeds.
Therefore, virtue is called "the feet."
Thus, this is "restraint" (*saṃyama*) by way of restraining, and "control" (*saṃvara*) by way of warding off.
By both terms, it is explained as both restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*) and control of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). As for the etymological meaning here:
it restrains (*saṃyameti*) transgression and agitation, or it restrains the person; it does not allow that person to agitate through transgression—thus it is "restraint. Of transgression...
It is called *saṃvara* because it restrains and closes off the gateway of entry. It is called *mokkha* because it is supreme or because it serves as a door.

For just as the fourfold nutriment of sentient beings enters through the mouth and pervades all the limbs and members, so too does the wholesome [dhamma] of the four planes enter for the yogin by way of the door of virtue (*sīla*) and accomplish the attainment of his goal. Therefore it is said: "liberation" (*mokkha*).

"Foremost" (*pāmokkha*) means "at the head" (*pamukhe*); the meaning is "the precursor," "the best," or "the preeminent. Regarding the phrase "for the attainment of wholesome states" (*kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā*), it should be understood as the foremost, the precursor, the best, or the preeminent for the sake of acquiring the wholesome states belonging to the four planes of existence.

"Bodily non-transgression" refers to the threefold good conduct of body (*kāyasucarita*). "Vocal" refers to the fourfold good conduct of speech (*vacīsucarita*). "Bodily and vocal" refers to both of these together.
By this, he shows that the virtue of the eightfold right livelihood (*ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla*) is fully encompassed.

"Restrained" (*saṃvuta*) means closed; the meaning is one whose sense faculties are restrained, whose sense faculties are closed. For just as a house with its doors closed is called a "restrained house," [so too is the practitioner].
"Sheltered from the wind" is what is meant; likewise, here one whose sense faculties are restrained is called "restrained.

"By means of the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means by both the Pātimokkha and the restraint, or by the restraint known as the Pātimokkha. The terms beginning with "endowed" have already been explained in their respective places.
With the seven phrases beginning with "he conducts himself," the dwelling in the postures of a bhikkhu established in the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is described.

513. In the exposition of conduct and resort (*ācāra-gocara*), although the Blessed One, desiring to explain the conduct of a recluse and the resort of a recluse, set forth the phrase: "Endowed with conduct and resort:

there is conduct, there is non-conduct," he nevertheless first mentioned the path that must be abandoned—the dangerous, deviant path—just as a man skilled in the way, when pointing out the road, says: "Leave the left and take the right."
He points out the safe path and the straight path that should be taken later;

in the same way, the King of Dhamma, who is like a man skilled in paths, having first pointed out the improper conduct censured by the Buddha that is to be abandoned, and desiring to point out proper conduct afterwards, said:
"In this regard, what is improper conduct? and so forth. For the path pointed out by such a man would indeed lead to success.
Whether [one does so] or not, the path proclaimed by the Tathāgata is unfailing; like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra, it never misses its mark and converges precisely upon the city of Nibbāna.
Therefore it was said: "‘A man skilled in the way,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
Or rather, just as the application of ornaments such as garlands, perfumes, and ointments is fitting for a person who has washed away sweat, dirt, and grime from head to foot,

so too is the cultivation of wholesome qualities fitting for one who has abandoned unwholesome states; therefore, having first explained improper conduct— which is like the sweat, dirt, and grime that must be abandoned— the [text] describes the application of ornaments such as garlands, perfumes, and ointments for one whose sweat, dirt, and grime have been removed.
Although he intended to explain proper conduct later on, he first stated, "In that regard, what is improper conduct? and so forth.
Therein, "transgression by way of body" refers to the threefold misconduct of body; "transgression by way of speech" refers to the fourfold misconduct of speech;
and "transgression by way of both body and speech" refers to both of these together. Thus, he demonstrated the transgression specifically of the eightfold virtue of right livelihood.

However, since one does not practice misconduct through body and speech alone, but also practices it through the mind, it was therefore said, "All immorality is misconduct," in order to demonstrate that.
Therein, having analyzed and shown a specific instance of misconduct, he said:
"Here, someone [gives] by means of the gift of bamboo," and so forth. In this context, "by means of the gift of bamboo" refers to the gift of bamboo given for the sake of requisites.

Indeed, it is not permissible for one to give bamboo that has been brought from a monastery or from the forest and protected and guarded by oneself to supporters with the thought, "In this way they will provide requisites for me.
For one who makes a living in such a manner lives by wrong livelihood through improper search.
Such a person incurs censure in this very life and, in the future life, becomes a fulfiller of the states of misery. [This applies even to] bamboo belonging to one's own private property.
If one gives for the sake of supporting a family, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for corrupting the family.

If one gives what belongs to another individual with a thieving mind, one is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods. This same principle applies even in the case of property belonging to the Saṅgha. However, if one gives such property out of a sense of ownership, one incurs the offense of disposing of valuable goods (*garubhaṇḍavissajjana*).
But which bamboo is a heavy article, and which is not? First, as for that which is unplanted and grown of its own accord:
it is a heavy article only within the area demarcated by the Saṅgha, but beyond that it is not a heavy article;
however, in the place where it has been planted, it is a heavy article in every respect. Furthermore, it is a heavy article even if its size is limited to the measure of an oil-tube.
Not below that amount. However, if a monk has need of an oil-tube or a walking-stick, it may be accepted after performing a service (*phātikamma*).
The service performed must be worth the same as the object, or more; less is not permitted.
Even manual labor is not permitted if it is merely for the purpose of fetching water or clearing away weeds.
It is proper to make that [place] stable. Therefore, it is proper to take [the goods] after removing soil from a pond, having had steps laid down, or having leveled uneven ground.
If it is taken without performing the *phātikamma* (ritual of dedication), it must be used only by one dwelling there;
when departing, one must leave it as property belonging to the Saṅgha. If it was taken through forgetfulness...
Wherever one has gone, one should bring back from there whatever was brought along. If there is danger on the way, one should proceed after leaving behind the dwelling that has been reached.
When people go to the monastery and ask for bamboo, the monks do not dare to give it, thinking, "It belongs to the Saṅgha.
If the people then ask repeatedly or even threaten them, the monks should say: "Take it after having paid the fine."
It is permissible to speak [of this]; it does not constitute the "gift of bamboo.

If they give axes, hatchets, and so forth for the purpose of clearing away timber, or if they give hard or soft food, it is not permissible to accept them. However, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"When people who have had their houses burned by fire are taking things away, they should not be stopped."
If bamboo-sprouts arise for the Saṅgha in a bamboo grove, and the bamboo is destroyed while they do not have it split, what should be done?
It should be explained to people during their alms-round. If they do not wish to split it, they should be told, “You will receive an equal share.
If they still do not wish to, they should be told, “You will receive two shares. Even so...
If they do not wish [to give], one should say: "There is no point in being lost; when you have the opportunity, you shall perform the punishment—beat them and take them!
This is not called a gift of bamboo. The same rule applies even if a fire breaks out in a bamboo thicket or if the bamboos are being carried away by water.
The same course of reasoning applies to trees as well. However, as for a tree...

An object as small as the handle of a needle is considered heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*). Having had a tree belonging to the Sangha cut down, it is permitted to build a dwelling belonging to the Sangha even without asking the Sangha for permission.
However, for the purpose of cutting off further talk, it should indeed be done after having asked for permission.
Is it permitted or not permitted to make [a dwelling] for an individual (*puggalika*)? It is not permitted. However, by way of manual labor, in one case...
In the case of a house, one obtains only the space for a bed; among three houses, one obtains one house.
If the building materials belong to an individual but the ground belongs to the Saṅgha, having built one house, one obtains an equal share; among two houses, one obtains one house.
If trees belonging to the Saṅgha obstruct a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, one may remove them without asking the Saṅgha.
Is it allowable or not allowable? It is allowable. However, for the purpose of cutting off the path of speech, it must be removed only after having asked permission.
If there is a great gain for the Saṅgha dependent upon a tree, it must not be removed.
If a tree belonging to an individual obstructs a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, the owner of the tree should be informed. If he does not wish to have it removed, [the matter should be resolved].
Having had it cut down, it should be removed. To one who demands, "Give me the tree," the value of the tree should be assessed and the price paid.
This same principle applies even when a private dwelling encroaches upon a tree belonging to the Saṅgha, or when a private dwelling encroaches upon another private dwelling.
This is the same course of action regarding creepers as well. However, where a creeper is sold and is difficult to obtain, there—
Heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*). And this [begins] from the measure of half an arm upwards; below that, a piece of creeper is not heavy goods.
Regarding the giving of bowls and so forth, everything such as "by the giving of a bowl" or "by the giving of requisites" should be understood in the same manner as stated for the giving of bamboo.
However, regarding the status of being heavy goods here, this is the analysis: for even a bowl, where it is sold...
Perfume-sellers and others take [leaves] for the purpose of wrapping perfumes and so forth; in such rare instances, it constitutes a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*).
This, first of all, is the determination regarding ear-ornaments made from *kiṃsuka* leaves, palm leaves, and the like.
The palm leaf (*tālapaṇṇa*) should also be discussed in this very context, for even a palm leaf, when grown in a natural palm grove, belongs to the Saṅgha.
Precious goods [are considered lost] only within the defined area, and not beyond it. On the walls of the plastered rooms, everything is considered precious goods.
Its minimum measure is even a blank piece of paper eight finger-breadths in size. Even a blade of grass must be included here when making the assessment.
However, where there is no grass, they cover the area with muñja-grass, palāla-reeds, coconut leaves, and so forth.
Therefore, those [other grasses] are also included under the term "grass" (*tiṇa*).

Thus, any grass measuring a handful from among *muñja*, *palāla*, and so forth, or even a single leaf from among coconut leaves and the like, if it has been given to the Saṅgha, or if it grows there [in the monastery], or if it is grass grown on the Saṅgha’s grass-site outside the monastery, and is protected and guarded—it is considered "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*). Furthermore, regarding that [property] used for Saṅgha-affairs...
And when work on a shrine has been completed, it is permissible to give the surplus toward personal construction work. The same principle applies to the bamboo mentioned below as well.

Regarding the offering of flowers: in a place where it has been specifically designated, such as "Having distributed flowers among these many trees, bring them for the sake of rice-gruel, food, and clothing;
bring them for the repair of so many dwellings," the flowers are considered valuable goods (garubhaṇḍa).
[They] are. On the opposite shore, the novices gather flowers and make a heap. A distributor of flowers endowed with five qualities, having counted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, divides them into portions.
He is permitted to give [the flowers] even without having asked the Saṅgha if it is an assembly that has arrived;
however, one who is not authorized must give [them] only after having asked [permission]. But for whom does the bhikkhu [distribute] the flowers?

One may receive it for giving; for whom may one not receive it? Even if one has brought [the requisites] to the home of one's parents, or even if one has had them summoned from their home, one may receive it for saying, "Perform an offering to the site (vatthupūjā)";
however, one may not receive it for the purpose of providing ornaments. As for other relatives, one must not give [requisites] after having brought them [to the site];
rather, they should be given after having summoned them, saying, "Perform an offering. For other people, it is a place for honoring.
One should give without expecting anything in return; this is not called a gift of flowers. In a monastery, many flowers bloom.
When a bhikkhu is walking for alms and sees people, he may say, "There are many flowers in the monastery;
you should offer them. There is no fault in merely saying this. [Thinking,] "People will come bringing hard and soft food,"...
However, it should not be said by mind. If one does say so, one must not consume solid or soft food.
People, according to their own custom, ask, "Are there flowers in the monastery?
and say, "We will come to the monastery on such-and-such a day; do not let the novices pick the flowers. The monks [should instruct] the novices...
[The monks] had forgotten to mention it. The novices had gathered flowers and set them aside.
People approached the monks and asked, "Venerable sirs, we informed you on such-and-such a day, 'Do not allow the novices to gather flowers.
Why did you not stop them? [The monks replied,] "I forgot; I was mindful only until the moment they had gathered the flowers."
It should be said, "The offering has not yet been made. One should not say, "Take it; offer it. If he says so, the material gift must not be consumed.
Another bhikkhu informs the novices, saying, "The residents of such-and-such a village said, 'Do not pluck the flowers.'"
When people bring food offerings and give them as alms, they say, "We do not have many people [to serve];
please instruct the novices to gather flowers along with us. One should reply, "The novices will receive alms;
those who do not go on their alms-round, O lay followers, will know for themselves. Having obtained this much guidance, [one should proceed].
There is no fault in having a novice (sāmaṇera) pick flowers after making him one’s son or brother; this is not called a gift of flowers.
In the case of a gift of fruit, the fruit itself—just like the flower—is strictly considered a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa).

When there is an abundance of fruits and other produce in a monastery, people who are inconvenienced come and ask for them. The monks do not venture to give them, thinking, “This belongs to the Saṅgha. The people...
Being remorseful, they reviled and abused him. What should be done in that case?
One should demarcate the area by means of fruits or trees and establish an agreement:
"Those taking so many fruits from these particular trees, or those taking fruits from so many trees, shall not be restrained. But as for thieves or powerful men who act by force...
Those who take [the bath powder] should not be stopped; for if they are angry, they might destroy even the entire monastery. However, the danger must be explained. Regarding the gift of bath powder:
bath powders that have been ground are not "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*). But unground tree bark is indeed a heavy good.
As for the powder, it is permissible for one who is not ill to use it as a dye-ingredient. For one who is ill, any kind of powder is indeed permissible.
Clay should also be mentioned here as being included in this very category. Where clay is difficult to obtain, it is a "heavy article" (garubhaṇḍa) even in that case.
Even that clay, at its minimum limit, is only the measure of a lump of thirty palas of flour; below that, it is not a heavy article.
Regarding the giving of a tooth-stick, a tooth-stick that has not yet been cut is a heavy article. As for those novices who [receive it] from the Saṅgha...
When it is the turn for tooth-sticks, those who have not been assigned a specific share are not permitted to give any to their own teachers or preceptors.

However, those who have taken their turn by specifying, "This many tooth-sticks must be brought," are permitted to give any surplus to their teachers and preceptors. From the tooth-stick shed, one monk...
Many tooth-sticks should not be taken; only one should be taken each day.
Even for one staying separately, having counted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he should take as many as fall to his share and then depart.
If guests arrive in the interim, or if he is departing for another region, he should bring them back and place them back in the very place where they were taken from.

Regarding "flattery" (*cāṭukamyatā*) and so forth: flattery is said to be the speaking of exaggerated words out of a desire for affection, while placing oneself in a low position like a slave and smoothing over even another’s faulty speech.

"Bean-soup-like conduct" (*muggasūpyatā*) is a designation for making a livelihood through truth and falsehood combined, which is similar to bean soup. For just as when bean soup is being cooked, many beans...
Most ripen, while few do not; even so, in a person who makes a living by truth and falsehood, falsehood is abundant and truth is meager.

Or, just as there is no spot where a bean curry does not enter, even so for a person whose conduct consists of truth and falsehood, there is no speech that has not entered [with falsehood]; it is like a crossroads.
It stands ready to grant whatever stream [of wealth] one desires. Therefore, this lying of his is called "like bean soup. "Pāribhaṭayatā" means the state of being a hireling (*paribhaṭa*).
For *pāribhaṭayaṃ* is the work of a hireling, and *pāribhaṭayatā* is the state of that;
this is a designation for the employment of children through such means as providing ornaments and the like.
"Sending on foot" (*jaṅghapesanika*) means carrying messages and replies between various householders in different villages, districts, and so forth.

This "sending on foot" is permitted by way of going somewhere after receiving a message from one's own parents, or from those who are attending upon one's parents; or [for the sake of] a *cetiya* or the Saṅgha. One's own...
Or it is appropriate to carry the message even to carpenters who are performing work. People say, "We shall give alms, we shall perform worship;

announce it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus"; they give alms-food, medicine, or robes, saying, "Give this to such-and-such a thera"; or [they give] garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth, saying, "Perform worship at the monastery."
If they carry away items such as banners or flags, it is permissible to take everything; this does not constitute "sending on foot" (*jaṅghapesanika*).
For one who goes after receiving a message from others, there is an offense at every step.
Regarding the phrase "by any one of these": by any one of these, such as the gift of bamboo and so forth, [one performs] the work of a physician or the work of a storekeeper.
“Alms-round and alms-work,” “work for the arising of the Saṅgha or the arising of a shrine,” or by any such work that makes a livelihood through wrong livelihood;
“condemned by the Buddhas” means censured and prohibited by the Buddhas.
“This is called” means that all this together is termed “improper conduct. The description of proper conduct (ācāra) should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
514. Regarding the explanation of the "range" (*gocara*), the reason for mentioning what is not a proper range first should be understood according to the method already stated below.
In this context, "range" (*gocara*) refers to a place suitable for approaching for the sake of alms-food and so forth; an "unfit range" (*agocara*) is a place unsuitable for such purposes.
One whose range is prostitutes is "one who frequents prostitutes" (*vesiyagocara*); that is, a place approached by way of intimacy with friends.

The meaning [of this is as follows]. In that context, "prostitutes" (*vesiyā*) refers to those who live by their beauty. Anyone who approaches them—whether out of ease, habitual practice, friendship, intimacy, or affection—is said to have "frequented the domain of prostitutes.
Therefore, it is not proper to approach them in such a manner. For what reason? Because of the failure of protection.
For one who approaches in this way, even if the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*) has been long protected and guarded, in just a few days...
[If he goes] he is lost; even if he is not lost, he incurs censure. However, one who approaches for the sake of alms should approach having established mindfulness.
"Widows" refers to those whose husbands are dead or those whose husbands have gone abroad.
"Old maidens" refers to grown-up girls who are unmarried. "Eunuchs" refers to those who engage frequently in talk centered on worldly gain.
Those whose defilements are rampant and whose fever has not subsided are neuter.
The danger in approaching any of them should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The same principle applies to bhikkhunīs as well.

Furthermore, bhikkhus are those for whom the holy life is predominant, and so too are bhikkhunīs. Through mutual intimacy, in just a few days, they may lose the ascetic qualities that were protected and guarded.

They remove [the flowers]. However, it is permissible to go to inquire after the sick. When a bhikkhu has obtained flowers, it is likewise permissible for him to go for the purpose of making an offering or for the purpose of giving exhortation.
"A tavern" means a house for drinking liquor; it is not devoid of those intoxicated by liquor who create obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
In that regard, it is not proper to approach them together with them in a state of intoxication;
for there would be an obstruction to the holy life (*brahmacariya*). Regarding the phrases "he dwells in association with kings" and so forth:
"kings" refers to those who rule over a kingdom, whether they have been formally anointed or not. "Royal ministers" refers to those who possess great authority, equal to the sovereignty of kings.

"Endowed with": "Heretics" (*titthiya*) refers to outside wanderers who hold perverted views. "Disciples of heretics" (*titthiyasāvaka*) refers to those who provide requisites for them by way of their status as supporters.
The meaning is that one has come into association with these people.
"By unsuitable association" (*ananulomikena saṃsaggena*): so-called "unsuitable association" is that which is not in conformity with the three trainings.
Association with adversaries, by which one incurs an obstacle to the holy life, a transgression of the rules, and a loss of ascetic refinement;
namely: sharing grief, sharing joy, and sharing in pleasure and pain with kings, royal ministers, and high officials;
personally engaging in whatever duties or tasks arise; and [associating] with sectarian teachers and their disciples.

It is the state of having a single desire, inclination, and conduct; or it is intimacy characterized by affection, esteem, and familiarity that brings about such a state of desire, inclination, and conduct. In this context, association with kings, royal ministers, and high officials creates an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
With others—namely, the lay followers of other sects—it consists of adopting their tenets. Furthermore, [the purpose is] to break their doctrine and cause them to adopt one's own tenet.
It is proper to approach [such families] with composure.
Now, in order to show the improper resort by another method, the passage beginning "or those families which... is commenced.
Therein, "lacking faith" means devoid of faith toward the Buddha and the others; [thinking], "The Buddha is omniscient; the Dhamma leads to liberation..."
They do not have faith that “the Saṅgha has practiced well. They are “unconvinced” in the sense that they are unable to make their minds clear and undisturbed.
They are “abusive and reviling” means they are both abusive and reviling: “You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded! You are a camel! You are an ox! You are a donkey!
You are bound for the states of deprivation! You are bound for hell! You are a creature of the animal realm! There is no...”
"O Sugata, for you, only an unhappy destination (duggati) is to be expected"—thus they revile them with these ten grounds of abuse;
"Let it be, now we shall strike you, bind you, kill you"—thus they revile them by instilling fear;
such is the meaning. "Desiring what is harmful" means they do not desire welfare (attha), but desire only harm. "Desiring what is detrimental" means...
They desire only what is harmful; they do not desire what is beneficial. "Desiring discomfort" means they do not desire comfort, but rather desire only discomfort.
"Desiring lack of security from the yokes" means they do not desire the safety and fearlessness that come from being free of the four yokes, but rather desire only what is fearful.
Regarding the term "monks," here novices are also included. Regarding the term "nuns," here...

[This applies to] female trainees (*sikkhamānā*) and novice nuns (*sāmaṇerī*) as well. For all those who have gone forth under the Blessed One, as well as for the four assemblies who have taken refuge, such [families] are indeed those that do not desire their welfare.

"Such families" refers to families such as the *khattiya* (warrior-noble) clans and others. "Frequents" means he lives depending upon them. "Associates with" means he approaches them. "Waits upon" means again and again.
"He approaches. Regarding the phrase "this is called": this threefold improper resort—namely, one who frequents prostitutes and so forth being a prostitute-resorter;

one who is associated with kings and so forth being a king-resorter; and one who serves families lacking faith and so forth being a family-resorter—is to be understood as an improper resort (*agocara*).

In this manner, his lack of proper resort (*agocaratā*) should be understood. First, the class beginning with prostitutes should be understood as a non-resort because it is dependent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure, as it is said:
"And what, monks, is a monk’s non-resort, the domain of others? Namely, the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The class beginning with kings is a non-resort because it does not provide a supporting condition for the practice of meditation and because it produces the cycle of gain and honor.
It is not a proper resort because it causes the failure of right view, and because families lacking faith and so forth bring about mental distress through the loss of one's own faith.
Regarding the description of the proper resort (*gocara*), terms such as "not a resort of prostitutes" and so on should be understood by way of their opposites.

Furthermore, in expressions such as "become like a well," the phrase "become like a well" means they have become like a water-well; [it refers to] a lotus pond dug at a crossroads for the Saṅgha of monks.
They were like the houses of the great minister Citta, capable of being entered at one's ease.
It is said that in his house, a black pillar was always fixed. For the monks who arrived at the door of his house, there was never a lack of requisites;
on a single day, sixty kahāpaṇas would go out solely for the purpose of medicine. "Bright with the ochre robes" means by the monks and nuns.
They were made uniform in appearance by the radiance of the saffron robes worn by those clad in them, resembling the noble families of the merchant Bhūtapāla.

"Scented by the breezes from the sages" means that they were scented by the wind from the robes of the sages—namely the monks and nuns—as they entered and exited the houses, and by the bodily wind produced by their bending and stretching;
or alternatively, they were "cleansed of evil," being thoroughly purified by those winds.
515. In the description of seeing danger in even minute faults (*aṇumatta-vajja*): "minute" (*aṇumattāni*) means of small measure. "Faults" (*vajjāni*) means defects.
"Those which are faults" means those things which are faults in the sense of being censurable. "Trifling" (*appamattakāni*) means merely limited, of a small size.
"Insignificant" (*oramattakāni*) means insignificant because their measure is even smaller than limited. "Light" (*lahusāni*) means...
"Light": they are considered light. "To be done by restraint": they are countermeasures to be performed through restraint.
"To be done by self-control": they are to be performed by self-control; they are countermeasures to be performed by self-control. "To be done by the mere arising of thought":
they are countermeasures to be performed by the mere arising of thought. "Dependent on attention": by the mere mental advertence [of the mind].
The remedies that must be performed. What, then, are they? First, the Elder Suma, who dwelt in the daytime rest-hut, said:
"Those [offenses] which lead to non-offense and consist of a mere arising of thought are purified by the mere mental reflection, 'I shall not do such a thing again.
This is called the confession by determination. His pupil, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, however—
But he says: "This is the portion belonging specifically to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha.

Therefore, it should be understood that here even the lightest offenses—dukkaṭa and dubbhāsita—are what are meant. This is called the 'procedure for rehabilitation' (vuṭṭhāna-āvikamma). Thus, "in these" means in those of such a kind.
"One who sees the fault" (vajjadassāvī) means one whose nature is to see faults as defects. "One who sees danger" (bhayadassāvī) [means one who sees] the fourfold danger...
One who is habituated to seeing [things] as fearful because they are causes [of fear].

"One who sees the danger" means one who is habituated to seeing the danger here in various ways: because it brings about censure, because it results in suffering in the future, because it creates obstacles to higher qualities, and because it generates remorse.
"One who sees the escape" means one who is habituated to seeing whatever escape there is from that. But what is the escape in this case?
In the tradition of the Elder Ācariya, it is stated: "When there is the possibility of non-offense, the resolution and confession is the way out.
In the tradition of the Elder Antevāsika, it is stated: "When there is the possibility of an offense, the rising up from it and the confession is the way out.
In this context, such a bhikkhu is said to "see even minor faults as faults and as fearsome. To demonstrate this:

This method has been explained: namely, the atom (*paramāṇu*), the minute particle (*aṇu*), the dust mote of a water drop (*tajjārī*), the dust mote of a chariot wheel (*rathareṇu*), the tip of a louse egg (*likkhā*), the louse (*ūkā*), the grain of rice (*dhaññamāsa*), the finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), the span (*vidatthi*), the cubit (*ratana*), the staff-length (*yaṭṭhi*), the ox-yoke (*usabha*), the league (*gāvuta*), and the yojana.
Among these, the "atom" (*paramāṇu*) refers to a portion of space.
It does not come within the range of the fleshly eye; it comes only within the range of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
What is called a "minute particle" (*aṇu*) is perceived as a shimmering circle revolving within the rays of the sun that have entered through a crack in a wall or a hole in a palm tree.

What is called a "dust mote" (*tajjārī*) is that which, having broken off from paths for cattle, paths for humans, or carriage roads, stands suspended on both sides. What is called a "chariot-dust" (*rathareṇu*) is that which settles right there.
The *likkha* and so forth are well known. Among these, thirty-six atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute the measure of one minute particle (*aṇu*).

Thirty-six minute particles constitute the measure of one *tajjāri*. Thirty-six *tajjāri*s constitute one chariot-dust (*rathareṇu*). Thirty-six chariot-dusts constitute one *likkha*. Seven *likkha*s constitute one *ūkā*.
Seven *ūkā*s constitute one grain-measure (*dhaññamāsa*). The measure of seven grain-measures [constitutes one finger-breadth].
One finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). By that finger-breadth, twelve finger-breadths make a span (*vidatthi*). Two spans make a cubit (*ratana*). Seven cubits make a staff (*yaṭṭhi*).
Twenty such staffs make a fathom (*usabha*). Eighty fathoms make a quarter-league (*gāvuta*). Four quarters of a league make a league (*yojana*).
By that league, King Sineru, the monarch of mountains, is five hundred and sixty-eight thousand leagues in height.
The monk who is able to see even a minor fault as being like Mount Sineru, which rises six million eight hundred thousand yojanas high—
this monk is said to "see minor faults with fear. And the monk who sees even the lightest offenses,
such as a *dukkaṭa* or *dubbhāsita*, as being equal to the first *pārājika* offense— [this monk is also said to see minor faults with fear].
He is able to do so—it should be understood that this means he perceives even minor faults as faults and as a source of fear.
516. Regarding the explanation of the phrase "having undertaken, he trains in the training precepts": "the training of a bhikkhu" refers to the training that must be trained in by bhikkhus.
That is called the "training of a bhikkhu" whether it is common to bhikkhunīs or not common to them. "The training of a bhikkhunī" refers to...
The training to be practiced by bhikkhunīs: that too is called the bhikkhunī training, whether it is shared with the bhikkhus or not shared.
The training of sāmaṇeras, sāmaṇerīs, and sikkhamānās is also included herein.
The "training of upāsakas" refers to the training to be practiced by upāsakas; this applies to the five precepts and the ten precepts. The "training of upāsikās" refers to...
The training to be practiced by female lay followers (*upāsikā*) is also appropriate as the five precepts and the ten precepts.
In that regard, the training for monks and nuns extends up to the path of Arahantship; the training for male and female lay followers extends up to the path of Non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*).
