Herein, this monk trains only in those points of training that he himself ought to practice. As for the remaining trainings, they are mentioned merely for the sake of enumerating them.
These are spoken for the purpose of showing the meaning of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"In these trainings" means in these trainings of such a kind. "In every way and in all respects" means the entire training by means of the complete undertaking of the training.

"In every manner and in its entirety" means the whole training in every mode of practice that ought to be trained in. "Without remainder and exhaustively" means without remainder because there is nothing left over; [even] through forgetfulness...

Because even a training rule that has been broken can be restored to its original state, it is "complete. "Practicing after undertaking" means practicing after having undertaken and taken up [the precepts].

"Therefore it is said" means: for this reason, because one undertakes and trains in—and fulfills—all this training rule in every manner in which it is to be trained, therefore it is said: "one trains after undertaking the training rules."

517–8. Regarding the two terms "guarding the doors of the sense-faculties" and "moderation in eating," the purpose of the first statement concerning the dark side (the unwholesome) should be understood in the same manner as explained in the exposition on conduct (*ācāra*).

Furthermore, whatever needs to be said regarding the passages beginning with "What is lack of restraint of the doors of the sense-faculties? has all already been stated in the commentary on the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* (The Section on Enumerations).
519. In the explanation of "devotion to wakefulness" (*jāgariyānuyoga*), regarding the phrase "the first watch and the last watch of the night":
here, "the first watch" (*pubbaratta*) refers to the period before midnight; by this, both the first watch and the period after the meal are included.
"The last watch" (*apararatta*) refers to the period after midnight; by this, both the final watch and the period before the meal are included. However, the middle watch belongs to it [as well].
The opportunity for a bhikkhu to dispel drowsiness and fatigue is not included here. "Devotion to wakefulness" means devotion to wakefulness, that is, to the state of being free from sleep.
"Is devoted" means he is devoted to—that is, associated with—the practice and cultivation known as such devotion.
In its exposition, however, it says: "Here, a bhikkhu [during] the day"—that is, the three divisions of the day: forenoon, midday, and afternoon.

"Taken up. By means of walking and sitting—that is, by dwelling in these two postures alone for the entire day—he purifies the mind from obstructive states, that is, from the five hindrances or from all unwholesome states.
He cleanses it of those states; he liberates it from them. As for the possibility in this context, although...
It is not taken [as a blanket], but rather it must be taken by making it dependent upon the walking meditation path and the sitting posture.
"The first watch" refers to the entire first watch of the night. "The middle watch" refers to the middle watch, which consists of the sixth division of the night and day.
Regarding "the lion’s posture," there are four types: the posture of those who indulge in sensual pleasures, the posture of the hungry ghosts, the lion’s posture, and the posture of the Tathāgata.
The postures for lying down. Among these, "Monks, for the most part, those who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side"—this is the posture of one who enjoys sensual pleasures.
For among them, there is generally no one who lies on their right side. "Monks, for the most part, the departed spirits (petas) lie on their backs"—this is the posture of the departed spirits;
for, due to having little flesh and blood, they are composed of a mass of bones joined together and lie on one side.
They are unable to lie down and remain lying on their backs. Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, lies down on his right side...
[as before] ...and he is satisfied. This is the lion’s posture;
for, being full of vital energy, the lion, the king of beasts, places both fore-paws in one place and both hind-paws in another, and tucks his tail between his thighs.

Having placed [the foot] and having observed the location where the toes of the front and back feet were situated, he lies down with his head placed upon the tops of the two front feet. Even when waking after sleeping during the day, he does not wake in fear;
rather, lifting his head, he observes the locations where the front feet and so forth were situated. If any spot has been left vacant...
If it stands [facing him], thinking, "This is not suitable for your birth nor for your courageous nature," he becomes displeased and lies down right there,
not setting out for his range. But if it stands without turning away, thinking,
"This is suitable for your birth and for your courageous nature," he rises up, joyful and elated, and performs the lion’s yawn, shaking his mane.
Having shaken off [drowsiness] three times and having uttered the lion’s roar, he sets out for his almsround.

However, the posture of the fourth jhāna is called the "Tathāgata-posture. Among those, it is the lion’s posture that is intended here. For this is indeed called the supreme posture because its physical demeanor is preeminent in fiery energy (*tejo*).
"Placing foot upon foot" means placing the left foot upon the right foot. "Resting" means placing it slightly beyond, having set it down with a small overhang.
For when one ankle touches the other, or one knee the other, painful sensations arise frequently, the mind does not become one-pointed, and the bed becomes uncomfortable.

However, when placed so that they do not touch—having been set apart—painful sensations do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the bed becomes comfortable. Therefore it was said: "The feet..."
“Having placed one foot over [the other]. “Mindful and clearly comprehending” means being endowed with both mindfulness and the wisdom of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
By this, mindfulness and clear comprehension that are well-sustained are described.

“Having brought to mind the perception of rising” means having brought to mind in the consciousness the perception of rising that delimits the time for rising, thinking, “I shall rise at such-and-such a time.”
Having approached. For one who has lain down having acted in this way is fit to rise at the very time previously determined.

520–521. *Sātaccaṃ* (constancy) and *nepakkaṃ* (discernment): while practicing the application of wakefulness (*jāgariyānuyoga*), he is fit to exert both the energy known as constancy because it must be maintained continuously, and the wisdom known as discernment because it has reached maturity. Thus he is devoted and intent upon them.
The meaning is that he dwells devotedly. And here, energy is spoken of as a mixture of both mundane and supramundane;
wisdom likewise follows the course of energy—the meaning being that when energy is mundane, [wisdom] is mundane, and when it is supramundane, [wisdom] is supramundane.
"Of the states conducive to enlightenment" means of those states belonging to the side of the knowledge of the path, which is termed the awakening to the Four Noble Truths.

Of the states (*dhammānaṃ*). Up to this point, having taken all thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*) together, [the author] speaks of "the seven factors of enlightenment" (*satta bojjhaṅgā*) and so forth, showing that even through mundane development (*bhāvanā*), it is only the factors of enlightenment that are capable of occurring together upon a single object.
It should be understood that these are spoken of as a mixture of both mundane and supramundane. The rest here is of plain meaning, since it follows the method already explained below.
523. In the explanation beginning with "abhikkante" and so forth:
first, regarding "abhikkante paṭikkante," here "abhikkanta" refers to going forward, and "paṭikkanta" refers to returning. Both of these are found within the four postures.
In the case of walking, for instance, one who brings the body forward goes forward (*abhikkamati*), and one who turns back returns (*paṭikkamati*).
Regarding the term "name": even while standing in one place, when one bends the body forward, it is called "approaching" (*abhikkamati*);

when one draws it back, it is called "receding" (*paṭikkamati*). Regarding sitting as well, even while seated, when one moves toward the front part of the body facing nearby, it is called "approaching";
when one moves back toward the rear part of the body, it is called "receding. The same principle applies to lying down as well.
“He acts with full awareness” means he performs all his duties with full awareness, or he is one who acts only with full awareness.
For he indeed exercises full awareness regarding such things as going forward and so on; he is never devoid of full awareness in any situation.
Since that full awareness is necessarily associated with mindfulness, therefore in its description it says: “Mindful and fully aware, he goes forward...”
It is said: “Mindful and clearly comprehending, he steps back.
For whether he is stepping forward or stepping back, he is not muddled in mindfulness nor lacking clear comprehension;
rather, endowed with mindfulness and clearly comprehending through wisdom, he both steps forward and steps back—in all such actions as stepping forward and so forth.
One brings down fourfold clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). For fourfold clear comprehension consists of:

clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of the range of activity (*gocara-sampajañña*), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

In that regard, when the thought of going forward arises, instead of going merely by the power of the mind, one considers the purpose and the lack of purpose, [asking]: "Is there any purpose for me in going there, or is there not?"

Having grasped [the object], the discerning of its purpose is “clear comprehension of the purposeful” (*sātthaka-sampajañña*). In this context, “purpose” (*attha*) refers to spiritual progress (*vaḍḍhi*) by way of the Dhamma, such as through seeing a shrine (*cetiyadassana*), seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing an elder, or seeing the foul (*asubhadassana*).
For even after seeing a shrine or the Bodhi tree, one generates joy with the Buddha as its object; and by seeing the Saṅgha, one generates joy with the Saṅgha as its object.
Then, contemplating that very joy in terms of its waning and passing away, one attains Arahantship.

Having seen them there, he establishes himself in their instruction; seeing the foul therein, he arouses the first jhāna and, contemplating that very state in terms of its exhaustion and vanishing, he attains Arahantship. Therefore, seeing these [beings] is purposeful.
Some, however, say: "Even the increase of material goods is indeed purposeful, because one has set out to support the holy life by depending upon it."
In that journey, however, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable, the discernment of the suitable is "discernment of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).
For example: first of all, visiting a shrine (*cetiyadassana*) is purposeful.

But if, because of a great offering to the shrine, assemblies gather within a radius of ten or twelve leagues, and both men and women, according to their means, are adorned and prepared like figures in a painting—
They move about as it were; and therein, greed arises toward a desirable object, aversion toward an undesirable one, and delusion toward indifference.
Or else, one incurs an offense involving physical contact, or there is an obstacle to the life of celibacy (*brahmacariya*).
In this way, that place is unsuitable. It is suitable when the aforementioned obstacles are absent. This also applies to the vision of enlightenment (*bodhi*).

The same principle applies here. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if people have constructed a great pavilion within the village and hold a Dhamma discourse throughout the entire night, then—just as in the case previously described—there will be a gathering of people and obstacles.
In such a case, that place is unsuitable; if there are no obstacles, it is suitable. [This is so] for those who are accompanied by a large retinue.
The same principle applies to visiting the elders.
Contemplation of the foul (*asubha*) is also purposeful. To illustrate this point, there is this story:
it is said that a certain young bhikkhu went out with a novice to fetch tooth-sticks. The novice left the path and walked ahead.

Having seen the foul, he attained the first jhāna; making that very state his foundation, he contemplated conditioned phenomena, realized the three fruits, and stood having taken up a meditation subject for the sake of the higher paths.
A young man, not seeing him, called out, "Novice! He replied, "From the day I went forth, I have been a bhikkhu..."
Thinking, "Two such conversations have never been held together before; on another day I shall produce a further distinction," he replied, "What is it, venerable sir?
When told, "Come," he came with a singular form of address and said, "Venerable sir, go first by this path and stand for a moment facing east at the place where I am standing."
"Look! he said. Having done so, he attained that very distinction of the bowl. Thus, one foul object (asubha) arose for the benefit of two people.
Furthermore, while this is indeed purposeful, the foulness of a woman is unsuitable for a man, and the foulness of a man is unsuitable for a woman;
only that which is of a similar kind is suitable. This discernment regarding what is suitable is called "suitability-awareness" (sappāya-sampajañña).
But for one who has thus selected what is beneficial and suitable, having learned a range of practice— known as a meditation subject—

from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects according to his own mental preference, and then proceeding on his alms-round while maintaining that very subject, this is called "clear comprehension of the range.
To explain this, the following tetrad should be understood:
In this regard, a certain bhikkhu carries [the mind] forward but does not bring it back; another does not carry it forward but brings it back;
yet another neither carries it forward nor brings it back; and still another both carries it forward and brings it back.
Therein, that bhikkhu who, during the day, having purified his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting meditation, likewise [purifies it] during the first watch of the night...

Having spent the middle watch of the night in sleep, and having passed the last watch of the night in sitting and walking meditation, he performs the duties at the shrine terrace and the Bodhi-tree terrace early in the morning;
having sprinkled water on the Bodhi-tree and set out drinking water and water for washing, he undertakes and practices all the Khandhaka duties, such as those toward teachers and preceptors;
then, having attended to his bodily needs, he enters his lodging.
Having practiced the meditation subject while sitting cross-legged for two or three sessions until he felt a sense of warmth, he should rise at the time for the alms-round.
Taking his bowl and robe with the meditation subject foremost, he should leave his lodging and go to the shrine terrace while still attending to that meditation subject.
If it is the meditation subject of recollecting the Buddha, he should go to the shrine terrace without relinquishing it.
Upon entering, if there is another object of meditation, one should set it aside like a parcel held in the hand while standing at the foot of a staircase;
then, taking up the joy inspired by the Buddha as the object, one should ascend the terrace of the shrine.
If it is a large shrine, one should circumambulate it three times and pay homage at four places; if it is a small one, one should likewise circumambulate it.

Having done so, one should pay homage at eight places. Even when one has paid homage to the cetiya and reached the precinct of the Bodhi tree, one should pay homage to the Bodhi tree by showing full prostration as if in the very presence of the Blessed Buddha.
Having thus paid homage to both the cetiya and the Bodhi tree, he should go to the place where the goods were deposited and [inspect] the goods deposited there.

As if taking it up with his own hand, he takes up the meditation subject he has set aside, puts on his robe with the meditation subject foremost even while near the village, and enters the village for alms.

Then, seeing him, people think, "Our venerable one has arrived," and they go out to meet him, take his bowl, and seat him either in a rest-house or in their own house; having given him rice-gruel, they continue until the meal...
They do not leave until they have washed their feet, anointed them with oil, and sat down before him to ask questions or listen to the Dhamma.

Even if he does not speak to them, the commentators say that a discourse on the Dhamma must indeed be delivered for the sake of winning over the people. For a discourse on the Dhamma is never devoid of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

There is none. Therefore, having partaken of food with the meditation subject as his primary aim, and having delivered a blessing, even while being followed by people returning from the village, he departs from the village;
there he turns them back and sets out upon the path.
Then, novice monks and young bhikkhus who had departed earlier and finished their meal outside the village see him.

They went out to meet him and took his bowl and robe. It is said that the ancient bhikkhus did not perform their duties by looking at the faces of others, thinking, "He is our preceptor" or "He is our teacher," but performed them according to the established limits of propriety.
They asked him, "Venerable sir, who are these people? Are they relatives on your mother's side?"
“Is it because of their side of affection? “What have you seen that you ask this? “Their love and great respect for you.
“Friends, these people do for us what is difficult even for one’s own mother and father to do. Even our alms-bowls and robes belong to them alone;
by their power we know neither fear in times of danger nor hunger in times of famine. Such as they are...”
"There is no one who has been so helpful to us," he says as he goes along, speaking of their virtues. This is called "carrying [the meditation subject] but not returning it.
However, for one who performs the aforementioned duties and observances from early morning, the fire born of karma blazes up;
releasing the non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) and taking hold of the clung-to (upādinnaka), sweat breaks out from the body, and the meditation subject—

He does not enter the street; rather, having taken his bowl and robe early in the morning, he quickly pays homage at the shrine and enters the village for alms of rice-gruel just as the cattle are leaving.
Having received the gruel, he goes to a sitting hall and drinks it.
Then, by the mere act of swallowing it two or three times, the fire element born of karma consumes the [material] derived from the four great elements.
Having let go of what is not clung to, he takes up what is not subject to clinging; like one who has bathed with a hundred pots [of water],
having attained the cooling of the fever of the fire-element, he partakes of rice-gruel under the heading of his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*),

washes both bowl and mouth, attends to the meditation subject during the interval between meals, wanders for alms in the remaining places, and partakes of food under the heading of his meditation subject.
From that time on, he would come having taken up his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) which followed him in uninterrupted succession.

This is called "not carrying it away, but bringing it back. And such monks as these—having drunk the rice-gruel, initiated insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahatship in the Buddha’s Dispensation—are beyond counting.
Even in the Island of Ceylon alone, among those [who have done so] in various places...
"In the villages, in the rest-houses, there is no such seat where there are no bhikkhus who, having drunk rice-gruel, have attained Arahantship. He who dwells in negligence,
having cast aside his burden and broken all the rules of conduct, dwelling with his mind bound by the five kinds of mental thorns and fetters,
and without even forming the perception that "there is such a thing as a meditation subject," enters the village for alms with improper conduct...
Having lived in close association with householders and having both eaten and wandered about together with them, he goes out empty-handed—
this is called "neither taking away nor bringing back.
However, he who is described as "both taking away and bringing back" should be understood by way of the practice of going and returning.

For sons of good family who have gone forth in the Dispensation out of desire for the goal, even ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred living together in one place, establish a code of conduct and dwell thus:
"Friends, you have not gone forth out of debt, nor out of fear, nor because you are destitute of a livelihood; rather, you have gone forth here desiring to be released from suffering."
"Therefore, subdue any defilement that arises while walking right there where it arose; subdue any defilement that arises while standing, sitting, or lying down right there where it arose.
Having thus made this agreement, as they went on their almsround, at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gavuta, and one gavuta, they...
There are stones there, and while attending to the meditation subject with that perception, they walk along.
If defilement arises in anyone while walking, he restrains it right then and there. If he is unable to do so, he stops.
Then even those coming behind him stop. He thinks: "This bhikkhu knows the thought that has arisen in you; it is unbecoming."
Having reproached himself with "These are they," he develops insight and enters the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*).
If he is unable to do so, he sits down. Then, even one coming behind him sits down; such is the procedure.

Even if he is unable to enter the plane of the Noble Ones, he goes along suppressing that defilement and attending only to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), not dissociated from the meditation subject.
One lifts the foot with the mind; if one lifts it and then turns back, one returns to that very same previous spot, as did the Elder Mahāpuṣpadanta, the resident of the Ālindaka.
It is said that for nineteen years he lived fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning.
Even people along the road—plowing, sowing, threshing, and performing their labors—[saw him do so].
Seeing the Elder walking along, they conversed among themselves, saying, "This Elder turns back again and again as he goes;

is he perhaps lost on the way, or has he forgotten something? Without paying any heed to them, he practiced the duties of a recluse with a mind intent on his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), and within twenty years he attained Arhatship. On the day he attained Arhatship...
A deity dwelling at the end of his walking path lit a lamp with her fingers and stood there.
The Four Great Kings, Sakka the lord of the gods, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to attend upon him.
Seeing that radiance, the forest-dwelling Mahātissa Thera questioned him on the following day: "During the night, in the presence of the Venerable One..."
“There was a radiance. What was that radiance? The Elder, wishing to create a diversion, said, “Radiance can be the radiance of a lamp, or the radiance of a gem,” and so forth.
Then, being pressed with the words, “You must conceal it,” he admitted, “Yes,” and reported it.

And like the Mahānāga Thera who dwelt in the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa. He too, it is said, while fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning, resolved for seven years to remain only in the standing and walking postures, thinking, "First, I shall honor the Great Struggle (mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One.
Then, having fulfilled the practice of going forth and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahatship. He...
Lifting his foot with a mind still engaged in the meditation subject, and turning back as he lifts it with a mind dissociated from it, he goes to the village boundary.

Standing in a place where there might be suspicion—thinking, "Is this a cow, or is it a renunciant?"—he puts on his robe, washes his bowl with water from the armpit, and takes a mouthful of water. For what reason?
‘I must not cause even a moment’s distraction from my meditation subject by saying “May you live long” to people who come to give me alms or pay their respects.
However, when asked the date, such as ‘Today, venerable sir, what is the day?
or the number of monks, or a question [on the Dhamma], he swallows water and then reports it; but if there are no such inquirers about the date and so forth, [he does not speak].
At the time of departure, he goes forth having spat right there at the village gate.
He is like the fifty bhikkhus who entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery;
it is said that on the full moon of Āsāḷha they made a formal agreement: "We shall not speak to one another until we have attained arahantship. And as for the village, for alms—
Upon entering, they entered after taking a mouthful of water; when questioned regarding the day and other such matters, they proceeded according to the method already described.
There, the people, seeing the place where [the water] was spat out, realized: "One has come today; two have come today. And they thought thus:
"Why is it that these do not converse with us, or perhaps even with one another? If..."
“They do not even speak to one another; surely they have fallen into dispute. Come, let us ask them for forgiveness.
Having all gone to the monastery, they did not see even two monks in the same place among those fifty monks.
Then, a man with keen eyes among them said: “Sirs, such is not the dwelling place of those who create strife. It has been well swept.”
“The courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree have been well-swept; the drinking water and the water for washing are well-set out.

Thereupon, they turned back from that very spot. Those monks, having attained *arahantship* within that very rainy season, performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) of purity during the Great Invitation.
Thus, just like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, the monks who had entered the rains retreat at the Kalambutittha Monastery...
And as if lifting his foot with a mind intent solely on the meditation subject, he goes to the vicinity of the village;
having rinsed his mouth with water and observed the streets, he enters that path where there are no drunkards, gamblers, or other quarrelsome persons, nor any fierce elephants, horses, or the like.
While wandering for alms there, he does not move with excessive haste or speed.
He walks; for there is no such thing as a "speedy alms-round" ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*).
Rather, he proceeds remaining motionless like a water-cart that has reached uneven ground.
Having entered from house to house, he observes whether the people wish to give or not, and taking alms after waiting for the appropriate time, he [remains] either within the village...
Having come either outside the village or to the monastery itself, and having sat down in a suitable and comfortable place,
he attends to his meditation subject. Establishing the perception of repulsiveness in food, he reflects upon it by way of the similes of the axle-oil,
the wound-ointment, and the child’s flesh, and partakes of food endowed with the eight factors— neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment.
"Not for adornment... [and so on] ...but for comfort. Having finished eating and performed the duties regarding water, he allows the fatigue from the meal to subside for a moment;
then, just as before the meal, he attends to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) during the period after the meal, throughout both the first watch and the last watch of the night.
This is called "carrying it out and bringing it back."

Furthermore, while fulfilling this practice of going and returning—consisting of taking [the bowl] and bringing it back—if one is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), one attains Arahatship in the first stage of life; if not in the first stage, then in the middle stage;
if not in the middle stage, then in the final stage; and if not in the final stage, then at the time of death.
If he does not attain [the goal] at the time of death, then he becomes a son of the gods;
if he does not attain it as a son of the gods, then, having been reborn when no Buddha has appeared, he realizes pratyekabodhi;
if he does not realize pratyekabodhi, then in the presence of Buddhas he becomes one of swift higher knowledge—just like the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya.
Or one of great wisdom—such as the Elder Sāriputta; or one of great psychic power—such as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna;
or one who maintains the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)—such as the Elder Mahākassapa; or one with the divine eye—such as the Elder Anuruddha;
or one who is an expert in the Vinaya—such as the Elder Upāli; or one who is a preacher of the Dhamma—such as...
The Elder Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī, is one who dwells in the forest—just like the Elder Revata;
he is one who is learned—just like the Elder Ānanda; he is one who desires training—just like the Elder Rāhula, the Son of the Buddha.
Thus, in this tetrad, for him who both carries out and brings back [the task], his clear comprehension of the range of activity reaches its peak.
Furthermore, non-delusion regarding advancing and so forth is the clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*). This should be understood as follows:
here, when a bhikkhu is advancing or retreating, unlike the blind, foolish worldlings who, in regard to advancing and so forth, think, "The self advances;
by the self, advancing is produced," or "I am advancing; by me, advancing is produced."

Or they are deluded; but one who is not so deluded, when the thought "I am stepping forward" arises, the wind-element originated by that very consciousness arises together with it, producing intimation (*viññatti*).
Thus, through the expansion of the wind-element produced by mental activity, this collection of bones designated as "body" steps forward. As he thus steps forward, with each lifting of a foot—
In the two instances of lifting up and moving away, the earth element and the water element are deficient and weak, while the other two elements are predominant and powerful.

Likewise, in the two instances of letting go and setting down, the fire element and the air element are deficient and weak, while the other two elements are predominant and powerful. Similarly, this applies to the acts of placing and releasing.
In that regard, the material and immaterial phenomena occurring in lifting do not reach carrying away; likewise, those occurring in carrying away do not reach shifting;
those occurring in shifting do not reach releasing; those occurring in releasing do not reach placing down;
and those occurring in placing down do not reach resting. In each respective instance, [they remain] joint by joint.
Joining together, joining together, and uniting, uniting, they break apart with a *paṭapaṭa* sound like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan.
In this regard, who is it that goes forward as a single entity? Or for whom is there the going forward of a single being?

For in the ultimate sense, there is only the going of the elements (*dhātu*), the standing of the elements, the sitting of the elements, and the lying down of the elements; for in each respective part, together with the material forms (*rūpa*)—
"One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases;
the succession is uninterrupted, flowing like the current of a river.
Thus, non-delusion regarding such actions as stepping forward and so forth is called "clear comprehension of non-delusion."
The meaning of the phrase "he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning" is thus concluded.

Regarding the terms "looking ahead" (*ālokita*) and "looking aside" (*vilokita*): here, "looking ahead" means gazing straight forward, while "looking aside" means glancing toward the intermediate directions.
There are also other ways of looking, such as "looking down," "looking up," and "looking behind," by way of gazing downward, upward, and backward respectively.
Those [other types of clear comprehension] are not included here; however, these two alone are taken because they are appropriate. Or rather, by way of this heading, all of them are indeed included.

In that regard, when the thought “I shall look” has arisen, the discernment of the purpose (*atthapariggaṇhana*) without looking merely according to the impulse of the mind is “clear comprehension of purpose” (*sātthakasampajañña*). This is to be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as an eyewitness. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, if Nanda must look toward the eastern direction, he looks toward the eastern direction having fully attended with his whole mind, thinking:

‘May no covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states flow in upon me as I look toward the eastern direction. In this way, he is one who possesses purposeful clear comprehension. [If, bhikkhus,] Nanda must look toward the southern direction... [and so on for the other directions].
"Nanda must look toward the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, above, below, and the intermediate directions.
Having focused his entire mind, Nanda looks toward the intermediate directions: ‘As I am looking toward the intermediate directions in this way...
[and so on] ...he remains clearly comprehending."
Furthermore, here too, purposefulness and suitability should be understood by way of the same visiting of shrines and so forth mentioned previously.

However, the non-abandonment of the meditation subject itself is "clear comprehension of the range. Therefore, those whose meditation subjects are the aggregates, elements, or bases should look forward and around by way of their own respective meditation subjects;
or rather, those whose meditation subjects are the kasiṇas and so forth should do so by means of the primary meditation subject.
Internally, there is no such thing as a self that looks forward or looks around.
However, when the thought "I shall look" arises, simultaneously with that very consciousness, the wind-element originating from consciousness arises, producing intimation.
Thus, by means of the expansion of the wind-element produced by mental activity, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper one...
"It leaps upwards. There is no such thing as an opening by means of a mechanical device; rather, visual consciousness arises performing the function of seeing.
Understanding in this way is here called "clear comprehension through non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

Furthermore, clear comprehension through non-delusion should be understood here by way of (1) fundamental thorough knowledge (*mūla-pariññā*), (2) adventitiousness (*āgantuka*), and (3) temporariness (*tāvakālika*). First, by way of fundamental thorough knowledge:
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting (āvajjana), seeing (dassana), receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), determining (voṭṭhabbana), and the impulsion (javana) is the seventh.
Therein, the life-continuum proceeds accomplishing the function of a factor for the existence at rebirth (upapatti-bhava); having turned that back—
The functional mind-element accomplishes the function of adverting; with its cessation, the eye-consciousness accomplishes the function of seeing;
with its cessation, the resultant mind-element accomplishes the function of receiving;

with its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element accomplishes the function of investigating; with its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element [accomplishes the function of determining].
Accomplishing its function of determining, it causes the impulsion to run seven times following its own cessation.
In that process, even during the first impulsion, there is no looking forward or looking around by way of lust, hatred, or delusion, thinking "this is a woman" or "this is a man";

nor does such occur during the second impulsion... [and so on] ...nor during the seventh impulsion. However, among these, just as among warriors on a battlefield, [the moments arise] in an upward and downward sequence.
When [the body] has split and fallen apart, looking forward and looking around with attachment and so forth occurs, thinking, "This is a woman," or "This is a man.
In this way, first, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood here by way of "full understanding of the root.
However, when a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door, from the moment the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) vibrates onwards, by way of accomplishing its respective functions...
When the adverting consciousness and the others have arisen and ceased, at the very end the impulsion (javana) arises.
That [impulsion] is like a visitor in the eye-door, which has become a dwelling place for the previously arisen adverting consciousness and the rest.
Just as when a visitor has entered another's house to beg for something, even though the owners of the house remain silent, he issues his commands; so too does this [impulsion].

It is not logical; for if, while the mind-door of the eye—which has become like a house—is itself neither lustful, nor hateful, nor deluded, it is illogical that lust, hatred, and delusion should arise [in the mental states].
Thus should non-delusive clear comprehension be understood by way of the "state of being a visitor.
Furthermore, those consciousnesses that arise at the eye-door, ending with the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), together with...
They break up right there along with the associated states; they do not see one another, and thus they are fleeting and temporary.

In this regard, just as when all the human inhabitants of a house have died, it is not fitting for the one survivor—who is himself subject to death at that very moment—to take delight in dancing, singing, and so forth; even so, when [only] one door remains among those accompanied by their associated states...
Since the adverting consciousness and the others have ceased right there at their respective moments, it is not fitting for the remaining impulsion— which is subject to death at that very instant—
to find delight through the modes of lust, hatred, or delusion. In this way, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood by way of its temporary nature.
Furthermore, this should be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya).

For herein, both the eye and visible forms constitute the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha); seeing is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); the feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha);
perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); and contact and so forth are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Thus, of these five aggregates...
In the coming together [of conditions], looking forward and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it that looks forward alone?
Who is it that looks around? Likewise, the eye is the eye-base; visible form is the visible-form base; seeing is the mind-base;
and feeling and the other mental factors associated with it are the mental-object base. Thus, in the coming together of these four bases, looking forward and looking around are discerned.
In that regard, who is it that looks forward?
Who is it that looks around? Likewise, the eye is the eye-element; visible form is the visible-form element; seeing is the eye-consciousness element;

and the mental states associated with it, such as feeling and so forth, are the mental-object element. Thus, looking forward and looking around occur through the coming together of these four elements.
It is perceived. In that regard, who is it that looks forward? Who is it that looks around?

Likewise, the eye is the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); visible form is the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*); adverting consciousness is the proximity, contiguity, proximity-decisive-support, absence, and disappearance-conditions;
light is the decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*); and feeling and the other mental factors are the co-nascence and other conditions. Thus, through the concurrence of these conditions—

Looking ahead and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it that looks ahead? Who is it that looks around? Thus, here too, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.
Regarding "in bending and in stretching": this refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. In that context, the bending and stretching occurs solely through the power of the mind.

"Clear comprehension of purpose" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) is the discernment of what is beneficial and what is not beneficial regarding the bending and stretching of the hands and feet, rather than doing so without such discernment; therein,
for one who stands with the hands and feet bent or stretched for too long,
painful sensations arise from moment to moment, the mind fails to attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) [is lost].
He falls away and does not attain distinction. However, when he bends at the proper time and stretches at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise;
his mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject reaches full development, and he attains distinction.
In this way, "discerning what is beneficial and what is detrimental" should be understood.

Furthermore, when there is something to be done, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable, the grasping of what is suitable is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).
Herein is the method: it is said that young bhikkhus were learning their recitations on the courtyard of the Great Cetiya.
Behind them, young bhikkhunīs were listening to the Dhamma. There, one young man, stretching out his hand, made physical contact [with a bhikkhunī].
For that very reason, he was born as a householder. Another monk extended his foot toward a fire;
his foot was burned, having struck a bone. Another monk extended it toward an anthill; he was bitten by a venomous snake.
Another monk extended it toward the pole of a robe-closet; a jewel-serpent bit it. Therefore, one should not extend [the foot] toward such unsuitable places.
One should extend [the limbs] when it is appropriate. This is what is meant here by "clear comprehension of the appropriate" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).
"Clear comprehension of the resort" (*gocara-sampajañña*), however, should be illustrated by the story of the Elder Mahā-Tissa:
it is said that while the Elder was sitting in his daytime resting place conversing with his pupils, he suddenly drew back his hand and then placed it back in its original position.
Having set it down, he bent his arm slowly. His pupils asked him, "Venerable sir, why did you first bend your arm suddenly, then set it back in its place, and finally bend it slowly again?
"Friends, ever since I began to attend to my meditation subject, I have never before bent my arm without having first released my attention from the meditation subject."
"But now, while conversing with you, I have let go of my meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and flexed my limbs.
Therefore, having placed it back in its original position, I am flexing them again. "Excellent, Bhante! A bhikkhu indeed ought to be like this.
Thus, even in this case, it should be understood that 'clear comprehension of the resort' (gocara-sampajañña) consists precisely in not abandoning the meditation subject.
‘There is no such thing as a self within that bends or stretches.

Rather, through the diffusion of the air-element of mental activity in the manner described, bending and stretching occur just like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet by means of pulling strings.
This thorough understanding here should be known as “clear comprehension of non-delusion.”

Regarding "the wearing of the outer robe, the bowl, and the robes": here, "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to the use of the outer robes by way of wearing them as undergarments and upper garments, and the use of the bowl by way of receiving alms-food and so forth. In that regard, concerning the wearing of the outer robes first:
for one who goes for alms after having worn and put on [the robes], it is said: "The acquisition of material goods is for the warding off of cold," and so forth.

And by way of method, the meaning is precisely that which has been stated by the Blessed One; it is on account of that meaning that "clear comprehension of what is beneficial" (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.
For one whose nature is fond of heat and who is weak, a fine robe is suitable; for one who is sensitive to cold, a thick double-layered robe is suitable.
What is the opposite of this is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is simply unsuitable. By means of providing [repairs such as] patches and so forth...
That [wealth] becomes an impediment for him. Likewise, robes of various kinds such as those made of wool or fine linen are objects of greed for thieves;
for such things create obstacles to the dwelling alone in the forest and even pose a threat to one’s life.

In the absolute sense, however, that which is acquired through wrong livelihood such as fortune-telling and the like, and the unwholesome states that arise in one who indulges in it—[these are the impediments].
When unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, that is unsuitable; the opposite is suitable.

By way of this, "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*) should be understood here, and by way of not abandoning the meditation subject, "clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocara-sampajañña*) should also be understood.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that puts on the robe; it is solely through the expansion of the air-element in the form of mental activity of the kind already described.
But there is the act of putting on a robe. In this regard, the robe is insentient and the body is also insentient.
The robe does not know, “The body has been clothed by me,” nor does the body know, “I have been clothed by a robe.
It is merely elements concealing a collection of elements, like a piece of cotton cloth concealing a painted figure. Therefore, it is not...
Having obtained a beautiful robe, one should feel joy; having obtained an unattractive one, one should not feel dejection.

For regarding the Nāgavammika tree at the cetiya and others, some pay honor with garlands, perfumes, incense, cloth, and so forth, while others pay dishonor by striking them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, weapons, and the like.
Yet those trees, such as the Nāgavammika, [are neither pleased nor displeased] by them.
They produce either joy or dejection. In the same way, one should not feel joy upon receiving a beautiful robe, nor dejection upon receiving one that is not beautiful.
It is by means of such reflective consideration as it occurs that "clear comprehension through non-delusion" is to be understood here.

Even when taking up the bowl, one should not seize it hastily; rather, by way of the purpose to be achieved through the taking up of the bowl—thinking, "Having taken this, I shall obtain alms while wandering for food"—it should be understood as "clear comprehension of what is beneficial" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
Furthermore, for one who is emaciated or weak, a heavy bowl is unsuitable; for anyone [who is ill], a bowl with four or five patches is [recommended].
It is difficult to clean and indeed unsuitable. For a bowl that is hard to wash is not proper; it becomes a hindrance even while one is washing it.
A bowl with the color of a gem is likewise alluring and, for the same reasons stated regarding the robe, is unsuitable.
Furthermore, [a bowl] obtained through hinting (*nimittakamma*) and so forth, or one by using which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, is unsuitable.

This is exclusively unwholesome; the opposite is wholesome. In this context, by way of that [wholesome state], "clear comprehension of suitability" (*sappāyasampajañña*) is to be understood as "clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocarasampajañña*) precisely through the non-abandonment of the meditation subject.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that takes up the bowl; it occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element in the form of mental activity of the kind already described.
However, there is such a thing as taking up a bowl. In that case, the bowl is insentient and the hands are also insentient.
The bowl does not know, “I am being held by the hands,” nor do the hands know, “The bowl is being held by us.

It is merely elements grasping a collection of elements, like the grasping of a glowing-hot bowl with tongs. Thus, it is by way of reflection on what has thus occurred that one should understand this.
‘Non-delusive clear comprehension’ (asammohasampajañña) should be understood.
Furthermore, just as compassionate persons, upon seeing destitute people in a shelter for the destitute— whose hands and feet are severed, from whose wound-mouths pus, blood,
and swarms of worms are trickling, and who are surrounded by blue flies— provide them with bandages and cloths to bind their wounds;
And they present medicines with skull-cups and such. In that regard, some receive cloths that are soft, while others receive those that are coarse;
some receive medicine bowls that are well-shaped, while others receive those that are ill-shaped.
They are neither pleased nor displeased by this, for [they consider] the cloth merely as a covering for the wound, and the medicine bowl merely as a container for the medicine.
And they have need of a bowl for the medicine. In the same way, that bhikkhu who regards his robe as a bandage for a wound,

his alms-bowl as a vessel for medicine, and the alms-food obtained in the bowl as the medicine itself— this one should be understood as one who acts with supreme clear comprehension through unconfused clear comprehension in the wearing of the outer cloak, the bowl, and the robes.

Regarding "asita" and the others: "asita" refers to the eating of alms-food and so forth; "pīta" refers to the drinking of rice-gruel and so forth; "khāyita" refers to the chewing of flour-cakes and so forth;
"sāyita" refers to the tasting of honey, molasses, and so forth. Therein, the eightfold meaning described by way of the method beginning with "not for amusement" is called "meaning" (*attha*).
Through that, "clear comprehension of purposefulness" (*sātthakasampajañña*) is to be understood.
Regarding coarse, fine, bitter, sweet, and so forth: whatever food causes discomfort for a particular person is unsuitable for them.

Furthermore, that which is obtained through practices such as divination (nimitta-kamma), or that which, when eaten by one, increases unwholesome states and causes wholesome states to decline, is exclusively unsuitable; the opposite is suitable. It is with reference to this [unsuitability] that it is said here:
‘Clear comprehension of what is suitable’ should be understood as the non-abandonment of the meditation subject; and ‘clear comprehension of the domain’ should be understood in the same way.
There is no so-called “eater” within that consumes anything.

Rather, it is solely by the expansion of the air-element of mental activity that the taking up of the bowl occurs. It is solely by the expansion of the air-element of mental activity that [the food] goes into the hand in the bowl.

This is called "introducing. Through the expansion of the air element produced by mental activity alone, there occurs the forming of a mouthful, the lifting of the mouthful, and the opening of the mouth.

No one opens the jawbone with a key or a mechanical device; rather, through the expansion of the air element produced by mental activity alone, there occurs the placing of the mouthful in the mouth, the upper teeth performing the function of a pestle, and the lower teeth performing the function of a mortar.
And it performs the function of a hand for the tongue. Thus, there, thin saliva from the tip of the tongue and thick saliva from the root of the tongue smear it.

That [food], turned over by the hand of the tongue upon the lower teeth as a mortar, moistened with the water of saliva, and crushed by the pestle of the upper teeth—there is no one who puts it inside with a ladle or a spoon.
It enters by means of the air element (*vāyodhātu*). Once it has entered, there is no one who makes a bed of straw and holds it;
it remains solely by means of the air element. While it remains, there is no one who makes a hearth, kindles a fire, and cooks it;
it is cooked solely by means of the fire element (*tejodhātu*). Once it is cooked, there is no one who [stirs it] with a stick or a staff...
Or there is no separate "ejector" outside [the body]; it is the air element alone that ejects.
Thus, the air element brings in and carries out, sustains and turns over, crushes and dries up, and ejects.
The earth element sustains, turns over, crushes, dries up, and ejects. The water element moistens.
And it maintains its own integrity. The fire element digests what has been ingested. The space element provides a clear passage.

The consciousness element, by means of appropriate application here and there, exerts itself. In this way, through the reflection on the process as it occurs, "clear comprehension of non-delusion" is to be understood.

Furthermore, "clear comprehension of non-delusion" should be understood here through the contemplation of the tenfold repulsiveness consisting of: (1) going, (2) seeking, (3) enjoyment, (4) the dwelling place, (5) the storehouse, (6) the unripened, (7) the ripened, (8) the fruit, (9) the secretion, and (10) the smearing.
A detailed exposition on this point, however, should be taken from the description of the perception of repulsiveness in food in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Regarding the business of excrement and urine": this refers to the performing of excretion and urination.
In that regard, for one who does not relieve themselves when it is time, sweat breaks out from the entire body, the eyes roll, the mind does not become one-pointed, and other diseases arise;
however, for one who does relieve themselves, none of that occurs—this is the meaning here. Of that...
By way of this, "clear comprehension of what is beneficial" (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.
For one who voids excrement or urine in an improper place, there is an offense, infamy increases, and there is a danger to life;
however, for one who does so in a suitable place, none of that occurs—this is what is meant here by "what is suitable. By way of that...

‘Clear comprehension of what is suitable’ (*sappāya-sampajañña*) and ‘clear comprehension of the domain’ (*gocara-sampajañña*) should be understood precisely through the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Internally, there is no such thing as a “self” that performs the act of passing excrement or urine;

rather, the act of passing excrement and urine occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) resulting from mental activity (*cittakiriyā*). Just as, when an abscess has ripened, pus and blood issue forth through the bursting of the abscess without any desire on its part...

It issues forth; and just as water issues from an overfilled water vessel against its will, so too feces and urine accumulated in the receptacle for digested food and the bladder issue forth, even against their will, when pressured by the force of the wind.
And this feces and urine issuing forth in this manner belongs neither to that bhikkhu himself nor to another; it is merely—
It is merely an outflow from the body. How so? Just as when one discards old water from a water-pot, it belongs neither to oneself nor to others;

it is simply the act of clearing it away. It is in this way that "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (asammohasampajañña) should be understood here by means of the reflection occurring in such a process.

Regarding "walking" and so forth: "walking" means in the act of going; "standing" means in the act of standing; "sitting" means in the act of sitting; "lying down" means in the act of reclining. In these cases, full awareness of one's actions (*sampajañña*) should be understood in the same manner as explained previously under "excellent conduct" (*abhikkanta*) and so on.
Furthermore, there is this other method: one bhikkhu walks while thinking of something else, while reflecting on something else;
another bhikkhu walks without ever relinquishing his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Likewise, one bhikkhu stands...
When sitting or lying down, he lies down thinking of one thing while reflecting on another. However, one person lies down without even relinquishing his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

But since this much alone does not make it clear, they illustrated it by means of walking meditation (*caṅkama*). For a bhikkhu who, having descended to the walking path, stands at the eastern end of the path and examines:
"The material and immaterial phenomena occurring at the eastern end of the walking path..."
Without reaching the western end of the walking path, they cease right there; even those occurring at the western end of the walking path cease right there without reaching the eastern end;
those occurring in the middle of the walking path cease right there without reaching either end;
and the material and immaterial phenomena occurring on the walking path cease right there without reaching their destination.

‘Having ceased while standing, it proceeded to sitting; having proceeded from sitting, it ceased right there without reaching lying down’—grasping in this way, even as he grasps, he causes the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) to descend;
rising, he rises only after taking up the meditation subject.
This bhikkhu is called one who acts with clear comprehension regarding going and so forth.
In this way, however, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) remains unclear in the sutta. A meditation subject that is unclear should not be undertaken.
Therefore, a bhikkhu who is able should lie down after walking, standing, sitting, and lying down in this manner, having thus encompassed [the situation]:
"The body is insentient; the bed is insentient. The body does not know, 'I am lying on the bed. The bed also..."
He does not know: "The body is lying on me," nor does he think: "The insentient body is lying on an insentient bed.
While thus repeatedly scrutinizing, he causes his mind to sink into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); upon waking, he wakes only after having grasped his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
This is what is called "one who acts with clear comprehension while sleeping."
"In waking" means in the state of wakefulness. In this regard, a bhikkhu who discerns that "when there is no occurrence of the process consisting of activity, there is no such thing as waking;

when the range of the process consisting of activity is occurring, there is what is called waking," is one who acts with clear comprehension in waking. Furthermore, having divided the night and day into six periods, [he applies himself] to five...
Even while tending to the body parts, one is called "practicing full awareness" when awake.
Regarding "in speaking": therein, a monk who discerns that "when the sound-base, which is derived form, does not occur, there is no speaking;
when it occurs, there is speaking," is called "practicing full awareness in speaking."

He is one who acts with clear comprehension when speaking. Even when teaching the Dhamma under the heading of the "bases of liberation," or even when engaging in discourse based on the ten topics of talk—having abandoned the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk—he is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speech.
Regarding silence (*tuṇhībhāve*): therein, when there is the occurrence of the sound-base (*saddāyatana*), which is derived form (*upādārūpa*), [the absence thereof] is silence.
A scrutinizing bhikkhu is said to be "one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence" when he thinks: "There is no name;

it exists in the non-occurrence [of speech]. Even one who has taken up a meditation subject according to his own preference among the thirty-eight objects and is seated, or even one who has attained the second jhāna, is indeed called "one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence."
And here, one posture is mentioned in two places.
It should be understood that in the passage "when going forward and returning," it is described in terms of traveling on the road for one who goes to and returns from the village for alms;
whereas in the passage "when walking, standing, sitting, and lying down," it is described in terms of the minor postures such as dusting and sweeping within the monastery.
524. Therein, the entire passage beginning with "What is mindfulness?
and so forth is of plain meaning. 526. What does he show by the phrase "secluded"?
He shows this bhikkhu’s place of attendance, his path of yoga, and his suitable lodging. For one who possesses such virtues within, that [lodging] is appropriate.

Dwelling in the forest. But for one who lacks these [qualities], it is unsuitable. For such a person, dwelling in the forest is like the forest-dwelling of black monkeys, bears, hyenas, leopards, deer, and the like.
Why? Because they have entered there out of mere desire. Indeed, he has no purpose rooted in forest-dwelling;
he ruins both the forest-dwelling and those who live in the forest, and he engenders a lack of confidence in the Teaching.
But for one who possesses such virtues within, he alone is worthy of it.
For by relying on forest-dwelling, having established insight and attained Arahantship, he attains final Nibbāna;
he adorns the entire forest life, he leads the way for those who dwell in the forest, and he causes the whole Dispensation to flourish. Therefore, the Teacher [entrusted this] to one of such a kind.
Showing the place for a bhikkhu’s attendance, the path of yoga, and a suitable lodging, he said, “He resorts to a secluded lodging,” and so forth.
Therein, “secluded” means empty, quiet, and noiseless. To demonstrate this very meaning, it was said, “and that which is uncrowded,” and so on.
Therein, “uncrowded” means not crowded together, not congested. Therein...
If, in the vicinity of a lodging, there is a mountain thicket, a forest thicket, or a river thicket extending even for a quarter-league (gāvuta) or half a league (addhayojana),
such that no one is able to approach at an improper time— this is called "unfrequented" despite being nearby. However,
that which is half a league or a full league away is called "unfrequented" solely by virtue of its distance.

527. It is called *senāsana* because one lies down (*seti*) and sits (*āsati*) upon it. To show its classifications, "bed (*mañca*), chair (*pīṭha*)" and so forth are stated. Therein, "bed" refers to four kinds of beds:
the stuffed-cotton bed (*masāraka*), the bound-cushion bed (*bundikābaddha*), the crab-legged bed (*kuḷīrapādaka*), and the detachable-legged bed (*āhaccapādaka*).

Likewise for the chair. "Cushion (*bhisī*)" refers to five kinds of cushions: the woolen cushion (*uṇṇābhisī*), the cloth cushion (*coḷabhisī*), the grass-cloth cushion (*vākabhisī*), the straw cushion (*tiṇabhisī*), and... [the fifth].

"Leaf-mat" (*paṇṇabhisī*): "Cushion" (*bimbohana*) refers to a pillow for the head. It should be one span and four finger-breadths in width, and in length, it should be the same as the width of the bed.
"Vihāra": a dwelling constructed with a walkway all around, having designated places for staying by night and by day within.
"Half-roofed house" (*aḍḍhayoga*): a house curved like a garuḍa. "Palace" (*pāsāda*): [as previously defined].
A long palace (*dīghapāsāda*) is one constructed by taking two *kaṇṇikā* (corner-towers).

An *aṭṭa* is a specific type of dwelling with thick walls made of bricks, four or five stories high, built for the purpose of repelling rival kings and the like. A *māḷa* is a circular pavilion similar to a dining hall;
however, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that it is a square palace comprised of a single peak. A *leṇa* is a mountain... [text ends]
A dwelling place that has been constructed by digging into a slope or by building a wall in a location where it would otherwise be insufficient;
a cave, which may be a natural chasm in the ground where a lamp is required day and night, or a mountain cave or an underground cavern;
the foot of a tree, which is the area beneath a tree, whether enclosed or unenclosed; and a bamboo thicket, which is a grove of bamboo.
"Or where the monks withdraw" means: setting aside these beds and so forth, whatever place the monks assemble in—that place fit for their assembly—is all considered "lodging. 528.
"Frequents" means he approaches it. "Frequenting thoroughly" means he approaches it well, being without longing due to his delight in that place.
"He serves" means he serves by way of wearing [the robes]; "he attends upon" means he attends upon while remaining settled and free from longing.
"He associates with" means he associates properly by fulfilling the duties regarding the lodgings.
Now, in order to show the divisions of that which was called "secluded," [the text says] "a forest, the foot of a tree," and so forth.
It has been undertaken. In this context, first according to the method of the Vinaya, it is stated: "With the exception of the village and its precincts, the remainder is the forest (arañña).
According to the method of the Suttanta, with reference to a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, it is stated:
"A forest dwelling (āraññaka) is a resting place that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant. Both of these, however, are teachings given by way of a specific method (pariyāyadesanā).
[This is] the name. Since the Abhidhamma is a teaching according to the direct method (*nippariyāya*), in order to show the forest by way of the Abhidhamma terminology, it is said:
"having gone out beyond the threshold-stone" (*indakhīla*); the meaning is "having gone out outside the threshold-stone.
Because the foot of a tree and so forth are naturally easy to understand, [the text] says simply "the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*) and so on.
It has been said. Furthermore, in this context, "at the foot of a tree" refers to any secluded spot at the base of a tree that provides cool shade. "A mountain" refers to a rocky peak;

for there, having performed one's water-related duties by the mountain springs and sitting in the cool shade of a tree while the various directions are visible and being fanned by a cool breeze, the mind becomes one-pointed. "A glen" (kandara) refers to...
*Kam* means water; *daritam* means split by that water, a mountain region which they call a *nitumba* or a river-glen (*nadīkuñja*).
For there, the sand is like silver plates, the dense forest on top is like a canopy of jewels, and water flows like a mass of gems. Having descended into such a glen, [one drinks] water.

Having drunk [water], cooled his limbs, spread out the sand, and arranged his rag-robe (paṃsukūlacīvara), the mind of one who sits and practices the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) becomes one-pointed.
A "mountain cave" (giriguhā) is the space between two mountains, or a single great hollow resembling a tunnel.
The characteristics of a charnel ground (susāna) are described in the *Visuddhimagga*.
531. "Forest-dwelling" (*vanapattha*) refers to a place beyond the vicinity of a village, outside the range of human habitation, where people neither plough nor sow.
For this very reason, it is said in its definition: "Forest-dwelling is a designation for remote lodgings," and so forth.
Alternatively, since among the tree-root dwellings and the rest, only this one is presented by dividing [the category] into its parts, therefore, according to the sequence of their enumeration:

It should be understood that, rather than providing a detailed exposition for each individual term, the exposition is given for all the final members [of the list]. "An open space" (*abbhokāsa*) means an uncovered place.
However, one who so desires may build a cloth-tent (*cīvarakuṭi*) there and dwell. "A heap of straw" (*palālapuñja*) is a pile of straw.
For they take straw out from a large heap of straw and construct a dwelling resembling a mountain slope or a cave; likewise, they do so above bushes, thickets, and the like.
Having thrown straw [into the fire] and sitting below it, they practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*); it is with reference to this that this was said.
In the description of the forest-dwelling (*vanapattha*), "with hair-raising" (*salomahaṃsa*) means where a thrill of horror arises for one who has entered;
such terrifying lodgings. "Remote" (*pariyantānaṃ*) means situated at a distance. "Not frequented by people" (*na manussūpacārānaṃ*)...
[It refers to] those standing beyond the forest edge that is frequented by people for the purpose of plowing and sowing. "Difficult to master" (*durabhisambhavānaṃ*) means:
they cannot be dwelt in by those who have not attained the taste of seclusion (*viveka-sāda*), having overcome [the obstacles]. 532.
In the description of "little noise" (*appasadda*) and so forth: "little noise" means little noise with respect to the sound of speech.
533. *Appanigghosaṃ*: it is "without noise" because it lacks the sound of the city's clamor.
Since both of these [terms] are one in the sense of sound, it is stated in its definition: "That which is 'little-sound' is the very same as that which is 'without-noise'. *Vijanavātaṃ*:
it is "free from the wind of people," meaning it is devoid of the bodily wind of those who move about. It is also called *vijanavādaṃ*.

"Reading": the meaning is that it is devoid of the talk of people. Since that which is free from noise is precisely what is devoid of both the movement of people and the talk of people, therefore in its definition it is said:
"That which is free from noise is itself that which is devoid of people. "A place for human seclusion" means a place for the private activities of humans.
However, because that place is devoid of the movement of people, it is said in its description:
"That which is secluded from people is itself that which is remote from human habitation. "Suitable for seclusion" means appropriate for solitude.
Furthermore, because that place is necessarily remote from human habitation, it is said in its description: "That which is remote from human habitation..."
"That indeed is suitable for seclusion," it is said. 534.

Regarding the description of "gone to the forest" and so forth, the forest has already been explained. Likewise with the foot of a tree. All remaining dwellings, however, are included under the term "empty place. 535.
"Having folded his legs crosswise" means having bound the posture by placing the thighs all around. "Holding the body erect" means...
Having placed the upper body straight and set the eighteen vertebrae edge-to-edge, for one sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend.
Thus, those pains that would arise moment by moment due to their bending do not arise; and since they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed.
The meditation subject does not fall away; it attains growth and expansion.
(536) "The body is erect, established, and composed"—this too was said with reference to this very same meaning.
(537) "Having established mindfulness facing the front" means having placed mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject, near the face.
The meaning is "having made [it] so. For this very reason it was said: "This mindfulness is established, well-established, either on the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth.
And here, the "sign of the mouth" (mukhanimitta) should be understood as the middle portion of the upper lip where the breath from the nose strikes;
alternatively, "pari" has the sense of encompassing (pariggaha), and "mukha" has the sense of an outlet (niyyāna).

“Satī” means the sense of establishing; thus it is called “mindfulness facing the face. In this regard, the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*: “Having established mindfulness that has discerned the way out.
Herein, this is the summary: “Having made mindfulness the means of discerning the escape.
(538) The exposition on covetousness is self-evident. However, here is the brief commentary: “Covetousness for the world...”
"Having abandoned": the world, in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating, consists of the five aggregates of clinging.
Therefore, the meaning here is: having abandoned lust for the five aggregates of clinging and having suppressed sensual desire.
(539) "With covetousness departed": because it has been abandoned by way of suppression, it is "with covetousness departed," not in the manner of eye-consciousness; this is the meaning.
541. "He purifies the mind of covetousness" means he purifies the mind from covetousness;
the meaning is that he acts in such a way that it both releases the mind from it and, having released it, does not take hold of it again.

Furthermore, in the passages of the *Niddesa*, the meaning should be understood as follows: "By practicing [it], he cleanses it; by developing it, he purifies it; by cultivating it repeatedly, he thoroughly purifies it."
The same method applies to "moceti" and so forth.
542–543. The meaning of "having abandoned ill-will and hatred," etc., should also be understood according to this very method.
It is called *byāpāda* because by means of it the mind becomes corrupted and abandons its natural state, like spoiled rice; it is defiled (*padussati*) by reaching a state of transformation.
It is called *padosa* because it corrupts or destroys another. Both these terms are synonyms for anger itself. For this very reason it is said:

"Whatever ill-will (*byāpāda*) there is, that is corruption (*padosa*); whatever corruption there is, that is ill-will. And because this has been defined in an all-inclusive sense, it is stated simply as "one whose mind is free from ill-will" (*abyāpannacitta*), rather than saying "one who is compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings."
546. *Thīna* is a sickness of the mind; *middha* is a sickness of the mental factors (*cetasika*). *Thinamiddha* is both *thīna* and *middha*.
They are "peaceful" because these two states are peaceful by virtue of their cessation-nature. It is with reference to this that the distinction in expression is made here. 549.
"Perceiving light" means being endowed with a purified perception free from hindrances, capable of cognizing the light seen both by night and by day.
550. "Mindful and clearly comprehending" means endowed with both mindfulness and knowledge. These two are mentioned because they are supportive of the perception of light. 553.

Furthermore, regarding the terms "freedom from sloth and torpor," "due to the perception of light," and "because of being abandoned" found in the explanatory passages, these are merely synonyms for one another.
Therein, "abandoned" (*catta*) means the cause of abandonment. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. This term "abandoned" (*catta*) here—
This was stated by way of relinquishing one’s own being (*sakabhāva*). “Because it has been vomited out” (*vantattā*) is further stated by way of showing the state of not taking it up again.

“Because it has been released” (*muttattā*) is stated by way of liberation from the continuity [of existence]. “Because it has been abandoned” (*pahīnattā*) is stated by way of the absence of any location even for that which has been released.
“Because it has been relinquished” (*paṭinissaṭṭhattā*) is stated by way of showing the casting off of what was previously taken up.
"Because it has been relinquished by one who is binding [the mind]" means that it has been overcome and relinquished through the power of meditation (*bhāvanābala*).

"Relinquished by way of what has been abandoned" means that abandonment occurs precisely through the mode of suppression (*vikkhambhana*); thus it is relinquished in such a way that it does not again ascend into the continuity (*santati*) of the mind.

"It becomes luminous" means it possesses radiance. It is "opened" in the sense of being free from obstruction; it is [described as] "free from defilement" in the sense of being devoid of secondary afflictions (*upakkilesa*).
They are purified. They are cleansed in the sense of being luminous.

556. Regarding "restlessness and remorse": here, restlessness (*uddhacca*) is the state of being agitated; remorse (*kukkucca*) is the transgression regarding an object due to a lack of resolve toward that object. Here too, the difference in phrasing—“they are peaceful”—should be understood according to the same method as before.
558. “One who has crossed over doubt”: having crossed over and transcended doubt, he stands [beyond it]. In the *Niddesa* as well, he is called “one who has crossed over.”
This is stated by way of showing that one has not submerged in doubt. "Crossed over" (*uttiṇṇo*) is said by way of showing the transcendence of that [doubt].
"Completely crossed over" (*nittiṇṇo*) is said by way of showing the state of having crossed over calamities after having overcome them through the power of meditation.

"Gone to the further shore" (*pāraṅgato*) means having gone to the further shore of doubt, which is characterized by the state of being free from doubt. "Attained the further shore" (*pāramanuppatto*) means having reached that very further shore through application to meditation.
"Attained": thus he shows the fruitfulness of his practice.
(559) "Free from doubt" (*akathaṃkathī*): one who is devoid of the kind of vacillation that occurs as "How is this?
How is this? "In regard to wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*): in regard to blameless states. "He does not doubt" (*na kaṅkhati*): he has no doubt such as "Are these indeed wholesome?"
"He does not give rise [to doubt]. "He does not doubt" means he does not find it difficult or wearying to determine those phenomena according to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"He is free from perplexity" (*akathaṃkathī*) means he is devoid of the kind of hesitation that asks, "How indeed are these wholesome?
"Free from perplexity" and "one whose perplexity has departed" are synonyms for the same state. As for the etymological meaning here: he has emerged from perplexity (*kathaṃkathā*).
"Free from doubt" (*nikkaṅkha*): one from whom doubt has departed is "one free from doubt.
