562. "Corruptions" (*upakkilesa*): they are the very nature of corruptions. For they defile the mind by approaching it; therefore, they are called "corruptions. 563. "Weakening wisdom":
because when these hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) arise, they weaken both mundane and supramundane wisdom that has not yet arisen...
They do not allow wisdom to arise; even when the eight attainments or the five higher knowledges have arisen, they cut them off and cause them to fall away.

Therefore, they are called "the factors that weaken wisdom. The statement, "Wisdom that has not yet arisen does not arise, and wisdom that has already arisen ceases," was also said with reference to this very meaning. The rest here is as follows:
Everything [in this section] is already clear in meaning because it has been explained here and there below.

564. Regarding the explanations of "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*) and so forth, whatever needs to be said has already been stated below in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* (The Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness), in the exposition of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and right here in various places.
For indeed, [this applies] even to the expositions of the second, third, and fourth jhānas.
Just as those jhānas were described below as "a jhāna with three factors" or "a jhāna with two factors," so too,
instead of stating it that way, they are taken together with the factors such as confidence (*sampasāda*) by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*),
based on the statement beginning with "internal confidence" (*ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ*), according to the method starting with: "Jhāna is confidence, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind."
"The specific jhāna is pointed out"—this is the distinction here.

588. Regarding the explanation of the phrase "which the Noble Ones declare," although all such terms as "they declare" and "they teach" are indeed synonyms for one another, nevertheless, [the text proceeds] by way of the summary beginning with "equanimous, mindful, dwelling in happiness."
They explain; they teach by way of exposition; they make known by way of detailed exposition;
they establish and set forth the meaning in various ways; they reveal it by showing the reasons for each respective meaning;
they analyze it by showing the distinctions of the phrasing; and they bring out its hidden state and its profundity for the sake of the listeners' knowledge.
They produce a foundation and make [the truth] clear; by all these modes, they dispel the darkness of ignorance of the listeners and reveal [the truth]. This is how the meaning should be understood.
Also, in the exposition on "transcending" (*samatikkama*), the meaning should be understood as follows:

because one has emerged from various states through those respective factors, one is "transcending"; because one has reached a higher plane, one is "surpassing" (*vītikkanta*); and because there is no falling away from that state, one is "having transcended" (*samatikkanta*).
Commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya.
2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya. 623.
In the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya, the textual arrangement follows the same method as that presented previously in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa. Therefore...
In this regard, the meaning of all the jhānas indicated by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional states should be understood according to the method explained therein.
Furthermore, the entire classification into the pure ninefold set and so forth is exactly as described there.
This concludes the commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchakavaṇṇanā) 638.
In the Section of Questions, the state of the jhānas as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the text itself.

Regarding the triads of objects, however, it should be understood that because three of the jhānas have the sign (*nimitta*) as their object, they cannot be defined by way of having a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, among these, the supramundane [jhanas] at the time of the path or the time of the fruition may have an immeasurable object. Regarding the statement that "the fourth jhana may have a limited object," there are thirteen types of wholesome fourth jhanas:

the fourth jhana as the basis for all (sabbatthapādaka), the fourth jhana of the supernormal power of transformation (iddhividha), the fourth jhana of the knowledge of the divine ear (dibbasotañāṇa), the fourth jhana of the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa), and the fourth jhana of the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa).
The fourth [jhāna] based on the divine eye knowledge, the fourth based on the knowledge of rebirth according to karma, the fourth based on the knowledge of future existences,
the fourth consisting of the base of infinite space and so forth,
and the supramundane fourth. Among these, the fourth based on the universal foundation has only an inexpressible object.
In the fourth type of supernormal power (*iddhividha*), for one who transforms the body by means of the mind and performs miracles with an invisible body,
the object is limited (*parittārammaṇa*) because it has the body as its object. For one who transforms the mind by means of the body and,
having performed a miracle with a visible body, goes to the Brahma-world, the object is exalted (*mahaggatārammaṇa*) because it has the attainment-consciousness (*samāpatticitta*) as its object.
The fourth [knowledge], the divine ear-knowledge (*dibbasotañāṇa*), has a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) because its objective field is sound.

The fourth, the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), has a limited object at the time of knowing sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) consciousness; it has a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*) at the time of knowing fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) consciousness;
and it has an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇa*) at the time of knowing supramundane (*lokuttara*) consciousness. One who has attained the knowledge of others' minds...
However, an ordinary person knows only the minds of other ordinary persons, not those of noble ones. A stream-enterer knows the minds of both stream-enterers and ordinary persons;
a once-returner knows the minds of once-returners and the two lower types;
a non-returner knows the minds of non-returners and the three lower types; and one whose taints are destroyed knows the minds of all.

When recollecting the aggregates of the sense-sphere during the knowledge of past lives, it has a limited object; when recollecting the aggregates of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, it has a sublime object;

when recollecting that "in the past, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints were destroyed cultivated the path and realized the fruit," it has an immeasurable object; and when recollecting names and clans, it has an indeterminate object.
The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the divine eye, has a limited object because its objective referent is color.

The fourth, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), has a limited object when recollecting sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) karma; it has a sublime object when recollecting fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) or immaterial-sphere (*arūpāvacara*) karma.

The fourth, the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*), has a limited object when knowing rebirth in the future within the sense-sphere; [it has a sublime object] when [knowing rebirth] in the fine-material or immaterial realms.

At the time of knowing rebirth, it has a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*); at the time of knowing that "in the future, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed will develop the path and realize the fruit," it has an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇa*);
and at the time of recollecting names and clans in such a manner as "in the future there will be a king named Saṅkha," it has an indeterminate object (*navattabbārammaṇa*).

The fourth [jhānas] of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness have an indeterminable object. The fourth [jhānas] of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have a sublime object.
The supramundane fourth has an immeasurable object.
Even in the case of functional [jhānas], this is the classification of objects for these twelve jhānas. Three jhānas have the Path as their object.

If either reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) or knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) were to take the path as its object, those three jhānas would not be "having the path as their object" because they do not occur in that manner;
however, by way of being co-nascent causes, they may be "rooted in the path.

Alternatively, when the development of the path is dominated by energy (*vīriya*) or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), they have the path as their predominance (*adhipati*). At times when desire (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) are predominant, and at the time of the fruit, they are not to be so designated.

Regarding "the fourth jhāna": here too, among the thirteen types of wholesome fourth jhānas, all instances of the fourth jhāna serving as a basis (sabbatthapādaka), the fourth jhāna of the supernormal powers of transformation (iddhividha), the divine ear (dibbasota), the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), and the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma (yathākammūpagañāṇa)—as well as the fourfold formless-sphere (āruppa) fourth jhāna—cannot be said to have the Path as its object (maggārammaṇa) and so forth.

However, the fourth jhāna of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya), the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa), and the knowledge of future existences (anāgataṃsa) does have the Path as its object. Furthermore, it cannot be said that they are "rooted in the Path" (maggahetuka) or "dominated by the Path" (maggādhipati); this applies to the supramundane (lokuttara) fourth jhāna.
It does not have the Path as its object; however, at the time of the Path, it has the Path as its cause by way of being a co-nascent cause (*sahajātahetu*).

It has the Path as its predominance (*adhipati*) when the development of the Path is dominated by energy (*viriya*) or investigation (*vīmaṃsā*). When the development of the Path is dominated by desire (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*), and at the time of the fruit (*phala*), it cannot be so described.
This same method applies to the twelve meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) from the perspective of functional states (*kiriyā*) as well.

The three jhānas should not be described [in terms of time] because they do not occur with reference to even a single dhamma among those such as the past; thus they should be understood as "not to be described.
As for the fourth jhāna: among the thirteen types of wholesome fourth jhānas, the fourth jhāna that serves as a basis for all (sabbatthapādaka) has only an "undeterminable" object.

The fourth jhāna pertaining to the various kinds of psychic power (iddhividha), when transforming the mind by means of the body, has a past object because its attainment-consciousness takes that [past state] as its object.
At the time of resolving, "In the future, may these flowers not wither; may the lamps not go out; may a single mass of fire arise;
may a mountain arise," it has a future object. At the time of transforming the body by means of the mind, because it has the body as its object, it has a present object.
The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the divine ear, has a present object because it has sound as its object.
The fourth, the knowledge of the minds of others (*cetopariyañāṇa*), has a past object at the time of knowing a mind that arose and ceased within the last seven days;
it has a future object at the time of knowing a mind that will arise within the next seven days.
[As it is said: "Just as this worthy one’s mental formations are directed, immediately following this consciousness, such-and-such a thought..."

“He will think it; even if he explains it at great length, it will be exactly so and not otherwise. For by this sutta, the occurrence of the knowledge of others’ minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) alone is demonstrated.

When it occurs with reference to the present—whether by way of the duration of the present (*addhāna-paccuppanna*) or the continuity of the present (*santati-paccuppanna*)—it has the present as its object (*paccuppannārammaṇa*). A detailed discussion on this point, however, is found in the commentary on the *Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa* below.
They should be understood in the same manner already stated.
The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of past lives, has the past as its object when recollecting past aggregates; it has an indeterminate object when recollecting names and clans.
The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the divine eye, has the present as its object because its object is physical form (vaṇṇa).
The fourth [jhāna] of the knowledge of rebirths according to one’s kamma has only past kamma as its object; thus, it has a past object (*atītārammaṇa*).

The fourth [jhāna] of the knowledge of future existences has a future object when it recollects future aggregates, and an indeterminate object (*navattabbārammaṇa*) when it recollects names and clans.

The fourth [jhāna] of the base of infinite space and the base of nothingness has only an indeterminate object. The fourth [jhāna] of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
The object is exclusively past. The supramundane fourth jhāna has an object that is not to be specified.
This same method applies to the twelve functional (kiriyā) fourth jhānas as well.

Regarding the statement "three jhānas have external objects": they are called "external-object" because they proceed by taking as their object a sign (nimitta) that exists externally to the internal self.
"Fourth jhāna": here too, among the thirteen types of fourth jhānas that are wholesome, the "foundation-of-all" fourth jhāna has only an external object.

The fourth jhāna of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*)—whether it be the transformation of the mind by means of the body or the transformation of the body by means of the mind—has an internal object because one's own body and mind are its objects;
as it is said in the method beginning with, "He even displays an external hand," and so forth.
At the time of its occurrence, it has an external object.

Regarding the fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the divine ear: when it has as its object the sounds within one's own belly, it has an internal object; when it has as its object the sounds of another, it has an external object; and by way of both, it has an internal-external object.
The fourth, the knowledge of the penetration of minds, has only an external object.

The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of past lives, has an internal object at the time of recollecting one’s own aggregates, and an external object at the time of recollecting both the aggregates and the name and clan of another.

The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of the divine eye, has an internal object when one’s own form is the object, an external object when another’s form is the object, and both internal and external objects when both are the object.

The fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of rebirths according to one’s kamma, has an internal object at the time of knowing one’s own kamma; it has an external object at the time of knowing another’s kamma; and by way of both, it has an internal-external object.
The fourth, the knowledge of future existences, has an internal object at the time of knowing one’s own future rebirth;
it has an external object at the time of recollecting another’s aggregates as well as at the time of recollecting their name and clan; and by way of both...
The fourth jhāna with internal and external objects has both internal and external objects.

The fourth jhāna of the base of infinite space has external objects. The fourth jhāna of the base of nothingness has indeterminable objects. The fourth jhānas of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have internal objects.
The supramundane fourth jhāna has exclusively external objects. This same method applies to the twelve functional (kiriyā) jhānas as well.

In this Analysis of Jhāna (Jhānavibhaṅga), however, the Fully Enlightened One has explained the jhānas as being a mixture of both mundane and supramundane in the Suttanta-bhājaniya, as well as in the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya and the Pañhāpucchaka.
For these three methods (nayā) constitute a single exposition because they are mixed with the phenomena (dhamma) belonging to the three planes.
Thus, this Analysis of Jhāna is also presented by dividing it after having extracted its three cycles (teparivaṭṭa).
The explanation of the Analysis of Jhāna in the Commentary on the Vibhaṅga, which Dispels Delusion, is finished. 13.
The Analysis of the Illimitables (Appamaññāvibhaṅga).
1. Commentary on the Suttanta-Bhājaniya (Exposition according to the Discourses) 642.
Now, in the immediately following *Appamaññā-vibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Illimitables), "four" is the numerical limit.

They are called "illimitables" (*appamaññāyo*) by virtue of their being illimitable in their pervasiveness. For these [states] either pervade immeasurable beings by way of their object, or they themselves are immeasurable.
They are called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*) because they pervade even a single being in their entirety by way of a pervading immeasurability.
"A bhikkhu here" means a bhikkhu in this dispensation. "Accompanied by loving-kindness" means endowed with loving-kindness.
"With the mind" means with the consciousness. "One direction" means toward one direction, starting from a being first embraced [as an object].
This is stated by way of pervading beings included in a single direction. "Pervading" means having touched and made into an object.
"Dwells" means he maintains the dwelling in the postures (iriyāpatha) established upon the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
"Likewise the second" means that just as he dwells having pervaded any one direction among the directions such as the east, in exactly the same way, immediately thereafter—
The meaning is: "a second, a third, and a fourth.
Thus, by that same method, it is said: "above" means the upper direction. "Below and across"—in the same way, this refers to the downward direction and the horizontal direction.
And here, "below" (*adho*) means underneath; "across" (*tiriyam*) means the intermediate directions. In this manner, [it is applied] to all directions.

"In the circle of the hermitage, he directs and also brings back the mind associated with loving-kindness as if it were a deer"—by this much, the directed pervasion of loving-kindness is shown after encompassing each individual direction.
However, the passage beginning with "in all places" (sabbadhi) is stated for the purpose of showing the non-directed [pervasion].

Therein, "in all places" (sabbadhi) means everywhere. "In all respects" (sabbattatāya) refers to all the various classifications such as inferior, middling, superior, friends, enemies, neutrals, and so forth.
"By means of selfhood" means not making a distinction such as "this is another being," but rather by means of equality with oneself;
or alternatively, "by means of all-selfhood" means without wavering even slightly outward from every state of mind. "Possessing all" (*sabbāvanta*) means possessing all beings;
the sense is "connected with all beings. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of beings (*sattaloka*).
However, because such methods as "by the vast" have already been shown here, it is stated again: "accompanied by loving-kindness.
Alternatively, since the word "thus" (*tathā*) or the word "in this way" (*iti*) is not repeated here—as it was in the case of the directed pervasion—it is therefore stated again:
"with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness"; or rather, this is stated by way of a conclusion. Regarding the term "vast" (*vipula*): here...
And its vastness is to be understood by way of pervasion. By way of plane, however, it is sublime; by way of proficiency, it is immeasurable;
and by way of having sentient beings as its object, it is immeasurable. Through the abandoning of the adversary of ill will, it is without enmity (*avera*);

through the abandoning of mental distress, it is without affliction (*abyāpajjha*), meaning it is free from suffering. This, first of all, is [the explanation] of the passage beginning with "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness."
The meaning of the matrix (mātikā) established by way of this method.

643. Now, regarding this word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya) stated by way of the method beginning with, “And how, bhikkhus, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness,” since this meditation subject (kammatthāna) is suitable for one of a hateful temperament (dosacarita), therefore, in such a manner...
This loving-kindness reaches absorption (appanā) with respect to a person. To first show that person who serves as the object for this loving-kindness, it is said:
"Just as if, for example, a certain person," and so forth. In that context, *seyyathāpi nāma* is a particle used in the sense of a simile;
the meaning is "just as if one were [to see] a certain person. *Piya* means endearing. *Manāpa* means heart-gladdening. Therein:
One is called "dear" (*piya*) either because of former association or because of present benefit;

one is called "pleasant" (*manāpa*) due to being endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). Alternatively, dearness should be understood through generosity and impartiality, while pleasantness through affectionate speech and beneficial conduct.
And since the abandonment of this ill-will (*byāpāda*) occurs through dearness, loving-kindness (*mettā*) then radiates happiness.
Because of being pleasing, neutrality does not persist, and a sense of shame and dread of blame (hiri-ottappa) arises;
then, when protected by shame and dread of blame, loving-kindness (mettā) does not decline. Therefore, having made that a simile, this was said: "dear and pleasing.
"One should practice loving-kindness" means one should pervade with loving-kindness; the meaning is that one should direct and extend loving-kindness toward that person. In the same way, all...

The meaning of "beings" (*satta*) is as follows: just as one would exercise loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward a dear person, so too, by means of that loving-kindness which has reached absorption and attained mastery, one gradually extends it to all beings—even those designated as neutral or hostile.
*Metti*, *mettāyana*, and so forth, have already been explained in their respective contexts.
644. The statement "it blows across" (*vidisaṃ vāti*) or "it blows sideways" (*tiriyaṃ vāti*) was spoken for the purpose of explaining the meaning of this [term].

645. "Having pervaded" (*pharitvā*) means having touched by way of making it an object (*ārammaṇa*). "Having resolved upon" (*adhimuñcitvā*) means having released with intensity; the meaning is: having released in such a way that what is released is well-released, well-stretched out, and well-expanded. 648. Regarding the exposition beginning with "in all ways" (*sabbadhi*):

since these three terms are each inclusive of everything, the phrase "all by all" (*sabbena sabbaṃ*) and so forth was stated in order to show their meaning as one. Its meaning has already been explained above.

650. In the exposition of "Vipulādi" (the vast, etc.): because that which, having reached absorption, is "vast" by way of pervading infinite beings, it is necessarily "lofty" by way of its plane. And that which is lofty is "immeasurable" by way of its immeasurable object.
That which is immeasurable is "harmless" by way of destroying adversaries. And that which is harmless, because of the destruction of ill-will, [is "peaceful"].

It is free from ill will. Therefore it was said: "That which is vast is sublime," and so forth. Furthermore, here the term *averam* (free from enmity) has been stated as *abyāpajjam* (free from ill will) by way of a change in grammatical gender.
Or rather, the construction should be made with the mind (*mano*): that immeasurable consciousness is the mind free from enmity;
that which is free from enmity is free from ill will. Moreover, in this context, each preceding term [is the basis] for the succeeding one.
It should be understood that "of the upper" means the upper [part] for the upper [part], or "of the lower" means the lower [part] for the lower [part].

(653) Just as one might say of a person who is destitute and poorly provided for—this was said to show the kind of person who serves as the basis for compassion; for it is toward such a person that powerful compassion arises. In this regard:
"Duggata" means one who has come to a state of being possessed by suffering (*dukkha*). "Durupeta" means one who is endowed with bodily misconduct and so forth.

Alternatively, a person who stands in darkness due to the loss of family, wealth, and so on, is "duggata"; one who stands in a state of having darkness as their ultimate destination because of being endowed with bodily misconduct and so forth is "durupeta.
This is how the meaning should be understood here.
663. “One person who is dear and pleasing”—this too was said in order to show the person who serves as the basis for *muditā* (appreciative joy).

In this context, one should understand that he is "dear" (*piya*) because he stands in a state of radiance by way of his destiny, clan, wealth, and so forth; and he is "pleasing" (*manāpa*) because he stands in a state of being destined for glory due to being endowed with good conduct of body and so on.
673. “Neither agreeable nor disagreeable”: this too is stated to show the person who serves as the basis for equanimity.

In this context, it should be understood that one is “neither agreeable” because the state of being a friend has not been attained, and “not disagreeable” because the state of being an enemy has not been attained.
Whatever else might need to be said here has all already been stated below in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* (The Section on the Arising of Consciousness).
The method of cultivation for these meditation subjects has also been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
This concludes the commentary on the Suttanta-bhājaniya. 2.
Commentary on the Abhidhamma-bhājaniya.

The *Abhidhammabhājanīya* is analyzed according to the same method of analysis as used below for the section on the arising of consciousness (*cittuppādakaṇḍa*) regarding the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional; its meaning should also be understood there according to the method already stated.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (*Pañhāpucchaka*):

In the Section of Questions, the status of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] as wholesome and so forth should be understood in accordance with the text itself. Regarding the triplets of objects (*ārammaṇattika*),...
However, all [these states] in the three triads have only nine objects of consciousness. In the triad of internal objects, they are "external objects.

But in this Exposition of the Illimitables (*Appamaññāvibhaṅga*), the Fully Enlightened One has spoken of only mundane illimitables in the Suttanta-analysis (*Suttantabhājanīya*), as well as in the Abhidhamma-analysis (*Abhidhammabhājanīya*) and the Questions-and-Answers (*Pañhāpucchaka*). For these three methods (*naya*) have the same delimitation because they are mundane.
Thus, this Exposition of the Illimitables (*Appamaññāvibhaṅga*) has also been presented by analyzing it after extracting its three cycles.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Illimitables within the *Sammohavinodanī*,
the commentary on the Vibhaṅga, is concluded.
14. Analysis of the Training Rules (Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga) 1.
Commentary on the Exposition According to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 703.
Now, in the subsequent Analysis of the Training Rules, "five" is the numerical limit. "Training rules" (sikkhāpadāni) means...

"Training precepts" (*sikkhāpada*); the meaning is "sections of training. Furthermore, all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) mentioned above are "training" (*sikkhā*) because they are to be practiced.
Among the five factors of virtue (*sīla-aṅga*), whichever factor it may be, it is a "footing" (*pada*) in the sense of being the foundation for those trainings;

thus, they are called "training precepts" (*sikkhāpada*) because they are the footing for the trainings. "Taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*): the taking away (*atipāta*) of a living being (*pāṇa*), its destruction, its killing.
Meaning: *Veramaṇī* means abstention (*virati*). *Adinnādānā* means from taking what is not given; the meaning is the seizing of what is possessed by another.
*Kāmesu* refers to sensual objects (*vatthukāma*). *Micchācārā* means wrong conduct by way of defiled desire (*kilesakāma*).
*Musāvādā* means from speaking what is untrue. *Surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā*: herein, *surā* refers to flour liquor, cake liquor, and rice liquor.

The five types of *surā* (fermented liquor) are those prepared from flour, and those "connected with ingredients" (*sambhārasaṃyutta*). The five types of *āsava* (distilled spirits) are those called *meraya*, namely: flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, molasses-liquor, honey-liquor, and that which is connected with various ingredients.
Both of these are *majja* (intoxicant) in the sense of being intoxicating.

The volition by which one drinks them is a "basis for negligence" (*pamādaṭṭhāna*) because it is a cause of negligence; therefore, they are called "the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants."
This, then, is the meaning of the presentation of the matrix (*mātikā*) here.

704. In the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanīya*), however, the entire passage beginning with "at whatever time [it is] pertaining to the sense-sphere" (*yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ*) is of plain meaning because it follows the method already explained below.
Furthermore, since it is not only abstention (*virati*) that is a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), but volition (*cetanā*) as well is indeed a training rule.
Therefore, the second method was presented in order to demonstrate that. Furthermore, since these two factors alone do not constitute the training rule (*sikkhāpada*),
but rather fifty-six factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) are also training rules by virtue of being objects to be trained in,
the third method was also presented.

In this regard, the training precept (*sikkhāpada*) is twofold: the figurative training precept (*pariyāya-sikkhāpada*) and the non-figurative training precept (*nippariyāya-sikkhāpada*). Among these, abstinence (*virati*) is the non-figurative training precept.
For that is what appears in the Canon as "abstaining from taking life" (*pāṇātipātā veramaṇī*); it is not volition (*cetanā*).
One abstains from various things by means of that [abstinence] itself, not by means of volition. However, he has presented it by bringing volition into the picture.

The same applies to the other states associated with volition. For at the time of transgression, the volition of enmity is called "immorality" (*dussīlya*); therefore, it is described as "morality" (*susīlya*) even at the time of abstention. Contact and the other [mental factors] are included because they are associated with that volition.

Now, for the purpose of stimulating knowledge regarding these training precepts (*sikkhāpada*), the analysis of these [offenses] such as killing living beings should be understood according to their nature, components, object, feeling, root, kamma, blameworthiness, and application.

In this context: "By way of nature" means that all five, beginning with the destruction of life, are indeed volitional states (*cetanā-dhamma*). "By way of constituent parts," all five are likewise courses of action (*kamma-patha*).
"By way of object": the destruction of life has the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) as its object; taking what is not given has either a sentient being or formations (*saṅkhāra*) as its object;
sexual misconduct has a woman or a man as its object; false speech has either a sentient being or formations as its object; and the drinking of fermented liquor has formations as its object.
‘In terms of feeling’: killing living beings is painful feeling. Taking what is not given has three kinds of feeling;
for when one takes what is not given while being joyful and glad, it is pleasant feeling; at the time of fear, it is painful feeling;
and for one who takes it while being neutral, it is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Sexual misconduct has either pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. False speech—
Taking what is not given has three types of feeling. Drinking intoxicants has pleasant and neutral feelings. As for their roots:
killing living beings is rooted in hatred and delusion. Taking what is not given is at times rooted in greed and delusion, and at times rooted in hatred and delusion.
Sexual misconduct is rooted in greed and delusion. False speech is at times rooted in greed and delusion, and at times...
[The first three] have hatred and delusion as their roots. Drinking intoxicants has greed and delusion as its roots.
Regarding "by way of action," false speech here is verbal action; the rest are exclusively bodily action.

Regarding "by way of blameworthiness," there is killing that is slightly blameworthy and there is that which is greatly blameworthy; the same applies to taking what is not given and so forth. Their distinctions have already been shown below.
But there is this other method: the killing of a *kunthakipillika* (a small ant) is of slight blame; that of one larger than it is of greater blame;
that too is of slight blame compared to the killing of a larger bird; that of a larger bird is of greater blame than that;
then [the killing] of a lizard, then of a hare, then of a deer, then of a gayal, then of a horse, then of an elephant is of greater blame.

The killing of a human being is a very grave offense; more so than that, the killing of an immoral person; more so than that, the killing of a person possessing the virtue of an ox; more so than that, the killing of one who has gone for refuge; more so than that, the killing of one who observes the five precepts;
more so than that, the killing of a novice monk; more so than that, the killing of an ordinary monk; more so than that, the killing of a stream-enterer;

more so than that, the killing of a once-returner; more so than that, the killing of a non-returner; and the killing of one whose taints are destroyed is indeed the most extremely grave offense of all.
Taking what is not given from the property of one who is immoral is slightly blameworthy; it is more blameworthy than that from the property of one whose virtue is like that of cattle;
more so from one who has gone for refuge; more so from one who observes the five precepts; more so from a novice monk; more so from an ordinary monk;
more so from a stream-enterer; more so from a once-returner; and more so from the property of a non-returner. Than that—
In the case of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), it is indeed extremely blameworthy.
Sexual misconduct is slightly blameworthy when committed against a woman who is immoral; more blameworthy than that is [misconduct] against one who has the character of a cow;

more so against one who has gone for refuge; more so against one who observes the five training rules; more so against a female novice (sāmaṇerī); more so against an ordinary bhikkhunī; and more so against a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

For a once-returner (*sakadāgāminī*), it is more blameworthy than that; for a non-returner (*anāgāminī*), it is even more blameworthy upon transgression; and for a bhikkhunī whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsavā*), it is exclusively and most blameworthy.
Regarding false speech (*musāvāda*), speaking falsely for the sake of a mere *kākaṇika* coin is slightly blameworthy; more so for the sake of half a *māsaka*, and more so for a *māsaka*.
Speaking falsely for the sake of five māsakas, half a kahāpaṇa, one kahāpaṇa, or for an object of even greater value, is a grave offense (mahāsāvajja).
However, for one who speaks falsely and thereby causes a schism in the Saṅgha, it is an absolutely grave offense.

Regarding the drinking of fermented liquor: drinking a mere *pasata* measure is a minor offense, while drinking a measure of an *añjali* is a grave offense; yet for one who drinks a large quantity sufficient to move the body and commits acts such as plundering villages or towns, it is indeed an absolutely grave offense.

For among the [five] courses of action, killing an *arhat* (one whose taints are exhausted) after having encountered the taking of life is a great offense; stealing what belongs to an *arhat* after having encountered taking what is not given;
violating a nun who is an *arhat* after having encountered sexual misconduct;

causing a schism in the Saṅgha through false speech after having encountered lying; and destroying villages or market towns after having drunk much liquor capable of moving the body, following the drinking of intoxicants.
It is a great offense. Among all these [offenses], however, the schism of the Saṅgha through false speech is the greatest offense;
for it is a great evil capable of causing one to be cooked in hell for an eon.

Regarding "by way of application": the taking of life may be both by one's own hand and by command; likewise with the taking of what is not given. Wrong conduct, false speech, and the drinking of intoxicants are only by one's own hand.
Thus, having understood here the analysis of killing living beings and so forth by way of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*) and other factors,

one should also understand the analysis of the abstinence from killing living beings and so forth by way of their intrinsic nature, constituent parts, object, feeling, root, kamma, breach, undertaking, and application.
In this context: "By way of dhamma" means that, according to the sequence of the conventional categories of virtue (*pariyāyasīla*), there are simply five dhammas consisting of volition (*cetanā*).

"By way of factors" means that these are precisely the five courses of kamma (*kammapatha*). "By way of object": abstaining from taking life takes the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of another as its object and desists from one's own volition of enmity. The same method applies to the others as well. For all of these—
Taking as their object a thing that ought to be transgressed against, they desist by means of volitions of aversion alone.
Regarding "from the standpoint of feeling": all such feelings are either pleasant or neutral. Regarding "from the standpoint of the root":

for one who desists with a consciousness associated with knowledge, the roots are non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for one who desists with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, the roots are non-greed and non-hatred.
‘In terms of action’: here, the abstention from false speech alone is verbal action (*vācī-kamma*); the rest are bodily actions (*kāya-kamma*). ‘In terms of breach’:
whatever a householder transgresses, that very part becomes broken and shattered, while the remainder is not shattered.
Why? Because householders have unbound morality; they guard only whatever they are able to observe. As for novices...
However, when one transgresses even a single one, all of them are broken. Not only these, but the remaining precepts are also indeed broken.
Yet, their transgression is based on the matter of a formal penalty (*daṇḍakamma*);

once the penalty has been performed with the thought, "I shall not do such a thing again," the virtue becomes complete. Regarding "from undertaking": it means that one personally resolves, "I undertake the five precepts."
They are undertaken both by one who makes a formal resolution and by one who undertakes them individually.
Even when one sits in the presence of another and undertakes them by saying, "I undertake the five precepts," they are indeed undertaken whether they are undertaken individually or collectively.
As for the "mode of application," it should be understood that all of these involve only manual application (*sāhatthika-payoga*).

712. Now, in order to show those training rules (sikkhāpada) which are spoken of as five by way of being categories of training, this section on training (sikkhāvāra) beginning with "Which things are training?

is commenced. Therein, since all wholesome states (dhamma) belonging to the four planes are "training" because they are to be trained in, therefore, in order to show them, [the text] begins with "At whatever time, pertaining to the sense-sphere... and so forth.
Thus it was said. Therein, the meaning should be understood by expanding the text according to the method already explained below in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*.
However, here only a mere summary has been shown.
This concludes the commentary on the *Abhidhammabhājanīya*.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchaka) 714.
In the Section of Questions, the nature of the training rules (sikkhāpada) as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the text itself.

Regarding the triads of objects (ārammaṇattika), however, those training rules which are stated here to have "beings" (satta) as their object should be understood as such because they are designated by the term "being."

They take only formations as their object; and because all these [abstinences] are described solely by way of abstinence from what has been encountered, they are said to have "limited objects" and "present objects.
Furthermore, since the basis from which one abstains is entirely external, it should be understood that all of them have external objects.

In this analysis of the training rules (sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga), however, the Fully Enlightened One has explained only the mundane training rules both in the Abhidhamma-Bhājanīya and in the Pañhāpucchaka. For both these methods, being mundane, have the same delimitation.
Thus, this analysis of the training rules is presented by dividing it after having extracted two cycles of permutations.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Training Precepts (*Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*) within the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, is finished. 15.
The Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (*Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*).
1. The Exposition of the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya) 1. Explanation of the Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāra-vaṇṇanā) 718.
Now, in the immediately following Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga), "four" is the numerical limit. "Analytical knowledges" (paṭisambhidā) means...

Furthermore, since it is said later, "Knowledge regarding meaning is the discrimination of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), etc., it should be understood that these are not the divisions of anything else, but rather the divisions of knowledge itself.
Thus, by the phrase "four discriminations" (*catasso paṭisambhidā*), the meaning of "the four divisions of knowledge" is included.
"Discrimination of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) means discrimination with respect to meaning.
The meaning is: knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding the meaning (*attha*), which is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the various distinctions of meaning.

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. For indeed, knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), which is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the various distinctions of phenomena, is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*). [Likewise,] it is the knowledge capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the various distinctions of linguistic expression (*nirutti*)... [that is the analytical knowledge of language].
Knowledge that has reached distinction regarding expression (nirutti) is called the analytical knowledge of expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā).

Knowledge that has reached distinction regarding ingenuity (paṭibhāna), which is capable of observing, clarifying, and defining its various manifestations, is called the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Now, in order to explain the analytical knowledges as they were set forth by dividing them, he said: "Knowledge regarding meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning," and so forth.
In this context, "the goal" (*attha*) is, in brief, cause and fruit. For that is to be sought, to be reached, and to be attained by way of its cause;

therefore it is called "the goal. In detail, however, these five things should be understood as "the goal": whatever is produced by conditions, Nibbāna, the meaning of what was spoken, kamma-result, and functional consciousness. For one who reflects upon that goal...
Knowledge that has reached the analysis of that meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
"Dhamma" is, in brief, a condition. For it is called "dhamma" because it ordains, sets in motion, and brings about this or that;
thus it is called dhamma. In detail, however, it is any cause whatsoever that produces a fruit, as well as the Noble Path.
What has been spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five things should be understood as "dhamma.
For one who reflects upon that dhamma, the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that dhamma is the analytical knowledge of dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā).
In that regard, "knowledge of the expression of the language of dhamma" refers to the conventional terminology (sabhāvanirutti) concerning both that meaning and that dhamma; of that...

When one reflects upon that expression—the sound of conventional terminology—having made it the object, the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that expression of conventional terminology is the *niruttipaṭisambhidā*. Thus, this *niruttipaṭisambhidā* is said to have sound as its object, not conceptual designation (*paññatti*) as its object. Why?
Because having heard the sound, [one knows]: "This is conventional terminology; this..."

They do not know [the distinction between] "this is the primary derivation" (*sabhāvanirutti*) and "this is not the primary derivation. For one who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāppatta*) knows that when "contact" (*phasso*) is stated, "this is the primary derivation";
but when "contacts" (*phassā*) or "contact" (*phassaṃ*) is stated, he knows that "this is not the primary derivation.
The same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [aggregates]. Furthermore, he knows other words consisting of nouns, verbs, prefixes, and suffixes, but...
"Does he know?"— insofar as, having heard a sound, he knows "this is a natural expression,
this is not a natural expression," in that same measure he will also know that [other thing]. However, having rejected the claim that this is the function of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā),
this case was stated.
It is said that the Elder Tissadatta, having taken a golden stylus at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), made this proclamation: “In which of the eighteen languages shall I speak?
However, he made this proclamation based on his mastery of learning (*uggaha*), not on his possession of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
For by means of his great wisdom, he had mastered each respective language by speaking it again and again; thus, it was from his mastery of learning...
Standing thus, he invited [them] to speak.
Having stated that beings indeed learn speech, this was further explained here:
for when children are young, their parents place them on a couch or a seat and perform various tasks while speaking various words.
The children establish the respective languages of those [parents], thinking, "By this [parent] this was said; by that [parent] this was said.

As time passes, they come to know every language. If the mother is a Tamil and the father an Andhaka, the child born to them will speak the Tamil language if he first hears his mother's speech; if he [hears] his father's speech...
If he hears first, he will speak the Andhaka dialect; but if he hears neither of the two, he will speak the Māgadhī dialect.
Even one who has been reborn in a great forest where no village exists and there is no one else to speak, when he utters speech according to his own nature, will speak only in the Māgadhī dialect.
This applies likewise in the hells, the animal realm, and the sphere of hungry ghosts.

In the human world and in the world of the devas, the Māgadhī language alone is predominant everywhere. Therein, the remaining eighteen languages—such as those of the Oṭṭhas, Kirātas, Andhakas, Yonakas, and Damilas—undergo change;
this single Māgadhī language, known as the "speech of Brahmā according to reality" (yathābhūta-brahmavohāra) and the "noble speech" (ariya-vohāra), does not change.
Even the Perfectly Enlightened One, when committing the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas to the textual tradition (tanti), [employed it].
He rendered it into the Māgadhī language itself. Why? Because in this way, it is easy to bring out the meaning.

For when the word of the Buddha has ascended the textual tradition (tanti) in the Māgadhī language, its arrival within the range of hearing of those who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) is itself a mere elaboration (papañca);
yet, as soon as it strikes their ears, the meaning presents itself through hundreds and thousands of methods. However, for others...

The textual tradition recorded in speech must be mastered by striking it again and again [with the mind]. Yet, even after mastering much, an ordinary person (puthujjana) does not attain the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
It is not that a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) lacks the attainment of analytical knowledge;
rather, for one who takes all-pervading knowledge as the object and reflects upon that knowledge among the various types of knowledge, there arises a knowledge that has reached differentiation.

"Knowledge is the analytical knowledge of inspired speech. Furthermore, it should be understood that these four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) undergo differentiation in two stages and become clear through five causes. In which two stages?

In the stage of the trainee (sekha-bhūmi) and in the stage of the adept (asekha-bhūmi). In this regard, [the analytical knowledges of] the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and the Elder Mahākassapa...
The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of the eighty great elders, such as the Elder Mahākaccāyana and the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita,

had reached the stage of one beyond training (*asekkha-bhūmi*). The analytical knowledges of the Elder Ānanda, the householder Citta, the lay follower Dhammika, the householder Upāli, the female lay follower Khujjuttarā, and others like them, [reached] the stage of one in training (*sekkha-bhūmi*).
"Have reached analysis": they reach analysis within these two stages.
By what five causes do the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become clear? By attainment, by study, by hearing, by inquiry, and by previous application.
Therein, "attainment" refers to Arahantship; for one who has reached that, the analytical knowledges [become clear].
They become clear. "Learning" (pariyatti) refers to the word of the Buddha; for one who masters it, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) become clear.
"Hearing" (savana) refers to hearing the Dhamma; for one who listens to the Dhamma with due care, the analytical knowledges become clear.
"Inquiry" (paripucchā) refers to the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā); for one who explains the meaning of the text already mastered, [the analytical knowledges become clear].
The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become lucid. "Former practice" (*pubbayoga*) means the state of being engaged in former practice;

it is the state of having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of carrying it forward and bringing it back in a previous existence. For one engaged in former practice, the analytical knowledges become lucid.
In this regard, for the Elder Tissa, the son of the householder Punabbasu, who had attained Arahantship, the analytical knowledges became lucid.

It is said that after learning the Buddha’s word on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, he went to the other shore and, having learned the Buddha’s word in the presence of the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita, was returning when, at the landing place where he boarded the ship, a doubt arose in him regarding a single point.
He turned back from a journey of one hundred yojanas to go into the presence of his teacher; while on the way, at the house of a certain householder—
He spoke a question. Having gained confidence, the man gave him a woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces of money.
He too, having brought it, gave it to his teacher. The Elder had it pounded with an axe and made a border for his sitting mat.
"For what purpose? [the man asked]. "For the sake of favoring future generations," he replied. For this was his thought: "Having contemplated the path we have traveled..."
"In the future, my fellow practitioners will think that their own practice must be perfected.
Having resolved his doubts in the presence of his teacher, the Elder Tissa disembarked at Jambukolapaṭṭana. At the time for sweeping the courtyard of the shrine, he reached Vālikārāma and swept it.
Seeing the place he had swept, [the people thought], "This is a place swept by a monk who is free from passion."
They asked the Elder a question for the sake of testing him. Because the Elder had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), he answered every question that was asked.
However, the analytical knowledges of the Elder Tissadatta and the Elder Nāgasena became clear through their mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
The analytical knowledges of the novice Sudhamma became clear through his attentive hearing of the Dhamma. He...
It is said that a nephew of the Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, attained Arahatship at the very moment of his ordination;
while sitting in the place of his maternal uncle, the Elder, to listen to the exposition of the Dhamma, he mastered the Three Piṭakas.

However, it was the Elder Tissadatta who, as he explained the meaning of the texts he had learned, attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) with clarity. [This concludes] the section on the practice of going and returning.
However, there was no end to those former practitioners who had come after fulfilling [the preliminary requirements], having mastered the meditation subject up to the level of adaptation (anuloma),
and had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) in their clarity.

Among these causes, however, these three— mastery of the scriptures (pariyatti), listening (savana), and interrogation (paripucchā)— are the powerful causes for the specific distinction [of the Dhamma].
Is prior application (*pubbayoga*) a powerful condition for attainment, yet not for its differentiation? It is a condition for attainment, but not in that same way [for differentiation].

For whether there was prior study, listening, and interrogation in the past or not, without the contemplation of formations (*saṅkhārasammasana*)—both in the past and now—there is no such thing as the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
However, when these two [prior application and the contemplation of formations] come together, they constitute the analytical knowledges.
"Having supported them, they make them clear.
This concludes the commentary on the Section on Compendium (Saṅgahavāra). 2. Commentary on the Section on Truths (Saccavārādi).

719. Now, in order to analyze the *paṭisambhidā* (analytical knowledges) by way of demonstrating the classification of those five meanings and five phenomena that were included in the section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*), the section on classification is commenced again by means of the method beginning with "four," and so forth.

This is fivefold, consisting of the section on the truths (*saccavāra*), the section on causes (*hetuvāra*), the section on phenomena (*dhammavāra*), the section on the modes of conditions (*paccayākāravāra*), and the section on the summary of the teachings (*pariyattivāra*).
Among these, [the first deals with] Nibbāna, which is to be attained through the condition of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) that has arisen from conditions.

The "Chapter on Truths" (*saccavāra*) was spoken in order to show the state of phenomena (*dhamma-bhāva*) of the Noble Path—which brings about the fruit of Nibbāna—and the state of meaning (*attha-bhāva*) of that fruit.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Causes" (*hetuvāra*) was spoken in order to show the state of phenomena of any cause that produces a fruit, and the state of meaning of that cause and its fruit. In that regard:
Furthermore, by way of the sequence of cause and fruit, the discrimination of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) was first explained out of order. Then,

the "section on phenomena" (*dhamma-vāra*) was stated in order to show the state of being the meaning (*attha-bhāva*) of those various phenomena— classified as material and immaterial— that are born from their respective causes,
and to show the state of being the phenomenon (*dhamma-bhāva*) of each of those specific causes of material and immaterial phenomena, such as aging and death.

Furthermore, the "Section on the Mode of Conditions" (Paccayākāravāra) was stated to show the state of being a condition for existence and the state of being phenomena— such as birth and so forth— for the arising of aging, death, and the rest. Subsequently,

the "Section on the Discourses" (Pariyattivāra) was stated to show the state of being a phenomenon for each respective teaching comprised within the scriptures, and the state of being the meaning for the meaning of those teachings as attained through the conditions comprised within those very teachings.

And in this regard, since the meaning is understood by knowing what has been spoken, the discrimination of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) is first explained according to the sequence of what was spoken and its meaning, rather than in the reverse order.

Furthermore, for the purpose of showing the divisions of the Dhamma as study, the section of detailed exposition preceded by the question, "In that context, what is the discrimination of phenomena? is stated. Therein:
The entire body of the teaching (tanti) is grasped in its entirety by means of the nine divisions beginning with "Sutta.

In this instance as well, by way of what has been spoken—namely, "this is the meaning of this utterance, this is the meaning of that utterance"—the entire body of the teaching alone is grasped in its entirety.
This concludes the commentary on the *Suttantabhājanīya*.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya) 725.
Therein, three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are mundane (lokiya). The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane (lokuttara).
For it is also supramundane by way of the path and fruition knowledges that have Nibbāna as their object. [This is stated] in the Exposition of the Abhidhamma.
This is analyzed by way of four sections according to the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional [consciousness].

Therein, it should be understood that for every single description of consciousness, four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) are analyzed by way of all those wholesome consciousnesses that were previously analyzed in the "Section on the Arising of Consciousness" (*Cittuppādakaṇḍa*). The same method applies to the unwholesome consciousnesses as well. Regarding the sections on the resultant and the functional:

Because they are included under the meaning of resultant and functional [consciousness], the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are analyzed as three each for every single resultant consciousness and functional consciousness, excluding the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā). However, the text is abbreviated, showing only the general outline;
it should be understood according to the detailed exposition that has already been given below.

But why is it that, whereas in the sections on the wholesome and the unwholesome it was stated, "Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)," it is not stated here in this way:
"Knowledge regarding those phenomena of which these are the results is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā)"?
Because it has already been stated above. If that is so, [one might ask] because it was stated above, "Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning."
Should it not be said here that this analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is also not to be mentioned? It is not the case that it should not be mentioned. Why?

Because it was not mentioned below in reference to the arising of resultant and functional consciousnesses. Furthermore, in the section on the functional [consciousness], the statement "of those states these are the functionals" would simply not be appropriate;
therefore, in both these sections, only three analytical knowledges are analyzed.

In that context, "by whatever language there is the designation of those phenomena" means that by whatever language there is the designation of those phenomena stated in the manner beginning with "there is contact for them," such as "this is contact" and "this is feeling.
In that regard, "knowledge of the expression of the language of phenomena" refers to the knowledge regarding that meaning and those phenomena which occurs through that [language].
Knowledge of the expression of the Dhamma is knowledge of the verbal designation of intrinsic nature.

Here too, it is precisely the knowledge that has arisen by taking the sound of the expression as its object that is being spoken of. "By which knowledge" means by which analytical knowledge of ready wit (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*).
"He knows those knowledges" means he knows the other three analytical knowledges.
Now, in order to show how that knowledge functions with respect to those knowledges—just as it knows them—it is said:
"These knowledges illuminate this meaning. In this context, "illuminate this meaning" means they illuminate, reveal, and define this particular meaning. Thus, regarding the knowledges...
"Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge that occurs in these three ways among the three types of knowledge; this is called the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
In this regard, although this analytical knowledge of perspicuity knows the function of the other analytical knowledges—thinking, "This is the function of this one;
this is the function of that one"—it itself is not able to perform those functions.
It is like a preacher of the Dhamma who is well-versed compared to one who has heard little. It is said there were two monks:

one was learned, the other had heard little. They both learned the same path of a Dhamma discourse together. Among them, the one who had heard little possessed a beautiful voice, while the other had a dull voice.
As they traveled from place to place, the one with the lesser learning, by virtue of his own excellence of voice, [captivated] the entire assembly...

Having stirred them up, he preached the Dhamma. As they listened to the Dhamma, their minds became joyful and glad, and they said, "From the way he preaches the Dhamma, he must surely be one who has mastered the Three Piṭakas.
But the learned monk said, "You will know whether he is a master of the Three Piṭakas or not once you have heard the Dhamma. Although he spoke thus, [the others did not heed him].
However, just as he is unable to preach the Dhamma by agitating the entire assembly, so too he lacks the capacity for such discourse.

In this regard, although he possesses the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*), one should understand that—just as a man of little learning cannot emulate one who is well-versed—he recognizes the duties of the others but is himself unable to perform those duties. The rest is self-evident.

746. Having thus analyzed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) by way of the arising of wholesome states of consciousness and so forth, he now says, "Again, the four analytical knowledges," etc., in order to show the field that serves as their place of origin.

Therein, the statement "three analytical knowledges [arise] from wholesome states of the sense-sphere in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge" is said with reference to those in training (sekkhā). For even for them, at the time of reflecting upon the Dhamma...
Taking as its object the fivefold Dhamma mentioned above, the discrimination of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) arises within the four types of wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge.
Likewise, at the time of reviewing language, taking sound as its object, the discrimination of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) arises;
and at the time of reviewing knowledge, taking all-pervading knowledge (sabbatthaka-ñāṇa) as its object, the discrimination of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) arises.
Regarding the phrase "from functional [consciousness] in four," this is stated with reference to those who are beyond training (asekkha).

For at the time of reviewing their own states, having made the fivefold state mentioned above the object, the discrimination of dhamma arises in the four types of functional consciousness associated with knowledge.
Likewise, at the time of reviewing language, having made sound the object, [the discrimination of language arises].

The analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*); and at the time of reviewing, the knowledge that takes all-pervading knowledge as its object is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).

As for the statement that "the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) arises in these [three] as well," this is said with reference to those in training (*sekkhā*) and those beyond training (*asekkhā*).
For, at the time when those in training review the meaning, they take as their object the meaning classified as described above.
Having done so, it arises in the four wholesome consciousnesses associated with knowledge, as well as at the time of the Path and its Fruits,
within the Path and the Fruits themselves. Furthermore, for one who is beyond training (an arahant),

it arises in the four functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge— taking as its object the very same categories of meaning mentioned above— at the time of reviewing the Fruit, and also at the time of the Fruition, specifically the highest fruit of recluseship (arahattaphala).

Thus, this method has been shown for the purpose of demonstrating the planes, showing that these [states] of those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha), when arising, arise within these planes.
This concludes the commentary on the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya*.
3. Commentary on the Section of Questions (Pañhāpucchaka) 747.
In the Section of Questions, the status of the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) as wholesome and so forth should be understood according to the canonical text itself.
Regarding the triads of objects, however, the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) takes only sound as its object; therefore, it has a limited object (parittārammaṇā).

The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) has a limited object when it reflects upon meanings comprised of sense-sphere resultant and functional states that have arisen through conditions;
it has a sublime object when reflecting upon the aforementioned categories of fine-material and immaterial-sphere meanings;
and it has a supramundane object when reflecting upon the meaning of supramundane resultants and the ultimate meaning, Nibbāna.

For one who is reviewing it, [the analytical knowledge of] the object is immeasurable. The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā) has a limited object when reviewing wholesome, unwholesome, and conditional phenomena of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara);
it has a sublime object when reviewing wholesome phenomena and conditional phenomena of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara);
[and it has a supramundane object when reviewing] wholesome phenomena of the supramundane (lokuttara).

For one who reflects upon conditioned phenomena (*paccayadhamma*), it has an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇā*). The analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*) has a limited object (*parittārammaṇā*) for one who reflects upon the wholesome, resultant, and functional knowledges of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*);
it has a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇā*) for one who reflects upon the wholesome, resultant, and functional knowledges of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, knowing their objects;
and [it has a supramundane object] for one reflecting upon the wholesome and resultant knowledges of the supramundane (*lokuttara*).
For one who is reviewing, it has an immeasurable object (*appamāṇārammaṇā*).
As for the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), by way of its co-nascent cause (*sahajātahetu*), it may have the Path as its cause (*maggahetukā*);

by way of the cultivation of the Path where energy (*vīriya*) is predominant, it may have the Path as its dominant influence (*maggādhipati*); by way of the cultivation of the Path where desire (*chanda*) or consciousness (*citta*) is predominant, it is not so classifiable; and at the time of the fruit (*phala*), it is likewise not so classifiable.

At the time of reviewing the path, the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) has the path as its object; for one who reviews the path by treating it with reverence, the path is predominant by way of objective predominance (ārammaṇādhipati).
At the time of reviewing the knowledge of the path, the analytical knowledge of inspired speech (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) has the path as its object;
for one who reviews the path by treating it with reverence, the path is predominant. At the time of reviewing the remaining knowledges...

[The analytical knowledge of language] has an object that is not to be expressed. The analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) takes only present sound as its object; thus, it has a present object.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) has a past object for one who reviews a past result-meaning, a kamma-result meaning, or a meaning arisen from conditions;
it has a future object for one who reviews the future; and [it has a present object] for one who reviews the present.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) has a present object when one is reflecting on supramundane ultimate reality;
it has an indeterminate object when one is reflecting on that which is beyond description. When reflecting on past wholesome, unwholesome, or conditioning phenomena, it has a past object;
when reflecting on the future, it has a future object; and when reflecting on the present, it has a present object.
The analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) has the past as its object when one reviews past wholesome knowledge, resultant knowledge, or functional knowledge;
it has the future as its object when reviewing the future; and it has the present as its object when reviewing the present.

The analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) has external objects as its object because its object is sound. Among the other three, the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā)...
For one who reviews what has arisen through conditions as being internal, for the sake of result or for the sake of functional [kamma], it has an internal object;
for one who reviews it externally, it has an external object; for one who reviews it both internally and externally, it has an internal-external object;
and for one who reviews the ultimate reality, it has an external object only. The discrimination of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā) concerns the wholesome and unwholesome within oneself.
At the time of reviewing the condition-dhamma internally, it has an internal object; at the time of reviewing wholesome or unwholesome condition-dhammas externally, it has an external object;
and at the time of reviewing wholesome or unwholesome condition-dhammas both internally and externally, it has an internal-external object.
The analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*) consists of the knowledge of wholesome resultant and functional consciousness internally.

At the time of reviewing, knowledge of wholesome, resultant, and functional [consciousness] has an internal object; it has an external object... pe ...and at the time of reviewing, it has both an internal and external object.

Here too, three of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are mundane; the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is both mundane and supramundane. For in this *Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*...
The Fully Enlightened One has explained even these three methods as a single exposition because they are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
For in all three of these, the three analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are mundane, while the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is both mundane and supramundane.
Thus, this *Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga* has also been presented by analyzing it after having extracted those three turnings.

The explanation of the Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (*Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*) in the Commentary on the Analysis (*Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*), which Dispels Delusion (*Sammohavinodanī*), is completed. 16.
The Analysis of Knowledge (*Ñāṇavibhaṅga*).
1. Commentary on the Singlefold Chapter, etc.

751. Now, immediately following that, in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga*, a detailed exposition has been made according to the sequence of the words set forth, after first establishing the table of contents (*mātikā*) by way of ten sections beginning with "the basis of knowledge as singlefold" and ending with "the tenfold."
Therein, "by way of one kind" means by way of a single mode or a single portion. Regarding the term *ñāṇavatthu*:

it is called *ñāṇavatthu* because it is both knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and a basis (*vatthu*) for various kinds of attainments; alternatively, it is called *ñāṇavatthu* because it is the basis for knowledge in the sense of being its locus.
However, here it should be understood as *ñāṇavatthu* in the former sense. For this very reason, at the conclusion of the section on the singlefold classification:
“Wisdom that analyzes the basis as it actually is—thus, in one way, is the basis of knowledge,” so it is said.

“The five consciousnesses” refers to the five beginning with eye-consciousness. “Are not roots,” and so forth, should be understood according to the method already explained below in the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
Whatever remains to be said here in brief will be made clear in the section of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*). As follows:
And here, whatever needs to be said regarding the sections beginning with the "Pairs" (Duka) matrix will be made clear in those very places.
However, the mere outline of the presentation should be understood here as follows. For herein, there are two types [of verses] in brief:
those by way of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* matrix, such as "Not a cause, rootless," and those not by way of a matrix, such as "Impermanent, overcome by aging. By way of these seventy-eight divisions...
The single-item matrix (ekaka-mātikā) is set forth by way of individual terms.
The two-item matrix (duka-mātikā), however, is set forth by way of thirty-five dyads that correspond to the pairs [of the Abhidhamma].

The three-item matrix (tika-mātikā) is set forth by way of four external triads corresponding to the triads, such as "wisdom consisting of reflection" (*cintāmayā paññā*), and "wisdom that is fruition" (*vipākā paññā*).

By means of the fourteen matrices (mātikā) stated according to unrestricted wisdom; by means of the thirteen stated according to the first term of the triad of applied thought (vitakka) with restricted wisdom;
by means of the seven stated according to the second term with restricted wisdom;
by means of the twelve stated according to the third term with restricted wisdom; and by means of the first term of the triad of rapture (pīti) with restricted wisdom.

The matrix of triplets (tikamātikā) is set forth by means of eighty-eight triplets: by thirteen stated according to the first term, likewise by thirteen according to the second term, and by twelve according to the third term, which are determined by way of wisdom (paññā).

As for the matrix of fours (catukkamātikā), it is [set forth] by twenty-one tetrads beginning with "knowledge of the ownership of kamma" (kammassakatañāṇa); as for the matrix of fives (pañcakamātikā)...
The fivefold matrix by two sets of five; the sixfold matrix by one set of six;
the sevenfold matrix by eleven sets of seven as briefly stated thus, "Seventy-seven bases of knowledge"; the eightfold matrix by one set of eight; and the ninefold matrix by one set of nine.
10. Commentary on the Tenfold Matrix.
760. The *Dasakamātikā* (The Tenfold Schedule) is set forth by means of a single decade beginning with “the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

In this context, “ten” (*dasa*) is a numerical limit. “Of a Tathāgata” (*tathāgatassa*) refers to one who has come (*āgata*) as did the ancient seers such as Vipassī and others, and who has gone (*gata*) as they went.
“Powers of a Tathāgata” (*tathāgatabalāni*) refers to those qualities not shared with others.

They are the powers of the Tathāgata himself; or alternatively, the meaning is "powers arrived [at him] in the same way that the powers of previous Buddhas arrived through the perfection of their store of merit. In this regard, the Tathāgata’s power is twofold: physical power and knowledge-power.
Of these, the physical power should be understood according to the lineage of elephants. For this has been said by the ancients:
Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tambapiṅgala, Gandha, Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta—
these are the ten breeds of elephants.
In this context, "Kāḷāvaka" should be understood as a breed of ordinary elephants.
The physical strength of ten men is equal to that of one Kāḷāvaka elephant; the strength of ten Kāḷāvakas is equal to that of one Gaṅgeyya;
the strength of ten Gaṅgeyyas is equal to that of one Paṇḍara; and the strength of ten Paṇḍaras is equal to that of one...
The value of ten *tamba* elephants is equal to that of one *piṅgala* elephant; the value of ten *piṅgala* elephants is equal to that of one *gandhahastin*;
the value of ten *gandhahastins* is equal to that of one *maṅgala*; the value of ten *maṅgala* elephants is equal to that of one *hemavata*;
and the value of ten *hemavata* elephants is equal to that of one *uposatha*.
That which is the strength of ten Uposatha elephants is the strength of one Chaddanta elephant. That which is the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants is the strength of one Tathāgata.
