This very thing is also called the power reckoned as Nārāyaṇa.
By the calculation of ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand koṭis of elephants; by the calculation of men, it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men.
This, first of all, is the physical power of the Tathāgata.
As for his power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*), that which has come down here in the scripture is the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*).

In the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*, there is the knowledge of the ten powers, the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the unshakable knowledge regarding the eight assemblies, the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth (*yoni*), and the knowledge that delimits the five destinations (*gati*).

The seventy-three knowledges (ñāṇa) recorded in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the seventy-seven knowledges, and likewise many thousands of other knowledges—this is what is called the "power of knowledge" (*ñāṇabala*).
Here too, it is specifically the power of knowledge that is intended; for knowledge is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.

"Endowed with these powers" means possessed of, fully endowed with, these ten powers of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*). "The place of the bull" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means the preeminent position, the supreme position;
or alternatively, "bulls" (*āsabhā*) refers to the previous Buddhas, and it means their place.
Furthermore, a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred cattle, a *vasabha* is the leader of a thousand cattle; or a *usabha* is the leader of a hundred bulls (*vaja*).

The bull is the eldest of a thousand bulls; he is the best of all cattle, the overcomer of all dangers, white, beautiful, the bearer of great burdens, and unshakable even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts—the *nisabha*.
It is this that is intended here by the term *usabha*. Indeed, this is also a synonym for it.
That which belongs to the *usabha* is *āsabha*. "Place" (*ṭhāna*) refers to [the bull] having pressed down upon the earth with its four feet.
An immovable position. This, moreover, is called "bull-like" (*āsabha*) because it is like a bull.

For just as a bull known as a "leader" (*nisabha*), endowed with the strength of a bull, stands in an immovable position by pressing down upon the earth with all four feet, even so the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, [stands] upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of intrepidity.
Having pressed down upon the world with its devas, he stands unshakable in his immovable state, incapable of being moved by any adversary or enemy.
Standing thus, he claims that bull-like position (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*), approaches it, does not renounce it, and attributes it to himself.
Therefore it is said: "He claims the bull-like position."
"In the eight assemblies" means in the eight types of assemblies. "He roars the lion’s roar" means he roars the best roar, the fearless roar;
or he roars a roar similar to that of a lion. This meaning should be illustrated by the *Sīhanāda Sutta*.

Or, just as a lion is called a "lion" (*sīha*) because of his endurance (*sahana*) and his slaying (*hana*), so too the Tathāgata is [called a lion] because of his endurance of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and his slaying of the doctrines of others.
It is called a "lion. The roar of the lion thus spoken of is the "lion's roar.

In this regard, just as a lion, endowed with lion-strength, fearless in every respect, and free from horripilation, lets out a lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, fearless in the eight assemblies and free from horripilation, [utters his roar] beginning with "Such is form," and so forth.
By means of his method, he roars the lion’s roar, endowed with the various graces of teaching. Therefore it is said: “He roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies.
Regarding the phrase “he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel”: here, *brahma* means supreme, excellent, and pure. Furthermore, this word *cakra* (wheel) refers to:
prosperity, a characteristic mark, a chariot part, and a mode of conduct.
The term *dāna* is seen in the sense of "giving," as well as in the context of the "jewels" (*ratana*), the "Dhamma," and the "wheels" (*cakra*) beginning with the wheel of sovereignty.
Here, however, it is intended in the sense of the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*).
One should analyze that in two ways. For instance, in such passages as: "Monks, there are these four wheels possessed by which gods and humans [attain their status]," this [term]—
It is seen in prosperity: in the phrase “wheels have grown on the soles of his feet,” it refers to a mark (lakkhaṇa).
In the phrase “like the wheel of one who drives,” it refers to a chariot part (rathaṅga). In the phrase “four-wheeled, nine-gated,” it refers to the modes of deportment (iriyāpatha).
In the phrase “Give, enjoy, and do not be negligent; set the wheel in motion for all living beings,” it refers to giving (dāna). [And] “the divine wheel-treasure...”
In the phrase "he appeared," it refers to the Wheel of Jewels (*ratana-cakka*). In the phrase "the wheel set in motion by me," it refers to the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhamma-cakka*).

In the phrase "the wheel revolves upon the head of the man struck by desire," it refers to the chest-wheel (*ura-cakka*). In the phrase "even with a wheel whose edge is as sharp as a razor," it refers to the wheel as a weapon (*paharaṇa-cakka*).
In the phrase "a thunderbolt-wheel (*asanivicakka*)," it refers to the circle of a thunderbolt (*asanimaṇḍala*). But here, this term is understood as the Wheel of Dhamma.

Furthermore, that Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). Therein, the knowledge of penetration is developed through wisdom and brings about the noble fruit for oneself;
the knowledge of teaching is developed through compassion and brings about the noble fruit for disciples.
Therein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen. For, from the time of the Great Departure...

From the moment the path of Arahatship arises until the moment of the fruition, it is called "arisen"; or from the Tusita heaven until the moment the path of Arahatship arises on the Great Enlightenment Seat (Mahābodhipallaṅka) until the moment of the fruition, it is called "arisen";

or from the time of the prophecy by Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the moment the path of Arahatship arises until the moment of the fruition, it is called "arisen. The knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa) is also [likewise].
That which occurs while it is occurring is twofold. For as long as it occurs up until the stream-entry path of Aññā Koṇḍañña, it is called "occurring at the moment of the fruit.
Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, while the knowledge of teaching is mundane.
Yet both of these are the unique, direct knowledge of the Buddhas alone, not shared by others.

Now, in order to show in detail those ten powers endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his pre-eminent place—those which were introduced at the very beginning as "the ten powers of a Tathāgata"—it is asked: What are the ten?
Here, the Tathāgata says: "The possible as possible," and so forth. In that context, "the possible as possible" means the cause as cause.
By way of cause. For a cause is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit abides therein;
since it arises and proceeds in dependence upon that, it is therefore called a ground. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever states are the causes and conditions for the arising of whatever states, those are the grounds for them," and "whatever states are not... [the rest of the passage follows].
Understanding that "these causes are not conditions for the arising of this or that state," he understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible.

"By which" means by which knowledge. "This too is of the Tathāgata" means that this knowledge of the possible and the impossible is called a power of the Tathāgata; such is the meaning. This same method of application should be understood for all subsequent passages.
"Of the undertaking of kamma" means of wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed after having undertaken it; or "the undertaking of kamma" is simply the kamma itself.
"By way of place and cause" means by way of both condition and cause. In this context, destiny, the basis, time, and effort are the "place" for the result, while the kamma is the "cause."
"Leading everywhere" means leading to all destinations, both to good destinations and to bad destinations. "The way" means the path.
"He understands it as it really is" means that even when many people are killing a single living being, he understands according to this principle: "The volition of this one will lead to hell;
the volition of this one will lead to the animal realm"—thus, regarding even a single object, he understands the wholesome and unwholesome volitions.
He understands the intrinsic nature of the practices without error.
"Many elements" means having many elements by way of the eye-element and so forth, or by way of the sense-sphere of desire and so forth.
"Diverse elements" means having elements of various kinds due to the distinct characteristics of those very same elements. "The world" refers to the world of aggregates, bases, and elements.
"He understands according to reality" means he penetrates the specific nature of those various elements without error.
"The state of having diverse inclinations" refers to the condition of having diverse inclinations through inferior and other such dispositions.
"Of other beings" refers to preeminent beings. "Of other persons" refers to those other than them who are inferior beings; these two terms have the same meaning.
Alternatively, these two terms are stated in two ways according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

"The knowledge of the higher and lower faculties" (*indriyaparopariyatta*) means the superior state and the inferior state, as well as the increase and decrease, of the faculties such as faith (*saddhā*) and so forth.

"Of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments" refers to the four meditations beginning with the first, and [the eight liberations] beginning with "one possessing form sees forms."
Of the eight liberations, the three concentrations beginning with "with applied thought and sustained thought," and the nine successive attainments beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.
"Corruption" refers to states conducive to decline. "Purification" refers to states conducive to distinction.
"Emergence" refers to the cause by which one emerges from the jhānas and so forth.
"Recollection of past abodes" (*pubbenivāsānussati*) means the recollection of the aggregates (*khandha*) in which one formerly dwelt.
"Passing away and rebirth" (*cutūpapāta*) means both passing away (*cuti*) and rebirth (*upapāta*).

"The destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*) means Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the taints (*āsavanirodha*) consisting of the destruction of the taints such as the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*).
"These" refers to those which were previously called "the ten powers of a Tathāgata"; by saying "these are they," he brings them to completion.

Having thus understood the word-by-word commentary on this sequence, one should now consider that the Tathāgata, first of all, by means of the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*), [discerns] for the sake of the beings to be trained the possibility and impossibility regarding the attainment and non-attainment of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).
He sees the absence of the obstruction of defilements (kilesāvaraṇa), because he sees the state of mundane right view and because he sees the absence of the state of fixed wrong view.
Then, by means of the knowledge of the ripening of kamma, he sees the absence of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa), because he sees rebirth with three roots.

By means of the knowledge of the path leading everywhere, he sees the absence of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa), because he sees the absence of deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma).

Thus, by means of the knowledge of the many elements and the diversity of elements regarding those who are unobstructed, he perceives their specific temperament for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma in accordance with it, because he sees the differentiation of their elements.

Then, by means of the knowledge of their diverse inclinations, he perceives their inclination, so that he may teach the Dhamma according to their inclination even without employing formal methods. Then, having thus perceived their inclinations—

To teach the Dhamma according to their capacity and strength, he perceives the individual differences among their faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta*) by means of the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*),

because he sees the sharpness or dullness of their faith and the other faculties. Furthermore, even though they have thus fully understood the differences among their faculties, if they are far away, then—
because he has attained mastery over the jhānas and so forth through the full understanding of those states— he [perceives them] by means of a specific supernormal power (*iddhi-visesa*).

He approaches them quickly. Having approached, he perceives their cultivation of previous births through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), and he perceives the specific states of mind they have attained through the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) obtainable by the power of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

Then, because he is free from delusion regarding the path leading to the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) by virtue of the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the destruction of the taints. Therefore...
It should be understood that these ten powers have been explained in this successive order. This concludes, for now, the commentary on the meaning of the matrix (mātikā).
(1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Singles (Ekakaniddesa): 761.
Now, regarding the matrix as it has been set forth, beginning with the method "The five consciousnesses are not causes alone," etc., [the following is commenced].
In the section on the exposition (*niddesa-vāra*), the phrase "not only a cause" (*na hetumeva*) is an exposition that excludes the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*).

Regarding this, whatever should be said by way of the method beginning with "Cause is fourfold: cause as cause, cause as condition, supreme cause, and common cause," all of that has already been stated in the commentary on the meaning of the passages in the *Rūpa-kaṇḍa* such as "All matter is not only a cause.
This applies to the phrases "only without cause" (*ahetukameva*) and so forth.
The letter *ma* should be understood here by way of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*); the meaning is "only those without roots" (*ahetukā*). This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.

Furthermore, among the categories of phenomena (*dhamma*) such as "phenomena that are roots" and "phenomena that are not roots," the five types of sensory consciousness are neither "phenomena that are roots" nor "phenomena with roots.
Rather, they are exclusively "not roots" and exclusively "without roots. These [points] also...
The meaning here in all these phrases is to be understood according to this method. The phrase "only indeterminate" (*abyākatameva*) is stated by way of the indeterminate as result (*vipākābyākata*).
The phrase "only with an object" (*sārammaṇameva*) is by way of an apprehended object (*olubbhārammaṇa*).

For there are two kinds of objects: the object as condition (*paccayārammaṇa*) and the apprehended object. However, in this context, the apprehended object alone is primary, though the object as condition is also present.
It is indeed obtainable. The phrase "only non-mental" refers specifically to consciousness (*citta*) among the three non-mental categories—consciousness, matter, and Nibbāna.

They are "not un-included" (*no apariyāpanna*); because they are included within the realms of existence (*gati*), included within death, included within the cycle of saṃsāra, and included within the states of becoming (*bhava*), they are indeed "included" (*pariyāpanna*), not "un-included. They are "non-leading-out" (*aniyyānika*) because they do not lead out from the world or from the cycle of existence. [Regarding] that which has arisen...

Regarding the phrase "to be cognized by mind-consciousness alone": in the *Rūpakanda*, because eye-consciousness and the others arise only with respect to present forms and so forth, even mind-consciousness—which has past and other objects as its domain—is treated as falling within the stream of the fivefold consciousness.

Thus it is said: "That which has arisen is cognizable by the six consciousnesses. As for the fivefold consciousness, although they are present, [they are restricted] to eye-consciousness and the rest.
They do not become objects for [the other five types of] consciousness; they belong only to mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*). Therefore, it is said: "to be cognizable by mind-consciousness alone.

"Only impermanent" means they are indeed impermanent in the sense of having existed and then ceased. "Overcome by aging" means they are indeed overcome by aging because they have been overwhelmed by aging.
762. "Having arisen bases and arisen objects" is a negation of the future; for they do not arise with respect to bases and objects that are yet to come.
"Having as their basis what is pre-arisen" and "having as their object what is pre-arisen" is a negation of simultaneous arising.
For these do not arise in dependence upon a simultaneously arisen basis or object; rather, having themselves arisen later, they arise in relation to bases and objects that are pre-arisen.
"Having internal bases" is stated by way of the internal and internal-most; for those [consciousnesses] have the five internal sensitive organs as their bases.
They arise having made a basis. "External objects" means having external forms and so forth as their objects. In this regard, a fourfold classification should be understood:
the five sense-consciousnesses are internal because they have internal sensitive matter as their bases;

at the time when mind-consciousness arises having made the heart-physical form its basis, it is internal with an external basis; [and] the three [mental factors] associated with the five sense-consciousnesses...

The external aggregates that have internal bases are the three aggregates associated with mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) at the time they arise having made the heart-base their basis; these are "external" and "having external bases.
"Having unmixed bases" means having non-ceased bases; for they do not arise dependent upon a ceased or past base. The same principle applies to their having unmixed objects (*asambhinnārammaṇatā*).
In such passages as "another [base] for eye-consciousness and another object," the base for eye-consciousness is one thing and its object is another; likewise for ear-consciousness and the rest.
Eye-consciousness does not arise even after passing from an eon to an eon if it takes as its base any one of the ear-sensitivity or others, or as its object any one of sounds or others.
Furthermore, it arises having the eye-sensitivity as its base and visible form as its object. Thus, for this consciousness, the base, the door, and the object are fixed;
it does not transfer to another base, door, or object, but arises only with a fixed base, a fixed door, and a fixed object.
The same method applies to ear-consciousness and the others as well.

763. “They do not experience one another’s range and domain”: here, the meaning is that the eye does not experience the range and domain of the ear, nor does the ear experience that of the eye; thus, each does not experience the range and domain of the other.
For if one were to collect various forms as objects—such as blue and so forth—and present them to the ear-faculty, saying, “Come now, [experience] this!”...
“Determine and analyze it: ‘What indeed is this object? Even without eye-consciousness, the eye itself would speak by its own inherent nature:
“Hey, blind fool! Even if you were to run for a hundred years or a thousand years, where else could you find anyone who knows this except me?
Bring it here and place it within the range of the eye; I shall [reveal] this.”
"I shall know the object—whether it be blue or yellow. For this is not the domain of another;
this is my own domain alone. This same method applies to the remaining types of consciousness as well. Thus, these [consciousnesses] are said not to experience one another's range or domain.
"While attending" means while attending by means of adverting (āvajjana) itself.

"Of one who attends" means of one who attends by means of adverting (*āvajjana*) alone. For these consciousnesses arise only at the time they are brought to mind by adverting and at the very time they are attended to.

"Not uninterrupted" means that they do not arise without being interrupted—that is, without an interval—by another consciousness. By this, their state of immediate succession (*anantaratā*) is rejected.

"Neither before nor after" means that by this, the simultaneous arising of all of them is rejected. "Not immediately following one another" means that by this, their state of immediate succession (*samanantaratā*) is rejected.
766. *Āvaṭṭanā*, *ābhoga*, and so forth—these four are all names for adverting itself. For it is called *āvaṭṭanā* because it turns back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*);
it is called *ābhoga* because it bends toward that same continuum; it is called *samannāhāra* because it attends to visible forms and so on;
and it is called *manasikāra* because it directs the mind toward those very objects. Thus, in brief, this is the function of adverting for the five types of consciousness.
The capacity to perform functions such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth is excluded.
"It does not discern any phenomenon" means it does not discern even a single wholesome or unwholesome state as expressed in the verse, "Phenomena are preceded by the mind.
"Except for the mere impact" means setting aside the mere impact of visible forms and so forth. This is what is meant:

Even a very wise person, setting aside forms and other objects that have come into range, does not discern any other single phenomenon among the wholesome or unwholesome with the five types of sensory consciousness.
In this context, eye-consciousness consists merely of seeing;
ear-consciousness and the others consist merely of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. [Consciousness] is free from these mere acts of seeing and so forth.
There is no other designation for these [states] such as "wholesome" and so forth.
"Even by the mind-element" means even by the receiving mind-element (*sampaticchana-manodhātu*). Here, the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion.

Therefore, [it means] neither by the mind-element, nor by the subsequent mind-consciousness-elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), nor indeed by any of the five-door consciousnesses, is there any wholesome or unwholesome [state].
"One understands the Dhamma"—this is how the meaning should be understood here.
The same method applies to such passages as "he does not assume any posture" and so forth.
For by means of the five-door consciousnesses, one does not assume any posture such as walking, nor does one initiate bodily action or verbal action, nor wholesome or unwholesome [action].
One undertakes the Dhamma, but does not enter into concentration—whether mundane or supramundane—and does not emerge from concentration—whether mundane or supramundane;
one does not pass away from a state of existence, nor is one reborn into another state of existence.
For all this activity, ending with the discernment of wholesome and unwholesome states and so forth, is performed by means of the mind-door consciousness alone.
It does not arise through the five doors; thus, in performing all these functions, the cognitive processes (*vīthicitta*) accompanied by conascent impulsions (*sahajavana*) are excluded.
Just as these [five-door] processes lack these functions, so too they lack the entering into the path of certainty (*niyāmokkama*) and so forth.

For one does not enter the certainty of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*) or the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*) by means of a five-door impulsion; nor does this impulsion [perform those functions].
It occurs taking name and clan as its object, not the designations such as the kasiṇas and so forth;

it does not proceed by way of insight that has the characteristics [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self] as its object, nor by way of powerful insight leading to emergence; it does not occur taking material or immaterial phenomena as its object, nor Nibbāna;

and with this, the knowledge of the analytical powers (paṭisambhidāñāṇa) does not arise, nor the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (abhiññāñāṇa), nor the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (sāvakapāramīñāṇa).

There is no knowledge of individual enlightenment (paccekabodhiñāṇa), nor is there omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). However, this entire variety [of states] is obtained only in the javana consciousness of the mind-door (manodvārika-javana).

Regarding the statements "he does not sleep," "he does not wake up," and "he does not see a dream": by means of all five-sense-door (pañcadvārika) consciousness as well, one neither descends into sleep, nor does one sleep, nor does one wake up, nor does one see any dream whatsoever. In these [cases]:
In three instances, the process-consciousness (vīthi-citta) is excluded along with the impulsion (javana).

For instance, when a person is sleeping and a great fire is lit and a lamp is brought near the eye, the first adverting consciousness (āvajjana) at the eye-door does not turn back toward the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
rather, it adverts only through the mind-door (manodvāra). Then, after the impulsion has occurred, [the mind] returns to the life-continuum.

It descends. On the second occasion, the adverting consciousness pertaining to the eye-door turns back the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Thereafter, the processes beginning with eye-consciousness and ending with impulsion (javana) proceed.

Immediately after that, the life-continuum proceeds again. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is turned back by the adverting consciousness pertaining to the mind-door, an impulsion of the mind-door proceeds.
Having known [the object] with that consciousness, [one wonders]: "What is this? in this [world]?
He knows: ‘There is light in the proper place.

Likewise, while he is sleeping, when musical instruments are sounded near his ears, or fragrant or foul-smelling flowers are brought near his nose, or ghee or molasses is placed in his mouth, or when there is a blow with the hand upon his back—
When [the object] has been given, the adverting consciousnesses of the ear-door and so forth do not turn back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*);
rather, it is only the mind-door adverting that turns back. Then, after the impulsion (*javana*) has impelled, it sinks back into the life-continuum.

On the second occasion, the adverting consciousnesses of the ear-door and so forth do turn back toward the life-continuum. Thereafter, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses, ending with the impulsion, proceed.

Immediately after that, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum has been turned back by mind-door adverting consciousness, mind-door impulsion consciousness impels.
Having known [the object] with that consciousness, one discerns: "What is this sound in this place—is it the sound of a conch, or the sound of a drum?
or "What is this smell in this place—is it the smell of roots, or the smell of heartwood? or "What...
When this flavored substance is placed in my mouth—whether it be ghee or molasses—people say, "Who struck me on the back?
The blow was very hard! Thus one awakens by means of the mind-door javana alone, not by the five sense-doors.
One sees even a dream by that same [mind-door] alone, not by the five sense-doors.
Furthermore, one who sees this dream sees it for four reasons:
either from a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*), or from what was previously experienced, or from the instigation of a deity, or from a prognostic sign.

In that regard, one whose elements are disturbed through association with conditions that cause the disturbance of bile and so forth sees a dream "from a disturbance of the elements. And while seeing, he sees various kinds of dreams.
He sees—like one falling from a mountain, like one traveling through the sky, and as if pursued by wild beasts, elephants, thieves, and the like.
Seeing "from what was previously experienced," he sees an object previously experienced.
For one seeing "through the intervention of a deity," deities act for his benefit or detriment, or for his welfare...
Or they bring forth various kinds of objects for his benefit or for his harm. By the power of those deities, he sees those objects.

Seeing them as a precursor, he sees a dream that serves as a premonitory sign—whether for benefit or for harm—of the matter about to arise through the influence of merit or demerit, just like the mother of a Bodhisatta.
For the sake of obtaining a son, as in the case of the five great dreams of the Bodhisatta or the sixteen dreams of the King of Kosala.
Among these, a dream that one sees due to a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*) or from what has been previously experienced is not true.
That which one sees through the intervention of a deity may be either true or false; for deities, when angry, [act] by means of a stratagem...
Desiring to destroy [the teaching], they even present things in a distorted manner. Here is an example:
it is said that at the Nāgamahāvihāra in Rohaṇa, a great elder had a certain *nāga*-tree cut down without even consulting the Saṅgha of monks.
The deity dwelling in the tree, being angry with the elder, first enticed him and then said, "In seven days from now..."
The attendant announced in a dream, "The king will die. The Elder brought that report and informed the king's women.
They all broke out into a great wailing at once. The king asked, "What is this?
They reported, "It was spoken thus by the Elder. The king counted the days, and when seven days had passed, he became angry with the Elder.
He had his hands and feet cut off.

Furthermore, whatever one sees as a premonitory sign (pubbanimitta) is invariably true. Moreover, even through the combination or variation of these four primary causes, there is indeed a variation in dreams.
And it is only those who are still in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana) who experience this fourfold dream.
Those who have not abandoned the perversions see [it]; those beyond training (asekkha), having abandoned the perversions, do not see it.
But as for that which is seen, does one see it while asleep, or while awake? Or perhaps one sees it neither while asleep nor while awake?
In this regard, if one were to see it while asleep, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma would arise. For by means of the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta)...
He sleeps. And that object, such as the sign of a form and so forth, is not associated with lust or other defilements.
Such types of consciousness arise for one seeing a dream. Now, if he were to see [the act] upon waking, it would entail a contradiction with the Vinaya.

For whatever one sees upon waking, one sees with a consciousness pertaining to worldly affairs (*sabbohārika-citta*). And when a transgression is committed by means of a consciousness pertaining to worldly affairs...
There is indeed no such thing as "no offense. However, regarding a transgression committed while seeing a dream, there is invariably no offense at all.
Now, if one sees neither while asleep nor while awake—that is, if one does not see what is called a dream—would it not follow that dreams simply do not exist?
They do not fail to exist. Why? Because one sees while overcome by *kapimiddha* (monkey-sleep). For this has been said: [text follows].
—“O Great King, one who is overcome by monkey-sleep sees a dream. “Overcome by monkey-sleep” means being possessed of monkey-slumber.

For just as a monkey’s sleep is characterized by rapid shifting, so too is that sleep which is characterized by rapid shifting due to being interspersed again and again with wholesome and other types of consciousness;
one who is possessed of that state in its occurrence, wherein there is a repeated emergence from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), [sees a dream].
One sees a dream. Therefore, this dream may be wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome (*akusala*), or indeterminate (*abyākata*).

In this regard, it should be understood that for one who performs such acts as venerating a shrine, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma during a dream, it is wholesome; for one who commits acts such as the taking of life, it is unwholesome;
and when free from both extremes at the moments of adverting and the subsequent object-impulsion, it is indeterminate. By means of a dream alone...
Even at the time of saying, “It is as if seen by me,” or “It is as if heard by me,” it remains indeterminate (*abyākata*).
What then of wholesome or unwholesome karma performed in a dream—is it with result (*savi-pāka*) or without result (*avipāka*)? It is with result;

however, because of its weakness, it is unable to draw forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Once rebirth-linking has been given by another karma, it becomes something to be experienced during the course of existence (*pavatte vedanīya*).

Thus, wisdom is the discernment of the object as it truly is (*yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā*). For the five types of consciousness, the state of being without a cause (*ahetvaṭṭha*) is their state as it truly is (*yāthāvaṭṭha*).

Because it discerns that object as it truly is, it is called "discernment of the object as it truly is. Likewise, for the five types of consciousness, the state of being without a cause, the state of being overcome by aging, and the state of not seeing dreams are their states as they truly are. That state as it truly is...
"It clarifies the basis as it actually is" is the clarification of the basis according to its true nature (*yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā*).

Thus, that which was set forth in the matrix (*mātikā*) below as "wisdom that clarifies the basis according to its true nature" should be understood as this very wisdom that clarifies the basis according to its true nature.
And by means of this alone, there is thus the singlefold ground of knowledge; in this way, the enumeration of knowledges is given according to each individual category.
Or, there is a delimitation of knowledge by way of a single aspect.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the singlefold (Ekakaniddesa). (2. Commentary on the exposition of the twofold (Dukaniddesa).

767. In the exposition of the bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*) by way of two kinds: regarding the wholesome in the four planes, there is the wisdom of the wholesome pertaining to the four planes belonging to those in training (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*).

Regarding the five meanings stated in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga*, it is called "making the meaning manifest" (*atthajāpikā*) because it makes manifest, generates, and brings into operation the meaning known as fruition (*vipāka*) that is included within its own respective plane.
[It is also so called] when an Arahant arouses direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) or attainment (*samāpatti*).

For one who is arousing [the higher knowledge], it is "functional-indeterminate" (*kriyā-abyākata*); this refers to sense-sphere functional wisdom (*kāmāvacara-kiriya-paññā*) at the time of the preliminary work for both direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

For that wisdom is called "wisdom that makes its object manifest" (*atthajāpikā paññā*) because it makes manifest, generates, and brings into operation the objective state known as functional activity, which is distinguished by the types of direct knowledge and meditative attainments.
Furthermore, there is this other method from the commentaries not found in the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*): even that previous sense-sphere functional [wisdom]...
It is a condition for subsequent sense-sphere functional states by way of being their immediate antecedent and so forth;

since it also makes manifest that state of functioning, it is called "wisdom that makes an object manifest" (*atthajāpikā paññā*). The same method applies to the fine-material and immaterial spheres as well.
In the exposition of the second term, regarding "resultant states in the four planes," wisdom [is a condition] for sense-sphere resultants by way of being a conascent condition and so forth.

"Having been brought about for the sake of sense-sphere resultant [states], it remains"—thus it is "that which has its purpose brought about" (*jāpitatthā*). This same method applies to the wisdoms that are resultants of the fine-material sphere and so forth.

Alternatively, all these are "that which has its purpose brought about" (*jāpitatthā*) because they have been brought about (*jāpitā*), generated (*janitā*), and made to occur (*pavattitā*) by their respective causes, and they themselves constitute a state of purpose (*atthabhūtā*).
This also applies to the functional wisdom (*kiriyapaññā*) mentioned in the context of the superknowledge (*abhiññā*) arisen in an Arahant and the attainment (*samāpatti*) arisen [in him].
The same method applies here. Furthermore, there is this other way from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka*):

for even the functional wisdom (*kiriyapaññā*) of the sense-sphere maintains its existence by making manifest the meaning known as "functional of the sense-sphere" through such relations as co-nascence (*sahajāta*).

The same method applies to the functional wisdom of the fine-material and immaterial spheres as well. Or rather, all of these [types of wisdom] maintain their existence by means of their respective causes.
"Recited" (*jāpita*) means brought forth, set in motion, and being itself the meaning; thus it is "that which has recited meaning" (*jāpitattha*).
All else here is clear because it follows the method already stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*. This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (*Dukaniddesa*).
(3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Triads, 768.

Regarding the exposition of the bases of knowledge in three ways: "in those established by yoga" means that "yoga" is called wisdom (*paññā*); thus the meaning is "in those established by wisdom, transformed by wisdom.
Regarding "bases of action" (*kammāyatana*): here, action itself is the base of action; or alternatively, [it refers to the spheres of sense-experience].

That which is both action (*kamma*) and a field (*āyatana*)—such as the fields of livelihood and so forth—is called the "field of action" (*kammāyatana*). The same principle applies to the fields of crafts (*sippāyatana*) as well.
In that regard, action is twofold: inferior and superior. Therein, the inferior is such as the work of a carpenter, the work of a flower-sweeper, and so on;
the superior is such as agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and so on. Craftsmanship (*sippa*) is also twofold: inferior and...
And the superior. Therein, "inferior craft" refers to such things as the craft of the basket-maker, the weaver, the potter, the leather-worker, and the barber.
"Superior craft" refers to such things as finger-calculation, arithmetic, and writing;
indeed, it is knowledge itself that constitutes a branch of learning (*vijjāṭṭhāna*). That which is taken here is strictly lawful. It is like the *Nāgamaṇḍala-paritta* and so forth.
Furthermore, medical treatises such as *phudhamanaka*, *mantasādasa*, *sālākiya*,
and *sallakattiya* are not included here because they were entered into as branches of craft (*sippāyatana*) with the thought,

"Teacher, I wish to train in this craft. In that regard, one wise person, for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of humanity and by his own nature, [constructed] houses, palaces, vehicles, ships, and so forth.

He produces [them]. For, standing in the performance of benefit with the thought, "These people are suffering without a place to dwell," he produces houses distinguished by length, squareness, and so forth; he builds palaces of one or two stories and so on for the purpose of warding off cold and heat;
and [he provides vehicles] for the purpose of dispelling fatigue of the legs, thinking, "In the absence of vehicles, wandering about is indeed suffering."
He produces carts, wagons, litters, and so forth; thinking, "In the absence of ships, there would be no traveling upon the oceans and such," he produces ships of various kinds.
He does not see all this being made by others, nor does he learn it from what has already been done, nor does he hear it from those who are speaking;
rather, he performs it through his own natural disposition and reflection. Thus is he possessed of wisdom.
For even that which is performed by one’s own nature becomes exactly like that performed by others who have learned it;
this, first of all, is the method regarding lowly work.
Regarding superior work as well: "In the absence of agricultural work, the livelihood of human beings would not proceed"—thus thinking, a certain wise man [acted].
For the sake of a comfortable living, he acquires farming implements such as yokes and ploughs; likewise, he engages in various kinds of trading and cattle-rearing.
He sees none of this being done by others... [as before] ...it is exactly as if he himself had done it.
This is the method regarding superior work.

Furthermore, in both types of craft-branches (*sippāyatana*), one wise person, for the sake of providing a comfortable livelihood for humanity, originated low crafts such as the craft of the reed-worker;
the *muddā* known as finger-calculation; the calculation known as *acchinnaka*; and writing, which is divided into the various types of matrices (*mātikā*) and so forth.
He did not see any of this being performed by others... [as before] ...it was exactly as if he himself had done it.
This is the method regarding the sphere of crafts.

Furthermore, a certain wise person, for the sake of treating humans afflicted by non-human beings, reptiles, and so forth, develops fields of knowledge such as righteous *nāga*-circles and spells; these, when performed by others, do not [produce the same effect].
He does not see [the work], nor does he learn it from others who have done it, nor does he listen to those explaining it; rather, he performs it through his own natural capacity for reflection.
For what is performed by one possessed of wisdom through his own natural capacity is exactly the same as what is performed by others after they have learned it.
"Ownership of action" (*kammassakata*) means the knowledge that understands: "This action is one's own (*saka*); this is not one's own."
"Conformable to the truths" (*saccānulomika*) refers to insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). For that is called "conformable to the truths" because it conforms to the four truths.
Now, in order to show the manner of its occurrence, it is said: "Or 'form is impermanent,'" and so forth.

And here, only the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) has been mentioned, not the characteristics of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) or non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*); however, they are indeed included by implication according to their meaning.
They are to be seen thus: "For that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self.
"That which is of such a nature" means that which has the aforementioned characteristics as described above, being in conformity with reality.

All terms beginning with "acceptance" (*khanti*) are indeed synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*). For that [wisdom], by way of seeing without opposition, is the cause among the five causes previously mentioned, such as the sphere of action (*kamma-āyatana*), and so forth.

It is "conformable" (*anulomika*) because it conforms. Likewise, it is conformable because it conforms to the conduct for the welfare of beings, it conforms to the Truth of the Path, and it conforms to Nibbāna, the ultimate truth; thus, it is conformable.
All these reasons are called "patience" (*khanti*) because one endures, bears, and is able to see them; "view" (*diṭṭhi*) because one sees; and "inclination" (*ruci*) because one finds it pleasing.
It gladdens, thus it is *mudi*; it contemplates, thus it is *pekkhā*. All those phenomena, such as the bases of action (*kammāyatana*) and so forth, endure contemplation;

and specifically, the phenomena comprised within the five aggregates, when contemplated again and again by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, endure that contemplation—thus it is "acceptance through contemplation of the Dhamma" (*dhammanijjhānakhanti*).
"Obtains without having heard from another" means that he obtains it by reflecting for himself, without hearing the instructive words of another.
"This is called" means this is called wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*). Furthermore, this does not arise in just anyone;
it arises only in well-known Great Beings (*mahāsatta*). Even among them, the knowledge conforming to the truths (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) arises in only two.
It arises for Bodhisattvas. It should be understood that the remaining types of wisdom arise for all those of great wisdom who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*).

Regarding the phrase "obtains it by hearing from another": this refers to obtaining it either by seeing others performing or having performed the spheres of action (*kammāyatana*) and so forth, or by hearing the words of anyone speaking about them, or even by learning them in the presence of a teacher.
It should be understood that all those [knowledges] acquired are indeed acquired only by hearing from another.

"Of one who has attained" means of one possessing meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); the meaning is that the wisdom occurring within the attainment is called "consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya*).
"Concerning giving" means depending upon giving; the meaning is "conditioned by the volition of giving. "The attainment of giving" means giving.

"Of one who attains"; the meaning is "of one who reaches. "That which arises" means that wisdom associated with the volition of giving which thus arises is called "wisdom consisting in giving" (*dānamayā paññā*).

Furthermore, this consists of the prior volition, the volition of release, and the subsequent volition of one who thinks, "I shall give a gift," while actually giving the gift, and while reviewing that gift after having given it.
It arises in three ways.

Regarding the phrase "taking virtue as one's object, one attains virtue": here too, it is specifically wisdom consisting of virtue (*sīlamayā paññā*) associated with the volition of virtue that is intended.
This [wisdom] also belongs to one who thinks, "I shall fulfill virtue," to one who is fulfilling virtue, and to one who, having fulfilled virtue, reflects upon it.

It arises in three ways: as prior volition (*pubba-cetanā*), as the volition of releasing (*muñca-cetanā*), and as subsequent volition (*apara-cetanā*). Those consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya*) have already been explained above. 770.

Regarding higher virtue (*adhisīla*), higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), and so forth, virtue and the others should be understood in two ways: virtue (*sīla*) and higher virtue (*adhisīla*); mind (*citta*) and higher mind (*adhicitta*);
wisdom (*paññā*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*). In this context: "Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise..."

"By way of being included in this textual tradition: 'That element remains as the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā), the fixed course of phenomena (dhammaniyāmatā),' both the five precepts and the ten precepts are called 'virtue' (sīla). For that exists whether a Tathāgata has arisen or not arisen.
Who prescribe them when he has not arisen? Ascetics, wanderers, omniscient Bodhisattvas, and wheel-turning monarchs prescribe them."
When a Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared, the community of monks, the community of nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers establish [the training rules].
However, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha—being superior to all other virtues—arises only when the Tathāgata has appeared, not when he has not appeared.
And only Omniscient Buddhas establish it. "In the case of a transgression regarding this matter..."
For this designation “this is so-and-so” is not within the domain of others; it is the domain of the Buddhas alone, the power of the Buddhas.

Thus, because the restraint of the Pātimokkha is higher virtue (adhisīla), in order to demonstrate the wisdom regarding that higher virtue, it was said: “of one who is restraining the restraint of the Pātimokkha,” and so forth.
Furthermore, by way of being included within the very same system mentioned above, the eight attainments that lead to the round of existence are called "consciousness" (*citta*).
For that exists both when a Tathāgata has arisen and when he has not arisen. When he has not arisen, who produces them?
Ascetics and wanderers, as well as omniscient Bodhisattvas and wheel-turning monarchs (*cakkavatti-rājāno*). When the Blessed One has arisen, even monks and others who seek excellence [produce them].
[The jhānas] arise only while [the path] is being generated. However, the eight attainments that lead to insight (*vipassanā*) are superior to all other states of consciousness;
they arise only when a Tathāgata has appeared, not when one has not appeared. And it is only the omniscient Buddhas who define these.

Thus, because the eight attainments constitute the higher mind (*adhicitta*), in order to demonstrate the wisdom of the higher mind (*adhicittapaññā*), [the text mentions] the attainments of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.
"Of one entering [attainment]," and so forth, has been stated.
Furthermore, by way of being included within the very same sequence mentioned below, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma is called wisdom (*paññā*).
For that exists whether a Tathāgata has appeared or not; when he has not appeared, it exists by way of the giving of Velāma, the giving of Dāna-vessantara, and so forth.
When it has arisen, there is no limit to the great gifts bestowed by those possessing that knowledge.
However, the wisdom of the path and fruit (*maggaphala-paññā*) surpasses all other forms of wisdom; it proceeds extensively only when a Tathāgata has appeared, not when he has not.
Thus, because the wisdom of the path and fruit is supreme wisdom (*adhipaññā*), in order to demonstrate wisdom through this superior wisdom, [the text speaks] regarding the four...
"Regarding the paths," and so forth, was said.

Herein, it might be asked: among these six categories—namely, virtue (sīla) and higher virtue (adhisīla), mind (citta) and higher mind (adhicitta), and wisdom (paññā) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā)—on which is insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) dependent?
It is dependent on higher wisdom (adhipaññā). Therefore, just as [the size of] a smaller measure...

Just as a parasol or banner that exceeds the standard measure is called an "excessive parasol" or an "excessive banner," so too, this morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) is called "higher morality" (adhisīla) in relation to the five precepts and the ten precepts.

Likewise, the eight attainments that lead to insight (vipassanā-pādakā aṭṭha samāpattiyo) are called "higher mind" (adhicitta) in relation to the eight attainments that lead to the round of existence (vaṭṭa-pādakā). [And] the wisdom regarding one's own actions as one's own property (kammassakata-paññā)...
It should be understood that insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*), and fruition-wisdom (*phala-paññā*) are what is called “higher wisdom” (*adhipaññā*).

771. In the exposition of skill in gain (*āya-kosalla*) and so forth: since “gain” (*āya*) means increase, and that is twofold—through the abandoning of the harmful and the arising of the beneficial—and “loss” (*apāya*) means decrease, and that too is twofold—through the loss of the beneficial and the arising of the harmful—it is therefore in order to demonstrate this [that it is said]:

"It attends to these states," and so forth, was said. "This is called" means that the wisdom regarding the non-arising and abandoning of these unwholesome states, and the arising and persistence of wholesome states—this is what is called skill in acquisition (*āyakosalla*).
Furthermore, the wisdom regarding the non-arising and cessation of wholesome states, and the arising and persistence of unwholesome states—[this is called skill in relinquishment].
—The meaning is: "This is what is called skill in loss. Now, let skill in gain be wisdom;
but how does skill in loss come to be called wisdom? For it is only one possessed of wisdom who thinks:
"When I attend in this way, unarisen wholesome states do not arise and arisen ones cease; unarisen unwholesome states arise, and arisen..."
He understands: "It is increasing. Having understood this, he does not allow unarisen unwholesome states to arise;
he abandons those that have arisen. He brings about the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he brings to full development those that have arisen.
Thus, skill regarding the state beyond perdition is also to be understood as wisdom. Furthermore, all wisdom that constitutes the means for that [state] is skill in means (*upāyakosalla*).

This, however, should be understood as occurring when there is urgent business or when fear has arisen, specifically by way of knowing the reasons for acting immediately in order to remedy that [fear].
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of Threes.
(4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads, §793.

Regarding the exposition of the bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*) by way of fourfold classification, in the passage beginning "there is what has been given" (*atthi dinnaṃ*), the meaning should be understood through this method: "there is a fruit due to the condition of what has been given.
As for the phrase "this is called": it is that knowledge which [discerns] "this is one's own karma, this is..."
The meaning is that one knows: "I am not able [to avoid the results]. This is called the knowledge of being the owner of one's own kamma (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*).
In this context, the threefold misconduct of body, the fourfold misconduct of speech, and the threefold misconduct of mind—this is what is called "not one’s own kamma.
However, the tenfold good conduct across the three doors is indeed "one’s own kamma," whether it belongs to oneself or to another.
Or rather, all unwholesome action is not called "one's own karma. Why? Because it destroys one’s welfare and produces harm.
Whether it belongs to oneself or to another, all wholesome action is indeed called "one's own karma. Why? Because it prevents harm and produces welfare.
Standing upon this knowledge of the ownership of action (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*), which is capable of such understanding, one should give much in alms.
There is no limit to the number of those who, having given gifts, fulfilled the precepts, observed the Uposatha, and experienced happiness upon happiness and prosperity upon prosperity,
have attained Nibbāna. For example, it is like a man with wealth who,
having loaded five hundred carts with ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, as well as salt, sesame, rice, and other provisions, sets out upon a wilderness road.
When some business arises, because all necessary provisions have been taken, one does not worry nor is one anxious, but reaches safety with ease;
even so, standing upon this knowledge of the ownership of kamma, having given much in alms...
[and so on] ...there is no way of counting those who have attained Nibbāna. This excludes those who have attained conformity with the Truths.

"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to all remaining wholesome wisdom associated with the taints (*sāsava*), excluding the insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) that has received the name "conformity to truth" (*saccānulomika*) because it conforms to the Noble Truths and the ultimate truth; the meaning is that this is precisely the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*).

Regarding the statement, "The knowledge of one possessing the Path (*magga-samangī*) is also knowledge regarding suffering": here, the single knowledge of the Path is included in four instances by virtue of its single penetration (*ekappaṭivedha*) into the four truths.
796. Regarding "knowledge of the Dhamma": here, let it be granted that path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) is called "knowledge of the Dhamma" by virtue of its single penetration of the four truths.
But how is fruition-wisdom (*phala-paññā*) called "knowledge of the Dhamma"? It is so by virtue of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*).
For both these kinds of wisdom, being independent of others and directly perceiving the noble truth of the Dhamma, [function] through their function and through their object.
It should be understood that "knowledge of the Dhamma" refers to the knowledge regarding the Dhamma because it occurs therein.

In the phrase "by means of this Dhamma," the term "Dhamma" is used here according to the conventional designation for its objective range (*gocara*), because path-knowledge has the Dhamma as its range; or else, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative.
The meaning is: "by having known this Dhamma"; that is to say, by means of the path-knowledge established after having known the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "By seeing" means by vision.

The meaning is: "by one who stands having seen the Dhamma. By "one who has attained" (pattena) is meant: by one who has attained the Dhamma because of standing after having reached the Four Noble Truths.
By "known" (viditena): the Four Noble Truths have been known and made manifest by means of path-knowledge;
therefore, that Dhamma is called "known. By "one who has fathomed" (pariyogāḷhena) refers to the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"By one who stands having thoroughly investigated. "He leads the method" means that he leads, carries, and directs the method regarding both the past and the future.
However, this is not the function of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*); it is the function of reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
Yet, the Teacher made path-knowledge act like the leading of a method with respect to the past and the future. Why? Because it has the path as its root. For one who has cultivated the path...
There is indeed what is called reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā). Therefore, the Teacher made the knowledge of the path itself the guide, similar to a leader.

Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: by means of this knowledge of the path—which has the four truths as its objective domain—and having that knowledge as the cause, one leads the guide known as the reviewing knowledge regarding the past and the future.
Now, in order to show the manner in which he leads [the teaching] by that method, he said: "Whatever [monks], in the past time... and so forth.

Therein, *abbhaññaṃsu* means they knew, they penetrated. *Imaññeva* (this very same) refers to the fact that this suffering is not exactly the same as that which they knew in the past and that which they will know in the future;
rather, it is stated thus in the sense of similarity. Even in the past...
For, setting aside craving, they have penetrated that the aggregates of the three planes alone are the truth of suffering;
they have penetrated that craving alone is the truth of origin, Nibbāna alone is the truth of cessation, and the Noble Path alone is the truth of the path.
They will penetrate it in exactly the same way in the future, and they are penetrating it in exactly the same way at present; thus, it is by way of similarity.
“It is this very [knowledge],” it is said. This is called subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*); it is called knowledge of following along, knowledge of leading, and knowledge of cause.
Knowledge of penetration (*pariyāya-ñāṇa*) is knowledge of the delimitation of consciousness. “Of other beings” means of all beings except oneself.

The other [term] is a synonym for that same thing. "Having encompassed their mind with his own mind, he understands" means that by means of his own consciousness, he delimits their consciousness according to its states—such as being with lust, and so forth—and knows it in its various modes.

Regarding the phrases "with lust," and so on, what ought to be said has already been stated below in the *Vibhaṅga* on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhāna*). However, this is the distinction: here, [he understands] either an unsurpassed mind...
"Or a liberated mind": here, even the supramundane is included; for even that which has not reached insight (avipassanūpaga) remains within the range of knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa).

"The remaining wisdom": setting aside the three types of wisdom beginning with knowledge of phenomena (dhamme ñāṇa), all other wisdom is called conventional knowledge (sammutiñāṇa) because it is generally recognized as such. As for the etymology here: knowledge regarding convention (sammutimhi ñāṇam) is conventional knowledge.
797. "Wisdom in wholesome states of the sense sphere": for this wisdom invariably brings about death and rebirth within the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).

Therefore, it is said to be "for accumulation, not for diminution. However, because supramundane path-wisdom (*lokuttara-magga-paññā*) indeed diminishes both death and rebirth, it is said to be "for diminution, not for accumulation.

Wisdom pertaining to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) accumulates both death and rebirth, yet it diminishes defilements (*kilesa*) and the phenomena rooted in defilements by way of suppression; therefore, it is said to be "for accumulation..."
And it is said, "for both accumulation and diminution. The remaining [types of wisdom] neither accumulate nor diminish rebirth-linking and death;
therefore, they are said to be "neither for accumulation nor for diminution.
The phrase "but he does not penetrate the higher knowledges" is stated with reference to the wisdom of the first jhāna. That...
Because it is to be attained through seclusion from sensual desires, it leads to disenchantment with the defilements. By means of this, one becomes free from lust for sensual desires;

however, because one has not yet reached the state that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), one does not penetrate the five direct knowledges, nor does one penetrate the Truths, since [this concentration] has a sign as its object.
Thus, this wisdom leads to disenchantment but not to penetration. "That very same" refers to the first jhāna.
Having attained it, he stands firm. "Being one who has become free from lust for sensual pleasures" means he is free from lust by virtue of those very sensual pleasures having been suppressed.
"He penetrates the direct knowledges" means he penetrates the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

This is said with reference to the wisdom of the fourth jhāna; for the wisdom of the fourth jhāna penetrates the five direct knowledges both by way of being their foundation (*pādaka*) and by its own nature.
It penetrates even for the attainment of the development of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Therefore, it serves for penetration (*paṭivedha*).
However, because one becomes disenchanted with the defilements by means of the wisdom of the first jhāna alone, it does not serve for disenchantment (*nibbidā*).

As for this wisdom of the second and third jhānas, to which category does it belong? It belongs to the category of the first jhāna by way of mental joy (*somanassa*), and to that of the higher jhānas by way of being without applied thought (*avitakka*).
And also the fourth jhāna. Thus, this [wisdom] should be practiced either based on the first jhāna or based on the fourth jhāna.

"For the sake of disenchantment and for the sake of penetration": path-wisdom is "for the sake of disenchantment" because it becomes disenchanted with the entire round of existence (vaṭṭa), and it is "for the sake of penetration" because it penetrates the sixth direct knowledge (abhiññā).
799. Regarding the phrases "one who has attained the first jhāna" and so forth:

when one who has attained the first jhāna that is not yet well-mastered emerges from it, perception and attention accompanied by sensual desire arise and assail him—that is, they strike and urge him—by way of the object [of the jhāna].
Through those perceptions and attentions that have leaped into sensual desires, his wisdom regarding the first jhāna...
It declines and falls away; therefore it is called "partaking of decline. "Conforming to that" means having a nature corresponding to that.
"Mindfulness stands still" is said with reference to wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*), not right mindfulness (*sammāsati*).
For when one who has a nature conforming to the first jhāna sees the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime, and, relishing and delighting in it, attachment arises, [that is wrong mindfulness].
Through his lack of attachment, that wisdom of the first jhāna neither diminishes nor increases; it becomes a factor of stability.

Therefore it is said: "wisdom partaking of stability. "Accompanied by non-thinking" means that for one who attends to the second jhāna, which is free from thinking, as peaceful and sublime, it is accompanied by non-thinking by way of its object. "Occurring" means because it has become familiar.
They press and urge one who has emerged from the first jhāna for the sake of attaining the second jhāna.

By means of those perceptions and acts of attention that leap into the second jhāna above it, that wisdom of the first jhāna is said to "partake of distinction" because it is the basis for the arising of the second jhāna, which is distinguished [from it]. "Accompanied by disenchantment" refers to that very same...
It is accompanied by insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which is designated as "disenchantment" (nibbidā) for one who has emerged from the first jhāna.
For insight-knowledge becomes disenchanted and weary when the differentiation of the jhāna factors is occurring; therefore, it is called "disenchantment.
"Exerting themselves" means they prick and urge [the mind] toward the realization of Nibbāna. "Associated with dispassion" means associated with Nibbāna, which is designated as "dispassion" (virāga).

It is associated with dispassion (*virāgūpasañhita*). Because it proceeds with the thought, "By means of this path, it is possible to realize fading away (*virāga*) and Nibbāna," it is called "associated with dispassion.
The perception (*saññā*) and attention (*manasikāra*) concomitant with that [wisdom] are likewise called "associated with dispassion.
By way of those perceptions and attentions, that wisdom of the first jhāna serves as the penetration of the Noble Path.
It is called "partaking of penetration" because it serves as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). Thus, in these four instances, only the wisdom of the first jhāna has been discussed.
The meaning in the case of the wisdom of the second jhāna and so forth should also be understood by this same method.
801. "Of one who produces concentration with difficulty and with effort" refers to one who, in the preliminary stage, produces supramundane concentration.
"At the time of coming" means having come after suppressing the defilements while being exhausted by difficulty, hardship, suffering,
exertion, and application. "Slowly realizing that state" means that once the defilements have been suppressed,
having dwelt for a long time in the preparatory service of insight (vipassanā-parivāsa), one slowly and gradually realizes that state known as supramundane concentration (lokuttara-samādhi).
"For one who recognizes, penetrates, and attains"—this is the meaning. "This is called" refers to that wisdom which arises in this manner;

because it is difficult due to the practice of suppressing the defilements and because the wisdom of the preparatory stage of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa-paññā*) is sluggish, even though it arises in a single moment of consciousness during the time of the Path (*magga-kāla*), this wisdom is called "difficult progress" (*dukkha-paṭipadā*) by way of its approach.
It is called "slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiññā*). The meaning in the three subsequent sections should also be understood by this same method. 802.
"One who does not obtain concentration at will": one who is not able to obtain concentration whenever he wishes is said to be "one who does not obtain it at will.
For such a person, there is no basis for striving to attain higher and higher levels of concentration.
The meaning is that he is one who possesses jhāna that is not highly proficient.

"Spreading the object only slightly" means that having performed the preliminary work upon an object as small as a coin or a saucer, and having attained absorption right there, he spreads that very same unextended object only slightly;
such is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. [The term *nanikāmalābhī* is used] because it is the opposite of one who obtains only limited desire.

For one who has attained mastery in jhāna is here called "one who obtains [it] at will. And because it is the opposite of an unextended object, the "vast" (vipula) is said to have an extended object. The rest is exactly as before.
This knowledge regarding aging and death is stated with reference to Nibbāna alone as its object, by way of the single penetration of the four truths.

The phrases beginning with "with reference to aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) are stated by way of the determination of the truths (*saccavavatthāpana*) during the prior stage, at the time when [the mind] occurs in reference to each individual subject. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads. (5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads.
804. In the description of the fivefold bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*):

"Wisdom that arises pervading rapture" refers to the wisdom in the first two jhānas, which is called the pervasion of rapture (*pītipharaṇatā*). "Wisdom that arises pervading bliss" refers to the wisdom in the [next] three jhānas, which is called the pervasion of bliss (*sukhapharaṇatā*).
"Wisdom that arises pervading the minds of others" refers to the wisdom of penetration into others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), which is the pervasion of mind (*cetopharaṇatā*).
The wisdom that arises pervading light is called the "pervasion of light" (ālokapharaṇatā) of the divine eye-wisdom (dibbacakkhu-paññā).

The knowledge of reflection (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) is called the "sign of reflection" (paccavekkhaṇānimitta). For this very reason it was said: "In two jhānas, wisdom is the pervasion of rapture (pītipharaṇatā)," and so forth.
And therein, the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of pleasure are like the two feet, while the pervasion of the mind and the pervasion of light are like the body.
The two hands are like the two factors; the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge is like the middle part of the body; and the sign of review is like the head.
Thus the Blessed One, having fashioned the five-factored right concentration like a person complete with limbs and minor members, demonstrated it.
This is the five-factored right concentration: by means of these five factors, which correspond to the hands, feet, and head...
"Endowed with right concentration" refers to the concentration of the foundational jhāna.

In such passages as "this concentration is pleasant in the present," it is the concentration of the fruit of arahantship that is intended. For that is "pleasant in the present" because it is pleasant at every moment of absorption.
Each preceding [moment] is [the cause] for each subsequent moment of the bliss of concentration.
Because it is a condition, it has a pleasant result in the future. It gives rise to a peaceful, subtle, resultant consciousness that is sublime and sweet in form.

For when one has emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure arises in dependence on the tangible object of a pleasant contact that pervades the entire body. By this method as well, it has a pleasant result in the future. [It is so called] because of the defilements...

It is "noble" (ariya) because it is far removed (āraka). It is "free from worldly bait" (nirāmisa) due to the absence of the bait of sensual desire, the bait of material goods, and the bait of the world.

It is "not practiced by base men" (akāpurisasevita) because it is practiced by Great Beings such as the Buddhas. It is "peaceful" (santa) because of the serenity of its factors, the serenity of its object, and the serenity of all the distress of the defilements.
It is "sublime" (paṇīta) in the sense of being insatiable. It is [the state] of the subsiding of defilements, because it is attained through the subsiding of defilements.
Or, it is "attained through subsidence" because it is attained by one for whom [the defilements] have subsided; for "subsided" and "subsidence" are identical in meaning.
Or, it is "attained through subsidence" because it is attained by an Arahant whose defilements have subsided.
It is "attained through unification" because it is reached by means of unification, or simply because it is reached through unification. This refers to weak, mundane concentration.

Because he has not yet attained [the higher stages], he is not one who has "restrained and barred by effort" (sasaṅkhāra-niggayha-vārita-gata), even though he restrains opposing states and wards off defilements with a mind that involves effort and application.

And when entering that concentration or emerging from it, because he has reached a fullness of mindfulness, he enters with mindfulness and emerges with mindfulness, according to the time limit previously determined.
or he enters into attainment mindfully and emerges mindfully. Therefore, when one reflects thus:
"This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future," there arises within him a personal knowledge independent of others;
this is one factor. This same method applies to the remaining factors as well. Thus, by means of these five kinds of reviewing knowledge—
This concentration is called "right concentration possessing five kinds of knowledge.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads. (6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Hexads.

805. Regarding the description of the bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*) by way of sixfold division: "knowledge of the supernormal powers" (*iddhividhe ñāṇaṃ*) is the knowledge pertaining to the supernormal powers that proceed in such a manner as "having been one, he becomes many," and so forth.

By this, it is specifically the wisdom of absorption (*appanā-paññā*)—belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata*), free from applied and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicāra*), momentary in a single conscious instant (*ekacittakkhaṇika*), and accomplishing states such as multiplicity—that is being described.

"Knowledge of the purification of the ear-element" (*sotadhātu-visuddhiyā ñāṇaṃ*) refers to [the knowledge] regarding the objects of sound, which are divided into those that are distant or near, and so on.

"Knowledge by means of the divine ear-element. By this too, it is precisely the wisdom of absorption (appanā-paññā) that is described—wisdom which is without applied thought or sustained thought, accompanied by equanimity, belonging to the fine-material sphere, having as its object sounds beyond the range of the natural ear, and lasting for a single moment of consciousness. "Knowledge of the minds of others" is knowledge in the discernment of the minds of other beings.

By this too, it is precisely the wisdom of absorption of the aforementioned type, having as its object the minds of others such as those with lust and so forth, and lasting for a single moment of consciousness.
"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge associated with the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati).

By this, too, it is precisely the wisdom of absorption (appanā-paññā) lasting for a single moment of consciousness that is described, which is associated with the mindfulness (sati) that recollects the aggregates (khandhas) inhabited in previous lives in the manner already stated.
"Knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings" (sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇaṃ) refers to the passing away (cuti) and the reappearance (upapāta) of beings.

"Knowledge" (ñāṇa): By this too, it is precisely the wisdom of absorption (appanā-paññā) lasting for a single moment of consciousness, which has the color-element as its object for beings passing away and being reborn in the manner already described, that is spoken of.
"Knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge that knows the discernment of the Truths;
this is exclusively supramundane (lokuttara). The remaining [knowledges] are mundane (lokiya).
Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold Set. (7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevenfold Set, etc. 806.

In the exposition of the bases of knowledge in seven ways, by way of the method beginning with "With birth as condition, aging and death," [it is shown] according to the process of occurrence and cessation.

Having explained the reviewing knowledge with respect to each of the eleven factors of dependent origination according to the three periods of time, it is further stated—by way of summary—that very same knowledge as "the knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) through such modes as its nature of decay (*khayadhammatā*).
In this context: "With birth as condition, there is aging-and-death; in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death."
The two types of knowledge are stated with reference to the present time.

Likewise, there are two types of knowledge regarding the past time and two types of knowledge regarding the future time—thus making six. Together with the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), there are seven.

In this context, the "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" is the knowledge of the mode of conditions (*paccayākārañāṇa*). For the mode of conditions is so called because it is the cause for the persistence of the occurrence of phenomena.
It is called "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhiti*); knowledge therein is "knowledge of the stability of phenomena. This is a designation for these six kinds of knowledge.
