Thus, by taking these seven [knowledges] for each factor, there are seventy-seven [knowledges] across the eleven factors.
In that context, "subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*) means having the nature of passing away; "subject to vanishing" (*vayadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing.
"Of the nature of fading away" (*virāgadhamma*) means having the intrinsic nature of fading away. "Of the nature of cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*) means having the intrinsic nature of ceasing.
What is stated by this? The contemplation (*sammasana*) of the preceding insight is stated by means of the subsequent insight.
What is thereby stated? Contemplation upon contemplation (*paṭivipassanā*) seven times is stated. For by the first knowledge, all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*)—
Having seen [the aggregates] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, that knowledge must be seen by a second [knowledge]; the second by a third;
the third by a fourth; the fourth by a fifth; the fifth by a sixth; and the sixth by a seventh.
Thus, seven insights and counter-insights have been explained.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Septads (Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā). 807.

In the exposition of the eight bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), "wisdom in the path of stream-entry" (*sotāpattimagge paññā*) refers to the wisdom within the path of stream-entry. By this, only the associated wisdom (*sampayuttapaññā*) is spoken of. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Octads (Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā).
808. Regarding the description of the nine bases of knowledge, "in the attainments of successive dwellings" means in those attainments known as successive dwellings.

Their status as "successive dwellings" should be understood in the sense that they are to be dwelt in successively and in regular order; their status as "attainments" should be understood in the sense that they are to be entered.
Therein, the wisdom associated with the attainment of the first jhāna consists of eight types, beginning with the wisdom of insight (paññā).
It should be understood. The ninth is the wisdom of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇapaññā*). For that arises in one who reviews the attainment of cessation as peaceful and sublime.
Therefore it is said: "the knowledge of reviewing for one who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the ninefold [classification].
(10. Explanation of the Exposition of the Tens:
The Exposition of the First Power. 809.
In the exposition of the ten bases of knowledge, "impossible" (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the cause; "no occasion" (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the condition.

By both [terms], he rejects the very notion of a cause. For a cause is called the "basis" (*ṭhāna*) and the "opportunity" (*okāsa*) for its own fruit because it exists in dependence upon that [fruit]. "By which" (*yaṃ*) means by whatever cause.

"One endowed with right view" (*diṭṭhisampanno*) refers to a noble disciple who has entered the stream, being perfected in the vision of the Path. "Any conditioned thing" (*kañci saṅkhāraṃ*) refers to the conditioned formations belonging to the four planes of existence.
"Any single formation whatsoever": he might approach it as permanent, meaning he might grasp it as "permanent.
"This possibility does not exist": this reason does not exist; it is not found. "That an ordinary person": by which reason an ordinary person [would do so].
"This possibility exists": this reason exists; for, due to the view of eternalism, he [grasps] any [formation] among the formations belonging to the three planes.

The meaning is that one would grasp a formation as permanent. However, because the formations of the fourth plane are characterized by an abundance of heat, like an iron ball heated all day, they do not become an object for flies—that is, for views—or for other unwholesome states.
By this same method, the meaning should be understood regarding [grasping] any formation as pleasant, and so forth. "One would approach it as pleasant" means...
This was said with reference to the grasping after pleasure by way of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), namely: “The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death.
However, when a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*)—whose mind is dissociated from such views—is overcome by fever, he seeks to allay that fever;
just as one terrified of a mad elephant seeks safety, or as the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, who desired purity, [sought] dung, so too [the disciple regards] any conditioned thing (*saṅkhāra*) as pleasant.

It approaches. In the discourse on the self-theory (*attavāda*), in order to include the designations such as the *kasiṇas*, it is stated as "some state" (*kañci dhamma*) rather than "formations" (*saṅkhāra*).
Here too, the delimitation should be understood for the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) by way of the four planes, and for the worldling (*puthujjana*) by way of the three planes;
or alternatively, in all instances, the delimitation for the noble disciple may also be by way of the three planes alone.
For whatever the worldling grasps, from that very thing the noble disciple disentangles his grasp.
Indeed, whatever the worldling grasps as permanent, pleasant, and self, the noble disciple disentangles that grasp by grasping it instead as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

In the passage beginning with “Mātaranti,” it is only one’s own biological mother who is meant by “mother. By “arahant,” an Arahant who has become a human being and whose taints are destroyed is intended.
But could a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) ever deprive another of life? That too is impossible.
Even if someone were to say to a noble disciple who has passed into another existence—even one who does not know his own status as a noble disciple: “Kill this ant,” [it would still be impossible].
Even if they were to deprive him of life, saying, ‘Take over the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch throughout the entire interior of the world-system,’ he would not deprive him of life.
Or even if they were to say to him, ‘If you do not have this man killed, we shall cut off your head,’ they might indeed cut off his own head, yet he would never kill that person.
This is for the purpose of showing the extreme blameworthiness of the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
And this was said for the purpose of illustrating the power of the noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). This is the intended meaning here:

the state of being a worldling (puthujjana) is blameworthy, since it is for such a person that one might even commit the immediate offenses (ānantariya-kamma) such as matricide. The noble disciple, however, possesses great power;
he does not perform such deeds.
"With a corrupt mind" means with a mind associated with hatred, a murderous intent.
"Should shed blood" means that he should cause even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly to flow from a living body.

"Should split the Saṅgha" means that he should split the Saṅgha—which consists of those sharing the same communion and standing within the same boundary—by five means; for it has been said: "By five [means], Upāli..."

“The Saṅgha is split by means of formal acts (kamma): by a motion (apalokana), etc., among the four types of formal acts; by a recitation (uddesa), among the five recitations of the Pātimokkha; by speaking (voharanta), that is, by conversing;

and by means of proclamation (anussāvana) and the distribution of voting tickets (salākaggāha). In this context, “by a formal act” means by any one of the four formal acts, such as the motion and so forth.
“By a recitation” means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. “Speaking” means conversing, through various [forms of discourse].
By means of these occurrences, he was pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma. Regarding the phrase "by means of a proclamation":
"Do you not know my noble birth and my state of being one who has gone forth, as well as my great learning?

It is not fitting for you even to entertain the thought that someone like me would cause one to adopt what is contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Teacher’s instruction."
By means of an announcement made by whispering into their ears in such a manner as, "Is Avīci cool to me like a grove of blue lotuses?

Do I not fear the states of misery? and so forth; and by means of the drawing of lots, having thus announced it, steadied their minds, and rendered them of a nature not to turn back, [he says], "Take this lot. This is the drawing of lots.
And here, the act itself is the authority, whether it be the formal announcement (*uddesa*) or the measurement;
however, the preliminary stages consist of the consultation (*vohāra*), the proclamation (*anussāvana*), and the taking of the voting sticks (*salākaggāha*).

For even when the consultation is conducted by way of illustrating the eighteen grounds (*vatthu*) in order to generate consent therein, and the voting sticks have been taken after the proclamation, the Saṅgha remains undivided. But when, having thus had four or more [monks] take the voting sticks...
When they perform either a formal act (*āveṇika-kamma*) or a recitation (*uddesa*) separately, then the Saṅgha is said to be "split.
Thus, it is impossible for a person endowed with right view (*diṭṭhisampanna*) to split the Saṅgha.

Up to this point, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*), such as matricide and so forth, have been shown—those which an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) commits, but not a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).
To clarify their meaning:
the detailed exposition should be understood by way of kamma, the door, and likewise duration, ripening, commonality, and so forth.

In this regard, first concerning "by way of action": for here, even if one who has become a human being deprives of life a mother or a father who has also become a human being—even if their gender has changed—the action constitutes an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense.

Even if one were to fill the entire *cakkavāḷa* with golden stūpas the size of the Great Cetiya, thinking, "I shall ward off the ripening of that [kamma]," [it would not be enough]. The entire *cakkavāḷa*...

Even after giving a great alms-offering to the community of monks seated for a meal, and even after wandering about without ever letting go of the corner of the Blessed Buddha’s outer robe, one is reborn in hell alone upon the dissolution of the body.

But he who, being himself a human, [kills] his mother or father who has become an animal; or being himself an animal, [kills] one who has become human; or being an animal [kills] another animal—[is likewise reborn in hell].
Or if one deprives an animal of life, that action is not an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense;
however, it is a grave action, and it remains as having merely approached the status of an *ānantariya*. This question, moreover, is stated with reference to those of human birth.
Herein, the "fourfold set on sheep," the "fourfold set on battle," and the "fourfold set on thieves" should be explained. [For example: "I am killing a sheep."
For even by way of intention, a person who kills his mother or father—who are human beings standing in the place of a sheep—incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
However, one who kills a sheep with the intention that it is a sheep, or with the intention that they are his mother or father, does not incur an immediate retribution.
But one who kills his mother or father with the intention that they are his mother or father certainly incurs it.
This same method applies to the other two tetrads as well. And just as these tetrads are to be understood regarding mother and father, so too they are to be understood regarding an Arahant.
Only by killing a human Arahant does one incur an immediate retribution (ānantariya) offense, not by killing a *yakkha* or a spirit;

however, that deed is indeed grave, being equivalent to an immediate retribution offense. And regarding a human Arahant, [the offense is incurred] even during his time as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Even if a blow from a weapon or poison is administered, if he attains *arahantship* and dies by that very means, it is indeed the killing of an *arahant*.
However, if one who has attained *arahantship* consumes a gift given while he was still a worldling (*puthujjana*), that gift is considered as having been given to the worldling himself.
For one who kills other noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), there is no immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), yet the karma remains heavy.
It is exactly like an ānantariya offense.
Regarding the shedding of blood: because the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible, there is no such thing as the flowing of blood from a wound to the skin caused by another’s assault.
Rather, the blood merely collects in one place within the body itself. By Devadatta...
A splinter that had broken off from the rock he had pierced struck the edge of the Tathāgata’s foot;
the foot became filled with blood inside as if it had been struck by an axe. For one who acts in such a way, an act of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) occurs.
However, Jīvaka, with the Tathāgata’s consent, cut the skin with a blade, removed the foul blood from that place, and [treated the wound].
He made it convenient. For one acting in such a way, there is only meritorious karma.
Now, as for those who destroy a shrine (*cetiya*) when the Tathāgata has attained *parinibbāna*, cut down the Bodhi tree, or take action against the relics—what becomes of them?
Their karma is grave, similar to an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). However, [if they act] toward a stupa containing relics...
Or it is permissible to cut down a tree that is damaging a statue or a branch of the Bodhi tree.

Even if birds perched there void their excrement upon the shrine, it is still permissible to cut them down; for the bodily relic-shrine (sarīracetiya) is more venerable than a shrine used for offerings (paribhogacetiya).
It is also permissible to cut down and carry away even the root of a Bodhi tree if it is obstructing the site of a shrine.
However, if a branch of the Bodhi tree obstructs the Bodhi house, it is not permitted to cut it down for the sake of protecting the building;
for the house exists for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. The same principle applies to the Seat House (āsana-ghara).
But in a Seat House where a relic has been enshrined, it is appropriate to cut a branch of the Bodhi tree for the purpose of protecting that [relic]. For the purpose of tending to the Bodhi tree—
It is indeed permissible to cut off a branch that robs one of vitality or a place that is putrid; merit is even gained in such acts, just as in the maintenance of the body.

When a schism in the Saṅgha occurs while the Saṅgha within the boundary has not assembled, if one forms a separate faction and performs an act—whether by making a formal declaration, by reciting the proclamation, or by distributing voting tickets—there is both a schism and an act of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). This applies even if one acts with the perception that the assembly is united.

However, it is permissible [to act] with the perception that the assembly is united. For one who acts with the perception that it is united, there is neither schism nor an immediate offense (*ānantariya-kamma*).
Likewise, it is so when the assembly consists of fewer than nine members. But at the very minimum limit, for one who causes a schism in a Saṅgha of nine persons, there is an immediate offense.
For those followers who speak what is not Dhamma, it is a highly blameworthy deed; [but for those who speak according to the Dhamma...]
It is blameless. In that regard, this sutta concerning schism in the Saṅgha applies specifically to nine persons:
"Upāli, there are four on one side and four on the other; the ninth proclaims and distributes voting tickets, saying:
'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve this. In this way, Upāli, there is a fracture in the Saṅgha."
“And there is schism in the Saṅgha. Upāli, when there are nine or more than nine [monks], there is both a fracture in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, among these five, schism in the Saṅgha is verbal action; the others are bodily actions. Thus the analysis should be understood also by way of action.
As for “by way of door,” all of these arise from both the bodily door and the verbal door. The former...
In this context, although the four [offenses] arise from the door of speech by way of the application of commands and the science of spells, they fulfill only the door of the body.
The schism of the Saṅgha, for one who effects a split by means of hand gestures, arises from the door of the body but fulfills only the door of speech.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood also by way of the doors.
‘Because it lasts for an eon (*kappa*)’: here, it is the schism of the Saṅgha itself that lasts for an eon.
For having created a schism in the Saṅgha either when an eon is forming or during the middle of an eon, one is released only upon the destruction of the eon.

Even if one creates a schism in the Saṅgha today, thinking, “The eon will be destroyed tomorrow,” one is released on that very day; one suffers in hell for only a single day. Such is the manner of its creation.
But [the fifth] does not exist. The remaining four kamma-s are indeed *ānantariya* (immediate), and they do not persist for the duration of an eon (*kappaṭṭhitiya*).
Thus, the analysis should be understood here even with respect to their persistence for an eon.

Regarding the term "manifest" (*pākata*): for one who has committed all five of these kamma-s, it is the schism in the Saṅgha itself that [determines rebirth] by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
It ripens. The remaining [actions] are classified under such categories as "there was action, but there was no ripening of action," and so forth.
In the absence of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, the shedding of blood [ripens]; in its absence, the killing of an arahant;
and in its absence, if the father is virtuous while the mother is unvirtuous—or if she is not likewise virtuous—the killing of a father ripens by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). If...
“Mother” means the mother. Even when two people are equal—whether in virtue or in misconduct—it is only the killing of a mother that ripens by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
for a mother performs difficult tasks and is of great benefit to her children. Thus, the analysis (*vinicchaya*) here should be understood even from common experience.
Regarding the phrase “by commonality and so forth”: the first four [offenses] are common to all, both householders and those gone forth. Schism in the Saṅgha...

However, because of the statement: “Upāli, it is not a bhikkhunī who causes a schism in the Saṅgha; nor a sikkhamānā, nor a sāmaṇera, nor a sāmaṇerī, nor an upāsaka, nor an upāsikā who causes a schism in the Saṅgha.

It is a bhikkhu, Upāli, who—being of regular status (pakatatta), belonging to the same community (samānasamvāsaka), and standing within the same boundary (samānasīmā)—causes a schism in the Saṅgha,” it belongs only to a bhikkhu of the aforementioned description.

It does not belong to another; therefore, it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all these [states] are accompanied by painful feeling and associated with hatred and delusion;
thus, the analysis here should also be understood by way of commonality and the rest.
"Another teacher" means: even in another existence, [thinking] "this teacher of mine is capable of performing the duties of a teacher."
That one should take a sectarian teacher (titthakara) as "this is my Teacher"—such a thing is impossible; this is the meaning.
That one would be reborn for an eighth existence—even one of the very dullest wisdom—would pass beyond the seventh existence and be reborn for an eighth:
such a thing is impossible. For it is with reference to the seventh existence at the very utmost limit that he is said to be "destined for enlightenment and bound for the ultimate goal."
It has been said. But what determines that? Is it the past cause (*pubbahetu*) that determines it, or is it the path already attained, or is it the three higher paths?
This is merely a name adopted by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). There is no such thing as a "determined person" (*niyato puggalo*).
For if one says, "The past cause determines it," then the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the three higher paths is being stated.
If [the path] exists, it follows that there is an absence of the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the first path. Thus, it would follow that its arising occurs without cause or condition.
If it were said that "the attained path determines [the destiny]," then the three higher paths would be rendered purposeless, while the first path alone would have its own function;
one would have to attain final *nibbāna* after having exhausted the defilements by means of the first path alone. [Regarding the statement: "The three higher paths..."
When it is said, "he determines [the path]," the first path is without its specific function; only the three higher paths possess their own functions.
The three higher paths must be realized without having first produced the first path, and the defilements must be exhausted without the first path having arisen.
Therefore, no other factor determines [the result]; rather, it is insight (vipassanā) itself that leads to the three higher paths.
He brings them to a conclusion. For if their insight proceeds sharp and courageous, they produce only one more existence, attain Arahantship, and pass away into Parinibbāna.
One of duller wisdom attains Arahantship and passes away into Parinibbāna in the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth existence.
One of the very dullest wisdom [attains it] in the seventh.
Having produced one more existence, he attains *arahantship*; there is no rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in an eighth existence. Thus, this is merely a name taken by the Fully Enlightened One.
For the Teacher, having weighed him with the balance of Buddhahood and determined it through his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*), [declared]:
"This person, possessing supreme great wisdom and keen insight, shall produce only one more existence and attain *arahantship*."

Thinking, “He will attain arahantship,” he gave him the name “Ekabījī” (One-seed). Thinking, “This person, having produced a second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth existence, will attain arahantship,” he gave him the name “Kolaṅkolo” (One who goes from family to family).
Thinking, “This person, having produced a seventh existence, will attain arahantship,” he gave him the name “Sattakkhattuparamo” (One who has seven births at most).
However, there is no person who is fixed (*niyata*) for seven existences.
Yet, even a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), if he is of dull wisdom in any respect, attains final nibbāna (*parinibbāti*) before reaching an eighth existence.

Even one like Sakka, if he delights in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), goes only to a seventh existence. Even if he dwells in negligence in every way during that seventh existence, [he does not go beyond it].
Insight-knowledge reaches maturity. Having become disenchanted even with a slight object, one attains Nibbāna.

For even if, in his seventh existence, while he is falling asleep or walking away, someone were to stand behind him and strike off his head with a sharp sword, or drown him in water, or [strike him with] a thunderbolt...
Even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon his head, even at such a time there is no passing away with rebirth-linking;
rather, having attained Arahantship, he attains final Nibbāna. Therefore it was said: “That he should take birth for an eighth existence—such a case is impossible.
“In one world-system” means in a ten-thousandfold world-system. For there are three fields: the field of birth, the field of authority, and [the field of influence].
Regarding the phrase "the field of objects" (*visayakkhetta*): therein, the "field of birth" (*jātikkhetta*) refers to the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*).

For that system shakes at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb, at the time of his birth, at the time of his awakening, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the relinquishing of the life-force, and at his final *parinibbāna*.

However, a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) is called the "field of authority" (*āṇākhetta*). This is because [the power] of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, the Mora Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Ratana Paritta, and others [extends throughout it].
In this regard, authority prevails. However, there is no limit to the extent of the "field of objects.

For regarding the Buddhas, it is said: "As far as knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge. The knowable is bounded by knowledge, and knowledge is bounded by the knowable.
Thus, for them, there is nothing that is not within their range.
Regarding these three fields, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system apart from this Cakkavāḷa, whereas there is one stating that they do not.
There are three Piṭakas: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
There are three Councils: the council of the Elder Mahākassapa and the council of the Elder Yasa...

The *saṅgīti* refers to the *saṅgīti* of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa. Regarding these three councils, once the Buddha-word contained in the Tipiṭaka has been compiled, there is no sūtra stating that Buddhas arise elsewhere outside this Cakkavāḷa;
rather, there is one stating that they do not arise [elsewhere].
“Neither before nor after” means not prior and not subsequent; it is said that they do not arise simultaneously, but rather arise either before or after.

In this context, from the time he sat at the seat of enlightenment with the resolve, “I shall not rise until I have attained enlightenment,” until his taking of rebirth-linking in the mother’s womb, these should not be understood as being “prior. [This refers to] the Bodhisatta’s...
For at the moment of taking rebirth, by the very shaking of the ten thousand world-systems, the field of birth is delimited, and the arising of another Buddha is prevented.
It should not be understood that [the Buddha's presence] ends after his parinibbāna;
rather, as long as even relics the size of a mustard seed remain, he remains. For as long as the relics persist, the Buddhas persist. Therefore...
Within this interval, the arising of another Buddha is indeed precluded; however, once the Parinibbāna of the relics has occurred, the arising of another Buddha is not precluded.
For there are three kinds of disappearances: the disappearance of the scriptures (pariyatti), the disappearance of realization (paṭivedha), and the disappearance of practice (paṭipatti).
In this context, "learning" refers to the three Piṭakas; "penetration" refers to the penetration of the Truths; and "practice" refers to the path.

Among these, both penetration and practice may exist or may not exist. For at one time there are many monks who have attained penetration, such that one must point with a finger and say, "This monk is an ordinary person. Even in this very [time]...
It is said that at one time on the island of Laṅkā, there was not even a single bhikkhu who was still a worldling (puthujjana).
Those who fulfill the practice (paṭipatti) are sometimes many and sometimes few; thus, both realization (paṭivedha) and practice may exist or may not exist.

However, for the endurance of the Dispensation (sāsana), the study of the scriptures (pariyatti) alone is the measure. For a wise person, having heard the Tipiṭaka, fulfills both [realization and practice].
Just as our Bodhisatta, having realized the five higher knowledges and the seven meditative attainments in the presence of Āḷāra,
asked him about the preliminary practice for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and he replied, "I do not know it"; thereafter,
having gone into the presence of Uddaka and compared the distinctions he had attained, [he asked] about the preliminary practice for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He asked; he explained; immediately upon his words, the Great Being accomplished it.
In the same way, a wise bhikkhu, having heard the scriptures (pariyatti), fulfills both [the teaching and the practice].
Therefore, when the scriptures remain, the Dispensation (sāsana) remains. But when they disappear, first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is lost.
Among these, the *Paṭṭhāna* disappears first. Gradually, later on, the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* disappears.
When that has disappeared, while the other two Piṭakas remain, the Dispensation (*sāsana*) indeed remains.
Therein, as the Sutta Piṭaka is disappearing, first the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* [disappears], starting from the Elevenfold Section (*ekādasaka*).
First, the Ekaka disappears. Immediately thereafter, the Saṃyuttanikāya disappears, starting from the Cakkapeyyāla up to the Oghataraṇa.
Immediately thereafter, the Majjhimanikāya disappears, starting from the Indriyabhāvanā up to the Mūlapariyāya.
Immediately thereafter, the Dīghanikāya disappears, starting from the Dasuttara up to the Brahmajāla.
It disappears. Even the question of one or two verses extends over a long distance;

it is unable to sustain the teaching, like the questions of Sabhiya and like the questions of Āḷavaka. It is said that these [questions] from the time of the Buddha Kassapa were unable to sustain the teaching in the interim.
Furthermore, even when two of the Piṭakas have disappeared, the Dispensation (sāsana) continues to endure as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains.

When the Parivāra and the Khandhakas have disappeared, it continues to endure as long as the Ubhatovibhaṅga remains. When the Ubhatovibhaṅga has disappeared, it continues to endure as long as the Mātikā remains.
When the Mātikā has disappeared, it continues to endure as long as the Pātimokkha, the going-forth (pabbajjā), and full ordination (upasampadā) remain.
The Dispensation (sāsana) endures; its outward signs (liṅga) persist for a long duration.
However, the lineage of white-robed ascetics was unable to sustain the Dispensation from the time of the Buddha Kassapa onwards.

From the moment of the final penetration of the Truths (sacca-paṭivedha) and the final breach of morality (sīla-bheda), the Dispensation is said to have declined. From that point on, the arising of another Buddha is not precluded.

There are three kinds of *parinibbāna*: the *parinibbāna* of defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*), the *parinibbāna* of the aggregates (*khandha-parinibbāna*), and the *parinibbāna* of the relics (*dhātu-parinibbāna*).
Among these, the *parinibbāna* of defilements occurred at the seat of enlightenment; the *parinibbāna* of the aggregates occurred at Kusinārā;
and the *parinibbāna* of the relics will occur in the future. It is said that when the Dispensation declines, in this island of Tambapaṇṇi...
The relics will assemble and proceed to the Mahācetiya; from the Mahācetiya they will go to the Rājāyatana-cetiya on Nāgadīpa, and from there they will go to the Mahābodhipallaṅka.
Even from the abode of the Nāgas, from the world of the gods, and from the Brahma-world, the relics will go specifically to the Mahābodhipallaṅka.
Not even a relic the size of a mustard seed shall perish along the way. All [of them].
The relics, gathered together upon the Great Enlightenment Throne like a single mass of gold, will emit rays of six colors as one solid whole.
These rays will pervade the ten-thousandfold world system. Then, the deities of the ten-thousandfold universe, having assembled, will cry out:
"Today the Teacher passes into Parinibbāna; today the Dispensation declines; this is now the final sight!"
Thinking, "This is ours," they will manifest even greater compassion than on the day of the Ten-Powered One’s final passing (parinibbāna).
With the exception of those non-returners whose taints are exhausted, the rest will not be able to maintain their own composure.
From among the relics, the fire-element will arise and ascend as far as the Brahma-world. Even if there remains a relic the size of a mustard seed...
It will become as a single net; when the relics have been completely exhausted, it will be cut off.
When such great power has been displayed and the relics have vanished, the Dispensation (sāsana) is said to have vanished. As long as it does not vanish in this way, it is called "not the last.
Thus, that they should arise neither before nor after one another—such a situation is impossible.
But why do they not arise neither before nor after one another? Because it would lack wonder (*anacchariyattā*).
For Buddhas are wonderful persons (*acchariyamanussa*), as it is said: "Bhikkhus, when one person arises in the world, he arises as a wonderful person.
Who is that one person? Bhikkhus, it is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And if two or four [were to arise]...
If eight or sixteen [Buddhas] were to arise together, they would not be marvelous.
For in a single monastery, even two shrines do not receive such great offerings and honor; likewise, monks do not become marvelous simply by being numerous, and thus Buddhas would be no different.
Furthermore, it is because there is no distinction in their teaching. For that which is divided into the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth—
If one person were to teach the Dhamma, it would have to be taught by that same person after having arisen again; thus, it would not be marvelous.
However, when the Dhamma is taught by one [Buddha], the teaching itself is marvelous. Furthermore, because there would be no dispute [if there were many].
And if many Buddhas were to arise, it would be like the disciples of many teachers saying, "Our Buddha is handsome, our... [and so on].
They might dispute, saying, ‘The Buddha has a sweet voice,’ or ‘He is a recipient [of offerings],’ or ‘He is meritorious’;
for this reason also, they do not arise. Furthermore, this reason was explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda.
For it is said there: “Venerable Nāgasena, this was spoken by the Blessed One: ‘It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question that...’”
"It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in a single world-system.
Furthermore, venerable Nāgasena, all Tathāgatas teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
they discourse upon the four noble truths; and they train others in the three trainings.
They train others, and while instructing them, they instruct them in the practice of heedfulness.
If, venerable Nāgasena, the teaching of all Tathāgatas is one, their discourse is one, their training is one, and their instruction is one, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise simultaneously?
By the arising of even a single Buddha, this world becomes filled with light.
“If there were a second Buddha, this world would become even more brilliantly illuminated by the radiance of two Buddhas.
Furthermore, two Tathāgatas teaching would teach with ease, and two Tathāgatas instructing would instruct with ease.
Show me the reason for this, so that I may be free from doubt.”
“Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the domain of a single Buddha; it sustains the qualities of only one Tathāgata.
If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain them;
it would shake, tremble, reel, sink, incline, bend, scatter, dissolve, and be utterly destroyed, and it would not remain in its place.”
“Suppose, great king, there were a boat that could carry only one person. When one person had boarded it, that boat would be just level with the water.

Then a second person might come along, similar in lifespan, complexion, age, stature, and in every limb and member—neither thin nor stout. If he were to board that boat, would it not, great king, [sink]?”
“Would it be able to support even two? “No, venerable sir; it would move, shake, lean, incline, bend, scatter, be blown away, be destroyed; it would not remain stable, but would sink into the water.
“In the same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the support for only one Buddha, for only one Tathāgata.”
It sustains his qualities. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him;
it would shake... [and so on] ...it would not remain stable.
"Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were to eat food until he was full, filling his throat and reaching up to his neck."
“Then, being satisfied, full, and satiated, having become languid and unable to lift his staff, he would eat that same amount of food once again.
Would that man, Great King, be happy? “Certainly not, venerable sir;
having eaten it once, he would die. “In the same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the domain of a single Buddha... [and so on].”
“...it would not find a place [to stand].
“But, venerable Nāgasena, does the earth tremble because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma?
“In this case, Great King, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to their very rims. Having taken a jewel from one cart...”
“Suppose they were to pour [the contents] into a single cart. Would that cart, Great King, be able to bear the weight of the jewels from both carts?
“No, venerable sir. Its nave would give way, its spokes would break, its rim would collapse, and its axle would snap.
“But why so, Great King? Because of the excessive weight of the jewels?”
“Does the cart break? “Yes, venerable sir. “In the same way, great king, the earth trembles because of the excessive burden of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, great king, this reason has been set forth to illustrate the power of the Buddha.
Listen now to another appropriate reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously. If, great king, [two Buddhas were to arise]...”
If two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, a dispute would arise among their assemblies:

"Your Buddha is ours; our Buddha is yours," and they would become divided into two factions. Just as, O Great King, a dispute might arise among the retinues of two powerful ministers: "Your minister is ours; our minister is yours," and they become divided into two factions.
It happens; even so, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise simultaneously, a dispute would arise within their assemblies:
‘The Buddha belongs to you’ and ‘The Buddha belongs to us,’ and they would become divided into two factions.
This, Great King, is one reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
“Listen further to another reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
If, Great King, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same moment, the statement ‘the Buddha is supreme’ would be false;
likewise, [the statements] ‘the Buddha is the eldest,’ ‘the Buddha is the best,’ ‘the Buddha is the most distinguished,’ and ‘the Buddha is the highest’ would be false.”

The statement that "the Buddha is supreme," "the Buddha is peerless," "the Buddha is unequaled," "the Buddha is equal to the unequaled," "the Buddha is incomparable," "the Buddha is without counterpart," and "the Buddha is without rival" would be false.
Great King, you should accept this as a valid reason for why there cannot be two perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
They do not arise at the same moment.
"Furthermore, Great King, it is the natural disposition of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world at a time.
For what reason? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an omniscient Buddha. Moreover, Great King, whatever..."
In the world, that which is great is indeed singular. Great, O King, is the earth, and it is one alone; great is the ocean, and it is one alone;
great is Sineru, the king of mountains, and it is one alone; great is space, and it is one alone; great is Sakka, and he is one alone;
great is Mahābrahmā, and he is one alone; so too is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"He is great, being alone in the world. Wherever they arise, there is no room for others.
Therefore, Great King, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arises in the world alone.
"Well explained, venerable Nāgasena, is this question by means of similes and reasons."
"In one world-system" means in a single *cakkavāḷa*. By this very phrase, ten thousand *cakkavāḷas* below are included;
these too should be delimited by a single *cakkavāḷa*. For when Buddhas arise, they arise in this very *cakkavāḷa*;
however, once the place of arising has been restricted, [they do not arise] in other *cakkavāḷas* than this.
It is already excluded by the statement "they do not arise. Regarding the phrase "neither before nor after":

here, "before" refers to the period prior to the manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*), and "after" refers to the period subsequent to its disappearance. In that regard, the disappearance of the Wheel-Treasure occurs in two ways:
either through the death of the wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) or through his going forth into homelessness (*pabbajjā*). And as it is disappearing...
However, that [sign] disappears on the seventh day from either his death or his renunciation. Beyond that, the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is not prohibited.
But why do two wheel-turning monarchs not arise in a single world-system (cakkavāḷa)?
Because it would cut off disputes, because it would prevent rarity, and because of the great power of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana). For if two were to arise, [the thought would occur]: "Ours..."
A dispute might arise, such as, "Our king is great; our king is great!
And it would not be extraordinary for there to be a wheel-turning monarch in one continent and a wheel-turning monarch in another.

Furthermore, that great majesty which is capable of bestowing sovereignty over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands would diminish. Thus, [it is for] the sake of cutting off disputes...
Because of the extraordinary nature of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*) and its great majesty, two do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

As for the statement, "If she were an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One," let alone the state of Buddhahood—which involves the development of omniscient qualities and the capacity to ferry the world across [to liberation]—even a mere aspiration toward it cannot be fulfilled by a woman.
"Human birth, possession of the [male] gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher..."
“Going forth, the perfection of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
These, indeed, are the causes for the perfection of the resolution. Thus, for a woman who is unable to fulfill even this resolution...
Regarding the question "From where does Buddhahood arise?", it is said: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a woman should be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.

Alternatively, since a store of merit fulfilled in every aspect produces a personal existence (attabhāva) that is likewise fulfilled in every aspect, only a man becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.

In such cases as "Could a woman be a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavattī)? and so forth, because a woman lacks the private parts concealed by a sheath and other such characteristics, her marks are not fulfilled; because she cannot possess the seven jewels by virtue of being a Woman-Jewel (itthiratana);
and because there can be no personal existence (attabhāva) superior to all men—therefore, "It is impossible, it is out of the question that a woman..."

It was said, “He would be a wheel-turning monarch. And since even the three positions such as that of Sakka are supreme, whereas the female gender is inferior, therefore those [positions] such as that of Sakka are also prohibited for her.
But is it not the case that just as the female gender does not exist in the Brahma-world, so too the male gender does not exist there?
Therefore, [the statement] “that a man should exercise the status of Brahmā—this is possible” [would also be incorrect].
Should it not be said [that a woman cannot become a Great Brahmā]? No, it should not be so said. Why?

Because a man is reborn there. For by "the state of a Brahmā" (brahmatta), the state of a Mahābrahmā is intended. And here, a woman, having developed jhāna and passed away, is reborn into the company of the Brahmapārisajja devas, but not as a Mahābrahmā. A man, however, is not [reborn] there...
It cannot be said that [the state] arises. And here, although both genders are equally absent, the Brahmās have the form of males, not the form of females.
Therefore, this is well-stated.

Regarding the passage beginning with "of bodily misconduct," etc., just as seeds of the nimba tree, the kosātaki creeper, and so forth, do not produce a sweet fruit, [so too does misconduct not produce a pleasant result].
Just as they produce what is unpleasant and not sweet, so too bodily misconduct and the like do not produce a sweet result,
but produce only what is not sweet. And just as seeds such as sugarcane and rice produce fruits that are sweet and of excellent flavor,
and not unpleasant or bitter, so too bodily good conduct and the like produce only a sweet result.
It is not unwholesome. And this has also been said:
"As is the seed one sows, so is the fruit one reaps;
the doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil."
Therefore, it was said: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who possesses bodily misconduct... and so forth.

Regarding the terms "one who possesses bodily misconduct" and so on, there are five kinds of possession (*samaṅgitā*): possession by way of accumulation, possession by way of volition, possession by way of kamma, possession by way of result, and possession by way of manifestation.
Among these, at the moment of accumulating wholesome or unwholesome kamma...

‘Possession of accumulation’ is what is meant. Likewise, ‘possession of volition. However, as long as they have not reached Arahantship, all beings are called ‘possessors of karma’ with reference to the karma accumulated in the past that is ready to yield its result—this is ‘possession of karma.
‘Possession of result,’ on the other hand, is to be understood only at the moment of the result itself. As long as...

For those beings who have not yet attained Arahantship, hell appears to them as they pass away from here and there and are reborn in hell through its various manifestations such as masses of flames and cauldrons of molten iron; the mother’s womb appears to those entering it;
and the deva-world appears to those being reborn among the devas through its manifestations such as the wish-fulfilling tree and celestial palaces. Such is the sign of rebirth.
It appears. Thus, because they are not yet freed from this appearance of the sign of arising, it is called "possession of appearance" (*upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā*).
That very [appearance] wavers, while the others are motionless. For even when hell appears, the world of the gods may appear;
even when the world of the gods appears, hell may appear; even when the human world appears, the animal realm may appear; and in the animal realm...
And even when one has established [the mind], the human world still presents itself.
Here is an illustration: it is said that at the foot of Soṇagiri, in the Acela monastery, there was a certain preacher of the Dhamma named the Elder Soṇa.
His father was a hunter named Sunakhavājika. Although the Elder tried to restrain him, he could not establish him in self-restraint.
Being unable [to do otherwise], thinking, "May this poor man not perish," he reluctantly ordained him when he was old.
As that man lay on his sickbed, hell appeared before him. From the foot of Mount Soṇa, large dogs arrived and surrounded him as if wishing to devour him.
Terrified by great fear, he cried out, "Stop them, dear Soṇa! Stop them, dear Soṇa!"
“What is it, Great Elders? “Do you not see, dear one? they replied, and explained the situation to him.
The Elder Soṇa thought, “How indeed could my father, such as I am, be reborn in hell? I shall be his support.
Having had various flowers brought by the novices, he performed offerings of flower garlands and seats upon the terrace of the shrine and the terrace of the Bodhi tree.
Having had his father carried on a litter to the courtyard of the shrine and having laid him down upon the litter, he said:
"O Great Elder, this offering of mine has been made for your sake; saying, 'This, O Blessed One, is my gift from a person in distress,' please pay homage to the Blessed One and gladden your heart.
Seeing the offering, the Great Elder did as requested and gladdened his heart.
At that very moment, the heavenly world appeared before him;

the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and the celestial palaces, along with the divine dancers, stood as if surrounding him. He said, "Go away, Soṇa! Go away, Soṇa!
"What is this, Great Elder? "My dear, these are your mothers who are coming. "The Elder, heaven has appeared!"
‘[He thinks], “I am the Great Elder. Thus it should be understood that the possession of attendance (*upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā*) wavers.
Among these types of possession, here it is stated as “one who possesses bodily misconduct,” etc., by way of the possession of the kamma consisting in volition of accumulation (*āyūhanacetanā*).
The rest is self-evident in all respects.
Commentary on the Exposition of the First Power.
Exposition of the Second Power: 810.

Regarding the phrase "obstructed by the excellence of destination" (*gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni*) in the exposition of the second power: they are obstructed and prevented by the excellence of destination.

These have been refuted. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Herein, "perfection of destination" (*gatisampatti*) refers to a successful destination, namely the world of the devas and the world of humans.

"Failure of destination" (*gativipatti*) refers to a failed destination, namely the four states of misery (*apāya*). "Perfection of the physical basis" (*upadhisampatti*) refers to the excellence of the personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Failure of the physical basis" (*upadhivipatti*) refers to the inferiority of the personal existence. "Perfection of time" (*kālasampatti*) refers to a perfect time, reckoned as a period when the human race is ruled by a righteous king.
"Failure of time" (*kālavipatti*) refers to a degenerate period characterized by bad kings and wicked people. "Perfection of effort" (*payogasampatti*) is right application.
"Failure of effort" (*payogavipatti*) is wrong application.
In this regard, a certain person may have many evil karmas; these would ripen for one who is situated in a failure of destiny (*gativipatti*).

However, having been reborn among gods or humans through a single wholesome kamma within a fortunate destination (*gatisampatti*), there is no opportunity for unwholesome states in such a place; rather, it is exclusively an opportunity for the wholesome.
Thus he understands that those karmas do not ripen because they are obstructed by the attainment of a fortunate destination.
Another person may also have many evil kamma-formations. These would ripen for one who stands in the failure of the physical basis (*upadhivipatti*).

But he, by means of a single wholesome kamma, stands in the success of the physical basis (*upadhisampatti*), with well-proportioned limbs and members, handsome, beautiful to behold, like a divine calf.
Even if he is born as a slave from the womb of a slave-woman, such is his personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Thinking, "This is not suitable for one of defiled karma," they do not have him perform tasks such as elephant-keeping, mule-herding, horse-keeping, or cattle-herding;
instead, having him dressed in fine garments, they appoint him to positions such as treasurer. If she is a woman, they do not have her cook elephant fodder and so forth;
rather, having given her clothes and ornaments, they appoint her as a bed-guardian or—
They do so, or they place them in a position of favor, like Somadevī.
It is said that during the reign of King Bhātikarājaka, when many people who ate beef were seized and presented to the king, they were asked, "Are you able to administer punishment?
and they replied, "We are not able. Then the king had them appointed as cleaners in the royal courtyard. Among them was a daughter who was beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring.
Seeing her, the king brought her into the inner palace and established her in a position of favor. Her remaining kinsmen also lived happily through her power;

for even evil karmas are unable to yield their fruit within such a physical existence. Thus he understands that [karmic results] do not ripen when obstructed by the excellence of material conditions (*upadhi*).
A certain person has many evil karmas. These would ripen for one who stands at a failure of time;
however, he is reborn at a time when a first-era world-ruler, a wheel-turning monarch, or a Buddha has appeared—during an age of men possessing excellent kingship.
For one reborn at such a time, it is impossible for unwholesome karma to give its result.
"There is no opportunity [for them]; there is only the opportunity for what is exclusively wholesome. Thus he understands that those [karmas] obstructed by the perfection of time do not ripen.
Furthermore, another person may have many evil karmas; these might ripen if he were situated in a failure of application (*payoga-vipatti*).

However, he—being established in the perfection of application through a single wholesome deed, abstaining from killing and so forth, and possessing good conduct of body, speech, and mind—[is thus protected].
It fulfills [the conditions]. In such a state, there is no opportunity for unwholesome karma to ripen; it is exclusively an opportunity for the wholesome.
Thus, one understands that those [karmas] obstructed by the perfection of the means do not ripen.
Furthermore, another person may have many evil karmas; these would not ripen for one who stands in the perfection of rebirth.
Thus, by means of a single evil deed, he is reborn precisely in a state of miserable destiny. There, those karmas approach him and yield their result in turn:
at times they cause him to be reborn in hell, at times in the animal realm, at times in the sphere of hungry ghosts, and at times among the asuras;
even over a long period of time, he is unable to lift his head from the states of misery.

They do not give. Thus he understands: "Being prevented by the excellence of the destination (gatisampatti), they are unable to yield their result; only by resorting to the failure of the destination (gativipatti) do they ripen.
Furthermore, another person may have many evil kamma-formations; these would not ripen for one who stands in the excellence of the physical basis (upadhisampatti).
However, on account of a certain evil deed, he was established in the very ruin of his physical basis; he was ugly, misshapen, ill-proportioned, hideous, and like a *pisāca*.

If he were born as a slave from the womb of a female slave, they would make him perform all kinds of filthy tasks suited to him, down even to the work of throwing away flower refuse. If [he were] a woman...
Thinking, "These are suitable for her," they compel her to perform all kinds of defiled tasks, such as preparing food for elephants.

Even though she was born into a noble family, royal officers, while performing a sacrifice, bind her and take her away, perceiving her as a "house-slave," like the wife of a great householder in the village of Kotalavāpī.
Thus, because she is obstructed by the excellence of material acquisitions (*upadhi-sampatti*), [she does not attain the higher realms].
He understands that those [karmas] which are unable to yield their result ripen due to the failure of the basis (*upadhivipatti*).
There may also be many evil deeds belonging to another person; these might not ripen for one who has attained the perfection of time.

However, by means of a single evil deed, during a failure of time—during an era of bad kingship, a time of non-humans, when it is turbid and sapless, and when the lifespan is ten years—[the result ripens].
He is reborn [in a state] where, when the five products of the cow are cut off, kudrūsaka grain becomes the first food.
Although he is reborn in the human world, his livelihood is similar to that of wild animals and cattle. At such a time, there is no opportunity for wholesome karma to ripen;
it is exclusively unwholesome. Thus, because they are obstructed by the failure of the right occasion, they are unable to yield their result.
He understands: "Due to the failure of time, [these karmas] ripen.
Another person also has many evil karmas; those might not ripen for one who stands in the success of application.
But he, standing in the failure of application, commits the ten unwholesome karmas, such as the destruction of life. To him, that...
They seize them together with their stolen goods and present them to the king. The king subjects them to many judicial punishments and has them executed.
Thus, he understands that kamma which was unable to yield its result because it was warded off by the perfection of the means, ripens instead due to the failure of those means.
In this way, evil kamma that was warded off by the four perfections, failing to give its result, gives it when the four failures occur.
Suppose, for instance, a certain man were to please a king by some service or other.
Then the king, having granted him a position of authority, might bestow upon him a province. Being unable to enjoy it properly, he might break it up like a monkey breaking a bag of food;
[whether it be] whatever vehicle, or mount, or male slave, or female slave, or park, or estate [he receives].
Or if he sees someone of noble appearance, he would seize them all by force. People would not be able to say anything because he is a royal favorite.
He would come into conflict with another royal minister who is even more favored.
That other man, having seized him and beaten him soundly until he was thoroughly bruised, would have him dragged along, rubbing his back against the ground, and then report it to the king.
Having approached him, he would have him arrested, saying, "Your Majesty, such-and-such a person is plundering your realm.
The king, having had him bound in prison, would cause a drum to be beaten throughout the city, asking, "By whom was what taken from whom?
The people, coming forward, would raise a tumultuous outcry of thousands, crying, "This was taken from me! This was taken from me!"
The king, becoming even more enraged, would torment that man in various ways in the prison, have him executed, and say:
"Go, throw him into the charnel ground and bring back his shackles. This should be understood as being exactly like that.
For it was at the time when that man, having pleased the king through some service, had obtained a position of authority.
Just as for an ordinary person there is a time when, through some meritorious deed, they are reborn in heaven;

or as when someone seizes the property of people after dividing up a country, there is a time when no one is able to say anything to him—so too, when one is reborn in this heaven, it is a time when unwholesome karma finds no opportunity to ripen. One day, while he was with a certain high-ranking royal favorite...

The time when he, having become dispassionate toward that [object], was beaten by the angry man, informed the king, and cast into prison, is like the time when this being, having fallen from heaven, is reborn in hell. The time when people cry out, "This has been taken from me!
This has been taken from me! is like the time when all unwholesome kamma [comes forth] upon his rebirth in that hell.
The time has come for them to gather together. It is like the time for collecting shackles after they have been discarded in a charnel ground;
when each individual deed is exhausted, they do not lift their heads from hell until the other deed has also ripened, remaining in hell for the duration of an entire *kappa*.
For there are beings who, having performed deeds that endure for a *kappa*, remain in hell for one entire *kappa*.
One, not two, not a hundred, not a thousand. Thus, it is said that beings who are reborn [in such states] exceed the path of calculation.
In passages such as, "There are certain undertakings of wholesome kamma that do not ripen because they are obstructed by a failure of destination," this same application should be understood.
Here, a certain person has many wholesome kamma; those [kamma] [ripen] in a fortunate destination...
[The wholesome deeds] would have matured for him had he remained [in that state]. However, due to one evil deed, he was reborn in a miserable destination, either in hell or among the asuras.
In such a place, wholesome karma is unable to yield its result; it is only unwholesome karma that can do so with absolute certainty.
Thus, he understands that those karmas of his did not mature because they were obstructed by the miserable destination.
Another person may also have performed many wholesome deeds that would ripen for him had he been established in the excellence of his physical basis (*upadhi*).
However, because he was established in the failure of his physical basis due to a single evil deed, he becomes ugly, like a *pisāca*.
Even if he were reborn in a royal family, upon the death of his father, [the people might say], "What is the use of this kingdom for one so devoid of splendor? and [refuse it].
He does not obtain it. Even if he is reborn in the houses of generals and the like, he does not obtain the position of a general and so forth.
To clarify this point, the story of King Dīpa should be told: it is said that when his sons were born, the king was pleased with the queen and granted her a boon.
Having received the boon, she set it aside. When the prince reached the age of seven or eight years...
He had a cock fight in the royal courtyard. One cock flew up and pecked out the prince’s eyes.
When the prince was fifteen or sixteen years old, his mother, the queen, thinking, “I shall secure the kingdom for my son,” approached the king and said:
“Your Majesty, at the time of the prince’s birth, you granted him a boon. I have kept it reserved; now—”
“I will take it. “Very well, Queen, take it. “Your Majesty, there is nothing that I have not already received from you.
But now, I request the kingdom for my son. “Queen, your son is physically deformed;
it is not possible to give him the kingdom. “Since you are unable to grant me the boon I desire, why—”
“Did you grant him a boon? Being pressed very hard, the king said, “It is not possible to give your son the sovereignty over the entire island of Laṅkā;
however, let him dwell in Nāgadīpa after being installed under the royal parasol. Thus he sent him to Nāgadīpa.
He became known as Dīparāja. Had he not been blind, he would have possessed all the splendors and retinues of sovereignty over the entire Tambapaṇṇidīpa, which extends for three hundred yojanas.
"He would have obtained the kingdom. Thus he understands that those [deeds] obstructed by the failure of conditions do not ripen.
There may also be many wholesome deeds belonging to another; these might ripen for one established in the perfection of time.
However, due to a single evil deed, during a failure of time—in an era of bad kings, a time of non-humans, when it is turbid, sapless, and short-lived—[the wholesome deeds do not ripen].
He is reborn at the very limit of existence. And at such a time, wholesome karma is unable to yield its result.
Thus he understands that deeds are not ripened when obstructed by a failure of time.
Furthermore, another person may possess many wholesome karmas; these would ripen for one who stands in the perfection of application.
But this person, standing in failure of application, kills a living being... [and so on] ...fulfilling all forms of immorality.
Likewise, families of the same social standing do not form marriage alliances with him;
thinking, "This man is a wicked person—a womanizer, a drunkard, or a gambler," they avoid him from afar. His wholesome karmas are unable to ripen. Thus...

He understands that deeds obstructed by failure in application do not ripen. Thus, wholesome kamma that would otherwise yield a result does not ripen because it has been obstructed by the four failures, even though one has attained the four successes.
Furthermore, another person may possess many wholesome kamma deeds; these might fail to ripen for one who remains in a failure of destination.
However, he was reborn solely in a fortunate state of existence (*gati-sampatti*) due to a single wholesome deed (*kalyāṇakamma*).
There, those karmas approached him and gave their results in turn: at times they caused him to be reborn in the human world, and at times in the deva world.
Thus, because they were unable to yield their results due to being obstructed by a misfortune of state (*gati-vipatti*), they did so by means of his fortunate state.
He understands: "They are ripening.
Another person also has many wholesome kamma-formations; these would not ripen for one who stands in the failure of the physical basis (upadhivipatti).
However, by means of a single wholesome kamma, he is established in the very success of the physical basis (upadhisampatti), being handsome and beautiful to behold.
He is gracious, resembling Brahmā’s son Vasiṣṭha. Because he stands upon the excellence of his acquisitions (*upadhi*), his wholesome deeds yield their fruit.

If he is reborn in a royal family, even though there are other elder brothers present, they consecrate him alone in the kingdom, thinking: “This person’s personal existence (*attabhāva*) is successful;
when the white umbrella is raised over him, there will be well-being for the world.”
One reborn in such places as the palace of a viceroy obtains, upon the death of his father, the position of viceroy, commander-in-chief,

treasurer, or merchant chief. Thus one understands that kamma, being unable to yield its result because it was obstructed by misfortune regarding material possessions, ripens instead through the attainment of prosperity regarding material possessions.
Another person may also possess many wholesome deeds (*kalyāṇakamma*). These would not ripen for one who exists during a failure of time (*kālavipatti*).
However, he was reborn through a single wholesome deed at a time of temporal perfection (*kālasampatti*), during the era of men with excellent kings.
For one reborn in such a flourishing time, the wholesome deed yields its fruit.
In this regard, the story of the Elder Mahā-Soṇa should be told:
it is said that during the time of the Brahmin Tissa’s reign, twelve thousand bhikkhus resided at Cittala Mountain and likewise at the Tissamahāvihāra.
In both great monasteries, for three years, a swarm of large rats devoured everything in a single night, leaving nothing but the straw.
At Cittalapabbata, the community of monks left the monastery, thinking, "The formal observance will take place at Tissa Mahāvihāra;
we shall go there and dwell. At Tissa Mahāvihāra as well, the community of monks left the monastery, thinking, "The formal observance will take place at Cittalapabbata;
we shall go there and dwell. Thus, from both sides, they gathered on the bank of a certain deep ravine.
Having gathered together and inquired, and knowing that the cycle of existence had come to an end, the twenty-four thousand bhikkhus thought, "What shall we do by going there?
They entered a deep mountain glen and forest, sat down, and while remaining in that very posture, they attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
Later, when the danger had subsided, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus [approached] Sakka, the king of the gods.
Having taken the relics and gathered them together, he constructed a cetiya.
The bandit Brāhmaṇatissa also ravaged the countryside. The Saṅgha, having assembled and deliberated, sent eight elders to the presence of Sakka, saying, "Please ward off this bandit.
Sakka, the king of the devas, said, "Venerable sirs, it is not possible for me to [stop] the bandit who has arisen..."
"To ward it off, let the Saṅgha go to the other side of the ocean; I shall act as the ocean-guardian.
The Saṅgha went from all directions to Nāgadīpa and had a great three-storied ship constructed at the port of Jambukola.
One story was submerged in the water. On one [story], the Bhikkhu-saṅgha sat down; on the other, they placed their bowls and robes.
The three elders who were the leaders of those assemblies were the Elder Cūḷasīva, the reciter of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the Elder Isidatta, and the Elder Mahāsoṇa.
Two of those elders said to the Elder Mahāsoṇa: "Friend Mahāsoṇa, board the great raft.
"But what about you, venerable sirs? "Friend, death in the water is one and the same as death on land."
“We will not go. However, by depending on him, the lineage of the Dispensation will endure in the future.
Go then, friend. Having spoken thus even up to three times, they were unable to make the Elder ascend [the ship] and turned back, saying, “Venerable sir, we will not go while you do not come.”
Then the Elder Cūḷasīva said to the Elder Isidatta: "Friend Isidatta, in the future the succession of the Dispensation will stand supported by the Elder Mahāsoṇa;
do not let him go out of your hands. "But what about you, venerable sir?
"I shall go to pay homage at the Great Shrine. Having thus instructed the two elders, he traveled by stages on his alms-round until he reached the Mahāvihāra.
He arrived there. At that time, the Mahāvihāra was empty. Eraṇḍa trees had grown in the courtyard of the cetiya;

the cetiya was surrounded by shrubs and covered with moss. The Elder, as if showing the utmost reverence to a Buddha still living, paid homage to the Mahācetiya, entered the Sāla hall in the western direction, and looking about, [saw] such a state...
Thinking, "The site of the reliquary stupa for the bodily relics of one who has attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of glory has become desolate," he sat down.

Then, a deity dwelling in a tree not far away, assuming the form of a traveler, took a measure of rice and a lump of sugar and approached the Elder, asking, "Where are you going, venerable sir? "I am going to the southern region."
“Lay follower,” [the Elder said]. “I too wish to go to that very place; let us go together, venerable sir. “I am weak;
I shall not be able to go at your pace, lay follower. You go on ahead.
“I too will go at your pace,” [the lay follower replied], and he took hold of the Elder’s bowl and robe. And when they had ascended the embankment of the Tissavāpi pond—
Having had a bowl brought and prepared a drink, she gave it to him. As soon as the Elder had drunk it, his strength was restored.
The deity, having contracted the earth, reached an abandoned monastery near the Veṇu River, maintained the Elder’s dwelling place, and gave it to him.
On the following day, as soon as the Elder had rinsed his mouth, she cooked rice-gruel and gave it to him; after he had drunk the gruel, [she provided] a meal.
Having cooked it, she offered it to him. The Elder covered his bowl with his hand, saying, "Set this aside for you, lay follower.
Thinking, "I will not go far," the deity placed the food into the Elder's very bowl;
then, taking the bowl and robes of the Elder who had finished his meal, she set out on the road, contracting the distance until they reached the banks of the Jajjara River.
Having led him there, he said, "Venerable sir, this is the dwelling place of the leaf-eating people; smoke is visible.
I shall go on ahead," and after paying homage to the Elder, he departed for his own abode. The Elder dwelt throughout the entire period of danger depending upon those leaf-eating people.
The Elder Isidatta, too, traveling by stages on his journey, arrived at the Aḷa country. There, the people—
They split the slightly ripened madhuka fruits, took the seeds, and discarded the husks.
The Elder said, "Friend Mahāsoṇa, alms-food is now visible," and having had his bowl and robe brought, he put on his robe, took out his bowl, and stood there.
Seeing the Elder standing there, the young children thought, "He must have some need for this."
Having wiped away the sand and placed the bark of the *madhuka* fruit into their bowls, they gave it to them; the elders consumed it.
That very food remained their sustenance for about seven days.
Gradually, they reached the village of Coriya. People, having gathered lilies, threw away the lily stalks.

They arrived. The Elder said, "Friend Mahāsoṇa, alms-food is now visible," and having had his bowl and robe brought, he put on his robe, took out his bowl, and stood there. The village boys cleaned lotus stalks, placed them in the bowl, and gave them to him;
the Elders consumed them. That was his only food for about seven days.
Traveling by stages, they reached a village gate in the dwelling place of people who lived on leaves.
There, as the parents of a certain girl were going into the forest, they said, "If some noble person comes, do not let him go anywhere;
tell him where we live, mother. When she saw the elders, she [did so].

Taking a bowl, she had him sit down. Since there was no kind of grain in the house, she took an axe and, having pounded the bark of the *guñja* and *coca* trees together with the leaves of the *guñja* creeper, she formed them into three balls.
She placed one ball in the bowl of the Elder Isidatta and one in the bowl of the Elder Mahāsoṇa, thinking, "I shall place the remaining ball in the bowl of the Elder Isidatta."
He extended his hand. His hand turned around and placed itself within the bowl of the Elder Mahāsoṇa.

The Elder Isidatta said, “In the past, during the time of the Brahmin Tissa’s fear, when I offered a mere guñja-fruit alms-gift, by the excellence of the place and the time, what measure of ripening will that karma produce?
Having consumed it, they went to their dwelling place. She too [returned] from the forest...
When his parents arrived, he informed them, "Two elders have come. I have pointed out their place of residence to them.
Both of them went to the presence of the elders, paid homage, and made this request: "Venerable sirs, we shall look after you with whatever we receive;
please dwell right here. The elders, for the duration of all the times of fear, lived depending upon them.
When the bandit Brāhmaṇatissa was slain, the Great King raised the royal parasol.
Hearing that the danger had been pacified and the countryside was flourishing, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from beyond the ocean disembarked at Mahātittha port by boat.
Inquiring, “Where does the Elder Mahāsoṇa dwell? they went into the presence of the Elder, who was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus. The Elder...
He arrived at the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery in the village of Kālakā. At that time, about seven hundred families resided in the village of Kālakā.
During the night, a deity, while wandering about, thought:
"The Elder Mahāsoṇa has reached the Maṇḍalārāma Monastery accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus. Each one [brought] a cloak worth nine cubits and a value of one kahāpaṇa."
“Give almsfood,” they said to the people. On the following day, the elders entered Kālakagāma for alms.
The people had them sit down and gave them rice-gruel. The elder Tissabhūti, a resident of Maṇḍalārāma, sat there as the senior of the Saṅgha.
A certain great lay follower paid homage to him and asked, “Venerable sir, who is the elder named Mahāsoṇa?”
At that time, the Elder was a novice sitting at the edge [of the assembly].
The Elder stretched out his hand and said, "This one, lay followers, is named Mahāsoṇa. The lay follower paid homage to him and reached for his bowl. The Elder would not give it to him.
The Elder Tissabhūti said, "Friend Soṇa, just as you do not know him, we too do not know him in this way; for those possessed of merit, the deities..."
“They bring [offerings] to maturity; give the bowl and provide for your fellow celibates,” he said. The Elder gave him the bowl.

The great lay follower took the bowl, went and filled it with alms-food worth a kahāpaṇa, made a nine-cubit cloth into a base, brought it back, and placed it in the Elder’s hand. Another lay follower [did the same] for the Elder—seven times.
They gave seven hundred robes and seven hundred portions of alms-food to the Elder alone.
The Elder, having shared these with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, gradually reached the Mahāvihāra;
there he washed his face, paid homage to the Mahābodhi, paid homage to the Mahācetiya, and standing in the Thūpārāma, put on his robe.
Accompanied by the community of monks, he entered the city through the southern gate;
from the gate as far as the assembly hall, he received alms-food worth sixty kahāpaṇas. From that point on, however, there was no limit to the honor shown him.
Thus, due to the failure of the time, even the honey-fruit and its rind, as well as the lotus-stalks, became difficult to find.
During that period of prosperity, such great gains arose.
To the Venerable Kaṇikāravanatthera as well, fear of the Brahmin Tissa arose while he was still a novice.
Both the novice and his preceptor did not go to the other sea, thinking, "We shall dwell depending on people who eat leaves."

They turned toward the borderlands. After seven days without food, the novice saw a palm fruit on a palm tree in a certain village area and said to his preceptor, "Venerable sir, please wait a moment; I shall shake down the palm fruit.
"You are weak, novice; do not climb up," he replied. "I will climb, venerable sir," he said.
Taking his small axe, he climbed a palmyra tree and began to cut the fruit. The blade slipped and fell to the ground.
The Elder thought, "This youth has climbed the tree while still weary; what will he do now?
The novice, having repeatedly split off palm leaves, tied them to the handle of the axe and, striking them again and again, caused it to fall to the ground.
“Venerable sir, it would be well indeed if you were to insert the handle of the axe here,” he said.
The Elder, thinking, “This novice is endowed with skillful means,” inserted the handle of the axe and gave it to him. He raised the axe and brought down the palm fruits.
The Elder, having caused the axe to fall and having split the palm fruit that had rolled away, spoke to the novice when he had descended: “Novice,…”
“You are weak; eat this first. “Venerable sir, I will not eat until you have eaten,” he said.
Taking an axe, he split the palm fruits, removed the husks, put the kernels into a bowl, and gave them to the elder.
He himself ate as well. As long as there were palm fruits, he remained right there; when the fruits were exhausted—
