Gradually, they entered an abandoned monastery in a place inhabited by people who ate only leaves.
The novice monk attended to the Elder’s dwelling. After the Elder had given the novice his exhortation, he entered the monastery.
The novice thought, “There is no limit to the number of existences lost in unfavorable realms; I shall serve as an attendant to the Buddhas.”
Having gone to the courtyard of the shrine, he cleared away the weeds; for seven days, trembling from lack of food, he remained lying prostrate while pulling up the grass.
And some men wandering in the forest, having found honey and taken firewood as well as vegetable leaves, thinking it was a deer because of the movement of the grass, approached the novice.
Having gone there, they asked, "What are you doing, novice? "I am gathering a bundle of grass, lay followers.
"Is there anyone else here, venerable sir? "Yes, lay followers; my preceptor is inside the inner chamber. "Venerable sir, you should give it to the Great Elder and then eat it.
Having given honey to the novice and pointed out his own dwelling place, they said, "We..."
"We shall go breaking off branches. Taking the Elder with this signal, you may come, venerable sir," they said, and then they departed.
The novice, taking the honey, went into the presence of the Elder and, standing outside, said, "I pay homage to you, Bhante.
The Elder remained silent, thinking, "The novice must have come burning with hunger. He...
Again he said, "I pay homage, venerable sir. "Why, novice, do you not allow the weak monks to lie down comfortably?
"It is proper, venerable sir, to open the door. The elder rose up, opened the door, and asked, "What have you received, novice?
"Honey was given by the people; it is proper, venerable sir, to eat it."
“Novice, in this very way we shall become weary from eating; let us make a drink and drink it. The novice made a drink and gave it to them.
Then the elder said to him, “Novice, you ask about the dwelling places of people?
“They pointed them out themselves, venerable sir,” he replied. “Novice, if we go as early as tomorrow morning, we shall become weary; let us go this very day.”
Having had his bowl and robes taken up, he departed. Having gone there, they lay down not far from the dwelling place of the people.
During the night, the novice thought: "Since the time of my going forth, I have never before allowed the dawn to rise while staying within a village.
Taking his bowl, he went into the forest to bring about the rising of the dawn. The Great Elder—
Not seeing the novice at the place where he had lain down, he thought, "He must have been seized by man-eaters.
The novice, having caused dawn to rise in the forest, returned bringing water and a tooth-stick in his bowl.
[The teacher said: "Novice, where have you been? A thought arose in you regarding the elder monks; bring the penalty!"
“I will bring it, Bhante,” he replied. The Elder washed his face and put on his robe. Both of them went to the dwelling place of the people.
The people gave them tubers, roots, fruits, and leaves for their own use. After the Elder had consumed them, he returned to the monastery.
The novice brought water and said, “I shall wash your feet, Bhante. “Novice,…”
“Where did you go during the night? You have caused us to give rise to anxious thoughts.
“Venerable sir, I have never before allowed dawn to break within the village; I went to the forest for the purpose of breaking dawn there.
“Novice, disciplinary action is not appropriate for you; it is appropriate for us alone,” said the Elder, and right there on that spot—
The Elder gave the novice a warning: "We are now old;
it is not possible for us to know what will happen. You must protect yourself. It is said that the Elder was an Anāgāmin.
Later on, man-eaters devoured him. The novice, having protected himself, remained in such a place when the danger had subsided.
Having taken formal preceptors and received full ordination, he mastered the word of the Buddha and became a bearer of the Three Piṭakas; thus he became known as the Elder Vattabbaka-Nigrodha.
His father, the Great King, took over the reign. Monks arriving from across the sea asked, "Where is the Elder Vattabbaka-Nigrodha?
Where is the Elder Vattabbaka-Nigrodha? and went into his presence. There was a great assembly of monks.

He attended upon the Elder. Surrounded by a great community of monks, he eventually reached the Mahāvihāra, where he paid homage to the Mahābodhi, the Mahācetiya, and the Thūpārāma, and then set out for the city.
As he proceeded as far as the southern gate, the three robes appeared to him in nine places; from the moment he entered the city, there was great honor shown to him.
Thus, during a failure of the season, even palm fruits, tubers, roots, and leaves became difficult to find; whereas during a success of the season, such a great gain arose.
In this way, he understands that kamma, being unable to yield its result because it was obstructed by a failure of the season, ripens when a success of the season arrives.
Another person may also have many wholesome deeds (*kalyāṇakamma*). These would not ripen for one who stands in a failure of application (*payogavipatti*).
However, by being established in correct application through even a single wholesome deed, he fulfills the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*), guards the five precepts and the ten precepts.
For one reborn during a period of excellence (*kālasampatti*), kings and princesses adorned with every ornament [approach him].
“They send what is suitable for him,” they say; they send various kinds of gifts—such as vehicles, carriages, gems, gold, silver, and so forth—thinking, “This is suitable for him.
Even one who has gone forth into homelessness may possess great fame and great power. In this regard, there is this story: it is said that King Kūṭakaṇṇa...
He claimed as his own the Elder Cūḷasudhamma, who lived at Girigāmakaṇṇa. While staying at Uppalavāpi, he summoned the Elder.
The Elder came and resided at the Mālārāma Monastery. The king asked the Elder’s mother, "What does the Elder like?
"Roots, Great King," she replied. The king had roots brought and went to the monastery.
While giving to the elder, he was unable even to look up at his face. Having gone outside the monastery courtyard, the king asked the queen, “What is the elder like?
She replied, “Being a man yourself, you were not able to look up; how then could I possibly do so?
I do not know what he is like. The king thought, “In my kingdom, I am not even able to look up at the son of a householder who pays taxes.”
"Ah! How great indeed is the teaching of the Buddha! he exclaimed, clapping his hands. He claimed even the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka as his own.
A small boil had arisen on the elder’s finger. Thinking, "I shall see the elder," the king went to the monastery and, out of intense affection, took the finger into his mouth.
The boil burst within the mouth itself; the pus and blood flowed out without causing any pain to the elder.
With affection, he swallowed it as if it were nectar. Later, that same elder lay down upon his deathbed.
The king went there, placed a stool of impurities upon his head, and wandered about lamenting, "The axle of the Dhamma-chariot is breaking! The axle is breaking!
This wandering of the Lord of the Earth with a stool of impurities lifted upon his head—
"Whose path has been traversed? "The path of right application has been traversed.
Thus he understands: "Because they were obstructed by a failure of application, these [karmas] were unable to give their result; now, through the excellence of application, they ripen.
In this way, wholesome karma that was obstructed by the four failures, instead of giving its result, gives it by means of the four excellences.
In this regard, having established the actual fact, here is the simile: It is said that a certain great king, having become slightly angry with a minister, had him bound in prison.
His relatives, learning of the king’s anger, said nothing at first;
but when the king’s fierce rage had subsided, they made the king understand the minister’s innocence. The king released him.
He restored his position to its original state. Then there was no limit to the quantities of gifts arriving from here and there;
the people were unable to receive them all. In that situation, for the king, it was like the time he had been imprisoned in a jail for being slightly angry;
for the worldling, it was like the time of rebirth in hell. Then, for him—
The time of his rebirth in heaven is like the time when relatives, having persuaded the king, restore him to his former position.
The time when he is unable to accept the gift is like the time when, having attained the four types of prosperity,
one moves from the world of gods to the human world and from the human world to the world of gods— thus, from a state of happiness...

It should be understood that having led [the being] to a state of happiness alone, and having granted the fruition of happiness for even a hundred thousand aeons, one brings them to the attainment of Nibbāna.

Thus, having first illustrated the second power by way of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it should further be illustrated by the method of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) according to the formula: "There was karma;
there was the fruition of karma. In this context, "there was karma" refers to karma accumulated in the past.
It simply occurred in the past. However, with reference to that by which a result was given in the past, it is said: "There was a ripening of kamma.

But even when many [karmas] such as those to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) have been accumulated, only one—namely, that to be experienced in the present life—gives its result, while the others remain without result. One [kamma] to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) draws forth the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), while the others...

They are without ripening (*avipāka*). By one *ānantariya* (immediate) deed, one is reborn in hell; the remaining ones are without ripening. Among the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), by one [attainment] one is reborn in the Brahma-world; the others are without ripening. It is with reference to this that it was said: "There is no ripening of karma.
However, there is one who, having performed even much wholesome or unwholesome karma, reaches *arahantship* by relying on a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*).

The result of this karma is called "was not" (*nāhosi*). That which was accumulated in the past and gives its result in the present is called "karma that was, there is the result of karma" (*ahosi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko*).
That which, by the same method as before, reaches a state of non-resulting is called "karma that was, there is no result of karma" (*ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko*).
That which was accumulated in the past and will give its result in the future is called "karma that was... [there will be the result of karma].

There will be action and there will be the ripening of that action. That which, by the aforementioned method, will reach a state of non-ripening is called "action that has been, but there will be no ripening of that action.
That which is currently exerted and gives its ripening right now is "there is action, there is the ripening of action."
[This refers to] the name [of such views]. That which, by the same method as before, reaches a state of non-resultantness is called "there is action, there is no result of action.
That which is now accumulated and will give its result in the future is called "there is action, there will be a result of action.
That which, by the same method as before, will reach a state of non-resultantness is called "there is action, there will be no result of action."
That which is itself future, and whose ripening is also future, is called "there will be karma, there will be the ripening of karma.
That which is itself future, but which— by the same method as before— will reach a state of non-ripening,
is called "there will be karma, there will not be the ripening of karma."

"This is for the Tathāgata": by all these aspects, this knowledge of the Tathāgata regarding the diversity of kamma and the diversity of its results should be understood as the second power in the sense of being unshakable.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the second power. Now follows the exposition of the third power.
811. In the description of the third power, "the path" (*magga*) or "the way of practice" (*paṭipadā*) is simply a name for kamma. Regarding the terms "leading to hell" (*nirayagāminī*) and so forth:

in the sense of being devoid of enjoyment (*nirassāda*) and in the sense of being without delight (*nirati*), it is "hell" (*niraya*). Having gone upward and slanting across, they are "animals" (*tiracchāna*);
the animal realm itself is the "animal womb" (*tiracchānayoni*). By virtue of being a *peta*, one is a *petti*; the meaning is "having passed away from here and gone. The *petti* themselves...
The realm of ghosts (*pettivisaya*). Because of the predominance of mind (*manas*), they are humans (*manussa*); humans themselves constitute the human world (*manussaloka*).
They sport with the five strands of sensual pleasure, or because of their preeminent excellence of station, they are gods (*deva*); gods themselves constitute the divine world (*devaloka*).

"Fetter" (*vāna*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*); since that is not there, it is *nibbāna*. One goes to hell, thus one is "hell-bound" (*nirayagāmī*). This is said with reference to the path (*magga*).
This has been said. However, there is a practice that leads to hell. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
The Tathāgata understands all these modes of practice.
How so? For even when all the inhabitants of a village together deprive a single pig or a deer of its life, [the Tathāgata knows this].
The volition of all [those who kill] has exclusively the life-faculty of another as its object. However, that karma differs at the very moment of their undertaking it.
For among them, one acts having generated zeal with earnestness; another acts because he is pressured by others, being told, "Come, you too must do it";
and another acts while appearing to have the same intent, moving about without being resisted. Among these—
One is reborn in hell by that very same kamma, one in the animal realm, and one in the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).
At the very moment of the accumulation [of kamma], the Tathāgata understands: "Because it was accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in hell;
this one in the animal realm; this one in the sphere of hungry ghosts. Even as they are being reborn in hell, [he knows]: "This one... into the eight...
He understands: ‘He will be reborn in the great hells; he will be reborn in the sixteen secondary hells.
When being reborn in the animal realm, he understands: ‘This one will be footless; this one will be two-footed; this one will be four-footed; this one will be many-footed.
When being reborn in the sphere of hungry ghosts, he understands: ‘This one will be one whose thirst is parched...’
He understands: "This one is hungry and thirsty; this one lives on what is given by others. And regarding those karmas, he understands:
"This karma will not be able to draw forth rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi); it is weak, and its result will ripen in the acquisitions (upadhi) after rebirth-linking has already been given.
Likewise, when all the inhabitants of an entire village give alms-food together, the volition (cetanā) of all of them has the alms-food as its object alone.

That karma, moreover, is differentiated at the very moment of its accumulation by the method previously described. Among them, some will be reborn in the world of the gods, and some in the human world.
At the very moment of accumulation, the Tathāgata understands: "Because it was accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in the human world;
that one in the world of the gods. This applies even to those being reborn in the world of the gods.
‘This one will be reborn among the Paranimmitavasavatti devas; this one among the Nimmānarati devas; this one among the Tusita devas; this one among the Yāma devas;
this one among the Tāvatiṃsa devas; this one among the Cātumahārājika devas; this one among the earth-devas;
but this one will be reborn as the supreme king of the gods, while this one will be his attendant, performing the second or third office.’

Having sacrificed, he understands: ‘He will be reborn among humans. Regarding those being reborn among humans, he understands: ‘This one will be reborn in a khattiya family; this one in a brahmin family;
this one in a vessa family; this one in a sudda family. But this one, having become a king among humans, will be reborn;
that one, performing the second or third rank, will be reborn as an attendant.’

He understands. And regarding those karmas, he understands: ‘This karma will not be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; it will be weak, and its ripening will occur as a result within the existing aggregates after rebirth has been given.
Likewise, even while those who have established insight are practicing, by whatever method the insight was begun, [he understands]: ‘This [person] will attain Arahantship...’
"He will reach [the fruit]; he will not be able to attain Arahantship; he will be a non-returner (anāgāmī) only; he will be a once-returner (sakadāgāmī) only;

he will be a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) only; however, he will not be able to realize either the path or the fruit, but will remain fixed in insight (vipassanā) that takes the characteristics as its object;
he will be occupied only with the discernment of conditions (paccaya-pariggaha); he will be occupied only with the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-pariggaha)."
He understands: ‘This one will remain in the apprehension of the formless alone; this one will remain in the apprehension of form alone;
this one will define only the primary elements; this one will not be able to discern anything.
Even regarding those performing the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, he knows: ‘This will be merely the preliminary work for him; he will not be able to produce the sign.’
"He will not be able [to attain it]; however, he will be able to produce the sign, though he will not be able to reach absorption;
having reached absorption and made jhāna the basis, he will establish insight and attain Arahantship"—thus he understands.
This concludes the commentary on the description of the third power.
The Exposition of the Fourth Power (Catutthabalaniddesa) 812.

Regarding the exposition of the fourth power, "the diversity of the aggregates" means that one understands the differentiation of the five aggregates thus: "This is called the aggregate of form... [and so on] ...this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding those [aggregates], one understands: "The aggregate of form is of one kind... [and so on]"...
‘The aggregate of form is elevenfold; the aggregate of feeling is singlefold... [and so on] ...the aggregate of feeling is manifoldfold...
the aggregate of perception is singlefold... the aggregate of volitional formations is singlefold...
the aggregate of consciousness is singlefold... the aggregate of consciousness is manifoldfold. In this way, one understands the diversity of each aggregate. As for the diversity of the sense bases:
‘This is called the eye-base... [and so on] ...this is called the mind-object-base. Among these, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while two belong to the four planes.
In this way, one understands the diversity of the bases. As for the diversity of the elements: ‘This is called the eye-element...

[and so on] ...this is called the mind-consciousness-element. Among these, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere, while two belong to the four planes. In this way, one understands the diversity of the elements.
Thus he understands the diversity of elements.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the diversity of the world through its many elements and various elements," this means that the Tathāgata understands not only the diversity of the world of appropriated formations, but likewise understands the diversity of the world of unappropriated formations as well.

It was taken [as an example] in order to show this: for Paccekabuddhas and the two Chief Disciples know only a portion, not the entirety, of the diversity of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) that is subject to grasping (*upādinnaka*);
moreover, they do not know the diversity of the world that is not subject to grasping (*anupādinnaka*).
But the Omniscient Buddha [knows it all], such that when a particular element is predominant, he knows of a particular tree...
One trunk is white, this one is black; this one is smooth, this one is rough;
this one has thick bark, this one has thin bark; due to the predominance of such-and-such an element, the leaf of this tree becomes of such-and-such a color, shape, and so forth;
but due to the predominance of such-and-such an element, the flower of this tree is blue, or yellow.
It is red, white, fragrant, or foul-smelling; through the predominance of this particular element,
the fruit becomes small or large, long or short, round, well-shaped or ill-shaped, smooth or rough,
fragrant or foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, or astringent.
‘With the predominance of this particular element, this tree has a thorn that is sharp, very sharp, straight, curved,
copper-colored, black, blue, or white’— in this way he understands the diversity of the world of non-clung-to formations.
For this is the power of the omniscient Buddhas alone, and not of others.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Fourth Power.
The Exposition of the Fifth Power. 813.

Regarding the exposition of the fifth power: "those of inferior inclination" means those whose underlying tendencies (*adhyāśaya*) are inferior; "those of superior inclination" means those whose underlying tendencies are noble.
"They serve" means they rely upon and cling to [them]. "They associate with" means they approach them. "They attend upon" means they approach them again and again.
For if the teachers and preceptors are not virtuous while the co-residents are virtuous, those co-residents do not even approach their own teachers and preceptors;
rather, they approach only those monks who are similar to themselves and worthy of association.
They approach [their teachers]. If the teachers and preceptors are monks of suitable character while others are unsuitable, even those [unsuitable ones] do not approach their teachers and preceptors;
they approach only those who are similar to themselves and of inferior inclination.
To show that such approaching is not only the case now, but also in the past and the future, he said: "In the past time... and so forth.

That has already been explained in its literal sense. But what determines this: that the unvirtuous associate only with the unvirtuous, the virtuous only with the virtuous, the witless only with the witless, and the wise only with the wise?
It is the element of inclination (*ajjhāsayadhātu*) that determines it. It is said that a number of bhikkhus were wandering for alms as a group through a certain village.
The people, having brought much food and filled their bowls, gave it to them, saying, "Eat according to your respective portions," and then dismissed them.
The monks also said, "Friends, the people are employing us in work related to the relics.
Then the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya, together with five hundred monks, went to the Cetiya on Nāgadīpa to pay homage.
While traveling, he was invited by people in a certain village. With the Elder there was one unsuitable monk, and in his own resident monastery there was also one unsuitable monk.

As the two monastic communities were entering the village, although neither of those two individuals had ever seen the visiting monk before, nor had the resident monk ever seen the visitor, [they both joined the procession].
Even though this was so, they stood to one side, having gathered together and conversed with frequent laughter.
Seeing them, the Elder said, "The Perfectly Enlightened One, knowing [our thoughts], spoke the *Dhātusaṃyutta*.

Having thus stated that "the element of disposition (*ajjhāsayadhātu*) determines [the teaching]," this very meaning should be illustrated by the *Dhātusaṃyutta*. For, on Mount Vulture Peak (*Gijjhakūṭapabbata*),...

While the Blessed One was lying on his sickbed, he observed Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and the others—who were staying around him for protection—each walking back and forth with their own respective retinues. He then addressed the monks:
“Monks, do you see Sāriputta walking back and forth together with a large number of monks? “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Venerable sir,” [he said]. “All these bhikkhus, bhikkhus, are of great wisdom”—all this should be recited in full.
The commentary on the explanation of the fifth power.
The explanation of the sixth power.

814. In the exposition of the sixth power (*chaṭṭhabalanniddesa*): "They lie" (*āsayanti*) means that where beings lie or dwell—that is, their place of residence, whether it be a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*) or knowledge according to reality (*yathābhūtañāṇa*). "They lie latent" (*anusayanti*) refers to the defilement (*kilesa*) that has not been abandoned and remains latent.

"Conduct" (*carita*) refers to the wholesome and unwholesome actions performed by body and so forth. "Inclination" (*adhimutta*) refers to one's underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*). Regarding the terms "one with little dust" (*apparajakkha*) and so on: [the explanation follows].
Those who have little or limited dust of lust, hatred, and delusion in the eye consisting of wisdom are "those with little dust" (*apparajakkhā*).
Because that [dust] is great, they are "those with much dust" (*mahārajakkhā*). By both of these terms, he indicates beings with weak defilements and those with great defilements.
Those whose faculties such as faith are sharp are "those with sharp faculties" (*tikkhindriyā*); those whose faculties are dull are "those with dull faculties" (*mudindriyā*).
Those whose dispositions (*āsaya*) and other factors are excellent are "of good character" (*svākāra*). The opposite are "of bad character" (*dvākāra*).
Those who perceive the reasons explained and can be made to understand with ease are "easily instructed" (*suviññāpayā*). The opposite are "difficult to instruct" (*duviññāpayā*).
Those who are suitable for the penetration of the Noble Path and possess the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) are "capable" (*bhabbā*). The opposite are "incapable" (*abhabbā*).
815. Having thus established the matrix (mātikā) for the sixth power, he now explains it according to its sequence, beginning with:

"And what is the disposition (āsaya) of beings? and so forth. In this regard, the meaning of such views as "the world is eternal" has already been stated in the commentary on the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* (The Chapter on the Exposition).
"Thus, based on the view of existence" means: thus, based on the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). Eternalism.
For here, "existence-view" (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) is mentioned, as is "annihilation-view" (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*).
Indeed, because all views are subsumed under the views of eternalism and annihilationism, all beings who follow views are dependent upon these two views alone.
And this has been said: "Kaccāna, this world for the most part relies upon a duality."
—“both existence and non-existence. Here, “existence” refers to eternalism (*sassata*), and “non-existence” refers to annihilationism (*uccheda*).
This, first of all, is the disposition of ordinary beings (*puthujjana*) who rely upon the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Now, in order to show the disposition of pure beings who rely upon the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), [the text says]: “But by not approaching either of these two extremes,” and so forth.
It has been said. Therein, "or these very ones" refers to these very same [views]. "Both extremes" refers to the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism.
"Without approaching" means without clinging. "Conditionality in things dependently arisen" refers both to conditionality itself and to the things that have arisen dependently.
"Conformable acceptance" is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "As it really is" (refers to...)

Or "knowledge" refers to path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*). This is what is meant: that insight which has been attained regarding both dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently originated phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna-dhammā*), without falling into either of these two extremes of eternalism or annihilationism;

and that higher path-knowledge which follows from it—this is the disposition of beings, and this is [the knowledge] of all those who are based on the round of existence as well as those who are based on its cessation.
"It is the abode of beings; it is their dwelling place. This is the teachers' explanation of the identical meaning. However, the caviller says:
"Does not the so-called 'path' proceed by destroying one's dwelling? Are you not saying that the path is a dwelling? He should be asked:
"Are you a reciter of the *Ariyavāsa* [Sutta], or not? If he says, "I am not," [then the point is established].
If he says this, he should be told, "You do not know because you are not a reciter. If he says, "I am a reciter," he should be told, "Bring forth a sutta.
If he brings it forth, that is well; if he does not bring it forth, he himself should bring it forth:
"Monks, there are these ten noble abodes which the Noble Ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in."
For this sutta illustrates the state of being a dwelling place for the Path. Therefore, it is indeed well-spoken.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, knowing the inclinations of beings, knows even at a moment when these types of views do not arise whether insight-knowledge or path-knowledge is present.
And this has been said:
“He knows one who indulges in sensual pleasures as: ‘This person is heavy with sensual pleasures, inclined toward sensual pleasures, intent upon sensual pleasures.
He knows one who indulges in renunciation as: ‘This person is heavy with renunciation, inclined toward renunciation, intent upon renunciation.

[He knows one who indulges in] ill will… [and so on]… non-ill will… sloth and torpor… [and so on]… perception of light as: ‘This person is heavy with renunciation, inclined toward renunciation, intent upon renunciation.’”
He knows one who is practicing thus: “This person values the perception of light, has a tendency toward the perception of light, and is intent upon the perception of light.

(816) In the description of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*) is called the underlying tendency of lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāgānusaya*) because it is not yet abandoned.

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. “Whatever in the world is of a lovely nature” means whatever is of a pleasant kind in this world. “Of a pleasurable nature” means of a delightful kind.
The "basis of gratification" is a desirable object. Regarding the phrase "the underlying tendency to lust underlies beings here":
in this desirable object, the underlying tendency to lust underlies beings in the sense that it has not been abandoned.
Just as for one submerged in water, there is only water below, above, and on all sides, even so, the arising of lust in beings occurs toward a desirable object.

"Practiced and repeatedly practiced. Likewise, there is the arising of repulsion toward an undesirable object. Thus, "in these two states" means in these two states consisting of desirable and undesirable objects which possess sensual lust and repulsion.

"Overcome by ignorance" means that ignorance has followed along by way of making them its object while being associated with sensual lust and repulsion. "Associated with that" means by way of being associated with that ignorance and being of one side with it.
"Singlefold": conceit, views, and doubt constitute nine types of conceit, sixty-two types of views, and doubt with eight bases.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) is here included within the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). 817.
In the exposition of conduct (*carita*), thirteen volitions are the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), twelve are the formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), and four...

The formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*). Among these, that which belongs to the sense sphere is of limited range (*parittabhūmaka*), while the other is of great range (*mahābhūmaka*).
Alternatively, among these three, whichever has a small result is to be understood as being of limited range, and whichever has a great result is of great range. 818.
The exposition of resolve (*adhimutti*) has already been explained below. But why is this resolve mentioned again, even though it was stated below?
"Taken"? This [term] was taken previously in the section on the individual demonstration of power; here it is for the purpose of showing the state of having sharp or dull faculties in beings. 819.

In the description of those with great defilement (*mahārajakkha*), "gone to excess" (*ussadagata*) means gone to abundance (*vepullagata*). And this description is given in reverse order according to the sequence of abandoning. 820. "Not gone to excess" (*anussadagata*) means not gone to abundance.

In the description of those with sharp and dull faculties, the "faculties as decisive supports" (*upanissayaindriya*) are what are being discussed. Regarding the purpose for giving this description in reverse order here, it should be understood in the same manner as stated below.

823. Likewise, in the exposition of the "bad aspects" (*dvākāra*) and so forth: "evil dispositions" (*pāpāsaya*) refers to unwholesome latent tendencies (*akusala-āsaya*). "Evil conduct" (*pāpacarita*) refers to those who fulfill unmeritorious volitional formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*). "Devoted to evil" (*pāpādhimuttika*) refers to those who delight in self-identity (*sakkāya*) and have a disposition toward the round of existence (*vaṭṭajjhāsaya*). 824.

In the exposition of the "good aspects" (*svākāra*), because there is no such thing as a "beautiful underlying tendency" (*kalyāṇānusaya*), the term "beautiful underlying tendencies" is not mentioned. The remainder should be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated. 826.

In the exposition of the "capable and incapable," "by the obstruction of karma" (*kammāvaraṇa*) means by the fivefold deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*). "By the obstruction of defilements" (*kilesāvaraṇa*) means...
"Fixed by wrong view" refers to the obstruction of fruition (*vipākāvaraṇa*), which is rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) without root-cause (*ahetuka*).
Since even those with two root-causes lack penetration of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), it should be understood that rebirth-linking with two root-causes is likewise an obstruction of fruition.
"Lacking faith" means being devoid of faith toward the Buddha and the others. "Lacking desire" means being devoid of wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
The people of Uttarakuru have entered a state devoid of desire. They are "of poor wisdom" because they are deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-paññā*).
However, even one whose life-continuum is complete in wisdom is still called "of poor wisdom" if that life-continuum does not serve as a basis for the supramundane (*lokuttara*).
Regarding the phrase "incapable of entering into the certainty of rightness in wholesome states," it refers to wholesome states...
They are incapable of entering the path known as the fixed course of rightness regarding phenomena. 827.
"Not by obstruction of kamma" and so forth should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated above. This is the distribution of two kinds of knowledge:

the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties and the knowledge of their dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya*). For herein, by means of the knowledge of their dispositions and underlying tendencies—
The knowledge of the degrees of the faculties (*indriyaparopariyattiñāṇa*) is also divided. Thus, these two knowledges, when combined together, become what is called one power-knowledge (*balañāṇa*).
This concludes the commentary on the description of the sixth power. Now follows the description of the seventh power.
828. In the exposition of the seventh power: one who meditates is a meditator (*jhāyī*). "Four meditators" refers to four types of persons who are called meditators.

Therein, in the first tetrad, first of all, the first person, while being actually an attainer of attainment, perceives: "I am not an attainer"; and while having the same meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he perceives: "It is not my meditation subject.
This one should be understood as an obtainer of meditation that is not yet proficient.
The second, though not having attained meditative absorption, thinks “I have attained it”; though it is not a meditation subject, he perceives it as “a meditation subject.
This is called one who “meditates while asleep. Having slept and awakened, he conceives it thus.
The third, being one who has attained absorption, thinks “I am an attainer of absorption”; though it is indeed a meditation subject, he perceives it as “a meditation subject.”
This person should be understood as one who has attained mastery over the jhānas. The fourth person, however, is indeed a non-attainer;

thinking "I am a non-attainer," he perceives what is not a meditation subject as "a meditation subject. Thus, in this context, two types of people—though they are merely reciters—are called "meditators" because they have entered among the ranks of meditators.
In the second tetrad, [the practitioner] who suppresses the factors obstructive to concentration with effort and exertion [is slow].
"Enters" means: one who emerges suddenly after remaining for one or two thought-moments is said to "emerge quickly.
One who, with ease, clears away the factors obstructive to concentration is said to "enter quickly.
One who emerges after passing the time limit without emerging according to the predetermined duration is said to "emerge slowly."
The other two [tetads] should also be understood by this same method. These four types of persons are all attainers of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

In the third tetrad, one who is skilled in discerning the defining characteristics of the factors—such as determining that "this jhāna has five factors" and "this has four factors"—is called "skilled in concentration" (*samādhikusala*) regarding concentration. Having suppressed the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), within the casket of the mind...
One who is unable to establish the mind is called "unskilled in concentration" and "not proficient in attainment.
The other three types should also be understood in this same manner. These four are indeed possessors of attainment (*samāpatti*).
Now, in order to show those meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) by depending on which these individuals have become known as "meditators" (*jhāyin*), he said: "The four jhānas," and so forth.
Therein, the four jhānas and the three liberations have been explained in meaning already in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*.
The meaning of the remaining liberations should also be understood according to the method stated therein.

Furthermore, in this context, they are called "liberations" because, in their respective order, they are liberated from opposing states at the moment of absorption and because they resolve upon their objects.
It is called "liberation" (vimokkha). However, the eighth is called "liberation by removal" because it is entirely liberated from perceptions and feelings (saññā-vedayita).

Among the concentrations, according to both the fourfold and fivefold systems, the concentration of the first jhāna is called "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra). In the fivefold system, the concentration of the second jhāna is called "concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (avitakka-vicāramatta). This applies to both the fourfold and the fivefold systems.
In the three higher jhānas, concentration is called “concentration without applied thought and sustained thought” (avitakka-avicāra-samādhi).

For among the eight attainments in their successive order, both the name “concentration” (samādhi) and the name “attainment” (samāpatti) apply. Why? Because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā).
In the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), because that [one-pointedness] is absent, it does not bear the name “concentration.”

A state partaking of decline (*hānabhāgiyo dhammo*) is the intrusion of sensual desire and so forth into the perception and attention of one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so on that are not yet well-mastered.

A state partaking of distinction (*visesabhāgiyo dhammo*) is the intrusion of the second jhāna and so forth into the perception and attention of one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so on that are well-mastered.
By the phrase "purification is also emergence," it refers to well-mastered purification.
"Emergence" (vuṭṭhāna) has been explained. For each lower, mastered jhāna serves as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for each higher one;

therefore, even purification (vodāna) is called "emergence. By the phrase "emergence from each respective concentration," the so-called "emergence from the life-continuum" (bhavaṅga-vuṭṭhāna) is indicated;
for it is by means of the life-continuum that there is emergence from all jhānas.
...occurs. However, they emerge from cessation only through the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). This is called "emergence independent of the texts" (*pāḷimuttakavuṭṭhāna*).
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the seventh power. Now follows the exposition of the eighth power, etc.

829. In the exposition of the eighth power, everything beginning with "various kinds of past lives" has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. In the exposition of the ninth power as well, everything beginning with "with the divine eye" has been explained in that same place.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Ninth Power.
Exposition of the Tenth Power.
831. In the exposition of the Ten Powers (*dasabala*), "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of fruition (*phalasamādhi*);

"liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) refers to the knowledge of fruition (*phalañāṇa*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout. This, then, is the teachers' explanation of the identical meanings. However, an opponent says:
"There is no such thing as the knowledge of the ten powers as a separate entity; this is merely a classification of the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) itself."
That should not be viewed in that way. For the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) is indeed one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) is another.
The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions. The knowledge of omniscience, however, knows both those and what remains beyond them.

Even among the knowledges of the ten powers, the first knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause; the second, only the diversity of kamma and the diversity of its results; and the third, only the delimitation of kamma.
The fourth is precisely the diversity of elements; the fifth is precisely the inclinations and dispositions of beings;
the sixth is precisely the sharpness or dullness of the faculties; the seventh is precisely their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other factors;
the eighth is precisely the continuity of the aggregates in previous existences; the ninth is precisely the death and rebirth-linking of beings; the tenth—
It is precisely the delimitation of truth. However, omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa) understands both what is to be known by these [other knowledges] and what is superior to them.
Yet it does not perform all the functions of those [knowledges]. For that [omniscience], being jhāna, cannot attain absorption; being psychic power (iddhi), it cannot perform transformations;
and being the path (magga), it cannot eradicate defilements (kilesa).

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked thus: "Is this so-called 'knowledge of the ten powers' (dasabalañāṇa) with applied thought and sustained thought (savitakkasavicāra), without applied thought and with sustained thought only (avitakkavicāramatta), without applied thought and without sustained thought (avitakkāvicāra);
belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara);
mundane (lokiya) or supramundane (lokuttara)? One who knows will say: "In sequence, the first seven knowledges are with applied thought and sustained thought. Then [he will say]: "The latter two..."

He will say, "The knowledges are without applied thought and without sustained thought. He will say, "The knowledge of the destruction of the taints may be with applied thought and sustained thought, may be without applied thought and with sustained thought only, or may be without applied thought and without sustained thought.

Likewise, he will say, "In sequence, there are seven belonging to the sense-sphere, then two belonging to the fine-material sphere, and at the end, one supramundane. Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of omniscience...
"He will say: 'It is precisely with applied thought and sustained thought, precisely pertaining to the sense-sphere, and precisely mundane.
Thus, the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience is another.
(From the *Sammohavinodanī*, the Commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*).
The Commentary on the Analysis of Knowledge is finished.
17. The Analysis of Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga). 1.
Commentary on the Singlefold Matrix, etc. (Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā).
832. Now, in the subsequent *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, a detailed exposition has been made following the sequence of the terms established after first setting forth the matrix (*mātikā*).
Therein, this is the delimitation of the arrangement: first, seventy-three single items beginning with "pride of birth" (*jātimada*) were set forth;
then, eighteen pairs beginning with "anger and resentment" (*kodha ca upanāho ca*); and thirty-five [groups] beginning with the "unwholesome roots" (*akusalamūla*).
The triads; the fourteen tetrads such as the four taints (āsava); the fifteen pentads such as the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana);
the fourteen hexads such as the roots of dispute (vivāda-mūla); the seven heptads such as the underlying tendencies (anusaya); the eight octads such as the bases of defilement (kilesavatthu);
the nine nonads such as the bases of resentment (āghātavatthu); the seven decads such as the bases of defilement; and [the categories] of the internal...

It should be understood that all these eighteen groups—beginning with the eighteen modes of craving based on the [five aggregates] and so forth—are included within these eight hundred defilements. This, then, is the section on their classification.
(1. Commentary on the Exposition of Single Items.
843–844. Now, regarding the section on the exposition that begins with the method "In this regard, what is pride of birth?
as it follows the matrix (mātikā) as it was laid down: "dependent on birth" means relying upon birth. And here, "dependence" (paṭicca) is spoken of in the sense of existence;
therefore, the meaning here is "when birth exists. The same method applies to "dependent on clan," and so forth. By way of intoxication...

*Madō*: the mode of intoxication is *majjanā*; the state of being intoxicated is *majjitattaṃ*. *Māno*, *maññanā*, and so forth, have meanings already explained below in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*.

"This is called" means that when such a birth exists, the pride that arises depending on that birth and proceeds in the mode of intoxication is called "pride of birth" (*jātimada*). This arises among all four castes, including the *khattiyas*. One who is endowed with birth...
For a khattiya thinks: "There is no other like me; the rest are born as khattiyas only by rising from among others.
I, however, am a khattiya of ancient lineage," and thus he conceives pride. The same method applies to brahmins and the others as well.
The meaning should be understood through this very means in the descriptions of pride regarding clan and so forth. For even a khattiya thinks: "I am of the Koṇḍañña clan; I am of the Ādicca clan."
One conceives pride. A brahmin also conceives pride, thinking, "I am of the Kassapa clan; I am of the Bhāradvāja clan.
A merchant and a worker also conceive pride based on their respective family clans.
Even the eighteen guilds likewise conceive pride, thinking, "We were born into this particular guild."

Among these, *ārogyamada* (the conceit of health) is the conceit arising from self-satisfaction, thinking: "I am healthy, while others are full of disease; even for my part, there is no such thing as illness, not even enough to draw blood with a cow's horn.

*Yobbanamada* (the conceit of youth) is the conceit arising from self-satisfaction, thinking: "I am young; the physical frames of other beings are like trees standing on a precipice, whereas I stand in the prime of life."

The conceit arisen through the mode of self-exaltation, thinking: “I have lived long, I am living long, I shall live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I shall live happily,” is called the conceit of life (*jīvitamada*).

The conceit arisen through the mode of self-exaltation, thinking: “I am a gainer of gains, while other beings have little gain; moreover, there is no measure for my gains,” is called the conceit of gain (*lābhamada*).

The conceit that arises through self-delusion, thinking, “Other beings receive this or that, but I receive requisites such as robes that are well-made and exquisite,” is called the intoxication of honor (*sakkāramada*).
Furthermore, when people walk treading upon the heels of other bhikkhus and do not even bow to them,
saying, “This is a recluse,” yet upon seeing me they immediately bow down, treating me with reverence like a stone parasol or like a mass of fire— [this is also intoxication].
The conceit arising from the sense of self-importance, thinking, “I have made myself difficult to overcome,” is called the intoxication of respect (*garukāramada*).

The conceit arising from the sense of self-importance, thinking, “Any question that arises is resolved by my mouth alone; even when going on almsround, they go surrounding me, placing me at their head,” is called the intoxication of precedence (*purekkhāramada*).
First, regarding a householder with a large retinue: “Even a hundred men or a thousand men surround me.”
Furthermore, in the case of homelessness, the conceit arising from the vanity of thinking, "A hundred ascetics or even a thousand ascetics attend upon me;
others have small retinues, whereas I have a large retinue and a pure retinue," is called *parivāramada*.
As for wealth (*bhoga*), although it is already included by the mention of "gain" (*lābha*), it is placed here as a separate category.

He has been addressed by name; therefore, the pride that arises from intoxication, thinking, "The remaining beings do not obtain even enough for their own consumption, whereas for me there is no limit to the wealth stored in my treasury," is called *bhogamada* (pride of wealth).
"In dependence on beauty" means in dependence on both the beauty of the body and the beauty of one's virtues. [Thinking: "The remaining beings are ill-favored and ugly..."

But I am handsome and pleasing; other beings are devoid of virtue and have no wide renown, whereas my fame is well-known among gods and humans—‘Thus the Elder is learned, thus he is virtuous, thus he is endowed with the ascetic qualities.
Pride arising from such self-exaltation is called the intoxication of beauty.
The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, “Other beings are of little learning, whereas I am well-versed,” is called the intoxication of learning (*sutamada*).

The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, “Other beings lack eloquence, whereas for me there is no limit to my eloquence,” is called the intoxication of eloquence (*paṭibhānamada*).

The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, “I am one who knows antiquities; I know such-and-such lineage of Buddhas, royal genealogies, histories of provinces, histories of villages, the divisions of days and nights, and the conjunctions of constellations and moments,” is called the intoxication of antiquarian knowledge (*rattaññumada*).

The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, "The remaining bhikkhus have become alms-food eaters only halfway through their lives, but I am one who has been an alms-food eater since birth," is called the intoxication of being an alms-food eater (*piṇḍapātika-mada*).

The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, "Other beings are despised and held in contempt, but I am neither despised nor held in contempt," is called the intoxication of not being despised (*anavaññāta-mada*).
The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, "The deportment of others is unpleasing, but mine is pleasing," is called the intoxication of deportment (*iriyāpatha-mada*).

The conceit arising from self-admiration, thinking, “The remaining beings are like crows with clipped wings, whereas I am of great psychic power and great majesty,” or “Whatever action I perform, that succeeds,” is called the conceit of psychic power (*iddhimada*).
By the mention of a retinue below, fame (*yasa*) is already included; however, in this context, the conceit of attendants (*upaṭṭhākamada*) is also taken.
This should be illustrated by both the householder and the homeless one. For a certain householder among the eighteen guilds...
In the case of one who is the eldest among his [family], he thinks, "I establish the rest of the men; I am the one who directs them.
Likewise, even a certain homeless one (anagārika) may be the eldest in some context, and through the inflation of pride, thinking, "The other bhikkhus act according to my instruction;
I am the eldest," there arises what is called the intoxication of fame (yasamada).

The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking, “Other beings are immoral, but I am virtuous,” is called the pride of virtue (*sīlamada*). The conceit arising from the sense of self-satisfaction, thinking,
“At a time when other beings lack even one-pointedness of mind sufficient for a single drink of water from a chicken’s trough, I, however,
am an attainer of both access and absorption concentration,” is called the pride of meditation (*jhānamada*).
The conceit arising from the sense of pride, thinking, “Other beings are without craft, but I am skilled,” is called *sippamada* (pride in one’s craft).
The conceit arising from the sense of pride, thinking, “Other beings are short, but I am tall,” is called *ārohamada* (pride in one’s stature).
The conceit arising from the sense of pride, thinking, “Other beings are either short or tall, but I am well-proportioned like a banyan tree (*nigrodhaparimaṇḍala*),” [is called *saṇṭhānamada*].

Pride that has arisen [thinking] "The physical build of other beings is ugly and repulsive, but mine is pleasing and handsome" due to such self-exaltation is called pride in physical build (*saṇṭhānamada*). Pride that has arisen due to self-exaltation [thinking] "In the bodies of other beings there are many defects, but in my body there is not even a hair’s breadth of fault" is called pride in health (*ārogyamada*). [And so on for youth, life, power, wealth, etc. Pride that has arisen due to self-exaltation [thinking] "Other beings are inferior to me in birth, lineage, clan, learning, wisdom, and wealth, but I am superior to them" is called pride in superiority (*adhimāna*). Pride that has arisen due to self-exaltation [thinking] "I am equal to those who are equal to me in birth, lineage, clan, learning, wisdom, and wealth" is called pride in equality (*samānādhimāna*). Pride that has arisen due to self-exaltation [thinking] "I am superior to those who are inferior to me in birth, lineage, clan, learning, wisdom, and wealth" is called pride in inferiority (*ūnamāna*). Pride that has arisen due to self-exaltation [thinking] "I have attained what I have not yet attained, I have mastered what I have not yet mastered, I have realized what I have not yet realized" is called pride of overestimation (*abhimāna*). Pride that has arisen due to self-exaltation [thinking] "I am the teacher, I am the leader, I am the chief, I am the best, I am the most excellent, I am the highest, I am the foremost, I am the pre-eminent, I am the unequalled, I am the peerless, I am the matchless, I am the incomparable, I am the unsurpassed, I am the supreme, I am the ultimate, I am the best of all" is called pride of conceit (*mānātimāna*). The conceit that has arisen is called the conceit of fullness (pāripūrimada).
Having thus explained conceit with its basis by this much, he now says "What is pride? and so forth, in order to show the conceit produced without a basis. That is self-evident in meaning.
In the description of negligence (pamāda), "relinquishment of the mind" refers to not restraining mindfulness within these aforementioned states.
The relinquishing of the mind; the meaning is the absence of mindfulness. "Non-renewal of relinquishment" means the failure to renew relinquishment;

the meaning is repeated abandonment. "Lack of earnestness in performance" refers to the lack of earnestness in performing these wholesome states such as giving, whether by way of the person's lack of diligence or the lack of care regarding the object to be given.
Constant state is *sātacca*; the absence of constant state is *asātacca*. The lack of continuous performance is *asātaccakiriyatā*.
Just as a crane goes a little way and then stops, not moving continuously, even so is a person who, having given a gift or performed an act of worship on one day, [desists].
Having heard the Dhamma or having performed the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), one performs it again only after a long time and does not carry it out continuously;

such an action of his is called "an unstable action" (anaṭṭhitakiriyatā). "A sluggish mode of living" (olīnavuttitā) refers to a state of sluggishness due to the very absence of that expansion characterized by continuous performance.
"Relinquishing zeal" (nikkhittachandatā) refers to the lack of zeal and energy for wholesome action.
"Abandonment of the burden" (*nikkhittabhāva*) means the laying down of the yoke of energy (*vīriyadhura*); the sense is a shrinking back of the mind.

"Lack of resolve" (*anadhiṭṭhāna*) is the state of not being established in the performance of what is wholesome. "Lack of application" (*ananuyoga*) is non-exertion. "Negligence" (*pamāda*) is heedlessness.
The phrase "whatever negligence is of such a kind" is used because there is no limit to the synonyms for the meaning (*attha*) and the synonyms for the expression (*byañjana*).

This is the exposition of its mode. This is what is meant: that negligence which has been shown from the beginning, and whatever other negligence of such a mode and such a nature—being called "negligence" by way of the act of neglecting, and "state of having neglected" by way of the condition of having neglected—this is called negligence.
As to its characteristic, however, it has the characteristic of the loss of mindfulness regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In that very context, the mode of non-attention (*vissaṭṭhākāra*) should be understood through mindfulness.
847. In the exposition of stiffness (*thambha*): it is "stiffness" in the sense of being rigid. Here, the rigidity of the mind—like that of a stiff cloth on a clothesline—is what is described.
The state of stiffening is "stiffening" (*thambhanā*). The condition of one who has stiffened is "stiffenedness" (*thambhitatta*).
The state of a harsh person is harshness (*kakkhaḷiya*). The state of a rough person is roughness (*phārusiya*).
Uprightness of mind (*ujucittatā*) is the state of a mind established in straightforwardness by way of not performing that proper conduct (*sāmīci*), such as the absence of salutation and so forth.
The state of one who is stubborn and not pliant is inflexibility (*amudutā*). "This is called" means this is called "stiffness" (*thambho*).
A person endowed with this [defilement] is like a python that has swallowed the head of a plough, or like a bellows filled with air;
upon seeing a shrine or an elder, he is unable to bow down and moves only within his own limits.
This should be understood as having the characteristic of inflation of the mind.
848. In the exposition of *sārambha* (aggression): *sārambha* is so called by way of the act of aggression.
Aggression by way of counter-attack is *paṭisārambha*. The state of being aggressive is *sārambhanā*. Counter-attacking with aggression is *paṭisārambhanā*.
The state of one who has counter-attacked is *paṭisārambhitattaṃ*. "This is called" means this is called *sārambha*. As for its characteristic:
It is called "the characteristic of superior performance" (*karaṇuttariya-lakkhaṇa*), by which a person endowed with it performs twice, then twice again that amount.
Being a householder, when one person has prepared one dwelling site, another prepares two sites;
another four, another eight, and another sixteen. Being a homeless one (*anagārika*), when one person has taken up one *nikāya*...
Thinking, "I will not be below him," one person takes two, another three, another four, and another five.
Indeed, it is not proper to take [alms] out of a spirit of rivalry; for this is an unwholesome side, a path leading to hell.
However, from the perspective of the wholesome side, when someone gives one *salākabhatta* (ticket-meal), one should give two; when they give two, one should give four.

It is permissible to give [it]. Even for a bhikkhu, when another has already mastered one Nikāya, if he stands on the side of non-attachment and thinks, "It is comfortable for me to recite having mastered two Nikāyas," it is permissible for him to master more than that. 849.
In the exposition of contentment (*atricchata*), just as in the *Ariyavaṃsa Sutta* the phrase "the state of being base and low" is used as a synonym for "the state of being inferior," so too...
It is the lack of contentment with whatever robes and so forth one has obtained;

or, for a householder, it is the lack of contentment with whatever forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile objects one has obtained. "Desire for more" (*bhiyyokamyatā*) means the longing for distinction.
It is "desire" (*icchā*) in the sense of wishing; it is either "that which has come to desire" (*icchāgatā*), or it is the very mode of wishing. One's own gain...
Excessive desire (*aticchā*) is the state of wanting too much; *atricchatā* (excessive greed) is the same. Terms such as "lust" (*rāga*) and so forth have meanings already explained above.
"This is called" means that this is called by the name *atricchatā*. *Atricchatā* is also its name.

By way of characteristic, however, it is dissatisfaction with all one’s own gains and longing for the gains of others—this is the characteristic of excessive greed. For a person who is excessively greedy...
What one has obtained for oneself appears inferior even if it is excellent, while what another has obtained appears excellent even if it is inferior;

whether it be rice gruel, boiled rice, or bread cooked in a single vessel, that which falls into one's own bowl appears inferior, while that which falls into another's bowl appears excellent. This lack of moderation, moreover, occurs even among those who have gone forth.
[This applies] to householders as well as to animals.
In this regard, there are these instances: it is said that a certain householder, having invited thirty bhikkhunīs, gave them a meal with cakes.
The senior of the community (saṅghattherī), after having the cakes distributed into the bowls of all the bhikkhunīs, [ate] only what she herself had received afterwards.
"Go ahead and eat. The King of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "I shall eat meat roasted on coals," took his queen and entered the forest.
Upon seeing a *kinnarī*, he abandoned his queen and followed after her.

The queen turned back, went to the hermitage, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and having attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), she sat down.
Seeing the king approaching, he sprang up into the air and departed. The deity dwelling in the tree uttered this verse:
"Through excessive desire and the intoxication of greed, one thus falls away from one's welfare, just like me, Asitābhū."

"Just as he who desired the Kinnarī Candā was deprived and fell away from the princess Asitābhū, so too, through excessive greed for what is unrighteous, our wealth is diminished and we are ruined"—thus did the deity jest with the king.
Also, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a merchant’s son named Mittavindaka, who was faithless and lacked confidence;
his mother said to him, "Dear son, today, having observed the Uposatha, listen to the preaching of the Dhamma in the monastery all night long, and I will give you a thousand pieces."

Having been told this, out of greed for wealth, he undertook the precepts of the Uposatha, went to the monastery, and perceiving that "this place is free from fear," he lay down beneath the Dhamma-seat and slept the entire night; then he returned home.
Early in the morning, his mother cooked rice-gruel and offered it to him. He took a thousand pieces of money and drank the gruel. Then this thought occurred to him:
—“I shall gather wealth. He desired to set out upon the ocean by ship.
Then his mother stopped him, saying, “Dear son, there is forty million pieces of wealth in this family;
enough with going. Disregarding her words, he insisted on going. She stood before him. Then, becoming angry, he said to her, “This woman of mine…”
Thinking, "He is standing in front of me," he struck his mother with his foot; she fell down, and he passed by using her as a stepping-stone.
When the mother rose up, she said, "O son, having committed such an act toward a mother like me, will there be happiness for you in the place where you go?
As he was traveling after boarding a ship, on the seventh day, the ship...
He stood there. Then those people said, "Surely there is a wicked man here; give out the voting sticks!
As the sticks were being distributed, they fell to him alone three times. They gave him a raft and cast him into the ocean.
He went to an island and was enjoying prosperity together with *vimāna*-petīs, when they told him, "Do not go further ahead."
Although he was being told this, seeing a prosperity twice as great as that, he eventually saw a man bearing a razor-wheel.
To him, that wheel appeared like a lotus flower. He said to him, "Sir, give me this lotus you are wearing.
"This, sir, is not a lotus; it is a razor-wheel," he replied.
Saying, "So you have deceived me! Have you never seen a lotus before? he replied, "Indeed, having smeared yourself with red sandalwood, you do not wish to give me a lotus flower as an ornament.
He thought, "This man too has performed an action similar to what I did, and now wishes to experience its fruit. Then he said to him, "Come now!"
Having said this, he placed a wheel upon his head and fled. Knowing the significance of this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“From four he reached eight, from eight sixteen;
from sixteen thirty-two—thus the wheel of desire, having approached, struck him who was beyond all measure.”
“The wheel turns upon the head of the man who is driven by desire.
Now, another minister, being devoid of desire, overstepped his own territory and entered the territory of another.
There, having been beaten, he fled and entered the dwelling place of a certain ascetic; having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha, he lay down there.
Thus, when questioned by the ascetic, "What have you done?", he recited these verses:
"Utterly despising my own home,
through excessive greed I went to the village of Mallaputta."
Then people, having come out from the village,
beat me with clubs. With my head split open and my limbs smeared with blood, I lay there.
I have returned to my own abode;
therefore, I observe the Uposatha.
Out of lack of desire, may you not come here again.
850. In the exposition of *mahicchatā* (great desire): one who desires great things, or whose desire for them is great, is "one of great desire" (*mahiccha*);

the state of being such is *mahicchatā*. As for its characteristic: it is the seeking after the esteem of qualities one does not possess, and a lack of moderation in both receiving and using [possessions].
This is the characteristic of *mahicchatā*. For a person of great desire is like a merchant with a tortoise-shell box.
Just as a woman, taking ornaments with her hand and placing those suitable for the lap into it,
directs them to the public while they look on, saying, "Mother, take this one;
take that one," even so does he [the monk] direct his own meager virtue, learning, ascetic qualities, or even merely his dwelling in the forest.
He desires to be esteemed even by the great multitude; and having been so esteemed, he accepts the requisites brought even by carts, without saying, "Enough.
For three things cannot be filled: a fire by fuel, the ocean by water, and one of great desire by requisites.
The mass of fire, the ocean, and the person of great desire—
even when given many requisites, these three cannot be satisfied.
For a person of great desire is unable to satisfy even the mind of his own mother who gave birth to him, let alone his attendants.
In this regard, there are these instances: It is said that a certain young bhikkhu was fond of flour-cakes.
His mother, wishing to test his conduct, thought, "If my son knows moderation in receiving gifts, I shall provide him with nothing but cakes for the entire three-month rains retreat.
On the day of the entry into the rains residence, while testing him, she first gave him one cake.
When that was finished, he ate a second; when that too was finished, he ate a third. The youth did not say, "Enough," but simply continued eating.

His mother, realizing his lack of moderation, thought, "Today my son has eaten all the cakes for the entire three-month period," and from the following day onward, she gave him not even a single cake.
Tissamahārāja, while giving daily alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at Cetiyapabbata, was addressed by the people of the realm:
“Great King, why do you resort to this one place alone? Is it not fitting to give elsewhere?
On the following day, he caused a great almsgiving to be given in Anurādhapura. Not even a single bhikkhu knew moderation in receiving. Each and every one—
Two or three people threw away the hard and soft food they had received. On the following day, the king invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to Cetiyapabbata;
when they had arrived at the royal palace, he said, "Give me your bowls. Not a single bhikkhu gave him a bowl, saying, "Enough, Great King;
one shall receive almsfood according to one's own measure. Thus, everyone took only what was appropriate for their portion.
They accepted [the food]. Then the king said: "See, among your monks not even one knows moderation.
Yesterday there was nothing left over; today what was taken was meager, yet what remains is abundant.
He was pleased with their moderation, but displeased with the lack of moderation of the others.
851. In the exposition of *pāpicchatā* (evil desire), regarding such passages as "Being faithless, may people know me to be faithful," what does one who desires thus do?
Being faithless, he displays the appearance of faith; those who are immoral and so forth display the appearance of being virtuous and so on.
How? First, when people come to the monastery on a great festival day, the faithless person sweeps the grounds with a broom.

Taking [the broom], he sweeps the monastery and discards the refuse; perceiving that he has been seen by people, he goes to the shrine courtyard (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*), where too he sweeps and discards the refuse, levels the sand, washes the seats, and sprinkles water at the Bodhi tree.
Seeing this, people think, "There is surely no other monk who tends to the monastery."
Thinking, "This very venerable elder, who is faithful, looks after this monastery," they would invite him at the time of departure and then leave.
Even an immoral monk, in the presence of his supporters, would approach a master of the Vinaya and ask:
"Venerable sir, while I was departing, my ox became agitated; as it ran, it trampled the grass. While I was sweeping, the grass was cut [by the hooves]."
"While I am walking back and forth, small creatures die. When I spit without mindfulness, it falls upon the tips of the grass;
what happens there? "There is no offense, friend, if it was unintentional, done without mindfulness, and unknown," he was told.
But he said, "Venerable sir, it appears to me as if it were a grave matter; please investigate thoroughly. Hearing this, the people [said], "To us..."
"The noble one is scrupulous even about such a small thing! What would he do regarding something more serious?
There is no one with virtue like him"—thinking thus, those who have faith pay him honor. Even one of little learning, sitting in the midst of his attendants, says:
"Such-and-such a person is a master of the Three Piṭakas; such-and-such a person is a master of the Four Nikāyas; they have learned the Dhamma from me."
People, being impressed, thought, “There is no one so learned as our noble master;
it is said that such-and-such and such-and-such have learned the Dhamma in his presence,” and they paid him honor.
Being fond of company, on great festival days he would have a long bench and a backrest brought out at the edge of the monastery.
He sat at the foot of a tree for his midday rest. People came and asked, "Where is the Elder?
They replied, "The Gaṇṭhikaputtas are indeed like knots; therefore, at such a time as this, the Elder does not sit here.
He dwells at the edge of the monastery in a daytime station on a long walking path. Having spent a portion of the day there, he [placed his hand] upon his forehead...
Having fastened the monkey-sutras and taken hold of the bench, he would come and sit at the door of the courtyard.
People would say, "Venerable sir, where have you been? We did not see you when we returned. He would reply, "Lay followers, the interior of the monastery is crowded;
this is a place for young novices to wander about. We sat in the daytime resting-place on the sixty-cubit walkway."
He makes known his own state of seclusion.
Even a lazy man, sitting in the midst of attendants, says: "Lay followers, did you see the falling of a meteor?
When asked, "We did not see it, Venerable Sir; at what time did it happen?", he replies, "At the time when we were walking to and fro."
He asks, "Did you hear the sound of the earthquake? "We did not hear it, Bhante," they reply.
When asked, "At what time?", he says, "In the middle watch of the night, while we were standing without leaning against our wooden supports.
He then asks, "Was there a great radiance? Did you see it? When they ask, "At what time, Bhante?", he replies, "At the moment I was descending from my walking meditation path."
He speaks thus. People, being inspired with faith, thinking, "Our elder remains walking the meditation path throughout all three watches of the night;
there is no one so diligent in energy as this noble one," pay him honor.
Even when sitting in the midst of his attendants, though he may be forgetful, he thinks, "At such-and-such a time, I mastered the Dīghanikāya."
"At such-and-such a time he was a Majjhima, at another a Saṃyutta, and at another an Aṅguttara;

there is no looking around in between, for wherever he wishes to speak, the tradition comes forth as if it had already mounted his lips. But these other bhikkhus live like goats, twitching their mouths.
People, being inspired by the thought, "There is no one with mindfulness established like that of this noble one," paid him honor.
Even when not in a state of meditative absorption, he would ask questions of the commentator in the presence of his supporters:
“How does one develop the kasiṇa? To what extent is the sign said to have arisen? To what extent is access concentration reached?
To what extent is absorption reached? How many factors are there in the first jhāna? In the second, the third, and the fourth jhāna?”
“How many factors [are there]? he asked. When they had spoken according to what each had learned, he smiled and said, “Why, friends, is it not so for you?
When they replied, “It is permissible, venerable sir,” he indicated that he himself possessed the attainment.
People, believing that “this noble one has attained meditative absorption,” were inspired with faith and offered him honor.
Even one of little wisdom, sitting in the midst of his attendants, might say such things as:
"As I was looking over the Pañcattaya in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Path came to me with its own power. Indeed, the study of the scriptures is not difficult for us;
yet, being preoccupied with study, one is not released from suffering," and so forth, thereby proclaiming his own great wisdom.
He illuminates [the truth]. But by speaking thus, he strikes a blow at the Dispensation. There is no such great thief as this one;

for one who merely upholds the scriptures is not liberated from suffering. Even though his taints were not yet exhausted, when he saw some village children, he asked, "What do your parents say about us?
They replied, "Venerable sir, they say you are an Arahant. He remarked, "How clever those householders are!"
Thinking, "It is not possible to deceive [them]," he demonstrates his own state of being one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
Furthermore, others here should be understood as the "jar-Arahant," the "branch-Arahant," and so forth.
It is said that a certain deceiver, having buried a jar inside a chamber, would enter it at the time when people were arriving. When people asked, "Where is the Elder? [he would remain hidden].
When it was said, “In the inner chamber,” they entered and searched; not seeing him, they came out and said, “The Elder is not there.
When it was said, “The Elder is right in the inner chamber,” they entered again. Then the Elder, having emerged from the jar, was seated upon a bench.
Thereupon they asked, “Venerable sir, we previously went out without seeing you; where were you?”
When it was said, “We have gone,” he revealed his own state of having destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) by saying, “Monks indeed go wherever they wish.
Furthermore, another rogue lived in a leaf-hut on a mountain; and behind that leaf-hut, in a place where there was a precipice—
