There was a single *kacchaka* tree. Its branch extended forward and took root in the ground at the far end.
When people came along the road and invited him [to a meal], he took his bowl and robes, descended by means of the branch, and showed himself at the village gate.
Then, when people followed after him and asked, "By which path did you come, venerable sir? he replied:
By saying, “It is not proper to ask the path by which the ascetics have come; they come by whichever way they please,” he reveals his state as one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

However, a certain man with pierced ears, having recognized that [the ascetic] was a deceiver, thought, “I shall catch him,” and one day, seeing him descending by means of a side-branch, he cut it off from behind and left him stranded with only a small portion remaining.
Thinking, "I will descend from this branch," he jumped down with the sound "Tha! and his clay bowl broke.
Thinking, "I have been discovered," he went out and fled. The state of having evil desires is *pāpicchatā*.

By way of its characteristic, however, it should be understood as the concealing of non-existent qualities and a lack of moderation in receiving [offerings]; this is the characteristic of *pāpicchatā*.
852. In the explanation of *siṅga*: it is *siṅga* in the sense of piercing; this is the name for the "horn" of defilement, which is reckoned as urbanity (*nāgarikabhāva*).
*Siṅgārabhāva* is the state of being graceful (*siṅgāratā*), or the manner of performing gracefulness. *Caturabhāva* is cleverness (*caturatā*); likewise, *cāturiya*.
*Parikkhatabhāva* is the state of being polished (*parikkhatatā*); this refers to a state of firm gracefulness established by having been thoroughly honed.
This is the name; the other [terms] are synonyms for it. Thus, by all these words, the state of being a "lustful deer" (kilesasiṅgāratā) alone is described.

In the exposition of *tintiṇa*: *tintiṇa* means "wasting away. The mode of wasting away is *tintiṇāyanā*. The state of one who has wasted away through such wasting, that is, of one possessed of *tintiṇa*, is *tintiṇāyitatta*.
The state of greediness is *loluppa*. The other two are expositions of its modes and its nature.

“Seeking after” (pucchañjikatā) means the piercing and trembling in the place where gain is obtained, as well as a lowly way of living. “Desiring excellence” (sādhukamyatā) means yearning for things that are increasingly refined.

Thus, by all these terms, the manner of disparaging through the influence of defilements—like a dog drinking sour gruel from a dog trough who, upon seeing another dog, growls “This belongs to you! This belongs to me!”—is described.
854. Regarding the explanation of restlessness (*cāpalya*): the decoration of robes by means of beating them, smoothing them out, and so forth, is "decoration of robes" (*cīvaramaṇḍanā*).
The decoration of the alms-bowl by means of giving it a jewel-like color, polishing its surface, and so forth, is "decoration of the bowl" (*pattamaṇḍanā*).
The decoration of one's private lodging by means of murals and the like is "decoration of the lodging" (*senāsanamaṇḍanā*). "Of this putrid body" refers to this human corpse. For just as...

Just as even a newly born jackal is reckoned as nothing other than an old jackal, and even a climbing creeper, though it grows, is reckoned as nothing other than a rotten creeper, so too this human body, though it has the color of gold, is called nothing other than a putrid body.
The adornment of it by the virtuous with garments, coverings, and the like—of various colors such as red and pale—is merely for its sake. Or rather, [it is for the sake] of outsiders...
"Requisites" (*parikkhārānaṃ*) means: with the exception of the bowl and robes, it refers to the remaining requisites.

Alternatively, that which is called "adornment of the robe" or "adornment of the bowl" is either the adornment of the body by means of those requisites, or it is "adornment" in the sense of setting them down after having adorned [the body] with those external requisites;
thus should the meaning here be understood. Regarding the phrase "adornment and embellishment" (*maṇḍanā vibhūsana*): here...
Adornment (*maṇḍanā*) should be understood as the act of filling out what is deficient; beautification (*vibhūsana*) as the application of skin-coloring and the like.
Play (*keḷanā*) means sporting. Sporting about (*parikeḷanā*) means playing around. Greediness (*giddhikatā*) is the state of being possessed by greed;
"greediness" (*giddhikatta*) is a synonym for that same state. Fickleness is restlessness (*capalatā*); likewise, it is called flightiness (*cāpalya*). This is what is called "flightiness."
It is said that a person endowed with this, even if they are a hundred years old, becomes like a child born on that very day.
855. In the exposition of dissimilar conduct (*asabhāgavutti*), "grasping in opposition" means grasping what is contrary [to the Dhamma].
"Constant contrariness" means taking pleasure in acting in a way that is hostile and opposed. "The state of non-regard" is disrespect (*anādariya*); likewise is "the quality of disrespect."
The state of being without respect is *agāravatā*. The failure to perform the duty of a senior is *appatissavatā*.
"This is called" means this is called *asabhāgavutti*; the meaning is "a dissimilar way of life.
Endowed with which, a person does not even look back at a mother or father who is ill, nor [act] for the sake of what belongs to the father because of the mother.
Together with [her husband], she quarrels with her father for the sake of what belongs to her mother;
she leads a life contrary to her nature, quarreling with her elder or younger brother for the sake of what belongs to her parents,
speaking shameless words, and failing to perform the duties and services toward her teacher or preceptor.
He does not attend to the sick; he voids excrement or urine at a place where there is a shrine of the Buddha, the Blessed One;
he spits or discharges mucus there; he carries an umbrella; he goes about wearing sandals;

he feels no shame before the disciples of the Buddha; he shows no respect toward the Saṅgha; and he fails to show reverence toward those who occupy positions of honor, such as maternal uncles, paternal uncles, and so forth.

He does not establish moral shame and moral dread. As he proceeds in this way, all these activities—even toward objects such as his mother—are what is called "conduct that is discordant with the nature of things.

856. In the description of discontent (*arati*), "in remote places" means in distant or secluded locations; "in superior wholesome states" means in the phenomena of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

*Arati*: the negation of delight (*rati*). *Aratitā*: the state of not finding pleasure. *Anabhirati*: the condition of being without delight. *Anabhiramaṇā*: the mode of not finding delight. *Ukkaṇṭhitā*:
the mode of longing or yearning. *Paritassitā*: agitation resulting from that very state of longing. 857. In the description of *tandi* (lassitude):
*Tandi* is natural indolence. *Tandiyanā* is the mode of being indolent. *Tandimanakatā*... [is the state of having become indolent].
Languor (*tandi*) is the state of the mind being overcome. The state of being lazy is laziness (*ālasya*). The mode of proceeding toward laziness is the tendency toward laziness (*ālasyāyanā*).
The state of one who has become lazy is sluggishness (*ālasyāyitatta*). Thus, by all these terms, physical lethargy due to the defilements is described.
In the exposition of yawning (*vijambhitā*): *jambhanā* means quivering. Repeated yawning is *vijambhanā*. *Ānamanā* means bending.
*Bowing forward* is bending toward the front. *Bowing back* is bending toward the rear. *Bowing down* is bending all around.
*Bowing up* is the raising of the body upward, just as a weaver, having risen from his loom, grasps something and straightens his body;
it is the erecting of the body. *Afflicted by disease* means being possessed of arisen illness. Thus, by all these terms—
By way of defilement, only the shaking of the body is spoken of.
859. In the description of "drowsiness after eating": *bhuttāvissa* means "of one who has eaten. *Bhattamucchā* is a languor caused by food;
for through heavy food, one becomes as if fallen into a swoon. *Bhattakilamatha* is the state of being exhausted by food.
“Feverishness regarding food” (*bhattapariḷāha*) means distress caused by food. For at that time, one’s faculties are impaired by the arising of feverishness, and the body decays.
“Bodily rigidity” (*kāyaduṭṭhulla*) is the lack of serviceability of the body due to food.

860. The description of mental sluggishness (*cetaso līnatta*) has already been explained in the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. It should be understood that by all these terms, the state of illness of the mind through the influence of the defilements (*kilesa*) is described.
861. In the exposition of hypocrisy (*kuhanā*): "Of one dependent upon gain, honor, and fame" means of one who relies upon gain, honor, and reputation;

the sense is "of one who yearns for them. "Of one with evil desires" means of one who wishes to display non-existent virtues. "Of one overcome by desire" means of one who is afflicted by desire; the sense is "of one who is oppressed by it."
From here on, since three bases for hypocrisy (*kuhanavatthu*) have been taught in the *Mahāniddesa* by way of the use of requisites,
hinting, and dependence on postures, the following passage beginning with "or by [the use of] what is called the use of requisites" is commenced in order to show all three of them.
In that context, when one who is invited with robes and so forth— and who actually has need of them— [acts out of] evil desire...

By means of declining [the offerings] out of dependence [on the Dhamma], and having recognized that those householders were firmly established in faith toward him, he [acted] solely out of a desire to favor them when they, employing various means, presented him with excellent robes and other requisites, thinking: "Oh, how modest this noble one is! He does not wish to accept anything at all; it would indeed be a great gain for us if he would accept even a small thing."

By making it known through acceptance, from that time forward, the act of deceiving which serves as the cause for the presentation of eighty cartloads [of requisites] should be understood as the basis for hypocrisy termed "the utilization of requisites. And this has been said in the *Mahāniddesa*:
"What is the basis for hypocrisy termed the utilization of requisites? Here, householders invite a bhikkhu..."
[He provides] robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Yet, being of evil desires, overcome by longing,
and seeking more of these requisites— robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— he, out of a desire for further gain,
renounces his robe, renounces his almsfood, renounces his lodging, and renounces his medicinal requisites for the sick.
Thus he spoke: "What is the use of an expensive robe for a recluse?
It is fitting that a recluse should gather rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shopkeeper's shop, and having made them into a patched cloak, wear it.
What is the use of expensive almsfood for a recluse? It is fitting that a recluse should maintain his life by the practice of gleaning, by the scraps of food collected in his bowl."
He would think: "What is the use of a costly dwelling for a recluse?

It is fitting that a recluse should be a tree-root dweller, a charnel-ground dweller, or an open-air dweller. What is the use of costly medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness for a recluse?
It is fitting that a recluse should prepare medicine from fermented urine or a fragment of myrobalan. Taking that as his basis...
He wears coarse robes, eats coarse almsfood, uses a coarse lodging, and uses coarse medicinal requisites for the sick. Householders know of him thus:
“This ascetic is of few desires, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, and a proponent of the ascetic practices.”
They invite him again and again with robes... [and so on] ...with requisites. He says this:
"When three things are present, a faithful clansman produces much merit: when faith is present, a faithful clansman produces much merit;
when the gift is present... [and so on] ...when those worthy of offerings are present, a faithful clansman [produces much merit]."
"One generates much merit. You have faith, the object to be given exists, and I am the recipient.
If I do not accept it, you will be excluded from the merit;
this is of no use to me, yet I accept it out of compassion for you alone. From that time on...
He accepts much robe-cloth, much almsfood... [and so on] ...he accepts medicinal requisites.
Whatever such grimacing, grimacery, hypocrisy, scheming, and state of being hypocritical—this is called the ground for hypocrisy known as the "use of requisites.
Furthermore, it is the deceiving of others by one who is of evil desire through speech that indicates the attainment of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) in various ways.
This should be understood as the ground for hypocrisy known as "hinting" (*sāmantajappana*). As it is said: "What is the ground for hypocrisy known as hinting?
Here, someone with evil desires, driven by longing and aiming for esteem, thinking 'In this way people will hold me in high regard,' utters speech based on the noble Dhamma:
'The ascetic who wears such a robe is one of great influence.'"
He says: "Whoever carries such an alms-bowl, an iron dish, a water-pot, a water-strainer, a key, sandals, a waist-band, or a shoulder-pack—that ascetic is one of great influence. He says:
"He who has such a person as his preceptor, teacher, co-resident pupil, fellow-student, friend, or close associate..."
He is a companion who dwells in such dwellings— whether in a detached house, a palace, a turret, a cave, a grotto, a hut,
a peaked-roofed house, a watchtower, a multi-storied building, a barn, a loft, a shed, a pavilion, a hall, or at the foot of a tree— and he says,
"That ascetic is one of great influence."

“Or else, being excessively fickle, prone to frowning, deceitful, crafty, talkative, and seeking to win over others by his appearance, he delivers such a discourse—deep, hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane, and connected with emptiness—thinking: ‘This ascetic is one who has attained these kinds of peaceful meditative absorptions. Such as this...”
“Frowning, frown-making, scheming, schemingness, schemedness—this is called the ground for scheming known as hinting.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the ground for scheming based on deportment is the deception practiced by one who is of evil desires through a mode of conduct intended to inspire confidence.
As it is said: “What is the ground for scheming known as deportment? Here, someone…”
One who has evil desires, being overcome by desire and intent on gaining reputation, thinks, "In this way people will esteem me," and thus he composes his gait, composes his posture while lying down;
he goes with deliberation, stands with deliberation, sits with deliberation, and lies down with deliberation;
he walks as if concentrated, stands as if concentrated, sits, and lies down.

He maintains [this], becoming like one who meditates on the threshold. Whatever such posing, fixing, adjusting, grimacing, grimacery, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of scheming of the postures there is—this is called the ground for scheming known as the postures.
In that context, “by what is reckoned as the utilization of requisites” means by the utilization of requisites reckoned in this way.
“By whispering nearby” means by speaking in close proximity. “Of the posture” means of the four postures.
“Arranging” means initial placing, or placing with care. “Placing” is the manner of placing. “Adjusting” means the act of composing;
what is meant is the making of oneself attractive. “Frowning” means by showing the state of having the face drawn up at the front.
"Bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ" means the contraction of the face. One whose nature is to frown is "bhākuṭiko";
the state of being such a person is "bhākuṭiyaṃ. "Kuhanā" is the act of deceiving; the practice of deceiving is "kuhāyanā"; the state of one who has deceived is "kuhitattaṃ.
In the exposition of "lapana," "ālapanā" refers to seeing people who have come to the monastery and saying, "For what purpose, sirs, have you come?"
"Shall I invite the bhikkhus? If so, you go; I shall follow behind, taking the bhikkhus with me"—this is "addressing" (*ālapanā*) as initial conversation.
Alternatively, presenting oneself by saying, "I am Tissa;

the king is well-disposed toward me, and such-and-such and such-and-such royal ministers are well-disposed toward me"—this is "addressing" (*ālapanā*) as self-presentation. "Addressing" (*lapanā*)... [is defined as above].
*Puṭṭhassa* (when asked): speaking in the manner already described while being questioned. *Sallapanā*:

speaking well after giving an opening to one who is afraid of causing displeasure to householders. *Ullapanā*: speaking by exalting [the person], saying, “He is a great householder, a great ship-owner, a great lord of almsgiving.
*Samullapanā*: speaking by exalting [the person] from every side. *Unnahanā*: [enticing].
"Upāsakas, you gave alms at such times in the past; why do you not give now?
Thus, until they say, "Venerable sir, we shall give, but we find no opportunity," and so forth, it is called "binding from above" or "wrapping.
Alternatively, seeing someone with sugarcane in their hand, he asks, "Where have you come from, upāsakas? "From the sugarcane field, venerable sir."
‘Is that sugarcane there sweet? ‘It must be known, Bhante, after eating it. ‘Upāsaka, it is not proper for a bhikkhu to say, “Give me sugarcane.
Such talk as this, which is a form of enticement even when one is trying to avoid it, is *unnahanā*.
*Samunnahanā* is enticement again and again from every side. *Ukkācanā* is [the urging]: ‘This family...’
"He knows me alone; if any gift arises here, he gives it to me alone"—this is "raising up" (*ukkhipana*), which is to say "hinting" (*ukkācana*).
It is a form of instigation (*uddīpanā*).
Herein, the story of the oil-seller (*telakandari*) should be told: two monks, it seems, entered a certain village and [sat] in the rest-house...
Having sat down, they saw a young girl and called her over. When she had come, one among them asked another:
"Venerable sir, whose daughter is this girl? "This is the daughter of our supporter, Telakandarikā, friend.
When her mother gives me ghee while I am at home, she gives it with a whole jar; this girl also gives it with a whole jar, just like her mother," he said, laughing.

*Samukkācanā* is repeated praising from every side. *Anuppiyabhāṇitā* is merely the repeated speaking of what is pleasing, without regard for whether it accords with truth or accords with the Dhamma. *Cāṭukamyatā* is the state of living in servility;
behaving by placing oneself in a subordinate position. *Muggasūpyatā* is the state of being like bean soup. Just as in the case of beans...

Just as when some among those being cooked do not cook while the rest do cook, so too, that person whose speech contains only a small amount of truth while the remainder is false is called a "bean-soup man" (*muggasūpī*). His state is "bean-soup-ness" (*muggasūpyatā*).
"Fawning" (*pāribhaṭyatā*) is the state of being a fawner. For one who, like a nurse toward a noble child, carries [him] on the hip or on the shoulder...
"Paribhaṭati" means he carries [the bowl] around; the meaning is that he maintains it. The action of such a person who carries [it] around is "pāribhaṭayaṃ";
the state of being such a carrier is "pāribhaṭayatā.
In the description of "nemittikatā" (hinting), "nimitta" refers to any bodily or verbal action that incites others to give requisites. "Nimittakamma" is the skill in making such hints.
The story here is as follows: A certain alms-collector went to the door of a smith who was his supporter.
When asked, "What is it, venerable sir? he extended his hand through the folds of his robe and made a gesture as if striking with an axe.
The smith said, "I have understood, venerable sir," and having fashioned an axe, he gave it to him. "An occasion" refers to a discourse connected with the four requisites.
Regarding "the work of illumination": having seen some cowherds, he asked, "Are these calves milk-calves or curd-calves?
When they replied, "They are milk-calves, venerable sir," he said, "They are not milk-calves; if they were milk-calves, the monks too would receive milk.
Having informed the children's parents in this manner and other such ways, he [set them on the path].
The giving of milk-rice and so forth constitutes the making of a manifestation. "Whispering nearby" (*sāmantajappā*) means speaking while remaining close at hand.
In this regard, the story of the Jātaka-reciter should be told.

It is said that a certain elder who was a reciter of the Jātakas, desiring to eat, entered the house of his supporter and sat down. She, being unwilling to give, while saying "there is no rice," [took] the rice...

Desiring to fetch [provisions], she went to the house of a neighbor. The bhikkhu entered the inner room and, looking about, saw sugarcane in the corner by the door, sugar in a vessel, salted fish-scales in a basket, rice in a jar, and ghee in a pot;
having seen these, he came out and sat down. When the mistress of the house arrived, thinking, "I have not obtained any rice," the Elder said, "Laywoman, today there is almsfood..."
"I saw a sign beforehand that it would not succeed," he said. "What was it, venerable sir?
"I saw a snake like a stalk of sugarcane placed in the corner of a door-panel; looking at it with the thought, 'I shall strike it,' I saw a stone like a lump of sugar placed in a vessel;
and [the mark] made by the struck snake was like a salt-fish scale placed in a basket."
The hood; his teeth, which were like rice in a cooking pot, as he desired to bite that clod of earth;

and then, when he was enraged, the saliva mixed with poison issuing from his mouth, resembling ghee placed in a jar—thinking, "I cannot deceive this shaveling," she gave him sugarcane, cooked rice, along with ghee, molasses, and fish.
"‘I am not a slave-girl’—thus, inciting by drawing near should be understood as *sāmantajappā* (indirect incitement).
*Parikathā* (circumlocution) is speaking by repeatedly turning the matter around so that one obtains what is desired. 864.

In the description of *nippesikatā* (depreciation), *akkosanā* (reviling) is reviling by means of the ten grounds for reviling. *Vambhanā* (contempt) is [speaking] after having treated [the person] with contempt."
“Speaking” (*kathana*) means this. “Reproaching” (*garahana*) is the attribution of faults in such a manner as, “He is faithless, he has no confidence,” and so forth.

“Excluding” (*ukkhepanā*) is the act of excluding someone by speech, saying, “Do not speak of this person here. “Complete exclusion” (*samukkhepanā*) is excluding someone after making the case all-encompassing, providing it with its basis and its reason.
Alternatively, “exclusion” (*ukkhepanā*) is the act of excluding someone who is not giving by saying, “Oh, what a generous patron!”
‘A great lord of alms-givers’—this is a thorough disparagement, a complete disparagement. ‘Casting out’ means mocking by saying, “What is the life of this one who eats only seeds?

‘Throwing together’ means mocking even more thoroughly by saying, “Why do you call him a non-giver when he constantly says, ‘I have nothing for anyone’? ‘Bringing low’ refers to the state of being a non-giver.
Or the proclaiming of dispraise. Proclaiming in every way is thorough proclaiming.
"A carrier of dispraise" means carrying dispraise from house to house, village to village, and district to district, thinking, "In this way, out of fear of dispraise, he will give [to me].

"One who eats the flesh off the back of others" means speaking dispraise behind someone's back after having spoken sweet words to their face; for this is [the conduct] of one who is unable to look one in the face.
It is like eating the flesh on the back of those who are face-to-face; therefore, it is called "backbiting" (*parapiṭṭhimamsikatā*).
This is called "denigration" (*nippesikatā*) because, like a bamboo scraper, it scrapes away or wipes off another's virtue as one would scrape off ointment;
or because, like the pursuit of fragrance by grinding fragrant substances, it grinds away the virtues of others.
Having crushed [the truth], this is the way of seeking gain; therefore, it is called "hinting" (*niṣpeṣikatā*). 865.
In the exposition on "seeking gain by means of gain," "seeking" (*nijigīsanatā*) means searching.

"Obtained from here" means obtained from this house. "There" means in that particular house. "Desiring" (*eṭṭhī*) means longing for. "Seeking" (*gaveṭṭhī*) means searching. "Searching thoroughly" (*pariyeṭṭhī*) means...

"Seeking again and again": having given whatever alms-food was obtained from one place to the children of various families, and finally receiving milk-rice, the story of the monk who had gone there should be told here.
"Esaṇā" and so forth are synonyms for "eṭṭhi" and so forth; therefore, "eṭṭhi" means seeking (*esanā*), "gaveṭṭhi" means searching (*gavesanā*), and "pariyeṭṭhi" means...
This is how the construction should be understood here.
In the exposition of "being held in high esteem": "by birth" means by the excellence of birth such as being a khattiya; "by clan" means by a distinguished clan such as the Gotama clan;
"by family lineage" means by the status of a great family; "by beauty of complexion" means by the possession of a body endowed with beauty.

For the body is called "the lotus" (*pokkhara*); the meaning is that it is so called because of its excellence of color and its beautiful form. The phrases beginning with "by wealth" have meanings that are already evident.
"He arouses conceit" means that by means of any one of these bases, he brings about or exercises the conceit, "I am superior.

(867) In the exposition of conceit toward equals, "he arouses conceit" means that by means of any one of these bases, he brings about the conceit, "I am equal. This is the difference here in terms of meaning; however, there is no difference in the actual text (*pāḷi*).

868. In the exposition of inferiority (*hīnamāna*): "He indulges in self-depreciation" means he brings about a lowly sense of inferiority. "Self-depreciation" (*omāna*) refers to a base, lowly sense of inferiority.

"Self-depreciation" (*omaññanā*) and "the state of being self-depreciated" (*omaññitatta*) are expositions of its mode and its nature. "Contempt" (*hīḷanā*) is the loathing of oneself on account of birth and so forth. "Excessive contempt" (*ohīḷanā*) is an exceeding degree of such loathing.
"The state of being excessively contemptuous" (*ohīḷitatta*) is an exposition of its nature. "Self-disparagement" (*attuññā*) is making oneself out to be inferior.

*Jānanā* means knowing. *Attāvaññā* means despising oneself. *Attaparibhava* means the conceiving that arises from disparaging oneself by thinking, "I am merely born with such [inferior] qualities as birth and so forth.
Thus, these three types of conceit (*māna*) are explained without reference to a specific person, but rather in terms of the bases such as birth and so on.
Among them, each one arises in relation to all three—those who are superior, equal, and inferior. In that regard, "I am superior" refers to...

The conceit "I am superior" is a conceit according to reality only for one who is actually superior; for others, it is a conceit not according to reality. The conceit "I am equal" is a conceit according to reality only for one who is actually equal;
for others, it is a conceit not according to reality. The conceit "I am inferior" is a conceit according to reality only for one who is actually inferior;

for others, it is a conceit not according to reality. In this context, what is the conceit of one who is superior thinking "I am superior," and so forth? These nine types of conceit are explained with reference to the person.
Among those, three arise for each one. In this context, "places" means he establishes [them].
"Depending on that" means depending on that placing [of oneself] as superior. Here, however, the conceit "I am superior to the superior" arises in both kings and renunciants.
For a king thinks, "In terms of kingdom, wealth, or vehicles, who is there equal to me? and so forth.
He conceives pride. Even one who has gone forth conceives this pride, thinking, "Who is there equal to me in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so forth?
(870) Pride such as "I am equal to one who is superior" also arises among these very people.
For a king conceives this pride, thinking, "What difference is there between me and other kings in terms of kingdom, wealth, or vehicles? Even one who has gone forth...
He conceives this conceit: "What difference is there between me and another bhikkhu in terms of virtue, ascetic practices, and so forth?
Furthermore, the conceit "I am inferior to one who is superior" arises among these very same persons.
For a king who does not possess a kingdom, wealth, or vehicles, [thinks]: "My title 'king' is merely a pleasant convention."
One conceives this conceit: "I am called a king. Even when one has gone forth, one conceives this conceit: "I have little gain and honor;
I am merely a speaker on the Dhamma, learned, and an elder"—this is mere talk. One conceives this conceit: "What am I called a speaker on the Dhamma? What am I called learned?
What am I called an elder, since I have no gain and honor?"
872. Pride such as "I am superior to my equal" arises in ministers and others. For instance, a minister or a provincial official might think:
"What other royal person is my equal in wealth, vehicles, mounts, and so forth?
or "What distinction is there between me and others? or "The title 'minister' is merely a name for me; even my mere food and clothing..."
"I have nothing. What does this man call himself—a 'minister'?"—with such thoughts he conceives these forms of pride.

(875) In one who is inferior, pride such as "I am superior" arises; it arises in those such as slaves. For a slave thinks, "Whether by birth on my mother's side or my father's side, what other slave is there who is my equal?
Others, being unable to live otherwise, become known as slaves for the sake of their mothers' wombs.

He conceives these conceits: “I am superior because I was born [into a higher lineage],” or “What difference is there between me and this slave named So-and-so, since we are both equally pure on both sides by virtue of our ancestral lineage? or “I entered into slavery through the fault of my womb;
however, in terms of the excellence of my parents, I have no status as a slave. How can I be called a slave? It is such conceits as these that he forms.
And just as a slave does, so too do the outcaste, the scavenger, and others; they indeed give rise to conceit.

In this context, the conceit that arises in one who is superior, thinking "I am superior," is conceit based on reality (*yāthāvamāna*); the other two are conceits not based on reality (*ayāthāvamāna*).
Likewise, the conceit that arises in one who is equal, thinking "I am equal," or in one who is inferior, thinking "I am inferior," is conceit based on reality.

The other two types of conceit are not according to reality (*ayāthāvamāna*). Among them, that which is according to reality is to be abandoned by the path of Arahatship; that which is not according to reality is to be abandoned by the path of Stream-entry.
Having thus explained conceit with a basis (*savatthuka*), he now states "What is conceit? and so forth, in order to show only the conceit produced without a basis (*avatthuka*).

In the exposition of excessive conceit (*atimāna*), one does not refer to a person by way of being "superior" and so on, but rather defines it solely by way of the bases such as birth and the rest. Therein, "he conceives excessively" means he conceives by overstepping [the truth], thinking, "There is no one equal to me in terms of birth and the rest."

880. In the exposition of *mānātimāna* (excessive conceit), the phrase "that which is of such a kind" refers to the conceit that has arisen in the form: "Previously I was equal to this person; now I am superior, and he is inferior.
This is stated in order to show that, like a heavy burden upon a heavy burden, it is called *mānātimāna* by taking the previous state of equality as its basis.

881. The description of self-depreciation (*omāna*) is exactly like the description of inferiority-conceit (*hīnamāna*). However, it is called “the conceit ‘I am inferior’” by way of the person to be trained (*veneyya*); this is what is known as self-depreciation. Furthermore, in this context:
“You have a birth, but your birth is like that of a crow; you have a clan, but your clan is like that of a *caṇḍāla*; you have a voice, but your voice is like that of a crow.”
"Self-depreciation" (*sāro*) should be understood as this sense of inferiority that occurs by placing oneself below others.
In the description of overestimation (*adhimāna*): "perceiving one has attained what one has not attained" means perceiving that one has attained the Four Truths when one has not yet attained them.
"Without having done" means while the task to be performed by the four paths remains undone. "Without having realized" means while the Dhamma of the Four Truths has not been realized.
"Unrealized" (*asacchikata*) means not made manifest through the attainment of Arahatship. This is called "conceit" (*adhimāna*); this is what is termed "conceit regarding what has been attained.
Now, for whom does this arise, and for whom does it not arise? First of all, it does not arise in a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).

For he, having become joyful through the reviewing of the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements, [is established] in the penetration of the noble qualities.
He is free from doubt. Therefore, conceit such as "I am a once-returner" and so forth does not arise in stream-enterers and the others;

it does not arise even in one who is immoral, for the latter has no hope at all of attaining noble qualities. Nor does it arise in one who possesses virtue but has abandoned his meditation subject and is devoted to the pleasure of sleep and the like.
But for one of pure virtue who is diligent in his meditation subject, it arises when he has defined name-and-form,
crossed over doubt by discerning conditions, applied the three characteristics, and is comprehending formations as one whose insight has been commenced.
Once it has arisen, one who has attained pure serenity or one who has attained pure insight stops it midway.

For even if one does not perceive the manifestation of defilements for ten, twenty, or thirty years, one might still conceive the thought, “I am a stream-enterer,” or “a once-returner,” or “a non-returner.
However, one who has attained serenity and insight establishes himself only in Arahantship.
For by the power of concentration his defilements are suppressed, and by the power of insight formations are thoroughly grasped.
Therefore, for sixty years, eighty years, or even a hundred years, the defilements do not manifest; his mental activity is that of one whose taints are exhausted.

Seeing no manifestation of defilements over such a long period, he does not wait in between but conceives the thought, "I am an Arahant," just like the Elder Mahānāga of Uccamālaka and the Elder Mahādatta of Haṅkanaka.
...and like the Elder Cūḷasumana, who dwelt in the Niṅkapoṇṇa meditation hall on Cittala Mountain.

Herein is an illustration of one such case: it is said that there was a certain Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, who had broken through to the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), whose taints were utterly exhausted, and who served as the instructor for a great community of monks. One day, while at his own daytime resting place—
Having sat down, he reflected, "Has our teacher, the Elder Mahānāga of Uccatālīṅka,
reached the culmination of the ascetic’s task, or not? Seeing that he was still at the stage of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), and knowing that if he did not go,
the elder would surely pass away as an ordinary person, he rose into the air by means of psychic power and approached the elder who was seated in his daytime resting place.
Having descended, paid homage, and performed the customary duties, he sat down to one side. When asked, "Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an improper time?
he replied, "Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question. Then, being told, "Ask, friend;
knowing, I shall explain," he asked ten thousand questions. The Elder [answered] each question as it was asked.
He answered the question without hesitation. Then, when asked, “Venerable sir, your knowledge is exceedingly sharp.
When did you attain this Dhamma? he replied, “Friend, sixty years ago. “Venerable sir, do you also employ meditative concentration?
“This is not difficult, friend. “In that case, venerable sir, please conjure up an elephant.”

The Elder conjured up an entirely white elephant. “Now, venerable sir, act in such a way that this elephant comes toward you with its ears pricked, its trunk extended, its tail tucked in, having thrust its trunk into its mouth and letting out a terrifying, trumpeting cry.
The Elder did so, and as the elephant approached with great speed, he displayed a terrifying form.

Seeing this, he rose and began to flee. The Elder Khīṇāsavatthera reached out his hand, caught him by the corner of his robe, and said, “Venerable sir, does one who has destroyed the taints feel timidity?
At that moment, realizing his own state as an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), he said, “Friend Dhammadinna, be my support,” and sat down on his heels at the elder’s feet. “Venerable sir...”
"I have come to be your refuge; do not worry," he said, and then taught them the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having taken up the meditation subject, the elder ascended the walking path (*caṅkama*) and, at the third step, attained the supreme fruit of *arahantship*.
It is said that the elder was of a temperament characterized by hatred (*dosacarita*).

883. In the exposition of the conceit “I am” (*asmimāna*): “conceit that ‘I am form’” (*rūpaṃ asmīti māno*) is the conceit arisen as “I am form. “Inclination” (*chando*) is simply the inclination following after conceit. The same applies to the underlying tendency (*anusaya*). This same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates as well. 884. In the exposition of wrong conceit (*micchāmāna*):
regarding the phrases “by means of a base sphere of action” (*pāpakena vā kammāyatanena*), etc., a “base sphere of action” is the work of fishermen, fish-trappers, hunters, and the like.
A “base sphere of craft” (*sippāyatana*) refers to [the work] in casting nets for fish, making traps, and so forth.
And there is skill in such things as binding with nooses and impaling on stakes. A "base branch of knowledge" (*pāpakaṃ vijjāṭṭhānaṃ*) refers to any science intended for the harming of others.
"Base learning" (*pāpakaṃ sutaṃ*) refers to that connected with the Battle of the Bhāratas, the abduction of Sītā, and so forth.

"Base eloquence" (*pāpakaṃ paṭibhānaṃ*) refers to eloquence associated with ill-spoken words, such as the fabrications of plays and lamentations. "Base virtue" (*pāpakaṃ sīlaṃ*) refers to the "vow of silence" (*ajasīla*) and the "vow of the cow" (*gosīla*).
Speech, too, consists only of what is not born and does not lead to birth. However, an evil view is any view whatsoever among the sixty-two types of speculative views.

885. Regarding the explanation of thoughts concerning relatives and so forth: a thought that arises with reference to relatives, based on a worldly affection dependent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure—such as “my relatives live happily, endowed with prosperity”—is precisely what is called a thought concerning relatives (*ñātivitakka*). [As it is said: “We have come to destruction...”
However, a reflection that occurs in the form, "Faith has gone; they are confident," is not what is called *ñātivitakka* (reflection on relatives).

When one is delighted by the thought, "Our country is well-supplied with food and rich in crops," the reflection that arises through the influence of worldly affection is called *janapadavitakka* (reflection on the country).
When one thinks, "In our country, people are faithful and confident; [their] destruction... [and so forth].
However, when it occurs as "we have gone, we have gone," it is not what is called "reflection on the country.
"Reflection for the sake of immortality" or "immortal reflection" is *amaravitakka*.

In this context, for one who performs ascetic practices such as squatting and exertion, thinking, "When suffering has been worn away by these means, the self will be happy and immortal in the future life"—it is through that [reflection]...
Thought associated with the practice of austerities is called "thought for the sake of immortality. However, when one who holds a speculative view is asked, "Do you teach eternalism?

and so forth, he resorts to evasion, saying: "It is not thus for me; it is not otherwise for me; it is not so for me; it is not not so for me. Such [thought] of his is associated with that speculative view.

Applied thought (*vitakka*). Just as a fish called "immortal" (*amara*) cannot be killed once caught in the water because it dashes hither and thither and does not come to a hold, so too, because it does not settle upon any single side, it is called "immortal" (*amara*) since it does not die.
Combining both of these [meanings] together, this is what is called "immortal applied thought" (*amaravitakka*), as it has been stated.
888. "Connected with compassion for others" means being connected with a worldly affection that merely resembles compassion.
Regarding "rejoicing together" and so forth: when his attendants rejoice or grieve, he rejoices or grieves twice as much as they do;
when they are happy, he becomes twice as happy, and when they are suffering, he becomes twice as suffering.
It occurs. Regarding "when duties and tasks have arisen": when those tasks, whether great or small, have arisen.
"Or he engages himself": while accomplishing those various duties, he transgresses the formal precepts (*paññatti*) and violates his own austerity (*sallekha*).
"Whoever therein": whoever, in that state of social intimacy or in that engagement, possesses thoughts rooted in the household life.
—this is what is called a thought associated with compassion for others.
889. “Associated with gain, honor, and renown” means being associated by way of taking as an object both the acquisition of robes and so forth, as well as honor and fame.
890. “Associated with non-contempt” means: “Oh, may others not despise me; may they not strike or harass me.”
“They would speak” refers to the thought that arises together with the aspiration for not being despised. Regarding the phrase “which there is worldly”:

this refers to the thought that arises when the mind has arisen with the thought, “May others not despise me,” while remaining dependent on the "house" consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure. The rest is clear in all respects.
Commentary on the Singlefold Exposition.
(2. Commentary on the Twofold Exposition. 891.
Among the twofold expositions, the exposition of anger and the others are to be understood according to the method already stated above. However, regarding those not mentioned above:

In the *Upanāha-niddesa* and other such texts, "resentment" (*upanāha*) is defined as follows: because it "binds on" (*upanayhati*) a subsequent anger (*kodha*) after a prior one, it is called resentment.

The act of binding on is "binding" (*upanayhanā*). The state of having been bound on is "the state of being resentful" (*upanayhitattaṃ*). "Fixing" (*aṭṭhapanā*) refers to fixing immediately after the initial arising, or fixing within a boundary.
"Placing" (*ṭhapanā*) refers to placing in its natural state. "Stabilizing" (*saṇṭhapanā*) refers to doing so repeatedly from every side.
The establishment of resentment (*āghāta-ṭṭhapanā*). "Connecting" (*anusaṃsandana*) means making [the subsequent anger] one with the first arisen anger, without showing any interval between them.
"Following along" (*anuppabandhana*) means the joining of the later [anger] with the former. "Strengthening" (*daḷhīkamma*) means making it firm.
"This is called" refers to that which has the characteristic of binding on; its function is the non-relinquishing of enmity (*vera-appaṭinissajjana-rasa*).
It is called "rancor" (*upanāha*). A person possessed of this is unable to relinquish their enmity;
thinking, "It is utterly improper for him to speak to me thus," they pursue the matter again and again. It burns like a flaming brand of putrid dung;
it does not become pure, being like a polished hide or like a rag smeared with fat and oil.

892. *Makkha* (sycophancy) is so called by way of the state of smearing. Even while proceeding to smear the virtues of others, one first smears oneself for one's own sake, just as excrement [smears] the dung-scraper;
this is the meaning. Following that, there are two descriptions of modes of manifestation.
*Niṭṭhuriyaṃ* (harshness) is the state of being harsh; the meaning is the spitting of phlegm [in contempt], thinking, "Relying on that, even this much does not exist."

“Harsh action” means the performance of harshness. For when a householder living in dependence on another householder, or a bhikkhu living in dependence on another bhikkhu, becomes angry at even a slight matter and acts with harshness—
spitting upon him as if treading on him with the foot while saying, “I have nothing at all to do with that person”— that action of his is called “harsh action.”
It is so called. From the perspective of its characteristic and so forth, this *makkha* (sycophancy) has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others;
its function is the destruction of those [virtues]; it is manifested as the concealing of deeds well-performed by others. *Paḷāsa* means to boast;
the meaning is that, having displayed the virtues of another, one makes them equal to one's own virtues. Of *paḷāsa*...
"Āyana" means "paḷāsāyana. Since it is both a "paḷāsa" (contempt) and an "āhāra" (nutriment) for one's own victory, it is called "paḷāsāhāra.
"Grounds for dispute" means the cause of dispute. "Yugaggāha" means taking up an equal burden. "Appaṭinissagga" means the non-relinquishing of what has been grasped by oneself.
As for its characteristics and so forth: this contempt has the characteristic of taking up an equal burden; its function is to make one's own qualities equal to those of others.
It has the manifestation of attending by means of the measure of others' virtues. For a person who is envious does not give way to a second;

he stands with his chest thrust out. Even when another monk has cited many suttas and reasons in the circle of discussion, he says: "What difference is there between your position and mine? Is it not the same? and so on.

He says, "Our words are exactly the same, like gold that has been broken [into pieces]. The description of envy (*issā*) and avarice (*macchariya*) has already been explained in their respective contexts.

894. In the description of deceit (*māyā*): "He speaks a word" means that, even while knowing, "The monks who transgress the designation (*paṇṇatti*) bring upon themselves heavy consequences, but for us there is no such thing as a point of transgression," he speaks as if he were peaceful. By way of the body...
"He exerts himself" means that he performs physical actions with the thought, "Let no one know that this evil deed was done by me.
It is called *māyā* because it is like an optical illusion (*cakkhumohana*) that conceals existing faults. The state of one who possesses such deceit is *māyāvitā*.

Because beings rely excessively (*aticca*) upon this for the purpose of concealing their evil once again after having committed it, it is called *accāsara*. [This occurs] through bodily and vocal actions.
It is *vañcanā* (deceit) because one deceives by seeing things otherwise. It is *nikati* (fraud) because beings act dishonestly through it; the meaning is that they act wrongly.

It is *vikiraṇā* (dissimulation) because one diverts the wicked by saying, "I do not do such a thing. It is *pariharaṇā* (concealment) because one avoids [the truth] by saying, "I do not do such a thing.
It is *gūhanā* (hiding) because of the covering up [of faults] by means of body and so forth. It is *parigūhanā* (complete concealment) because of hiding [them] in every respect.
It is called *chādanā* because one conceals evil through bodily and verbal actions, just as one covers excrement with grass and leaves. It is *paṭicchādanā* because it is a concealment on all sides.
It is *anuttānīkamma* because one does not show it by making it plain. It is *anāvikamma* because one does not show it by making it manifest.
It is *vocchādanā* because it is a thorough concealment. Because of the tendency to commit evil yet again due to having performed such concealment, [it is called *paticchādanā*].
"Evil action. This is called "deceit": this is what is meant by that which has the characteristic of concealing what has been done.
A person endowed with it is like a charcoal fire covered by ashes, like a tree stump hidden by water, or like a sword wrapped in a cloth.
In the exposition of *sāṭheyya* (deceitfulness): *saṭha* means that which is not rightly spoken because it displays non-existent qualities.
It is crooked in every respect, thoroughly crooked. "That which therein" means that which is in that person. *Saṭha* refers to the display of non-existent qualities, a form of hypocrisy (*kerāṭiya*).
*Saṭhatā* is the state of being crooked. *Kakkaratā* is a harsh and rough quality, like a lotus stalk, which cannot endure being touched.

*Kakkariyanta* is also a synonym for that same thing. By the two terms *parikkhattatā* and *pārikkhattiya*, what is stated is a firm crookedness (*daḷhakerāṭiya*) as if it were buried and established [within].

"This is called" means this is called *sāṭheyya* (deceit), which has the characteristic of proclaiming qualities that do not exist in oneself; by being possessed of which, it is impossible to know whether a person’s belly or back [is crooked].
With its left side it is a pig, with its right side a goat or antelope;
with its cry it is a jackal, and with its horns an old ox.
Thus it is like the "pig-yakṣa" (yakkhasūkara) described. The explanations of ignorance (*avijjā*) and the other [factors] have already been stated according to their meaning.

902. In the explanation of "lack of rectitude" (*anajjava*): "lack of rectitude" (*anajjava*) means the state of being non-straight. The nature of lack of rectitude is "lack of rectitude-ness" (*anajjavatā*).

"Crookedness" (*jimhatā*) is crookedness like that of the moon. "Deviousness" (*vaṅkatā*) is deviousness like that of cow's urine. "Wrinkledness" (*kuṭilatā*) is deviousness like the tip of a ploughshare.
By all these terms, only the crookedness of body, speech, and mind is described.
In the explanation of *amaddava*: non-softness is *amudutā*. The mode of being non-soft is *amaddavatā*. Hardness is *kakkhaḷiyaṃ*.
Harshness is *phārusiyaṃ*, due to the absence of affection that produces softness. The state of mind standing straight because of not living in a lowly manner is *ujucittatā*.
The repetition of the term *amudutā* is for the purpose of qualifying it as "that which is reckoned as *amudutā*."
“Rectitude of mind, not that which is called rectitude through straightforwardness. 903.
The descriptions of intolerance and so forth should be understood as being the opposites of the descriptions of patience and so forth. 908.

In the description of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), “internally” refers to the existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*); “externally” refers to the existence of form and the formless (*rūpārūpabhava*). For although...
Beings dwell for only a short time in the sensual existence (kāmabhava), namely during the fourth quarter of an eon;
during the other three quarters, the sensual existence is empty and void. They dwell for a long time in the fine-material and immaterial existences (rūpārūpabhava);
nevertheless, because their deaths and rebirth-linkings (cutipaṭisandhi) are numerous in the sensual existence and few in the fine-material and immaterial existences, [wherever...]
Where there are many deaths and rebirths, there too attachment (*ālaya*), aspiration (*patthanā*), and longing (*abhilāsa*) are many;
where they are few, there they are few. Therefore, sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is called "internal," while form and formless existences (*rūpārūpabhava*) are called "external.

Thus, the fetter that binds one to sense-sphere existence—which is reckoned as internal—is called the "internal fetter" (*ajjhattasaṃyojana*); [the fetter] regarding those things reckoned as external...
The fetters pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial realms are called the external fetters (*bahiddhā-saṃyojana*).
Each of these is fivefold. Therefore it is said: "There are five lower-fettering [fetters] and five higher-fettering [fetters]. Herein, this is the etymological explanation:
"lower" (*oraṃ*) refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*); because they produce rebirth there and thus partake of that lower realm, they are called "lower-fettering" (*orambhāgiyāni*).
"Higher" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpadhātu*). Because they lead to rebirth there, they "belong to the higher" (*uddhambhāgiyāni*).
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the dyads. (3. Commentary on the exposition of the triads.
909. In the Exposition of the Triads, the manifestation of the root of the round [of existence] is explained by means of the three unwholesome roots.

Among the unwholesome thoughts and so forth, it should be understood that "thought" (vitakka) is so called by way of the act of thinking, "perception" (saññā) by way of the act of perceiving, and "element" (dhātu) in the sense of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
In the Exposition of Misconduct, the first method is analyzed by way of the courses of action (kamma-patha), while the second is by way of all-encompassing kamma.
The third [type of craving] arises solely by way of the volition that has already been produced.
914. In the exposition of the taints (*āsava*), according to the method of the Suttas, only three taints are mentioned. 919.
In the exposition of the searches (*esanā*), it is stated briefly in the manner beginning with "Therein, what is the search for sensual pleasures? as the lust for the seeking of sensual pleasures.

The search for sensual pleasures (*kāmesanā*) is as described by the method beginning with "the desire for existence regarding states of being" (*bhavesu bhavacchanda*). The search for existence (*bhavesanā*) is the passion for seeking existence.

The search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*) should be understood as the search for the holy life that is approved by those who hold to views, as described by the method beginning with "the world is eternal.
Furthermore, it should be known that it is not only lust and views that constitute these searches.
Furthermore, the karma associated with that [craving] is itself a search; therefore, the second method is analyzed in order to demonstrate it.

In this context, "associated with that" should be understood as being associated with its concomitants (*sampayutta-ekaṭṭha*). Among these, that which is associated with sensual lust (*kāmarāga-ekaṭṭha*) occurs only among beings of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);

however, that which is associated with lust for existence (*bhavarāga-ekaṭṭha*) occurs among the Great Brahmas (*mahābrahmāṇaṃ*) when they have emerged from meditative attainment and are walking about.
At the time of relishing the factors of jhāna, there is unwholesome bodily action; at the time of relishing by breaking into speech, saying “Oh, what happiness!
Oh, what happiness!”, there is verbal action; and at the time of relishing by means of the mind alone, without moving the limbs of the body or uttering words, there is mental action.
Furthermore, for all those who hold views, these actions certainly exist through the practice of walking meditation and so forth, by way of their adherence to extreme views.
920. In the *Vidhāniddesa*, in passages such as “In what way do they call one virtuous? In what way do they call one wise?”, *vidhā* means mode or appearance (*ākārasaṇṭhāna*).

In passages such as “The bases of knowledge are of one kind,” it means a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*). In passages such as “He does not waver among the various modes (*vidhāsu*),” it means conceit (*māna*).
Here too, conceit is what is called *vidhā*. For it is so called because it “disposes” (*vidahati*) itself by way of superiority and so forth. In the sense of establishing (*ṭhapanaṭṭhena*)...
Or it is threefold. Therefore, the manifestation of conceit that has arisen as "I am better" should be understood as the establishment of conceit that manifests as "I am better.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. 921.
In the description of fear, "fear dependent on birth" means the fear that has arisen with birth as its condition. "Terrifying" means...
The description of the modes: *chambhitattaṃ* (trembling) is the shaking of the limbs due to fear. *Lomahaṃso* (horripilation) is the bristling of the body hairs, their state of being raised upward.
Having shown fear by way of its function through these two terms, it is then shown by way of its intrinsic nature as "terror of the mind" (*cetaso utrāso*).
In the description of darkness (*tama*), ignorance is spoken of under the heading of doubt: "Darkness, obscurity, delusion, the flood of ignorance."
For ignorance is called "darkness" because of the statement, "It is a great terror.
However, the teaching was presented under the heading of doubt for the sake of making the instruction easy to understand by way of the three time periods.

In that regard, one who is doubting concerning the past time, wondering, "Was I a khattiya in the past, or was I a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudra? Was I dark, fair, short, or tall?"—[this refers to the past period].
"Is doubtful" means: being doubtful, thinking, "Will I in the future be a khattiya, or a brahmin, or a vessa...
[and so on] ...or tall?", one is said to be doubtful concerning the future time.
Being doubtful, thinking, "Am I at present a khattiya, or a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda? Or am I form, or feeling, perception, mental formations... [and so on].
One who is doubtful about "consciousness" is said to doubt with reference to the present time.
In this regard, although there is no one— whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda—
who does not know their own status as a khattiya, brahmin, vessa, or sudda, yet a being who has obtained a life-continuum...
Having heard of the distinctions in color and so forth among the life-principles (*jīva*) of Kṣatriyas and others, one who is doubting—thinking, "What indeed is our internal life-principle like?
Is it blue, or yellow, red, or white? Is it four-cornered, six-cornered, or eight-cornered?"—is said to doubt in this way. 923.
*Titthāyatanāni* means bases that have become fords (*tittha*), or the bases (*āyatana*) of the sectarians (*titthiya*). In this context, a "ford" (*tittha*)...
The sixty-two views are as follows. "Heretics" (*titthiyā*) refers to those for whom these views are pleasing and acceptable.
The meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) has already been explained above. In this context, because all proponents of views, when arising, arise within these very three points;
and when converging, they converge and assemble within these very same points—regarding their status as proponents of views—
And because these very things are their causes, they are called "bases of the sects" (*titthāyatanāni*) in the sense that they have arisen as those sects (*titthāni*);
and in that same sense, they are also called "bases of the sectarian teachers" (*titthiyānaṃ āyatanāni*). A "person" (*purisa-puggala*) is a sentient being (*satta*).
Although when one says "man" (*purisa*) or "person" (*puggala*), it is indeed the sentient being that is meant, this is nevertheless a conventional discourse (*sammuti-kathā*).
"Name" refers to that which is called according to how one knows it. "Experiences" (*paṭisaṃvedeti*) means he knows what has arisen in his own continuum;
or it means he makes it experienced, or he undergoes it. "Caused by what was done previously" (*pubbekatahetu*) means due to a cause performed in the past;
the meaning is that he experiences [the result] solely through the condition of karma performed in the past. This is the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas. But for those who speak thus...
Rejecting both kamma-experienced feeling and functional feeling, they accept only resultant feeling.
Among the eight types of afflictions, such as those arising from bile, they reject seven and accept only the eighth.
And among the three types of kamma, such as that to be experienced in this very life, they reject two and accept only that to be experienced in a subsequent existence.
They accept [the four types of consciousness], yet among the four volitions classified as wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional, they accept only the resultant volition.
"By the cause of creation by a Lord" (*issaranimmānahetu*) means by the reason of creation by a Lord;
the meaning is that one experiences [feeling] because it was created by a Lord, such as Brahmā or Pajāpati. This is the doctrine of the Brahmins. For this is their intention: these three feelings...
"It is impossible to experience [suffering] in the present based on what was done by oneself, or based on the command of another, or based on what was done in the past, or without cause or condition;
rather, these are experienced solely due to the creative act of a Supreme Lord (Issara-nimmāna).
However, those who hold such a view do not accept even one of the eight types of afflictions mentioned above, but instead reject them all.
Likewise, regarding all categories such as those to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) and so forth, they reject everything without accepting even a single one.
"Without cause, without condition" means that one experiences [results] without a cause or a condition, that is, without any reason whatsoever.
This is the doctrine of the Ājīvakas. Those who speak thus likewise reject even one of the causes or diseases mentioned below.
They reject everything. 924.
"Possessions" (*kiñcana*) means obstructions (*palibodha*). Lust is a possession: when lust arises, it binds and obstructs sentient beings;
therefore, it is called a "possession. The same applies to hatred and delusion. "Defilements" (*aṅgaṇa*) refers to [the thought]: "Indeed, there is filth in the courtyard..."
In the passage where it says "they do not find," *aṅgaṇa* refers to a bare patch of ground at the place one has arrived.

In the passage where it says "he strives for the removal of that very dust or *aṅgaṇa*," it refers to any kind of dirt or mud. In the passage where it says "being full of *aṅgaṇa*," it refers to various kinds of intense defilements (*kilesa*).
Here too, that same *aṅgaṇa* consisting of defilements is intended. For this very reason, he said, "lust is *aṅgaṇa*," and so forth.

*Malāni* means things that cause defilement (*malinabhāva*). Lust (*rāga*) is a stain (*mala*): when lust arises, it makes the mind defiled and causes it to grasp at stains; therefore, it is called a stain. The same method applies to the other two as well.

In the description of "the uneven" (*visama*), it is said that lust and so forth are "the uneven" because they are the cause of stumbling and falling: for beings stumble over lust and the like, as well as over bodily misconduct and so forth, and having stumbled, they fall away from the Teaching and from a happy rebirth. Therefore, it is stated that lust is the uneven, etc.
"Fire" (*aggi*) is so called in the sense of burning (*anudahana*). "The fire of lust" (*rāgaggi*) means that when lust arises, it burns and consumes sentient beings;
therefore, it is called "fire. The same applies to hatred and delusion. In this regard, there is an instance:
it is said that a certain young bhikkhunī, having gone to the Uposatha hall at the Cittalapabbata monastery, stood looking at the form of the gatekeeper. Then, for her—
Passion arose within her. Having meditated with that very [passion], she passed away. As the bhikkhunīs were walking by, they said, "This young woman is standing there;
call her! One of them went and took her by the hand, saying, "Why are you standing? As soon as she was grasped, she turned over and fell down.
This, first of all, is the story regarding the non-consumption of passion. Now, regarding the non-consumption of hatred:
The Manopadosika devas are to be understood [in this way]. Because they do not burn away delusion, the Khiḍḍāpadosika devas are to be understood [in this way];
for through the power of delusion, their mindfulness fails them. Therefore, by means of their play, they pass the time for taking food and die.
"Astringent" (kasāva) means dregs, devoid of nutritive essence. Among lust and the other [defilements], and among bodily misconduct and the rest, there is not even one thing that is refined.
There is nothing possessing vitality; therefore, it is said that "lust is a stain," and so forth.

925. *Assādadiṭṭhi* means a view associated with gratification. "There is no fault in sensual pleasures" means he says there is no fault in indulging in sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) due to the defilement of lust (*kilesakāma*).
*Pātabyataṃ* means the state of being drunk, the consuming, or the swallowing. One who speaks thus—
For he, as it were, drinks and swallows the defilement-desire within the object-desires, and thus partakes of them.

"Self-view" (*attānudiṭṭhi*) means a view that follows after a self. "Wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) means a base or inferior view. Now, since the first of these is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), the second is the personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), and the third is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), therefore, in order to demonstrate this meaning, [the text states] "eternalist view."
He says, "the view of gratification," and so forth.
The description of discontent (*arati*) and the description of cruelty (*vihesā*) have already had their meanings explained. Unrighteous conduct is *adhammacariyā*;

the meaning is the practice of what is unrighteous, or the performance of unrighteous acts. It is uneven conduct, or the practice of uneven (unjust) action; thus it is "uneven conduct" (*visamacariyā*).
The explanations for *dovacassatā* (obstinacy) and *pāpamittatā* (bad friendship) have already been stated.

Because it occurs with respect to various signs as its objects, perception regarding those diversities is "diverse perception" (*nānattasaññā*). Alternatively, because the perception of sensual desire is one thing and the perceptions of ill-will and so forth are another, it is called "diverse perception" because the perceptions are diverse.
Regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure, [it refers to] one whose mind has abandoned them in the explanations of indolence and negligence.

Lethargy (*kosajja*) should be understood as a state of sluggishness due to a lack of application to the cultivation of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*); negligence (*pamāda*) is the state of being heedless through the act of neglecting one's duties.
The descriptions of "lack of contentment" and so forth have already been explained.
In the exposition of disrespect (*anādariya*), disrespect is the state of lacking respect due to not heeding instruction (*ovāda*). It is the mode of being disrespectful.
Lack of respect (*anādaratā*). Lack of reverence (*agāravatā*) is the state of being without reverence in the sense of not dwelling in a state of deep veneration.

Lack of deference (*appatissavatā*) is the state of not dwelling in a state of honoring the eldest. Non-acceptance (*anaddā*) is the act of not accepting. Non-acceptingness (*anaddāyanā*) is the manner of not accepting.

The state of one who does not accept is non-acceptingness (*anaddāyitattaṃ*). The state of one who lacks virtue is lack of virtue (*asīliyaṃ*). Disregard (*acittīkāra*) is the failure to exercise respectful consideration.

932. Lack of faith (*assaddhabhāva*) is faithlessness (*assaddhiya*). The mode of not believing is non-belief (*asaddahanā*). Non-acceptance (*anokappanā*) is the failure to grasp after having formed a conviction and entered into it. Lack of serene confidence (*anabhippasāda*) is in the sense of not being tranquilized.
Ignorance of what should be said (*avadaññutā*) is the state of not understanding the words "Give! or "Do it! due to stubbornness and stinginess. 934.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas," by the inclusion of the term "Buddhas," the Pacceka-buddhas are also included.
"Desire not to associate" means the lack of desire to go near them. "Desire not to hear the True Dhamma":
the True Dhamma consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; it is the lack of desire to listen to that. "Desire not to master": the lack of desire to learn by heart.
"A state of mind intent on finding fault": the state of having a mind disposed toward criticism. Since, in its actual meaning, this is indeed criticism, therefore—

To demonstrate that, it was said: "In this context, what is 'objection' (*upārambha*)? and so forth. Therein, it is an "objection" by way of the act of objecting. Repeated objection is "continued objection" (*anupārambha*);
the manner of objecting is "the act of objecting" (*upārambhanā*). Repeated act of objecting is "continued act of objecting" (*anupārambhanā*).
The state of one who has not been objected against is "the state of being unobjected against" (*anupārambhitatta*). "Contempt" (*uññā*) is knowing [something] while placing it below [oneself].
*Avaññā* means despising. *Paribhavanaṃ* is contempt. *Randhagavesitā* is the seeking of faults;
or, one who seeks a fault is a "fault-seeker" (*randhagavesī*), and the state of being such is "the seeking of faults.

"This is called" means that this, characterized by the observation of the faults of others, is called "reproach" (*upārambha*); a person endowed with which is like a tailor who, having spread out a cloth—
He looks only for flaws; in the same way, having defiled all the virtues of another, he settles upon their very faults.

(936) *Ayoniso manasikāra* is unmethodical attention. Regarding the impermanent as permanent means that which occurs in thinking "this is permanent" with respect to a basis that is indeed impermanent.
The same method applies to [the misconceptions] such as "pleasure in what is suffering," and so forth. It is by way of being contrary to the Truths.
And "not in conformity" refers to the four truths. All terms such as "turning of the mind" (*cittassa āvaṭṭanā*) are synonyms for adverting (*āvajjanā*) itself.
For adverting turns the life-continuum consciousness toward an object, hence it is the "turning of the mind. It turns repeatedly, hence it is "repeated turning" (*anāvaṭṭanā*).
It inclines toward an object, hence it is "inclination" (*ābhogo*). It directs the mind toward an object other than the object of the life-continuum, hence it is "directed attention" (*samannāhāro*).
It is a thorough application. It is called *manasikāra* because it arises following after that very object and attending to it; "it attends" means it establishes [the mind].
This is called "unskillful attention" (*anupāya-manasikāra*), which is characterized by attention to a wrong path and is termed "unwise attention" (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
By means of this, a person [fails to perceive] the truths such as suffering as they truly are.
He is unable to advert [to the object].

Regarding the description of following a wrong path (*kummaggasevanā*), in order to show that which is called "following a wrong path" when one follows a wrong path, the second question—"In this context, what is the wrong path?"—is posed. The rest is entirely clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Exposition of Threes (*Tikaniddesa-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
(4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Tetrads 939.
Regarding the "arising of craving" in the Exposition of the Tetrads: "on account of robes" means that craving arises for the sake of robes with the thought, "Where shall I obtain pleasing robes?
Regarding "on account of this or that state of being" (*itibhavābhavahetu*): here, *iti* is a particle used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*); as for example...
The meaning is that it is for the sake of robes and so forth, and likewise for the sake of various states of existence (*bhavābhava*).
Here, "various states of existence" refers to superior and more superior things such as oil, honey, and molasses.
It should be understood that the four noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*) were taught in their specific sequence for the purpose of abandoning these four arisings of craving.
"One who goes to a wrong course through desire" means that through desire—that is, through affection—one goes to a wrong course and does what should not be done.

The same principle applies to the other terms as well. In this context, when one, out of desire—thinking, "This person is my friend, or has been seen by me, or is a close associate, or a kinsman, or he gives me a bribe"—makes someone who is not the owner the owner, this is [desire-bias].

One is said to "go by way of bias" (chandāgati) when, out of natural animosity or due to anger arisen at that very moment, one who thinks "this person is my enemy" deprives the rightful owner of their ownership.
One is said to "go by way of hatred" (dosāgati) when, through dullness and delusion, one says this or that and deprives the rightful owner of their ownership. Furthermore, one who...

Thinking, “This person is a royal favorite or dependent on someone in power; they might even do me harm,” one who, out of fear, makes a non-owner the owner—this is what is called going by way of fear.

Or again, when distributing something in a place where it is to be shared, one gives an extra portion out of affection, thinking, “This person is my friend, or someone I have seen before, or someone I am intimate with,” while [thinking of another], “This person is my enemy.”
One gives less out of ill will; out of delusion, not knowing what has been given or not given, one gives less to some and more to others;
or, fearing that "if this person does not receive [this], they might even cause me harm," one gives more to them.
This fourfold type of person is said to follow the biases of favoritism (*chandāgati*) and so forth in their respective order. Noble ones do not [follow] this.
They go, thus it is "going" (*agati*); because the ignoble ones go by means of this going, it is "going on a wrong path" (*agatigamana*).

This pair is stated with reference to all four [defilements] in common. Going by means of desire is "desire-going" (*chandagamana*); this is stated with reference to hatred and the others individually.
Going in a state of discord, placing attachment to one's own side and aversion toward the other side before oneself, is "factional going" (*vaggagamana*).
This was stated by way of what is common to both desire (*chanda*) and hatred (*dosa*). "Water-going" (*vārigamana*) means going like water according to its downward slope;
this was stated by way of what is common to all four [mental disturbances].

Regarding the perversions (*vipariyāsa*), they are called "perversions" because they seek objects such as impermanence and so forth in a perverted manner, such as by taking them to be permanent and so forth.
The perversion of perception is *saññā-vipariyāsa*. The same method applies to the other two [perversions of mind and view].

Thus, these are four based on the four objects (*vatthu*), and twelve based on the objects of perception and so forth. Among those, eight are abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
The perversions of perception and mind regarding the foul as beautiful are abandoned by the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-magga*).

They become attenuated and are abandoned by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). It should be understood that the perversion of perception and mind which takes what is painful to be pleasant is abandoned by the path of arahantship (*arahattamagga*).
Regarding "un-Aryan expressions": these are the base expressions of un-Aryans, of those who are lowly. "Speaking of what was seen" means: "seen..."
"By me"—thus it was spoken. And here, the meaning should be understood by way of the respective volition that originates [the speech].
It has already been stated that volition is expressed by the word "together" (*saha*). The same method applies to the second tetrad as well.
For there is no Noble One (Ariya) who, having not seen, would say "I have seen," or having seen, would say "I have not seen"; only a non-Ariya speaks thus.
He speaks. Therefore, for one who speaks thus, these eight volitions (cetanā) together with speech should be understood as ignoble modes of speech (anariya-vohāra).
Among the misdeeds (duccarita), the first tetrad is stated by way of volition rooted in enmity (veracetanā), while the second is by way of verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita).

Regarding fears (bhaya), in the first tetrad, fear arising in dependence on birth is "fear of birth" (jātibhaya); the same method applies to the others. In the second tetrad, fear arising from a king is "fear of a king" (rājabhaya); the same method applies to the others.
In the third tetrad, "the four fears" refers to the aforementioned fears for one descending into the waters of the great ocean.
It is said that in the great ocean there is a wave called the Mahinda-wave which rises sixty yojanas; the Gangā-wave rises fifty;
and the Rohaṇa-wave rises forty yojanas. The fear arising in dependence on such waves is "wave-fear."
[This is] the name. Fear arising from a crocodile is "crocodile-fear" (*kumbhīlabhaya*). Fear arising from a whirlpool in the water is "whirlpool-fear" (*āvaṭṭabhaya*).
A *susukā* is called a fierce fish; fear arising from that is "susukā-fear" (*susukābhaya*).
In the fourth tetrad, "fear of self-reproach" (*attānuvādabhaya*) refers to the fear that arises for one who reproaches oneself for having committed evil deeds.
The fear of being reproached by others (*parānuvādabhaya*) is the fear arising from being censured by another.

The fear of punishment (*daṇḍabhaya*) is the fear arising in dependence upon the punishment administered by a king for a householder, or the disciplinary punishment of the Vinaya for one who has gone forth.

The fear of an unhappy rebirth (*duggatibhaya*) is the fear arising in dependence upon the four states of misery. Thus, by these four tetrads, what are called the sixteen great fears have been explained.
