In the tetrad on views, the view called "Timbaruka’s" is explained. Therein, for one who regards feeling as self—thinking, "Pleasure and pain are self-made"—the view arises that feeling itself has made the feeling.
This being so, it follows that the feeling must have existed even previously; thus, this becomes the eternalist view (*sassata-diṭṭhi*). [The phrase] "as true and real" means...

"Truly and firmly. The view that arises from one who regards the cause of feeling as something other than the present feeling itself—thinking, "This feeling has been produced by another feeling"—is the view [of eternalism]. When this is so, the annihilation of the preceding causal feeling follows;
thus, this is called the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). [The view that it is] both self-made and made by another...
The view that arises from grasping the meaning as previously stated—namely, "half is self-made, half is made by another"—is called the view of eternalism and annihilationism (*sassatucchedadiṭṭhi*).

The view that arises from grasping that pleasure and pain occur without any cause whatsoever is the view of no-cause (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*). The rest here is clear in meaning, as it follows the method explained below.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Fours is finished.
(5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives: 940.
In the Exposition of the Fives, because those for whom personality-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the other [fetters] have not been abandoned are reborn even in the Peak of Existence (*bhavagga*),...
Having dragged these [five] along, they cause one to fall into the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava) itself; therefore, they are called "lower fetters" (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana).
Thus, these five do not prevent one from going, but having gone, they bring one back.

The five beginning with attachment to the fine-material realm (rūparāga) also do not prevent one from going, but they do not allow one to return. The five beginning with lust (rāga) are called "attachments" (saṅga) in the sense of clinging, but they are called "arrows" (salla) in the sense of having entered [the heart].
941. *Cetokhilā* means states of rigidity, like refuse or like stumps, within the mind.
"He doubts the Teacher" means he doubts either the Teacher’s physical body or his qualities. Doubting the body, he doubts:
"Does a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man exist, or does it not? Doubting the qualities, he doubts: "Is there one capable of knowing the past, future, and present..."
He doubts whether "there is omniscient knowledge" or "there is not. To "doubt" (*vicikicchati*) means that while investigating, he is distressed;
he encounters suffering and is unable to reach a decision. To "not resolve" (*nādhimuccati*) means that he does not obtain the conviction that "this is exactly so.
To "not have confidence" (*na sampasīdati*) means that, having entered into the qualities [of the Buddha], he is not turbid because of his state of being free from doubt.
He is unable to come to a conclusion.

Regarding "the Dhamma": this refers both to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) and the Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedha-dhamma*). One who has doubt regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures thinks:
"They say that the word of the Buddha consists of the Three Baskets and eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma; does this actually exist, or does it not?"

He is doubtful. Being doubtful regarding the Dhamma of realization, he doubts: "They say that insight is the outflow of the path, the fruit is the outflow of the path, and Nibbāna is the relinquishment of all conditioned things; does that exist, or does it not exist?
He is doubtful regarding the Saṅgha: "By way of such phrases as 'one who has entered upon the straight path,' they have entered upon such a practice..."
He doubts whether or not there exists what is called the Saṅgha, which is a collection of eight persons consisting of four who stand on the path and four who stand in the fruit.
Doubting the training, he doubts whether or not there exists what they call the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
"Bonds of the mind" (*cetasovinibandhā*): they are called "bonds of the mind" because they bind the mind and seize it as if making a fist.
"Sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers to both sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) and defilements (*kilesakāma*). "In the body" (*kāye*) means in one's own body. "Forms" (*rūpe*) means external forms.
"As much as required" (*yāvadattha*) means as much as one desires. "To fill the belly" (*udarāvadehaka*) means to fill the stomach; for it is so called because it covers the belly.
"Rubbing the belly" is what is meant by that term. "The pleasure of lying down" refers to the pleasure of beds and chairs, or the pleasure of the season.
"The pleasure of the side" is the pleasure that arises for one who lies turning over, such that there is comfort for both the right and left sides. "The pleasure of torpor" is the pleasure of sleep.
"Devoted to" means he dwells engaged and intent upon these. "Having directed his mind toward" means having formed a longing for them.

Regarding the passage beginning with "By virtue" (*sīlena*): "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "Vow" (*vata*) refers to the undertaking of a vow. "Austerity" (*tapa*) refers to the practice of asceticism.
"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to abstaining from sexual intercourse. "I shall become a god" means I shall become a god of great power; "or some other god" means among gods of little power.
They are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇāni*) because they obstruct and prevent wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).

"The mother has been deprived of life" means that a human mother, one's own biological mother, has been deprived of life by a human being. "The father" likewise refers only to a human father. "An Arahant" likewise refers only to a human Arahant. "With a malicious mind" means with a murderous intent. "One who possesses perception" means one endowed with perception.
"Immortal" means eternal. "In this way some declare" means that some declare thus; the sense is that some declare in this manner.
Up to this point, the sixteen views of those who maintain that there is perception after death (*saññīvāda*) have been explained. "One without perception" means devoid of perception.

By this phrase, the eight theories of non-percipient existence (*asaññīvāda*) are stated. By the third phrase, the eight theories of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*) are stated.
"Or of an existing being" (*sato vā pana sattassa*) means: or of a being that is actually present. "Annihilation" (*uccheda*) means cutting off.
"Destruction" (*vināsa*) means non-appearance. "Cessation of existence" (*vibhava*) means the disappearance of being. All of these are merely synonyms for one another.
In this regard, two kinds of people adopt the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi): both those who possess supernormal powers and those who do not.

Among them, one who possesses such powers adopts the annihilationist view after seeing with the divine eye the passing away (cuti) of an Arahant but not their reappearance (upapatti); or, one who is only able to see the passing away itself and not the rebirth.
One who does not possess such powers adopts it out of greed for sensual pleasure, thinking, "Who knows about the next world?"
Or, by means of the thought, "Just as leaves fallen from a tree do not grow again, so too are sentient beings," one grasps at annihilationism.
However, in this context, the seven doctrines of annihilationism are explained by way of craving and views, having been conceptualized both in that manner and otherwise;
for this is a summary statement of them. [The seventh is] Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*).

Regarding the phrase "or else one" (*vā pana eko*): here, "the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived phenomenon (*paccakkhadhamma*). This is a designation for the state of existence acquired in various places.
"Nibbāna in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*) means Nibbāna within the present life; the meaning is that suffering is stilled right in this very selfhood (*attabhāva*).
This is a summary statement encompassing the five proponents of Nibbāna in the present life.
942. "Enemies" refers to those with hostile intentions. "Calamities" refers to destructions. "Impatience" refers to non-acceptance.
"Unpleasant" means one who is not to be loved because of being repulsive to see or hear; it is "unmindful" (amanāpa) because the mind does not settle upon him due to his repulsiveness.
"Full of enmity" means having much enmity. "Full of faults" means having many defects.
"Fear regarding livelihood" means the fear that arises in dependence upon one's livelihood, which is to say, one's mode of life. This exists for both the householder and the homeless renunciant.
In this regard, first, much unwholesome karma has been committed by the householder on account of his livelihood;
consequently, at the time of death, when hell appears before him, fear arises. Much improper search has also been conducted by the homeless renunciant.
It comes to pass. Then, at the time of his death, when hell appears before him, fear arises.

This is called the fear of livelihood (*ājīvikabhaya*). "Fear of ill-repute" (*asilokabhaya*) means the fear of censure. "Fear of timidity in assemblies" (*parisā-sārajjabhaya*) means that for a person who has committed evil, as he approaches an assembled gathering, a fear characterized by timidity arises. This is the fear of timidity in assemblies.
The other two [terms] are indeed clear. 943.

Regarding the sections on "nibbāna in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammanibbāna*): "by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcahi kāmaguṇehi*) refers to the five divisions of sensual desire, such as agreeable forms and so forth, or to the bonds.
"Endowed" (*samappito*) means being thoroughly endowed or closely attached. "Possessed" (*samaṅgībhūto*) means being fully equipped.
"He enjoys" means that he moves and shifts his sense faculties as he pleases among those strands of sensual pleasure, directing them hither and thither;

or alternatively, it means he dallies, delights, and plays. And here, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures: human and divine. Human sensual pleasures should be understood as being like those of King Mandhātu;
divine sensual pleasures belong to the king of the gods who wields power over the creations of others (*paranimmitavasavatti*).
"Resembling the strands of sensual pleasure. For they say that one who has entered into such sensual pleasures has attained the supreme *diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna* (nirvana in the present life).
In this context, "supreme *diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna*" means the highest *diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna*; the sense is "the most excellent.

In the second section, [sensual pleasures] are impermanent in the sense of passing away after having come to be; they are suffering in the sense of oppression; and they are subject to change in the sense of abandoning their original nature.
They should be understood as subject to change. "Their change and alteration" means the alteration, termed change, of those sensual pleasures.
Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise according to the manner stated: "What was mine, that is no longer mine. In this context, sorrow has the characteristic of inward brooding;
lamentation has the characteristic of outward wailing dependent upon that; and [pain] has the characteristic of physical oppression.
Dukkha has the characteristic of bodily affliction; domanassa has the characteristic of mental distress;
upāyāsa has the characteristic of despondency. "Vitakka" is thought that proceeds by way of directing the mind onto an object.
"Vicāra" is sustained application that proceeds by way of continued examination. By this and that: by this thought and that sustained application, this first jhāna is coarse.
It appears as if it were thorny.
"Consisting of rapture" (pītigata) means rapture itself. "The elation of the mind" (cetaso uppilāvitam) means that which causes the mind to become uplifted.

"The mental engagement of the mind" (cetaso ābhoga) means that, having emerged from the jhāna, there is a repeated mental engagement and attention toward that bliss. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads is finished.
(6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Hexads: 944.

In the Exposition of the Hexads, because one who is angry, or through anger, or one who adheres to their own views, or through adherence to their own views, falls into quarreling, strife, and dispute, therefore anger and the rest are called "roots of dispute."

In the *Chandarāga-niddesa*, after stating that "desire-and-lust based on the household" refers to phenomena based on the household because they are rooted in desire-and-lust for sensual pleasures, it is said, "regarding agreeable forms," and so forth, in order to show them again by way of their classification. Therein, "agreeable" means desirable things that increase mental pleasure.
"Antagonistic" means the very bases of antagonism. "Disagreeable" means undesirable things.
945. "Lacking respect for those who should be respected" means being devoid of reverence. "Lacking deference" means lacking support, behaving without humility.

In this context, however, it refers to a bhikkhu who, while the Teacher is still living, does not attend upon him at the three appointed times; who walks with sandals on when the Teacher is walking without sandals;
who walks on a high walkway when the Teacher is walking on a low one; [and] below...
In the spring, he dwells above; at the place where the Teacher is seen, he covers both shoulders, holds a sunshade, wears sandals, bathes, and voids excrement or urine;
or, when the Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, he does not go to pay homage at the shrine;
yet at the place where the shrine is visible—that is, at the place where the Teacher is seen—he performs everything that was prescribed.

This is what is called disrespect toward the Teacher. Furthermore, when the proclamation for the hearing of the Dhamma has been made, he does not go respectfully, he does not listen to the Dhamma respectfully, he sits chatting, he does not grasp it respectfully, and he does not recite it respectfully—this is what is called disrespect toward the Dhamma.
Furthermore, when a senior bhikkhu has not requested him... [he teaches] the Dhamma... [this is what is called disrespect toward the Saṅgha].
To teach, to answer questions, to walk, stand, or sit while jostling senior bhikkhus,
to fold one's robe like a bolster or to clasp one's hands together [in a disrespectful manner], to cover both shoulders while in the midst of the Saṅgha,
or to carry a sunshade and sandals— this is called disrespect toward the Saṅgha. For when disrespect is shown toward even a single bhikkhu, disrespect has indeed been shown toward the Saṅgha.
[He] exists. However, one who does not fulfill the three trainings is said to have disrespect for the training.

One who does not cultivate the characteristic of heedfulness is said to have disrespect for heedfulness. One who does not perform the two kinds of hospitality is said to have disrespect for hospitality.
"States conducive to decline" refers to those states that cause decline. "Delight in work" refers to [delight] in building projects or in the distribution of robes and so forth.
Or, it is delight in worldly tasks and being intent upon them. Delight in talk (*bhassārāmatā*) is being intent upon talk by way of frivolous chatter (*tiracchānakathā*).
Delight in sleep (*niddārāmatā*) is being intent upon sleep. Delight in company (*saṅgaṇikārāmatā*) is being intent upon company.
Delight in socializing (*saṃsaggārāmatā*) refers to socializing through hearing, socializing through seeing, socializing through conversation, and socializing through shared enjoyment.

"Physical contact" (*kāyasaṃsagga*) refers to being engaged in or occupied with the five kinds of contact. "Delighting in proliferation" (*papañcārāmatā*) refers to being engaged in or occupied with the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views.
946. Regarding "mental explorations of joy" (*somanassupavicāra*) and so forth: they are called "mental explorations of joy" because they explore together with joy.
"Having seen a form with the eye" means having perceived a form by means of visual consciousness. "A basis for joy" means [a basis] for joy.
It is the cause by way of its object (*ārammaṇa*). "It ranges over" means that it ranges over by way of the occurrence of investigation (*vicāra*) therein.
By this method, the meaning should be understood for all three sets of six; for instance, "but applied thought (*vitakka*) is associated with that. 947.

"Worldly" (*gehasita*) means dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "Gladnesses" (*somanassāni*) are mental pleasures. "Distresses" (*domanassāni*) are mental pains. "Equanimity" (*upekkhā*) is the feeling of equanimity associated with ignorance; "ignorance-equanimity" (*aññāṇupekkhā*) is also a name for these very same states.
948. In all instances where the word "vā" (or) occurs in the phrase "Atthi me attā vā," it has the sense of an alternative; thus, what is meant is that such a view arises.
Herein, the eternalist view (*sassataditthi*)—namely, "There is a self for me"—grasps the existence of a self at all times.
"Truly and really" means from the standpoint of what is actual and firm; that is to say, "This is the truth" by way of being well-established and steadfast.
"There is no self for me"—this, however, is the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), because it grasps the non-existence of an existing being here and there.
Alternatively, the former [view] is the eternalist view (*sassatadṛṣṭi*) because it grasps that [the self] exists in the three times;

grasping that only the present exists is the annihilationist view. The latter [view] is also [an annihilationist view] because it grasps that [the self] does not exist in the past and future, as in the statement: "The oblations end in ashes."

The annihilationist view is like that of those who have already grasped a [wrong] view; the eternalist view of the fortuitous originationist is like that of one who grasps that there is nothing in the past.

Or, regarding the phrase "I perceive self by means of self": having grasped the aggregates as "self" under the heading of the aggregate of perception—since one perceives the remaining aggregates through perception—one thinks, "By this self, I perceive this self. Thus...

"It is by means of self, [perceiving] non-self": having grasped the aggregate of perception itself as "self" and the other four aggregates as "non-self," because one knows them through perception, it occurs thus. "Or by means of non-self, [perceiving] self":
having grasped the aggregate of perception as "non-self" and the other four aggregates as "self," because one knows them through perception, it occurs thus.
All [these] are indeed views of eternalism and annihilationism.

However, such expressions as "the speaker" (*vada*) and "the feeler" (*vedayya*) are modes of dogmatic adherence specifically to the view of eternalism. In this context, "speaker" (*vada*) means one who speaks;
it is said to be the performer of verbal action. "Feeler" (*vedayya*) means one who feels; it is said to mean one who knows and experiences.
[He] exists. Now, in order to show what he experiences there, it is said: "In this and that [place], for a long time, [the results of] wholesome and unwholesome [deeds]," and so forth.
Therein, "in this and that" means in those various wombs, destinies, stations, abodes, and classes of beings, or in [various] objects.
"For a long time" means for a long duration. "Experiences" (paccanubhoti) means he feels (paṭisaṃvedayati). "He was not born [and did not exist]"—he...
The self (*attā*), by virtue of its nature of being unborn (*ajātidhamma*), is not said to have been born; the meaning is that it has always existed.
For that very reason, it did not exist in the past, nor will it exist in the future. For that which has been born has existed, and that which will be born will exist.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "it was never not born": because it exists at all times, it was never at any point not born in the past, nor will it ever be not born in the future.
"It will not be. "Permanent" (*nicca*) means devoid of arising and passing away. "Stable" (*dhruva*) means firm and substantial. "Eternal" (*sassata*) means existing at all times.
"Of a nature not subject to change" (*avipariṇāmadhamma*) means a state that does not abandon its own natural condition; like a *kakaṇṭaka* plant, it does not undergo various transformations.
Thus, this is called the "view of all taints" (*sabbāsava-diṭṭhi*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold Set. (7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevenfold Set: 949.

In the exposition of the sevenfold set, they are called *anusaya* (latent tendencies) because they lie latent (*anusenti*) in the sense of being firmly established and in the sense of not having been abandoned within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
They are called *saṃyojanāni* (fetters) because they yoke and bind sentient beings. They are called *pariyuṭṭhānāni* (obsessions) because they obsess by way of active manifestation.
Sensual lust itself as an obsession is "sensual-lust-obsession" (*kāmarāga-pariyuṭṭhāna*). The same method applies to the others as well. 950.

They are "unrighteous states" (*asaddhammā*) because they are the qualities of those who are non-existent, or because they are base qualities. They are "misconducts" (*duccaritāni*) because they are behaviors corrupted by faults such as lust and so forth. They are "conceits" (*mānā*) because one conceives [of oneself] in various ways.
951. In the exposition of views (*diṭṭhiniddesa*): "Possessing form" (*rūpī*) means having form. "Consisting of the four great elements" (*cātumahābhūtika*) means made of the four great elements.

"Belonging to mother and father" (*mātāpettika*) refers to what belongs to the mother and father. What is that? It is the semen and blood. "Born and produced from what belongs to mother and father" (*mātāpettikasambhava*) means born and arisen from the maternal and paternal [elements].
Here, by way of the term "form-body," one speaks of the human existence as "self. The second [view] rejects that and [speaks of] the divine existence.
He speaks. "Divine" means born in the world of the devas. "Belonging to the sense-sphere" means included among the six classes of sense-sphere devas.
"One who eats physical food" means one whose sustenance is physical food. "Mind-made" means produced by means of meditative absorption (jhāna).
"Complete in all limbs and parts" means endowed with every limb and part. "With unimpaired faculties" means having perfect faculties—those which exist in the Brahma-world.

This is stated by way of the shape of the former [the first formless realm] and by way of the shapes of the others. "One who has reached the base of infinite space" means one who has attained the state of the base of infinite space.
The same method applies to the others as well. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Septad.
(8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Eightfold [Set] 952.

In the Exposition of the Eightfold [Set], the defilements themselves are the bases for defilement (*kilesavatthu*). "Bases for laziness" (*kusītavatthu*) means the bases for one who is lazy or indolent;
the sense is that they are the grounds for indolence. "Work that ought to be done" refers to tasks such as the distribution of robes (*cīvaravicāraṇā*) and so forth.
It ought to be done. "He does not arouse energy" means he does not arouse either of the two kinds of energy.

"For the attainment of the unattained" refers to the attainment of the states of jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit which have not yet been attained. "For the reaching of the unreached" is for the sake of reaching those very same states which have not yet been reached.
"For the realization of the unrealized" is for the sake of realizing those very same states which have not yet been realized. "This is the first" refers to the thought: "Now, let me lie down."
Thus, sinking down is the first ground of indolence. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Regarding the phrase "he thinks it is a month’s accumulation": here, "a month’s accumulation" means a month [of stored food]; the intention is that he is as heavy as a month’s accumulation of food when it has become moldy. "He has recovered from illness" means that having been ill, he has subsequently recovered.
954. Regarding the phrase "in the eight worldly conditions": here, "worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) means the conditions of the world. One who is liberated from these is called...
They do not cease even for Buddhas; therefore, they are called "worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*). "Striking back" (*paṭighāta*) means the mode of being struck back.
"Attachment to gain" (*sārāga*) is the attachment that arises by way of sensual-based joy, thinking, "I am receiving gain";
it strikes back at the mind. "Aversion to loss" (*paṭivirodha*) is [the state] by way of dejection, thinking, "I am not receiving gain."
It is a conflict that has arisen; that too strikes back at the mind. Therefore, it is called "resistance" (*paṭighāta*).

Regarding fame and the rest as well, their arising should be understood in this way: "I have a large retinue," "I have a small retinue," "I have attained praise," "I have met with blame," "I have attained happiness," "I have fallen into suffering.
"Noble speech" (*anariyavohārā*) means the speech of the ignoble ones.
957. *Purisadosā* means faults of men. *Na sarāmi* means: “I do not remember, I do not perceive the place where this deed was committed by me”;
thus, through lack of mindfulness, he unravels it—that is, he releases himself. *Codakam-eva paṭippharati* means: being opposed, he strikes back;
he stands by way of a retort. *Kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ* means: “What [does it matter] to you?”... [the rest of the sentence follows].
"By what is said by a fool who is incompetent—namely, 'How can you speak when you do not even know the basis for the offense nor the formal charge?'—it is meant to point this out.
'Even you, it seems, thinking you should speak while knowing nothing at all,' he thus overwhelms him.
'He counter-accuses' means that by saying 'As for you too... and so forth, he levels a counter-charge. 'Confess' means that which leads to confession."
"Show [your offense]; emerge from that which leads to emergence; once established in the pure state, you shall accuse another"—this is what he indicates.
"He evades one matter with another" means that by means of another reason or statement, he conceals another reason or statement.
When told, "You have fallen into an offense," he asks: "Who has fallen? What has been fallen into? How has it been fallen into? In what has one fallen?"

He says, "Who are you addressing? What are you saying? When told, "You have seen such-and-such a thing," he either does not lend an ear, saying, "I did not hear it," or he diverts the conversation externally.
Regarding how he diverts the conversation externally: when asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense?
he replies, "I went to Pāṭaliputta. When told again, "We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta," [he continues to deflect].

When one says, “I have gone from there to Rājagaha,” and is asked, “Whether you go to Rājagaha or to the house of a brahmin, you have fallen into an offense,” how does one distract by means of externals when saying things such as, “I obtained pork there”? “Anger” (*kopa*) is the state of being provoked;
“hatred” (*dosa*) is the state of being corrupted. Both of these are names for anger itself. “Discontent” (*appaccaya*) is the mode of dissatisfaction.
This is the name for displeasure (*domanassa*). "Manifests" means shows or makes known.
"Speaks with brandished arms" means he speaks words of shamelessness while waving his arms. "Harasses" means torments or oppresses.
"Without taking to heart" means not grasping with respect, but rather despising; the meaning is that he is disrespectful.
*Atibāḷhaṃ* means excessively firm or excessive in measure. *Mayi byāvaṭā* means having become occupied with me.
*Hīnāyāvattitvā* means having returned for the sake of the inferior state of a householder; the meaning is "having become householders. *Attamanā hothā* means be joyful in heart:
"Receive what is to be received by me; dwell in the place where I dwell; may you have a comfortable dwelling through me."
He speaks with the intention of asking, "What is it? (958).
The term *asaññivāda* refers to a doctrine that proceeds by way of non-perception (*asaññī*); those who hold such a doctrine are called *asaññivādā*.

In the case of views such as "the self possesses form" (*rūpī attā*), the view of "possessing form" arises when one who has attained [meditative mastery] takes the kasiṇa-form to be the self; whereas for one who has not attained it, it arises through mere reasoning alone.

It is like that of the Ājīvakas. Furthermore, only those who have attained the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti) develop the view "I am formless" by apprehending the sign of the formless attainment as a self;
whereas those who have not attained it do so through mere reasoning alone, as in the case of the Nigaṇṭhas.
However, one need not seek a definitive cause here for the state of being non-percipient (asaññībhāva). For a proponent of such views (diṭṭhigatika) is like a madman, saying whatever comes to mind.
"He grasps. "Both material and immaterial" is stated by way of grasping a mixture of the material and the immaterial.

This view arises both for one who has attained the meditative absorptions (samāpatti) of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and for the mere rationalist (takkika). "Neither material nor immaterial," however, is exclusively the view of the rationalist.
"Finite" is the view of one who grasps a limited kasiṇa as the self. "Infinite" refers to an immeasurable kasiṇa. "Both finite and infinite" [refers to grasping both].
The view that arises by grasping the kasiṇa—whether limited above and below, or unlimited across—as "self" is [the view] "neither finite nor infinite.
This is simply the speculative view (*takki-diṭṭhi*). The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the *Aṭṭhaka-niddesa*.
(9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines (Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā) 960.

In the exposition of the nines, the "nine bases for resentment" (*āghātavatthūni*) are mentioned specifically in terms of their arising toward sentient beings. "Stains of men" (*purisānaṃ malāni*) means the stains belonging to men. "Ninefold" (*navavidhā*) means consisting of nine sections or nine divisions.
963. "Dependent upon craving" (*taṇhaṃ paṭicca*) means relying upon craving. "Search" (*pariyesanā*) refers to the search for objects such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth. For that [search]...
When craving exists, there is gain. "Gain" refers to the acquisition of objects such as forms and so forth; for that indeed occurs when there is seeking.
"Decision," however, is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and applied thought. Among these, "One should know the decision regarding pleasure;
having known the decision regarding pleasure, one should devote oneself to internal pleasure"—this is the decision by way of knowledge.
“‘Investigation’ (vinicchaya) means two kinds of investigation: the investigation of craving (taṇhā-vinicchaya) and the investigation of views (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya).

Thus, the one hundred and eight modes of craving’s movement (taṇhā-vicari-tā) that have been handed down constitute the investigation of craving. The sixty-two views constitute the investigation of views.
However, in this sutta—“Desire, O Lord of Devas, has its source in thought” (vitakka)—it is thought itself that is called “investigation.”
Having arrived, and having obtained gain—whether desirable or undesirable, beautiful or ugly—one determines it by means of thought alone:
“This much will be for the sake of the object of visible form; this much for the sake of the objects of sound and so forth;
this much will be mine; this much will belong to another; this much I shall consume; this much I shall store away.”
Therefore it was said: “In dependence on gain, there is discrimination.
Regarding “lust and passion”: when an object has been thought over by such unwholesome thinking, both weak lust and strong lust arise.
For here, “desire” (*chanda*) is a designation for weak lust. “Clinging” (*ajjhosāna*) means “I” and “mine.”
It is a powerful resolution. "Possession" (*pariggaha*) means making something one's own by way of craving and views.
"Avarice" (*macchariya*) is the inability to endure sharing with others. For this very reason, the ancients explain its etymological meaning thus:
"It is called 'avarice' (*macchariya*) because it occurs with the thought, 'Let this wonder be mine alone; let it not be a wonder for another.'"
“It is so called. *Ārakkho* means thorough protection by means of locking doors, guarding with a key, and so forth.

*Adhikaroti* means “it undertakes”; this is a name for a cause (*kāraṇa*). *Ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ* is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*); the meaning is “for the sake of the cause that is protection.
*Daṇḍādānaṃ* is the taking up of a staff for the purpose of restraining others among the acts such as taking up a staff. [The same applies to] the single-edged blade, etc.
*Satthādānaṃ* (taking up a weapon) means the grasping of a weapon. *Kalahā* (quarrel) refers both to quarrels of body and quarrels of speech.
The former [instances] are oppositions or conflicts (*viggaha*), while the latter are disputes (*vivāda*). *Tuvaṃ tuvaṃ* is a term of disrespect; the meaning is "you, you. 964.
*Iñjitāni* means stirrings or fluctuations. By all the phrases beginning with "the stirring 'I am'" (*asmīti iñjitaṃ etam*), it is pride (*māna*) that is described.
For even the conceit that occurs as "I am" is indeed a fluctuation; so too is that which occurs as "this I am," and even that which occurs as "I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.

Conceit is also spoken of by the rest of the novices. For conceit is a "fluctuation" because it fluctuates, a "conceiving" because it conceives, a "quivering" because it quivers, and a "proliferation" because it proliferates.
It is "conditioned" because it is conditioned by various causes.
And so it is said. The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of Nines. (10. The Commentary on the Exposition of Tens.

966. In the exposition of the ten [bases], the defilements themselves are the bases for defilement. As for the bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*), they are stated here together with the resentment that arises even toward inappropriate objects such as stumps or thorns, by way of such thoughts as, "He has done me harm.

970. Among the wrong states (*micchatta*), "wrong knowledge" (*micchāñāṇa*) is the delusion that arises in the mode of reviewing one's own actions after having committed evil through the planning of means for sinful deeds, thinking, "I have done well.
"Wrong liberation" (*micchāvimutti*) is the perception of being liberated while one is actually not liberated.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the Exposition of the Decads. The commentary on the Exposition of the Wanderings of Craving.
973. In the exposition of the "modes of craving" (*taṇhāvicarita*), "modes of craving" refers to the occurrences and manifestations of craving.
"Based upon the internal" means based upon the internal pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*). This genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"The thought 'I am' arises" means that, based upon this internal pentad of aggregates, there arises from a grasping at a collective whole by way of craving, conceit, and views.
‘I am’ (asmī) occurs; the meaning is: when that [conceit] exists.
In such cases as “I am thus” (itthasmī), when there is the grasping of a self as a whole, there follows a twofold grasping: both by way of non-comparison and by way of comparison.

Therein, "by way of non-comparison" means that without approaching another mode, having made one's own state itself the object, one thinks “I am thus”; [this refers to] among the khattiyas and so forth.
The meaning is that it occurs by way of craving, conceit, and views, such as “I am this benefactor.

This, first of all, is grasping without comparison (*anupanidhāya*). Grasping with comparison (*upanidhāya*), however, is twofold: by way of equality and by way of inequality. To show that, it is said:
“I am thus” (*evam-asmi*) and “I am otherwise” (*aññathā-asmi*). Therein, “I am thus” is grasping with comparison by way of equality.
The meaning is: "Just as this khattiya, just as this brahmin, so am I. However, "I am otherwise" is a grasping based on dissimilarity; the meaning is:
"Unlike this khattiya and unlike this brahmin, I am otherwise—either inferior or superior.
These, first of all, are the four modes of craving's movement with reference to the present. [As for] "I shall be," and so forth...
However, these four [views] are stated with reference to the future. The meaning of the remainder should be understood in the same manner as explained for the preceding tetrad.
"I am" (*asmī*) means "I am eternal. "I am existing" (*sāmīti*) means "I am non-eternal. There is also a reading: "I am not" (*asamīti*) or "I am existing" (*satasmīti*).
In that context, "existent" (*asaṃ*) is a designation for the permanent; "perishing" (*sīdati*) is a designation for the impermanent. Thus, "existing" (*sataṃ*) is a designation for the impermanent.
Thus, it should be understood that these two [views] are stated by way of eternalism and annihilationism.
The four following views, beginning with "I might be," are stated by way of speculative doubt. Their meaning should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the preceding tetrad.
However, the four beginning with "Perhaps I might be" are stated by way of aspiration and imagining, thinking, "May I indeed come to be."
These have been stated. They are to be understood according to the same method as that explained for the preceding tetrad.
Thus, among these—two with the view as their head, four with the pure as their head, three rooted in the head, and three [more]—one should discern these eighteen.
For among these, the two expressed by way of eternalism (sassata) and annihilationism (uccheda) are called the "two heads of views" (diṭṭhisīsa).

"I am" (asmī), "I shall be" (bhavissanti), "I might be" (siyanti), and "I might not be" (apāhaṃ siyanti)—these four are the "pure heads" (suddhasīsa) alone. "In this way I am" (itthasmī) and so forth—these three times three make twelve, which are called the "heads based on the root" (sīsamūlaka).
Thus, these are eighteen: the two heads of views, the four pure heads, and the twelve based on the root.
The phenomena consisting of the wanderings of craving (*taṇhāvicaritadhammā*) are to be understood.
Now, in order to analyze and demonstrate those phenomena in their proper sequence, the passage beginning with "And how does the thought 'I am' arise? is commenced.

In this context, "without making any phenomenon exempt" means without leaving out even a single phenomenon—such as form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth—from the process of non-separation (*avinibbhoga*).
The meaning is: having taken them not one by one, but having taken them as a whole.
“He acquires the desire ‘I am’” means that, having grasped the five aggregates without remainder, he acquires the craving “I. The same method applies to conceit and views as well.
In this context, although this is a description of the wandering of craving, conceit and views do not exist apart from craving.

Therefore, they are mentioned here by virtue of being associated with that [craving]. Alternatively, all three types of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) have been indicated under the heading of craving (*taṇhā*).
In order to explain them in accordance with that indication, pride and views were included.
Or, while demonstrating the proliferation of craving, he spoke thus in order to show the remaining proliferations along with it as well.

"When that exists, these proliferations exist": the meaning is that when those three kinds of proliferation have arisen in the manner described by "one acquires the desire 'I am'," then again these proliferations—namely, "I am thus," and so forth—come to be.

In such cases as "I am a khattiya," one thinks "I am a khattiya" by virtue of being anointed, a general, a minister, and so on; "I am a brāhmaṇa" by virtue of being a master of mantras, a priest, and so on;
"I am a vessa" by virtue of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so on; and "I am a sudda" by virtue of wearing clothes made of bark or grass.
The meaning should be understood in this manner: by means of the insignia of a householder, one thinks, "I am a householder.

Thus, "it occurs that 'I am such-and-such'" means that, having produced within oneself the appearance of a khattiya or other status among the khattiyas and so forth, one thinks, "I am of such-and-such a kind.

Just as among those who are khattiyas and so on—just as he is a khattiya by virtue of his consecration, his position as commander-in-chief, his ministers, and so forth—so too [does one think of oneself].
The meaning should be understood according to this method: "a khattiya. In the second method, the meaning should be understood according to this method:
"Just as he is a khattiya by virtue of his consecration, ministers, and so forth, I am not such a khattiya; rather, I am either inferior or superior to him.
This same method applies to the explanations beginning with "will be," and so on.
975. Having thus analyzed the modes of craving based on the internal [aggregates], he now says, "In that regard, which are they?
and so forth, in order to analyze the modes of craving based on the external. Therein, "based on the external" means based on the external pentad of aggregates (*khandha*).
This genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative. "By this" means by this form (*rūpa*).
Or... pe... or by consciousness. As for the remainder, it should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on the enumeration (uddesavāra).
However, in the section on the exposition (niddesavāra), "having made a separation" means having performed an analysis (vinibbhoga).
In such passages as "by this one acquires the desire 'I am'," and so forth, [the meaning is] "by this form... pe... or by consciousness," thus [referring to] the five aggregates partially.
Having grasped this, one obtains [the notions] such as "I" through desire and so forth; thus the meaning should be understood.

In cases such as "I am a khattiya," the meaning should be understood in the same manner as before: "By means of this parasol, or sword, or consecration, or ministers of state, etc., I am a khattiya. Here, the only distinction is the word "by means of this" (*iminā*).
Just as in the phrases "he is a khattiya" and so on, the phrase "by means of this" that was mentioned is itself the distinction. Therefore, according to that [principle], just as...

“Khattiya”—in this way, one should understand the meaning in all instances by applying it thus: “I too am a khattiya because of this sword, or this parasol, or these ministers of consecration and so forth.

Having made the five aggregates non-existent [as a self] by means of this thought, “I am permanent,” and having grasped even a single phenomenon such as form and so forth as “I,” [one thinks]: “By means of this sword or this parasol, I...”
“He conceives it as permanent and eternal. The same method applies to the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*). The rest is to be understood according to the method already stated everywhere.
Thus, there are thirty-six such [views] in the past; that is, thirty-six for each individual in the past. There are thirty-six in the future;
that is, thirty-six for each individual in the future. There are thirty-six in the present; that is, for each individual...
According to the principle of "as many as are obtained," there are thirty-six for many [beings] in the present.
However, it should be understood that for all beings, there are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present.

For beings are infinite, distinguished by various types of craving, conceit, and views that are not identical. As for the phrase "there are one hundred and eight modes of craving's wandering" (*aṭṭha-taṇhā-vicari-sataṃ*), here [the number] designated as one hundred and eight...
"It is a wandering of craving" (taṇhāvicaritaṃ) is how the meaning should be understood. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the wandering of craving. Now begins the commentary on the exposition of the spheres of views (diṭṭhigata).
977. Regarding the exposition on views (*diṭṭhigataniddesa*) in the *Brahmajāla-vyākaraṇa*: this refers to the discourse named the *Brahmajāla*, the first sutta of the *Dīghanikāya*.
"Spoken by the Blessed One" means uttered by the Teacher himself. In the passage beginning with "the four eternalists" (*cattāro sassatavādā*), [it is said]:
"And those venerable recluses and brahmins, based on what, referring to what, are proponents of eternalism (*sassatavādā*) regarding the self and the world?"

The classification and the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* by way of the passage beginning, “And they proclaim the world on four grounds,” and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Khuddakavatthu Vibhaṅga* in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.
18. Analysis of the Heart of the Teaching (Dhammahadayavibhaṅga) 1.
Explanation of the Section on the Comprehensive Summary (Sabbasaṅgāhikavāravaṇṇanā) 978.
Now, immediately following that, the textual division of the Analysis of the Heart of the Teaching (Dhammahadayavibhaṅga) should be understood as follows:
For here, first of all, the "Comprehensive Section" is stated by way of the twelve categories, beginning with the aggregates (khandha).
The second is the "Section Showing the Arising and Non-arising" of those very same phenomena within the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu) and so forth.
The third is the "Section Showing the Included and Unincluded" within those very realms. The fourth [deals with] the moment of arising in the three planes.
The fifth is called the section on the vision of those phenomena according to their different planes.

The sixth is called the section on the vision of the karma that produces rebirth in the various destinies and the measure of the life-span. The seventh is called the section on those things to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth.
The eighth is called the section on those with objects and those without objects. The ninth is [the section] on those aggregates (*khandha*) and other phenomena...
The section on seeing is that which is summarized by way of the seen, the heard, and so forth. The tenth section on seeing is that which is summarized by way of the wholesome triad and so forth.

979. Thus, regarding the first of the ten sections that delimit the text—the all-inclusive section—when it is asked, "Within this interval from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence (bhavagga), how many aggregates (khandha) are there? [the answer is given as] "One... pe ... four, or six."
Demonstrating his own power of knowledge by saying, "There is no one else capable of explaining them as five," he gave an answer in accordance with the question: "The five aggregates.
For an answer given according to the question is called an "all-knowing" (sabbaññu) exposition.

This same method applies to the [questions on] the twelve bases and so forth. The detailed classification of the aggregate of form and the others is found in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other such texts.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. 2.

Commentary on the Section on Arising and Non-arising: 991. In the second section, those phenomena which arise in the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and for those beings born in the sensual realm (*kāmadhātu*)—
Whether they are included within the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) or not included therein—all of them taken together are called "the five aggregates of the sense-sphere element," and so forth.
This same method applies to the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and the others as well.

However, because beings included within the fine-material element lack the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*) and so on, the bases such as the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) do not perform their respective functions; therefore, in the fine-material element—
It was stated [above] that there are six bases (*āyatana*) and nine elements (*dhātu*), and so forth.

Since there is no such thing as an "unincluded element" (*apariyāpanna-dhātu*) either by way of a spatial location or by way of the arising of beings, it was therefore not said "in the unincluded element," but rather, in order to show each specific thing that is unincluded, it was stated:
"In the unincluded, how many aggregates (*khandha*)? and so forth.
3. Commentary on the Section on the Included and the Unincluded 999.
In the third section, “included in the sense-sphere realm” (*kāmadhātu-pariyāpanna*) means included in the sense of partaking of the sense-sphere realm;

the meaning is that they are dependent upon it, contained within it, and thus reckoned simply as belonging to the sense-sphere realm. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. “Included” (*pariyāpanna*)...
They are delimited by way of existence (*bhava*) and by way of sphere (*okāsa*). "Not included" (*apariyāpanna*) means not delimited in that manner.
4. Commentary on the Section on the Vision of Phenomena (*Dhammadassanavāra*): 1007.
In the fourth section, "eleven bases" (*āyatana*) refers to those excluding the sound base (*saddāyatana*), for that [sound base] is exclusively [present] at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
[It] does not arise. In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
In the section on the "sevens," instead of stating it by way of destination as "of the devas and asuras," it is stated without distinction as "of those born from a womb" (*gabbhaseyyaka*).
Therefore, wherever womb-born beings occur, there their seven bases (*sattāyatana*) are to be understood; likewise their elements (*dhātu*). The rest here [is as follows].
The meaning is already clear. What needs to be said regarding the fifth section has already been stated in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*.
6. Commentary on the Section on Productive Karma and Life-Span (1). Productive Karma.
1021. In the sixth section: they are called *devas* because they shine (*dibbanti*) with the five strands of sensual pleasure or with various kinds of special supernormal powers (*iddhivisesa*).

"Devas by convention" (*sammutideva*) are those who are called "god" or "goddess" according to worldly convention. "Devas by rebirth" (*upapattideva*) are those who are gods by virtue of having arisen in the world of the gods (*devaloka*).
"Devas by purification" (*visuddhideva*) are those worthy of worship by all other gods, being gods through the purification of all defilements (*kilesa*).
"Kings" refers to Khattiyas who have been consecrated by coronation. "Queens" refers to their chief consorts.
"Princes" refers to the sons born to consecrated queens from consecrated kings.
"Having performed the Uposatha rite" means having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors on the fourteenth day and other such occasions. Now...
Since limited meritorious karma such as giving is a condition for human prosperity, and that which is performed to a moderate degree is a condition for superior human prosperity,
and even within the state of superiority there are various distinctions that serve as conditions for various states such as being a wealthy Khattiya householder and so forth—
it is for this reason that, in order to show the diversity of rebirths by way of that [karma], he said: "Some are wealthy householders," and so on.
In this context, "mahāsālā" means those who have great essence (*sāra*); however, by changing the letter *ra* to *la*, it is called "mahāsālā.
They are householders who are great-sāl trees, or great-sāl trees among householders; thus they are "gahapatimahāsālā.
The same method applies to the other [categories] as well. In that regard, one whose house contains forty crores of wealth deposited as a hoard at its very foundation, and of kahāpaṇa coins—
Five *ambaṇas* of daily expenditure go out from his house—this is called a "great householder.

But he in whose house there is eighty million pieces of wealth stored away as a reserve, and ten *ambaṇas* of *kahāpaṇas* go out as daily expenditure—this is called a "great brahmin. Furthermore, in whose house... [the end of the passage].
A treasure of a hundred million coins lies stored away, and twenty ambuṇa-measures of kahāpaṇa coins come out for daily use—this is what is called a "wealthy noble.
"Sahabyataṃ" means companionship; the meaning is that they are reborn as peers. Regarding the terms "of the Cātumahārājikās," and so forth:
The realm known as the Cātumahārājika is situated in the middle of Mount Sineru.
Among them, there are those dwelling on mountains and those dwelling in the sky; their succession extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.
The Khiḍḍāpadosika, Manopadosika, Sītavalāhaka, Uṇhavalāhaka, Candima the son of a deva, and Suriya the son of a deva—all these, too, dwell within the Cātumahārājika deva-world.
Thirty-three people were reborn there; thus they are called the Tāvatiṃsas. Furthermore, it is said that "Tāvatiṃsa" is simply the name of those deities.
Among them, some dwell on mountains and some dwell in the sky; their lineage extends as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
The same applies to the Yāma and other deities. For even within a single divine world, the lineage of the deities does not extend beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain.
There is no [other] name [for them]. In that regard, they are called *Yāma* because they have gone (*yātā*), proceeded (*payātā*), and arrived (*sampattā*) at divine bliss.

They are called *Tusita* because they are contented (*tuṭṭhā*) and delighted (*pahaṭṭhā*). They are called *Nimmānarati* because, when they desire to enjoy more than the naturally provided objects, they create enjoyments according to their wish and take delight in them.
They are called *Paranimmitavasavatti* because, having understood the mental inclinations of others, they exercise mastery over the enjoyments created by those others.

Among the Brahmapārisajja and other realms, those who are the attendants (*pārisajjā*) and companions (*paricārikā*) of the Mahābrahmās are the Brahmapārisajjas. Of them...

1025. They have limited radiance, thus they are the *Parittābha* (Limited Radiance) devas. They have immeasurable radiance, thus they are the *Appamāṇābha* (Immeasurable Radiance) devas.
Their radiance issues forth from their bodies and spreads out, streaming forth as if breaking off again and again like the flame of a torch;
thus they are the *Ābhassara* (Radiant) devas. These three classes of beings also dwell on the same level within the plane of the second jhāna, yet their lifespans differ.
1026. Because "limited beauty" belongs to them, they are the *Parittasubhā* (Limited-Beauty). Because "immeasurable beauty" belongs to them, they are the *Appamāṇasubhā* (Immeasurable-Beauty).

Because they are "overspread and strewn with beauty"—that is, their bodies are a single mass of radiance, as glorious as a glowing lump of gold placed within a golden casket—they are the *Subhakiṇhā* (Utterly Beautiful).
These three classes of beings also dwell on a single level within the plane of the third jhāna; however, their lifespans differ.
1027. *Ārammaṇanānattatā* (diversity of object) means the state of diversity of the object. The same method applies to *manasikāranānattatā* (diversity of attention) and so forth.
Herein, for one the earth-kasiṇa is the object... [and so on] ...for another the white-kasiṇa;
this is the diversity of object. One attends to the earth-kasiṇa... [and so on] ...another to the white-kasiṇa; this is the diversity of attention.
"One has desire for the earth-kasiṇa... one has desire for the white-kasiṇa"—this is the diversity of desire (*chanda-nānatta*).
"One makes an aspiration for the earth-kasiṇa... one makes an aspiration for the white-kasiṇa"—this is the diversity of aspiration (*paṇidhi-nānatta*). "One resolves by way of the earth-kasiṇa...
one resolves by way of the white-kasiṇa"—this is the diversity of resolution (*adhimokkha-nānatta*). "One [resolves] by way of the earth-kasiṇa..."
“He directs the mind... [etc.]... one [does so] by means of the white kasiṇa”—this is the diversity of directing (abhinīhāra-nānatta).
“One possesses the wisdom that delimits the earth kasiṇa... [etc.]... one possesses the wisdom that delimits the white kasiṇa”—this is the diversity of wisdom (paññā-nānatta).

Among these, attention to the object (ārammaṇa-manasikāra) was explained in relation to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). Zeal (chanda), aspiration (paṇidhi), resolve (adhimokkha), and directing (abhinīhāra) occur both in access concentration (upacāra) and in absorption (appanā).
Wisdom (*paññā*), however, is said to be a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.

"Of non-percipient beings" (*asaññasattānaṃ*) means of those beings who are devoid of perception (*saññā*). For some, having gone forth into certain heretical sects (*titthāyatana*), seeing the fault in the mind—thinking, "Based on the mind, there arise attachment, aversion, and delusion"—they [aspire to] the state of being without mind (*acittakabhāva*).
Having generated the perception, "This is beautiful; this is Nibbāna in the present life," they develop the fifth attainment leading to rebirth there and are reborn in that state.
At the moment of their rebirth, only the single aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) arises.
Having arisen while standing, they remain standing; having arisen while sitting, they remain sitting; having arisen while lying down, they remain lying down.
Remaining as if lying down, they persist for five hundred eons like figures made by a painter.
At the conclusion of that period, that material body vanishes and sense-sphere perception arises; thus, by the arising of that perception, those devas are known to have passed away from that body.

They are called *vehapphala* because their fruits (*phala*) are vast (*vipula*). They are called *avīha* because they do not diminish (*na hāyanti*) nor do they fall away (*na vihāyanti*) from their own attainment.

They are called *atappa* because they do not torment (*tappanti*) any being. They are called *sudassa* because they are beautiful to behold (*sundarā dassanā*), handsome (*abhirūpā*), and pleasing (*pāsādikā*).

They are called *sudassī* because they see well (*suṭṭhu passanti*), or because their vision is beautiful (*sundaraṃ etesaṃ dassanaṃ*). [They are so named] by virtue of all these qualities and their excellence of existence (*bhava-sampatti*).
Because there is no one younger (*kaniṭṭha*) here, they are called *Akaniṭṭha*.
Those who have reached the base of infinite space are "those who have reached the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā*). The same method applies to the others as well.
Thus, there are six sense-sphere realms (*kāmāvacara*), nine Brahma-worlds, five Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), four formless [realms], and the Asañña-satta and Vehapphala [realms].
Together with the twenty-six divine worlds, there are twenty-seven including the world of humans.

In that context, when the Fully Enlightened One was defining the lifespan of humans and of the gods, he also defined the lifespan in the four states of misery (apāya) and among the earth-dwelling deities (bhummadeva).
Why is that? First, in the case of hell, karma alone is the measure. As long as...
Their karma is not exhausted, and thus they do not pass away. The same applies to the remaining woeful planes.

For the deities of the earth as well, karma alone is the determining factor. Among those reborn there, some remain for only seven days, some for half a month, some for a month, and there are even those who remain for an entire eon.

Among those humans, even while remaining in the state of a householder, some become stream-enterers, and they also attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
Among them, the stream-enterers and others remain as householders for as long as life lasts.
However, those whose taints are exhausted either attain final nibbāna or go forth into homelessness. Why? Because arhatship is the supreme quality, whereas the mark of a householder is inferior.
Because of that inferiority, they are unable to maintain the supreme quality; therefore, they either desire final Nibbāna or desire to go forth into homelessness.

However, the earth-deities (bhummadeva), even after attaining Arahatship, remain for as long as their lifespan lasts. Among the six classes of sense-sphere deities (kāmāvacara-deva), stream-enterers (sotāpanna) and once-returners (sakadāgāmin) remain for as long as their lifespan lasts;
non-returners (anāgāmin) ought to go to the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), while those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) ought to attain final Nibbāna.
Why? Because there is no place for them to dwell. All those in the fine-material and immaterial realms remain there for as long as life lasts.
Among them, those who have attained the stages of stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) born in the fine-material realm do not return here again;
they attain final nibbāna right there. These are indeed called "jhāna non-returners" (*jhāna-anāgāmin*).

But for those who have attained the eight meditative absorptions (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*), what determines [their rebirth]? It is the jhāna that is familiar to them; they arise by means of whichever one is familiar to them.
When all are familiar, what determines it? It is aspiration (*patthanā*); wherever one aspires for rebirth, there alone one is reborn.
In the absence of aspiration, what determines it? It is the attainment entered into at the time of death.
At the time of death, there is no one who has entered [a lower attainment]; what then determines it?

It is the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti*). For such a person is reborn exclusively in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Among noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) born in the nine Brahma-worlds, there is rebirth there as well as rebirth in higher planes, but never rebirth in lower planes. However, for worldlings (*puthujjana*), there is rebirth there as well as [rebirth] below.
There is rebirth both above and below. For noble disciples in the five Pure Abodes and the four formless realms, there is rebirth both in those very places and in higher ones.
An Anāgāmin born in the plane of the first jhāna, having purified the nine Brahma-worlds, attains final Nibbāna while stationed at the summit.
These are the Vehapphala, the Akaniṭṭha, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These three divine worlds are called the "supreme existences. Non-returners reborn in these three places do not go upward nor downward;
they attain final nibbāna right there. This is the incidental discussion here. 7.
Commentary on the Section on What is to be Directly Known, etc. (Abhiññeyyādivāra)

1030. In the seventh section, the state of being "to be directly known" (*abhiññeyyatā*) should be understood by way of the direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) that grasps the specific characteristics [of phenomena].

The state of being "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyyatā*) is to be understood by way of the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning. Furthermore, in such passages as "the aggregate of form is to be directly known, to be fully understood, and not to be abandoned," this should be understood precisely by way of the full understandings of knowing and scrutinizing. The truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is to be directly known.
In the passages beginning with "to be fully understood" and "to be abandoned," [the distinction] is by way of the full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*).
In the eighth section, the state of having an object and not having an object should be understood by way of eye-consciousness and so forth, which have visible forms and so forth as their objects.
The ninth section is of plain meaning. As for the tenth section, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in its respective places.

Thus ends the commentary on the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* in the *Sammohavinodanī*, the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*.
The Conclusion:
And thus far,
while teaching the Abhidhamma, the Teacher, who is reverent toward the Dhamma and devoted to those who revere the Dhamma—
In the city of the gods, amidst a retinue of thousands of celestial hosts,
the peerless person, the Protector, spoke this second work called the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*,
adorned with eighteen *vibhaṅgas* and possessing the quality of being worthy of praise.
At the request of the ascetic Buddhaghosa—
who possesses steady virtue, an unerring intellect, and keen wisdom—
I have composed this commentary on the meanings that are most subtle, for the purpose of elucidating their significance.
Because it dispels delusion, it is called the *Sammohavinodanī*.
Having taken the essence of the ancient commentaries,
this work has reached its conclusion without hindrance through the recitation sections of the text.
Just as it was with the forty-four [treatises], so too with this one—
may all beings reach their goal, their stainless aspirations fulfilled.
And whatever merit has been gained by me in composing this work for the sake of the endurance of the True Dhamma;
May the world, including the devas, attain the perfection of that which has been accomplished by him.
May the Dhamma endure for a very long time; may the world always delight in the Dhamma;
and may the provinces be constantly endowed with security, abundant alms-food, and other blessings.
Adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a multitude of virtues such as moral discipline, conduct, sincerity, and gentleness;
capable of plunging into the depths of both his own and other systems of tenets; possessed of analytical discernment;

a great grammarian whose unimpeded radiance of knowledge shone throughout the Teacher’s Dispensation—the various divisions of the Tipiṭaka scriptures along with their commentaries—endowed with the grace of sweet and noble speech that flowed forth from the happiness born of perfection in composition.
By the one named Buddhaghosa—so called by his teachers—who was a speaker of the fitting and the ultimate, the most eminent of debaters, and a great poet;

who was adorned with qualities such as the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā) and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) that accompany them; whose intellect was firmly established in superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma); and who served as an ornament to the lineage of the Elders (thera) dwelling at the Mahāvihāra, who were lamps of the Elder tradition.
This commentary on the Vibhaṅga, called the Sammohavinodanī, has been composed by the Elder.
May it endure as long as the world lasts,
showing the way to the purification of wisdom for sons of noble family who seek to cross over the world.
Even the name "Buddha" belongs only to that Pure-minded One,
the Peerless, the Elder of the World, the Great Seer— so it is proclaimed throughout the world.
The *Sammohavinodanī*, the Commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, is hereby completed.
